choices: To exclude haemorrhage before a thrombolytic is given
To confirm the infarct that the deficit already suggests
To measure the volume of tissue already infarcted
To grade the collateral supply to the affected side
quiz.answer: To exclude haemorrhage before a thrombolytic is given
quiz.explain: At 40 minutes an ischaemic infarct is usually invisible on CT, and a normal scan is the expected result rather than evidence against the diagnosis. What CT does deliver within minutes, anywhere, in a patient who may be restless and vomiting, is the one finding that turns a life-saving treatment into a lethal one: intracranial haemorrhage. It also excludes some structural mimics. Measuring infarct core and grading collaterals are real tasks with real consequences for thrombectomy selection, but they belong to CT perfusion and CT angiography acquired in the same visit, after the haemorrhage question is settled. Diffusion-weighted MRI would show the infarct within minutes, and where it is available immediately it is used, but availability and speed decide this at 40 minutes.

quiz.prompt: A metal fabricator is booked for a lumbar spine MRI. Screening reveals that a fragment was removed from his eye at work some years ago, with no imaging performed at the time. He has no ocular symptoms now. What should happen before he enters the scan room?
choices: Orbital radiographs to look for a retained fragment
A slit-lamp examination on the morning of the scan
A written declaration that his vision is normal now
A reduced specific absorption rate for the study
quiz.answer: Orbital radiographs to look for a retained fragment
quiz.explain: A ferromagnetic intraocular foreign body is one of the few hard exclusions in MRI screening, because the static field can rotate or translate a fragment lying against the retina and cause blindness in a patient who came in for a back problem. Two plain radiographs of the orbits, or CT where radiography is equivocal, are the accepted screen, and a negative screen clears the patient. Symptoms and visual acuity do not settle it, since a small retained intraocular or intraorbital fragment is often asymptomatic, and a self-reported history of an injury years ago is exactly the situation the screen exists for. Specific absorption rate governs radiofrequency heating of tissue and is the wrong lever here, since the hazard is mechanical force from the static field, which is present from the moment he walks through the door.

nodes.title: Ultrasound Physics, Doppler and Artefacts
nodes.goal: Set frequency, focus and gain for the question in front of you, work Doppler within the limits its physics imposes, and read ultrasound artefacts as evidence rather than as noise.

quiz.prompt: A 6 MHz transducer emits a pulse two cycles long. Taking the speed of sound in soft tissue as 1540 m/s, calculate the best achievable axial resolution. Answer in millimetres, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency: 1540 divided by 6 million is 0.257 mm. Two cycles make a spatial pulse length of 0.513 mm, and two reflectors can be separated along the beam only if they are more than half a pulse length apart, giving 0.26 mm. Two lessons follow. Higher frequency shortens the wavelength and improves axial resolution directly, and heavy damping, which shortens the pulse to one or two cycles, improves it again, which is why broadband probes resolve better than the ringing ones of an earlier generation. And axial resolution is roughly constant with depth, whereas lateral resolution depends on beam width and is best only at the focal zone, while elevational resolution depends on the thickness of the array and is the one that quietly averages a small lesion into the tissue beside it.

quiz.prompt: You are imaging to a depth of 20 cm with a speed of sound of 1540 m/s. Calculate the highest pulse repetition frequency at which every echo still returns before the next pulse is sent. Answer in hertz, to the nearest whole hertz.
quiz.explain: Each pulse travels out and back, so 0.4 m of path at 1540 m/s takes about 260 microseconds, and at most 3850 pulses can be sent per second. Depth therefore rations everything downstream. The Nyquist limit is half the pulse repetition frequency, here 1925 Hz, so deep vessels alias at velocities that would never trouble a carotid at 2 cm, which is why the renal artery in a large patient is the classic aliasing problem. Frame rate falls for the same reason, and falls further with a wide sector, deep focus or several focal zones, so a fast-moving structure imaged deep is imaged badly. Push the repetition frequency past this limit and echoes from the previous pulse arrive during the next listening interval and are placed too shallow, which is range ambiguity.

quiz.prompt: A 4 MHz pulsed Doppler beam meets blood moving at 1.0 m/s with an insonation angle of 60 degrees, in tissue with a speed of sound of 1540 m/s. Calculate the Doppler frequency shift. Answer in hertz, to the nearest whole hertz.
quiz.explain: The shift is twice the transmitted frequency, times the velocity, times the cosine of the angle, divided by the speed of sound: 2 x 4 x 10^6 x 1.0 x 0.5 divided by 1540 gives about 2597 Hz. The factor of two is there because the blood both receives and re-radiates the sound, and the answer lands in the audible range, which is why the spectral trace is also a sound worth listening to. Two consequences shape practice. At 90 degrees the cosine is zero and flow vanishes entirely, so a vessel running across the screen must be heel-toed or the beam steered. And because velocity is recovered by dividing by the cosine, the same few degrees of angle error that hardly matter at 20 degrees become a large velocity error beyond 60 degrees.

quiz.prompt: A carotid duplex is performed with the angle cursor set at 78 degrees to the vessel, because that is how the plaque sits in the available window. The peak systolic velocity reads 180 cm/s. What should be done with that measurement?
quiz.answer: Re-insonate at 60 degrees or less before quoting any velocity
choices: Re-insonate at 60 degrees or less before quoting any velocity
Report it, since the machine has already applied angle correction
Report it after multiplying the value by the cosine of that angle
Report the ratio to the distal vessel rather than the velocity
quiz.explain: Velocity is derived by dividing the measured shift by the cosine of the angle, and the cosine falls away steeply as the angle approaches 90 degrees, so the correction becomes a large multiplier applied to a small number. A few degrees of cursor error at 60 degrees produces an error of the order of ten per cent; the same error near 80 degrees can shift the velocity by tens of per cent, in either direction. Every published stenosis threshold assumes an angle of 60 degrees or less, so a velocity obtained at 78 degrees cannot be compared with them at all. The machine has indeed already applied the correction, which is precisely why re-applying a cosine by hand is wrong. Velocity ratios do cancel some systematic error and are useful in tortuous or heavily calcified vessels, but both of their components still need valid angles. The fix is a different window, beam steering, or an approach more parallel to the flow.

quiz.prompt: Colour Doppler of a native renal artery at 11 cm depth shows a mosaic of colour in mid-stream with no plaque, and the spectral trace wraps so that the systolic peaks appear below the baseline. Which single change is most likely to resolve it?
quiz.answer: Raise the velocity scale, which raises the pulse repetition frequency
choices: Raise the velocity scale, which raises the pulse repetition frequency
Raise the colour gain so that peak velocities display more brightly
Raise the wall filter so that the low-velocity signal is removed
Raise the transducer frequency so that the flow is sampled sooner
quiz.explain: Aliasing happens when the Doppler shift exceeds half the pulse repetition frequency, and the machine, sampling too slowly to know which way the phase turned, wraps the signal to the opposite direction. Raising the scale raises the repetition frequency directly and is the first move. Shifting the baseline buys the rest of the range in one direction. Choosing a lower-frequency probe helps, because the shift is proportional to the transmitted frequency, so a higher-frequency probe makes aliasing worse rather than better. Insonating at a larger angle reduces the shift as well, though it costs velocity accuracy. Reducing the imaging depth raises the ceiling on repetition frequency. And continuous-wave Doppler has no Nyquist limit at all, at the price of range resolution. Colour gain changes brightness and sensitivity, not the limit, and the wall filter removes low velocities, which is the opposite of the problem here.

quiz.prompt: A painful testis is scanned on a machine left on the preset from a carotid list. No colour flow is seen in either testis, though both look normal in grey scale. What should be done before absent perfusion is reported?
quiz.answer: Lower the velocity scale and the wall filter, and raise the colour gain
choices: Lower the velocity scale and the wall filter, and raise the colour gain
Report absent flow and refer urgently for scrotal exploration
Change to a lower-frequency curvilinear probe and rescan the scrotum
Apply harmonic imaging and spatial compounding to the whole study
quiz.explain: A carotid preset carries a high pulse repetition frequency and a high wall filter, both designed to reject exactly the slow flow that a testis has, so the study as performed is blind rather than negative. The low-flow preset drops the scale, minimises the wall filter, raises colour gain to just below the point where noise fills the box, and keeps a high-frequency linear probe. The single most valuable habit is a transverse image with both testes in the field, so the normal side proves the settings were capable of showing flow. Power Doppler is more sensitive to slow flow and is angle-independent, at the cost of direction and a tendency to flash with movement. Even then, absent flow supports torsion but a study with flow does not exclude it, since intermittent and partial torsion both occur, and a convincing clinical picture goes to theatre regardless of the pictures.

quiz.prompt: A right upper quadrant scan shows a rounded echogenic focus apparently in the lung base, the same distance above the diaphragm as a similar-looking liver lesion lies below it. What is the appropriate action?
quiz.answer: Treat it as a mirror-image artefact and scan from another window
choices: Treat it as a mirror-image artefact and scan from another window
Report a pulmonary metastasis and arrange a staging CT scan
Report a diaphragmatic hernia containing the liver lesion
Raise the output power to see through the diaphragm better
quiz.explain: The diaphragm and aerated lung form a near-total specular reflector. Sound that bounces between that interface and a structure in the liver takes a longer path home, and the machine, which assumes a single straight there-and-back journey, places the extra delay deep to the mirror, at exactly the same distance beyond it. The duplicate is identical and equidistant, which real basal lung disease never is. Confirm by scanning intercostally or from another angle, so that the geometry changes and the copy moves or disappears. The same mechanism duplicates the subclavian artery on colour above the pleura. Read positively, the artefact is useful: seeing it means aerated lung is there, so its loss can be the first clue to pleural fluid or consolidation. Raising output power adds energy and thermal index without changing geometry, and reporting a metastasis or a hernia commits a patient to a pathway built on an echo.

quiz.prompt: A liver study shows a broad bright band across the mid-field with a darker band beneath it, and the same appearance is present in every patient scanned on that machine this morning. What is the first thing to correct?
quiz.answer: Reset the time-gain compensation sliders to a smooth curve
choices: Reset the time-gain compensation sliders to a smooth curve
Reduce the overall output power and repeat the sweep
Change to a higher-frequency probe for the same views
Turn off tissue harmonic imaging for the whole study
quiz.explain: Time-gain compensation amplifies late-returning echoes more than early ones, to undo the roughly 0.5 dB per centimetre per megahertz that tissue takes out of the beam. A slider pushed out of line over-amplifies one depth and leaves the next under-amplified, producing precisely this horizontal banding, and the giveaway is that it repeats in every patient because it belongs to the console rather than to anatomy. Distinguish it from a genuine attenuating layer, such as thick subcutaneous fat, and from posterior enhancement, which is confined to the column beneath a fluid structure. Receive gain is adjusted before output power, since power raises the acoustic energy actually delivered and its thermal and mechanical indices, and the ALARA principle asks that it be the last thing raised. A steatotic liver attenuates more and needs both a steeper compensation curve and a lower frequency, and the extra attenuation is itself the diagnostic sign.

quiz.prompt: An indeterminate 3 cm renal lesion with possible enhancement is found on ultrasound in a man whose eGFR is 18 mL/min/1.73m2 and who can hold still only briefly. Which study answers the question of vascularity most safely here?
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound using a microbubble agent
choices: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound using a microbubble agent
Iodinated contrast CT under intravenous hydration cover
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI with a group I agent at low dose
Unenhanced MRI with chemical shift and diffusion imaging
quiz.explain: Microbubbles are a pure blood-pool agent: they stay intravascular, they are destroyed by the beam and cleared through the lungs, and they are not excreted by the kidney, so there is no nephrotoxicity at any level of renal function. The examination is also real-time, so a patient who can co-operate for a minute is enough, and the continuous observation shows enhancement in thin septa that a single CT phase can miss. Two honest caveats: Bosniak 2019 is written for CT and MRI, so a contrast-enhanced ultrasound classification is applied by analogy rather than by that version's own criteria, and microbubbles carry a small risk of anaphylactoid reaction with cardiopulmonary cautions. Group I gadolinium agents are the higher-risk group for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, so that option is backwards; if MRI is needed, a group II agent is the appropriate choice. Unenhanced MRI simply declines to answer the question asked.

quiz.prompt: A patient with treated hepatitis C has a two-dimensional shear wave elastography result of 7.5 kPa, taken without fasting, with an interquartile range of 40 per cent of the median. How should this be handled?
quiz.answer: Repeat it fasted, since the measurement quality fails the usual criteria
choices: Repeat it fasted, since the measurement quality fails the usual criteria
Report advanced fibrosis and start endoscopic variceal surveillance
Report normal stiffness and discharge from further liver follow-up
Proceed to liver biopsy, since elastography has proved inconclusive
quiz.explain: Elastography estimates stiffness from the speed of a shear wave, and its result means nothing without its quality metrics. The widely used criterion is that the interquartile range should be no more than 30 per cent of the median, and measurement should be made fasting for at least two to three hours, because postprandial portal hyperaemia raises stiffness on its own. A spread of 40 per cent in a non-fasted patient is an uninterpretable number, not a low one. Had it been valid, the Baveno VII thresholds would apply: below 10 kPa argues against compensated advanced chronic liver disease, 10 to 15 is suggestive, and above 15 makes it highly likely. The confounders that raise stiffness without fibrosis are worth carrying: a hepatitis flare with raised transaminases, right heart failure and hepatic congestion, cholestasis, infiltration and a recent meal. Repeat properly rather than commit a patient to endoscopy or biopsy on a bad reading.

quiz.prompt: A sonographer cannot demonstrate shadowing behind a 6 mm echogenic focus in the gallbladder, and the image is being acquired with spatial compounding on and several focal zones spread through the field. State what you would change and why.
quiz.answer: Turn spatial compounding off and place a single focal zone at the level of the focus, using the highest frequency that still reaches it. Compounding insonates from several angles and averages the frames, which fills the shadow in behind a small stone, while a tight focal zone narrows the beam at that depth so less sound passes around the stone and the shadow returns.
quiz.explain: Spatial compounding is on by default because averaging several steering angles suppresses speckle and fills in angle-dependent dropout, which flatters soft tissue. The same averaging softens the very artefacts we use as evidence: acoustic shadowing behind a stone and posterior enhancement behind a cyst are both angle-dependent by nature. A small stone also fails to shadow when the beam at that depth is wider than the stone, so most of the sound simply travels around it, which is why a single focal zone placed at the stone matters more than any other setting. Tissue harmonic imaging usually sharpens shadowing rather than degrading it, because the harmonic beam is narrower and carries less clutter. When shadowing still cannot be shown, colour Doppler over the focus looking for twinkling is the next test.

quiz.prompt: A 4 mm echogenic focus in the renal sinus does not shadow convincingly, but colour Doppler over it produces a rapidly changing mosaic of colour deep to it, with a spectral trace of random noise rather than a pulsatile waveform. State what you conclude and how you would set the machine to make the sign more reliable.
quiz.answer: This is twinkling, which arises from a rough, strongly reflective surface, so the focus is a small stone rather than sinus fat or a vessel. Make it reliable by placing the colour box tightly over the focus with the focal zone at or just beyond it, raising the colour scale and pulse repetition frequency, and reducing colour gain until noise clears, since true twinkling persists while random colour noise does not.
quiz.explain: Twinkling is a rapidly alternating band of colour behind a rough calcified interface, accompanied by a spectral trace that looks like noise because there is no coherent motion generating it; the accepted explanation involves intrinsic phase jitter in the machine's own transmit and receive chain being unmasked by a strongly reflective irregular surface. It earns its place clinically because it can reveal small renal stones that are too small to shadow, and it distinguishes a stone from sinus fat, which produces no colour, and from a vessel, which produces a coherent, cardiac-cycle waveform. It is machine- and setting-dependent, so a negative result on one system means little. Other rough surfaces twinkle too, including encrusted stents, calcified plaque, and the cholesterol crystals in adenomyomatosis, where the same physics also yields comet-tail reverberation.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these transducer frequencies in order of increasing depth of penetration in soft tissue.
quiz.answer: 15-MHz 9-MHz 5-MHz 2.5-MHz
quiz.explain: Attenuation in soft tissue runs at roughly half a decibel per centimetre per megahertz, so it scales with frequency: a 15 MHz beam is losing signal about six times faster over the same path than a 2.5 MHz one, and the trade between resolution and depth is fixed by physics rather than by preference. That maps directly onto the probe you pick up: 12 to 18 MHz linear for thyroid, testis, superficial masses and vessels; 7 to 12 MHz for the paediatric abdomen and the appendix in a slim adult; 3 to 6 MHz curvilinear for the adult abdomen; and 1 to 3 MHz phased array for adult cardiac work between the ribs and for very large patients. Harmonic imaging costs a little penetration, because the received harmonic is far weaker than the fundamental, and repays it by cutting near-field clutter and reverberation, which is why a cyst looks convincingly anechoic with it switched on.

nodes.title: Image-guided Biopsy and Drainage
nodes.goal: Plan an image-guided biopsy or drainage that is safe to perform - the right modality, a defensible tract, haemostasis corrected to the right threshold, the right catheter, and a team that knows what to do when it goes wrong.

quiz.prompt: A 3 cm lesion sits high and posteriorly in segment VIII of the liver, just under the dome. Ultrasound demonstrates it only through an intercostal window that crosses the costophrenic recess. What is the best plan?
quiz.answer: Plan on CT and take a subcostal, angled tract below the recess
choices: Plan on CT and take a subcostal, angled tract below the recess
Go through the recess in held expiration, accepting the risk
Abandon biopsy and manage on imaging features and follow-up
Use a fine needle rather than a core to make a pleural pass safe
quiz.explain: Crossing the pleural reflection turns a liver biopsy into a chest procedure: pneumothorax, and if the lesion is infected or contains bile, empyema or a bilious effusion. The variables you can actually change are respiratory phase and approach angle. In held expiration the diaphragm rises and the recess descends, which is the wrong direction; in held inspiration the liver descends below the costal margin, and an angled subcostal tract directed cephalad reaches segment VIII while staying extrapleural. That route also crosses a cuff of normal parenchyma, which tamponades the tract and is why a directly subcapsular or exophytic approach is avoided when a parenchymal one exists. Needle calibre changes bleeding risk, not the anatomy of a pleural pass. And abandoning a biopsy that would change management is a decision with its own harms - it is not the cautious option, merely the passive one.

quiz.prompt: A 6 cm presacral collection after anterior resection needs drainage, and CT shows the only percutaneous window is transgluteal. Where should the needle pass?
quiz.answer: Medially, close to the sacrum and below the piriformis muscle
choices: Medially, close to the sacrum and below the piriformis muscle
Laterally, close to the greater trochanter and above piriformis
Through the mid-gluteal region at the level of the sciatic notch
Through the ischiorectal fossa, angling upwards to the collection
quiz.explain: The sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and run laterally, so the safe corridor is the medial one: as close to the sacrum as the sacrospinous ligament permits, and inferior to piriformis, which keeps the needle medial and caudal to both structures. A lateral or mid-gluteal pass at the level of the notch is precisely where the nerve and the superior gluteal artery lie, and an arterial injury there is difficult to compress and may need embolisation. Two practical corollaries. Transgluteal drains hurt, and the patient deserves to be warned and given adequate analgesia, since pain is a common reason these catheters are pulled early. And where a transrectal or transvaginal route under ultrasound is available for a low pelvic collection, it is often shorter, less painful and avoids the gluteal anatomy altogether.

quiz.prompt: A patient with cirrhosis needs a percutaneous core biopsy of a liver lesion. The INR is 1.9 and the platelet count is 42 x 10^9/L. What does the SIR 2019 consensus support before proceeding?
quiz.answer: Correct the INR towards 1.5-1.8 and transfuse platelets above 50
choices: Correct the INR towards 1.5-1.8 and transfuse platelets above 50
Proceed as things stand; both values are acceptable for this case
Transfuse platelets above 20 and accept an INR of up to 3.0 here
Defer indefinitely; the coagulopathy of cirrhosis is not correctable
quiz.explain: The 2019 Society of Interventional Radiology consensus sorts procedures into low and high bleeding risk and attaches different thresholds to each. Percutaneous core biopsy of a solid organ, including the liver and the kidney, sits in the high-risk group, where the recommendation is an INR at or below 1.5 to 1.8 and platelets at or above 50 x 10^9/L. The lower thresholds - platelets above 20, INR tolerated up to 2.0 to 3.0 - belong to the low-risk list: thoracentesis, paracentesis, superficial aspiration and biopsy, and most catheter exchanges. The point worth carrying beyond the numbers is that in cirrhosis the INR is a poor predictor of bleeding, because procoagulant and anticoagulant factors fall together and the assay only sees one side. Transfusing plasma to chase a number adds volume and portal pressure; a transjugular route, which also measures the pressure gradient, is often the better answer.

quiz.prompt: A loculated abscess drains poorly through an 8 French catheter and you consider upsizing to 12 French. Treating the catheter as a rigid tube with laminar flow, so that flow varies with the fourth power of the internal radius, by what factor would the flow rate increase? Answer as a number, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The radius ratio is 12 over 8, which is 1.5, and 1.5 to the fourth power is 5.06, so about a fivefold gain from what looks like a modest change of catheter. Since three French equals one millimetre of outer diameter, 8 F is 2.7 mm and 12 F is 4.0 mm. Poiseuille's law is why doubling the French number multiplies flow sixteenfold, and why arguing about a single French size is rarely worth it. Real pus is not a Newtonian fluid, though, and in practice a side-hole blocked by fibrinous debris stops flow long before the physics becomes relevant, which is why the decision is driven by what came back on the aspirating syringe. Thin serous fluid drains happily through 8 to 10 F; frank pus, old haematoma or necrotic debris wants 12 to 14 F or larger, plus regular saline flushing to keep the side holes open.

quiz.prompt: In a service where 20 per cent of CT-guided lung biopsies are complicated by pneumothorax, and one quarter of those pneumothoraces require a chest drain, how many drains would you expect across 200 consecutive biopsies? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Twenty per cent of 200 is 40 pneumothoraces, and a quarter of those is 10 drains, which is a drain rate of 5 per cent. Those proportions are representative: series of CT-guided lung biopsy report pneumothorax in roughly 15 to 25 per cent, with drainage needed in around 5 per cent of biopsies overall. The distinction matters for consent, because the two numbers mean different things to the patient. A pneumothorax that is small, asymptomatic and stable changes nothing about her day; a drain means admission. Quote the number that maps onto the consequence. The risk rises with emphysema anywhere along the tract, with small and deep lesions, with crossing a fissure, with larger needles and, above all, with the number of separate pleural passes - which is the argument for coaxial technique, where one pleural puncture yields several cores.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the steps of Seldinger-technique catheter placement into an abdominal abscess in the order they are performed.
quiz.answer: access-needle guidewire tract-dilatation catheter-advancement wire-removal
quiz.explain: The whole safety argument for Seldinger over trocar technique lives in step two: once the wire is coiled in the cavity, access is secured and everything afterwards is done over it, so a dilator or catheter that will not pass can be exchanged without losing the target. Trocar technique - catheter, stiffening cannula and needle advanced as one assembly in a single pass - is faster and reasonable for a large, superficial, easily seen collection, but it gives you one attempt and no wire to fall back on. Practical points around the sequence: aspirate a sample for microbiology before you flush anything in, dilate only to the size you intend to place, keep the wire under vision as the dilators go, and form and lock the pigtail as the wire comes out. Then confirm the position, secure the catheter properly, and record the volume and character of what drained.

quiz.prompt: A patient on clopidogrel following a drug-eluting stent placed eight weeks ago needs a percutaneous renal biopsy for suspected glomerulonephritis. What is the right approach?
quiz.answer: Discuss with cardiology before any hold, and consider a transjugular route
choices: Discuss with cardiology before any hold, and consider a transjugular route
Hold the clopidogrel for five days and proceed, as SIR 2019 advises
Proceed on clopidogrel, since renal biopsy is a low bleeding risk case
Hold clopidogrel for seven days and bridge with heparin in the interval
quiz.explain: Both halves of the naive answer are individually defensible and together they are wrong. SIR 2019 does classify renal biopsy as high bleeding risk and does suggest withholding clopidogrel for five days. But a drug-eluting stent at eight weeks is inside the period where interrupting dual antiplatelet therapy risks stent thrombosis, an event whose case fatality is far higher than that of a renal haematoma. This is a decision that belongs to a conversation, not to a protocol, and the cardiologist may say the biopsy can wait a month. If it cannot, a transjugular renal biopsy lets the tract be tamponaded or coiled from within the vein, which is why it exists for exactly this patient. Heparin bridging is the classic error: it substitutes for warfarin, which acts on the coagulation cascade, and does nothing for a platelet-mediated mechanism.

quiz.prompt: You are planning a CT-guided biopsy of a retroperitoneal node. Using that case as the example, set out what makes a tract unsafe, naming at least four structures or features you would refuse to cross and saying why each one matters.
quiz.answer: The criterion is the safest path, not the shortest. I would not cross bowel, because a needle through colon or small bowel seeds the retroperitoneum with organisms and can produce an abscess or a fistula. I would not cross a major vessel - the aorta, cava, renal or mesenteric vessels - and I would use intravenous contrast or Doppler to be sure a suspected node is not an aneurysm or a vascular tumour. I would not cross the pancreas, because a needle tract through it risks pancreatitis and a pancreatic fistula. I would not cross the pleura or the costophrenic recess for an upper retroperitoneal target, because that converts the complication list into pneumothorax and empyema. And I would avoid a nerve or the neurovascular bundle running at the inferior margin of a rib, entering over the superior edge instead. Where a choice exists, passing through a cuff of normal solid organ that will tamponade is safer than a free peritoneal route.
quiz.explain: A safe window is a positive thing you construct, not the absence of an obvious obstacle. Build it from four questions. What is between the skin and the target on every slice of the planned angle, in the respiratory phase the patient will actually hold? What will bleed, and can it be compressed or tamponaded if it does? What is contaminated, and what would contamination cost here? And what could I not fix in this room? Two anatomical details repay memorising: the intercostal artery is protected in the costal groove laterally but runs unprotected and tortuous within about 6 cm of the midline posteriorly, and in the elderly it can wander mid-space; and a hypervascular lesion, a hydatid cyst or a phaeochromocytoma is a reason not to put a needle in at all until the diagnosis has been considered.

quiz.prompt: A 19 year old has a destructive lytic lesion of the distal femur with aggressive periosteal reaction and a soft tissue mass. The local orthopaedic team asks you to biopsy it on tomorrow's list. What do you do, and why does the position of the tract matter more here than almost anywhere else?
quiz.answer: I would not biopsy it locally. I would complete the imaging first - MRI of the whole bone and staging - and refer the patient to the regional sarcoma centre so that the biopsy is performed there, or at least along a tract agreed with the surgeon who will operate. The reason is that a biopsy tract through a suspected primary bone sarcoma is contaminated with tumour and must be excised en bloc with the specimen at the definitive resection. A tract placed through the wrong compartment, through a neurovascular bundle's plane, or transversely across the limb, can make that excision impossible and convert a limb-sparing operation into an amputation. Getting the biopsy technically right is worth nothing if the route has closed off the operation.
quiz.explain: This is the strongest version of a general rule: before the needle, ask who will treat this and what your tract does to their options. Primary bone and soft tissue sarcoma is the classic, and the evidence that unplanned local biopsy worsens outcomes is why national pathways route these lesions to specialist centres. Two neighbouring rules belong with it. A testicular mass is never approached percutaneously - it is explored inguinally with cord control, because a scrotal route changes the lymphatic drainage. And elsewhere, tract seeding is real but rare: cumulative rates of the order of a few per cent are reported for hepatocellular carcinoma, and mesothelioma is the other name usually cited. Rare is not the same as ignorable, which is why coaxial technique and a route that a future resection could take are good habits everywhere, not just in the femur.

quiz.prompt: Aspiration of a 9 cm post-appendicectomy collection returns thick, foul, particulate pus that barely moves through the 18 gauge needle. What catheter would you place?
quiz.answer: A 14 French locking pigtail, with regular saline flushes
choices: A 14 French locking pigtail, with regular saline flushes
An 8 French locking pigtail, upsized later if it blocks
A 6 French pigtail, since the tract should stay narrow
A 10 French straight catheter without a locking loop
quiz.explain: The character of the aspirate decides the calibre, not the size of the cavity. Fluid that will not pass an 18 gauge needle will not pass an 8 French side hole for long, and planning to upsize later means a second procedure for a patient who is already septic. Thin serous fluid drains through 8 to 10 F; viscous pus, haematoma or necrotic debris needs 12 to 14 F or more. The locking loop is not a detail: catheter dislodgement is the commonest reason a drain stops working, and a straight catheter in a mobile patient is asking for it. Prescribe flushing - typically 10 mL of saline two or three times a day - and record the output. If output falls while the patient stays septic, image before concluding the abscess has resolved: a blocked or displaced catheter, an undrained locule, or an enteric fistula are the usual explanations.

quiz.prompt: A 78 year old on home oxygen is having a painful drainage under conscious sedation with midazolam and fentanyl. Two minutes after a top-up she is unrousable, her respiratory rate is 6 and her saturations are 84 per cent on 4 litres. What comes first?
quiz.answer: Open the airway, give high flow oxygen and support ventilation
choices: Open the airway, give high flow oxygen and support ventilation
Give flumazenil 200 micrograms and repeat until she rouses
Give naloxone 400 micrograms intravenously and then reassess
Call the arrest team and begin chest compressions immediately
quiz.explain: Airway and breathing before pharmacology. A head tilt and chin lift, an airway adjunct, high-flow oxygen and bag-mask ventilation fix the physiology immediately, while any drug takes a minute or two to work and may not be the right drug. Reversal agents come second and with caveats: naloxone should be titrated in small increments of 100 micrograms or so and has a shorter half-life than fentanyl, so re-sedation follows and the patient must be watched; flumazenil can precipitate seizures and is avoided in anyone on long-term benzodiazepines. She has a pulse and a rhythm, so compressions would be wrong. The part that actually prevents this is upstream: continuous capnography, one person whose only task is monitoring the patient, reduced doses for age and for chronic respiratory disease, and small increments with enough time between them to see the effect before giving more.

quiz.prompt: Set out what should happen to a patient in the four hours after a CT-guided lung biopsy in a day-case service, and state two circumstances in which you would not discharge them that afternoon.
quiz.answer: Immediately after the needle comes out, roll the patient puncture-site down to help seal the pleural breach, then observe with regular observations and pulse oximetry. An erect chest radiograph at about one hour is the key check, since most pneumothoraces are apparent by then. If it is satisfactory and the patient is comfortable, continue observation for a further two to three hours before discharge with written advice on what to do if breathlessness or chest pain develops, and with a responsible adult to stay overnight within reasonable reach of a hospital. I would not discharge if the radiograph shows a pneumothorax that is enlarging or symptomatic, or has needed a drain; and I would not discharge if the social criteria fail - nobody at home, or a long journey from any emergency department - however good the radiograph looks. More than a trace of haemoptysis is a third reason to keep them.
quiz.explain: British Thoracic Society guidance built this pathway around one observation: the great majority of post-biopsy pneumothoraces declare themselves within the first hour, but a minority appear later, which is why the advice sheet and the accompanying adult are as much a part of the safety net as the radiograph. Two refinements worth knowing. The rollover manoeuvre and, in some services, a blood patch or saline instilled through the coaxial cannula as it is withdrawn, aim to reduce the leak at the moment of maximal risk. And a small, stable, asymptomatic pneumothorax does not need a drain: it needs a repeat film and a patient who understands what to watch for. Systemic air embolism is the rare catastrophe to know about - sudden neurological deficit or arrest during or just after the biopsy - managed with 100 per cent oxygen, head-down left lateral positioning and urgent hyperbaric referral.

quiz.prompt: The team is scrubbed and the patient is draped for a renal biopsy. The pause immediately before the needle goes in exists chiefly to catch one of the following. Which one?
quiz.answer: That the side on the consent form matches the side on the images
choices: That the side on the consent form matches the side on the images
That the histopathology request card has been completed correctly
That the sedation drugs have been drawn into labelled syringes
That the post-procedure observation chart is at the bedside ready
quiz.explain: All four are good practice, and three of them belong earlier in the checklist. The pause immediately before the needle exists for the never-events: wrong patient, wrong side, wrong site, wrong procedure. Laterality is the classic failure and it is not a failure of care but of geometry and assumption - images can be displayed flipped, a referral can name the wrong kidney, the prone patient's left is on your right, and by this point the patient is draped and sedated and can no longer correct you. So the pause is spoken aloud, by the whole team, against two independent sources: the signed consent form and the images on the screen. Add allergies, the coagulation results and antibiotic prophylaxis to the same thirty seconds. Consent itself belongs earlier and unsedated, with the specific numbers for this procedure - here, the risk of significant bleeding and of needing transfusion or embolisation.

nodes.title: Measuring Tumour Response
nodes.goal: Select target lesions, compute the sum of diameters, assign a RECIST 1.1 category, and recognise growth on immunotherapy that needs confirming rather than acting on.
articles: Response evaluation criteria in solid tumors

quiz.prompt: A baseline CT for a trial shows a 12 mm short-axis mediastinal node and a 22 mm liver metastasis, and the reader must decide whether the node can serve as a target lesion. What short-axis measurement in millimetres must a lymph node reach before RECIST 1.1 allows it to be selected as a target? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Nodes are the exception to the ten-millimetre rule, because normal nodes are visible and measurable and a ten-millimetre node may be entirely healthy. The bands are: 15 mm or more in short axis is measurable and may be selected as a target; 10 mm up to 15 mm is pathological but goes on the non-target list; under 10 mm is regarded as non-pathological and is not recorded at all. Short axis is used because it is the dimension least dependent on the plane of section, and it is the short axis that enters the sum of diameters - the one place in the system where the sum mixes two different measurements, longest diameter for everything else and short axis for nodes. One consequence follows directly: since a node's contribution can never fall below its normal size, a complete response requires target nodes to fall below 10 mm rather than to disappear.

quiz.prompt: At follow-up a reader records a target mediastinal node as 24 mm, having measured its long axis; at baseline the same node was recorded as 18 mm short axis. The sum of diameters accordingly rises and the software flags progression. What is the primary problem with this assessment?
choices: The node was measured in a different axis from baseline
The node should have been dropped as a target lesion
Nodal disease is recorded as non-target in this system
The reader should have used the mean of the two axes
quiz.answer: The node was measured in a different axis from baseline
quiz.explain: Reproducibility is the entire value of a response criterion: the number matters far less than the fact that it was obtained the same way every time. A node's long axis can be twice its short axis, so switching axes between timepoints can manufacture a 20 per cent rise out of a node that has not changed at all, and the consequence is a patient taken off a working treatment. The rule is that a node is measured in short axis at every timepoint, on the same imaging technique, ideally by the same reader with the same window settings, and that a target lesion once chosen is followed to the end even if it becomes difficult to measure. When a lesion genuinely becomes unmeasurable - it fragments, or is obscured - that is stated and handled explicitly, rather than fixed by quietly measuring something else.

quiz.prompt: The baseline sum of target diameters is 92 mm. The sum falls to 45 mm at the best response and then measures 54 mm on the current scan, with no new lesions and no change in non-target disease. Calculate the percentage increase from the nadir, to the nearest whole number. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 54 minus 45 is 9 mm, and 9 divided by 45 is 20 per cent. Progression requires two criteria to be met together: a relative increase of at least 20 per cent above the nadir, and an absolute increase of at least 5 mm. Both are satisfied here, at exactly 20 per cent and 9 mm, so this is progressive disease. Notice which number is the reference. Progression is judged against the nadir, the smallest sum recorded at any point including baseline, not against baseline itself - measured against the 92 mm baseline this patient is still 41 per cent down and would look like a continuing partial response. Using the wrong reference in this direction keeps patients on treatments that stopped working months ago.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a single target lesion has a nadir sum of 15 mm; on the current scan it measures 19 mm, with no new lesions and no change in the non-target disease. The trial coordinator reports progression on the strength of the 27 per cent rise. What is the correct assessment?
choices: Stable disease, as the absolute rise is under five millimetres
Progressive disease, as the relative rise is above twenty per cent
Progressive disease, as growth from the nadir was unequivocal
Not evaluable, as one target lesion is too few to assess
quiz.answer: Stable disease, as the absolute rise is under five millimetres
quiz.explain: The absolute five-millimetre requirement exists exactly for this situation. On a small lesion a percentage is treacherous: a 4 mm change on a 15 mm lesion is 27 per cent, and it is also well within the disagreement of two competent readers measuring the same lesion on the same scan, or of the same reader on a different day. Requiring both criteria stops measurement noise being reported as biology. The distinction between the two progressive-disease options is worth sitting with, because both invoke real rules - relative growth from the nadir, and unequivocal worsening - and neither rescues a 4 mm change. A single target lesion is entirely permissible, though it makes the assessment more fragile, which is one reason protocols prefer several. Progression could still arrive by another route on the same scan: a new lesion, or unequivocal progression of non-target disease, either of which would give progressive disease whatever the sum did.

quiz.prompt: A patient entering a trial has, at baseline: three liver metastases of 34, 22 and 12 mm; a 25 mm lung mass previously irradiated and unchanged since; two lung nodules of 11 and 9 mm; a 17 mm short-axis para-aortic node; sclerotic deposits in the right ilium; and a 30 mm simple renal cyst. Say which lesions you would take as targets, and justify the selection rules you applied.
quiz.answer: Take four targets: the 34 mm and 22 mm liver metastases, the 11 mm lung nodule and the 17 mm short-axis para-aortic node. The rules that produce this list are these. A lesion must be measurable, which on CT with 5 mm slices means at least 10 mm in longest diameter, or at least 15 mm in short axis for a node, so the 9 mm lung nodule is excluded, and the simple renal cyst is excluded outright because it is not tumour. No more than five targets in total and no more than two per organ, which is why only two of the three liver lesions are taken - the 34 mm and 22 mm, ahead of the measurable but smaller 12 mm lesion - chosen as the largest and the most reproducibly measurable, not merely the largest. Targets should represent all the involved organs, so a lung lesion and a node are included rather than filling the quota from the liver. A previously irradiated lesion is treated as non-measurable unless it has demonstrably progressed since, so the 25 mm lung mass moves to the non-target list, as do the sclerotic bone deposits, which have no measurable soft tissue component. Everything not selected is still recorded and followed qualitatively as non-target disease.
quiz.explain: Target selection is where most of the error in a trial dataset is introduced, because it happens once, early, and is never revisited. Two of the exclusions here are frequently forgotten. A previously irradiated lesion is unreliable because fibrosis holds its size regardless of what the tumour inside it is doing, so it neither shrinks convincingly nor grows convincingly; it becomes eligible again only if it has already progressed. Sclerotic bone deposits are unmeasurable for a related reason - the sclerosis is the healed bone reaction, and it may increase as the tumour responds, so a blastic lesion that gets denser is not growing disease. Choosing reproducibly measurable lesions matters more than choosing large ones: a lesion abutting the diaphragm or the heart border, or one bisected by an artefact, will generate spurious change at every timepoint.

quiz.prompt: Put these four RECIST 1.1 overall response categories in order, from the greatest reduction in tumour burden to the greatest increase.
quiz.answer: complete-response partial-response stable-disease progressive-disease
quiz.explain: Complete response is the disappearance of the target lesions, with any pathological node falling below 10 mm short axis. Partial response is a fall of at least 30 per cent in the sum of diameters, measured against baseline. Progressive disease is a rise of at least 20 per cent from the nadir together with an absolute rise of at least 5 mm, or a new lesion, or unequivocal progression of non-target disease. Stable disease is the wide middle ground - anything that is neither a 30 per cent fall nor a 20 per cent rise. The bands are deliberately asymmetric and deliberately broad, because most of what lies between them is measurement noise rather than biology; a system with narrow thresholds would report a great deal of change that no reader could reproduce. Stable disease is a category in its own right and not a failure to categorise, and in most protocols it carries a minimum duration before it can be claimed.

quiz.prompt: A protocol asks the reader to state whether a patient has met the criterion for a partial response. The baseline sum of target diameters was 80 mm. What is the largest current sum, in millimetres, that still qualifies as a partial response? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A partial response requires a decrease of at least 30 per cent from the baseline sum, so the ceiling is 80 multiplied by 0.7, which is 56 mm: a sum of 56 qualifies and 57 does not. Two features of the arithmetic deserve holding together. Partial response is measured against baseline while progression is measured against the nadir, so the two categories use different reference points and a patient can be simultaneously well below baseline and unequivocally progressing. And because the criterion is applied to a sum, shrinkage in one lesion can offset growth in another, which is part of why a new lesion counts as progression whatever the sum is doing. Where response rate is the primary endpoint of a non-randomised trial, a response must additionally be confirmed on a repeat assessment at least four weeks later.

quiz.prompt: After six cycles the liver and lung target lesions are no longer identifiable. The single target node, 21 mm short axis at baseline, now measures 8 mm short axis. The reader is minded to record a complete response and asks whether the residual node prevents it. What is the correct assessment?
choices: Complete response, as the node is below ten millimetres
Partial response, as measurable nodal tissue still remains
Complete response, as node size is disregarded on follow-up
Stable disease, as the node has not entirely disappeared
quiz.answer: Complete response, as the node is below ten millimetres
quiz.explain: Nodes do not vanish - healthy people have them - so the system sets the bar for a target node at below 10 mm in short axis rather than at zero. This node at 8 mm has cleared that bar, and with every other target lesion gone the target response is complete. Two riders keep the bookkeeping honest. The node's 8 mm is still recorded in the sum of diameters at each timepoint, so the sum of a patient in complete response is not zero, which surprises readers who expect the arithmetic to bottom out. And the overall response depends on more than the targets: any non-target disease must also have resolved, with any pathological nodes below 10 mm and tumour markers back within the normal range, before an overall complete response can be recorded.

quiz.prompt: The sum of target diameters has fallen from 96 mm to 55 mm, a 43 per cent reduction. The same scan shows a 7 mm enhancing liver lesion that was unequivocally absent before, is not explicable as artefact, and lies within a region imaged identically at baseline. What is the overall response?
choices: Progressive disease, because a new lesion has appeared
Partial response, as the new lesion is not measurable
Stable disease, pending a confirmatory scan in six weeks
Partial response, with the new lesion recorded separately
quiz.answer: Progressive disease, because a new lesion has appeared
quiz.explain: A new lesion is progression in its own right, regardless of what the sum of diameters has done, and this is one of the few places where the criteria abandon arithmetic entirely. The new lesion need not be measurable and it is not added into the sum; its existence is the finding. What the criteria demand instead is that it be unequivocal, and the qualifications matter: a small node visible only because this scan was reconstructed more thinly, a lesion in an area not previously imaged, or a finding attributable to infection or collapse is not a new lesion. Where a finding is genuinely equivocal the reader says so, treatment continues, and the next timepoint decides - and if it is then confirmed, the date of progression is backdated to the earlier scan. Immunotherapy is precisely where this rule strains, and it is why the immune-adapted criteria place new lesions in a separate compartment rather than treating them as an automatic endpoint.

quiz.prompt: A patient's target sum has fallen 22 per cent, but the previously mild peritoneal disease is now sheet-like with a new moderate volume of ascites, and the patient has deteriorated clinically. Explain how RECIST 1.1 handles non-target disease of this kind and what standard the change has to meet.
quiz.answer: Non-target disease is not measured; it is judged qualitatively and can only be recorded in one of three ways - complete response, non-complete-response with non-progressive-disease, or unequivocal progression. Unequivocal progression is a deliberately high bar. The worsening must be substantial enough that, taken with the whole picture, the overall tumour burden has increased to a degree that would justify stopping treatment, even though the target lesions are stable or shrinking. A modest apparent increase in a non-measurable deposit does not qualify, precisely because non-target assessment is subjective and the target sum is the quantitative anchor that keeps the whole system reproducible. Sheet-like peritoneal disease with new ascites in a deteriorating patient does meet that bar, and the case is recorded as progressive disease despite the 22 per cent fall in the sum. Where the reader is unsure, the honest course is to seek a second opinion or to wait for the next timepoint rather than to let an impression overrule a falling sum.
quiz.explain: This provision exists because a purely measurement-driven system would otherwise be blind to the disease it cannot measure - peritoneal and pleural disease, leptomeningeal spread, lymphangitis, diffuse bone marrow involvement - and those are common patterns of failure. But the same subjectivity that makes the provision necessary makes it dangerous, which is why the wording sets the bar at a change that would itself justify discontinuing treatment. The practical test to apply is whether an oncologist shown these images alone, without knowing the target sum, would stop the drug. If the answer is a confident yes, it is unequivocal progression; if it requires argument, it is not, and the next scan will settle it. Note that ascites and effusions are treated with particular caution, since both have non-malignant causes and both can be induced by treatment.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks into pembrolizumab for melanoma, a scan shows the target sum up 28 per cent from the nadir with an absolute rise of 9 mm, and one new subcutaneous nodule. The patient feels well, is gaining weight, and has no new symptoms. Explain what may be happening biologically, and how the response assessment should proceed.
quiz.answer: This may be pseudoprogression. Checkpoint blockade recruits lymphocytes into the tumour, so a lesion can enlarge with inflammatory infiltrate and oedema rather than with tumour cells, and deposits that were previously subclinical can become visible for the same reason. It is uncommon - of the order of a few per cent, more often seen in melanoma than in most other tumours - so it is a hypothesis to be tested rather than assumed. Under conventional RECIST 1.1 this scan is progressive disease. Under the immune-adapted criteria it is unconfirmed progression, and in a patient who is clinically stable treatment continues with a confirmatory scan in four to eight weeks. If that scan shows further growth - a further increase in the target sum of at least 5 mm, or further growth of the new lesion - progression is confirmed and is dated to the first scan. If instead the disease is stable or has shrunk, the unconfirmed progression is reset and the patient continues on treatment. The clinical state is part of the assessment: a patient who is deteriorating is not left on a drug for another eight weeks on the strength of a hypothesis.
quiz.explain: The reason a second set of criteria was needed is that the original ones were built for cytotoxic drugs, where growth means growth. With immunotherapy an early increase in size can precede a durable response, and a rigid application of the original rules would discontinue treatment in the patients about to benefit most. The safeguard against the opposite error - keeping everyone on a failing drug in the hope of a late response - is the confirmation requirement plus the clinical condition, which is why 'clinically stable' is written into the rule rather than left to judgement. Two further points for the radiologist. Related patterns exist elsewhere: enlarging nodes on immunotherapy may be sarcoid-like reaction rather than metastasis, and a growing lesion after chemoradiotherapy or ablation may be treatment effect. And in high-grade glioma the same trap has its own rule, where new enhancement within the radiation field in the first weeks after chemoradiotherapy is treated as pseudoprogression unless proven otherwise.

quiz.prompt: A trial site submits a baseline CT reconstructed at 8 mm slice thickness. The reader identifies a 12 mm liver lesion and wants to take it as a target lesion. What does RECIST 1.1 require here?
choices: The lesion must be at least twice the slice thickness
The lesion must be re-measured in the coronal plane
The lesion may be used if it is seen on three slices
The lesion counts, as twelve exceeds the ten limit
quiz.answer: The lesion must be at least twice the slice thickness
quiz.explain: The ten-millimetre rule assumes slices of 5 mm or less. Where slices are thicker, the minimum measurable size becomes twice the slice thickness, so at 8 mm the lesion must be at least 16 mm and this 12 mm lesion is non-measurable and goes on the non-target list. Partial volume is the reason. A lesion smaller than about twice the slice thickness may never be caught in a slice that contains its true maximum diameter, so its apparent size depends on where the slices happened to fall relative to it - and that dependence reappears at the next timepoint as change that is purely an artefact of positioning. The general lesson outlives the specific number: response criteria are only as reproducible as the acquisition beneath them, which is why trials fix the technique - slice thickness, contrast phase, reconstruction kernel, timing - and require the same one at every visit.

nodes.title: Structured Reporting
nodes.goal: Write a report to a standard template, assign a RADS category that carries its own recommendation, and close the loop on a finding that needs acting on.

quiz.prompt: A department rewrites its CT reports to follow the standard section headings used in structured reporting. Put those five headings in the order they appear, from the top of the report.
quiz.answer: indication technique comparison findings impression
quiz.explain: The order is not decorative; each section exists so that a later reader can tell what question was asked, what was done to answer it, and what the answer was. The indication frames the study and is what makes an incidental finding incidental. The technique records contrast, phases and reconstruction, so that a reader in six months knows what the study could and could not have shown - a non-contrast scan reported as showing no liver lesion means something different from a portal-venous one. The comparison names the prior studies actually reviewed, and naming them is a claim that they were opened. The findings are the observation, and the impression is the answer. The impression is the part that is read, quoted in the notes and acted on, which is why it goes last and why it has to stand alone.

quiz.prompt: A CT report on a patient with weight loss runs to eleven lines of findings, one of which records a 3 cm hypoenhancing pancreatic mass with upstream duct dilatation. The impression reads, in full: 'Abnormal appearances as described above. Clinical correlation advised.' The surgeon telephones the next day to ask whether the scan showed anything to explain the symptoms. What is the substantive failure in this report?
choices: The impression did not answer the clinical question asked
The findings should have opened with the pancreatic mass
The mass needed a stated differential in the findings
The report should have advised a repeat scan at 3 months
quiz.answer: The impression did not answer the clinical question asked
quiz.explain: The mass was seen, measured and recorded, and still the report failed, because the section the referrer reads contained nothing. 'As described above' asks a clinician who has not seen the images to do the synthesis, and 'clinical correlation advised' hands back the decision the study was requested to inform. A usable impression names the finding, gives the most likely explanation, ranks the alternative worth acting on, and states the next step with a modality and an interval. The near-miss about ordering the findings is a real point of style - leading with the abnormality that matters does help - but a perfectly ordered findings section under an empty impression still leaves the surgeon telephoning. Nor is a differential in the findings section the fix: the findings section is for what was seen, and interpretation belongs in the impression where it will be read.

quiz.prompt: A diagnostic workup characterises a circumscribed, oval, non-calcified mass, and the radiologist assigns BI-RADS 3, probably benign, with short-interval follow-up rather than biopsy. What is the upper limit of the likelihood of malignancy, as a percentage, that this category permits? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: BI-RADS 3 means a likelihood of malignancy greater than zero but no more than 2 per cent, and that number is the whole content of the category: it is the risk at which surveillance - typically at 6, 12 and 24 months - is judged safer than a needle. Category 4A begins immediately above it, at more than 2 up to 10 per cent, so a lesion the reader privately puts at 5 per cent is not a 3, however benign it looks. The bands continue: 4B more than 10 to 50 per cent, 4C more than 50 to less than 95, and category 5 at 95 per cent or above, where a benign biopsy result is disbelieved rather than accepted. Two disciplines follow. A category 3 may be given only after a complete diagnostic evaluation, never off a screening study, and the patient's own circumstances - a planned pregnancy, an unreliable route back for follow-up, or a patient who will not tolerate the wait - can still justify sampling a lesion the imaging calls probably benign.

quiz.prompt: A screening mammogram shows an asymmetry seen on the craniocaudal view only. No spot compression views, no ultrasound and no prior films have been obtained. The reporting radiologist writes 'BI-RADS 4, suspicious, biopsy recommended'. Why is that assessment wrong even if the lesion later proves malignant?
choices: The workup is incomplete, so the assessment is category 0
A one-view asymmetry is category 2 until it is proven
Category 4 is reserved for lesions with a mass on ultrasound
A screening study permits category 1 or category 2 alone
quiz.answer: The workup is incomplete, so the assessment is category 0
quiz.explain: An assessment category is a statement about a completed evaluation, and category 0 exists to say that the evaluation is not finished and to name what is needed - additional views, ultrasound, or the prior films. Being lucky about the eventual outcome does not rescue a category that misdescribes the state of the workup, for two reasons. The patient is sent to biopsy without the cheap steps that resolve most one-view asymmetries as summation of normal tissue, and the unit's own audit is corrupted, because positive predictive value is computed from these codes and a 4 assigned before workup pollutes the denominator that the department is judged on. The distractor pinning category 4 to an ultrasound correlate inverts the logic: a mammographic finding with no sonographic correlate is not thereby benign, and a lesion may be sampled under stereotactic or tomosynthesis guidance instead.

quiz.prompt: An emergency department patient with abdominal pain has a CT reported four hours after they were discharged home. It shows a 4 mm non-obstructing renal stone and, incidentally, a 3.5 cm saccular aneurysm of the splenic artery. The referring emergency physician's shift ended two hours ago. Describe how this result should be handled and what has to appear in the record.
quiz.answer: Treat it as an actionable finding that the report alone will not carry safely, because the clinician it is addressed to has no further contact with the patient. Reach a person who can act - the on-call clinician who has taken over that shift's patients, or the patient's named responsible clinician - by direct person-to-person contact rather than by leaving the result in an electronic inbox, and confirm that they have understood what is being asked of them. Close the loop by establishing that a named individual accepts responsibility for arranging vascular referral and for informing the patient, since a message that is delivered but not accepted is not closure. Then document in the report itself, as an addendum, who was contacted, at what time, by what means, and what was agreed. The written record is the durable part: a telephone call that nobody documented is indistinguishable, months later, from a call that was never made.
quiz.explain: Actionable findings sort roughly into three tiers by how fast someone must act: findings that threaten life within minutes, such as a tension pneumothorax or a ruptured ectopic, which demand immediate voice contact; findings that need action within hours or days, such as this aneurysm; and incidental findings that need outpatient follow-up. Counterintuitively, it is the third tier that is most often lost, and discharge is the classic failure mode, because the report lands with a clinician whose episode of care has ended. Notice also what is not the answer: adding a strong recommendation to the report changes nothing if nobody reads it, and telling the patient alone offloads the follow-up onto the person least able to arrange it. The durable fix is systemic - a tracked register of communicated results with acknowledgement, rather than a radiologist's memory - and the documented addendum is what feeds it.

quiz.prompt: An audit of one unit's CT reports finds the phrase 'infection or infarction cannot be entirely excluded' in a third of them, with no ranking of the two possibilities and no recommendation attached. What is the practical cost of this habit to the referring team?
choices: The decision the report was meant to inform is handed back
The report becomes too long for a clinician to read
The differential given is too narrow for the appearances
The findings section duplicates what the impression says
quiz.answer: The decision the report was meant to inform is handed back
quiz.explain: Hedging is sometimes the honest thing: genuine uncertainty must be stated, and a report that manufactures confidence it does not have is worse than one that admits doubt. The failure here is unranked uncertainty with no exit. Two diagnoses with opposite treatments are offered with no statement of which is more likely, no feature that separates them, and no test that would. The workable form gives the favoured diagnosis, names the alternative that is worth acting on, and says what would discriminate - a specific test at a specific interval, or a specific piece of clinical information. 'Correlate clinically' becomes meaningful only when it names the correlation sought: a white cell count, a lactate, a travel history, the date of the last chemotherapy. Length is not the problem; a two-line impression can be entirely unhelpful, and a controlled lexicon exists precisely so that agreed words carry agreed meanings between readers.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old with a 40 pack-year smoking history has a CT for haematuria that incidentally shows a single solid 4 mm pulmonary nodule and no other lung abnormality. Applying the 2017 Fleischner Society recommendations for incidental nodules, at how many months is the optional follow-up CT offered to a patient at this level of risk? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A solid nodule under 6 mm carries a risk of malignancy below about 1 per cent, so no routine follow-up is recommended in a low-risk patient; in a high-risk patient - heavy smoking, upper lobe location, spiculation, emphysema or fibrosis, older age - the guidance offers an optional single CT at 12 months, and if it is unchanged nothing further is needed. Hold the neighbouring bands beside it, because the intervals are not intuitive: a single solid nodule of 6 to 8 mm is imaged at 6 to 12 months and then considered again at 18 to 24 months, while a nodule over 8 mm earns CT at 3 months, PET-CT or tissue sampling, since at that size the pre-test probability justifies the intervention. Equally important are the recommendations' boundaries: they apply to incidental nodules in patients aged 35 and over, and not to lung cancer screening, which has its own system, nor to the immunosuppressed, nor to patients with a known primary malignancy.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old on tacrolimus after renal transplantation has a CT showing three new solid 5 mm pulmonary nodules. A trainee proposes discharging the finding under the Fleischner recommendation that nodules under 6 mm need no routine follow-up. Why is that reasoning unsound here?
choices: This patient sits outside the population the guidance covers
Three nodules exceed the number the guidance permits
The guidance requires thin-section CT to have been used
The guidance applies to nodules found on screening CT
quiz.answer: This patient sits outside the population the guidance covers
quiz.explain: Two exclusions bite at once. The recommendations are written for patients aged 35 and over, below which granuloma and resolving infection dominate and a lifetime of surveillance radiation is a real cost; and they explicitly exclude immunosuppressed patients, in whom a new nodule may be fungal or bacterial infection that needs treating this week, not a lesion to be watched for a year. Known primary malignancy is the third exclusion, for the mirror-image reason. The distractor about screening inverts the truth and is worth naming: this framework is for incidental nodules, while nodules found in a lung cancer screening programme are handled by the screening system, whose thresholds are calibrated to a population enriched for cancer. The right action here is short-interval CT with a discussion about infection, plus attention to whether the nodules are new against any prior imaging.

quiz.prompt: Your hospital board asks why the breast unit reports in BI-RADS categories while the general CT service writes free text, and whether the categories add anything beyond jargon. Give the argument in terms of what a category does that a paragraph of prose does not.
quiz.answer: A category is a controlled term that carries a defined probability of disease and a single recommended action, so the same word means the same thing to every reader and to every referrer. That buys three things prose does not. It removes ambiguity, because 'probably benign' becomes a stated risk band rather than one radiologist's confidence on one day. It ties the report to management, since the recommendation follows from the category rather than from individual habit, which reduces the variation between readers that is otherwise invisible to everyone outside the reporting room. And it makes the output auditable: because every study leaves a coded outcome, the unit can link its categories to the eventual pathology and measure its own positive predictive value, recall rate and cancer detection rate, then feed those numbers back into practice. The cost is real and should be conceded: a rigid category can flatten an unusual case, which is why these systems keep an explicit route for the reader who needs to depart from them, and why the departure has to be justified in the report.
quiz.explain: The board's scepticism is reasonable and the weak answer - that categories are clearer - does not survive it, since a well-written paragraph is clear too. What a paragraph cannot do is be counted. A coded assessment turns every report into a data point, and once the data exist the unit can discover that one reader's recall rate is twice another's, or that its own category 4A biopsies come back malignant at a rate far from the published band, which is a signal no amount of eloquent prose generates. This is also why the systems tie a recommendation to each category: it converts a probability estimate into a decision, and it makes divergence between the category and the advice visible as an error rather than as a style. The honest caveat is that the categories are only as good as the criteria beneath them, which is why they are versioned and periodically revised against outcome data.

quiz.prompt: A liver MRI in a cirrhotic patient describes a 2.5 cm observation with non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement, non-peripheral washout and an enhancing capsule, and concludes: 'LI-RADS 4, probably hepatocellular carcinoma; recommend follow-up MRI in six months.' The hepatologist queries the report. What is the internal inconsistency?
choices: The features listed already meet the criteria for LR-5
The washout must be seen in the portal venous phase
A capsule is not a feature this system recognises
An observation this size is reported without a category
quiz.answer: The features listed already meet the criteria for LR-5
quiz.explain: In a patient at risk, an observation of 20 mm or more with non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement plus at least one additional major feature - non-peripheral washout, an enhancing capsule, or threshold growth - is LR-5, definite hepatocellular carcinoma, and LR-5 is the category on which many programmes treat without a biopsy. Two errors compound here. The category understates what the reader's own description establishes, and the recommendation then contradicts even the understated category, since neither LR-4 nor LR-5 is followed with routine six-month surveillance. That second error is the one worth generalising: in a reporting system the recommendation belongs to the category, not to the reader's mood, and a report whose advice disagrees with its own code is more dangerous than free text because it wears the uniform of a standard. The washout distractor contains a real technical point - with extracellular agents washout may be assessed in the portal venous or delayed phase, while with a hepatobiliary agent it is judged in the portal venous phase only - but it is a caveat about acquisition, not the inconsistency in this report.

quiz.prompt: Rewrite the sentence 'Small lung nodule noted, follow-up as clinically indicated' into a recommendation that can actually be acted on and tracked, and set out the elements that make the difference.
quiz.answer: Something of the form: '5 mm solid nodule in the right upper lobe, apical segment, unchanged from the CT of 12 March 2024. Recommend non-contrast chest CT at 12 months; no further imaging if it remains stable.' The elements are a measurement and a specific location, so that the next reader finds the same nodule rather than a different one; a comparison that states whether it is new, stable or growing and against which study by date; a named modality and technique, so the follow-up can actually answer the question; a specific interval rather than a discretionary one; an endpoint that says when surveillance stops, which prevents a nodule being followed indefinitely by inertia; and clarity about who arranges it. 'As clinically indicated' fails every one of these: it passes the decision to a clinician who has not seen the images, leaves nothing for a tracking system to key on, and cannot be audited afterwards, because no one can say whether the recommendation was followed.
quiz.explain: The test of a recommendation is whether an administrator with no clinical training could book the right study from it, and whether an auditor could later decide whether it happened. Vague advice fails both. There is a second reason to state the endpoint: surveillance that never terminates accumulates radiation, cost and anxiety, and generates its own incidental findings, so the exit condition is part of the clinical decision rather than an afterthought. Where a published framework governs the finding, citing it by name and version does additional work, because it tells the referrer that the interval comes from evidence rather than from the reader's preference, and it lets a future radiologist see which rule was applied when the rules change.

nodes.title: Interventional Radiology: Access, Embolisation and Drainage
nodes.goal: Gain and close vascular access safely, choose the embolic agent and the level of occlusion the target demands, plan a drainage route, and recognise the common complications early enough to act on them.

quiz.prompt: Put the steps of the Seldinger technique for arterial access in the order they are performed.
quiz.answer: puncture-vessel confirm-pulsatile-return advance-guidewire withdraw-needle railroad-sheath remove-wire-and-dilator
quiz.explain: The whole logic of Seldinger's method is that nothing wide ever passes through tissue unless a wire is already sitting in the lumen for it to follow. Puncture the anterior wall, confirm pulsatile return, then feed the guidewire until it advances without resistance. If it does not advance freely, stop and look rather than push, because a wire forced into a subintimal plane is where most access complications begin. Only then does the needle come out over the wire, with the wire held. The sheath and its dilator follow as a single unit and are withdrawn together, leaving the sheath behind. Keep a hand on the wire at every exchange: a wire lost into the vessel, or dragged out with the dilator, is the most avoidable event in the room.

quiz.prompt: A 6 French angiographic catheter is being selected for a case. What is its outer diameter? Answer in millimetres to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: One French is a third of a millimetre, so dividing the French size by three gives the outer diameter: 6 Fr is 2.0 mm, 5 Fr is about 1.7 mm, 9 Fr is 3.0 mm. The convention that catches people is that catheters are sized by their outer diameter while sheaths are sized by their inner diameter, so a 6 Fr sheath will take a 6 Fr catheter but its own outer diameter is roughly 2 Fr larger, making an arteriotomy nearer 8 Fr, about 2.7 mm.
