That difference drives the closure strategy and the access site complication rate, because those complications scale with the hole in the artery rather than with the catheter inside it. Microcatheters are quoted in French too, typically 2.0 to 2.8 Fr, and their usability is set by the inner lumen of the guide and the wire they will accept.

quiz.prompt: Forty minutes after sheath removal from a right common femoral puncture, a patient becomes tachycardic and hypotensive with lower abdominal and back pain. The groin looks unremarkable, with no palpable swelling and no bruit, and both feet are warm. What has most likely happened?
quiz.answer: Retroperitoneal haemorrhage from a puncture above the inguinal ligament
choices: Retroperitoneal haemorrhage from a puncture above the inguinal ligament
A pseudoaneurysm arising from a puncture of the superficial femoral artery
An arteriovenous fistula between the femoral artery and the adjacent vein
Acute limb ischaemia from thrombus at the site of the arteriotomy closure
quiz.explain: A puncture above the inguinal ligament enters the external iliac artery, where there is no femoral head behind the vessel to compress against, so blood tracks freely into the retroperitoneum while the groin stays deceptively normal. Hypotension with flank, back or lower abdominal pain after femoral access is retroperitoneal haemorrhage until proven otherwise: resuscitate, cross-match, and get a CT, or take the unstable patient straight to angiography for balloon occlusion or a covered stent. The alternatives look different. A pseudoaneurysm from a low puncture presents hours to days later as a painful pulsatile swelling with a bruit; an arteriovenous fistula gives a continuous bruit and rarely destabilises anyone; limb ischaemia gives a cold, pulseless leg rather than shock. Prevention is the real lesson: puncture over the lower half of the femoral head with fluoroscopy or ultrasound, never by palpation of the skin crease.

quiz.prompt: Two days after a 6 French femoral procedure a patient returns with a tender pulsatile groin swelling. Ultrasound shows a 3 cm sac with a 1 cm neck and to-and-fro flow within the neck. The overlying skin is intact and the leg is well perfused. What is the appropriate first treatment?
quiz.answer: Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection into the sac, away from the neck
choices: Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection into the sac, away from the neck
Immediate surgical exploration with direct repair of the arteriotomy
A covered stent placed across the neck from a contralateral approach
Observation alone, with repeat ultrasound at six weeks to show closure
quiz.explain: A post-catheterisation pseudoaneurysm with a narrow neck and intact skin is treated by ultrasound-guided thrombin injection, which thromboses the sac in the great majority of patients at one sitting. The needle tip goes into the body of the sac well away from the neck, and injection stops the instant flow ceases, so that thrombin cannot track into the femoral artery and embolise distally. Small pseudoaneurysms under about 2 cm often thrombose on their own and can reasonably be watched, but a symptomatic 3 cm sac is not one of them. Surgery is reserved for rapid expansion, threatened or broken skin, infection, distal ischaemia, or failure of thrombin. A covered stent in the common femoral artery is poor practice, since it lies across a flexion point and a future access site. Look for an accompanying arteriovenous fistula before treating, because that changes the plan.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old with bronchiectasis has massive haemoptysis. Angiography shows a hypertrophied, tortuous right bronchial artery and no spinal branch is seen. Say which embolic agent you would deliver, and explain why coils and very small particles are both poor choices here.
quiz.answer: Deliver calibrated particles of roughly 300 to 500 micrometres through a microcatheter positioned distally in the bronchial artery. Coils occlude the vessel proximally, which stops today's bleeding but blocks catheter access when haemoptysis recurs, and recurrence is common because collaterals refill the bed beyond the coil. Particles much smaller than 300 micrometres, and liquid agents, can pass through a spinal or bronchopulmonary anastomosis and cause spinal cord infarction or bronchial wall necrosis.
quiz.explain: The choice of embolic follows what the target needs. A vascular bed to be devascularised takes particles; a single high-flow vessel to be shut takes coils or a vascular plug; an arteriovenous malformation, or a bleed in a coagulopathic patient, takes a liquid agent such as glue or an ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymer, because it polymerises without needing the patient to clot. Bronchial arteries are a bed, and one that is very likely to be worked on again, since recurrent haemoptysis after bronchial artery embolisation is frequent over the following years, so preserving the route back in matters as much as today's haemostasis. The specific hazard is the anterior spinal artery, which can arise from an intercostobronchial trunk: look for it before you embolise, and size the particles so that they lodge before reaching anything you could not see. Gelatin sponge is temporary and is reserved for situations where recanalisation is actually wanted.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a bleeding posterior duodenal ulcer has failed two endoscopic attempts and remains transfusion-dependent. Catheter angiography shows no active extravasation and no pseudoaneurysm. What is the appropriate course?
quiz.answer: Empirical embolisation of the gastroduodenal artery, on both sides of the ulcer
choices: Empirical embolisation of the gastroduodenal artery, on both sides of the ulcer
Stop, and repeat angiography only once further bleeding is clinically documented
Embolisation of the left gastric artery, which supplies the posterior duodenal wall
A covered stent in the common hepatic artery, across the origin of the ulcer supply
quiz.explain: A duodenal ulcer that has defeated endoscopy is embolised whether or not extravasation is visible, because angiography sees only bleeding that is active during the run, and a negative study in a transfusion-dependent patient does not mean the vessel is safe. The gastroduodenal artery is occluded on both sides of the bleeding point, front door and back door, because the pancreaticoduodenal arcades reconstitute it retrogradely from the superior mesenteric artery: a proximal coil alone leaves the ulcer perfused from below while removing the route you would need to get back to it. The duodenum tolerates the occlusion thanks to that same dual supply. The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curve of the stomach rather than the duodenum, and a covered hepatic artery stent treats a hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm, a different problem. Waiting for documented rebleeding squanders the safest window to intervene.

quiz.prompt: CT angiography localises acute bleeding to a branch of the right colic artery in a patient with diverticular disease, and catheter angiography confirms the bleeding branch. Which technique keeps the risk of bowel infarction lowest?
quiz.answer: Advance a microcatheter to the vasa recta and deploy microcoils at that level
choices: Advance a microcatheter to the vasa recta and deploy microcoils at that level
Deliver 100 to 300 micrometre particles from within the right colic artery
Occlude the ileocolic artery proximally with a gelatin sponge slurry instead
Deploy a vascular plug in the superior mesenteric artery branch that supplies it
quiz.explain: The colon has little useful collateral once you are beyond the marginal artery, so lower gastrointestinal embolisation is always a trade between stopping the bleeding and infarcting bowel. Superselective microcoils in the vasa recta or the terminal branch closest to the bleeding point occlude the smallest territory available, usually one or two vasa recta, and ischaemic complications with that technique are uncommon and mostly self-limiting. Small particles do the opposite: they travel beyond the level you can see and lodge in the mucosal capillary bed, which is precisely the tissue that infarcts. Proximal occlusion with gelatin sponge or a plug lowers perfusion pressure across a wide segment while leaving collateral inflow to the bleeding point, so it risks ischaemia and may not achieve haemostasis. If you cannot reach the target vessel, stop and hand over rather than embolise from wherever the catheter happens to sit.

quiz.prompt: A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is being created for recurrent variceal bleeding, and the portosystemic pressure gradient before the shunt is 21 mmHg. To what value must the gradient be brought down, at most, for the shunt to be considered adequate for variceal bleeding? Answer in mmHg as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Variceal bleeding does not occur below a portosystemic gradient of about 12 mmHg, and that figure is the target after a shunt created for variceal haemorrhage: dilate until the measured gradient is 12 or less, and measure rather than assume, since the pressures often do not follow the angiographic appearance. Lower is not better. The more portal flow that bypasses the liver, the greater the risk of hepatic encephalopathy, which affects a substantial minority of patients after the procedure and is the commonest reason a shunt has to be reduced or occluded later. Refractory ascites is often managed with a slightly less aggressive reduction for that reason. Patient selection carries as much weight as technique: heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension and uncontrolled sepsis are the standing contraindications, because a shunt delivers a sudden rise in preload to a right ventricle that may not tolerate it.

quiz.prompt: Four patients with hepatocellular carcinoma are discussed at the multidisciplinary meeting. Which one is the appropriate candidate for transarterial chemoembolisation?
quiz.answer: Multifocal tumour confined to the liver, Child-Pugh A, with a patent portal vein
choices: Multifocal tumour confined to the liver, Child-Pugh A, with a patent portal vein
A single 2 cm tumour in a Child-Pugh A patient who is fit for surgical resection
Tumour thrombus filling the main portal vein, Child-Pugh B7, performance status 0
Diffuse tumour with refractory ascites and encephalopathy, Child-Pugh C, ten points
quiz.explain: Chemoembolisation is the standard treatment for intermediate-stage disease: multinodular tumour still confined to the liver, preserved liver function and good performance status, with no macrovascular invasion and no extrahepatic spread, which is BCLC stage B. The reason the other three fail is the same in each case, that the procedure deliberately infarcts liver tissue and the liver must be able to absorb that insult. A patient fit for resection or ablation should have the curative treatment rather than a palliative one. Main portal vein occlusion means the hepatic artery is now supplying tissue that has lost its other inflow, so embolising it risks hepatic infarction, although selective treatment is sometimes used with segmental thrombus in experienced hands. Decompensated Child-Pugh C disease belongs to transplant assessment or supportive care. Expect post-embolisation syndrome afterwards in most patients: that is the treatment working.

quiz.prompt: A woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease needs six months of intermittent adjuvant chemotherapy. The ward has requested a PICC. Say what device you would place instead, and give two reasons for the change.
quiz.answer: Place a totally implantable chest port. First, a PICC would consume the arm veins she is likely to need for an arteriovenous fistula if her kidney disease progresses to dialysis, and it can stenose the subclavian or brachiocephalic vein and make the whole limb unusable for access. Second, a port suits intermittent treatment over months: it sits under intact skin between cycles, carries a lower infection rate per catheter-day than a PICC, and interferes far less with washing, working and sleeping.
quiz.explain: Choosing venous access is a question of how long, how often, how fast, and what the patient will need next. Under two weeks in hospital calls for a non-tunnelled line; weeks to a few months of continuous or daily therapy suits a PICC; months to years of intermittent treatment suits a port; high-flow or frequent access, apheresis or dialysis needs a tunnelled cuffed catheter. Vein preservation cuts across all of it, and in advanced chronic kidney disease the cephalic and basilic veins are a future fistula rather than a convenient route today. Ask about the dialysis plan before you puncture anything, and where a PICC is unavoidable in such a patient, discuss it with the renal team and use the non-dominant arm they nominate. Choose the smallest catheter with enough lumens, since infection and thrombosis both track with size and with the number of lumens.

quiz.prompt: Thirty-six hours after transarterial chemoembolisation for hepatocellular carcinoma a patient has a temperature of 38.4 degrees, right upper quadrant pain, nausea and a white cell count of 14. Ultrasound shows no collection, a normal gallbladder and normal bile ducts. What is the most likely explanation?
quiz.answer: Post-embolisation syndrome from the infarcted tumour, needing supportive care
choices: Post-embolisation syndrome from the infarcted tumour, needing supportive care
A developing hepatic abscess within the treated segment, needing drainage
Non-target embolisation of the cystic artery, causing ischaemic cholecystitis
Catheter-related bloodstream infection seeded from the femoral access site
quiz.explain: Fever, pain, nausea and a raised white cell count in the first two to three days after embolisation are the expected inflammatory response to infarcted tissue. Most patients have some of it after chemoembolisation, and after uterine artery embolisation too. Treat with fluids, analgesia and antiemetics, warn the patient beforehand so that they are not frightened by it, and expect it to settle within a few days. Time course and trajectory separate it from the alternatives: an abscess declares itself later, with a collection and often gas, and is far likelier in a patient with a bilioenteric anastomosis or an incompetent sphincter of Oddi; ischaemic cholecystitis follows non-target embolisation and shows a distended, thick-walled gallbladder; a line infection has no reason to localise to the right upper quadrant. The fever that matters is the one still climbing on day five rather than falling, and that one gets re-imaged.

quiz.prompt: A 6 cm presacral abscess after anterior resection cannot be reached from the front because of bowel and bladder, so a transgluteal approach is planned. Where should the needle cross the greater sciatic notch?
quiz.answer: Medially and inferiorly, close to the sacrum and below the piriformis muscle
choices: Medially and inferiorly, close to the sacrum and below the piriformis muscle
Laterally through the notch, keeping well clear of the adjacent sacral cortex
Superiorly through the notch, passing immediately above the piriformis muscle
Through the sacrospinous ligament, angled forwards towards the ischial spine
quiz.explain: The sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels occupy the lateral part of the greater sciatic notch, so a transgluteal puncture is taken as close to the sacrum as the anatomy permits and inferior to the piriformis, where the corridor is relatively bare. Crossing laterally is the error that produces a lasting sciatic neuropathy or serious gluteal bleeding, and passing above the piriformis threatens the superior gluteal artery, which is hard to compress and awkward to catheterise if it bleeds. Transgluteal drains hurt, because the catheter crosses muscle that moves with every step, so exclude the shorter routes first: transrectal or transvaginal drainage is well tolerated for a collection abutting either wall, and endoscopic transrectal drainage may be available. Where no safe window genuinely exists, say so in writing rather than accept a marginal one.

quiz.prompt: During prostatic artery embolisation, cone-beam CT from the left prostatic artery opacifies a small branch running to the rectal wall. Say what you do before delivering any particles, and what you are preventing.
quiz.answer: Reposition the microcatheter distal to the origin of that branch and repeat the cone-beam CT to confirm the rectum no longer opacifies. If the branch cannot be bypassed, occlude it with a coil to protect it before embolising. This prevents non-target embolisation causing rectal ischaemia and ulceration, and the same manoeuvre protects branches running to the bladder, the seminal vesicles and the penis.
quiz.explain: Prostatic arterial anatomy is highly variable and richly anastomotic, and the pelvic branches it communicates with, middle rectal, vesical and internal pudendal, supply tissue that does not forgive infarction. Cone-beam CT before embolisation is what makes the procedure safe, because a two-dimensional angiographic run cannot tell you which organ a small branch is heading for. There are two responses and they are both simple: get distal to the anastomosis, which a microcatheter usually manages, or coil the branch so that particles cannot enter it. Particle size helps as well, since larger microspheres are less likely to traverse a small anastomosis. Non-target embolisation announces itself afterwards as rectal pain and bleeding, dysuria and haematuria, or penile ulceration, and avoiding it is most of what separates a good service from a bad one.

quiz.prompt: A haemodynamically stable 24-year-old has a grade IV splenic laceration with a contrast blush on the arterial phase and a moderate haemoperitoneum. Say what you would offer, and explain why occluding the proximal splenic artery does not infarct the spleen.
quiz.answer: Offer splenic artery embolisation to support non-operative management and preserve the spleen. A coil or plug placed in the proximal splenic artery, beyond the dorsal pancreatic branch, lowers the perfusion pressure reaching the injured parenchyma so that it can clot, while the spleen stays perfused through collateral supply from the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries. A single focal injury can instead be embolised selectively; multiple or diffuse bleeding points favour the proximal approach.
quiz.explain: Non-operative management succeeds in the great majority of haemodynamically stable patients with splenic injury, and embolisation extends it to the high AAST grades that once went straight to splenectomy. A contrast blush, a pseudoaneurysm or an arteriovenous fistula on the arterial phase is the finding that predicts failure of observation alone and identifies the patient who gains from the angiography suite. The mechanism worth holding on to is perfusion pressure rather than occlusion: the collateral network through the short gastrics and the gastroepiploic arcade keeps the organ alive while pressure at the tear falls far enough for haemostasis, which is also why splenic immune function is largely retained, though local policy on vaccination after proximal embolisation varies. Keep the coil beyond the dorsal pancreatic artery to avoid pancreatic ischaemia. The unstable patient still goes to theatre; embolisation is for the patient whose physiology grants you the time.

nodes.title: Airway Disease: Bronchiectasis, Small Airways and the Large Airway
nodes.goal: Diagnose bronchiectasis on criteria that will survive scrutiny, use distribution and expiratory imaging to work out a cause, distinguish the emphysema subtypes, and assess the large airway for fixed narrowing and for dynamic collapse.

quiz.prompt: On an axial HRCT image the internal diameter of a right lower lobe segmental bronchus is 6.0 mm and the adjacent pulmonary artery measures 4.0 mm. Calculate the broncho-arterial ratio. Answer as a decimal, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Six divided by four is 1.5, so the bronchus is half as wide again as its companion artery and the pair form the signet ring. A ratio above one is the classical criterion, but on its own it over-diagnoses: the ratio rises with age, at altitude, in chronic hypoxaemia and in pulmonary arterial hypoplasia, all of which shrink the artery rather than widen the bronchus, and it rises artefactually on expiratory images and on oblique cuts through a bronchus. The more specific findings are failure of the bronchus to taper over one to two centimetres of its course, and bronchi visible within about a centimetre of the costal pleura or touching the mediastinal pleura. Measure perpendicular to the bronchial axis, and always ask whether the patient has the symptoms to match.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old has a broncho-arterial ratio of about 1.1 in both lower lobes. The bronchi taper normally along their course, none is visible within a centimetre of the costal pleura, and the walls are not thickened. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: The ratio alone is insufficient here and bronchiectasis should not be diagnosed
choices: The ratio alone is insufficient here and bronchiectasis should not be diagnosed
The ratio exceeds one, which establishes cylindrical bronchiectasis in both bases
The ratio suggests traction bronchiectasis and a fibrotic process should be sought
The ratio is diagnostic once an expiratory acquisition has confirmed air trapping
quiz.explain: A mildly raised broncho-arterial ratio in an elderly patient with normal tapering, normal wall thickness and no peripheral bronchial visibility is far more likely to reflect an age-related fall in arterial calibre than a diseased airway. Tapering is the sign to lean on, because it is a property of the bronchus itself rather than of the ratio between two structures. The cost of getting this wrong runs in both directions. Over-calling commits a patient to lifelong airway clearance, sputum surveillance and repeated antibiotic courses, and it anchors every subsequent reader. Under-calling in someone producing sputum daily misses a diagnosis with real treatment. Traction bronchiectasis is a different animal, occurring inside fibrotic lung with reticulation and volume loss around it, and the fibrosis is the finding to report first.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old with poorly controlled asthma has central upper lobe bronchiectasis packed with mucus, and on the unenhanced study some of the mucus plugs are denser than the paraspinal muscle. What should be done next?
quiz.answer: Send total IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE, since this pattern suits allergic aspergillosis
choices: Send total IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE, since this pattern suits allergic aspergillosis
Send sputum for mycobacterial culture, since this pattern suits atypical mycobacterial disease
Send a sweat chloride test and genotype, since this pattern suits late presenting cystic fibrosis
Send immunoglobulin subclasses, since this pattern suits common variable immunodeficiency
quiz.explain: Mucus that is denser than muscle without contrast is high-attenuation mucus, and in a bronchiectatic asthmatic it is close to specific for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, reflecting calcium and metal salts within inspissated secretions. The distribution supports it: central and perihilar bronchiectasis with relatively normal peripheral airways, upper zone predominant, sometimes with finger-in-glove opacities from impacted branching bronchi. Confirmation is serological, resting on a raised total IgE with Aspergillus-specific IgE or immediate skin reactivity in a patient with asthma or cystic fibrosis, and treatment is corticosteroids with or without itraconazole. The alternatives all cause bronchiectasis with a different distribution: cystic fibrosis is upper zone but diffuse with hyperinflation, mycobacterial disease favours the middle lobe and lingula with tree-in-bud nodules, and immunoglobulin deficiency favours the lower zones with chronic sinus disease.

quiz.prompt: A 71-year-old lifelong non-smoking woman has cylindrical bronchiectasis confined to the right middle lobe and the lingula, with clusters of tree-in-bud nodules in the same regions. Say what you suspect and what would confirm it.
quiz.answer: This nodular bronchiectatic distribution suggests nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease, usually Mycobacterium avium complex. Confirmation needs repeated sputum samples sent for mycobacterial culture, or lavage culture if she cannot expectorate.
quiz.explain: Cylindrical bronchiectasis with tree-in-bud nodularity restricted to the middle lobe and lingula in an older, slim, non-smoking woman is the nodular bronchiectatic form of nontuberculous mycobacterial disease. Tree-in-bud tells you the small airways are filled, so the process is spreading endobronchially, and the same appearance occurs in aspiration and in post-infective bronchiolitis. The distinction matters because treatment is a multi-drug regimen lasting a year or more beyond culture conversion, with real toxicity, so imaging alone never starts it. The accepted microbiological requirement is two separate positive sputum cultures, or one positive bronchial lavage, alongside compatible symptoms and imaging. The other form, cavitary fibronodular disease in the upper lobes, occurs in older men with emphysema and looks much more like tuberculosis.

quiz.prompt: A patient two years after lung transplantation is breathless with a falling FEV1, and the inspiratory CT looks nearly normal apart from mild bronchial wall thickening. Say what acquisition you would add and what it would show if the small airways are the problem.
quiz.answer: Add an expiratory acquisition. Lobular or geographic regions that fail to increase in attenuation on expiration, giving mosaic attenuation with air trapping alongside bronchial dilatation, indicate constrictive bronchiolitis, the imaging counterpart of bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome.
quiz.explain: Constrictive bronchiolitis narrows and obliterates membranous bronchioles that are below the resolution of CT, so the inspiratory study is often unremarkable and the disease is diagnosed by what the lung fails to do rather than by what it shows. On expiration the affected lobules cannot empty and stay lucent while normal lung becomes denser, producing sharply bordered geographic air trapping, usually with bronchial wall thickening and eventually bronchial dilatation. The causes are worth carrying: chronic lung allograft dysfunction, chronic graft-versus-host disease after stem cell transplantation, rheumatoid arthritis, post-viral disease in children, and inhalational injury. Check the expiratory series is genuine by looking for forward bowing of the posterior tracheal membrane, and discount the small volume of physiological trapping seen in dependent lung, the lingula and the superior segments of the lower lobes.

quiz.prompt: A 42-year-old who has never smoked has uniform low attenuation with a strikingly sparse vascular tree in both lower lobes, rather than discrete punched-out holes. What should follow?
quiz.answer: Measure the alpha-1 antitrypsin level, because basal panlobular destruction suggests deficiency
choices: Measure the alpha-1 antitrypsin level, because basal panlobular destruction suggests deficiency
Measure the diffusing capacity alone, because basal low attenuation is a normal finding at this age
Arrange bronchoscopy urgently, because basal low attenuation of this kind indicates large airway obstruction
Arrange a ventilation study first, because basal low attenuation reflects redistribution of lung perfusion
quiz.explain: The three emphysema subtypes separate on distribution and on what is destroyed. Centrilobular emphysema destroys the lobular core, gives discrete lucencies with the central artery still visible as a dot, and is upper zone predominant in smokers. Panlobular emphysema destroys the whole lobule uniformly, favours the lower zones, and is the pattern of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, also seen after intravenous methylphenidate use. Paraseptal emphysema sits subpleurally and along the septa. Panlobular disease is the one most often missed, because there is no hole to point at: the give-away is simplification of the vascular tree, an oddly empty-looking lower lobe. Testing changes several things at once, since deficiency brings augmentation therapy into play, makes smoking cessation urgent, prompts family screening, and calls for liver surveillance.

quiz.prompt: A tall 24-year-old man presents with a second right-sided spontaneous pneumothorax. CT after drainage shows a single row of thin-walled subpleural lucencies in both apices, with normal lung between them and elsewhere. What is the significance?
quiz.answer: Apical paraseptal emphysema and blebs, which carry a real risk of further pneumothorax
choices: Apical paraseptal emphysema and blebs, which carry a real risk of further pneumothorax
Apical honeycombing from fibrosis, which calls for a full interstitial disease work-up
Apical cavitating infection, which calls for sputum culture before any further imaging
Apical cystic lung disease, which calls for screening for lymphangioleiomyomatosis now
quiz.explain: Paraseptal emphysema occupies the subpleural lung and the lung along the interlobular septa, and on CT it is a single layer of lucencies with thin or barely visible walls, favouring the apices and the paramediastinal regions. It is the substrate for apical blebs and bullae in tall young men, and the reason this matters is recurrence: after a second ipsilateral pneumothorax the risk of a third is high enough that surgical pleurodesis with bullectomy is usually offered, so the CT finding feeds directly into an operative decision. Do not confuse the single subpleural row with honeycombing, which is stacked in layers, thick walled, basal and surrounded by reticulation. Cystic lung diseases such as lymphangioleiomyomatosis give round, walled cysts distributed throughout the lung rather than only under the pleura.

quiz.prompt: On a dynamic expiratory CT the tracheal lumen at a fixed level measures 240 mm squared at end-inspiration and 96 mm squared during forced expiration. Calculate the percentage reduction in cross-sectional area. Answer as a percentage, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The lumen falls by 144 of 240 square millimetres, which is 60.0 per cent. The conventional threshold for tracheobronchomalacia is expiratory collapse of more than half the cross-sectional area, and it is best demonstrated on dynamic imaging during forced expiration or coughing rather than on a static end-expiratory acquisition, which underestimates it. Two qualifications keep this honest. Healthy volunteers can exceed fifty per cent on forced expiration, which is why some groups use a higher cut-off and why nobody should make the diagnosis without symptoms to match. And malacia frequently coexists with other airway disease: it is common in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, after prolonged intubation or tracheostomy, and in relapsing polychondritis, and it is a recurring explanation for the patient whose obstruction does not respond to bronchodilators.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have tracheal narrowing with wall thickening that at first glance looks circumferential. Say which single feature of the tracheal wall you would use to separate relapsing polychondritis from tracheal amyloidosis, and what that feature reflects.
quiz.answer: Look at the posterior membranous wall. Relapsing polychondritis thickens the anterior and lateral walls and spares the posterior membrane because the disease attacks cartilage, whereas amyloid is deposited circumferentially, involves the posterior membrane and often calcifies.
quiz.explain: The posterior wall of the trachea has no cartilage, so it sorts the differential of tracheal narrowing into two groups. The cartilage diseases spare it: relapsing polychondritis, which thickens and later collapses the anterolateral wall, and tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica, which studs the same walls with calcified submucosal nodules. The infiltrative and inflammatory diseases involve it: amyloidosis, which thickens the wall circumferentially with calcification, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, classically as a short subglottic stenosis, and post-intubation or post-tracheostomy stenosis. Relapsing polychondritis also declares itself outside the chest, in auricular and nasal chondritis and audiovestibular symptoms, and airway involvement drives its mortality, so add dynamic expiratory imaging: fixed narrowing and malacia often coexist, and only the second explains sudden collapse on coughing.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an intrathoracic trachea whose coronal diameter is half its sagittal diameter, with normal wall thickness and a normal extrathoracic segment. What should the report state?
quiz.answer: A sabre-sheath configuration related to COPD, needing no specific airway intervention
choices: A sabre-sheath configuration related to COPD, needing no specific airway intervention
A fixed tracheal stenosis from prior intubation, needing bronchoscopic reassessment
Tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica, needing biopsy of the submucosal nodules
Extrinsic compression by mediastinal fibrosis, needing contrast-enhanced reassessment
quiz.explain: Side-to-side narrowing with preservation of the front-to-back diameter, confined to the intrathoracic trachea and sparing the cervical segment, with a coronal to sagittal ratio of two thirds or less and a normal wall thickness, is the sabre-sheath trachea of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is a marker of the disease rather than a lesion needing treatment, and reporting it as a stenosis sends the patient for an unnecessary bronchoscopy. The alternatives look different: post-intubation stenosis is a short hourglass segment at cuff or stoma level and often involves the cervical trachea, osteochondroplastica produces nodular anterolateral wall thickening that spares the posterior membrane, and extrinsic compression displaces as well as narrows. Do look for coexisting malacia, which is common in the same patients and does change management.

quiz.prompt: A two-year-old had a witnessed choking episode. The inspiratory frontal film looks symmetrical, but on the expiratory film the right lung remains lucent and large while the left deflates, and the mediastinum shifts to the left. What does this indicate?
quiz.answer: Ball-valve obstruction of the right main bronchus with air trapping on that side
choices: Ball-valve obstruction of the right main bronchus with air trapping on that side
Complete obstruction of the right main bronchus with collapse of the right lung
A left-sided pneumothorax decompressing across the anterior junction on expiry
A normal paediatric expiratory film, since the mediastinum swings in small children
quiz.explain: Most inhaled foreign bodies in children are organic and radiolucent, so the radiograph is read for their effect rather than for the object. The commonest effect is obstructive hyperinflation, not collapse: the object acts as a ball valve, letting air past on inspiration when the airway widens and trapping it on expiration when the airway narrows. So the affected lung fails to deflate, stays lucent and large, and pushes the mediastinum away from it on the expiratory film. The right main bronchus is the more frequent site because it is wider and more vertical. In a child who cannot cooperate with expiration, lateral decubitus films substitute: the dependent lung should deflate, and a dependent lung that stays inflated implicates that side. A normal film never excludes a foreign body.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these investigations for a clinically stable child with a suspected inhaled foreign body in order of increasing invasiveness, as you would escalate when each proves unhelpful.
quiz.answer: inspiratory-radiograph expiratory-radiograph low-dose-CT rigid-bronchoscopy
quiz.explain: The ladder exists to keep children out of a general anaesthetic they do not need. A frontal inspiratory radiograph comes first and may show a radio-opaque object, collapse or hyperinflation. An expiratory film, or lateral decubitus films in a child too young to cooperate, is added when the inspiratory film is unremarkable, because air trapping is a functional sign and only appears on expiration. Low-dose CT sits next: it can show a non-opaque object directly and resolve the equivocal case at a modest dose. Rigid bronchoscopy is last on this ladder because it needs anaesthesia, but it is also the only step that treats as well as diagnoses. The ladder is for the stable, equivocal child; with a witnessed choking episode and unilateral signs, the child goes straight to bronchoscopy.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old with a lifelong productive cough has bronchiectasis concentrated in the middle lobe and both lower lobes, chronic pansinusitis, and dextrocardia with a right-sided gastric bubble. What should be pursued?
quiz.answer: Testing for primary ciliary dyskinesia, since situs inversus accompanies this distribution
choices: Testing for primary ciliary dyskinesia, since situs inversus accompanies this distribution
Testing for cystic fibrosis, since sinus disease accompanies this pattern of bronchiectasis
Testing for immunoglobulin deficiency, since sinus disease dominates this clinical picture
Testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, since lower zone disease dominates this picture
quiz.explain: Bronchiectasis in the middle lobe and lower lobes, chronic sinus disease and situs inversus is primary ciliary dyskinesia, and the combination with situs inversus is Kartagener syndrome, present in roughly half of these patients because embryonic nodal cilia determine laterality. Confirmation runs through nasal nitric oxide, high-speed video microscopy of ciliary beat and genetic testing. Distribution does most of the sorting among the causes of diffuse bronchiectasis: cystic fibrosis is upper zone predominant and diffuse with hyperinflation and mucus plugging, and presents far earlier; antibody deficiency such as common variable immunodeficiency gives lower zone bronchiectasis with sinus disease but no laterality defect, and is worth excluding in any unexplained case because immunoglobulin replacement changes the course. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes basal emphysema rather than bronchiectasis.

nodes.title: HRCT of the Lung
nodes.goal: Name the elementary HRCT patterns from the images, use nodule distribution and an expiratory series to narrow the cause, and place a fibrotic scan into the UIP categories.

quiz.prompt: On a 1 mm axial section the right upper lobe is uniformly hazier than the left. Pulmonary vessels and the walls of the segmental bronchi are still visible running through the haze, no bronchus is outlined by surrounding density, and the appearance persists unchanged on a prone series. Which reading follows?
choices: Ground-glass opacity, not consolidation
Consolidation with air bronchograms
Dependent atelectasis of the segment
Volume averaging from a thick slice
quiz.answer: Ground-glass opacity, not consolidation
quiz.explain: The distinction is made on what survives the haze. Ground glass raises attenuation without replacing the air, so vessels and bronchial walls are still traced through it; consolidation replaces the air, obliterates the vessels, and reveals bronchi as air bronchograms precisely because everything around them is now dense. The other two options are the technical mimics that the vignette has already excluded. Dependent atelectasis is common in the posterior basal lung, looks exactly like ground glass, and disappears when the patient turns over, which is the whole reason for the prone series. Partial volume averaging in a thick section blurs fine reticulation into apparent haze, and is excluded by the 1 mm reconstruction. Ground glass itself is not a diagnosis: it can be infiltration, oedema, haemorrhage, or fine fibrosis below the resolution of the scan, and its company decides which.

quiz.prompt: Inspiratory HRCT shows sharply demarcated geographic regions of low and high attenuation. On the expiratory series the darker regions do not change in attenuation or volume, while the denser regions become denser still and shrink. The vessels running through the darker regions are smaller than those elsewhere. What has the expiratory series established?
choices: Air trapping from small airways disease
Infiltrative ground-glass in the dense areas
Reduced perfusion from chronic thromboembolism
Motion artefact between the two acquisitions
quiz.answer: Air trapping from small airways disease
quiz.explain: Lung that behaves normally empties on expiration: it loses volume and rises in attenuation. Lobules whose supplying bronchioles are obstructed cannot empty, so they stay dark and stay the same size, and that fixed attenuation is the definition of air trapping. The vessel calibre had already told you which lung was abnormal. In small airways disease the lucent regions are the diseased ones and their vessels are narrowed by hypoxic vasoconstriction, whereas in infiltrative disease the dense regions are the diseased ones and vessel calibre is equal in both. Mosaic perfusion in chronic thromboembolic disease also shows lucent regions with small vessels, which is why the inspiratory scan alone cannot separate the two, and it is the expiratory series that does: perfused-but-ventilated lung still empties normally. In that direction, look also for an enlarged central pulmonary artery, mural thrombus and dilated bronchial arteries.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old with a dry cough and no occupational dust exposure has HRCT showing small nodules strung along the fissures, the subpleural surfaces and the bronchovascular bundles, most numerous in the upper and mid zones, together with symmetrical hilar and right paratracheal nodal enlargement. Which diagnosis does that combination favour?
choices: Sarcoidosis of the lung
Miliary tuberculosis
Lymphangitic carcinoma
Silicosis of the lung
quiz.answer: Sarcoidosis of the lung
quiz.explain: Nodules that follow the fissures, the pleural surface and the bronchovascular bundles are perilymphatic, because those are where the lung's lymphatics run, and that distribution narrows the field to sarcoidosis, silicosis and coal worker's disease, and lymphangitic spread of carcinoma. Upper and mid zone predominance with symmetrical hilar and paratracheal nodal enlargement in a young adult is sarcoidosis. Silicosis produces an almost identical perilymphatic upper zone picture and can calcify its nodes in an eggshell pattern, so the discriminator is the occupational history the vignette explicitly removes, which is worth remembering as the reason that history must be asked for. Lymphangitic carcinoma thickens the interlobular septa nodularly, is often basal and asymmetrical, and comes with a known primary. Miliary tuberculosis is random rather than perilymphatic: uniform 1 to 3 mm nodules scattered without regard to lobular anatomy, some abutting the pleura and some in the middle of a lobule.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old pigeon fancier has HRCT showing profuse ill-defined ground-glass nodules a few millimetres across, sitting in the centres of the secondary lobules and sparing the pleural and fissural surfaces, with patchy lobular areas of low attenuation that persist on expiration. Which reading fits?
choices: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Perilymphatic sarcoid nodules
Haematogenous lung metastases
Endobronchial spread of TB
quiz.answer: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
quiz.explain: Centrilobular nodules sit a few millimetres away from the pleura, the fissures and the interlobular septa, because the structure at the centre of the secondary lobule is the terminal bronchiole with its accompanying arteriole. Anything arriving by air lands there. Ill-defined ground-glass centrilobular nodules combined with lobular air trapping, in a person with an inhaled antigen exposure, is the classic non-fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis picture: cellular bronchiolitis fills the lobular centres and partial bronchiolar obstruction traps air in whole lobules. Sarcoid nodules are perilymphatic and would sit on the fissures the vignette says are spared. Haematogenous metastases arrive by blood, so they are random and favour the lung bases where perfusion is greatest. Endobronchial tuberculosis is also centrilobular, but it is dense and branching, the tree-in-bud of impacted bronchioles, rather than ground-glass, and it usually comes with cavitation elsewhere.

quiz.prompt: A fibrotic CT shows, in the upper lobes, subpleural lucencies lying in a single row against the pleura, thin-walled and without distortion of the adjacent vessels. In the lower lobes there are clustered cystic spaces of similar diameter, stacked several layers deep and sharing their walls, with traction bronchiolectasis running into them. Which reading of the lucencies is correct?
choices: Paraseptal emphysema above, honeycombing below
Honeycombing in both upper and lower lobes
Paraseptal emphysema throughout both lungs
Traction bronchiectasis mistaken for cysts
quiz.answer: Paraseptal emphysema above, honeycombing below
quiz.explain: Honeycombing is defined by architecture, not by the presence of holes: clustered cystic airspaces of broadly similar diameter, usually a few millimetres to about a centimetre, subpleural, sharing their walls, and stacked in rows two or more layers deep, in lung that is distorted. Paraseptal emphysema is a single subpleural layer of lucencies separated by intact interlobular septa, upper zone predominant, with no distortion of the surrounding lung and no traction on the airways. Getting the pair the wrong way round is one of the commonest sources of interobserver disagreement in fibrosis reporting, and it is not cosmetic: honeycombing is the single feature that separates a UIP pattern from a probable UIP pattern, so a misread row of emphysematous spaces can promote a scan to definite UIP and start a patient on antifibrotic treatment for a disease they may not have.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with bibasal crackles and restrictive spirometry has HRCT showing reticulation with peripheral traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis, subpleural and basal in distribution, a little superimposed ground glass, and no clustered cystic spaces anywhere. Which category does the 2018 international guideline place this scan in?
choices: A probable UIP pattern
A definite UIP pattern
Indeterminate for UIP
An alternative diagnosis
quiz.answer: A probable UIP pattern
quiz.explain: The guideline sorts a scan into UIP, probable UIP, indeterminate for UIP, or a pattern suggesting an alternative diagnosis. Subpleural and basal predominant reticulation with peripheral traction bronchiectasis or bronchiolectasis, with mild ground glass permitted and honeycombing absent, is probable UIP; honeycombing is what would have made it UIP. Indeterminate is reserved for a scan with subtle subpleural basal fibrosis that will not commit either way, or one whose features are mildly discordant. An alternative diagnosis is called when the scan says something else outright, through upper or mid zone predominance, a peribronchovascular distribution, extensive ground glass, profuse micronodules, discrete cysts, widespread mosaic attenuation and air trapping, or consolidation. The categories matter because they carry management: a UIP pattern in the right clinical setting is accepted as a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without surgical lung biopsy, and a probable UIP pattern, after multidisciplinary discussion in a patient with no exposure and no connective tissue disease, very often is too.

quiz.prompt: A fibrotic HRCT is upper and mid zone predominant with a peribronchovascular distribution, and on the inspiratory images three distinct densities coexist within a single section: normal lung, ground glass, and sharply demarcated lobular lucency. Which reading does the pattern support?
choices: Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Fibrotic NSIP from scleroderma
Sarcoid fibrosis of the upper zones
quiz.answer: Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis
quiz.explain: Three densities in one section is the sign that hypersensitivity pneumonitis does two things at once: it infiltrates the lung, giving ground glass, and it obstructs bronchioles, giving lobular air trapping, and it leaves normal lung between the two. The 2020 international guideline names this three-density pattern on the inspiratory series as typical of fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which is useful precisely because it does not require an expiratory scan to be recognised. Zonal distribution argues the same way: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is basal and subpleural, and an upper and mid zone peribronchovascular fibrosis is not it. Fibrotic NSIP is basal, is often strikingly subpleural-sparing, and shows ground glass with fine reticulation rather than lobular lucency. Sarcoid fibrosis is also upper zone and peribronchovascular, but it comes with perilymphatic nodules, nodal enlargement and traction of the hila upward.

quiz.prompt: An older HRCT protocol acquires 1 mm axial sections at 10 mm intervals through the chest, rather than a volumetric dataset. What percentage of the lung volume appears in the images? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: One millimetre out of every ten is imaged, so nine tenths of the lung is not represented at all. The technique was designed for diffuse disease, where a sample of the lung answers the question, and it fails for anything focal: a 6 mm nodule lying between two sections does not exist. That is why volumetric thin-section acquisition, reconstructed at about 1 mm with a sharp high-spatial-frequency kernel, has become the default. It gives the same interstitial detail, plus coronal and sagittal reformats that show the craniocaudal gradient on which the UIP categories depend, maximum intensity projections that transform the assessment of nodule profusion and distribution, and minimum intensity projections that make mosaic attenuation and air trapping conspicuous. What volumetric acquisition does not replace are the two supplementary series: prone images, to separate dependent atelectasis from early subpleural fibrosis, and expiratory images, without which air trapping is invisible.

quiz.prompt: A report describes mosaic attenuation and stops there. Set out the three families of cause, the vessel-calibre clue that separates the first from the third, and the extra acquisition that settles the question.
quiz.answer: Mosaic attenuation has three families of cause: small airways disease with air trapping, occlusive vascular disease with mosaic perfusion, and patchy infiltrative disease in which it is the denser lung that is abnormal. In the first two the lucent lung is the diseased lung and its vessels are reduced in calibre relative to those in the denser regions, because ventilation or perfusion is reduced there; in infiltrative disease vessel calibre is equal in the two, because the dense areas are ground glass rather than the lucent areas being underperfused. The acquisition that settles it is an expiratory series. Lobules with air trapping fail to increase in attenuation and fail to reduce in volume, while all normally ventilated lung, including the lung of mosaic perfusion and of infiltrative disease, becomes uniformly denser. Chronic thromboembolic disease is then supported by an enlarged central pulmonary artery, mural or webbed thrombus, and dilated bronchial arteries.
quiz.explain: Mosaic attenuation is a description, and left as a description it is nearly useless to the referrer, because the three causes lead to a bronchodilator, an anticoagulant or an immunosuppressant. Two observations do almost all the work of separating them. The first is deciding which lung is abnormal, and vessel calibre answers it: reduced vessels mark the abnormal lucent lung of airways or vascular disease, equal vessels mark ground glass as the abnormality. The second is the expiratory series, which is the only way to demonstrate air trapping and costs one extra breath-hold at low dose. Two cautions belong with them. Dependent lung in a normal patient is denser and can be mistaken for a mosaic, which prone imaging resolves. And a small amount of air trapping in the dependent lower lobes, particularly in older people and smokers, is a normal finding, so the sign has to be geographic and out of proportion before it is reported as disease.

quiz.prompt: Two thoracic radiologists agree about everything on a fibrotic HRCT except whether one row of subpleural lucencies is honeycombing. Explain concretely what hangs on that single disagreement.
quiz.answer: Honeycombing is the feature that separates a UIP pattern from a probable UIP pattern, given that the rest of the scan is subpleural and basal and nothing suggests an alternative diagnosis. A UIP pattern, in the right clinical context and after multidisciplinary discussion, is accepted as sufficient to diagnose idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without surgical lung biopsy. A probable UIP pattern keeps bronchoalveolar lavage or surgical biopsy on the table for some patients and moves more of the weight of the diagnosis onto the multidisciplinary meeting and the clinical picture. The error in the other direction matters just as much: calling paraseptal emphysema or clustered traction bronchiolectasis honeycombing overdiagnoses UIP, and can commit a patient with a different, potentially treatable fibrosing disease to antifibrotic therapy and to a prognosis that is not theirs. So the disagreement decides an invasive test, a drug and a prognosis, which is why the honest report describes the morphology in detail and takes the case to the meeting rather than asserting the label.
quiz.explain: Interobserver agreement on honeycombing is famously imperfect, and the guideline is built in the knowledge of that, which is why it defines the term by architecture and why the multidisciplinary discussion, not the radiologist alone, makes the diagnosis. Two practical habits reduce the disagreement. The first is to check the morphology against the definition every time rather than by gestalt: stacked layers, shared walls, similar diameters, subpleural, in distorted lung. The second is to look at the coronal reformats and the upper zones before committing, because emphysema declares itself by its zonal distribution and by the absence of traction, and traction bronchiolectasis declares itself by continuity with an airway when it is tracked across contiguous slices.

quiz.prompt: A request asks you to exclude pulmonary fibrosis from a routine contrast-enhanced chest CT reconstructed at 5 mm with a soft tissue kernel. Say why the existing data cannot answer it, and specify what an HRCT protocol adds and what each addition is for.
quiz.answer: Thick sections apply partial volume averaging across a whole secondary lobule, so fine reticulation is smeared into apparent ground glass and small honeycomb cysts are unreadable, and a soft tissue kernel deliberately removes the high spatial frequencies that the fine interstitium is made of. HRCT means thin sections of about 1 mm reconstructed with a sharp kernel, in current practice from a volumetric acquisition so that coronal and sagittal reformats show the craniocaudal gradient on which the pattern categories depend, and maximum intensity projections show nodule profusion and distribution. Prone images are added to distinguish dependent atelectasis in the posterior basal subpleural lung, which disappears when the patient turns over, from early subpleural fibrosis, which does not. Expiratory images are added because air trapping cannot be seen on inspiration at all. Intravenous contrast is unnecessary and can be a nuisance, since dense enhancing vessels obscure fine peripheral detail, and the dose of a dedicated study is spent on the questions the referrer actually asked.
quiz.explain: The two reconstruction parameters are not interchangeable with each other or with anything else, and they are the reason a routine chest CT is not a low-grade HRCT but a different examination. Slice thickness sets how much lung is averaged into a voxel, and the secondary pulmonary lobule is only one to two and a half centimetres across, so a 5 mm section averages structures the diagnosis depends on. The kernel sets which spatial frequencies survive reconstruction, and a soft kernel is chosen for mediastinal soft tissue precisely because it suppresses the frequencies that fine lung detail occupies. Both can be re-reconstructed from raw data if it still exists, which is always worth asking before the patient is recalled. The prone and expiratory series cannot be recovered that way, because they are acquisitions rather than reconstructions, and that is the practical reason to protocol the study properly at the outset.

quiz.prompt: The 2018 international guideline sorts the HRCT appearance in suspected idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis into four categories. Put them in order, from the appearance that argues most strongly for a UIP pattern to the one that argues against it.
quiz.answer: UIP probable-UIP indeterminate alternative-diagnosis
quiz.explain: UIP: subpleural and basal predominant fibrosis, often heterogeneous, with honeycombing, with or without peripheral traction bronchiectasis. Probable UIP: the same distribution with reticulation and peripheral traction bronchiectasis or bronchiolectasis, mild ground glass permitted, but no honeycombing. Indeterminate: subtle subpleural basal fibrosis that will not commit, or fibrosis with a few features that sit awkwardly with UIP. Alternative diagnosis: findings that point elsewhere, such as upper or mid zone predominance, a peribronchovascular or perilymphatic distribution, extensive ground glass, profuse micronodules, discrete cysts, widespread mosaic attenuation with air trapping, or consolidation. The ladder is a statement about diagnostic confidence rather than about disease severity, and the rungs carry different consequences for whether tissue is needed, which is what makes the ordering worth knowing rather than merely worth reciting.

nodes.title: Mediastinal Masses and the Nodal Map
nodes.goal: Localise a mediastinal mass to its ITMIG compartment, narrow it with tissue characteristics and serum markers, and report the nodal map in the terms the surgeon needs.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old has a 5 cm soft-tissue mass on CT lying behind the pericardium, in front of a coronal plane drawn 1 cm posterior to the anterior margin of the vertebral bodies, and pushing the oesophagus to the left. Which reading of the case follows from where it sits?
quiz.answer: Visceral compartment, so nodal disease and foregut cysts lead
choices: Visceral compartment, so nodal disease and foregut cysts lead
Prevascular compartment, so thymic epithelial tumours lead
Paravertebral compartment, so nerve sheath tumours lead
Visceral compartment, so a retrosternal goitre is likeliest
quiz.explain: The ITMIG compartments are drawn on axial CT, and their boundaries are lines you can actually find. The prevascular compartment runs from the sternum back to the anterior surface of the pericardium; the visceral compartment runs from there back to a coronal plane 1 cm behind the anterior margin of the vertebral bodies; everything behind that plane, out to the posterior margin of the transverse processes, is paravertebral. This mass is behind the pericardium and ahead of the vertebral line, so it is visceral, and the visceral differential is dominated by lymph nodes, foregut duplication cysts and oesophageal disease. Thymic tumours belong to the prevascular compartment and nerve sheath tumours to the paravertebral, so neither fits the position given. A retrosternal goitre can descend into the visceral compartment, but it is only a goitre if the images show it continuous with the cervical thyroid, and that was not described. The odd-looking 1 cm offset exists because paravertebral tumours are commonly centred a little anterior to the vertebral body; drawing the line on the body itself would misassign them.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old woman who has just finished chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma has a diffusely enlarged thymus that keeps its arrowhead shape. On chemical-shift MRI a region of interest over the thymus measures 384 signal units on the in-phase image and 246 on the opposed-phase image. Calculate the signal intensity index, ((in-phase minus opposed-phase) divided by in-phase) times 100. Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: (384 - 246) / 384 = 0.3594, so 35.9 per cent. What the number means is more useful than the arithmetic. Opposed-phase imaging cancels signal wherever fat and water protons share a voxel, so a tissue that is lymphoid cells interspersed with fat loses signal, while a tissue that is solid tumour does not. Normal and hyperplastic thymus keep that fatty interspersion, so they drop; thymoma, thymic carcinoma and lymphoma are cellular masses without microscopic fat and stay bright. A substantial drop like this one, in a gland that is diffusely enlarged and has kept its bipyramidal shape, says rebound hyperplasia after chemotherapy rather than relapse - and rebound hyperplasia is FDG-avid, which is exactly why the PET alone will not settle it. Two limits are worth carrying: below about sixteen years of age the normal thymus is fat-poor and the test loses its footing, and beyond about forty the gland is usually fat-replaced anyway, so a soft-tissue prevascular mass in that age group is abnormal whatever the chemical shift shows.

quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old has an incidental smoothly marginated 3 cm prevascular lesion measuring 42 HU on unenhanced CT with no measurable enhancement afterwards. MRI shows uniform very high T2 signal throughout and no internal enhancement. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: A thymic cyst: no tissue diagnosis or surgery is needed
choices: A thymic cyst: no tissue diagnosis or surgery is needed
A thymoma: refer for surgical resection of the lesion
A lymphoma: arrange PET-CT and an image-guided biopsy
Indeterminate: repeat the CT in three months to compare
quiz.explain: Attenuation is the trap. Cyst fluid that is proteinaceous or has bled measures well above water, and 40-something Hounsfield units in a small lesion is also inflated by partial volume from the surrounding fat, so a cyst can look convincingly solid on CT. The pair of findings that settles it is uniform very high T2 signal with absent enhancement; no thymic epithelial tumour and no lymphoma looks like that. Thymoma enhances and is intermediate on T2. Lymphoma is homogeneous soft tissue, usually with nodal disease elsewhere, and is intensely FDG-avid. Waiting three months is not neutral - it commits the patient to another scan and to months of not knowing, for a lesion already characterised. Two caveats before you sign it off benign: a multilocular cyst, unlike the simple unilocular thymopharyngeal remnant, arises in inflammation and can harbour tumour in its walls, so a solid enhancing nodule within a multilocular lesion is resected; and a cyst that grows on interval imaging deserves the same suspicion.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old man has a 9 cm heterogeneous prevascular mass with central necrosis. Serum AFP is 1,850 kU/L and beta-hCG is normal. The multidisciplinary meeting asks whether to biopsy before starting treatment. What do you advise, and on what reasoning?
quiz.answer: No biopsy is needed: a markedly raised AFP means a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour whatever a core would show, so chemotherapy can start on the markers, and biopsy only adds delay and sampling error.
quiz.explain: Pure seminoma does not make alpha-fetoprotein. A markedly raised AFP therefore proves non-seminomatous elements are present, and it does so more reliably than a core from one part of a heterogeneous 9 cm mass, which may sample only necrosis or only the seminomatous component. Treatment is platinum-based combination chemotherapy started on the markers, with resection of any residual mass afterwards; a mediastinal non-seminomatous germ cell tumour is poor-prognosis by site alone, so the delay a biopsy buys is a real cost. Two habits follow. First, request testicular ultrasound - a mediastinal germ cell tumour is usually primary, but a burnt-out testicular primary changes the picture, and there is a recognised association with Klinefelter syndrome. Second, be careful with the alternatives: mature teratoma contains fat and calcium with normal markers and is a surgical problem, not a chemotherapy one; seminoma is a homogeneous lobulated mass with a normal AFP and at most a modest hCG rise, and it is exquisitely chemo- and radiosensitive.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old woman treated for stage II nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma has an end-of-treatment PET-CT. The residual prevascular mass measures 3.4 cm, down from 9 cm, and its FDG uptake is above mediastinal blood pool but below liver. How should this be reported and what follows?
quiz.answer: Deauville 3, complete metabolic response: stop and survey
choices: Deauville 3, complete metabolic response: stop and survey
Deauville 4, partial metabolic response: give more therapy
Deauville 5, progressive disease: change the chemotherapy
Deauville 2, but the residual size still means partial response
quiz.explain: The Deauville five-point scale reads uptake against two internal reference organs and nothing else. Score 1 is no uptake, 2 is uptake at or below mediastinal blood pool, 3 is above blood pool but at or below liver, 4 is moderately above liver, and 5 is markedly above liver or any new disease. Uptake above blood pool but below liver is score 3, and in standard practice scores 1 to 3 at the end of treatment are a complete metabolic response. Size does not enter the scale, which is the point of the fourth option: nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma characteristically leaves a bulky sterile fibrotic mass in the prevascular compartment that never shrinks to nothing, and calling that partial response by CT criteria led to years of unnecessary radiotherapy. One nuance worth knowing: in response-adapted trials that de-escalate treatment on an interim scan, score 3 is sometimes handled cautiously rather than as a clean pass, so state the score itself and let the clinical protocol decide what it means.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old with stridor has a 7 cm mass in the visceral compartment displacing the trachea to the right. Unenhanced attenuation is 96 HU, there are coarse calcifications, and contiguous images show the mass to be continuous with the right thyroid lobe. Which feature is doing the most diagnostic work here?
quiz.answer: Continuity with the cervical thyroid on contiguous slices
choices: Continuity with the cervical thyroid on contiguous slices
High unenhanced attenuation from intrinsic iodine content
The coarse calcification within the solid part of the mass
Displacement of the trachea towards the opposite side
quiz.explain: High baseline attenuation is thyroid tissue's most characteristic feature, because the gland concentrates iodine, and intense prolonged enhancement supports it - but haemorrhagic nodes, dense treated lymphoma and some vascular masses can also measure high, so the finding is suggestive rather than decisive. Coarse calcification appears in thymoma, teratoma, treated lymphoma and old granulomatous nodes. Tracheal displacement is mass effect and says nothing about tissue. Continuity with the cervical thyroid on unbroken contiguous images is the one observation only a goitre produces, and it is the reason you scroll up rather than reason about numbers. What the surgeon then needs from you is different again: the inferior extent relative to the arch and brachiocephalic vessels, the minimum tracheal calibre and the length of narrowing, whether the mass reaches behind the trachea or oesophagus, and whether it crosses to the contralateral side - retrotracheal or posterior mediastinal extension is what turns a collar incision into a sternotomy.

quiz.prompt: A 33-year-old has an incidental 4 cm rounded paravertebral mass at T7 with splaying of the adjacent ribs and widening of the neural foramen. The thoracic surgeon plans a thoracoscopic resection. What further imaging information must your report supply, and why does it change the operation?
quiz.answer: Whether the tumour extends through the foramen into the spinal canal, which needs MRI of the thoracic spine, because a dumbbell tumour requires a combined neurosurgical approach rather than thoracoscopic resection alone.
quiz.explain: A widened neural foramen is a warning, not a diagnosis, and CT is poor at showing what lies within the canal. Peripheral nerve sheath tumours arise on intercostal nerves and grow along them, so a proportion are dumbbell lesions with an intraspinal component. Resecting the thoracic half first can avulse the intraspinal half, bleed into the canal and leave a cord injury, so the operation becomes a staged or combined neurosurgical and thoracic procedure - which is why MRI of the spine belongs in your recommendation before anyone books a list. Two other habits round this out. Look at the shape: a rounded mass centred on a single interspace suggests a nerve sheath tumour, whereas an elongated, vertically oriented mass spanning several vertebral levels suggests a sympathetic chain tumour such as ganglioneuroma or, in a child with calcification and vascular encasement, neuroblastoma. And exclude the impostors before calling anything a tumour: extramedullary haematopoiesis, a paravertebral abscess with disc and endplate destruction, and a lateral meningocoele all sit in the same place.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT for a right upper lobe adenocarcinoma shows a 14 mm short-axis node anterior to the trachea, lying to the left of the sagittal midline but to the right of the left lateral tracheal border, at the level of the aortic arch. How should this node be assigned and what follows?
quiz.answer: Station 4R, making it ipsilateral N2 and possibly operable
choices: Station 4R, making it ipsilateral N2 and possibly operable
Station 4L, making it contralateral N3 and inoperable
Station 3a, prevascular, and therefore ipsilateral N2
Station 10R, a hilar node, and therefore N1 disease
quiz.explain: In the IASLC map the border between the right and left paratracheal stations is the left lateral wall of the trachea, not the sagittal midline. A node anterior to the trachea and left of the midline is still 4R provided it does not cross that tracheal border - which matters enormously here, because 4R for a right-sided tumour is ipsilateral N2 and potentially resectable after multidisciplinary discussion, while 4L would be contralateral N3 and takes surgery off the table. Station 3a is prevascular, anterior to the great vessels and not against the trachea; station 10 lies distal to the mediastinal pleural reflection, in the hilum. One more thing the report must not imply: 14 mm short axis is enlarged, but size is a poor discriminator, with roughly a quarter to a third of enlarged nodes reactive and a meaningful minority of normal-sized nodes harbouring tumour. Enlargement earns the node a needle, not a stage.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT for a left lower lobe primary shows enlarged nodes at stations 5 and 7, an enlarged node at station 10L, and a 12 mm short-axis node at station 4R. Using the IASLC map, how many separate mediastinal nodal stations - that is, stations counted as N2 or N3 rather than N1 - are involved? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Stations 5 (subaortic), 7 (subcarinal) and 4R are mediastinal; station 10L is hilar and therefore N1, not mediastinal. That gives three. The more important lesson is what the count does and does not decide. Stations 5 and 7 are ipsilateral or midline for a left-sided tumour and so are N2; station 4R is contralateral and so is N3, and the presence of any N3 station supersedes the N2 count entirely - this patient is N3 whatever the tally, and that is a non-surgical stage. The count matters when disease is confined to ipsilateral N2, because the ninth edition of the lung cancer TNM classification, in use since 2025, splits N2 into N2a for a single involved station and N2b for multiple stations, on evidence that single-station disease carries a distinctly better prognosis. That is why a modern report lists the stations individually by number rather than saying mediastinal nodes are enlarged: the count is now part of the stage.

quiz.prompt: The multidisciplinary team wants tissue from an enlarged subaortic (station 5) node before deciding on surgery for a left upper lobe tumour. The bronchoscopist has already sampled stations 4R and 7 by endobronchial ultrasound. What should you advise about station 5?
quiz.answer: It lies outside EBUS reach: VATS or anterior mediastinotomy
choices: It lies outside EBUS reach: VATS or anterior mediastinotomy
It is reachable at EBUS from within the left main bronchus
It is reachable at standard cervical mediastinoscopy instead
It is reachable at EUS from within the oesophageal lumen
quiz.explain: Sampling routes follow anatomy, and every route needs a window without a great vessel in it. Endobronchial ultrasound reaches what abuts the airway - stations 2, 4, 7, 10 and 11. Endoscopic ultrasound from the oesophagus reaches the posterior and inferior stations, 4L, 7, 8 and 9, and the left adrenal gland. Cervical mediastinoscopy covers 2R, 2L, 4R, 4L and the anterior part of 7. Stations 5 and 6 sit lateral to the aortic arch with the aorta and pulmonary artery interposed, so they are the classic blind spot of every needle technique and are sampled at left video-assisted thoracoscopy or anterior mediastinotomy. This matters most in exactly this tumour: the subaortic node is the first-echelon mediastinal station for a left upper lobe primary, so it is the one that decides the operation. Say in the report which stations are involved and which route can reach them - it saves the team a procedure that was never going to answer the question.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these steps in the assessment of a newly discovered bulky prevascular mass in a young man, earliest first.
quiz.answer: chest-radiograph contrast-CT serum-tumour-markers image-guided-biopsy
quiz.explain: The radiograph is usually how the mass announces itself; contrast CT characterises it, defines the compartment and plans access; serum markers come before any needle; biopsy is last and sometimes unnecessary. The order is not bureaucratic. A markedly raised AFP or beta-hCG makes the diagnosis of a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour on its own, so drawing markers first can spare the patient a procedure and start chemotherapy days earlier. When a biopsy is still needed, the CT is what makes it a good one: an anterior approach that avoids the internal mammary vessels, and enough core tissue for immunophenotyping, because fine-needle cytology will not subtype a lymphoma and a repeat is another week lost. There is one recognised exception to biopsying at all - a well-circumscribed prevascular mass with the appearances of an encapsulated thymoma in a patient fit for surgery is often resected without preoperative sampling, to avoid seeding the pleura along a transpleural tract.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old woman has facial swelling and distended chest wall veins. CT shows a 12 cm infiltrative prevascular mass encasing an occluded superior vena cava, with dense collaterals and mild tracheal narrowing. The team asks whether to start high-dose steroids overnight and biopsy tomorrow. What is your advice?
quiz.answer: Get tissue first if she is safe to lie flat, because steroids can lyse a lymphoma within hours and leave a non-diagnostic biopsy; flag the tracheal narrowing so the biopsy is planned with anaesthetic support.
quiz.explain: This is almost certainly primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma or Hodgkin lymphoma, and both are steroid-sensitive enough that a night of dexamethasone can render a core non-diagnostic or, worse, leave a partially treated lymphoma that cannot be subtyped or staged. Superior vena cava obstruction itself is rarely the emergency it looks like; the collaterals that make the chest wall veins so striking are also what keep the patient alive, and the genuinely time-critical problem is the airway. So the report should describe the tracheal calibre and the length of narrowing, whether the patient can lie supine, the level and length of the caval occlusion, and the collateral pathways - azygos, internal mammary, lateral thoracic - which the interventional team will want if a stent is needed. Endovascular stenting relieves symptoms quickly and can be done before or after sampling. If the airway genuinely will not permit a procedure, steroids are the right call, but that should be a decision made openly, not a default.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old presenting with new myasthenia gravis has a 4.5 cm prevascular mass on CT. Which additional feature would most change the surgical plan?
quiz.answer: Nodular soft tissue on the pleural surface beyond the mass
choices: Nodular soft tissue on the pleural surface beyond the mass
Punctate calcification within the capsule of the mass
A lobulated contour with a smooth fat plane preserved
Cystic change occupying about a third of the mass
quiz.explain: Thymoma spreads by contiguity and by dropping implants along the pleura rather than by nodal or haematogenous routes, so discontinuous pleural nodules are metastatic disease - Masaoka-Koga stage IVa - and they convert a straightforward total thymectomy into a case for induction chemotherapy and possibly extended pleurectomy. That is why every slice of the pleural surface, including the diaphragmatic and paravertebral reflections, is worth a deliberate look on a thymoma staging CT. The other options are noise: calcification and cystic change occur in encapsulated and invasive thymomas alike, and a lobulated contour with preserved fat planes is common in tumours that turn out to be entirely encapsulated. The CT features that genuinely suggest invasion are vascular or pericardial encasement, an irregular interface with adjacent lung, and pleural or pericardial nodularity; microscopic capsular invasion is simply not visible, which is why staging is ultimately surgical. Note too that in myasthenia the whole thymus is removed regardless of tumour size.

nodes.title: Pleura: Effusion, Pneumothorax and Malignancy
nodes.goal: Detect and quantify pleural fluid and air across modalities, separate empyema and malignant disease from simple effusion, and get a drain into the right space.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient lies supine. On ultrasound at the lung base, the maximal separation between the visceral and parietal pleura at end-expiration is 34 mm. Using the bedside estimate that volume in millilitres is twenty times the interpleural distance in millimetres, what volume does this predict? Answer in millilitres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: 34 x 20 = 680 mL. The estimate was derived in supine ventilated patients with the probe at the posterior axillary line at the lung base, and it is a working figure rather than a measurement - expect it to be right to within a couple of hundred millilitres, and do not use it in a seated patient or with loculated fluid. The reason it is worth knowing is the contrast with radiography.
