A frontal erect film needs roughly 200 mL before the lateral costophrenic angle blunts, a lateral film about 50 mL in the posterior sulcus, and a supine film can hide well over half a litre behind a veil of increased density. Ultrasound sees a few millilitres. So a supine intensive care film reported as showing no significant effusion is a statement about the projection, not about the chest, and the volume you quote should almost always come from ultrasound or CT. Volume alone never decides drainage: whether the fluid is infected, and whether the patient is breathless because of it, do.

quiz.prompt: An intubated patient has a supine anteroposterior film showing uniformly increased density across the whole right hemithorax, with pulmonary vessels still visible through it and no mediastinal shift. What is happening and what should you do next?
quiz.answer: Layering pleural fluid; confirm and quantify by ultrasound
choices: Layering pleural fluid; confirm and quantify by ultrasound
Complete lobar collapse; request an urgent bronchoscopy
Diffuse consolidation; start antibiotics and repeat film
A large haemothorax; call for immediate tube drainage
quiz.explain: Supine fluid layers along the posterior pleural space and is therefore spread across the whole hemithorax as a thin sheet the beam passes through. That produces a graded veil of increased density with the lung markings still visible through it, which neither consolidation nor collapse permits: consolidation fills the alveoli and obscures the vessels, and collapse takes volume with it and pulls the mediastinum towards the opacity. The other supine clues are worth collecting - an apical cap, loss of the hemidiaphragm outline, thickening of the paraspinal line, and blunting that never appears because there is no dependent costophrenic angle to blunt. Ultrasound answers the question in under a minute and does more than confirm: it measures the depth, shows whether the fluid is anechoic or complex, and marks the safe puncture site. Haemothorax is a statement about what the fluid is, which the density pattern cannot supply.

quiz.prompt: Ultrasound of a moderate effusion in a febrile patient shows freely mobile internal echoes swirling with the heartbeat, several fine septations, and parietal pleural thickening of 4 mm. What do these features tell you?
quiz.answer: An exudate is certain; anechoic fluid would not exclude one
choices: An exudate is certain; anechoic fluid would not exclude one
A transudate is likeliest; the echoes reflect cell debris
A chylothorax is likeliest given the swirling echo pattern
Little: these appearances are seen in transudates as well
quiz.explain: The test is asymmetric, and that asymmetry is the whole teaching point. Echogenic fluid, septations, loculation, parietal pleural thickening beyond about 3 mm and pleural nodularity are close to specific for an exudate - a transudate essentially does not produce them. But anechoic fluid tells you nothing, because most exudates are anechoic too, so the absence of these features cannot be used to call an effusion transudative. Swirling echoes appear in empyema, haemothorax and chylothorax alike, so they mark protein and cells rather than a particular fluid. Finding septations before you aspirate changes what you expect: septated fluid will not come out through a small catheter placed and forgotten. The biochemical arbiter remains Light's criteria - an exudate if the pleural-to-serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, or the pleural-to-serum LDH ratio exceeds 0.6, or the pleural LDH exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

quiz.prompt: Contrast CT in a septic patient shows a lentiform right pleural collection making obtuse angles with the chest wall, with thickened enhancing visceral and parietal pleura separated by the fluid, increased attenuation of the extrapleural fat, and internal loculation. What does this appearance commit you to, and how should it change the drainage plan?
quiz.answer: This is an empyema rather than a simple parapneumonic effusion, so a single small catheter is likely to fail: it needs a drain plus intrapleural fibrinolysis with alteplase and dornase alfa, and early surgical referral if it does not clear.
quiz.explain: The split pleura sign - two enhancing pleural layers with fluid between them - means the pleural surfaces are inflamed and thickened, not merely wet, and together with lentiform shape, obtuse angles, extrapleural fat stranding and loculation it says organising empyema. That changes the drain in two ways. First, a loculated collection is a set of compartments, and one catheter drains one of them; the fluid that will not come out is not a suction problem. Second, fibrinous septations respond to intrapleural alteplase with dornase alfa given together, the combination tested in the MIST2 trial, which improved drainage and reduced surgical referral where either agent alone did not. Bore size matters less than most people assume - small-bore catheters do as well as large ones for empyema provided they are flushed regularly - so the real decisions are fibrinolysis and a timely surgical opinion, since a collection that fails to clear needs video-assisted thoracoscopic decortication before the visceral peel becomes fixed.

quiz.prompt: A cavity with an air-fluid level abuts the chest wall. On CT it is round with a thick irregular wall, makes acute angles with the pleura, and destroyed lung and vessels can be traced right up to its edge. The air-fluid level measures the same width on the frontal and lateral projections. How should this be managed?
quiz.answer: Lung abscess: antibiotics, with drainage only if it fails
choices: Lung abscess: antibiotics, with drainage only if it fails
Empyema: place a chest drain and start fibrinolytic therapy
Empyema: refer directly for surgical decortication instead
Necrotic tumour: arrange biopsy of the wall before treating
quiz.explain: An abscess forms within lung and expands equally in all directions, so it is spherical: the air-fluid level is the same width whichever way you look at it, the angles with the pleura are acute, the wall is thick and irregular, and the vessels and airways of the lung it destroyed run up to it and stop. An empyema is confined to a potential space, so it is lentiform, makes obtuse angles, its air-fluid level is longer in one projection than the other, and it compresses and displaces lung rather than destroying it, with the vessels swept around the collection. The distinction earns its keep because the management diverges sharply: most lung abscesses drain through the bronchial tree and resolve on antibiotics, whereas passing a drain through aerated lung into an abscess risks a bronchopleural fistula and turns a treatable pneumonia into an empyema. Percutaneous drainage of an abscess is reserved for failure of medical treatment, and preferably where the cavity abuts the pleura without intervening lung.

quiz.prompt: On a frontal chest radiograph the average diameter of the collapsed lung is 8 cm and the average diameter of the hemithorax is 10 cm. Using Light's index, in which pneumothorax size as a percentage of the hemithorax is (1 minus lung diameter cubed divided by hemithorax diameter cubed) times 100, what is the size of the pneumothorax? Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 8 cubed is 512 and 10 cubed is 1000, so the lung occupies 51.2 per cent of the hemithorax and the pneumothorax is 48.8 per cent. The cube is why the eye is such a poor judge: a rim of air that looks like a fifth of the width is nearly half the volume, which is the reasoning behind the old rule that a 2 cm interpleural distance at the level of the hilum corresponds to roughly half the hemithorax. The rule itself has moved on. Where the 2010 British Thoracic Society guidance used that 2 cm measurement as the trigger for intervention, the 2023 BTS pleural disease guideline directs management by symptoms and by the presence of high-risk characteristics instead, after randomised evidence that conservative management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax is non-inferior to intervention with fewer adverse events. Size still belongs in your report, because it informs the discussion and the follow-up; it simply no longer decides it on its own.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated trauma patient becomes hypotensive with rising airway pressures. The registrar asks you to fit in a CT to look for a tension pneumothorax before decompressing. What is your answer, and what is the reasoning?
quiz.answer: Decline the scan and decompress at once: tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging only adds delay while obstructed venous return is what is killing him.
quiz.explain: The physiology explains the urgency. Air entering the pleural space under positive pressure with no way out raises intrapleural pressure above atmospheric, and the great veins - thin-walled and low-pressure - are compressed and kinked where they enter the mediastinum, so venous return and therefore cardiac output collapse. The patient dies of obstructed filling, not of hypoxia alone. A ventilated patient reaches that point in minutes, so a trip to the scanner is exactly the wrong direction. Needle decompression, followed by a chest drain, is the treatment, and a needle alone is temporary and often too short to reach the pleura in an adult chest. Two corollaries for the reporting radiologist. Radiographic signs - mediastinal shift away, a depressed or inverted hemidiaphragm, a splayed rib cage - are confirmation after the fact, not permission before it. And mediastinal shift on a film in a comfortable, haemodynamically stable patient is a large pneumothorax, not a tension pneumothorax.

quiz.prompt: A supine trauma film shows an abnormally lucent, deep left costophrenic sulcus with a sharply outlined left hemidiaphragm and cardiac border, but no visible pleural line. The patient is about to go to theatre for laparotomy under positive-pressure ventilation. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Treat it as a pneumothorax and drain before positive pressure
choices: Treat it as a pneumothorax and drain before positive pressure
Disregard it: a pneumothorax needs a visible pleural line
Repeat the film erect after theatre to see if it enlarges
Request a CT of the chest before allowing any anaesthesia
quiz.explain: In a supine patient pleural air rises to the anterior and basal pleural space rather than the apex, so the visceral pleural line is often projected en face and invisible. The signs are indirect: a deep, lucent lateral costophrenic sulcus, unusually crisp outlines of the hemidiaphragm, cardiac border or pericardial fat pad because air rather than lung now abuts them, and a lucent upper abdominal quadrant. Recognising them matters most in exactly this scenario, because positive-pressure ventilation forces more air across the visceral pleural defect with each breath and a small pneumothorax can tension quickly under anaesthesia. The observational data supporting watchful waiting for occult pneumothorax come from patients who are not being ventilated, so they do not apply here. CT would confirm the finding, but the finding is already actionable, and the transfer costs time the patient has better uses for.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old former boilermaker has a unilateral effusion. CT after drainage shows circumferential pleural thickening, nodularity along the mediastinal pleura, and thickening measuring 14 mm posteriorly. Calcified plaques are present on the contralateral diaphragm. What does this combination mean?
quiz.answer: Malignant pleural disease; the plaques are exposure alone
choices: Malignant pleural disease; the plaques are exposure alone
Benign asbestos pleural disease with a reactive effusion
The plaques have undergone malignant transformation here
Chronic empyema with fibrothorax and pleural calcification
quiz.explain: Four CT features carry high specificity for malignant pleural disease: circumferential pleural thickening, nodular thickening, parietal pleural thickening greater than 1 cm, and mediastinal pleural involvement. Three of them are present, and any one of them should send the patient for tissue. They are specific but not sensitive, so their absence does not reassure - a malignant effusion may show no pleural abnormality at all on CT. Note what the imaging cannot do: mesothelioma and metastatic pleural disease share these appearances, and histology decides. Ipsilateral volume loss with a contracted hemithorax that does not pull the mediastinum across, and involvement of the interlobar fissures, lean towards mesothelioma; a known primary with discrete pleural nodules leans towards metastasis. Pleural plaques are markers of asbestos exposure and do not themselves become malignant; they raise your suspicion only because they prove the exposure that mesothelioma shares. Report the extent - chest wall, diaphragm, pericardium - since that is what drives staging.

quiz.prompt: A retired dockworker is breathless with a restrictive spirometry pattern. CT shows a continuous sheet of pleural thickening on the left, 6 mm thick, extending over 10 cm craniocaudally and involving the costophrenic angle. There are discrete calcified plaques on the right. Which finding explains his physiology, and how do you tell the two apart?
quiz.answer: The continuous left-sided sheet is diffuse pleural thickening, which restricts the lung; it is continuous, involves the costophrenic angle and exceeds the conventional 5 cm width, 8 cm craniocaudal and 3 mm thickness, whereas discrete plaques spare the costophrenic angle and do not restrict.
quiz.explain: Plaques are discrete, well-circumscribed islands of parietal pleural collagen, typically posterolateral over the mid and lower ribs and on the diaphragmatic domes, often calcified, and characteristically sparing the costophrenic angles and the apices. They are a marker of exposure and, on their own, cause no symptoms and no measurable restriction. Diffuse pleural thickening is a different entity: a continuous sheet, conventionally at least 5 cm wide, 8 cm in craniocaudal extent and 3 mm thick, that involves the costophrenic angle and frequently follows a benign asbestos-related pleural effusion. It tethers the lung, so it does restrict, and in many jurisdictions it is compensable where plaques are not - which is a reason to be precise in the report rather than writing pleural thickening and leaving it there. One caution: diffuse thickening and early mesothelioma overlap, so nodularity, mediastinal involvement or progression on interval CT should prompt PET-CT and biopsy rather than reassurance.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the steps of inserting a large-bore surgical chest drain by blunt dissection in a spontaneously breathing patient, from first to last.
quiz.answer: ultrasound-marking local-anaesthetic blunt-dissection tube-insertion underwater-seal check-radiograph
quiz.explain: Each step guards against a specific disaster. Ultrasound marking must happen immediately before the procedure and with the patient in the position they will stay in - a mark made on a ward round and used an hour later after the patient has been sat up is a well-documented route to a drain in the liver or spleen. The site itself should sit within the safe triangle, bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line at the level of the nipple, and the tract should pass over the top of the rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle in the subcostal groove. Local anaesthetic goes down to the pleura, and drawing back fluid or air with it confirms you are aimed at the right space. Blunt dissection with forceps, then a finger sweep, replaces the trocar that used to spear organs. The tube goes to an underwater seal so that air can leave and cannot return, and only then does the check radiograph confirm position and re-expansion.

quiz.prompt: A drain placed for a pneumothorax has stopped bubbling, the pneumothorax persists, and the patient has developed extensive surgical emphysema. The film shows the tube tip in the upper hemithorax, and the radiopaque line along the tube is interrupted 2 cm outside the skin surface. What does that tell you?
quiz.answer: A side hole lies outside the pleura; the drain must be replaced
choices: A side hole lies outside the pleura; the drain must be replaced
The drain is kinked in the soft tissues and should be flushed
The drain sits within a fissure, which explains poor drainage
The lung is stuck against the tip, so suction should be raised
quiz.explain: The interruption in the radiopaque stripe marks the most proximal side hole, sometimes called the sentinel eye, and every side hole must lie inside the pleural space. An interruption seen outside the chest wall means air is being vented straight into the subcutaneous tissues, which is precisely the picture here: bubbling stops because the drain is no longer connected to the pleural space, the pneumothorax persists, and surgical emphysema spreads. The fix is a new drain through a fresh site, because advancing a tube that has already been in situ pushes a contaminated length inwards and invites empyema. Worth knowing about the alternatives: a drain in a fissure is a common finding and usually works acceptably, so it is not by itself a reason to replace; a kinked drain would not usually produce this stripe appearance; and raising suction on a malpositioned drain simply pumps more air into the chest wall. The other placements that must be corrected are intraparenchymal and intra-abdominal.

quiz.prompt: You are supervising drainage of a 3-litre malignant effusion that has been present for six weeks. The team plans to run it all off in one sitting. What limit do you set and why, and what symptom should stop them earlier?
quiz.answer: Drain no more than about 1.5 litres at a sitting and then clamp for a few hours, because rapid re-expansion of chronically collapsed lung risks re-expansion pulmonary oedema; chest tightness or persistent coughing should stop the drainage immediately.
quiz.explain: Lung that has been compressed for weeks has lost surfactant and has a leaky, remodelled microvasculature, and pulling it open quickly against a large negative intrapleural pressure floods the interstitium. Re-expansion pulmonary oedema is uncommon but can be severe and occasionally fatal, and the two risk factors that recur are a large volume removed rapidly and a long-standing collapse. Hence the convention of stopping at roughly 1.5 litres and clamping for several hours before continuing, and hence the instruction to stop for chest tightness or a persistent cough, which are the symptoms of the pleural pressure falling too far - manometry, where available, makes the same point numerically. Two further habits: never apply suction to a large chronic effusion at the outset, and expect a proportion of malignant effusions to be trapped lung, where the visceral pleura is encased and cannot re-expand at all. Recognising trapped lung on the post-drainage film matters, because pleurodesis will fail and an indwelling pleural catheter is the better answer.

nodes.title: Pneumonia, Tuberculosis and CO-RADS
nodes.goal: Read the pattern and distribution of a chest infection, place a COVID-19 CT on the CO-RADS scale, and separate active tuberculosis and the opportunistic infections of the immunocompromised from their mimics.

quiz.prompt: An unenhanced chest CT in a patient with four days of fever and cough shows multifocal bilateral ground-glass opacities of rounded shape in a peripheral and subpleural distribution, with areas of crazy paving, no effusion and no lymphadenopathy. No swab result is available. Give the CO-RADS category. Answer as a single whole number from 0 to 6.
quiz.explain: CO-RADS 5 is the very high level of suspicion and is reserved for the typical picture: bilateral, multifocal ground-glass, often rounded, peripheral and posterior in distribution, with crazy paving, subpleural bands, or an organising pneumonia pattern including the reversed halo. CO-RADS 4 covers findings that are suspicious but carry more overlap, such as unilateral or peribronchovascular disease, or ground-glass superimposed on severe pre-existing lung disease where the pattern cannot be read cleanly. CO-RADS 3 is genuinely equivocal, CO-RADS 2 fits another infection better, CO-RADS 1 is normal or clearly non-infectious, and CO-RADS 0 means the scan is technically uninterpretable. Note that CO-RADS 6 is not a radiological judgement at all: it is reserved for a patient with a positive RT-PCR, so a scan you would have called 5 becomes 6 the moment the swab returns.

quiz.prompt: A patient scanned for the same clinical question has centrilobular nodules with tree-in-bud opacities in the right lower lobe, a lobar consolidation containing air bronchograms, and a small parapneumonic effusion. Give the CO-RADS category. Answer as a single whole number from 0 to 6.
quiz.explain: CO-RADS 2 is the low-suspicion band, used when the findings are typical of an infection other than COVID-19. Tree-in-bud and centrilobular nodules are the signature of material filling terminal bronchioles, which is bacterial bronchopneumonia, aspiration or endobronchial tuberculosis, and they are conspicuously absent from the COVID-19 picture. Lobar consolidation with a parapneumonic effusion points the same way. In practice, effusion, lymphadenopathy, cavitation and tree-in-bud are the four findings that should push the category down rather than up. Two things are worth remembering about the scale. It grades suspicion of COVID-19, not severity, so a CO-RADS 2 patient may well be the sicker of the two. And it was designed for unenhanced CT in patients with moderate to severe symptoms, not as a screening tool for the asymptomatic.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these stages of tuberculous infection in the order they occur in one patient over a lifetime, from the first parenchymal lesion to disease reappearing years later.
quiz.answer: ghon-focus hilar-lymphadenopathy ranke-complex apical-reactivation
quiz.explain: Inhaled bacilli lodge in a well-ventilated part of the lung, typically the middle or lower zone, and produce the parenchymal Ghon focus. Lymphatic drainage carries them to the ipsilateral hilar and mediastinal nodes, and in children those nodes dominate the picture; on CT they characteristically show low-attenuation centres with rim enhancement, reflecting caseation. Healing calcifies both, and a calcified parenchymal focus with its calcified draining node is the Ranke complex, one of the commonest incidental findings on adult chest imaging. Reactivation, when it comes, favours the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes, where oxygen tension is highest and lymphatic clearance poorest, and it cavitates. Cavitation is the moment the patient becomes infectious, which is why the distribution of disease on a CT carries an immediate infection-control consequence.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these pulmonary infections in the order they typically appear after solid-organ transplantation, from the first post-operative days through to beyond six months.
quiz.answer: aspiration-pneumonia cytomegalovirus-pneumonia community-acquired-pneumonia
quiz.explain: The first month after transplantation belongs to the operation rather than to the immunosuppression, which has not yet had time to take full effect: aspiration around intubation, nosocomial bacterial pneumonia, fluid overload and surgical complications dominate. From roughly one to six months the pharmacological effect is at its deepest and the opportunists arrive, cytomegalovirus above all, with Pneumocystis, Aspergillus and Nocardia sharing the same window. Beyond six months, most patients on maintenance doses resemble the general community again and acquire the community's pathogens, with continued opportunistic risk confined to those needing heavy immunosuppression for rejection. Knowing where in this timeline a patient sits narrows a non-specific chest CT more reliably than any single sign on the images, and it is the first question to ask before describing ground-glass in a transplant recipient.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient in intensive care develops a new fever and her chest CT shows new consolidation. Say where you expect aspirated material to have settled in this patient, and why.
quiz.answer: Because she has been lying supine, aspirated material settles in the segments that are dependent in that position: the posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes, more often on the right because the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.
quiz.explain: Aspiration obeys gravity, so its distribution tells you the posture at the time it happened. Supine, as almost every ventilated patient is, the dependent segments are the posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes. Upright or seated, it is the basal segments of the lower lobes. Lying on one side, it is that side. The right lung is favoured throughout because the right main bronchus leaves the trachea at a shallower angle and has the wider lumen. Recognising the pattern changes the report from a generic hospital-acquired pneumonia to aspiration, and with it the antibiotic choice, the question of a swallow assessment, and the review of sedation, feeding and head-up positioning. Chemical pneumonitis from acid appears within hours and may clear within days; bacterial superinfection follows later and consolidates.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old from a high-incidence country has apical fibronodular change on CT and the registrar has reported it as old healed tuberculosis. Say which findings would make you call the disease active instead, and what you would do about it.
quiz.answer: Cavitation, clustered centrilobular tree-in-bud nodules and new or ill-defined consolidation all indicate activity; if any are present, isolate the patient and send sputum for smear, culture and nucleic acid amplification rather than reporting the scan as inactive disease.
quiz.explain: Imaging cannot prove inactivity, which is a microbiological verdict, but it can make activity very likely. Cavitation and tree-in-bud opacities are the two most useful signs: tree-in-bud represents bacilli-laden secretions filling terminal bronchioles, and tree-in-bud in a lobe remote from the cavity is bronchogenic spread, meaning the patient is coughing organisms into the room. Ill-defined consolidation, new nodules and an enlarging pleural effusion count too. Against that, upper-zone fibronodular opacity with volume loss, traction bronchiectasis and calcified granulomas favours old disease. But a report that calls such a scan inactive has overreached; the safer wording describes the findings, states that activity cannot be excluded on imaging alone, and asks for sputum. Getting this wrong puts an infectious patient onto an open ward, which is the sort of error that is discovered weeks later.

quiz.prompt: A 54-year-old smoker with fever has a rounded, well-defined 4 cm opacity in the right lower lobe that behaves clinically like a round pneumonia. Say what your report should ask for and why.
quiz.answer: Treat as pneumonia, but ask explicitly for repeat imaging in about six to eight weeks to document complete resolution, because in an adult a rounded opacity may be a malignancy and must be followed until it has cleared.
quiz.explain: Round pneumonia is largely a paediatric phenomenon, most often pneumococcal, in children under about eight years, in whom the collateral pathways of Kohn and Lambert are not yet developed and infection stays spherical rather than spreading through a segment. In an adult the same shape carries a real chance of being a carcinoma, an organising pneumonia, or a lymphoma, and the cheapest way to separate them is to show that it disappears. Six to eight weeks after treatment is the conventional interval: early enough to act on, late enough for a genuine pneumonia to have cleared. If it has not resolved, the next step is a contrast CT with bronchoscopy or percutaneous biopsy, not another course of antibiotics. Writing the interval and the reason into the report is what makes it happen; a recommendation to correlate clinically usually does not.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient has patchy multifocal peribronchial nodular consolidation in both lower lobes, without air bronchograms and without confinement by any fissure. What does this pattern tell the team about the disease they are treating?
quiz.answer: Bronchiolar spread, so expect a patchy, slower resolution
choices: Bronchiolar spread, so expect a patchy, slower resolution
Alveolar spread from one focus, confined by the fissures
Interstitial spread, with reticulation and septal thickening
Lymphatic spread along the bronchovascular bundles
quiz.explain: The three classical patterns each describe a route through the lung. Lobar pneumonia begins peripherally in one lobe and spreads through alveoli and the pores of Kohn until a fissure stops it, giving homogeneous non-segmental consolidation with air bronchograms because the airways remain patent; pneumococcus is the model. Bronchopneumonia begins in the bronchioles and spreads centrifugally into the surrounding lobules, giving patchy, often bilateral nodular consolidation without air bronchograms because the airways themselves are full of exudate. Staphylococci, Haemophilus, Pseudomonas and anaerobes behave this way, resolution is slower, and cavitation and scarring are commoner. Interstitial pneumonia, the viral, Mycoplasma and Pneumocystis pattern, gives reticulation, ground-glass and bronchial wall thickening, classically with a patient who sounds worse than the film looks.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old smoker with weight loss but no fever has a 5 cm right upper lobe cavity with a thick, irregular, nodular inner wall and no surrounding consolidation. What is the most appropriate next step?
quiz.answer: Contrast CT and bronchoscopy or biopsy for tissue
choices: Contrast CT and bronchoscopy or biopsy for tissue
A course of antibiotics with a repeat film in a month
Sputum for acid-fast bacilli and a period of isolation
Antifungal therapy for a suspected aspergilloma
quiz.explain: The wall does most of the diagnostic work. A cavity whose wall exceeds roughly 15 mm with an irregular, nodular inner margin, in a smoker with weight loss and without fever, is a squamous cell carcinoma until proved otherwise, and the priority is tissue. A thin, smooth wall favours an infected bulla, a healed abscess or a bleb. An acute pyogenic abscess is thick-walled too, but the patient is febrile, there is surrounding consolidation, and an air-fluid level sits dependently. Tuberculosis cavitates in the apical and posterior upper lobe segments with surrounding tree-in-bud, and sputum should indeed be sent in parallel here, since the two can coexist; what does harm is sending sputum and then waiting. An aspergilloma is a mobile fungus ball lying within a pre-existing cavity, not a nodular wall.

quiz.prompt: A 6-year-old recently arrived from a high-incidence country has right middle lobe consolidation and a bulky right hilar node whose centre is low in attenuation with an enhancing rim. What does this combination indicate?
quiz.answer: Primary tuberculosis, with necrotic nodal disease
choices: Primary tuberculosis, with necrotic nodal disease
Reactivation tuberculosis with endobronchial spread
Bacterial lobar pneumonia with reactive adenopathy
Lymphoma with post-obstructive consolidation
quiz.explain: In primary tuberculosis the nodes are the disease, particularly in children, and a low-attenuation centre with rim enhancement reflects caseous necrosis. That appearance is close to specific in the right clinical setting, shared mainly with non-tuberculous mycobacteria and some fungal infections. Reactive nodes accompanying a bacterial pneumonia are smaller and enhance homogeneously. Consolidation in primary disease has no zonal preference and often sits in the middle or lower lobes, unlike reactivation, which favours the apical and posterior upper lobe segments and cavitates. Lymphoma produces bulky, usually bilateral mediastinal masses without central necrosis before treatment. Two other faces of primary disease are worth holding on to: a pleural effusion, which is common in adolescents and young adults, and lobar collapse from a node compressing a bronchus.

quiz.prompt: A patient on long-term corticosteroids has three weeks of fever, and CT shows innumerable sharply defined 2 mm nodules of uniform size distributed evenly through both lungs, involving the subpleural surfaces and the fissures. What distribution should be reported, and what does it imply?
quiz.answer: Random: haematogenous seeding, so treat as miliary disease
choices: Random: haematogenous seeding, so treat as miliary disease
Centrilobular: airway spread, so seek an endobronchial source
Perilymphatic: sarcoidosis or lymphangitic spread of tumour
Upper-zone predominant: an inhaled organic dust exposure
quiz.explain: Distribution is the first question in any nodular pattern, and the secondary pulmonary lobule is the reference frame. Random nodules involve the subpleural surfaces and the fissures and ignore lobular architecture, which is what arrival through the bloodstream looks like: miliary tuberculosis, miliary fungal disease, or haematogenous metastases. Uniform size with weeks of fever in an immunosuppressed patient should prompt a telephone call before the report is typed, because untreated miliary tuberculosis is rapidly fatal and the workup, sputum, blood cultures and often bone marrow or liver biopsy, needs to start today. Centrilobular nodules spare the pleural surface and, with tree-in-bud, indicate airway spread. Perilymphatic nodules follow the fissures, the subpleural line and the bronchovascular bundles in a beaded fashion, which is sarcoidosis, silicosis or lymphangitis carcinomatosa.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 80 has a month of exertional breathlessness with a near-normal chest radiograph. CT shows symmetrical perihilar ground-glass sparing the immediate subpleural lung, a few thin-walled cysts, and no effusion or adenopathy. Which treatment should be started while confirmation is sought?
quiz.answer: Co-trimoxazole, with steroids added if hypoxaemic
choices: Co-trimoxazole, with steroids added if hypoxaemic
Intravenous ganciclovir for cytomegalovirus
Quadruple antituberculous therapy and isolation
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia
quiz.explain: This is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: onset over weeks, marked hypoxaemia with a chest film that looks better than the patient, and a CT showing perihilar or diffuse ground-glass that is often geographical and often spares the immediate subpleural lung. Thin-walled cysts or pneumatoceles appear in roughly a third and carry a genuine risk of pneumothorax, which is worth flagging before any positive-pressure ventilation. Pleural effusion and lymphadenopathy argue against the diagnosis. Treatment is co-trimoxazole with adjunctive corticosteroids where the arterial oxygen is low, and it is begun on suspicion because induced sputum or lavage takes time the patient may not have. Cytomegalovirus pneumonitis occurs at similarly low CD4 counts but adds nodules and consolidation; tuberculosis at this CD4 count often looks atypical, with adenopathy and lower-zone disease rather than upper-zone cavitation.

quiz.prompt: Twelve days into neutropenia following induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia, a patient has fever unresponsive to broad antibacterial cover, and CT shows three peripheral nodules each surrounded by a rim of ground-glass. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Start antifungal therapy for angioinvasive aspergillosis
choices: Start antifungal therapy for angioinvasive aspergillosis
Wait for a repeat CT in a week before treating anything
Start antituberculous therapy and isolate the patient
Escalate the antibacterial cover and repeat blood cultures
quiz.explain: The halo sign, a nodule or wedge of consolidation surrounded by ground-glass, is haemorrhage around an infarct caused by fungus invading a pulmonary artery branch, and in a profoundly neutropenic haematology patient it is invasive aspergillosis until proved otherwise. It appears early in the life of the lesion and fades within about a week, and treatment started while the halo is still visible does measurably better than treatment started later, so this is a finding to telephone rather than to report. Serum galactomannan and bronchoalveolar lavage support the diagnosis but should not delay the drug. As neutrophils recover, at roughly two to three weeks, the infarcted centre retracts and air dissects around it to give the air-crescent sign, which marks recovery rather than deterioration though it also signals a risk of haemoptysis. The halo is not unique to aspergillus: mucormycosis, other angioinvasive moulds, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and haemorrhagic metastases all produce it.

quiz.prompt: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes recovering from ketoacidosis has necrotic nasal turbinates on examination, and chest CT shows a large area of ground-glass surrounded by a complete thick ring of consolidation. What does this combination most urgently raise?
quiz.answer: Mucormycosis, needing urgent antifungals and surgery
choices: Mucormycosis, needing urgent antifungals and surgery
Organising pneumonia, needing a course of corticosteroids
Pulmonary tuberculosis, needing four-drug treatment
Pulmonary infarction from a segmental embolus
quiz.explain: The reversed halo, a central ground-glass core ringed by consolidation, was first described in cryptogenic organising pneumonia and remains commonest there, and it also belongs to the organising pneumonia phase of COVID-19, where it supports a CO-RADS 5. But context outranks the sign. In a diabetic patient emerging from ketoacidosis with necrotic sinonasal tissue, a reversed halo with a thick, nodular rim is invasive mucormycosis, which crosses tissue planes over hours to days and needs liposomal amphotericin and surgical debridement. Treating that as organising pneumonia with corticosteroids would accelerate it, which is what makes this differential worth knowing rather than merely interesting. Tuberculosis and sarcoidosis can also produce a reversed halo, in which case the ring tends to be composed of small nodules rather than solid consolidation.

nodes.title: Pulmonary Embolism and Pulmonary Hypertension
nodes.goal: Acquire and read a CTPA, tell true embolus from artefact, grade right heart strain, and set what you find against the pretest probability the clinician started with.

quiz.prompt: A CTPA on a breathless 34-year-old shows dense contrast in the superior vena cava, poor opacification of the main and lobar pulmonary arteries at about 90 HU, and low-attenuation unopacified blood filling the inferior vena cava and right atrium. The patient took a deep breath in on command. What has happened and what do you do?
quiz.answer: Transient interruption of contrast; repeat with quiet breathing
choices: Transient interruption of contrast; repeat with quiet breathing
Extensive central embolus; report a saddle pulmonary embolism
Bolus timed too late; repeat with a longer scan delay set
Poor cardiac output; repeat with a slower injection rate
quiz.explain: A deep inspiration drops intrathoracic pressure and draws a slug of unopacified blood up the inferior vena cava into the right atrium, where it dilutes the contrast arriving from the arm. The signature is a well-opacified superior vena cava alongside a poorly opacified pulmonary trunk, with unopacified blood visible in the inferior vena cava and right atrium. This is an artefact of the breathing instruction, not of the timing or the injection, which is why lengthening the delay makes matters worse by letting the interruption reach the lungs, and why the remedy is a shallow breath or quiet breathing with bolus tracking in the pulmonary trunk. It matters because the mixing interface throws up pseudo-defects that get reported as emboli, and because a genuinely occlusive central clot would show intraluminal filling defects rather than uniformly dilute opacification. As a working rule, a pulmonary trunk far below about 200 HU should be called technically inadequate rather than negative.

quiz.prompt: In a lower lobe a rounded soft-tissue-attenuation structure sits beside a segmental artery on one axial image and appears to occupy its lumen. On the adjacent images the structure is separate from the vessel and lies alongside a bronchus, and the artery opacifies normally above and below. How should this be reported?
quiz.answer: Not an embolus: a perivascular structure mimicking a defect
choices: Not an embolus: a perivascular structure mimicking a defect
A segmental embolus; start therapeutic anticoagulation now
An indeterminate defect; repeat the CTPA in twenty-four hours
A chronic web; refer for assessment for endarterectomy
quiz.explain: Three questions separate a clot from an impostor. Does the defect persist across consecutive images, or does it come and go with one slice? Is it intraluminal - surrounded by contrast in cross-section, the polo-mint appearance, or tracked as a longitudinal filling defect with contrast either side? And does the artery it sits in look right above and below? Here the answers are no, no and yes, so it is not an embolus. The commonest mimics are exactly this: a small lymph node or a mucus-filled or fluid-filled bronchus lying against the artery, given away by the fact that every pulmonary artery travels with a companion bronchus, so finding the bronchus identifies the intruder. Others include partial volume at a branch point, respiratory motion blurring a vessel, and flow-related mixing where poorly opacified blood streams into dependent lower lobe arteries. Reporting an equivocal subsegmental defect as definite embolus commits a patient to months of anticoagulation, so say what you actually saw.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old woman is assessed for possible pulmonary embolism. Her Wells score is 3, placing her in the 'PE unlikely' group on the two-level scale, and your department uses an age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off of age multiplied by ten, in micrograms per litre of fibrinogen-equivalent units. What cut-off applies to her? Answer in micrograms per litre, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: 78 x 10 = 780 micrograms per litre. The adjustment applies only above the age of 50; below that the conventional 500 threshold stands. Its justification is that D-dimer rises with age, so a fixed threshold is exceeded by nearly every elderly patient and the test stops discriminating; raising the bar with age substantially improves specificity, with the ADJUST-PE study showing no meaningful loss of sensitivity. Two conditions have to hold before you use it. The patient must already have been placed in a low or 'unlikely' pretest probability group by a formal rule - the adjustment rescues specificity, not a misapplied test. And the units must match the assay, because D-dimer units and fibrinogen-equivalent units differ by roughly a factor of two, and a laboratory reporting in the other convention needs a correspondingly different threshold. Applying an age-adjusted cut-off to a 'PE likely' patient is the error the rule cannot fix, because a negative result there still leaves too much probability behind.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old with pleuritic pain has no clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis and no haemoptysis, and you judge an alternative diagnosis more likely than pulmonary embolism. Her D-dimer is 780 micrograms per litre of fibrinogen-equivalent units. Applying the YEARS algorithm, what follows?
quiz.answer: No YEARS items, so the threshold is 1000: no imaging needed
choices: No YEARS items, so the threshold is 1000: no imaging needed
One YEARS item, so the threshold is 500: proceed to CTPA
No YEARS items, but 780 exceeds 500: proceed to CTPA now
YEARS is not valid outside pregnancy: proceed to CTPA now
quiz.explain: YEARS has three clinical items - clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis, haemoptysis, and pulmonary embolism as the most likely diagnosis - and a single D-dimer whose threshold depends on how many are present. None present raises the cut-off to 1000; one or more keeps it at 500. With no items and a D-dimer of 780 the diagnosis is excluded without imaging, which is the whole purpose of the algorithm: it cut CTPA use by around a seventh in the original study while leaving a very low three-month failure rate. It is not a pregnancy-only tool; the pregnancy-adapted version is a separate validated pathway that adds compression ultrasound of the leg when there are symptoms of deep vein thrombosis. The one rule that must not be broken is mixing pathways within a single patient - a Wells score used to select a threshold from YEARS, or vice versa, has no validation behind it and the failure rates simply do not transfer.

quiz.prompt: On axial CTPA images the maximal right ventricular short-axis internal diameter is 47 mm and the left ventricular short-axis internal diameter at the same level is 38 mm. Calculate the right-to-left ventricular diameter ratio. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: 47 / 38 = 1.24. A ratio of 1.0 or above marks right ventricular dilatation, and the 2019 European Society of Cardiology acute pulmonary embolism guideline accepts it as CT evidence of right ventricular dysfunction. It is a prognostic marker, not by itself a treatment trigger. In a normotensive patient, a raised ratio together with a raised troponin defines intermediate-high risk, which means a monitored bed and reperfusion held in reserve rather than given immediately; haemodynamic instability is what mandates immediate reperfusion, and that is a clinical, not a radiological, judgement. Two practical points: the measurement is more reproducible on a reformatted four-chamber plane than on axial images, which overestimate when the heart is rotated, and it should be made from inner wall to inner wall. Look also for the supporting signs - leftward bowing of the interventricular septum, reflux of contrast into the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins, and a dilated pulmonary trunk - and state them, because they are what the receiving team stratifies on.

quiz.prompt: Two normotensive patients on the same list have pulmonary embolism. The first has a saddle embolus with a right-to-left ventricular ratio of 0.8 and a normal troponin. The second has segmental clot only, a ratio of 1.3, septal bowing and a raised troponin. Which report should carry more urgency, and why?
quiz.answer: The second: risk in acute pulmonary embolism follows right ventricular function rather than clot bulk, so a ratio above 1 with septal bowing and a positive troponin puts that patient at intermediate-high risk, while a saddle embolus with a normal right ventricle is not itself high risk.
quiz.explain: Clot burden scores such as Qanadli and Mastora correlate only weakly with outcome once right ventricular function is accounted for, and the reason is physiological rather than statistical: what kills in acute pulmonary embolism is a right ventricle that cannot generate the pressure the obstructed vascular bed now demands. A young patient with a healthy right ventricle can accommodate a saddle embolus and look remarkably well, while a patient with limited cardiopulmonary reserve can decompensate on a segmental clot. That asymmetry has a practical consequence for the report: describe the distribution because it matters for the interventional options, but always state the ratio, the septal position and any caval contrast reflux, because those are what feed the risk stratification and determine where the patient is nursed. It also explains why the phrase 'massive pulmonary embolism' has been retired in favour of high-risk - the adjective described the clot when the point was the circulation.

quiz.prompt: A 28-year-old at 30 weeks' gestation has pleuritic pain and a normal chest radiograph. She is anxious about radiation reaching the baby. Which pathway best fits, and how do you frame the dose conversation?
quiz.answer: Perfusion imaging first; fetal dose is tiny, breast dose lower
choices: Perfusion imaging first; fetal dose is tiny, breast dose lower
CTPA first; fetal dose is tiny and breast dose is lower too
No imaging; treat empirically to avoid radiation exposure
MR pulmonary angiography; it avoids ionising radiation here
quiz.explain: With a normal chest radiograph, a perfusion or ventilation-perfusion study is a reasonable first test in pregnancy and is the one many guidelines favour, because the discriminator is not fetal dose but maternal breast dose: CTPA delivers tens of milligray to breast tissue that is proliferating and radiosensitive in pregnancy, while a perfusion study delivers a small fraction of a milligray there. Fetal dose from both sits in the fraction-of-a-milligray range, orders of magnitude below the roughly 100 mGy at which deterministic fetal effects are considered, so the honest sentence to the patient is that neither test poses a measurable risk to her baby and the choice is being made largely on her own breast dose and on which test is likelier to answer the question. Where the radiograph is abnormal, a perfusion study will often be uninterpretable and CTPA is preferred. Note also that CTPA is technically harder in pregnancy - the hyperdynamic circulation dilutes the bolus and transient interruption of contrast is commoner - so raise the flow rate, track in the pulmonary trunk and ask for a shallow breath-hold. MR angiography is not validated to exclude pulmonary embolism.

quiz.prompt: A CTPA in a large patient scanned at 120 kV has a pulmonary trunk attenuation of 160 HU with marked image noise, and there are indistinct low-attenuation areas in several segmental arteries. Which single change is most likely to make the repeat diagnostic?
quiz.answer: Lower the tube voltage and reconstruct iteratively
choices: Lower the tube voltage and reconstruct iteratively
Raise the tube voltage and lengthen the scan delay
Halve the injection rate and double the contrast volume
Widen the collimation and thicken the reconstructed slices
quiz.explain: Iodine attenuates far more strongly at lower photon energies, because the mean beam energy moves towards iodine's K-edge at about 33 keV, so dropping from 120 kV to 80 or 90 kV raises vessel attenuation substantially for the same iodine delivered. The price is noise, and that is exactly what iterative or deep-learning reconstruction, or a compensating rise in tube current, is for. Raising the tube voltage does the opposite and flattens the contrast you are trying to see. A longer delay does not concentrate a bolus that is simply too dilute, and halving the injection rate reduces the rate of iodine delivery, which is the quantity that governs peak arterial attenuation - volume without flow does not fix opacification. Thicker slices reduce noise but blur the subsegmental arteries the study exists to show, trading one non-diagnostic result for another. When the repeat is still inadequate, say so: 'no embolus demonstrated on a technically limited study' is a different report from 'no embolus'.

quiz.prompt: On CT the main pulmonary artery measures 34 mm at the level of its bifurcation and the ascending aorta measures 31 mm at the same level. Calculate the pulmonary artery to ascending aorta diameter ratio. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: 34 / 31 = 1.10. A ratio above 1 raises suspicion of pulmonary hypertension and is more specific in patients under about 50, in whom the aorta has not yet dilated with age; the corresponding absolute threshold is a main pulmonary artery of 29 mm or more, measured at the bifurcation perpendicular to the vessel's long axis. Both are supportive rather than diagnostic - sensitivity is only moderate, and a normal-calibre artery does not exclude the disease - because CT measures calibre, not pressure. The diagnosis belongs to right heart catheterisation, and under the 2022 ESC/ERS definition pulmonary hypertension is a mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg at rest, lowered from the previous 25 mmHg, with pre-capillary disease additionally requiring a wedge pressure of 15 mmHg or less and pulmonary vascular resistance above 2 Wood units. What CT genuinely contributes is the cause: mosaic perfusion with webs pointing to chronic thromboembolic disease, fibrosis or emphysema to lung disease, a dilated left atrium to left heart disease.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old remains breathless two years after a large pulmonary embolism. Echocardiography estimates a raised pulmonary artery systolic pressure. A CTPA has already been reported as showing no acute embolus. What is the right next test?
quiz.answer: A ventilation-perfusion scan, which is the sensitive screen
choices: A ventilation-perfusion scan, which is the sensitive screen
A repeat CTPA with a dedicated late arterial phase acquired
Right heart catheterisation before any further lung imaging
Cardiac MRI to quantify right ventricular volumes and mass
quiz.explain: Ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy remains the screening test for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension because a normal perfusion scan effectively excludes it, and its sensitivity exceeds that of CTPA, which is read for acute clot and readily passes over webs, bands, eccentric wall-adherent thrombus and subtle abrupt narrowing. The defects of chronic thromboembolic disease are typically large, wedge-shaped and mismatched, in contrast with the patchy, non-segmental defects of other pulmonary hypertension groups. Catheterisation is needed eventually to confirm pre-capillary haemodynamics, but it comes after the perfusion question is settled rather than instead of it. Once the diagnosis is suspected, the road map for the surgeon comes from a dedicated CT pulmonary angiogram or digital subtraction pulmonary angiography, which decides whether disease is proximal enough for pulmonary endarterectomy - potentially curative - or whether balloon pulmonary angioplasty and medical therapy are the route. Missing this diagnosis condemns a treatable patient to progressive right heart failure.

quiz.prompt: A CTPA shows a crescent of soft tissue lying against the wall of the right lower lobe artery and making obtuse angles with it; the vessel is narrower than its neighbours rather than expanded, and the lung shows mosaic attenuation with reduced vessel calibre within the darker regions. What do you conclude, and what should the report ask for?
quiz.answer: This is chronic rather than acute thromboembolic disease, given eccentric wall-adherent thrombus with obtuse angles, a narrowed rather than expanded vessel and mosaic perfusion, so the report should raise chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and request a ventilation-perfusion scan and referral to a pulmonary hypertension centre.
quiz.explain: Acute clot sits centrally in the lumen with contrast around it, makes acute angles with the wall, and distends the artery. Chronic material is organised and incorporated into the wall, so it is eccentric and crescentic, makes obtuse angles, and leaves the vessel narrowed or abruptly cut off rather than expanded; look also for intraluminal webs and bands, mural calcification, post-stenotic dilatation and hypertrophied tortuous bronchial arteries. The lung supplies the corroboration: mosaic attenuation in which the darker regions contain smaller, sparser vessels is perfusion mosaic and points to vascular obstruction, whereas mosaic from small airways disease shows unchanged vessel calibre and accentuates on expiratory imaging. Getting this right is the difference between anticoagulating a patient indefinitely and referring them for pulmonary endarterectomy, which can be curative. Note also that a proportion of patients with chronic thromboembolic disease have no history of acute embolism at all.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old with active cancer, unilateral leg swelling and tachycardia has a Wells score of 7. The junior doctor sends a D-dimer, which returns at 380 micrograms per litre of fibrinogen-equivalent units, and proposes discharge. What is wrong with that reasoning?
quiz.answer: With a high pretest probability a negative D-dimer cannot lower the posterior probability enough to exclude pulmonary embolism, because the test is only validated in the low-risk or 'unlikely' groups, so she needs a CTPA whatever the result.
quiz.explain: This is Bayes at the workstation. A test result moves a probability by its likelihood ratio; it does not set one. D-dimer earns its place through high sensitivity and therefore a very low negative likelihood ratio, which turns a small prior into a negligible posterior - but with a Wells score of 7 the prior sits somewhere around a half, and the same negative result still leaves a posterior in the region of five to fifteen per cent, far above the roughly two per cent failure rate accepted for sending someone home untreated. The same logic sets the boundary for the PERC rule: eight negative criteria are only meaningful when the clinician's gestalt probability is already below about fifteen per cent, because PERC lowers a small probability below the testing threshold rather than making a large one disappear. And when the prior is high and the CTPA is negative, the right reflex is to look at the leg veins and to reconsider the alternatives, not simply to reassure.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the stages of a bolus-tracked CTPA acquisition in the order they occur, from first to last.
quiz.answer: scout-topogram monitoring-slice contrast-injection threshold-trigger helical-acquisition
quiz.explain: The scout defines the coverage - lung apices to below the costophrenic angles - and lets you set the range before any contrast is committed. The monitoring image is then acquired and the region of interest placed within the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta, because it is pulmonary arterial opacification the study depends on. Injection follows, typically 4 to 5 mL per second of high-concentration contrast with a saline chaser that pushes the tail of the bolus out of the arm veins and reduces the dense streak artefact from the superior vena cava that ruins the right upper lobe arteries. Low-dose monitoring images then repeat until attenuation in the trunk crosses the trigger threshold, and the helical acquisition begins after the shortest diagnostic delay the scanner allows. Two refinements worth carrying: scanning caudocranially gets the lower lobes, where most emboli land, before respiratory motion sets in, and a lower tube voltage raises iodine attenuation so that contrast volume can come down.

nodes.title: Staging Lung Cancer on Imaging
nodes.goal: Assign T, N and M from the images, place a node in its IASLC station, and identify the findings that change the treatment plan.

quiz.prompt: A 3 cm right upper lobe adenocarcinoma is accompanied by a single FDG-avid node of 12 mm short axis in the left lower paratracheal region, with no other abnormality on PET-CT. The team asks whether lobectomy should still go ahead.
choices: It is N3, so sample it before abandoning surgery
It is N2, so proceed to mediastinoscopy
It is N1, so proceed to lobectomy as planned
It is M1a, so treat as metastatic disease
quiz.answer: It is N3, so sample it before abandoning surgery
quiz.explain: Station 4L is contralateral mediastinum for a right-sided primary, and contralateral mediastinal nodes are N3, which takes a patient off a primary surgical pathway. But avidity is not tissue. Granulomatous disease, anthracosis and nodes reacting downstream of an obstructed bronchus are all FDG-avid, and the positive predictive value of PET in the mediastinum is only moderate, so the single finding that would convert a resectable patient into an unresectable one is exactly the finding that must be proved. Endobronchial ultrasound reaches station 4L, and a negative needle result in a node with this much riding on it is followed by surgical staging rather than accepted. The converse discipline is just as important: normal-sized, PET-negative mediastinal nodes still conceal metastasis in a minority, which is why central tumours, large tumours and N1 disease go to invasive staging even after a clean PET-CT.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a right lower lobe carcinoma has an enlarged pretracheal node. It lies anterior to the trachea, its centre is a little to the left of the midline of the body, but it lies entirely to the right of the left lateral border of the trachea. How is it classified on the IASLC map?
choices: Station 4R, and therefore N2 disease
Station 4L, and therefore N3 disease
Station 3a, and therefore N2 disease
Station 10R, and therefore N1 disease
quiz.answer: Station 4R, and therefore N2 disease
quiz.explain: The IASLC map deliberately does not use the body midline to divide right from left paratracheal nodes. For stations 2 and 4 the boundary is the left lateral border of the trachea, so a node in front of the trachea and to the right of that line is 4R however it looks against the anatomical midline. The consequence is not academic: for a right-sided tumour, 4R is ipsilateral mediastinal, N2, and remains within a multimodality plan that can be given with curative intent, while 4L would be N3. Station 3a is prevascular, anterior to the great vessels and not in contact with the trachea. Station 10R is hilar, beginning below the lower border of the azygos vein where station 4R ends, and hilar nodes are N1. Naming the station rather than describing the node loosely is what lets the next person choose a sampling route.

quiz.prompt: A 4.5 cm left lower lobe squamous carcinoma has a small ipsilateral pleural effusion on CT, with no visible pleural nodularity or thickening. The plan is surgery or chemoradiotherapy depending on stage. What does the effusion require?
choices: Sampling, because it may make the disease M1a
Nothing, because it lacks pleural nodularity
Drainage, because it will limit radiotherapy
Repeat CT, because it may resolve on its own
quiz.answer: Sampling, because it may make the disease M1a
quiz.explain: A malignant pleural or pericardial effusion, and pleural or pericardial nodules, are M1a, which removes curative resection from consideration, so this is one of the highest-consequence findings on a staging CT. Most effusions in lung cancer are malignant, and the absence of visible nodularity does not exclude pleural deposits, which are commonly a few millimetres and below the resolution of the study. The classification is explicit about the exception: where the fluid is not blood-stained, is not an exudate, and repeated cytology is negative, and where clinical judgement attributes it to something else such as obstructive pneumonitis or cardiac failure, the effusion is excluded as a staging element. So cytology decides, not CT, and in an otherwise operable patient with repeatedly negative cytology, thoracoscopy is the next step rather than an assumption in either direction.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT in a patient with a 3.5 cm lung cancer shows a 2.4 cm left adrenal nodule and nothing else outside the chest. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Measure its unenhanced attenuation first
Call it M1b and treat as stage IV disease
Biopsy the adrenal gland under CT guidance
Proceed to surgery and monitor the adrenal
quiz.answer: Measure its unenhanced attenuation first
quiz.explain: Adrenal nodules are common in the general population, and most adrenal nodules in patients with lung cancer are still adenomas. An unenhanced attenuation of 10 HU or less establishes a lipid-rich adenoma; chemical-shift MRI answers the same question when unenhanced CT is unavailable, and contrast washout characterises a lipid-poor adenoma. Getting it right matters more here than in an incidental setting, because a solitary adrenal metastasis is the difference between a treatment given with curative intent and palliative systemic therapy. The M1b category exists because single-lesion, single-organ metastatic disease behaves differently from widespread disease, and an oligometastatic patient may have both sites treated radically. Biopsy is reserved for a lesion that imaging cannot characterise, and phaeochromocytoma should be considered before a needle is put into an adrenal gland.

quiz.prompt: A 2.5 cm right upper lobe adenocarcinoma is accompanied by a solitary 9 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe, biopsied and shown to be the same tumour type, with no nodal or distant disease. How does the second nodule count?
choices: T4, still within a curative-intent plan
M1a, so systemic treatment is indicated
T3, because it sits in the same lung
N1, because spread is intrapulmonary
quiz.answer: T4, still within a curative-intent plan
quiz.explain: Separate tumour nodules are graded by where they sit relative to the primary: the same lobe is T3, a different ipsilateral lobe is T4, and the contralateral lung is M1a. A T4 arrived at this way is not the same animal as a T4 by invasion of the mediastinum or a great vessel. With N0 disease this configuration is resectable and potentially curable, and it is one of the places where the stage label and the surgical reality diverge, which is a good reason to report the anatomy rather than only the letter. The other trap is assuming the second nodule is a metastasis at all. Synchronous second primaries are common in this population, and comparing histological subtype and molecular profile can turn one T4 tumour into two early-stage tumours, with quite different treatment.

quiz.prompt: A superior sulcus tumour abuts the subclavian artery and the T1 nerve root on CT, with an equivocal fat plane at both sites. Which examination best answers the resectability question, and what is it looking for?
choices: MRI, for brachial plexus and vertebral invasion
PET-CT, for occult nodal and distant disease
CT angiography, for subclavian artery invasion
Bone scan, for invasion of the first two ribs
quiz.answer: MRI, for brachial plexus and vertebral invasion
quiz.explain: At the lung apex the questions that decide the operation are soft-tissue ones: the brachial plexus, the subclavian vessels, the vertebral body, the neural foramina and the spinal canal. MRI with coronal and sagittal planes shows all of them, and CT, whatever its spatial resolution in bone, is poor at the plexus. Tumour reaching the plexus above the T1 root, encasing rather than abutting the subclavian artery, or invading the vertebral body extensively or entering the canal, is generally beyond resection; involvement of the T1 root and below, of the ribs, or of a limited portion of a vertebral body is within the scope of en-bloc resection after induction chemoradiotherapy at experienced centres. PET-CT is still needed, because a superior sulcus tumour is staged for nodal and distant disease like any other, but it does not answer the local question this patient's operability turns on.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a 5 cm tumour and ipsilateral mediastinal nodal disease has a PET-CT that shows no extrathoracic uptake, and has no neurological symptoms. What is still required before treatment is planned?
choices: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain
A repeat PET-CT after chemotherapy
A bone scan for skeletal metastases
No further imaging before treatment
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain
quiz.explain: Normal cerebral cortex takes up FDG avidly, so a metastasis sits against a bright background and PET-CT is unreliable intracranially. Dedicated brain imaging is recommended separately for locally advanced disease and for anyone with neurological symptoms, and contrast-enhanced MRI is substantially more sensitive than CT for small and posterior fossa deposits. The reason to do it before treatment is planned rather than afterwards is that the result changes the plan in either direction: an occult brain metastasis can convert a radical chemoradiotherapy plan into systemic therapy, or, if it is solitary and the thoracic disease is limited, into radical treatment of both sites with stereotactic radiosurgery or resection. A bone scan adds nothing after a PET-CT, which covers the skeleton with better sensitivity and specificity.

quiz.prompt: A peripheral part-solid adenocarcinoma measures 2.4 cm overall on lung windows, with a solid component of 1.8 cm, and there is no nodal or distant disease. Which of those measurements in centimetres is used to assign the clinical T category? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Since the eighth edition, a part-solid tumour is staged on the size of its solid component on CT, and at pathology on the size of the invasive component, because the ground-glass, lepidic part does not carry the same prognosis as invasive tumour of equal size. So 1.8 cm makes this T1b, where the whole-lesion measurement of 2.4 cm would have made it T1c. Both numbers belong in the report, since the referrer needs the total size to follow the lesion and the solid size to stage it. The same logic runs to the bottom of the scale: a pure ground-glass lesion up to 3 cm with no invasive component is staged as in situ disease, and one with an invasive component of 5 mm or less as minimally invasive. It runs upward too, in that growth of the solid component is what constitutes progression in a subsolid lesion.

quiz.prompt: In a patient with a left upper lobe tumour, an enlarged node lies in the space bounded above by the lower border of the aortic arch, below by the upper border of the left main pulmonary artery, and lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. Which IASLC station number is that? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: That is station 5, the subaortic or aortopulmonary window node, and left upper lobe tumours drain there characteristically. It is ipsilateral mediastinal for a left-sided primary, so N2. The practical weight of naming it correctly lies in access: neither cervical mediastinoscopy nor endobronchial ultrasound reaches station 5, so tissue requires a parasternal mediastinotomy, a video-assisted thoracoscopic approach or an extended cervical procedure. Station 6, the para-aortic node lying anterior and lateral to the ascending aorta and the arch, is equally out of reach of those routine techniques. This is the concrete reason a report should name the station rather than describe a node loosely as being in the upper mediastinum: the station determines who can biopsy it and how, and a vague description costs the patient an extra clinic visit or the wrong procedure.

quiz.prompt: Explain why an FDG-avid mediastinal node should be sampled before a patient is told that surgery is off, and set out which stations the two standard needle routes reach and which they do not.
quiz.answer: PET is sensitive but only moderately specific in the mediastinum: granulomatous disease, anthracosilicotic nodes, infection, and nodes reacting downstream of an obstructed bronchus are all avid, so an avid node in an otherwise operable patient is a hypothesis rather than a stage. Because upstaging from N1 to N2, or from N2 to N3, removes curative surgery, the finding that changes the plan is precisely the one that has to be proved, and pathological confirmation is the standard of care. Endobronchial ultrasound with transbronchial needle aspiration, EBUS-TBNA, reaches the paratracheal stations 2R, 2L, 4R and 4L, the subcarinal station 7, and the hilar and interlobar stations 10 and 11. Endoscopic ultrasound from the oesophagus reaches 4L, 7, 8 and 9, and can also sample the left adrenal gland and the left lobe of the liver. Neither reaches the subaortic station 5 or the para-aortic station 6, which need a parasternal mediastinotomy or a thoracoscopic approach. The converse error also matters: a negative needle result in a node with a high pretest probability does not exclude disease, and surgical staging follows.
quiz.explain: The rule underneath all of this is that a finding gets proved in proportion to what it costs the patient if it is wrong. A PET-positive node that merely confirms disease already evident elsewhere changes nothing and needs nothing; a PET-positive node that alone takes away an operation is worth an invasive test. Two extras are worth carrying. First, the two needle routes are complementary rather than alternatives, because they approach the mediastinum from opposite sides, and combining them raises the yield in the posterior and inferior stations that bronchoscopy cannot see. Second, the ninth edition of the classification, in force since 2025, subdivides N2 into single-station and multi-station disease because they carry different prognoses, which raises the value of a report that names each involved station rather than reporting mediastinal nodal disease in aggregate.

quiz.prompt: A staging CT reports no enlarged mediastinal nodes, and the team treats that as N0. Explain the two ways that inference can be wrong, and what determines whether invasive staging is needed anyway.
quiz.answer: The CT criterion is a short-axis diameter of 10 mm or more, and it fails in both directions. Nodes enlarge reactively in obstructive pneumonitis, infection and old granulomatous disease, so a good proportion of enlarged nodes are benign; and metastatic deposits sit inside normal-sized nodes, so a normal CT does not exclude N2 disease, with sensitivity around half. PET-CT improves on both figures without solving either, since deposits below its resolution are missed and lepidic adenocarcinoma and carcinoid tumours are poorly avid, while inflammatory nodes are avid. What determines whether invasive staging is done anyway is the pretest probability of mediastinal disease: a central tumour, a large tumour, enlarged or avid N1 nodes, and adenocarcinoma histology all raise it enough that a negative PET-CT is not accepted at face value, and endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) with or without surgical staging is performed before resection. A small peripheral tumour with a clean PET mediastinum carries a low enough residual risk to proceed directly to surgery.
quiz.explain: Size is a poor surrogate for tumour because it measures a consequence that inflammation produces just as readily. That is why nodal staging is a sequence of tests with rising invasiveness and rising accuracy, rather than a single measurement, and why the sequence is entered at the point the pretest probability justifies. The reporting habit that follows is to describe nodes by station, short-axis size and avidity, and to state the pretest features that raise concern, rather than issuing a bare N category from CT alone: the radiologist's job at this step is to set the probability that the next test is chosen against. The same reasoning explains why a positive result is confirmed when it removes an operation, and a negative result is confirmed when the probability was high to begin with.

quiz.prompt: Put these IASLC nodal stations in order of the level at which they are found, from the most cranial to the most caudal.
quiz.answer: station-2R station-4R station-7 station-8 station-9
quiz.explain: Station 2R is the upper paratracheal node, running down to the level where the caudal border of the left brachiocephalic vein crosses the trachea; 4R is the lower paratracheal node below that, down to the lower border of the azygos vein; 7 is subcarinal; 8 is paraoesophageal below the level of the carina; and 9 lies in the inferior pulmonary ligament, the most caudal mediastinal station of all. Two structural facts make the map worth learning rather than looking up each time. Stations 1 to 9 are mediastinal and become N2 when ipsilateral to the tumour and N3 when contralateral or supraclavicular, while stations 10 to 14 are hilar and beyond and are N1. And the boundaries are defined by structures visible on CT, precisely so that a radiologist and a surgeon assigning the same node from the same images arrive at the same number.

quiz.prompt: A single 3 cm peripheral lung cancer is being staged. Taking each site of direct invasion on its own, put them in order of the T category that site alone would confer, from the lowest to the highest.
quiz.answer: visceral-pleura chest-wall vertebral-body
quiz.explain: Invasion of the visceral pleura makes a tumour at least T2 whatever its size. Invasion through it into the parietal pleura or the chest wall makes T3, in company with the phrenic nerve and the parietal pericardium. Invasion of a vertebral body makes T4, in company with the mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus and carina. What is worth carrying is how badly CT performs at each of these boundaries. Contact with the pleura, loss of an extrapleural fat plane, and even a broad interface between tumour and chest wall do not prove invasion; the findings that do are frank rib destruction and an extrapleural soft-tissue mass. The step from T3 to T4 changes the operation and often the intent of treatment, so equivocal cases go to MRI, to careful review of sagittal and coronal reformats, or to assessment at thoracotomy, and the report should say which of those is being asked for.

nodes.title: The Chest Radiograph
nodes.goal: Read a chest radiograph to a fixed search pattern, localise disease by the silhouette sign, and separate a technically poor film from a diseased one.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old with cough and fever has a PA chest radiograph. The right heart border can no longer be traced against the adjacent lung, while the right hemidiaphragm stays sharp along its whole length. On the lateral there is a wedge of increased density overlying the heart, bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the front half of the oblique fissure. Where does the disease sit?
choices: The right middle lobe
The right lower lobe
The anterior mediastinum
The lingular segments
quiz.answer: The right middle lobe
quiz.explain: A border is drawn on a radiograph wherever soft tissue meets air-filled lung along the beam. The right middle lobe is the only lung that touches the right heart border, so consolidation there erases it, and the two fissures that bound the wedge on the lateral are the middle lobe's own boundaries. The right lower lobe sits posteriorly against the diaphragm: it would rub out the hemidiaphragm and leave the heart border intact, which is the reverse of what is described, and it is the commonest wrong answer because both lobes project over the lower zone on the frontal film. The lingula does the same job on the left, so it erases the left heart border. An anterior mediastinal mass does obscure the right heart border, but it displaces structures rather than filling a fissure-bounded wedge, and on the lateral it fills the retrosternal clear space instead of overlying the heart.

quiz.prompt: A supine AP radiograph of an intensive care patient shows the left hemithorax uniformly greyer than the right. Pulmonary vessels can still be traced through the grey to the periphery, there are no air bronchograms, the left hemidiaphragm is indistinct and the mediastinum is central. What accounts for it?
choices: Pleural fluid layering behind the lung
Consolidation of the whole left lung
Collapse of the left lower lobe
Air trapped anterior to the lung
quiz.answer: Pleural fluid layering behind the lung
quiz.explain: Supine, fluid runs to the dependent posterior pleural space and spreads as a sheet behind the whole lung, so the beam passes through fluid and aerated lung in series.
