The result is a veil of increased density with the vascular markings preserved through it, because the lung behind the veil still contains air. Consolidation replaces that air, so it obscures the vessels and usually shows air bronchograms. Lobar collapse loses volume, and the mediastinum and hilum would shift toward the opacity rather than staying central. Anterior air makes a hemithorax blacker, not greyer. The point that survives the case is that a supine film hides an effusion in plain sight: what would be a meniscus on an erect film becomes a whole-lung haze, and an erect or decubitus view, or five seconds of ultrasound, settles it.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient becomes suddenly hypotensive as airway pressures rise. The supine AP film shows the left costophrenic sulcus extending abnormally low and lucent towards the flank, an unusually crisp left heart border and pericardial fat pad, and no visible pleural line anywhere.
choices: Air in the pleural space anteriorly
Emphysema of the left lower lobe
A left-sided diaphragmatic rupture
Loculated fluid in the left fissure
quiz.answer: Air in the pleural space anteriorly
quiz.explain: In a supine patient the least dependent part of the pleural space is anterior and basal, not apical, so pneumothorax collects in front of the lung and runs down into the costophrenic sulcus. That gives the deep sulcus sign, a hyperlucent upper abdominal quadrant, and mediastinal and diaphragmatic borders that look sharper than they should because air rather than lung now abuts them. The absent pleural line is the trap: the visceral edge is only seen where the beam runs tangential to it, and here it does not, so waiting for a white line means missing a tension pneumothorax in a patient whose blood pressure is already falling. Lower lobe emphysema does not appear in minutes, a ruptured hemidiaphragm displaces abdominal contents into the chest, and loculated fluid is dense rather than lucent.

quiz.prompt: A ward PA film reported quickly is described as showing a widened upper mediastinum and a prominent right hilum, and a CT is requested on that basis. Reviewing the film, the spinous processes at T3 lie far closer to the medial end of the right clavicle than to the left, and the posterior ribs are noticeably longer on one side. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Repeat the radiograph with the patient square
Proceed to contrast CT of the mediastinum
Add a lateral to confirm the hilar mass
Arrange a follow-up radiograph in six weeks
quiz.answer: Repeat the radiograph with the patient square
quiz.explain: The spinous processes should sit midway between the medial ends of the clavicles; when they do not, the patient is rotated and the mediastinum is being projected obliquely. An obliqued mediastinum casts a wider shadow, and one hilum is thrown clear of the spine while the other is buried in it, so both of the reported abnormalities are manufactured by geometry. A repeat film costs one exposure and a minute, and it either removes the finding or confirms it. The discipline generalises: technique is assessed before findings, because every technical fault has a disease that it imitates. The one qualification worth carrying is that rotation is an explanation, not an excuse. In a patient after significant trauma, a mediastinum that still looks wide clinically goes to CT whatever the rotation.

quiz.prompt: A frontal radiograph shows a smooth ovoid opacity in the right superior mediastinum. Its lateral margin stays crisply outlined against aerated lung as it is traced upward, remaining sharp well above the level of the clavicles. What does that tell you, and where should the next examination look?
choices: It lies posteriorly, so image the neural foramina
It lies anteriorly, so assess the thymic bed
It lies within the neck, so scan the thyroid
It lies in the middle mediastinum, near the trachea
quiz.answer: It lies posteriorly, so image the neural foramina
quiz.explain: The anterior lung stops at the clavicles, while the posterior pleural apex extends several centimetres higher into the thoracic inlet. A mass in the anterior mediastinum therefore runs out of adjacent lung at the clavicle and its border dissolves there, meeting the soft tissues of the neck; a mass sitting posteriorly still has aerated lung beside it above the clavicle and keeps a sharp edge. That is the cervicothoracic sign, and it is a depth judgement made from a single projection. The reading changes what is looked for: a posterior mediastinal mass in this position is most often neurogenic, so the follow-up study is directed at the neural exit foramina and the cord, which usually means MRI. A retrosternal goitre, the classic anterior candidate, loses its border at the clavicle and is traced up into the neck instead.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old with night sweats has a PA film in which the cardiac silhouette looks grossly enlarged. Both hilar vascular shadows are still clearly visible, roughly 2 cm inside the lateral border of the enlarged shadow, and the left heart border is sharp. What does that tell you?
choices: The enlarged shadow is not the heart itself
The left atrium is enlarged behind the heart
There is a large pericardial effusion present
The pulmonary arteries are dilated centrally
quiz.answer: The enlarged shadow is not the heart itself
quiz.explain: This is the hilum overlay sign, and it is the silhouette sign used in reverse. Structures that touch each other efface each other; structures separated in depth are simply superimposed, and both are still seen. Hilar vessels visible well inside the border of a large central opacity therefore mean the opacity is not in contact with them, so it lies in front of or behind the hilum rather than arising from it. A genuinely enlarged heart, and a pericardial effusion filling the same outline, would abut the hila and push them laterally rather than leaving them projected within the shadow. In a young adult with night sweats the anterior mediastinum is where the answer lies, and the film has already told you to look there rather than at the heart.

quiz.prompt: A febrile patient's frontal film looks unremarkable. On the lateral view the thoracic vertebral bodies become progressively denser and whiter as they are followed downward towards the diaphragm, rather than progressively darker.
choices: Consolidation in a lower lobe
Consolidation of the lingula
A large anterior mediastinal mass
Air trapping in both lower lobes
quiz.answer: Consolidation in a lower lobe
quiz.explain: Descending the thoracic spine on a lateral film, there is progressively less shoulder girdle and soft tissue in the beam, so the vertebrae normally look blacker the further down you go. Anything that adds density in front of the lower spine reverses that gradient, and lower lobe consolidation is the usual cause: the spine sign. It matters because the lower lobes hide behind the heart and the diaphragm on the frontal view, which is exactly why the retrocardiac zone is a named review area and why the lateral is worth its dose. Lingular consolidation is anterior and would erase the left heart border instead. An anterior mediastinal mass fills the retrosternal clear space at the other end of the film. Air trapping makes lung blacker, not whiter.

quiz.prompt: An erect PA chest radiograph taken at full inspiration shows a maximum transverse cardiac diameter of 16.4 cm and a maximum internal transverse thoracic diameter, measured at the level of the domes of the diaphragm, of 29.8 cm. What is the cardiothoracic ratio? Give it to two decimal places. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 16.4 divided by 29.8 is 0.5503, so 0.55, and a ratio above 0.50 on a film of this kind is cardiomegaly. Each qualifier in the question is load-bearing. Erect, because supine increases pulmonary blood volume and widens the mediastinum. PA, because in an AP projection the heart lies far from the detector and is magnified. Full inspiration, because a shallow film raises the diaphragm and splays the heart transversely, which can add several centimetres of apparent width to a normal heart. And the ratio only measures a transverse shadow: concentric hypertrophy can leave it normal, a pericardial effusion can raise it with a structurally normal heart, so it is a screening observation rather than a diagnosis, and echocardiography is what settles the question.

quiz.prompt: A portable AP film is exposed with the x-ray source 100 cm from the detector, and the centre of the heart lies 20 cm in front of the detector. Treating the heart as a point object on the central ray, by what factor is its width magnified compared with an object lying against the detector? Give the factor to two decimal places. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Magnification is the source-to-detector distance divided by the source-to-object distance, that is 100 divided by 80, which is 1.25. The heart on this film is a quarter wider than it truly is, which is why a cardiothoracic ratio measured from a portable AP study routinely overcalls cardiomegaly and should not be quoted as one. Compare a departmental erect PA at 180 cm with the heart almost against the detector, perhaps 7 cm away: 180 divided by 173 is about 1.04, a four per cent magnification that the 0.50 threshold was built to tolerate. Two variables drive the difference, the shorter distance and the reversed geometry, and both are properties of the portable machine rather than of the patient.

quiz.prompt: A left lower lobe consolidation lies directly behind the heart, yet the left heart border stays sharp; a lingular consolidation of the same size erases it. Explain the physical rule that produces this difference, and state the one thing the sign gives you that a single frontal projection otherwise cannot.
quiz.answer: A border appears on a radiograph only where two tissues of different attenuation lie in contact along the path of the beam, and in the chest that means soft tissue against aerated lung. Consolidated lung has essentially the attenuation of soft tissue, so where it touches the heart the interface vanishes and the border is lost. The lingula lies immediately lateral to and in contact with the left heart border, so lingular consolidation effaces it. The left lower lobe lies posterior to the heart, and aerated lung still intervenes at the border itself, so the outline survives even though solid lung lies behind it. The sign therefore supplies depth: it localises disease to the lobe or segment that touches the effaced structure, which is anatomical information a single frontal projection has no other way to give.
quiz.explain: The rule is about contact, not about superimposition, and that is the whole of it. Disease behind a structure is superimposed on it and adds density without removing the edge; disease against a structure removes the edge. Run the map in both directions and it becomes a localiser: right heart border to middle lobe, left heart border to lingula, right hemidiaphragm to right lower lobe, left hemidiaphragm to left lower lobe, ascending aorta and superior vena cava to the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, aortic knuckle to the apicoposterior segment on the left. The same logic warns you off the two failure modes: a border that is lost because the film is rotated or under-inspired rather than because lung is diseased, and a normal variant in which a hemidiaphragm border is faint because of an interposed colon.

quiz.prompt: A portable AP film in a septic 70-year-old is reported as showing cardiomegaly with bibasal pulmonary oedema. Before accepting that report, name four technical features of the film you would assess, and for each say how it can manufacture that appearance in a normal chest.
quiz.answer: Projection: an AP portable film magnifies the anteriorly placed heart by around a fifth to a quarter, so the cardiothoracic ratio is not valid and a normal heart looks big. Inspiration: a shallow film, with fewer than five to six anterior or nine to ten posterior ribs above the hemidiaphragm, raises the diaphragms, crowds the lower zone vessels into apparent basal shadowing and splays the heart transversely. Position: supine, blood redistributes to the upper zones and mimics the upper lobe diversion of cardiac failure, and any pleural fluid layers posteriorly as a diffuse haze rather than as a meniscus. Rotation: an obliqued mediastinum looks wide and one hilum looks prominent. Exposure and penetration: an underexposed film makes lungs look uniformly opaque and adds interstitial markings that are not there, and an overexposed one erases them. The remedy is to compare with a previous film of comparable technique, and to state the technical limitation in the report rather than to report through it.
quiz.explain: Every technical fault on a chest radiograph has a disease it imitates, which is why technique is assessed first and not as a courtesy at the end. The four faults here converge on one clinical picture, and a single film carrying all four will show a big heart, upper zone vessels, hazy bases and a wide mediastinum in a patient with normal lungs. Reading in the other direction is just as important: the same faults hide disease, since a shallow film buries a lower lobe behind the diaphragm and an overexposed one erases a fine reticular pattern. What makes the report defensible is the comparison. Serial portable films in the same patient are read as a series against each other, and a change in technique between two of them is the commonest reason a chest appears to have changed overnight.

quiz.prompt: A chest radiograph reported as normal is shown three months later to have contained a 2 cm cancer. Name four review areas where an overlying structure hides lung, and for each give one finding it characteristically conceals.
quiz.answer: The apices, where the clavicles, the first ribs and the overlying soft tissues obscure lung: an apical tumour or a small pneumothorax hides here. The retrocardiac region, where the heart overlies the left lower lobe: consolidation, a collapsed left lower lobe behind the heart, and a hiatus hernia are missed here, and the lateral view rescues them. Below the diaphragms, which are part of the film: free subphrenic gas, a raised hemidiaphragm and basal disease projected below the domes. The hila, where normal vessels are dense enough to hide a nodal mass or a central tumour, and where comparison of size, density and position between the two sides is the only defence. Beyond those four, the bones and soft tissues carry rib and shoulder lesions, absent breast shadows and surgical emphysema, and the lung periphery beyond the lung markings carries the pleural line of a small pneumothorax. The common feature is that all of them are looked at after the reader believes they have finished.
quiz.explain: Satisfaction of search is the real mechanism behind most missed lesions, and a fixed review sequence is the only reliable countermeasure, because it runs whether or not the reader has already found something. The areas are not arbitrary. They are precisely the places where a dense structure is superimposed on lung, so that a lesion has to be more conspicuous than usual to be seen. Two practical additions make the sequence work: comparing the two sides directly, since the chest is nearly symmetrical and asymmetry is easier to see than abnormality, and always comparing with the oldest available previous film rather than only the most recent, since a nodule that grew slowly is invisible against yesterday and obvious against three years ago.

quiz.prompt: On a lateral chest radiograph, at the level of the mid-heart, put these structures in order from the most anterior to the most posterior.
quiz.answer: sternum right-ventricle left-atrium descending-aorta vertebral-body
quiz.explain: The lateral view exists to supply the depth the frontal view cannot. Behind the sternum lies the retrosternal clear space, which should be dark down to the level where the right ventricle meets the anterior chest wall; a filled retrosternal space is an anterior mediastinal mass until proven otherwise. The right ventricle forms the anterior cardiac border, the left atrium the posterosuperior one, and behind them the descending aorta runs down in front of the spine, with the retrocardiac clear space between the posterior heart border and the spine. That anterior-to-posterior sequence is what turns a lateral into a localiser: an opacity that overlies the vertebral bodies and stops them darkening downward is posterior, one that fills the space behind the sternum is anterior, and one that does neither but obscures the heart border is beside the heart.

nodes.title: The Incidental Pulmonary Nodule
nodes.goal: Measure an incidental nodule to the Fleischner convention, judge solid from subsolid, and give the follow-up the guidance recommends or say why it does not apply.

quiz.prompt: A 63-year-old with a 40 pack-year smoking history has a CT pulmonary angiogram for pleuritic pain, negative for embolus. It shows a single solid nodule in the right lower lobe with a mean diameter of 4 mm, smooth margins and no calcification. There is no known malignancy and no immunosuppression. What does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend?
choices: An optional single CT at 12 months
A CT at 6 months and at 18 months
A CT at 3 months, then PET-CT
Immediate biopsy of the nodule
quiz.answer: An optional single CT at 12 months
quiz.explain: For a single solid nodule under 6 mm, low-risk patients need no routine follow-up, and high-risk patients are offered an optional CT at 12 months. The word optional carries the argument: even in a heavy smoker a nodule this size has under about a one per cent chance of being a cancer, so the recommendation is a discussion rather than an instruction, and features such as an upper lobe location, spiculation, coexisting emphysema or fibrosis, or a family history legitimately tip an individual decision. The 6 to 12 month schedule with a second scan at 18 to 24 months belongs to the 6 to 8 mm band, and going straight to PET-CT or biopsy at 4 mm subjects the patient to tests that cannot answer the question at that size. Note also what the study is: an incidental finding on a scan done for something else, which is the only setting the guidance addresses.

quiz.prompt: A first CT in a 60-year-old shows a solitary part-solid nodule in the left upper lobe, 14 mm overall with a 4 mm solid component. There are no symptoms of infection and no prior imaging exists. What is the next step?
choices: Repeat thin-section CT at 3-6 months
PET-CT to assess the solid component
CT-guided biopsy of the solid part
Lobectomy for presumed adenocarcinoma
quiz.answer: Repeat thin-section CT at 3-6 months
quiz.explain: The first duty with any subsolid nodule seen once is to establish that it is real and persistent, because a large proportion of subsolid opacities are transient: infection, haemorrhage, focal inflammation and organising pneumonia all look like this and are gone in three months. So a repeat thin-section CT at 3 to 6 months precedes any decision. If it persists with a solid component still under 6 mm, annual CT for five years follows, since a persistent part-solid nodule is often on the adenocarcinoma spectrum but grows slowly and the solid part is the invasive part. PET-CT at a 4 mm solid component is below the useful resolution of the technique and lepidic tumour is poorly avid in any case; percutaneous biopsy of a 4 mm target is unreliable; and resecting before persistence is established treats a proportion of patients for pneumonia they have already recovered from.

quiz.prompt: A persistent 12 mm pure ground-glass nodule is referred with a request for PET-CT to confirm that it is benign. The nodule shows no FDG uptake above background lung. How should that result be used?
choices: It does not lower the risk from this appearance
It confirms the nodule is benign, so discharge
It shows the nodule is inflammatory, repeat in 3 months
It means the nodule should be resected without delay
quiz.answer: It does not lower the risk from this appearance
quiz.explain: FDG uptake tracks glucose metabolism and, in practice, viable cell density. A persistent pure ground-glass nodule is characteristically atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, adenocarcinoma in situ or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma, all of which grow along intact alveolar walls with very little cellular bulk, so a negative scan is expected whether the lesion is benign or malignant, and it carries almost no information. Acting on it ends a surveillance programme that the guidance asks to run to five years, and the thing being watched for over those years is the appearance or growth of a solid component. PET-CT earns its place with solid nodules above roughly 8 mm, and even there it has the mirror-image problem of false positives from granulomatous and other inflammatory disease. Small size and low cell density are its two blind spots, and this nodule has both.

quiz.prompt: A CT report flags a new 5 mm nodule. On review it is a smooth, homogeneous, lentiform solid nodule in the right lower zone, in contact with the oblique fissure with its long axis lying along the fissure, and it has a thin linear tail running to the pleura. It was present at the same size on a scan four years earlier. What follow-up is needed?
choices: No follow-up: this is a lymph node
A CT at 12 months for stability
A CT at 3 months, then 12 months
PET-CT to characterise it further
quiz.answer: No follow-up: this is a lymph node
quiz.explain: A typical perifissural nodule is an intrapulmonary lymph node: solid, smooth, homogeneous, oval or triangular, in contact with or within a few millimetres of a fissure or the pleura, usually below the level of the carina, and often with a septal tail running to the pleural surface. In screening cohorts these have proved essentially never to be malignant, and the guidance exempts them from follow-up on morphology alone. Four years of stability settles the matter independently, since two years of unchanged size is the conventional evidence of benignity for a solid nodule. That convention is worth keeping separate in your mind from subsolid disease, where it does not hold: adenocarcinoma in situ can sit unchanged for years, so two years of stability in a ground-glass nodule proves nothing.

quiz.prompt: A 9 mm solid nodule found incidentally contains a focus measuring -70 HU on a region of interest placed on a thin section, together with a coarse central clump of calcification. What follows?
choices: Fat and calcium here indicate a hamartoma
The low attenuation indicates a cavity
This appearance requires PET-CT staging
This warrants CT again in 3 to 6 months
quiz.answer: Fat and calcium here indicate a hamartoma
quiz.explain: Macroscopic fat inside a pulmonary nodule, conventionally in the region of -40 to -120 HU, is close to diagnostic of a hamartoma, and with coarse popcorn-like calcification the diagnosis is secure and the nodule needs no follow-up at all. The rare exceptions worth knowing are lipoid pneumonia and fat-containing metastases from liposarcoma or renal cell carcinoma, which do not resemble this. Two cautions govern the measurement. It must be made on thin sections, because partial volume averaging with adjacent air can fabricate a fat-like value in a small nodule. And the calcification pattern must be one of the benign ones, which are central, laminated, diffusely solid and popcorn: eccentric or stippled calcium does not exclude malignancy, since a carcinoma can engulf a pre-existing granuloma. Recognising the nodule that needs nothing is as much a part of the algorithm as recognising the one that needs everything.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old two years after renal transplantation, on tacrolimus and mycophenolate, has three new solid nodules of 4 to 5 mm on a CT performed for fever. A trainee proposes an optional CT at 12 months, quoting the Fleischner recommendations. What is wrong with that?
choices: The guideline excludes patients like this one
The nodules are multiple, so the interval halves
The nodules are too small to be measured reliably
The patient's age puts her in the low-risk column
quiz.answer: The guideline excludes patients like this one
quiz.explain: The 2017 recommendations apply to incidental nodules in immunocompetent patients aged 35 and over who have no known primary malignancy, and they explicitly do not apply within a lung cancer screening programme, where a structured reporting system takes over. This patient fails on two counts, and each on its own would be enough. Immunosuppressed, new nodules with fever are an infection question until proved otherwise, and invasive fungal disease, nocardia, mycobacteria and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder are answered in days by a repeat scan, bronchoscopy or empirical treatment, not in a year. Under 35, the prior probability of lung cancer is low and the accumulated radiation of surveillance is comparatively costly, so benign and infective causes are managed clinically. Knowing when an algorithm does not apply is the part of it that most often gets skipped.

quiz.prompt: A part-solid nodule under annual surveillance measures 15 mm overall on this year's scan and on last year's, but its solid component has gone from 4 mm to 9 mm over those 12 months. The patient has no new symptoms. What should happen?
choices: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
Continue annual CT to complete five years
Repeat CT at 3 months to confirm growth
Treat for infection and rescan in 6 weeks
quiz.answer: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
quiz.explain: In a part-solid nodule the solid component is the invasive component, and it drives both the risk and, if this becomes a cancer diagnosis, the T category. A growing solid component, or one reaching 8 mm, takes the nodule out of surveillance and into PET-CT, sampling or resection. The trap the case is built around is that the overall diameter never changed: had only the total size been recorded, the nodule would have been called stable and left for another year, which is why the solid component is measured separately on every study, on the same thin-section lung-window images. Waiting a further three months to confirm growth repeats a measurement already made over a whole year and delays treatment of a lesion that has declared itself. At 9 mm the solid component is also large enough for PET-CT to be informative, which it was not when the component was 4 mm.

quiz.prompt: On a 1 mm axial section an incidental solid nodule measures 7.0 mm along its long axis and 3.8 mm along the perpendicular short axis on the same image. Applying the Fleischner measurement convention, what size in millimetres is recorded for this nodule? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The convention is the average of the long-axis and short-axis diameters obtained on the same image, rounded to the nearest whole millimetre, measured on thin sections in a lung window. Here 7.0 and 3.8 average to 5.4, which is recorded as 5 mm, and that places an elongated nodule whose longest measurement is 7 mm below the 6 mm threshold, so a low-risk patient needs no routine follow-up. Reporting the long axis alone would have committed the same patient to a year of surveillance for the same lesion. The convention exists because it is reproducible rather than because it is the truth about the object: a nodule is not a sphere, and averaging two orthogonal diameters is simply a rule two readers can both follow. Semi-automated volumetry is more reproducible again, and the guidance gives the equivalents, roughly 100 cubic millimetres at 6 mm and 250 at 8 mm, for departments that measure volume instead.

quiz.prompt: A solid nodule has a mean diameter of 6.0 mm. Treating it as a sphere, what mean diameter in millimetres corresponds to exactly one doubling of its volume? Give it to one decimal place. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Volume scales with the cube of diameter, so a doubling needs a diameter multiplied by the cube root of two, that is 1.26: 6.0 becomes 7.56, or 7.6 mm to one decimal place. The lesson is in how small that step is. A whole doubling of tumour volume shows up as 1.6 mm on a ruler, which is inside the interobserver variability of manual measurement of a small nodule, so a solid nodule can double without any reader being able to prove it, and two readers can disagree about growth that never happened. That is the argument for volumetry, which measures the quantity that is actually doubling, and for long enough intervals that real growth outruns the noise. Volume doubling times of roughly 100 to 400 days characterise most solid lung cancers; much faster than that suggests infection or inflammation, and much slower suggests a benign lesion or an indolent subsolid tumour, whose doubling times commonly run to several years.

quiz.prompt: A solitary pure ground-glass nodule of 9 mm is still present and unchanged on the confirmatory CT performed at 9 months. Counting from the first scan, for how many years in total does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend that surveillance continue? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A solitary ground-glass nodule of 6 mm or more gets a CT at 6 to 12 months to confirm that it persists, then CT every two years out to five years in total. Persistence has ruled out infection and haemorrhage; it has emphatically not ruled out tumour, because the lesions that produce a persistent ground-glass nodule grow so slowly that the two-year stability rule used for solid nodules carries no weight here. Five years is not a claim that risk falls to zero afterwards, but a judgement about the yield of continued scanning against its radiation and cost. What the surveillance is watching for is a change in character rather than a change in size: the appearance of a solid component, or the growth of one, is the event that signals invasion and moves the patient from watching to treatment.

quiz.prompt: The 2017 revision moved the threshold below which no routine follow-up is advised from 4 mm up to 6 mm. Justify that change, and say what it implies for a 5 mm solid nodule in a heavy smoker.
quiz.answer: The evidence, largely from screening cohorts, is that a solid nodule under 6 mm carries a risk of malignancy below about one per cent even in high-risk people, and that a year of CT surveillance changes very little for such a nodule, because growth of that magnitude sits inside the measurement noise and because a cancer that small is usually still curable when it later declares itself. Set against that near-zero yield are real costs: the radiation of repeated scans, the financial cost, the anxiety of being under surveillance, and the cascade of further imaging and procedures that follows a followed nodule. Raising the threshold therefore removes surveillance from a very large number of people with little loss of cancer detection. For a 5 mm nodule in a heavy smoker the guidance offers an optional CT at 12 months rather than requiring one: the judgement is handed to the clinician and the patient, and an upper lobe location, spiculation, emphysema or fibrosis, or a family history are legitimate reasons for an individual to take it.
quiz.explain: A threshold in a guideline is a statement about the balance of harms rather than a claim about biology, and reading it that way explains both the change and the hedging around it. Below 6 mm the yield of surveillance is so low that the harms of scanning dominate, so the recommendation is withdrawn; the nodules did not become safer in 2017. It also explains why the high-risk column says optional rather than recommended: at that risk level the decision is genuinely close, and the guideline declines to make it for the patient. The corollary for reporting is to give the referrer what the decision needs, which is the mean diameter measured by the convention, the solid or subsolid character, the location, the margin, and an explicit statement of which follow-up row the nodule falls in, rather than a bare description of a nodule.

quiz.prompt: A nodule reported as 7 mm last year is reported as 9 mm today, and the patient is referred as growing. Before accepting growth, list the conditions that must match between the two measurements, and say which single technique removes most of the remaining disagreement.
quiz.answer: Both measurements should come from thin sections, ideally 1 mm and at most about 1.5 mm, displayed in a lung window with comparable settings, made by the same convention, which is the average of long and short axis on the same image, and read in the same plane; a nodule measured on a 5 mm series last year against a 1 mm series today will appear to change for purely technical reasons, and partial volume averaging in the thicker series usually understates it. Respiratory phase and patient positioning should be comparable, since a nodule in dependent lung can be measured differently in atelectatic surroundings. Above all, the prior images should be re-measured personally rather than the previous report's number being taken on trust, since the two numbers being compared were produced by different readers. Manual diameter carries an interobserver variability of a millimetre or two, which is the same size as the change being argued about, and semi-automated volumetry is substantially more reproducible: it measures the quantity that actually doubles, and expresses change as a volume doubling time.
quiz.explain: Most reported growth in small nodules is measurement, not biology, and the discipline that prevents the error is comparing like with like and doing the comparison yourself. Two habits carry most of the benefit. First, always open the prior study rather than reading its report, because the number in a report is a different reader's judgement on possibly different data. Second, state the technique the measurement came from in your own report, so that whoever compares next year knows what to match. The deeper point is about what growth means once established: a change in diameter is hard to interpret, whereas a volume doubling time places the lesion on a scale where roughly 100 to 400 days is typical of solid malignancy, faster suggests inflammation, and much slower suggests something indolent or benign.

quiz.prompt: An incidental solid nodule is found on a CT performed for another reason. Put these five decisions in the order that gets the follow-up right, beginning with the one that can stop the algorithm before any measurement is made.
quiz.answer: eligibility benign-morphology solid-or-subsolid mean-diameter patient-risk
quiz.explain: First, whether the guidance applies to this patient at all: under 35, immunosuppressed, a known primary malignancy, or a nodule found within a screening programme, and it does not, so any table you consult afterwards gives the wrong answer confidently. Second, whether the nodule is already diagnosed by its morphology, since fat with popcorn calcification makes a hamartoma, a benign calcification pattern makes a granuloma, and a typical perifissural nodule makes an intrapulmonary lymph node, and each of these ends the matter with no follow-up at all. Third, solid or subsolid, because the two run on different tables and different timescales. Fourth, the mean diameter by the averaging convention, which selects the row. And last, the patient's risk category, which chooses between columns and, in the smallest band, between an optional scan and none. Risk comes last because it modifies a recommendation rather than generating one, and applying it first is how a heavy smoker with an obvious hamartoma ends up in five years of surveillance.

nodes.title: Acute Aortic Syndrome
nodes.goal: Protocol and read the CT for suspected acute aortic syndrome, classify what it shows, and say what that commits the patient to.

quiz.prompt: A CT for suspected acute aortic syndrome is acquired as three passes through the chest. Put those passes in the order the protocol runs them.
quiz.answer: unenhanced arterial delayed
quiz.explain: The unenhanced pass comes first, and it is the one most often skipped to save dose. An intramural haematoma appears on it as a crescent of attenuation higher than the unopacified lumen, and once the lumen holds iodine at three hundred Hounsfield units or more that crescent is invisible against it. The same pass shows displaced intimal calcification, a hyperattenuating crescent within aneurysm thrombus, and fresh blood in the pericardium or mediastinum. Then the arterial acquisition, which is the diagnostic pass and which should be electrocardiogram-gated through the chest so that root pulsation cannot imitate a flap. The delayed pass answers slow-flow questions - a false lumen that fills late, a contained leak, an endoleak after repair - and is the one that can reasonably be dropped when the arterial phase has already answered the question and the dose is worth saving.

quiz.prompt: A non-gated CT angiogram of the chest shows a thin linear lucency in the ascending aorta at the level of the sinotubular junction, running from the right anterior to the left posterior wall, present on two adjacent slices, with no separate enhancing lumen and no extension into the arch. The patient's pain has settled. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Repeat the acquisition with electrocardiogram gating
Report a limited dissection of the ascending aorta
Obtain a delayed acquisition through the aortic root
Report a chronic dissection and arrange surveillance
quiz.answer: Repeat the acquisition with electrocardiogram gating
quiz.explain: Every feature here is the signature of motion rather than disease: the right anterior to left posterior orientation, confinement to the root, presence on only a couple of slices, no second lumen and no extension. The aortic root swings through systole, and an ungated helical acquisition catches it in different positions on adjacent rotations, producing a line that mimics a flap almost exactly. Gating freezes it, and the repeat is cheap against the alternative, which is sending a well patient to sternotomy. A true flap runs over a length of aorta, separates two lumens that enhance differently, and usually extends beyond the root; it should also have a correlate on the unenhanced series in the form of displaced calcification or mural haematoma. Where gating is unavailable, demand that the line be reproducible over more slices, and consider transoesophageal echocardiography, which is not troubled by this artefact at all.

quiz.prompt: CT shows an entry tear 3 cm beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery, with the flap extending distally to the coeliac axis and also retrogradely around the arch to involve the ascending aorta. A registrar codes it Stanford type B on the grounds that the tear is distal to the arch. What does the surgical team need to be told?
choices: Type A, because the ascending aorta is involved
Type B, because the entry tear sits beyond the arch
Type B, with the arch component reported separately
Indeterminate, pending transoesophageal confirmation
quiz.answer: Type A, because the ascending aorta is involved
quiz.explain: The Stanford division rests on whether the ascending aorta is involved, and deliberately not on where the tear is, because involvement of the ascending aorta is what determines the operation. A dissected ascending aorta threatens the coronary ostia, the aortic valve and the pericardium, and untreated it carries a mortality of the order of one to two per cent per hour over the first day or two, so it goes to theatre; an uncomplicated type B is managed medically. Retrograde type A is exactly the case the classification exists to catch, and the trap is real, because the eye anchors on the entry tear once it has found it. DeBakey does classify by origin and extent - type I ascending and beyond, type II ascending alone, type III descending - and handles this pattern less cleanly, which is one reason Stanford dominates the acute conversation. The newer reporting standards keep A and B but add the zone of the entry tear and the proximal and distal extent, so the report states where the disease starts and stops rather than which of two boxes it fits.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old with tearing chest pain has a CT angiogram; no intimal flap is seen, but there is a smooth crescent of thickening in the wall of the descending aorta with an intimal calcification displaced inward. The unenhanced series was skipped to save dose. Explain what is likely present, how the omitted series would have settled it, and what the finding commits the patient to.
quiz.answer: The appearances are those of an intramural haematoma: blood within the aortic media with no demonstrable intimal tear and no flow in a false lumen, seen as a crescentic thickening that keeps a constant circumferential relationship to the wall rather than spiralling as a dissection flap does, and that displaces intimal calcification inward, so the calcium lies at the inner margin of the crescent. The unenhanced series is where it declares itself, as a crescent of attenuation higher than the unopacified lumen - of the order of fifty to seventy Hounsfield units acutely - a contrast that is destroyed once the lumen is filled with iodine, where the same crescent looks merely like mural thrombus or a thickened wall. The distinction matters because the management is that of dissection rather than that of atheroma: an intramural haematoma of the ascending aorta is treated as a type A event and usually operated on, while a descending one is managed medically with impulse control and close interval imaging, since a substantial minority progress to frank dissection, to ulceration or to rupture.
quiz.explain: Two features separate an intramural haematoma from atheromatous mural thrombus, and both are visible here. The haematoma lies outside the intima, so intimal calcification is pushed inward and sits at the crescent's luminal edge, whereas thrombus lies inside the intima with the calcification at its outer margin. And the haematoma has a smooth luminal surface and a constant circumferential relationship along the vessel, while thrombus is irregular, tends to sit on an ectatic atherosclerotic aorta, and varies in position from slice to slice. Attenuation settles it on the unenhanced series, which is the whole argument for that pass. Its appearance evolves: at a few days the haematoma loses attenuation and, on later imaging, an unenhanced study can no longer make the distinction - so a scan without the unenhanced series is not merely incomplete now, it forecloses the diagnosis retrospectively.

quiz.prompt: A patient with an uncomplicated type B dissection is admitted for medical management, and the first order is intravenous beta-blockade titrated towards a heart rate target. Below what heart rate, in beats per minute, is that titration conventionally aimed? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Impulse control targets the rate of rise of pressure as much as the pressure itself, because it is the shearing force on the flap with each ejection that propagates the dissection. Convention is a heart rate below 60 and a systolic pressure in the region of 100 to 120 mmHg, as far as perfusion of brain, kidneys and gut allows. The sequence of drugs matters as much as the targets: the beta blocker goes in before any vasodilator, because a vasodilator given alone provokes reflex tachycardia and raises the very quantity being treated - the classic error on the ward. Analgesia is part of the haemodynamic treatment rather than a comfort measure, since pain drives catecholamines and with them both numbers. For the radiologist, the relevance is that this treatment is the reason an uncomplicated type B does not go to theatre, and the reason the follow-up scan exists.

quiz.prompt: In a chronic type B dissection the interventional team asks which lumen the landing zone lies in. On the axial images one lumen is larger, meets the outer wall at an acute angle where the flap inserts, and contains thin linear strands crossing it. Which lumen is it, and which feature is the most reliable indicator?
choices: The false lumen, indicated by the acute beak-shaped angle
The true lumen, indicated by the strands that cross it
The false lumen, indicated by its larger cross-section
The true lumen, indicated by its thin surrounding wall
quiz.answer: The false lumen, indicated by the acute beak-shaped angle
quiz.explain: The beak sign - the acute, wedge-shaped angle between the flap and the outer wall at the edge of the lumen - is the most reliable single indicator of the false lumen, because it is the leading edge of the haematoma prising the media apart. The true lumen, bounded by intima, meets the wall at an obtuse angle. Cobwebs, those thin strands of incompletely sheared media, are highly specific for the false lumen but are seen in only a minority of cases, so they confirm when present and prove nothing when absent. Size is the least dependable of the three: the false lumen is usually the larger in chronic dissection, but acutely a compressed true lumen and a small false lumen are both common, so the sign misleads in both directions. The most secure method is not a sign at all - follow the lumen proximally into undissected aorta, and the one continuous with it is true. The consequence of getting this wrong is a stent graft deployed into the false lumen, occluding every branch that arises from the true one.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old with an acute type B dissection is on intravenous beta-blockade with the pain settled. Six hours later the serum lactate rises and the abdomen becomes tender; repeat CT shows the coeliac axis and superior mesenteric artery arising from a true lumen compressed to a slit at that level. What does this change?
choices: It makes the dissection complicated and needs intervention
It reflects the expected course and medical therapy goes on
It is treated by deepening the blood pressure reduction
It calls for anticoagulation to protect the mesenteric flow
quiz.answer: It makes the dissection complicated and needs intervention
quiz.explain: Malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion, refractory pain and refractory hypertension are the features that convert a type B dissection from a medical problem into an interventional one, most often thoracic endovascular repair to cover the entry tear and let the true lumen re-expand. Recognise the mechanism, because it dictates the treatment: this is dynamic obstruction, in which the mobile flap prolapses across the branch origin as the true lumen collapses, and it is relieved by restoring pressure and flow in the true lumen. Static obstruction, where the flap extends into the branch itself, may need a stent in that branch instead, and the two often coexist. Note that the intuitive move is the harmful one - lowering the pressure further collapses the true lumen and worsens dynamic malperfusion. This is also why the protocol runs to the femoral heads: the question is never only what the arch looks like but what every branch from the coronaries downwards is being perfused by.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old with a known 6.2 cm infrarenal aneurysm attends with two days of back pain and stable observations. On the unenhanced series a crescent of attenuation higher than the psoas muscle lies within the peripheral thrombus of the sac; there is no periaortic fat stranding and no extraluminal contrast. What should the report say?
choices: Impending rupture; discuss with vascular surgery now
Chronic contained leak; arrange elective repair
Mural thrombus; back pain is unrelated to the sac
Infected aneurysm; obtain blood cultures and MRI
quiz.answer: Impending rupture; discuss with vascular surgery now
quiz.explain: The hyperattenuating crescent sign is acute blood dissecting into the mural thrombus or the aneurysm wall, and it is one of the recognised signs of impending rupture, alongside focal discontinuity of intimal calcification, the draped aorta sign in which the posterior wall loses its convexity and drapes over a vertebral body, and periaortic stranding. It is visible only on the unenhanced series, since against an opacified lumen and an enhancing wall it disappears - the second reason that pass exists. Reference the attenuation against psoas muscle, which is the standard comparator. Stable observations are not reassurance: a contained retroperitoneal leak can be haemodynamically quiet for hours before it is not. The elective repair threshold, around 5.5 cm in men, has no bearing here, because a symptomatic aneurysm is treated on its symptoms and its signs rather than on its diameter.

quiz.prompt: A screening ultrasound finds an asymptomatic infrarenal aortic aneurysm in a 72-year-old man, and the vascular clinic explains that repair is offered once the maximum diameter reaches a threshold. Give that threshold in centimetres, to one decimal place. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 5.5 cm is the long-standing threshold in men: the diameter at which the annual risk of rupture overtakes the risk of the operation. Below it the aneurysm is watched with ultrasound at intervals that shorten as the diameter grows. Three qualifications belong with the number. Many services intervene at a smaller diameter in women, whose aortas are smaller to begin with and who appear to rupture at smaller absolute diameters. Rapid expansion - conventionally more than about a centimetre in a year - is an indication in its own right, whatever the absolute size. And a symptomatic aneurysm of any diameter is a different problem altogether, treated urgently. One measurement discipline underlies all of it: measure perpendicular to the centreline of the vessel, because an axial diameter through a tortuous aorta cuts it obliquely and overstates the true size, and a patient can be referred for surgery by a measurement artefact.

quiz.prompt: A hypertensive 74-year-old with heavy aortic calcification has a focal outpouching of contrast extending beyond the expected line of the lumen into the wall of the mid descending aorta, with adjacent wall thickening. Describe the lesion, say what distinguishes it from a saccular aneurysm and from a dissection, and explain what determines whether it is treated.
quiz.answer: This is a penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer: an atheromatous plaque that has ulcerated through the internal elastic lamina, letting blood into the media, so that contrast projects beyond the intimal line into the wall itself. It occurs on a background of heavy atheroma, typically in the mid to distal descending aorta, is focal rather than longitudinal, and the adjacent wall thickening is an intramural haematoma at its base. A saccular aneurysm is an outpouching of an intact if abnormal wall, without disruption of the intima and without surrounding haematoma. A dissection has a flap propagating longitudinally and separating two lumens that both carry flow, whereas an ulcer stays local. Treatment is driven by symptoms and behaviour rather than by the finding alone: persistent or recurrent pain, an enlarging associated haematoma, growth in depth or diameter on interval imaging, a new pleural effusion or signs of rupture push towards repair, usually endovascular, while an incidental ulcer in a well patient is managed with blood pressure control and interval imaging.
quiz.explain: Dissection, intramural haematoma and penetrating ulcer form one family, united by a media that has been breached, and they interconvert: an ulcer can produce a haematoma, a haematoma can develop an ulcer-like projection, and either can progress to frank dissection, pseudoaneurysm or rupture. That is why they are read together and why interval imaging is the common thread in management. One distinction is worth guarding. A de novo penetrating ulcer, in an atherosclerotic aorta with a focal contrast outpouching through calcified plaque, is not the same as an ulcer-like projection arising within an established intramural haematoma, which is a marker of instability in a lesion already being followed. The imaging appearance overlaps; the history separates them, which is one more argument for naming the prior studies in the report.

quiz.prompt: A department's chest pain protocol covers the aortic arch to the diaphragm with a single gated arterial phase, and a patient with a proven type A dissection is taken to theatre on that study. The surgeon asks for the scan to be repeated before the anaesthetic. What is the surgeon most likely to be missing?
choices: The extent of the flap and the state of the iliac vessels
The calibre of the pulmonary arteries at the hilum
The pattern of coronary calcification in the septum
The volume of contrast in the collecting systems
quiz.answer: The extent of the flap and the state of the iliac vessels
quiz.explain: A type A repair is done on cardiopulmonary bypass and needs an arterial cannulation site, so the surgeon needs the whole aorta down to the femoral vessels, and needs to know which of them is perfused by the true lumen. They also need the arch branches, since a flap in the innominate or a carotid changes the perfusion strategy and predicts stroke; the coronary ostia; the pericardium; and the aortic valve and root dimensions. The recommended range for suspected acute aortic syndrome is therefore from the thoracic inlet through to the femoral heads, with gating at least through the chest. Extending the range costs one more spiral and some dose, and it saves a second scan on a patient who has no time to spare for one. The general lesson is to protocol for the question rather than for the region where the pain is: the anatomy the referrer must act on is nearly always larger than the anatomy the symptom points to.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old presents with severe chest pain and inferior ST elevation. The cardiology team is preparing for primary percutaneous coronary intervention when the chest radiograph is reported as showing a widened mediastinum, and the blood pressure is found to differ by 30 mmHg between the arms. Set out the concern, and what it changes about the immediate plan.
quiz.answer: The concern is a type A dissection extending into a coronary ostium, most often the right, which is why the electrocardiogram shows inferior infarction: the dissection is the cause and the infarct is its complication. It matters because the reflex treatment for that electrocardiogram - thrombolysis, or dual antiplatelet therapy with heparin before angiography - is close to lethal in a dissected aorta that may already be leaking into the pericardium. The plan changes to immediate cross-sectional confirmation before any antithrombotic treatment: an electrocardiogram-gated CT angiogram from the thoracic inlet to the femoral heads, or transoesophageal echocardiography if the patient is too unstable to move, with cardiac surgery alerted in parallel rather than afterwards. The clinical features that should trigger that pause are the pressure or pulse differential between limbs, the widened mediastinum, pain that was maximal at onset or that has migrated, a new diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, and any focal neurological deficit.
quiz.explain: This is the highest-stakes overlap in acute cardiac imaging, and it runs in both directions: a dissection can present as an infarct, and the treatment for one is dangerous in the other. The right coronary is involved more often than the left because the dissection commonly propagates along the greater curvature of the ascending aorta towards it, which is why inferior ST elevation is the pattern to be suspicious of. The radiologist's contribution is to protect the pause - a chest radiograph reported promptly, and a gated CT that answers the aortic question and the coronary question on the same acquisition. Be aware of the counter-risk, since it is what makes the decision hard: delaying reperfusion in a genuine infarct costs myocardium, so the pause is justified by the specific clinical features above, not by generalised caution in every inferior infarct.

nodes.title: Cardiac MRI: Function, Oedema and Late Enhancement
nodes.goal: Read a cardiac MRI by its sequences, use the late enhancement pattern to separate ischaemic from non-ischaemic disease, and call viability, oedema and iron with the numbers that go with them.

quiz.prompt: A short-axis cine stack is contoured slice by slice and summed by the method of discs. End-diastolic volume is 210 mL and end-systolic volume is 130 mL. Report the left ventricular ejection fraction as a percentage, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Stroke volume is 210 minus 130, which is 80 mL, and ejection fraction is 80 divided by 210, or 38.1 per cent. Cardiac MRI is the reference standard for this number because summing discs across the whole ventricle makes no assumption about its shape, which is exactly where echocardiographic estimates go wrong in a remodelled or aneurysmal heart. Two habits protect the figure. Choose the basal slice consistently, because including or dropping one basal slice moves the volumes more than any other decision, and it is the commonest source of disagreement between two readers of the same study. And state your convention for the papillary muscles and trabeculae, since counting them as blood pool rather than as myocardium raises the reported volumes and shifts the fraction by several points. That matters here: 38 per cent sits just above the 35 per cent band that drives primary-prevention defibrillator decisions, so a technical difference of three points has a real consequence for the patient.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old with a dilated, globally hypokinetic left ventricle and unobstructed coronary arteries has a linear band of late enhancement running through the middle of the septal wall and sparing the subendocardium. Ejection fraction is 34 per cent. What does that band add to the decision in front of you?
quiz.answer: It marks non-ischaemic scar and raises the arrhythmic risk
choices: It marks non-ischaemic scar and raises the arrhythmic risk
It marks a small old infarct in the septal perforator bed
It marks acute oedema and calls for repeat imaging in weeks
It marks a nulling error and should be left out of the report
quiz.explain: The one rule that organises late enhancement is the layer it starts in. Ischaemic necrosis advances as a wavefront from the subendocardium outwards, so an infarct always takes the innermost layer and always sits inside a coronary artery territory; enhancement that spares the subendocardium cannot be an infarct, whatever the coronary anatomy suggests. That is why the septal perforator answer fails here. Mid-wall septal fibrosis is the characteristic non-ischaemic pattern in dilated cardiomyopathy, present in roughly a third of these patients, and it is not merely descriptive: it is associated with ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death independently of ejection fraction, so it belongs in the conversation about a defibrillator rather than in a list of incidental findings. Oedema is a T2 question, not a late enhancement one, and a nulling error is a diffuse grey wash across the whole myocardium rather than a discrete band with clean borders, which is what the inversion-time scout and a phase-sensitive reconstruction are there to settle.

quiz.prompt: On the inversion-time scout of a 74-year-old with concentric wall thickening and low voltages on the ECG, the myocardium darkens before the blood pool does, and the ten-minute images show diffuse enhancement of the subendocardial layer around both ventricles. Say what this gadolinium behaviour indicates and what you would ask the referring team to arrange.
quiz.answer: The reversed nulling and the diffuse subendocardial enhancement indicate cardiac amyloid, because amyloid expands the interstitium and holds gadolinium while clearing it fast from the blood; ask the team for bone scintigraphy with a DPD or PYP tracer and a serum and urine light chain screen.
quiz.explain: Amyloid deposition expands the extracellular space enormously, so the myocardium takes up and holds gadolinium while the blood clears it quickly. The result is the abnormal kinetics you have just seen: on the scout, myocardium nulls at a shorter inversion time than blood, which is the reverse of every normal study, and the late images show enhancement that is global and subendocardial rather than confined to one artery's territory, progressing to transmural in advanced disease. Native T1 and extracellular volume are raised strikingly, often above 40 per cent, and extracellular volume tracks amyloid burden well enough to follow treatment. The next step is not a biopsy but a fork: bone-avid tracer scintigraphy that is strongly positive with a negative light chain screen supports transthyretin amyloid without histology, whereas abnormal light chains mean AL amyloid, which is a haematological emergency and must be excluded first rather than assumed away.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old man has chest pain and a raised troponin ten days after a coryzal illness, with normal coronary arteries. The study shows enhancement in the subepicardial half of the basal inferolateral wall and regionally raised T2 in the same segments. What does the raised T2 add to the enhancement finding?
quiz.answer: It dates the injury as acute and meets an oedema criterion
choices: It dates the injury as acute and meets an oedema criterion
It confirms an infarct in the obtuse marginal territory instead
It indicates iron deposition and should prompt T2* mapping
It reflects fat within the wall and needs a fat-saturated repeat
quiz.explain: The 2018 revision of the Lake Louise criteria pairs the two kinds of evidence: one T2-based marker of oedema, either regional high signal on T2-weighted imaging or a raised T2 map value, together with one T1-based marker of injury, being raised native T1, raised extracellular volume, or non-ischaemic late enhancement. Both halves are present here, so this is acute myocardial inflammation rather than an old scar, and that distinction drives the advice on abstaining from competitive exercise for three to six months and on when to rescan. The distribution does the other half of the work: subepicardial and inferolateral is the classic myocarditis pattern, and its sparing of the subendocardium is what excludes infarction. Iron shortens T2 and T2* and makes myocardium dark, so it moves the signal the other way. Fat is bright on T1, drops out with fat saturation, and does not belong to this presentation.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and new second-degree heart block has patchy enhancement in the basal septum and in the epicardial half of the lateral wall, with a further focus in the right ventricular free wall. Stress perfusion is normal. What should follow from this study?
quiz.answer: Refer for FDG PET after a high-fat, low-carbohydrate preparation
choices: Refer for FDG PET after a high-fat, low-carbohydrate preparation
Refer for invasive angiography to exclude three-vessel disease
Repeat the scan in six weeks to look for resolution of oedema
Reassure and discharge, as insertion point scar is a benign finding
quiz.explain: Multifocal enhancement that ignores coronary territories, favours the basal septum and the epicardial layer, and crosses into the right ventricle, in a patient with hilar nodes and conduction disease, is cardiac sarcoidosis until proved otherwise; basal septal involvement is what interrupts the conduction system and produces the block. Late enhancement marks scar, and scar in sarcoid predicts ventricular arrhythmia and death, so this study has already changed the patient's risk category and opens the defibrillator conversation. What it cannot say is whether anything is still burning, and that is the question immunosuppression turns on. FDG PET with a preparation that starves normal myocardium of glucose, typically a prolonged fast on a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet with heparin, separates active inflammation from inert scar. Angiography answers a question the normal perfusion study has already closed, and watchful waiting in a patient with heart block is not a safe plan.

quiz.prompt: In the mid-inferior segment of a patient being assessed before revascularisation, the late enhancement occupies 5.6 mm of a wall that measures 8.0 mm thick at end-diastole. Report the transmural extent of the scar as a percentage of wall thickness, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 5.6 divided by 8.0 is 0.70, so the scar occupies 70 per cent of the wall. The transmurality of enhancement, not the presence of it, is what predicts recovery: segments with scar through less than a quarter of the wall recover contraction after revascularisation in the large majority of cases, segments beyond half are unlikely to, and the band between is genuinely uncertain and best reported as such rather than dressed up as a decision. At 70 per cent this segment should be reported as unlikely to recover. Two cautions travel with the rule. Thin, chronically scarred walls make the denominator small and the percentage unstable, so measure at end-diastole and say if the wall is thinned below about 5.5 mm, which is itself a poor sign. And dysfunction without any enhancement is stunned or hibernating myocardium, which is viable and should recover, so a segment that contracts poorly with a clean late enhancement image is an argument for revascularisation rather than against it.

quiz.prompt: During adenosine stress first-pass perfusion a thin dark rim appears along the subendocardium of the whole left ventricle at the moment of peak myocardial enhancement, persists for two heartbeats and has gone by the time the myocardium is fully enhanced. Rest perfusion and late enhancement are normal. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: A dark rim artefact, so the perfusion study is reported as normal
choices: A dark rim artefact, so the perfusion study is reported as normal
Circumferential subendocardial ischaemia from three-vessel disease
An inadequate adenosine dose, so the stress should be repeated
A subendocardial infarct that the late enhancement has missed
quiz.explain: The dark rim artefact lives at the boundary between bright blood and dark myocardium, where truncation of the Fourier series and a little motion produce a ringing band. Its signature is timing and thickness: it appears at the instant of maximal contrast gradient, is one or two pixels thick, follows the phase-encode direction, and disappears within a few beats. True hypoperfusion behaves differently. It persists well beyond peak enhancement, is thicker, and either matches a coronary territory or, in the balanced case, is genuinely circumferential and accompanied by symptoms, ST change and splenic switch-off confirming that the vasodilator worked. Balanced ischaemia in three-vessel disease is a real trap, and quantitative perfusion mapping in millilitres per gram per minute is what defeats it, since relative comparison has nothing normal left to compare against. An infarct invisible on ten-minute enhancement is not a thing; late enhancement is the more sensitive test of the two.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old with transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia has a myocardial T2* of 8 ms and a heavily loaded liver. Ejection fraction is 61 per cent and the ventricle looks entirely unremarkable on the cines. What should this study drive?
quiz.answer: Intensified chelation now, because the myocardium is severely loaded
choices: Intensified chelation now, because the myocardium is severely loaded
No change to chelation, since ventricular function is preserved
A search for myocarditis, since a low T2* indicates active oedema
More transfusion, since a low T2* here indicates poor ventricular filling
quiz.explain: Iron is strongly paramagnetic and destroys signal quickly, so the more iron there is, the shorter T2* becomes. A myocardial T2* below 20 ms indicates myocardial iron loading, and below 10 ms indicates severe loading, a value that carries a substantial risk of heart failure and arrhythmia within the following year. The whole clinical value of the measurement is that it turns abnormal before the ventricle does, so a normal ejection fraction is not reassurance, it is the expected finding in the window where intervention still works. Note also that liver and heart load and unload on different timescales, so ferritin and liver iron cannot stand in for the cardiac measurement in either direction: a heavily loaded liver with a normal heart is common, and so is the reverse. Iron shortens T2 and T2* rather than lengthening them, which is what separates this from the bright, oedematous myocardium of inflammation.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old man with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, proteinuria and burning neuropathic pain in his hands has a native T1 well below the normal range for your scanner, with enhancement confined to the basal inferolateral epicardium. Explain why the native T1 value is the measurement that settles the differential here.
quiz.answer: Almost everything that thickens myocardium, including amyloid, hypertension and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, raises native T1, so a low value points to Fabry disease, where stored glycolipid shortens T1; confirm with alpha-galactosidase A activity and genetic testing.
quiz.explain: Native T1 is a mapped tissue property, and the direction it moves is more informative than its exact value. Oedema, fibrosis, infiltration by amyloid and the fibre disarray of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy all lengthen it, so almost every cause of a thick wall raises native T1. Very few things shorten it, and the ones that do are storage: the globotriaosylceramide of Fabry disease, iron, and fat. In a man with hypertrophy, proteinuria and acroparaesthesia, a low native T1 with basal inferolateral late enhancement is the picture of Fabry, and that matters because it is one of the few causes of left ventricular hypertrophy with a specific treatment, in enzyme replacement or chaperone therapy, which is wasted if the case is filed as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. One caveat to carry: once fibrosis and oedema supervene in that lateral wall they push T1 back up, so a pseudo-normal segmental value in advanced disease does not exclude it, and pairing the map with T2* keeps iron from being mistaken for it.

quiz.prompt: A 66-year-old diabetic has two separate areas of late enhancement: one subendocardial and confined to the inferior wall and inferior septum, and one running through the middle of the anteroseptal wall while sparing the subendocardium. Say what you conclude from having both, and what your report should say.
quiz.answer: The subendocardial inferior enhancement is an old right coronary territory infarct, while the anteroseptal mid-wall band is non-ischaemic fibrosis, so report both patterns separately rather than forcing one diagnosis, and state the transmural extent of the infarct.
quiz.explain: Readers are taught to sort a study into ischaemic or non-ischaemic, and most studies do sort. Some patients have both, and the mistake is to let the first pattern found suppress the second. Apply the rule segment by segment: enhancement that involves the subendocardium and sits within a single artery's territory is infarction, and the inferior wall with the inferior septum is the right coronary distribution. Enhancement that spares the subendocardium is not infarction whatever else it is, and a mid-wall anteroseptal band belongs to the non-ischaemic group, in this patient most likely a cardiomyopathic process alongside his coronary disease. Reporting both matters practically, because the ischaemic component with its transmural extent drives the revascularisation discussion while the non-ischaemic scar carries independent arrhythmic weight, and a report that averages them into one diagnosis loses both.

quiz.prompt: A 33-year-old with asymmetric septal hypertrophy of 19 mm has patchy mid-wall enhancement at both right ventricular insertion points and through the hypertrophied septum, quantified at 22 per cent of left ventricular mass. Conventional risk assessment leaves him in an intermediate band. How does the enhancement bear on the decision?
quiz.answer: Extensive scar is a risk modifier that favours a defibrillator discussion
choices: Extensive scar is a risk modifier that favours a defibrillator discussion
Insertion point scar is expected in hypertrophy and adds nothing here
Scar of this extent argues against hypertrophic disease altogether
Scar burden counts chiefly when it sits in a coronary artery territory
quiz.explain: The point is the burden, not the presence. Small foci at the right ventricular insertion points are common in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and in other causes of right ventricular pressure loading, and on their own they carry little weight. Extensive enhancement is different: in the 2020 American guideline on hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, late enhancement of roughly 15 per cent of left ventricular mass or more is one of the modifiers used to tip a decision when conventional risk assessment, built on family history of sudden death, unexplained syncope, maximal wall thickness, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, apical aneurysm and systolic impairment, has not settled it. At 22 per cent this study moves the discussion towards a defibrillator. That the scar ignores coronary territories is consistent with the diagnosis rather than against it, and cardiac MRI is also earning its place here by measuring the true maximal wall thickness that echocardiography often understates and by finding apical aneurysms that echocardiography misses.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these cardiac MRI sequences in the order a standard adult protocol acquires them, from patient setup to the last series.
quiz.answer: localisers cine-function native-T1-mapping stress-perfusion late-enhancement
quiz.explain: Everything that has to be free of gadolinium comes first, and the order is dictated by that one constraint rather than by convenience. Localisers set the cardiac axes, the cines then give volumes, mass and wall motion, and native T1 and T2 mapping follow while the tissue is still untouched, because a single dose of contrast makes native mapping uninterpretable for the rest of the day. Contrast enters the study at stress perfusion, and late enhancement is acquired roughly ten minutes after the last dose, once normal myocardium has washed out and scar has not; imaged at three minutes it is not late enhancement, and normal myocardium is still bright. If extracellular volume is wanted, the post-contrast T1 map sits at the end, around fifteen minutes, paired with a haematocrit drawn the same day, since the calculation converts the myocardium-to-blood ratio into a tissue fraction using it. Get the order wrong and the numbers cannot be salvaged by any amount of post-processing.

nodes.title: Cardiac Masses, Thrombus and Devices
nodes.goal: Separate thrombus from tumour on cardiac MRI, place the common cardiac and pericardial masses and physiologies, and read implanted cardiac devices well enough to catch their complications.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old five months after an anterior infarct has a 2 cm mass sitting on the akinetic apical endocardium. First-pass perfusion shows no signal within it. Say which single sequence you would add and what result would let you report thrombus with confidence.
quiz.answer: Add a late enhancement acquisition with a long inversion time of about 600 ms: thrombus is avascular and takes up no gadolinium, so it stays uniformly black against grey myocardium and bright blood, whereas a tumour would enhance.
quiz.explain: Thrombus has no blood supply, so it does not perfuse on the first pass, does not enhance early, and retains nothing late. That is the whole discriminator, and the long inversion time sequence is simply the way to make it visible. At the standard inversion time of roughly 250 to 300 ms, chosen to null normal myocardium, thrombus is dark too and can hide or be mistaken for scar. Lengthening the inversion time to about 600 ms drives normal myocardium up to mid grey and leaves the avascular thrombus conspicuously black, and it also separates true thrombus from the slow-flow signal that collects in an apical aneurysm. Corroborate with context rather than relying on one sequence: thrombus sits on akinetic or aneurysmal wall or in a fibrillating appendage, is broad based, and does not invade. A mass that enhances is not thrombus, however apical it sits and however tempting the history.

quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old in sinus rhythm has recurrent syncope on standing and a 3 cm left atrial mass on a narrow stalk arising close to the fossa ovalis. It swings through the mitral orifice on the cines, is heterogeneously bright on T2 and enhances patchily. What should this study lead to?
quiz.answer: Refer for surgical excision, since this behaves as an atrial myxoma
choices: Refer for surgical excision, since this behaves as an atrial myxoma
Start anticoagulation and rescan in three months for resolution
Arrange a PET-CT, since a stalked atrial mass suggests a sarcoma
Leave it, as a prominent Chiari network needs no further action
quiz.explain: Every feature here points one way. Myxoma is the commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults, about three quarters of them in the left atrium, characteristically attached by a stalk to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis, mobile enough to prolapse through the mitral valve and produce positional syncope or obstruction, bright on T2 because the matrix is myxoid, and enhancing because it has a blood supply. That last point is what excludes thrombus, which is avascular and would neither enhance nor sit on a stalk in a patient in sinus rhythm with a normal-sized atrium, so anticoagulating and waiting risks an embolic stroke or sudden death from valve obstruction while the diagnosis is on the screen. Sarcoma is typically right-sided, broad based, invasive, and comes with a haemorrhagic effusion. A Chiari network is a fine right atrial web. Excision is curative, and multiple or atypically sited myxomas should raise the Carney complex, which brings family screening with it.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old with two embolic strokes and no atrial fibrillation has a 9 mm mobile mass with a frond-like surface on the aortic aspect of the aortic valve. She is afebrile and blood cultures are negative. What should the report drive?
quiz.answer: Surgical referral, since a mobile left-sided valve tumour keeps embolising
choices: Surgical referral, since a mobile left-sided valve tumour keeps embolising
Six weeks of antibiotics on the assumption that this is endocarditis
Anticoagulation alone, since a mass on a valve is usually a thrombus
Discharge, since a lesion of this size carries a negligible embolic risk
quiz.explain: Papillary fibroelastoma is the commonest tumour of the cardiac valves, usually under 15 mm, pedunculated, with a shaggy frond-like surface that shimmers on cine imaging and often gives a stippled edge. Its danger is embolic rather than haemodynamic, and the risk tracks mobility and left-sided position far more than size, which is why a mobile aortic valve lesion in a patient who has already thrown two emboli is usually excised, often with the valve preserved. The mimic that matters is a vegetation, and it is separated clinically rather than by imaging: fever, positive cultures, valve destruction, regurgitation, and abscess or pseudoaneurysm formation. Treating this as endocarditis without an organism commits the patient to six weeks of antibiotics and leaves the source of embolism in place.
