quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old with new temporal headache, jaw claudication and an ESR of 88 has temporal artery ultrasound showing hypoechoic circumferential wall thickening around the lumen that does not disappear when the probe compresses the vessel. What follows?
quiz.answer: The halo and compression signs support giant cell arteritis: start steroids without awaiting biopsy
choices: The halo and compression signs support giant cell arteritis: start steroids without awaiting biopsy
The appearance is within normal limits, as the wall is commonly thickened at this age
This is atherosclerotic plaque: report the eccentric calcified disease and modify risk factors
A vein has been mistaken for the artery: repeat the scan with a lower frequency probe
quiz.explain: The halo sign is a hypoechoic, homogeneous, circumferential rim of oedematous inflamed wall around the lumen, and the compression sign is its persistence when the probe compresses the vessel, which distinguishes it from an incompressible lumen. Cut-offs of roughly 0.4 mm for the temporal artery and 1.0 mm for the axillary artery are widely used, and both temporal and axillary arteries should be examined because large-vessel involvement is common and can be the only finding. Atherosclerotic disease is eccentric, echogenic or calcified, not a uniform hypoechoic ring. Do not delay steroids for imaging or biopsy in a patient with visual symptoms or classic features, but do image early, because the halo can resolve within days of starting treatment.

quiz.prompt: Three years after endovascular aneurysm repair, surveillance CT shows the sac has grown by 8 mm. The arterial phase shows no contrast outside the graft, but the delayed phase shows a focus of contrast at the posterior sac periphery continuous with a lumbar artery. How do you report it, and what should happen next?
quiz.answer: Type II endoleak from a lumbar artery, and the documented sac growth makes it treatable
choices: Type II endoleak from a lumbar artery, and the documented sac growth makes it treatable
Type I endoleak at the proximal attachment site, requiring urgent placement of a cuff
Type III endoleak through a fabric or junctional defect, needing urgent relining of the graft
Endotension with no demonstrable leak, so continue with routine annual surveillance imaging
quiz.explain: The delayed phase is what makes this diagnosis, which is why a single arterial acquisition is not adequate surveillance: retrograde filling through lumbar or inferior mesenteric branches is slow and frequently invisible early. Type II endoleaks are the commonest and most are benign, so the trigger for treatment is not the leak itself but sac behaviour, conventionally growth of 5 mm or more, at which point the branch is embolised. Type I leaks arise at the proximal or distal attachment zones and type III at a fabric tear or component junction; both pressurise the sac directly and are treated promptly. Endotension is sac expansion with no visible leak, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion reached only after a properly delayed study has been reviewed.

nodes.title: TAVI Planning CT
nodes.goal: Size the annulus, judge coronary and conduction risk, and choose the access route.

quiz.prompt: Two readers measure the same aortic annulus. One takes a 22 mm diameter off a single long-axis view of the root; the other reconstructs the plane through the three leaflet nadirs and reports an area-derived diameter of 25 mm. A valve chosen on the 22 mm figure leaks around its rim afterwards. What went wrong?
quiz.answer: A single linear diameter is just one chord across an oval ring
quiz.explain: The annulus is a virtual basal ring - a plane joining the three cusp nadirs, with no anatomical structure lying in it - and it is habitually oval, with a major-to-minor ratio of roughly 1.2 to 1.3. Any single long-axis view cuts that ring along one chord, and which chord it catches depends on how the plane happens to fall through a structure tilted in two directions, so the figure it yields is not the ring's size. Deriving a diameter from the traced area or perimeter uses the whole contour instead of one chord, which is why sizing charts are built on those figures and not on a caliper measurement. Note the direction of the error in 'Area-derived diameter overstates a ring that is not circular': by the isoperimetric inequality the area-derived diameter is the smallest of the conventions, not the largest.
choices: A single linear diameter is just one chord across an oval ring
An oblique long-axis cut stretches the ring along its long axis
Area-derived diameter overstates a ring that is not circular
The annulus shrinks once a stiff wire has crossed the valve

quiz.prompt: A planning dataset is reconstructed only in mid-diastole, where the coronary arteries are sharpest, and the annulus is traced there. What does sizing from that phase invite?
quiz.answer: Undersizing, with a leak around the frame or embolisation
quiz.explain: The basal ring is distensible and reaches its largest, roundest configuration in systole, when the outflow tract is pressurised; in diastole it is smaller and more oval. Measuring in diastole therefore biases the operator towards a smaller prosthesis, and a frame that fails to seal against the ring leaks around its outside or, if grossly small, embolises. The systolic-to-diastolic difference in annular area averages some 5 to 8%, so it need not cross a size boundary - but it is a one-way bias, and it runs towards the error that leaks. 'Oversizing, with rupture of the annulus during expansion' is the hazard of the opposite mistake, as is conduction block.
choices: Oversizing, with rupture of the annulus during expansion
Accurate sizing, since the fibrous annulus holds its shape
Undersizing, with a leak around the frame or embolisation
Oversizing, with new left bundle branch block after release

quiz.prompt: Planning CT shows a bulky shelf of calcium in the outflow tract just below the annulus. The operator intends a balloon-expandable valve at more than 20% area oversizing. What is the particular hazard of that combination, and what does it argue for?
quiz.answer: Annular rupture; cut the oversizing or use a self-expanding frame
quiz.explain: A balloon-expandable frame reaches its nominal size whatever is in the way, so the force of expansion is taken by whatever will not move. Rigid subannular calcium does not move: it is levered outward into the aortic root or the anterior mitral leaflet, and rupture there is frequently fatal. The two factors multiply - it was heavy outflow-tract calcification together with area oversizing beyond about a fifth that marked out the ruptures in Barbanti et al. (Circulation 2013), not either feature alone, which is why a modestly oversized frame in the same calcified root is a different proposition. A self-expanding frame applies gentler, sustained radial force and conforms around the calcium instead of displacing it, so it is the usual answer alongside restraint about oversizing and post-dilatation. 'Device migration; raise the oversizing and post-dilate the frame' inverts the remedy: more radial force against immovable calcium is the mechanism of the injury, not the escape from it.
choices: Coronary occlusion; place a protective wire in the left main stem
Annular rupture; cut the oversizing or use a self-expanding frame
Device migration; raise the oversizing and post-dilate the frame
Leaflet thrombosis; extend anticoagulation beyond the usual course

quiz.prompt: The left coronary ostium sits 8 mm above the annular plane, the left sinus measures 27 mm across, and the left cusp is 11 mm long and densely calcified. By what mechanism is that coronary threatened?
quiz.answer: The swept-aside cusp is longer than the ostium is high, in a sinus too small to hold it
quiz.explain: TAVI does not remove the native valve; it pins the diseased cusp against the sinus wall. The cusp is a hinged flap, so it sweeps up to a height set by its own length. If that length exceeds the ostial height and the sinus is too shallow to accommodate the displaced tissue, the cusp lies over the ostium like a lid, and a rigid calcified cusp holds that position. Open frame cells are not themselves obstructive, which is why strut position is a much weaker concern than cusp length, ostial height and sinus width taken together.
choices: The metal struts of the frame lie across the ostium and obstruct flow through the cells
The prosthetic leaflets swing out into the sinus and press on the ostium during systole
Calcium showers into the coronary as the balloon crushes the native cusp against the wall
The swept-aside cusp is longer than the ostium is high, in a sinus too small to hold it

quiz.prompt: A systolic annular contour is planimetered at 430 square millimetres. Treating that contour as a circle of the same area, what diameter in millimetres does it give? Give it to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The area-derived diameter is the diameter of the circle of equal area: d = 2 x sqrt(A / pi) = 2 x sqrt(430 / 3.1416) = 23.3986, so 23.4 mm to one decimal place. For any contour that is not a perfect circle this figure is smaller than the perimeter-derived diameter, and the gap widens as the ring becomes more oval - which is why stating which convention a number came from matters as much as the number itself.

quiz.prompt: Planning CT before TAVI shows a membranous septum only 3 mm long. Identify the structure that measurement locates, say what it predicts about the patient's course, and explain how it should shape the implantation plan.
quiz.answer: The His bundle penetrates at the inferior border of the membranous septum, so a short septum places the conduction tissue high in the outflow tract, immediately beneath where the frame will sit. If implantation depth exceeds the membranous septal length, the frame presses on the bundle and left bundle branch block or complete heart block may follow, making a permanent pacemaker likely. The plan should therefore aim for a shallow implant, avoid unnecessary oversizing, and provide for prolonged rhythm monitoring afterwards.
quiz.explain: The membranous septum is the roof of the conduction system's course: the bundle of His emerges at its inferior margin, beneath the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps. Its length is therefore a direct measure of how much room lies between the annular plane and the conduction tissue. The quantity that matters in practice is the difference between septal length and implantation depth (Hamdan et al., JACC Cardiovascular Interventions 2015) - a depth greater than the septum is the geometry that predicts pacing, and it is one of the few TAVI risks the operator can still change on the table. Block is a strong risk here rather than a certainty, so the honest plan is a shallow implant plus rhythm monitoring, not a pre-emptive pacemaker.

quiz.prompt: The right external iliac artery has a minimum luminal diameter of 5.0 mm with an unbroken ring of calcium in its wall; the left measures 7.5 mm, is soft-walled, but loops through two tight bends. The delivery sheath is 6.0 mm across. Which route should be taken?
quiz.answer: The left, since a stiff wire straightens bends that hard calcium would not yield to
quiz.explain: Two things decide a transfemoral route: the narrowest luminal diameter along the whole path relative to the sheath, and whether the wall can give. A 6.0 mm sheath in a 5.0 mm lumen is a ratio well above the value at which vascular complications climb, and circumferential calcium removes the vessel's capacity to stretch, so the wall dissects or ruptures rather than dilating. Tortuosity in a soft, adequately sized vessel is the far weaker constraint: a stiff wire straightens it. Alternative access is for cases where neither side offers calibre or compliance.
choices: The left, since a stiff wire straightens bends that hard calcium would not yield to
The right, since a short narrowed segment stretches once the sheath is pushed through
The left, once the two tight bends have been stented open at an earlier sitting
Both sides fail here, so the case should go to a transcaval or axillary route

quiz.prompt: An eGFR of 28 forces a reduced-contrast protocol, and the radiographer proposes dropping the aortic run from 120 kVp to 80 kVp. Why does that allow less iodine for the same luminal opacification?
quiz.answer: Photon energies sit nearer iodine's K-edge, so each gram attenuates more
quiz.explain: Iodine's K-edge sits at about 33 keV. Lowering the tube potential shifts the spectrum down towards it, photoelectric absorption per gram of iodine rises steeply, and the same milligram of iodine yields a higher CT number - so the injected load can be cut for equal opacification. The price is noise: fewer and softer photons reach the detector, so tube current must rise to compensate, and the trade works best in slimmer patients. 'Beam hardening disappears at low kV, so calcium stops masking the lumen' is the trap and is backwards - beam hardening from calcium is worse at low kVp, not better. 'Low-energy photons slip past iodine, so the lumen is left looking brighter' is self-contradictory: photons that pass through would leave the lumen darker, not brighter.
choices: Fewer photons reach the detector, so the reconstruction lifts image contrast
Low-energy photons slip past iodine, so the lumen is left looking brighter
Photon energies sit nearer iodine's K-edge, so each gram attenuates more
Beam hardening disappears at low kV, so calcium stops masking the lumen

quiz.prompt: The planning CT is used to compute the fluoroscopic angulation that shows the annulus edge-on. The report gives not one gantry position but a curve of paired LAO/RAO and cranial/caudal values. Why is there a curve rather than a single angle, and what does that let the operator do?
quiz.answer: Any beam lying in the annular plane qualifies, so overlap can be dodged
quiz.explain: The three cusp nadirs define a plane, and a plane contains not one direction but a whole family of them: any X-ray beam lying in that plane sees the annulus edge-on and projects the three nadirs onto a single line. The angulations that satisfy this therefore trace a continuous curve of paired LAO/RAO and cranial/caudal values rather than one gantry position, and that freedom is the useful part - the operator slides along the curve to a projection that also keeps the spine, the pacing wire and overlapping structures out of the way. Cardiac phase and respiration are separate variables and generate no such curve, and the curve is a property of the patient's root, not of the device. Hunting for the same view in the laboratory instead means repeated aortic root injections, spending contrast and dose on a patient who often has little renal reserve to spare.
choices: Any beam lying in the annular plane qualifies, so overlap can be dodged
The curve allows for cardiac motion, so a phase can be picked to suit
Each point on it suits one valve size, so the chart follows the device
The curve spans the respiratory range, so a breath-hold can be avoided

quiz.prompt: A Sievers type 1 bicuspid valve has a heavily calcified raphe between the fused cusps. The annular area points to a 26 mm balloon-expandable valve, but the intercommissural distance a few millimetres above the annulus is appreciably smaller. What follows if the annular figure alone is used?
quiz.answer: The frame is held at the raphe above the annulus and expands unevenly there
quiz.explain: In a tricuspid valve the basal ring is the narrowest point the frame must pass, so annular sizing works. In bicuspid disease the constraining level is often supra-annular, at the calcified raphe between the fused cusps, and it can be several millimetres narrower than the annulus. Size to the annulus alone and the frame is effectively oversized where it is actually gripped: it deforms into an ellipse, seals poorly and leaks, and the load falls on a rigid calcified raphe with rupture as the extreme. Note that 'The frame is undersized throughout and drifts up into the ascending aorta' has the geometry backwards - the frame is over-, not undersized at the level that grips it. This is why bicuspid planning adds a measurement at the supra-annular level rather than trusting the basal ring.
choices: The frame seats too low, so that the basal ring carries the whole radial load
The frame is undersized throughout and drifts up into the ascending aorta
The frame expands fully but the native raphe covers a coronary ostium
The frame is held at the raphe above the annulus and expands unevenly there

quiz.prompt: A systolic annular contour is planimetered at 470 square millimetres. The operator is considering a balloon-expandable valve whose fully expanded frame is a circle 26 mm in diameter. By what percentage would that frame oversize the annulus by area? Answer as a percentage, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The expanded frame has an area of pi x 13 squared = 530.9 square millimetres, and the oversizing is (530.9 - 470) / 470 = 0.1296, that is 13.0 per cent. Read that against the two failure modes on either side of it. Too little oversizing and the frame does not seal, so blood runs around its outside or the device embolises; balloon-expandable sizing charts therefore aim at a modest positive figure rather than a neutral one. Too much, and the expansion force is taken by whatever will not move, which is why oversizing beyond roughly a fifth in an outflow tract loaded with calcium is the combination associated with annular rupture. Note also that the number is only as good as the phase it came from: measure the same annulus in diastole and it will look smaller, so the calculated oversizing will read falsely high and tempt you into a valve that is actually too small.

quiz.prompt: Planning CT shows both iliofemoral routes to be unusable: the right external iliac artery is 4.5 mm with an unbroken ring of calcium and the left common iliac artery is occluded. The dataset already covers chest, abdomen and pelvis. Which alternative access routes would you assess on it, and for each, what decides whether it is usable?
quiz.answer: The subclavian or axillary artery is judged on its minimum luminal diameter along the whole course, on calcium and tortuosity, and on whether a patent internal mammary graft arises from it that the sheath would jail. The transcaval route needs a segment of infrarenal aorta lying close to the inferior vena cava with a calcium-free window on the aortic wall to cross, and the distance between the two vessels measured. Transapical access is judged on the left ventricular apex and the rib space overlying it, and transaortic or carotid access on a calcium-free ascending aorta or a patent carotid artery.
quiz.explain: The planning dataset already contains every one of these answers, which is why a report that stops at the femoral arteries wastes the scan. Each route has one dominant constraint. For the axillary and subclavian it is calibre and the internal mammary graft, since covering the origin of a graft that is feeding the heart is a serious matter. For transcaval it is the window: the crossing point must be aortic wall free of calcium, and the plan depends on knowing exactly where along the aorta that window sits. For transapical and transaortic it is the chest, and both are more invasive routes that have become uncommon as the others have improved. Say which route the anatomy supports and give the numbers behind it, rather than reporting only that the femoral route has failed.

quiz.prompt: Eighteen months after TAVI a patient is well and the echocardiographic gradients across the valve are unchanged from discharge. A CT performed for an unrelated reason shows crescentic hypoattenuated thickening on two of the three prosthetic leaflets. What does this represent, what acquisition would characterise it properly, and what should be done about it?
quiz.answer: This is hypoattenuated leaflet thickening, subclinical thrombus laid down on the aortic aspect of the cusps. Characterising it properly needs a retrospectively gated four-dimensional acquisition, because what matters is whether leaflet motion is restricted as well as thickened. With an unchanged gradient and no symptoms, the finding is followed rather than treated: most such thickening is subclinical and much of it resolves. Anticoagulation reliably clears it, but routine anticoagulation after TAVI produced more bleeding and death than an antiplatelet strategy in trial, so it is reserved for a rising gradient, restricted motion, or a thromboembolic event.
quiz.explain: Two words do the work here. Thickening is a static finding on a single phase; restricted motion is a dynamic one and needs images across the cardiac cycle, which is the whole reason a four-dimensional study is asked for rather than a single systolic phase. The distinction matters because the two carry different weight: thickening alone, with normal gradients, is common and mostly of no consequence, whereas reduced leaflet excursion with a climbing gradient is the beginning of valve failure. The GALILEO trial settled the management question in the unhelpful direction radiologists must nonetheless respect: a routine anticoagulant strategy after TAVI was worse, not better, than antiplatelet therapy. So the report describes what is seen, states whether motion was assessable, and stops short of prescribing.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a degenerated surgical bioprosthesis is being considered for a valve-in-valve TAVI. Working from the planning CT, explain why coronary obstruction is a greater danger here than in a native valve, and what you would measure to quantify that danger.
quiz.answer: In a native valve the displaced cusp is a short hinged flap and the sinus usually has room to hold it. In a valve-in-valve the failed bioprosthetic leaflets are pinned open by the new frame as a rigid cylinder at the level of the surgical stent posts, so the barrier sits higher, is fixed, and cannot be pushed aside. What is measured is the height of each coronary ostium above the surgical valve ring, the width of the sinus of Valsalva, the height and diameter of the sinotubular junction, and the distance from the projected new frame out to each ostium, together with the design of the failed valve, since externally mounted leaflets sit further out and obstruct more readily.
quiz.explain: The geometry to hold in mind is a cylinder inside a cone. Once the old leaflets are splayed vertically against the new frame, blood can only reach a coronary by passing between that cylinder and the aortic wall, or over the top of it through the sinotubular junction. So three measurements decide the risk together: how high the ostium sits, how much room lies between the projected frame and the ostium, and whether the sinotubular junction is high and wide enough to let flow come over the top. A narrow, low sinotubular junction converts an otherwise acceptable ostial height into a sealed sinus. Where the risk is real, the answer is planned in advance rather than improvised: leaflet laceration before implantation, a protective wire, or a decision that the patient belongs in theatre.

quiz.prompt: Put these vessels into the order a transfemoral delivery system meets them on its way from the groin puncture to the aortic valve.
quiz.answer: common-femoral-artery external-iliac-artery common-iliac-artery abdominal-aorta aortic-arch ascending-aorta
quiz.explain: The route is read retrograde, and the reason to walk it segment by segment is that the narrowest point anywhere along it governs the whole path: a generous common femoral artery is no comfort if the external iliac artery above it is 4 mm. Each segment also has its own question. At the puncture, where the common femoral artery crosses the femoral head and whether its anterior wall is calcified decides whether a closure device will work. The iliac segments give the minimum diameter and the calcium pattern. The abdominal aorta and the arch add atheroma and tortuosity, and a shaggy, ulcerated arch is a stroke risk to be flagged even when the calibre is ample. The ascending aorta and root then hand over to the valve measurements themselves.

nodes.title: Acute Stroke Imaging
nodes.goal: Read the hyperacute stroke CT and CT angiogram, and say what in the images selects this patient for thrombectomy.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old presents with sudden dysphasia and right arm weakness. On the unenhanced CT the left middle cerebral artery looks dense - but so do the right middle cerebral artery, the basilar artery and the superior sagittal sinus, and the brain parenchyma looks unremarkable. The haemoglobin is 197 g/L. What best accounts for the dense vessels?
choices: A high haematocrit raising attenuation throughout the vessels
Thrombus filling the left middle cerebral artery trunk
Mural calcification of the intracranial vessel walls
Iodinated contrast retained from a recent study
quiz.answer: A high haematocrit raising attenuation throughout the vessels
quiz.explain: The discriminator is symmetry and company. A thrombus is one clot in one artery, so the sign is unilateral and is judged by comparing the vessel with its fellow on the same slice; a raised haematocrit raises the attenuation of blood itself, so arteries, veins and dural sinuses rise together, and a dense superior sagittal sinus alongside dense arteries is the giveaway that the finding is in the blood rather than in one lumen. Mural calcification is denser still and sits as a rim in the wall, following the vessel rather than filling it, and it is usually bilateral and irregular. Retained contrast would opacify the vessels far more brightly and would come with a history. The trap in the last sentence of the stem is the normal-looking parenchyma: at ninety minutes a normal brain is entirely compatible with a large ischaemic core, so it argues for proceeding to CT angiography rather than for reassurance.

quiz.prompt: An unenhanced CT two hours after onset of a right hemiplegia shows early ischaemic change in the left insular ribbon, the left lentiform nucleus, and the cortical regions M1, M2 and M5. Every other region of the scoring template is normal. What ASPECTS does this study score? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: ASPECTS starts at 10 and subtracts one point for each of ten regions showing early ischaemic change: caudate, lentiform, internal capsule, insular ribbon and the cortical regions M1 to M3 at the ganglionic level, and M4 to M6 at the level just above the ganglia. Five involved regions leaves 5. The score matters because it stands in for core volume when perfusion imaging is unavailable, and the early-window thrombectomy trials enrolled largely at 6 or above, which is still where the guideline recommendation is strongest. Since 2023, SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT and RESCUE-Japan LIMIT have shown benefit in large cores down to an ASPECTS of about 3, so a low score is now a reason for discussion rather than an automatic exclusion. Two cautions in scoring: count established hypoattenuation or focal swelling rather than a subjective impression, and do not count an old infarct as new.

quiz.prompt: Ninety minutes after a middle cerebral artery occlusion the diffusion-weighted images are unmistakably abnormal while the unenhanced CT of the same territory looks close to normal. Account for the difference in terms of where the water is.
quiz.answer: Arterial occlusion causes energy failure within minutes, the sodium-potassium ATPase stops, and sodium and water move from the extracellular space into the intracellular compartment. This is cytotoxic oedema: total tissue water is barely changed, but water has been redistributed into a compartment where its Brownian motion is hindered, so the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) falls and the DWI signal rises. CT attenuation tracks total tissue water content, which has hardly altered at this stage; it falls only later, once ionic oedema and then breakdown of the blood-brain barrier draw new water into the tissue from the vasculature, which is why frank hypoattenuation lags the diffusion change by hours.
quiz.explain: The two studies are sensitive to different physical quantities, and that is the whole answer: diffusion imaging is sensitive to where water is, CT to how much of it there is. Knowing the time course keeps the reader out of two traps. The ADC falls immediately, reaches its nadir over the first days, pseudonormalises at around a week to ten days as cell lysis and vasogenic oedema raise diffusivity again, and then rises above normal; so a bright DWI with a normal or high ADC late on is T2 shine-through rather than new ischaemia, and a subacute infarct can look deceptively unimpressive on diffusion alone. At the front door the corollary is blunter: a normal CT does not exclude infarction and is not a reason to withhold treatment, whereas a normal DWI in the first hours makes infarction unlikely, with small brainstem lesions and profound hypoperfusion imaged before a core has formed as the exceptions worth remembering.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old wakes at 07:00 unable to speak, having been well at 22:00 the night before. MRI at 08:30 shows a left middle cerebral artery territory lesion that is bright on diffusion-weighted imaging with a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and no corresponding signal change on FLAIR. What does the discrepancy between the two sequences allow you to say?
choices: The lesion is probably less than about 4.5 hours old
The lesion is probably more than twelve hours old
The lesion is an artefact of a poor diffusion trace
The lesion is chronic and unrelated to the symptoms
quiz.answer: The lesion is probably less than about 4.5 hours old
quiz.explain: Diffusion turns positive within minutes, while FLAIR signal follows the rise in tissue water and becomes visible at roughly 4.5 to 6 hours; a lesion that is bright on diffusion but invisible on FLAIR therefore dates itself to the first hours. That mismatch is what the WAKE-UP trial used to select patients with an unknown onset time for thrombolysis, and it found benefit. Here the clock reads nine hours since last seen well and the tissue reads under four and a half - the tissue wins. The near-miss is 'more than twelve hours old', which runs the logic backwards: by twelve hours the FLAIR abnormality would be conspicuous, and a DWI lesion with matching FLAIR change is the appearance that argues against a hyperacute onset. A low ADC is what separates a true diffusion lesion from T2 shine-through, so it is quoted in the stem deliberately.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a suspected large-vessel occlusion arrives nine hours after last being seen well, and the hyperacute protocol runs from the scanner to the angiography suite. Put these acquisitions in the order the protocol performs them.
quiz.answer: unenhanced-CT CT-angiography CT-perfusion digital-subtraction-angiography
quiz.explain: The unenhanced study comes first and answers one question - is there blood? - because everything downstream, thrombolysis above all, depends on that answer, and the same images supply the ASPECTS. CT angiography is second, because finding the occlusion, and seeing the aortic arch and cervical vessels the catheter must travel through, decides whether thrombectomy is possible at all. Perfusion is third and is a selection tool rather than a diagnostic one: in the late window it separates a small core with a large penumbra from a completed infarct. Catheter angiography is last and is part of the treatment. Running perfusion before angiography spends contrast and minutes on a question that only matters once a target exists, and leaving the unenhanced study until last is how a haemorrhage gets thrombolysed.

quiz.prompt: CT perfusion nine hours after onset gives an ischaemic core, defined as relative cerebral blood flow below 30 per cent of the contralateral side, of 25 mL, and a Tmax greater than 6 s volume of 90 mL. What is the mismatch ratio? Give it to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The mismatch ratio is the whole critically hypoperfused volume divided by the core, 90 over 25, which is 3.6; the mismatch volume - tissue at risk but not yet lost - is the difference, 65 mL. DEFUSE 3 selected patients 6 to 16 hours from last seen well with a core under 70 mL, a ratio of at least 1.8 and a mismatch volume of at least 15 mL, and this patient clears each criterion comfortably. DAWN worked out to 24 hours using a clinical-core mismatch instead, pairing age and NIHSS against core volume. Two cautions travel with these maps: Tmax above 6 s marks critically delayed tissue rather than tissue certain to die, and in very early presentations the core map overstates the damage, so a large core in the first couple of hours deserves scepticism rather than an automatic exclusion.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old is found with weakness of the left leg much worse than the left arm, with the face spared, and is apathetic and incontinent of urine. Before the images are reviewed, which arterial territory should be scrutinised first?
choices: The right anterior cerebral artery territory
The right middle cerebral artery territory
The right posterior cerebral artery territory
The right anterior choroidal artery territory
quiz.answer: The right anterior cerebral artery territory
quiz.explain: The homunculus does the work. Leg and perineum lie on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery; face and hand lie on the convexity, which belongs to the middle cerebral artery. A leg-dominant deficit that spares the face is anterior cerebral until proved otherwise, and the apathy and incontinence fit the same vessel, since the medial frontal cortex and anterior cingulate share its supply. Middle cerebral occlusion gives face-and-arm weakness with aphasia or neglect; posterior cerebral gives a homonymous hemianopia and, when the thalamus goes, hemisensory loss; the anterior choroidal artery gives hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia from the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the optic tract, without cortical signs. One corollary: isolated anterior cerebral infarction is uncommon, and bilateral medial frontal infarction should prompt a look for an azygos anterior cerebral artery or for vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

quiz.prompt: A 69-year-old smoker has repeated brief episodes of right arm weakness, worse on standing up. MRI shows a chain of small acute infarcts in a line through the left corona radiata between the lateral ventricle and the cortex, and CT angiography shows a 90 per cent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. Which mechanism does the pattern of the infarcts favour?
choices: Failure of perfusion in the internal borderzone
Artery-to-artery embolism to cortical branches
Lipohyalinosis of a single lenticulostriate vessel
Cardioembolism to the middle cerebral trunk
quiz.answer: Failure of perfusion in the internal borderzone
quiz.explain: Geometry is the argument. The internal borderzone lies in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale, at the far end of the deep perforators and the penetrating pial arterioles - the last field the water reaches. When perfusion pressure falls behind a tight carotid stenosis, infarcts appear there as a rosary of lesions strung in a line, and the postural trigger for the symptoms is the clinical half of the same observation. Embolic infarcts scatter across different territories, sit at the grey-white junction and take wedge or scattered cortical shapes rather than a straight line; a single lacune from lipohyalinosis is one lesion, not a chain. The distinction changes treatment: a haemodynamic pattern behind a symptomatic 90 per cent stenosis argues for prompt revascularisation and for caution about dropping the blood pressure, whereas an embolic pattern shifts attention to the plaque surface and to the heart.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old taking a combined oral contraceptive has had three days of worsening headache and then a seizure. Unenhanced CT shows patchy haemorrhage with disproportionate surrounding oedema in both high parietal lobes, and the superior sagittal sinus looks dense. What does this combination point to?
choices: Venous infarction from dural sinus thrombosis
Bilateral anterior cerebral artery infarction
Haemorrhagic contusions from unwitnessed trauma
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
quiz.answer: Venous infarction from dural sinus thrombosis
quiz.explain: The pattern breaks the rules that arterial infarcts obey. Parasagittal lesions on both sides correspond to no single arterial territory; they are haemorrhagic early rather than late; and the oedema is out of proportion to the lesion because the mechanism is back-pressure rather than absent supply. Add a dense sinus and the diagnosis is venous. Confirm with CT or MR venography, where the empty delta sign is a filling defect within the enhancing sinus wall, and remember that a dense sinus alone can be nothing more than a high haematocrit. Bilateral anterior cerebral infarction, possible with an azygos vessel, would follow the medial surface forward from the genu of the corpus callosum and would not be haemorrhagic at three days. Contusions cluster at the skull base against the orbital roofs and sphenoid ridges. PRES sits posteriorly, parieto-occipital, and is predominantly vasogenic oedema. The management consequence is the striking part: the treatment is anticoagulation, in the presence of intracranial haemorrhage.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a large right middle cerebral artery infarct has a routine CT at sixteen days. The territory that was clearly hypoattenuating on day two now looks close to normal, and the report concludes that the infarct has resolved. Explain what has happened to the tissue, and how you would answer the report.
quiz.answer: This is the fogging phase. Between roughly the second and fourth week, macrophages infiltrate the infarct and new capillaries proliferate within it, so its attenuation rises back towards that of normal brain and the lesion becomes inconspicuous on unenhanced CT. The tissue is not recovering; it is being cleared, and the encephalomalacic cavity will appear later. The report should be answered by saying that a transiently normal-looking CT in this window is not evidence of resolution: the infarct remains demonstrable on MRI, where it stays abnormal on T2 and FLAIR, and it will enhance on contrast-enhanced CT or MRI because the blood-brain barrier is broken.
quiz.explain: Fogging is worth knowing because it appears exactly when the follow-up scan tends to be booked, and because it can hide a subacute infarct in a patient scanned late for the first time: a normal CT two weeks after an event is not evidence that no stroke occurred. The mechanism is the one that also produces gyriform cortical enhancement and, on MRI, cortical T1 hyperintensity from laminar necrosis at around two weeks - reperfused, infarcted cortex packed with macrophages. The trap on the other side is calling that subacute infarct a tumour, since it enhances and can show mass effect. What keeps the reader right is the shape and the history: a wedge that respects a vascular territory and reaches the cortical surface, in a patient whose deficit began on a known day.

quiz.prompt: A 77-year-old with atrial fibrillation was last seen well fourteen hours ago and has an NIHSS of 18. There is no haemorrhage, the ASPECTS is 8, CT angiography shows an occluded left M1 segment, and perfusion gives a core of 12 mL with 95 mL of critically delayed tissue. The on-call team proposes medical management because the six-hour window has passed. What is the strongest response?
choices: Imaging, not the clock, selects patients out to 24 hours
The scan should be repeated after twelve more hours
Intravenous thrombolysis alone is the option left
The core is too large for an endovascular approach
quiz.answer: Imaging, not the clock, selects patients out to 24 hours
quiz.explain: DAWN and DEFUSE 3 replaced the clock with a tissue clock, and guidelines followed: thrombectomy is recommended out to 24 hours from last seen well in patients who meet imaging criteria. This patient meets them with room to spare - an ASPECTS of 8, a 12 mL core and 95 mL of penumbra fourteen hours in, which is the imaging signature of a slow progressor with good collaterals. 'The core is too large' inverts the numbers on the screen. A repeat scan buys nothing except infarct. Intravenous thrombolysis is outside its own window here (4.5 hours, extended to 9 hours only in perfusion-selected patients in trials such as EXTEND), and in any case thrombolysis is not a prerequisite for thrombectomy. The practical lesson is that in the late window the question is never 'how long has it been?' but 'how much brain is still alive?'.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have an occluded M1 segment, an NIHSS of 16, and presented three hours after onset. On multiphase CT angiography the first fills the pial vessels of the affected hemisphere almost as well and almost as fast as the normal side; the second shows sparse and delayed pial filling. Explain what the difference predicts and how it should change what you do next.
quiz.answer: Collateral supply through the pial or leptomeningeal anastomoses determines how fast penumbra converts into core. The first patient is a slow progressor: at three hours the core will still be small and the penumbra large, the chance of a good outcome after successful thrombectomy is high, and there is time to complete the imaging properly and to transfer if the centre cannot treat. The second is a fast progressor whose core is already growing quickly, may already be large despite the short time from onset, and for whom every minute of delay costs tissue, so imaging should be curtailed to what is needed to get the patient onto the angiography table. Collateral status is also why time from onset predicts core volume so poorly, and why a late presenter with good collaterals can be a better candidate than an early one with poor collaterals.
quiz.explain: Collaterals are the variable that makes the same occlusion a different disease in two patients. They are graded on the extent and the timing of pial filling relative to the normal hemisphere, and multiphase CT angiography exists because a single-phase study confuses a slow-filling good collateral bed with an absent one - the phase was simply caught too early. Good collaterals predict a smaller final infarct, a better functional outcome and a lower risk of haemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion; poor collaterals predict the opposite and are the reason some patients arrive early and are already beyond help. Two things follow for practice: report collateral status rather than only the occlusion site, and treat a poor collateral pattern as a reason to compress the workflow rather than as a reason to give up, since the tissue that remains is exactly the tissue that will be lost during any delay.

nodes.title: Approach to an Intracranial Mass
nodes.goal: Place an intracranial mass in the intra-axial or extra-axial compartment, then narrow it with enhancement, diffusion and perfusion.

quiz.prompt: A rounded 4 cm mass sits against the right frontal convexity. Between the mass and the brain there is a thin rim of cerebrospinal fluid containing vessels, the cortical grey matter is displaced inwards away from the inner table, and the underlying white matter is buckled rather than expanded. Where has the mass arisen?
choices: Outside the brain, from the dural surface
Within the cortex of the frontal lobe
Within the subcortical white matter
Inside the frontal horn of the ventricle
quiz.answer: Outside the brain, from the dural surface
quiz.explain: The compartment question is answered before any question of histology, because it halves the differential at a stroke. The extra-axial signs are all displacements: a cerebrospinal fluid cleft, pial vessels running between the mass and the brain, grey matter pushed inwards so that the cortical ribbon lies between the mass and the white matter, buckling of the white matter, a widened subarachnoid space, and reaction in the adjacent bone. An intra-axial mass does the opposite - it expands cortex or white matter, effaces the subarachnoid space, and has brain rather than fluid at its margin. Being systematic matters because a large extra-axial mass invaginating deeply can look intra-axial on a single axial image; coronal images and the position of the cortical ribbon resolve it. The differentials then diverge completely: meningioma, dural metastasis, solitary fibrous tumour, schwannoma and lymphoma outside the brain; glioma, metastasis, abscess and demyelination within it.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old treated for breast cancer three years ago has headache. MRI shows four separate dural-based enhancing masses over both convexities and along the falx, and CT shows lytic destruction of the inner table beneath the largest, with no hyperostosis. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Dural metastatic deposits from the breast primary
Multiple meningiomas in a predisposed patient
Neurosarcoidosis involving the pachymeninges
IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis
quiz.answer: Dural metastatic deposits from the breast primary
quiz.explain: Multiplicity alone does not settle it, since meningiomas are multiple in neurofibromatosis type 2, after cranial radiation, and occasionally sporadically - but the bone does. Meningioma provokes bone: hyperostosis, a thickened sclerotic inner table, sometimes a permeative sclerotic pattern with tumour inside it. Metastasis destroys bone. Add a treated breast primary, the commonest source of dural metastases, and the diagnosis follows. The near-misses are worth holding: sarcoidosis and IgG4-related disease thicken the dura in a more sheet-like, less nodular fashion and come with other clues - in sarcoid, leptomeningeal enhancement around the basal cisterns and involvement of the infundibulum and cranial nerves - and neither destroys bone. Solitary fibrous tumour, the entity that absorbed haemangiopericytoma, is the trap for a solitary lesion: narrow dural attachment, prominent internal flow voids, and bone erosion rather than hyperostosis. Saying this out loud in the report matters, because dural metastases change the whole management conversation and 'dural-based masses, likely meningiomas' closes it down.

quiz.prompt: A convexity mass has a tapering rim of thickened enhancing dura extending from each of its margins, and the neurosurgeon takes this as confirming a meningioma. Explain what this sign does and does not establish, and why it still matters to the operation.
quiz.answer: The tapering enhancing dural thickening - the dural tail - establishes that the mass is extra-axial and dural-based, which is genuinely useful, but it does not establish histology. It is seen in most meningiomas and also in dural metastases, lymphoma, solitary fibrous tumour, schwannoma, sarcoidosis and other pachymeningeal disease, so it is sensitive rather than specific. Histologically the tail may be tumour infiltrating the dura or merely reactive, hypervascular, oedematous dura, and imaging cannot separate the two. It matters to the operation because the tail may contain tumour: completeness of resection of the dural attachment is what the Simpson grading records and what predicts recurrence, so the surgeon plans to excise or coagulate the involved dura rather than the mass alone, and the report should state how far the tail extends and what it runs into, such as a venous sinus.
quiz.explain: What a sign is worth depends on the population it is used in. In a series of convexity masses the dural tail is common in meningiomas and uncommon in gliomas, so it is a good compartment sign; among dural-based masses, where every lesion has one, it discriminates nothing. That is the general lesson: a sign that separates two categories well can be useless one level further down the tree, and the tail is the neuroradiological example. The other half of the lesson is surgical. Simpson grade 1 resection - the mass, its dural attachment and any abnormal bone - carries the lowest recurrence rate, and grades rise as attachment is left behind, so the extent of the tail is an operative planning measurement rather than a descriptive flourish.

quiz.prompt: A 54-year-old with fever and a recent dental extraction has a 3 cm ring-enhancing left frontal lesion with surrounding oedema. The enhancing rim is smooth, thin, and thinner on the side facing the ventricle, and the centre is markedly bright on diffusion-weighted imaging with an apparent diffusion coefficient well below that of normal white matter. What is the lesion?
choices: A pyogenic abscess containing pus
A metastasis with a necrotic centre
A glioblastoma with central necrosis
A tumefactive demyelinating lesion
quiz.answer: A pyogenic abscess containing pus
quiz.explain: Pus is viscous, cellular and protein-rich, so water motion within it is genuinely restricted: the cavity is bright on diffusion with a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and this is among the most reliable signs in neuroimaging for separating an abscess from a necrotic tumour. Tumour necrosis is liquefied and acellular and has a high coefficient. Two further clues sit in the stem. An abscess rim is smooth and thin and is characteristically thinner along its deep margin, because the deep white matter is less well vascularised than the cortex - which is also why abscesses rupture into the ventricle rather than outwards - and it is often low in signal on T2, sometimes with a dual rim on susceptibility imaging. A glioblastoma rim is thick, irregular and nodular. Cautions: a treated abscess loses its restriction, some tumours restrict after haemorrhage, and spectroscopy adds amino acids, acetate and succinate to the argument, so the clinical trajectory stays in the reasoning rather than being replaced by one sequence.

quiz.prompt: A solitary ring-enhancing mass in the right parietal lobe is surrounded by extensive T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity. Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion shows relative cerebral blood volume markedly elevated in the enhancing rim, and moderately elevated in the non-enhancing hyperintense region beyond it. What does the perfusion of the region beyond the enhancement favour?
choices: A glioma infiltrating past the enhancing margin
A solitary metastasis with vasogenic oedema
An abscess with surrounding cerebritis
Radiation necrosis of the white matter
quiz.answer: A glioma infiltrating past the enhancing margin
quiz.explain: Enhancement marks where the blood-brain barrier has failed, which in a high-grade glioma is only the core; the tumour cells themselves extend well beyond it along white matter tracts, into brain that looks merely oedematous. Those infiltrated regions carry neovascularity with them, so relative cerebral blood volume in the peritumoural T2 signal is raised. Around a metastasis the same region is pure vasogenic oedema - plasma driven out through leaky capillaries into the extracellular space, with no tumour cells in it - and its blood volume is low. That difference is one of the few imaging tools that separates a solitary metastasis from a glioblastoma when the conventional images look alike, and it is why the surgical margin and the radiotherapy volume differ so much between the two diagnoses. Caveats worth carrying: the sequence needs preload and leakage correction, because contrast escaping through a broken barrier corrupts the estimate; susceptibility from blood products and from skull base bone degrades the maps; and the finding shifts a probability rather than settling a diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion of a cerebral mass gives a leakage-corrected cerebral blood volume of 5.8 mL per 100 g in the most vascular part of the lesion, while a region of interest in normal-appearing contralateral white matter gives 1.6 mL per 100 g. What is the relative cerebral blood volume ratio? Give it to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 5.8 divided by 1.6 is 3.6. The ratio is what gets reported rather than the absolute value, because absolute blood volume from this technique depends on the arterial input function, the injection, the sequence and the vendor, and only the comparison against the patient's own normal white matter is stable across studies. Ratios of roughly 1.75 are commonly used to separate high-grade from low-grade glioma, and 3.6 sits well into the high-grade range - but the threshold shifts with technique and with the leakage correction applied, so it belongs in a report as a supporting argument rather than as a grade. Two traps: sample the most vascular part of the tumour, since a single large region of interest across a heterogeneous mass averages the answer away, and do not sample a vessel, which turns any tumour into a high-grade one instantly. The standing exception is the oligodendroglioma, which often has high blood volume from its dense capillary network despite being low-grade.

quiz.prompt: Rank these five tissues by their typical apparent diffusion coefficient, from the lowest value to the highest.
quiz.answer: abscess-pus lymphoma glioblastoma vasogenic-oedema cerebrospinal-fluid
quiz.explain: The apparent diffusion coefficient measures how freely water moves, so the sequence runs from the most crowded and most viscous compartment to free fluid. Pus is viscous and packed with inflammatory cells, debris and protein and sits at the bottom. Primary central nervous system lymphoma is the most cellular of the common tumours - small round cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and scant extracellular space - so its coefficient is low, generally below that of gliomas and below normal white matter, which is why a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with a low coefficient in an immunocompetent adult is lymphoma until proved otherwise. The solid part of a glioblastoma is cellular but heterogeneously so, and sits in the middle. Vasogenic oedema is extracellular water in a widened extracellular space and diffuses more freely than normal brain. Cerebrospinal fluid is essentially free water and is the highest, which is why it is dark on the high-b image and bright on the map. The practical rule that follows: read the map, not the diffusion-weighted image, because T2 shine-through makes anything T2-bright look restricted.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks after completing chemoradiotherapy for an MGMT-methylated glioblastoma, the MRI shows new enhancement at the resection margin with more surrounding FLAIR signal. The patient is clinically well and on a reducing dose of dexamethasone. Explain the two possibilities, what favours each, and what you would do.
quiz.answer: The two possibilities are true progression and pseudoprogression, a treatment effect in which radiation and temozolomide cause endothelial injury, inflammation and increased permeability, producing new or enlarging enhancement without tumour growth. Pseudoprogression is favoured here by the timing, since most cases appear within three months of finishing chemoradiotherapy; by MGMT promoter methylation, which is strongly associated with it; and by a patient who is clinically stable or improving. True progression is favoured by clinical deterioration, by enhancement appearing outside the high-dose radiation field, and by elevated relative cerebral blood volume, whereas pseudoprogression tends to show low blood volume; diffusion, spectroscopy and amino-acid PET add weight but none is definitive. The action is not to declare progression: continue treatment and repeat the MRI at a short interval of about four to eight weeks, since the RANO framework does not call progression within twelve weeks of radiotherapy unless the new enhancement lies outside the high-dose field or there is histological proof.
quiz.explain: The mirror image of this error is worth learning at the same time. Under an antiangiogenic agent such as bevacizumab, the drug restores the blood-brain barrier and the enhancement melts away within days without the tumour having shrunk - pseudoresponse - which is why response on such treatment is judged on the non-enhancing T2 and FLAIR component rather than on the enhancing volume. Both errors have one root: enhancement is a property of the barrier, not of tumour cells, so any drug or injury that changes the barrier changes the picture without changing the disease. The clinical stakes are real in both directions, since calling pseudoprogression as progression stops an effective treatment early, and calling progression as pseudoprogression leaves a growing tumour untreated for two more months.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old presents with a first seizure. MRI shows a non-enhancing, expansile mass in the left frontal lobe that is homogeneously and markedly hyperintense on T2, while on FLAIR the same lesion is suppressed centrally with a bright peripheral rim. What does this appearance favour?
choices: An IDH-mutant astrocytoma, not codeleted
An oligodendroglioma, 1p/19q codeleted
An IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, grade 4
A tumefactive demyelinating plaque
quiz.answer: An IDH-mutant astrocytoma, not codeleted
quiz.explain: The T2-FLAIR mismatch sign - homogeneous high T2 signal with relative FLAIR suppression except at the rim - is among the most specific signs in neuro-oncology, approaching complete specificity for IDH-mutant astrocytoma without 1p/19q codeletion, while its sensitivity is low, so its absence says nothing at all. The likely substrate is the loosely structured, microcystic, water-rich matrix of these tumours: free water is bright on T2 and is nulled by the FLAIR inversion pulse, whereas the rim contains more cellular infiltrated tissue that resists nulling. Oligodendrogliomas, the other IDH-mutant tumour, are heterogeneous, frequently calcified, tend to involve the cortex, and characteristically lack the sign. A glioblastoma in a 32-year-old is possible but would usually enhance and rarely look this homogeneous. Under the 2021 WHO classification these molecular groups are the diagnosis rather than a refinement of it, so a sign that predicts the group changes the conversation before the biopsy. Apply the criteria strictly: the mismatch must involve most of the lesion, and a focal or cystic mismatch does not count.

quiz.prompt: An immunocompetent 68-year-old has a periventricular mass that is hyperattenuating on unenhanced CT, enhances homogeneously and avidly, has a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and shows strikingly little necrosis for its size. Neurosurgery plans a biopsy in four days, and the medical team wants to start dexamethasone now for the surrounding oedema. What is the strongest objection?
choices: Steroids can make the biopsy non-diagnostic
Steroids raise the risk of bleeding at biopsy
Steroids will mask the restricted diffusion
Steroids promote leptomeningeal spread here
quiz.answer: Steroids can make the biopsy non-diagnostic
quiz.explain: The imaging describes primary central nervous system lymphoma: dense on unenhanced CT because the tumour is so cellular, homogeneously enhancing, low in apparent diffusion coefficient for the same reason, periventricular and abutting the ependyma, and with little necrosis in an immunocompetent patient - necrosis and ring enhancement being the rule in the AIDS-related form instead. Lymphoma is exquisitely steroid-sensitive: corticosteroids are lympholytic and can dissolve the enhancing mass within days, the old 'ghost tumour', leaving a biopsy that shows reactive gliosis and debris and forcing either weeks of waiting for the tumour to return or a second procedure. The radiologist's job when this pattern appears is therefore to say in the report that lymphoma leads the differential and that steroids should be withheld until tissue is obtained, unless impending herniation makes them unavoidable. The distractors fail in different ways: steroids do not cause bleeding, do not abolish the low coefficient of the tissue that remains, and do not disseminate the tumour.

quiz.prompt: A diffuse glioma in a young adult does not enhance at all, while the pituitary gland, the choroid plexus and a small meningioma in the same patient enhance intensely. Explain what enhancement is actually measuring, and what follows for judging whether a lesion is benign.
quiz.answer: Gadolinium enhancement measures delivery of contrast into the extracellular space, which requires that contrast can leave the vasculature. It therefore maps where the blood-brain barrier is absent or broken, not where tumour is. The pituitary, choroid plexus, pineal gland, dura and area postrema lie outside the barrier and have fenestrated capillaries, so they enhance normally, as does a meningioma, which is fed by dural vessels that never had a barrier. A diffuse glioma grows through brain whose capillaries retain intact tight junctions, so it can be extensive and still not enhance at all. It follows that absence of enhancement is not evidence that a lesion is benign - a non-enhancing diffuse astrocytoma is still a tumour that infiltrates and eventually progresses, and its grade is set by histology and molecular findings rather than by enhancement - and that enhancement in a treated tumour may reflect a barrier damaged by surgery, radiation or infarction rather than tumour itself.
quiz.explain: The consequences run in both directions and both are common errors. Reading enhancement as a proxy for malignancy under-calls the non-enhancing diffuse gliomas, which under the 2021 WHO classification may reach grade 4 on molecular grounds alone - homozygous deletion of CDKN2A/B in an IDH-mutant astrocytoma, for instance, makes it grade 4 without necrosis or microvascular proliferation being present. Reading it the other way over-calls, because a subacute infarct, an area of demyelination, radiation injury and postoperative granulation tissue all enhance briskly. The practical habit is to describe enhancement as a finding about the barrier, then argue about the cause using the company it keeps: territory, diffusion, perfusion, time course and what the patient has already been treated with.

quiz.prompt: An incidental convexity meningioma measured 24 mm in maximum diameter three years ago and measures 31 mm on the current study. Treating the lesion as a sphere, by what factor has its volume increased? Give the answer to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Volume scales with the cube of a linear dimension, so 31 over 24 cubed is 2.2: a 29 per cent increase in diameter is a 116 per cent increase in volume. That is why a surveillance report reading 'minimally increased, 24 to 31 mm' can be so misleading - the tumour has more than doubled. It is also why measurement error deserves respect, since 2 mm of interobserver variation on a 24 mm lesion swings the implied volume by more than a quarter; growth should be judged against the earliest available study rather than the immediately preceding one, and measured on the same plane and sequence each time. For meningiomas specifically, a demonstrable growth rate, T2 hyperintensity, absence of calcification, peritumoural oedema and younger patient age all favour a tumour that will keep growing, and a growing meningioma in an operable location is treated before it becomes a symptomatic one.

nodes.title: Brain Anatomy and Vascular Territories
nodes.goal: Localise a brain lesion to its arterial or venous territory from cross-sectional images, and say what that territory tells you about the vessel, the deficit and the mechanism.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old develops weakness of the right leg with only trivial arm involvement, a normal face, and striking abulia. CT at 24 hours shows hypoattenuation confined to the medial surface of the left hemisphere, running from the genu of the corpus callosum back to the paracentral lobule. Which occlusion best accounts for this?
quiz.answer: Occlusion of the left pericallosal artery, the A2 continuation of the anterior cerebral artery
choices: Occlusion of the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery in the sylvian fissure
Occlusion of the recurrent artery of Heubner arising at the left A1–A2 junction
Occlusion of the left pericallosal artery, the A2 continuation of the anterior cerebral artery
Occlusion of the left anterior choroidal artery just beyond the posterior communicating origin
quiz.explain: The homunculus is the whole argument. The leg and perineum sit on the medial surface at the paracentral lobule, and that surface, together with the genu and body of the corpus callosum and the medial frontal cortex, is anterior cerebral artery territory carried by the pericallosal and callosomarginal branches. Leg-dominant weakness with a spared face is therefore ACA until proven otherwise, and the abulia comes from the medial frontal and cingulate involvement. The middle cerebral artery's superior division supplies the lateral convexity, so it gives face and arm weakness with sparing of the leg — the mirror image. Heubner's recurrent artery supplies the caudate head and the anterior limb of the internal capsule; it produces a small deep infarct with facio-brachial weakness and dysarthria, not a strip of medial cortex. The anterior choroidal artery supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule, optic tract and medial temporal structures, classically hemiplegia with hemianaesthesia and hemianopia. When you see a medial strip, look next at the A1 segments and the anterior communicating complex, because a single dominant A1 can infarct both medial hemispheres at once.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old with a 90% left internal carotid stenosis is found on the ward after a hypotensive episode. Diffusion imaging shows a chain of three small round infarcts strung in a line through the left corona radiata and centrum semiovale, with a normal cortical ribbon and no cardiac source found. What does this pattern tell you?
quiz.answer: Internal borderzone infarction from haemodynamic failure behind a tight proximal internal carotid stenosis
choices: Internal borderzone infarction from haemodynamic failure behind a tight proximal internal carotid stenosis
Cortical borderzone infarction from cardioembolic showers reaching the distal anterior cerebral branches
Chronic small vessel disease of the perforators, unrelated to the carotid stenosis on this study
Distal middle cerebral artery branch occlusion producing a wedge of cortical and subcortical infarct
quiz.explain: There are two borderzones and they mean different things. The external, or cortical, borderzone lies between the surface branches of the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries and infarcts as a wedge running from the ventricle to the cortex; it is often embolic, with hypoperfusion impairing washout of emboli. The internal, or deep, borderzone lies between the lenticulostriate perforators from below and the long medullary branches descending from the cortical arteries above, in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale. It infarcts as a linear string of small lesions parallel to the lateral ventricle — the rosary bead appearance — and it is the most haemodynamic of all stroke patterns. A normal cortical ribbon argues against embolism, and diffusion restriction argues against old small vessel disease, which would be T2 hyperintense without restriction. The management consequence is the point: this patient needs perfusion assessment and an urgent decision about revascularising the carotid, plus avoidance of further hypotension, not simply another antiplatelet.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old is brought in with abrupt coma, a vertical gaze palsy and dense amnesia. MRI shows restricted diffusion in both paramedian thalami and a small V-shaped lesion on the anterior surface of the midbrain. State the arterial variant that explains this, and the one alternative diagnosis you must exclude before you commit to it, and how you would exclude it.
quiz.answer: This is the artery of Percheron: a single dominant thalamoperforator arising from one P1 that supplies both paramedian thalami and often the rostral midbrain. Before committing, exclude deep cerebral venous thrombosis by inspecting the internal cerebral veins, vein of Galen and straight sinus, with a CT or MR venogram if there is any doubt.
quiz.explain: Bilateral thalamic signal change is one of the few patterns in neuroradiology with a short and dangerous differential. The artery of Percheron is a normal variant in which both paramedian thalamic territories hang off a single perforator from one P1 segment, so one small occlusion infarcts both thalami; involvement of the rostral midbrain gives the V-shaped anterior mesencephalic lesion. The clinical triad of depressed consciousness, vertical gaze palsy and memory loss follows from the intralaminar nuclei and the rostral interstitial nucleus. The mimic that must not be missed is thrombosis of the deep venous system, because the internal cerebral veins drain exactly this territory and its treatment is anticoagulation, not stroke pathway care. Venous infarction tends to be more oedematous, less sharply diffusion-restricted, often haemorrhagic, and extends into the basal ganglia; the giveaway is a dense straight sinus or vein of Galen on the unenhanced CT. Top-of-the-basilar embolism and Wernicke encephalopathy round out the list, the latter favouring the medial thalami around the third ventricle with the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal grey.

quiz.prompt: Consider these five structures: the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the optic tract, the head of the caudate nucleus, the lateral geniculate nucleus, and the occipital cortex. How many of them lie within the usual territory of the anterior choroidal artery? Answer as a whole number, counting structures.
quiz.explain: The anterior choroidal artery arises from the supraclinoid internal carotid just distal to the posterior communicating artery and runs backwards along the optic tract into the temporal horn. Its territory is small but strategically dense: the posterior limb of the internal capsule (its inferior and posterior part), the optic tract, the lateral geniculate nucleus, the medial temporal structures including the uncus and part of the hippocampus, and the choroid plexus of the temporal horn. That gives three of the five listed. The caudate head belongs to the recurrent artery of Heubner and the medial lenticulostriates, and the occipital cortex belongs to the posterior cerebral artery. The reason to hold this territory in mind is the classical triad it produces — contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and homonymous hemianopia — from a lesion no larger than a lacune. If you see a small capsular infarct and the patient has a field defect, look for optic tract and geniculate involvement rather than assuming a second lesion.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old has sudden vertigo and vomiting, ipsilateral facial weakness of lower motor neurone type, ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss, ipsilateral limb ataxia and contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss in the trunk and limbs. Which vessel does this combination point to?
quiz.answer: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery, which also supplies the labyrinth through the internal auditory artery
choices: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery, which supplies the lateral medulla and the inferior cerebellum
The superior cerebellar artery, which supplies the dorsolateral pons and the superior cerebellar surface
A paramedian basilar perforator, which supplies the ventromedial pons and the descending corticospinal fibres
The anterior inferior cerebellar artery, which also supplies the labyrinth through the internal auditory artery
quiz.explain: Hearing loss is the discriminator. The internal auditory (labyrinthine) artery usually arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, so AICA is the one posterior circulation territory in which cochlear and vestibular failure sits alongside brainstem signs. Add lower motor neurone facial weakness from the facial nucleus in the caudal pons, ataxia from the middle cerebellar peduncle and flocculus, and crossed sensory loss from the spinothalamic tract, and the lateral pontine syndrome is complete. PICA gives the lateral medullary syndrome: vertigo, hoarseness and dysphagia from the nucleus ambiguus, Horner syndrome, crossed sensory loss — but hearing is preserved and the facial weakness, if any, is not of lower motor neurone type. SCA gives ataxia, dysarthria and sometimes a contralateral fourth nerve palsy, without hearing loss. A paramedian perforator gives a ventral pontine syndrome with contralateral hemiparesis and no vestibulocochlear features. In practice, sudden isolated deafness with vertigo in a vasculopath is an AICA warning and deserves urgent posterior circulation imaging rather than a labyrinthitis label.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these vessels in the order that blood drains from the deep grey structures of the brain to the neck.
quiz.answer: internal-cerebral-vein vein-of-Galen straight-sinus confluence-of-sinuses transverse-sinus sigmoid-sinus internal-jugular-vein
quiz.explain: The deep venous system is a fixed chain and knowing it lets you predict which structures swell when one link fails. The thalamostriate and septal veins meet at the venous angle behind the foramen of Monro to form the paired internal cerebral veins, which run back in the velum interpositum. They join the basal veins of Rosenthal, carrying blood from the medial temporal lobes and midbrain, to form the great cerebral vein of Galen beneath the splenium. The vein of Galen meets the inferior sagittal sinus to become the straight sinus, which runs in the falco-tentorial junction to the confluence of sinuses, then out through the transverse and sigmoid sinuses to the internal jugular vein. Thrombosis anywhere from the internal cerebral veins to the straight sinus produces bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia oedema, often haemorrhagic — the venous mimic of the artery of Percheron. Thrombosis further downstream, in a transverse or sigmoid sinus, is far more often silent or presents with raised pressure, because the cortical veins and the opposite side can compensate.

quiz.prompt: A 60-year-old has a painless isolated right abducens palsy. There is no proptosis, orbital movements are otherwise full, V1 sensation is intact and the optic nerve function is normal. On the thin-section post-contrast MRI you are about to report, which compartment deserves the closest scrutiny, and on what grounds?
quiz.answer: The cavernous sinus, because the sixth nerve runs free within it alongside the internal carotid artery
choices: The superior orbital fissure, because the sixth nerve passes outside the annulus of Zinn on its way to the orbit
The cavernous sinus, because the sixth nerve runs free within it alongside the internal carotid artery
Meckel's cave, because the sixth nerve traverses it before entering the orbit through the fissure
The internal auditory canal, because the sixth nerve accompanies the facial nerve out of the pons
quiz.explain: The anatomy explains the clinical pattern. In the cavernous sinus the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves are embedded in the lateral dural wall, insulated to some degree from what is happening in the venous channel itself. The abducens nerve is the exception: it runs free inside the sinus, immediately lateral to the cavernous internal carotid artery. Anything that expands or infiltrates the venous compartment — tumour, thrombosis, a carotid–cavernous fistula, inflammatory pseudotumour — therefore tends to strike the sixth nerve first, and an isolated abducens palsy with an otherwise quiet orbit should send you to thin-section coronal images of the cavernous sinuses before anywhere else. In the superior orbital fissure the sixth nerve is inside the annulus of Zinn, not outside it, and a fissure lesion would rarely spare the third and fourth nerves. Meckel's cave contains the trigeminal ganglion, not the sixth nerve, and the internal auditory canal carries the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves. Do not forget raised intracranial pressure, which stretches the sixth nerve at Dorello's canal and is a false localising sign.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows a small acute infarct confined to the posterior part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule on the left, with the putamen and globus pallidus entirely normal. Say which artery you would suspect, and give one additional finding on the same study that would support your suspicion.
quiz.answer: Suspect the left anterior choroidal artery rather than a lenticulostriate perforator, because the lentiform nucleus is spared. Support it by looking for extension into the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus or the medial temporal lobe and uncus, and by asking the team to test for a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
quiz.explain: Two vessels can infarct the internal capsule and telling them apart changes what you look for and what you predict. The lateral lenticulostriate perforators arise from M1 and supply the putamen, most of the globus pallidus, the caudate body and the superior part of the posterior limb; if the lentiform nucleus is normal, they are unlikely to be the culprit. The anterior choroidal artery, from the supraclinoid carotid, supplies the inferior and posterior part of the posterior limb and continues to the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus and medial temporal structures. So the extra finding you hunt for is downstream: signal change tracking along the optic tract or into the uncus, and a homonymous field defect on examination. This matters because the anterior choroidal origin is an atheromatous carotid segment and is also vulnerable during aneurysm clipping and coiling near the posterior communicating artery, so a fresh anterior choroidal infarct should turn your attention to the carotid, not to isolated small vessel disease.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old speaks fluently but with frequent paraphasias and cannot follow a two-step command. There is no limb weakness and no facial asymmetry. Formal fields show a right superior quadrantanopia. CT perfusion shows a deficit over the left posterior temporal and inferior parietal region sparing the precentral gyrus. Which occlusion fits?
quiz.answer: Occlusion of the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery beyond the bifurcation
choices: Occlusion of the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery beyond the bifurcation
Occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery M1 segment proximal to the lenticulostriate origins
Occlusion of the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery beyond the bifurcation
Occlusion of the left posterior cerebral artery P2 segment beyond the thalamogeniculate branches
quiz.explain: The middle cerebral artery bifurcates in the sylvian fissure into a superior and an inferior division, and the two produce almost opposite clinical pictures in the dominant hemisphere. The superior division feeds the frontal operculum and precentral cortex: expect face and arm weakness with a non-fluent, effortful aphasia and relatively preserved comprehension. The inferior division feeds the posterior temporal and inferior parietal cortex: expect fluent, paraphasic speech with impaired comprehension, often with no weakness at all, and a superior quadrantanopia because Meyer's loop sweeps forward through the temporal lobe. An M1 occlusion proximal to the lenticulostriates would add deep grey infarction and a dense hemiparesis.
