A P2 occlusion would give a homonymous hemianopia, usually complete or inferior, with alexia without agraphia if the splenium goes, but not this language pattern. The practical trap is that a patient with a pure inferior division occlusion has a high NIHSS driven almost entirely by language, looks unimpaired at the bedside on limb testing, and can still have a large vessel occlusion worth treating.

quiz.prompt: A skull base tumour is reported as filling the right jugular foramen and extending anteromedially into the right hypoglossal canal. Counting only nerves that traverse those two openings, how many cranial nerves are at risk on that side? Answer as a whole number, counting nerves.
quiz.explain: The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, along with the internal jugular vein and the inferior petrosal sinus; the hypoglossal canal, just anteromedial and inferior to it in the occipital bone, transmits the twelfth nerve alone. A lesion occupying both therefore threatens four nerves — IX, X, XI and XII — which together make up the classical Collet–Sicard pattern, and the clinical consequence is a patient who cannot protect their airway. That is why this specific extension deserves an explicit sentence in your report rather than a general statement about skull base involvement. Keeping the neighbouring openings straight is worth the effort: the internal auditory meatus carries VII and VIII, the foramen ovale carries V3, the foramen rotundum carries V2, the optic canal carries II with the ophthalmic artery, and the superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, V1 and VI. When a mass sits at the pars nervosa or pars vascularis, look also for the vertical segment of the carotid and for a high jugular bulb before anyone contemplates biopsy.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old on the combined oral contraceptive pill has a right temporal haemorrhagic lesion that does not conform to any arterial territory, with surrounding oedema out of proportion to its size. The right transverse sinus does not opacify on the venous phase. Which vein's drainage territory matches the lesion?
quiz.answer: The vein of Labbé, the inferior anastomotic vein draining the temporal convexity to the transverse sinus
choices: The vein of Trolard, the superior anastomotic vein draining the convexity to the superior sagittal sinus
The basal vein of Rosenthal, draining the medial temporal region into the great cerebral vein of Galen
The internal cerebral vein, draining the deep grey structures into the great cerebral vein of Galen
The vein of Labbé, the inferior anastomotic vein draining the temporal convexity to the transverse sinus
quiz.explain: Venous infarcts announce themselves by disobeying arterial boundaries, by bleeding early, and by having oedema disproportionate to the infarct. Once you suspect one, work out which vein and then look at the sinus it empties into. The vein of Labbé drains the lateral temporal convexity backwards into the transverse sinus, so a transverse or sigmoid sinus thrombosis produces exactly this temporal haemorrhagic lesion, sometimes with a rapid decline as the temporal lobe swells against the tentorium. The vein of Trolard runs upwards to the superior sagittal sinus and matches parasagittal high convexity lesions, which is why superior sagittal sinus thrombosis gives bilateral parasagittal haemorrhages. Rosenthal's basal vein and the internal cerebral veins belong to the deep system and produce thalamic and basal ganglia oedema instead. The next step here is a dedicated venogram and anticoagulation, which is given even in the presence of venous haemorrhage — the bleeding is a consequence of the outflow obstruction, not a contraindication to relieving it.

quiz.prompt: A referrer asks whether a left medial occipital infarct with an ipsilateral posterolateral thalamic infarct in the same patient means one vessel or two. Explain the single arterial configuration that accounts for both, and state the one variant on the CTA that would change where you look for the embolic source.
quiz.answer: One vessel: the posterior cerebral artery, whose P2 segment supplies the medial occipital cortex through its cortical branches and the posterolateral thalamus through the thalamogeniculate perforators. Look for a fetal origin of that posterior cerebral artery from the internal carotid, because it moves the search for an embolic source to the anterior circulation.
quiz.explain: It is tempting to call two lesions two events, but the posterior cerebral artery supplies both cortex and deep grey, and a single P2 occlusion can take out the calcarine cortex and the lateral thalamus together. The thalamic supply is regional: the tuberothalamic artery from the posterior communicating artery, the paramedian thalamoperforators from P1, the thalamogeniculate branches from P2 to the posterolateral thalamus, and the posterior choroidal arteries to the pulvinar and geniculate bodies. A posterolateral thalamic plus medial occipital pattern is the P2 signature. The variant that changes management is a fetal posterior cerebral artery, present in roughly a fifth to a quarter of hemispheres, in which the PCA arises from the internal carotid through a dominant posterior communicating artery with a hypoplastic or absent P1. In that patient an occipital infarct is a carotid territory event, so the carotid bifurcation, not the vertebrobasilar system, is where the workup belongs — and it also matters when planning any carotid intervention.

quiz.prompt: A patient with progressive right hemifacial numbness and wasting on chewing has an enhancing mass replacing the normal fat of the right Meckel's cave and reaching the skull base foramen immediately below it. Having found that, what should you do next in reading the study?
quiz.answer: Follow V3 through the foramen ovale and look for denervation change in the muscles of mastication
choices: Follow V2 through the foramen rotundum and look for a mass filling the pterygopalatine fossa
Follow V3 through the foramen ovale and look for denervation change in the muscles of mastication
Follow the facial nerve through the stylomastoid foramen and look for a mass in the parotid gland
Follow the lower cranial nerves through the jugular foramen and look for a carotid space mass
quiz.explain: Meckel's cave is a cerebrospinal fluid-filled dural pouch in the petrous apex holding the trigeminal ganglion, and it is a junction box: the ophthalmic division leaves through the superior orbital fissure, the maxillary division through the foramen rotundum, and the mandibular division through the foramen ovale into the masticator space. Because the patient has both sensory loss and weakness of chewing, the motor fibres travelling with V3 are involved, so the foramen ovale is the route to follow. The specific sign to hunt for is denervation of the masseter, temporalis and pterygoids — oedematous and T2 bright in the subacute phase, fatty and atrophic later — which can be the only clue that a small perineural tumour is present. Perineural spread from a skin or parotid malignancy classically travels this way, and it upstages disease and changes the radiotherapy field, so it is worth an explicit statement in the report. The maxillary route matters for palatal and midface tumours, and the facial and lower cranial nerve routes belong to different clinical pictures altogether.

nodes.title: CNS Infection and Enhancement Patterns
nodes.goal: Read enhancement as a statement about which barrier has failed in which compartment, and use diffusion, distribution and the clinical setting to separate abscess, encephalitis, parasitic cyst and the mass lesions of advanced HIV.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old has fever, headache and neck stiffness. Post-contrast T1 shows thin enhancement running down into the sulci over both convexities and coating the cerebellar folia; the falx and tentorium are of normal thickness and show no extra enhancement. What does this distribution tell you, and what follows from it?
quiz.answer: The pia-arachnoid and the CSF spaces are inflamed, so lumbar puncture will sample the disease itself
choices: The pia-arachnoid and the CSF spaces are inflamed, so lumbar puncture will sample the disease itself
The cortex itself has broken down, so add perfusion and spectroscopy before considering a biopsy
The dura alone is inflamed, so look instead for low CSF pressure and image the whole spine for a leak
A collection sits between dura and arachnoid, so measure its depth and refer it for surgical drainage
quiz.explain: Contrast enhances where there is no blood-brain barrier or where one has failed. Enhancement that dips into sulci and follows the folia is leptomeningeal: pia and arachnoid, the walls of the CSF space, so the CSF is where the organism will be found. Dural (pachymeningeal) enhancement is a different signature - thick, continuous, following falx and tentorium, never entering a sulcus - and points to intracranial hypotension, post-surgical change or dural infiltration. Note the limits of the sign: leptomeningeal enhancement is neither sensitive nor specific for bacterial meningitis. Plenty of proven pyogenic meningitis has a normal scan, and carcinomatous and granulomatous meningitis look identical. Imaging in suspected meningitis is done to find the complication and to check that lumbar puncture is safe, not to make or exclude the diagnosis, and it must never delay antibiotics.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old smoker with a new seizure has a 3 cm ring-enhancing lesion at the grey-white junction. The rim is thick, nodular and irregular, the rim is not dark on T2, and the cavity is dark on diffusion-weighted imaging with a high ADC. There is a second smaller ring lesion in the cerebellum. What is the most reasonable next step?
quiz.answer: Treat it as metastatic disease and stage the chest, abdomen and pelvis before any neurosurgical referral
choices: Treat it as subacute infarction and repeat the study in six weeks to watch the enhancement settle down
Treat it as metastatic disease and stage the chest, abdomen and pelvis before any neurosurgical referral
Treat it as a pyogenic abscess and arrange urgent aspiration with blood cultures and empirical antibiotics
Treat it as tumefactive demyelination and arrange spinal imaging with oligoclonal bands before any therapy
quiz.explain: The cavity is the discriminator. Pus is viscous and packed with inflammatory cells, so water is restricted: bright on diffusion, low ADC. Tumour necrosis is thin liquefied debris, so water moves freely: dark on diffusion, high ADC. The rim adds to the argument - abscess rims are thin, smooth, complete, often thinner on the ventricular side, and characteristically dark on T2 from free radicals in the inflammatory wall, while necrotic tumour rims are thick and nodular. Two lesions at the grey-white junction in a smoker complete the picture. Keep two traps in mind: a treated abscess loses its restriction, and some abscesses caused by fungi or by treated organisms behave atypically. Where doubt persists, aspiration answers the question and treats the patient at the same time.

quiz.prompt: On a diffusion study acquired at b = 0 and b = 1000 s/mm2, the centre of a ring-enhancing lesion measures 900 arbitrary signal units on the b = 0 image and 450 units on the b = 1000 image. Calculate the apparent diffusion coefficient of the cavity contents. Answer in units of 10^-3 mm2/s, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: Signal decays exponentially with the b value, so ADC = ln(S0 / Sb) divided by b. Here the signal halves, ln(2) = 0.693, and dividing by 1000 s/mm2 gives 0.69 x 10^-3 mm2/s. That number does clinical work. The cavity of an untreated pyogenic abscess sits low, typically below about 1.0 x 10^-3 mm2/s and often nearer 0.5, because pus is cellular and viscous. Necrotic tumour usually sits above the value of normal white matter, commonly 1.5 and higher. Normal adult white matter is around 0.7 to 0.8, so a lesion reading like white matter or lower is behaving like pus. Always read the ADC map itself rather than the trace image: a very T2-bright lesion can look bright on diffusion with a perfectly normal ADC, which is T2 shine-through, not restriction.

quiz.prompt: On day four of treatment for pneumococcal meningitis a 30-year-old loses two points of GCS. CT shows a thin crescent of extra-axial fluid over the left convexity that had been read as a sterile effusion. Which MRI finding would separate an infected collection from a sterile one, and what does that change?
quiz.answer: A subdural empyema shows restricted diffusion within the collection with an enhancing membrane, unlike a sterile effusion which follows CSF freely, and it changes the plan to urgent neurosurgical drainage alongside antibiotics.
quiz.explain: Sterile subdural effusions are common in treated meningitis, particularly in children, and they resolve on their own. An empyema is a surgical emergency, and CT alone will not tell them apart because both are thin crescents of near-CSF density. Diffusion does: pus restricts, effusion does not, and the empyema usually shows a thin enhancing membrane along its inner border. Look for the company it keeps - cortical vein thrombosis, adjacent gyral swelling and early venous infarction, since an empyema inflames the veins running through the subdural space. The deteriorating patient on adequate antibiotics is the trigger for rescanning, and a scan without diffusion has not answered the question you were asked.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old is confused and febrile with complex partial seizures. FLAIR shows swelling and hyperintensity of both medial temporal lobes, asymmetrically, extending into the insula and the inferior frontal cortex; the lentiform nuclei are spared, there is gyral restricted diffusion and a few foci of petechial haemorrhage. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Start intravenous aciclovir immediately and send CSF for viral PCR, accepting that a negative early PCR does not stop it
choices: Start levetiracetam alone for peri-ictal change and repeat the imaging in one week once the seizures are controlled
Start high-dose steroids for autoimmune limbic encephalitis and screen for an underlying malignancy with body CT
Start intravenous aciclovir immediately and send CSF for viral PCR, accepting that a negative early PCR does not stop it
Start intravenous thrombolysis for a middle cerebral artery infarct once the time of onset is confirmed by a reliable witness
quiz.explain: This is the herpes simplex distribution: limbic and paralimbic cortex - medial temporal, insula, inferior frontal, cingulate - bilateral but asymmetric, with cortical swelling, early restricted diffusion and a tendency to bleed. The sparing of the lentiform nucleus is the classic separator from middle cerebral artery infarction, which takes the basal ganglia and stops at a vascular boundary; herpes crosses vascular territories because it spreads along trigeminal and olfactory routes. Autoimmune limbic encephalitis looks similar but is usually more symmetric, less haemorrhagic and without restricted diffusion. Treatment is the point of the item: aciclovir is started on suspicion. Untreated mortality is high, PCR can be falsely negative in the first 72 hours, and the drug is comparatively safe.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the four evolutionary stages of a parenchymal neurocysticercosis lesion in the sequence that serial imaging would show, from the newly established viable cyst to its end point.
quiz.answer: vesicular colloidal-vesicular granular-nodular nodular-calcified
quiz.explain: The larva is invisible to the host while alive. In the vesicular stage the cyst follows CSF signal, holds an eccentric mural scolex, and shows no oedema and little or no enhancement because the parasite is immunologically quiet. As it dies the fluid turns proteinaceous - colloidal vesicular - the wall enhances as a ring and surrounding oedema appears, and this is when the patient usually seizes. In the granular nodular stage the cyst retracts to a small enhancing nodule with less oedema, and finally it becomes a small calcified nodule with no enhancement. Reading the stage matters practically: antiparasitic drugs are aimed at viable vesicular cysts and can provoke a severe inflammatory reaction, so steroid cover and a search for intraventricular and subarachnoid disease come first, and a purely calcified burden needs no antiparasitic treatment at all.

quiz.prompt: A 28-year-old from a high-prevalence country has three weeks of headache, low fever and a new sixth nerve palsy. Which imaging pattern would you report as fitting tuberculous meningitis, and why does calling it early matter?
quiz.answer: Thick enhancing exudate filling the basal cisterns, communicating hydrocephalus, and infarcts in the basal ganglia and internal capsule from perforator vasculitis; calling it early matters because treatment starts on the pattern long before culture returns.
quiz.explain: Tuberculous meningitis is a disease of the basal cisterns. Sticky exudate fills the suprasellar and ambient cisterns, encases the cranial nerves - hence the sixth and third nerve palsies - and blocks CSF resorption, giving communicating hydrocephalus in most cases. The same exudate strangles the lenticulostriate and thalamoperforating vessels, so infarcts appear in the basal ganglia, internal capsule and thalami, a distribution that is a strong clue in a young patient with no vascular risk. Tuberculomas may coexist and can be T2-hypointense centrally. Culture takes weeks and CSF microscopy is often negative, so the triad on imaging, with the right epidemiology, is what starts anti-tuberculous therapy and steroids. Hydrocephalus that progresses may need diversion, so it must be reported and followed, not just mentioned.

quiz.prompt: A man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 80 has headache and a right hemiparesis. MRI shows four ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and at the grey-white junction, with marked oedema; the cavities show high ADC, and thallium-201 SPECT shows no uptake above background. What is the appropriate course?
quiz.answer: Give empirical anti-toxoplasma therapy and rescan at two weeks, reserving biopsy for lesions that fail to shrink
choices: Give antifungal therapy for cryptococcal disease and repeat imaging after the induction course has finished
Give whole-brain radiotherapy for presumed primary CNS lymphoma once staging of the body has been completed
Give supportive care alone for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy while antiretroviral therapy is being started
Give empirical anti-toxoplasma therapy and rescan at two weeks, reserving biopsy for lesions that fail to shrink
quiz.explain: Multiplicity, a basal ganglia and grey-white junction distribution, heavy oedema and facilitated diffusion all favour toxoplasmosis, and the negative thallium study is the clincher. Toxoplasma lesions are abscesses without viable cells to take up thallium or FDG; primary CNS lymphoma is densely cellular and takes up both avidly, tends to be solitary and periventricular, shows subependymal spread and typically restricts diffusion. The eccentric target sign - a small enhancing nodule on one wall of a ring - is specific for toxoplasmosis when present, though it is often absent. Standard practice is a therapeutic trial: clinical and radiological improvement within about two weeks confirms it, and failure to respond is the trigger for CSF EBV PCR and biopsy. Cryptococcus more often gives dilated perivascular spaces and gelatinous pseudocysts rather than florid ring enhancement.

quiz.prompt: A man with HIV and a CD4 count of 40 has a solitary periventricular enhancing mass with subependymal spread and a low ADC. Thallium-201 SPECT shows intense uptake. What does the thallium study add, and what must you advise before any biopsy is booked?
quiz.answer: Avid thallium uptake supports lymphoma rather than toxoplasmosis because the tissue is densely cellular, so ask for CSF EBV PCR and biopsy, and advise that corticosteroids be withheld until tissue is taken because they can shrink the lesion and make it non-diagnostic.
quiz.explain: Thallium-201 and FDG are read the same way here: they are cellularity and metabolism probes, and an infectious abscess is neither cellular nor metabolically active in the way a lymphoma is. Combined with a solitary periventricular mass, subependymal creep and restricted diffusion from a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, the study shifts the working diagnosis decisively. The practical warning is the steroid one. AIDS-related primary CNS lymphoma is exquisitely steroid-sensitive; a dose given for oedema before biopsy can dissolve the enhancing tissue and leave the neurosurgeon with gliosis. If intracranial pressure forces steroids, say so explicitly in the report so that the timing is understood. CSF EBV DNA is a useful adjunct in this population, since the tumour is EBV-driven.

quiz.prompt: A patient on natalizumab for multiple sclerosis develops slowly worsening speech and right-sided clumsiness. FLAIR shows a confluent asymmetric subcortical white matter abnormality in the left frontal lobe that reaches the cortex and involves the U-fibres, with no enhancement and almost no mass effect. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Stop the drug and send CSF for JC virus PCR, warning the team that enhancement may appear as immune reconstitution develops
choices: Stop the drug and send CSF for JC virus PCR, warning the team that enhancement may appear as immune reconstitution develops
Continue the drug and treat this as an active demyelinating relapse, giving a further course of high-dose intravenous steroids
Stop the drug and treat this as a septic embolic shower, adding echocardiography and empirical broad antibiotics
Continue the drug and treat this as small vessel ischaemia, adding blood pressure control and an antiplatelet agent
quiz.explain: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is a lytic infection of oligodendrocytes by JC virus. It is asymmetric, confluent, spreads through subcortical white matter and characteristically involves the subcortical U-fibres, which small vessel ischaemia and HIV encephalopathy spare. It does not enhance and it does not push, because there is no intact immune response to generate inflammation and no mass to speak of. A leading edge of mildly restricted diffusion marks the advancing front. The management point is immune reconstitution: once natalizumab is withdrawn or antiretroviral therapy is started, the returning immune system attacks infected tissue and the lesion swells and enhances. That is expected, not treatment failure, and recognising it in the report prevents the drug being wrongly blamed or the patient being biopsied unnecessarily.

quiz.prompt: A shunted child has fever and irritability. Non-contrast CT shows slightly enlarged ventricles with a layered debris-fluid level in both occipital horns. MRI adds restricted diffusion in that dependent material and thin enhancement of the ependymal lining. What should the report drive?
quiz.answer: Urgent shunt tap and CSF sampling for ventriculitis, since the intraventricular debris restricts and the ependyma is inflamed
choices: Expectant management for choroid plexus prominence, which commonly mimics debris in the dependent occipital horns
Urgent shunt tap and CSF sampling for ventriculitis, since the intraventricular debris restricts and the ependyma is inflamed
Routine outpatient review for layering blood products after a small intraventricular bleed, with repeat imaging in about a month
Elective shunt revision for gradual proximal catheter blockage, since the ventricles have enlarged since the last scan
quiz.explain: Ventriculitis is easy to under-call because the ventricles may be only mildly larger and the CT change is subtle. The two findings that make the case are debris that restricts diffusion, which is pus rather than blood or choroid plexus, and ependymal enhancement, which marks inflammation of the ventricular lining. Blood products layer too, but they follow the expected signal evolution and do not enhance the ependyma. The consequence is time-critical: infected shunt hardware usually has to be externalised or removed, and organisms are recovered from a shunt tap rather than from a lumbar puncture. Ventriculitis also loculates, so mention any developing septation or trapped horn, because that changes where the catheter has to go.

quiz.prompt: A trainee asks why an inflammatory demyelinating plaque enhances for a few weeks and then stops enhancing while the plaque itself remains visible on FLAIR for years. Answer in terms of what contrast enhancement actually reports.
quiz.answer: Enhancement reports a breached blood-brain barrier letting contrast leak into the interstitium, not the presence of disease itself, so it fades once the barrier is repaired even though the tissue damage persists.
quiz.explain: Gadolinium does not cross an intact blood-brain barrier, so enhancement is a map of where the barrier has failed or where it never existed - dura, choroid plexus, pituitary, pineal, the vessels themselves. That single idea explains most of the patterns in this module: a leptomeningeal pattern means the disease is in the CSF compartment, an abscess rim enhances because inflamed granulation tissue is leaky while the pus inside has no vessels at all, and an active plaque enhances only during the weeks in which inflammation is actively opening the barrier. It also explains the negatives. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy does not enhance in an untreated immunosuppressed patient because there is no inflammatory response to open anything. Absence of enhancement is a positive finding, not a normal study.

nodes.title: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis and CSF Disorders
nodes.goal: Recognise venous rather than arterial parenchymal injury and prove it without falling for the normal-variant traps, and work up raised and low CSF pressure and hydrocephalus to the point where management changes.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old woman ten days post partum has a week of worsening headache and now a seizure. CT shows swelling and patchy hyperdensity in both parasagittal frontal lobes, more on the left, with a rim of oedema that crosses from anterior to middle cerebral supply and does not match either territory. What should be arranged?
quiz.answer: CT venography now, because bilateral parasagittal change that ignores arterial boundaries points to a sinus occlusion
choices: Digital subtraction angiography now, because bifrontal swelling in pregnancy is typical of a small vessel vasculitis
CT angiography now, because bilateral frontal change of this kind indicates an anterior communicating artery aneurysm
CT venography now, because bilateral parasagittal change that ignores arterial boundaries points to a sinus occlusion
MRI with contrast next week, because posterior reversible encephalopathy resolves and needs interval confirmation alone
quiz.explain: Territory is the first question in any parenchymal insult. Arterial infarcts obey boundaries drawn by supply; venous infarcts obey boundaries drawn by drainage, so they sit where the blocked sinus collects from - parasagittal and bilateral for the superior sagittal sinus, temporal for the transverse or vein of Labbe, thalamic and basal ganglia for the internal cerebral veins and straight sinus. Oedema out of proportion to any arterial map, in a young patient with a prothrombotic state such as the puerperium, dehydration, the combined pill or an underlying cancer, should send you to the venous system. Note the sequence of events: venous obstruction raises capillary pressure, so oedema comes first and haemorrhage follows as vessels rupture, which is why the density is patchy rather than a single clean haematoma.

quiz.prompt: In that same patient a contrast-enhanced CT is performed on day one of admission and shows an enhancing dural wall around a central filling defect in the posterior superior sagittal sinus. A colleague scanned three weeks later would like to know why the appearance can be normal by then despite persisting clot. What is the sound explanation?
quiz.answer: Organising thrombus develops its own vessels and enhances, so the filling defect fades even while the sinus remains occluded
choices: Thrombus is usually fully lysed within three weeks, so a normal study means the sinus has recanalised completely
Dural walls stop enhancing after two weeks of treatment, so the surrounding rim disappears and the sign is abolished
Contrast timing in later studies is invariably too early, so the sinus opacifies poorly and the filling defect becomes invisible
Organising thrombus develops its own vessels and enhances, so the filling defect fades even while the sinus remains occluded
quiz.explain: The empty delta sign is a triangle of enhancing dura around unenhancing clot on axial contrast-enhanced imaging, and it is genuinely time-dependent in both directions. Very early it can be absent because the collateral dural venous channels have not yet dilated to give a bright rim. After roughly two to four weeks the thrombus itself becomes vascularised and enhances, so it merges with the sinus lumen and can look patent even though it is not. That is the trap for a late referral: an isolated post-contrast study is not enough. Use the non-contrast series, where acute clot is dense, and a dedicated venographic acquisition, and be aware that on MRI the signal of thrombus marches through the same deoxyhaemoglobin-to-methaemoglobin evolution as any haematoma, so an early clot can be isointense and easily missed.

quiz.prompt: A registrar reports occlusion of the left transverse sinus on a time-of-flight MR venogram. Before that report goes out, what three normal-variant or technical explanations must you exclude, and how does each one declare itself?
quiz.answer: An arachnoid granulation is a small rounded CSF-density defect inside a patent sinus, a hypoplastic transverse sinus has a correspondingly small bony groove on CT with no parenchymal change, and a flow gap on time-of-flight is a saturation artefact that disappears on contrast-enhanced venography.
quiz.explain: Over-calling transverse sinus thrombosis is one of the commonest errors in neuroradiology, because a hypoplastic or atretic transverse sinus is present in a substantial minority of normal people, usually on the right-dominant pattern's smaller left side. Three checks settle it. First, look at the skull base on bone windows: a truly hypoplastic sinus runs in a small or absent groove, whereas a thrombosed sinus of normal calibre has a normal groove. Second, arachnoid granulations are small, round, sharply marginated, follow CSF, and sit where veins enter. Third, time-of-flight venography depends on inflowing unsaturated spins, so in-plane flow produces spurious gaps; contrast-enhanced MR venography or CT venography is not subject to that. The parenchyma is the final arbiter, since a real occlusion of consequence usually leaves a mark.

quiz.prompt: CT venography confirms extensive superior sagittal sinus thrombosis in the postpartum patient, and there is a 3 cm haemorrhagic venous infarct in the left frontal lobe. The neurology team asks whether the bleed contraindicates treatment. What is the correct position to state?
quiz.answer: Full-dose anticoagulation is still indicated, because relieving venous obstruction is what stops the bleeding into congested brain
choices: Full-dose anticoagulation is still indicated, because relieving venous obstruction is what stops the bleeding into congested brain
Antiplatelet therapy should replace anticoagulation, because it lowers venous pressure with a smaller risk of extension
Anticoagulation should be deferred for two weeks, because any parenchymal haemorrhage first needs radiological stability
Immediate surgical clot retrieval should replace medical therapy, because drug treatment rarely reopens a sinus that is fully occluded
quiz.explain: This is the counterintuitive rule worth carrying: haemorrhagic transformation of a venous infarct is not a contraindication to anticoagulation, it is a consequence of the untreated occlusion. The blood is there because capillary pressure upstream of the clot has risen until vessels rupture, and the treatment for that is to stop the clot propagating and let the collateral drainage open. Heparin followed by oral anticoagulation is standard, and outcomes in the randomised and registry evidence are good even in patients who present with a bleed. Endovascular therapy is reserved for deterioration despite anticoagulation, and decompressive surgery for life-threatening mass effect. The radiologist's contribution is to state the extent of the thrombus, the deep venous system involvement, and the degree of mass effect, since those drive escalation.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 has daily headaches, transient visual obscurations and pulsatile tinnitus. MRI shows flattening of the posterior sclerae, an empty sella, distended and tortuous optic nerve sheaths, and smooth bilateral stenosis of the distal transverse sinuses. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: These findings support raised intracranial pressure but do not establish it, so an opening pressure and formal perimetry are needed
choices: These findings are within normal limits for this age and habitus, so no further neurological or ophthalmic assessment is required
These findings support raised intracranial pressure but do not establish it, so an opening pressure and formal perimetry are needed
These findings establish idiopathic intracranial hypertension on their own, so acetazolamide can be started without any further tests
These findings indicate bilateral transverse sinus thrombosis, so full anticoagulation should begin while venography is arranged
quiz.explain: The imaging signs of intracranial hypertension are supportive, not diagnostic: posterior globe flattening, an empty or partially empty sella, distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space with a tortuous nerve, protrusion of the optic nerve head, and bilateral distal transverse sinus narrowing. Each occurs in people without the syndrome, and their absence does not exclude it. Diagnosis remains clinical and manometric, with papilloedema and a raised opening pressure on lumbar puncture after a normal parenchymal study. The sinus stenosis deserves a comment: it is usually smooth, bilateral and at the transverse-sigmoid junction, and it is generally a consequence of raised pressure rather than a cause, though a self-sustaining loop exists and venous stenting is used in selected refractory cases. Vision, not headache, is what is at stake, so perimetry is the urgent test.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has three months of headache that comes on within minutes of standing and settles when lying flat. MRI shows smooth continuous enhancement following the falx, the tentorium and the inner table, sparing the depths of every sulcus, with bilateral thin subdural collections and a distended anterior pontine venous plexus. What should follow?
quiz.answer: Work this up as intracranial hypotension, because dural enhancement that spares the sulci reflects compensatory venous engorgement
choices: Work this up as chronic meningitis, because diffuse meningeal enhancement of this pattern usually reflects an infection
Work this up as bilateral chronic subdural haematoma, because the collections themselves account for the smooth enhancing membranes
Work this up as intracranial hypotension, because dural enhancement that spares the sulci reflects compensatory venous engorgement
Work this up as leptomeningeal metastatic disease, because enhancement along the falx and tentorium reflects tumour seeding
quiz.explain: The distribution is the whole argument. Dural, or pachymeningeal, enhancement is thick, smooth and continuous, follows the falx, tentorium and convexity dura, and never dips into a sulcus. Leptomeningeal enhancement, whether from infection or from carcinomatosis, is thin, irregular and follows the pia into sulci and around folia. In low CSF volume the Monro-Kellie doctrine explains everything you see: as CSF volume falls, blood volume rises to compensate, so the dural venous plexuses engorge and the leaky dural vessels enhance avidly, the brain sags, and subdural fluid accumulates in the space that opens up. The orthostatic history is the strongest clue of all. The subdural collections are a consequence, and draining them without finding the leak is a well-known way to make the patient worse.

quiz.prompt: You are grading that patient's brain MRI with the Bern score. Pachymeningeal enhancement is present, the suprasellar cistern measures 3.5 mm, the venous sinuses are not engorged, bilateral subdural collections are present, the prepontine cistern measures 6.0 mm, and the mamillopontine distance is 6.0 mm. Give the total Bern score. Answer as a whole number of points.
quiz.explain: The Bern score (Dobrocky and colleagues, 2019) has three major signs worth two points each - pachymeningeal enhancement, engorgement of the venous sinus, and effacement of the suprasellar cistern at 4.0 mm or less - and three minor signs worth one point each: a subdural fluid collection, effacement of the prepontine cistern at 5.0 mm or less, and a mamillopontine distance of 6.5 mm or less. Here the enhancement scores 2, the suprasellar cistern at 3.5 mm scores 2, the subdural collections score 1, and the mamillopontine distance at 6.0 mm scores 1; the prepontine cistern at 6.0 mm is above threshold and the sinuses are not engorged, so both score nothing. That is 6 of a possible 9, which falls in the high-probability band of 5 or more and justifies proceeding to specialised myelography to hunt for the leak.

quiz.prompt: The spine MRI in that patient shows no epidural fluid collection at any level, and the referring team concludes there is no leak. Explain why that conclusion is unsafe and what study you would recommend instead.
quiz.answer: A CSF-venous fistula produces no epidural fluid collection, so a normal spine MRI does not exclude it; the study to request is lateral decubitus digital subtraction myelography or dynamic CT myelography, which shows CSF draining directly from a nerve root sleeve into a paraspinal vein.
quiz.explain: Three mechanisms cause spontaneous intracranial hypotension: a ventral dural tear, usually from a calcified disc or osteophyte; a leaking meningeal diverticulum; and a CSF-venous fistula. The first two spill fluid into the epidural space and are therefore visible as an epidural collection on heavily T2-weighted spine imaging. The third does not, because CSF is shunted straight into an adjacent paraspinal vein and never enters the epidural space, so conventional spine MRI is normal. Fistulas are found with the patient in lateral decubitus - the side down matters, since the leak must be dependent - during dynamic myelography with fluoroscopic or CT acquisition timed to the intrathecal contrast bolus. They are commonly treated with transvenous embolisation or surgical ligation. A high Bern score with a normal spine MRI should raise the suspicion, not lower it.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the structures through which cerebrospinal fluid passes in normal circulation, beginning at its production in the lateral ventricle and ending at its resorption.
quiz.answer: lateral-ventricle foramen-of-Monro third-ventricle cerebral-aqueduct fourth-ventricle arachnoid-granulations
quiz.explain: Holding this sequence in mind converts a pattern of ventriculomegaly into an anatomical level. If the lateral ventricles are large and the third is normal, the block is at the foramen of Monro - a colloid cyst is the classic culprit, and it can be unilateral. If the lateral and third ventricles are large and the fourth is normal, the block is at the aqueduct. If all four are large, either the block is at the outlets of the fourth ventricle or the obstruction is beyond the ventricular system altogether, in the subarachnoid space or at the granulations. Note also that choroid plexus is not the only source of CSF, and that lymphatic routes along cranial nerves and dural vessels contribute to clearance alongside the granulations, which is why the older picture of a single drainage point is an oversimplification.

quiz.prompt: On an axial CT at the level of the foramina of Monro, the maximal width across the frontal horns measures 48 mm and the maximal internal diameter of the skull at the same level measures 148 mm. Calculate the Evans index. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The Evans index is the maximal width of the frontal horns divided by the maximal inner table diameter on the same axial slice, so 48 divided by 148 gives 0.32. A value above 0.3 defines ventriculomegaly and is one of the entry criteria for considering normal pressure hydrocephalus. Two cautions keep it honest. It is a crude, slice-dependent, two-dimensional surrogate, and it rises with age and with atrophy, so an index above 0.3 does not by itself mean hydrocephalus - it means the frontal horns are wide, and the reason may be lost brain. Look for the supporting features that separate pressure from atrophy: a narrow callosal angle, tight high convexity sulci with disproportionately widened Sylvian fissures, and upward bowing of the corpus callosum, together with the clinical triad of gait apraxia, cognitive decline and incontinence.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old has months of headache and blurred vision on bending forward. CT shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with a rounded third ventricular recess, a normal-sized fourth ventricle, and periventricular interstitial low density around the frontal horns. Sagittal MRI shows no flow void in the aqueduct. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: The obstruction is at the aqueduct, so endoscopic third ventriculostomy is the diversion to discuss with neurosurgery
choices: The obstruction is at the arachnoid granulations, so a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is the diversion to arrange
The ventricles are enlarged from atrophy, so no diversion is needed and clinical review in six months suffices
The obstruction is at the outlets of the fourth ventricle, so posterior fossa decompression is the procedure that is needed
The obstruction is at the aqueduct, so endoscopic third ventriculostomy is the diversion to discuss with neurosurgery
quiz.explain: The level is read off the pattern. Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth places the block at the aqueduct, and loss of the normal aqueductal flow void on sagittal T2 supports it - though a flow void can also be lost from an artefact-free sequence, so it is corroborative rather than definitive, and a cine phase-contrast study settles it. Periventricular interstitial oedema, best seen as low density hugging the frontal horns, indicates transependymal CSF flow under pressure and separates active hydrocephalus from the wide ventricles of atrophy, where sulci are wide in proportion. The management consequence is real: an obstruction upstream of the fourth ventricle with a patent subarachnoid space is well suited to endoscopic third ventriculostomy, which bypasses the aqueduct without hardware, whereas communicating hydrocephalus generally needs a shunt.

quiz.prompt: A shunted teenager attends with headache and vomiting, and the CT ventricles look much the same size as on the scan from two years ago. Describe how you would nonetheless assess this shunt on imaging.
quiz.answer: Compare with the patient's own baseline scan taken when the shunt was working rather than with the largest previous ventricles, trace the whole catheter on a shunt series for disconnection, kinking or migration, and remember that stiff slit ventricles may fail to enlarge at all despite a blocked shunt.
quiz.explain: Shunt failure is a clinical diagnosis that imaging supports, and the single most useful habit is to pull up the patient's own well-functioning baseline rather than the immediately preceding study. Small interval change from a known good baseline is significant; sameness compared with a scan taken during a previous failure is meaningless. Ventricular size can mislead badly in the slit ventricle syndrome, where non-compliant ventricles do not dilate despite dangerously raised pressure, so a normal-looking CT never excludes obstruction. The shunt series covers the whole track on plain films to look for disconnection at connectors, fracture, kinking, and the tip lying outside the peritoneum. Add to that any new subdural collection, which points to overdrainage rather than blockage, and describe the valve setting if it is a programmable device that has been near a magnet.

nodes.title: Dementia and Neurodegeneration on MRI
nodes.goal: Score atrophy against the patient's age, separate the neurodegenerative phenotypes on MRI, recognise the hydrocephalus that may respond to shunting, and run ARIA surveillance on anti-amyloid therapy.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with two years of progressive episodic memory loss. On coronal T1 angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, the choroid fissures are widened, the temporal horns enlarged and the hippocampal height reduced, giving a medial temporal atrophy score of 2 on each side. Posterior atrophy is 0 and the frontal lobes look normal. What do you report?
quiz.answer: Medial temporal atrophy beyond the age cut-off, a pattern that supports Alzheimer disease
choices: Medial temporal atrophy beyond the age cut-off, a pattern that supports Alzheimer disease
Medial temporal atrophy still within the expected range at this age, so a normal study
Global cortical atrophy out of proportion to the rest, favouring a vascular contribution
Posterior-predominant atrophy out of keeping with the age, favouring a parietal syndrome
quiz.explain: The Scheltens medial temporal atrophy (MTA) scale runs 0 to 4 and is read on a coronal T1 angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, weighing three things together: width of the choroid fissure, width of the temporal horn, and height of the hippocampal formation. The score only means something once you attach an age. The cut-off in common use is a score of 2 or more below the age of 75, and 3 or more at 75 and above; scoring without that adjustment is how normal ageing gets reported as disease. At 68 with a score of 2 bilaterally this study sits above the threshold, and in an amnestic presentation that supports Alzheimer disease. The other readings do not fit what was measured: global cortical atrophy and frontal change were not present, and the posterior atrophy score was 0.

quiz.prompt: On an axial CT slice through the frontal horns, the maximal width across the frontal horns is 42 mm and the maximal internal diameter of the skull on the same slice is 130 mm. Calculate the Evans index. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The Evans index is the maximal width across the frontal horns divided by the maximal internal diameter of the inner table on the same axial slice: 42 divided by 130 gives 0.32. Above 0.3 counts as ventriculomegaly, and this patient clears it. The trap is treating that as a diagnosis. Evans is a screening measure only: it rises with atrophy as readily as with hydrocephalus, it drifts with the slice you choose and with head shape, and it is deliberately crude. What separates idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from ex vacuo dilatation is the disproportion around the ventricles: tight crowded sulci at the high convexity and midline, widened Sylvian fissures, and a callosal angle that has closed to an acute value. Report the index, then report those.

quiz.prompt: A 77-year-old with a magnetic gait, urinary urgency and mild inattention. MRI shows enlarged lateral ventricles, crowded tight sulci over the high convexity and at the midline, widened Sylvian fissures, and a callosal angle of 68 degrees measured on a coronal plane at the posterior commissure. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Disproportionate hydrocephalus with an acute callosal angle, a pattern that supports iNPH
choices: Disproportionate hydrocephalus with an acute callosal angle, a pattern that supports iNPH
Ventricular enlargement secondary to generalised atrophy, with sulci widened throughout
Obstruction at the cerebral aqueduct, with a spared fourth ventricle and raised pressure
Chronic small vessel disease with confluent periventricular change accounting for the gait
quiz.explain: This is the DESH pattern: disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus. The point of the word disproportionate is that the cerebrospinal fluid is redistributed rather than uniformly increased, so ventricles and Sylvian fissures enlarge while the sulci at the vertex and along the midline are squeezed shut. The callosal angle, measured on a coronal image perpendicular to the anterior-posterior commissure line at the level of the posterior commissure, falls below about 90 degrees in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, against roughly 100 to 120 degrees in health or in atrophy. Atrophy is excluded here because the convexity sulci are tight, not open. Aqueduct obstruction would enlarge the third ventricle and spare the fourth in a different way and would not crowd the vertex. Small vessel disease often coexists and does not explain the geometry.

quiz.prompt: A referrer asks how you separate the big ventricles of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from the big ventricles of atrophy. Give the discriminating findings in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: In iNPH the enlargement is disproportionate: the callosal angle is acute at under about 90 degrees, the sulci at the high convexity and midline are tight and crowded, and the Sylvian fissures are widened, whereas atrophy opens the sulci everywhere including the vertex.
quiz.explain: Ventricular size alone cannot make this call, which is why the Evans index disappoints on its own. The discriminators are all about disproportion. A callosal angle below roughly 90 degrees, tight crowded high convexity and medial sulci, and widened Sylvian fissures together form the DESH pattern and are the findings that correlate with shunt response. Atrophy does the opposite: cerebrospinal fluid expands into sulci uniformly, so the vertex is open and the callosal angle stays obtuse. Two extras are worth adding to the report because they move the multidisciplinary decision: focal sulcal dilatation trapped between crowded gyri, which is easily mistaken for atrophy, and any aqueductal flow void that raises the alternative of an obstructive cause. Comorbid small vessel disease should be described rather than used to dismiss the diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old with fluctuating attention, well-formed visual hallucinations and mild parkinsonism. MRI shows relatively preserved hippocampal volumes with mild global atrophy. FDG-PET shows occipital hypometabolism with metabolism in the posterior cingulate preserved relative to the precuneus and cuneus. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies, given spared medial temporal lobes and the cingulate island pattern
choices: Dementia with Lewy bodies, given spared medial temporal lobes and the cingulate island pattern
Alzheimer disease, since occipital hypometabolism is the earliest metabolic change it produces
Posterior cortical atrophy, which produces this same occipital and parietal metabolic deficit
Frontotemporal dementia, in which the hippocampi are characteristically preserved on volumetry
quiz.explain: Two features point the same way. Medial temporal structures are relatively spared in dementia with Lewy bodies, which is the opposite of the Alzheimer pattern and is the single most useful structural discriminator on a routine MRI. On FDG-PET the occipital cortex is hypometabolic, and within a hypometabolic posterior belt the posterior cingulate stands out as preserved next to the precuneus and cuneus, the so-called cingulate island. Alzheimer disease does the reverse: it hits the posterior cingulate and precuneus early and typically spares the occipital cortex. Posterior cortical atrophy is visually led but shows marked parieto-occipital atrophy and usually rests on Alzheimer pathology. Frontotemporal dementia shows frontal and anterior temporal loss. If the diagnosis remains uncertain, reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake supports Lewy body disease.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old presents with two years of disinhibition, apathy and loss of empathy, with preserved day-to-day memory. MRI shows asymmetric atrophy of the frontal poles and anterior temporal lobes with knife-edge gyri and widened anterior interhemispheric fissure; the parietal lobes and posterior hippocampi look normal. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, from the asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal loss
choices: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, from the asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal loss
Alzheimer disease, from the precuneus and posterior cingulate volume loss in this distribution
Vascular cognitive impairment, from the confluent deep white matter burden in this distribution
Dementia with Lewy bodies, from the preservation of cortex outside the occipital lobes described
quiz.explain: Frontotemporal degeneration is recognised by where the tissue has gone and by how asymmetric the loss is. Knife-edge gyri at the frontal poles and anterior temporal lobes, a gaping anterior interhemispheric fissure and a widened frontal horn contour on the more affected side are the structural signature, and episodic memory is comparatively preserved because the posterior hippocampus is not the target. Subtypes matter for the report: predominant orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate loss goes with the behavioural variant, severe left anterior temporal loss with semantic variant primary progressive aphasia, and left posterior frontoinsular loss with the non-fluent variant. Alzheimer disease is excluded by the intact parietal and posterior cingulate regions, vascular disease by the absence of a white matter or infarct burden, and Lewy body disease by the frontal, rather than occipital, emphasis.

quiz.prompt: You are setting up MRI surveillance for a patient starting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody. Explain in one or two sentences what the two forms of ARIA look like and which sequence detects each.
quiz.answer: ARIA-E is oedema, seen as gyral swelling with sulcal and parenchymal FLAIR hyperintensity, while ARIA-H is haemorrhage, seen as new microhaemorrhages or superficial siderosis blooming on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or gradient echo.
quiz.explain: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities split cleanly by sequence, so your protocol must carry both. ARIA-E is vasogenic oedema and effusion: FLAIR shows gyral swelling, subcortical white matter hyperintensity and sometimes sulcal hyperintensity, and it is usually parieto-occipital and often multifocal. ARIA-H is blood: new microhaemorrhages and new areas of superficial siderosis that bloom on SWI or T2* gradient echo and are invisible on FLAIR. Read them against the baseline study rather than in isolation, because only incident lesions count. Most ARIA is asymptomatic and detected on scheduled surveillance, but headache, confusion, visual change or seizure in a treated patient is an urgent scan, not a routine one. Report the site, the extent and the count, since severity grading and the decision to pause or stop dosing depend on those numbers.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these regions in the order that neurofibrillary tau pathology, and the atrophy that tracks it, typically involve them in Alzheimer disease.
quiz.answer: transentorhinal-cortex hippocampus temporoparietal-association-cortex primary-visual-cortex
quiz.explain: The Braak scheme describes tau spreading in a stereotyped path, and MRI atrophy follows it a step behind. The earliest stages sit in the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, which is why the medial temporal atrophy score is the first structural measure to move. Limbic stages then take the hippocampus, amygdala and posterior cingulate, and by this point the amnestic syndrome is usually clinically obvious. Isocortical stages spread into temporoparietal association cortex, giving the precuneus and parietal thinning that anchors an Alzheimer read and drives the posterior atrophy score. Primary sensory and motor cortex, including primary visual cortex, is involved last. Knowing the sequence explains two everyday observations: why an early scan can look normal, and why atypical presentations such as posterior cortical atrophy, which start out of sequence, warrant a different structural search.

quiz.prompt: A patient on an anti-amyloid antibody had 2 microhaemorrhages on the baseline SWI. Surveillance MRI before the fifth infusion shows 9 microhaemorrhages in total. How many incident microhaemorrhages does this represent? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Nine on today's scan minus two that were there at baseline gives seven incident lesions. The arithmetic is trivial and the concept is not: ARIA-H is graded on new lesions counted against the baseline study, never on the running total, so a report that quotes only the total invites either false alarm or false reassurance. On the radiographic severity scale used in the anti-amyloid trials, incident microhaemorrhages are graded mild at four or fewer, moderate at five to nine, and severe at ten or more; new superficial siderosis is scored within ARIA-H as well. Baseline matters in the other direction too, since more than four microhaemorrhages, an area of superficial siderosis or a prior macrohaemorrhage are grounds to withhold treatment under the appropriate use recommendations. Always compare against the same baseline sequence, because SWI finds more lesions than gradient echo.

quiz.prompt: An 86-year-old has a slowly progressive, largely isolated amnestic syndrome. MRI shows medial temporal atrophy scored 4 bilaterally with a strikingly small hippocampus on each side, posterior atrophy 0, and only mild global cortical atrophy. Amyloid PET is negative. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Limbic-predominant TDP-43 pathology with hippocampal sclerosis rather than Alzheimer disease
choices: Limbic-predominant TDP-43 pathology with hippocampal sclerosis rather than Alzheimer disease
Typical Alzheimer disease, in which a negative amyloid scan is the expected result at this age
Frontotemporal dementia, which characteristically opens with isolated hippocampal volume loss
Normal ageing, since hippocampal loss of this degree is anticipated in the ninth decade of life
quiz.explain: A very old patient, a syndrome that stays amnestic, hippocampal atrophy out of all proportion to the rest of the brain, and a negative amyloid scan together describe limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, in which hippocampal sclerosis is the structural correlate. It is common above 80 and is regularly misreported as Alzheimer disease, which matters now that treatment decisions hinge on amyloid status. Alzheimer disease would be expected to spread beyond the limbic system to the precuneus and parietal cortex and to be amyloid positive; a negative scan in a typical clinical picture argues against it rather than being expected. Frontotemporal degeneration begins frontally and anteriorly in the temporal lobe. And a score of 4 is well beyond the age-adjusted threshold of 3 that applies from 75 onwards, so this is not simple ageing.

quiz.prompt: A physician asks you what a positive amyloid PET actually establishes in a patient with cognitive decline. Answer in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: A positive scan shows tracer binding in cortical grey matter with loss of the normal grey and white matter contrast; it establishes that amyloid pathology is present but does not on its own prove that amyloid is the cause of the patient's cognitive syndrome.
quiz.explain: Amyloid tracers such as florbetapir, flutemetamol and florbetaben bind fibrillar plaque in cortical grey matter. A negative scan keeps white matter tracts bright against a dark cortical ribbon, so the grey and white matter boundary stays sharp; a positive scan fills the cortex, blurring or reversing that contrast. The read is essentially binary, and it is a pathology test, not a syndrome test. Amyloid is present in a substantial minority of cognitively normal older people, so a positive scan in a patient whose picture fits frontotemporal or Lewy body disease may be an incidental finding. Tau PET is the more topographical study, tracking a Braak-like distribution that correlates better with symptoms and atrophy. In current practice the biggest use of amyloid status is gatekeeping anti-amyloid therapy and the surveillance that comes with it.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old with a subjective memory complaint and normal formal cognitive testing is scanned. Global cortical atrophy scores 1, medial temporal atrophy scores 2 bilaterally and posterior atrophy scores 0, with no infarcts and only punctate white matter foci. What should your report say?
quiz.answer: Atrophy within the range expected at 82; report it as such and avoid implying degenerative disease
choices: Atrophy within the range expected at 82; report it as such and avoid implying degenerative disease
Atrophy beyond the range expected at 82; report a pattern that is consistent with Alzheimer disease
Atrophy chiefly posterior; report a parietal-predominant pattern and recommend amyloid imaging next
Atrophy chiefly frontal; report a frontotemporal pattern and recommend neuropsychological assessment
quiz.explain: This is the commonest way a structured read goes wrong. Every visual scale is age-dependent, and the thresholds move upward with each decade. For medial temporal atrophy the widely applied cut-off is 2 or more below 75 but 3 or more at 75 and above, so a score of 2 in an 82-year-old is unremarkable. Global cortical atrophy runs 0 to 3 and a score of 1 is mild and expected here. Posterior atrophy runs 0 to 3, and it is 0. The other options misdescribe the measurements: nothing posterior or frontal predominates. Writing that the appearances are within the expected range for the age is a positive finding, not a failure to commit, and it protects a worried patient from a diagnosis the images do not support. Note the burden and offer follow-up if the clinical picture changes.

nodes.title: Epilepsy: the HARNESS Protocol and What It Looks For
nodes.goal: Design and read a dedicated epilepsy MRI, find the lesions a routine brain study hides, and know what to do next when the protocol comes back negative.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old with drug-resistant focal seizures is referred to a surgical programme. The only imaging is a 1.5T study with 5 mm axial T2 and FLAIR and 5 mm axial T1, reported as normal two years ago. What do you arrange?
quiz.answer: Rescan at 3T with millimetric 3D T1 and FLAIR plus a high-resolution coronal T2 through the hippocampi
choices: Rescan at 3T with millimetric 3D T1 and FLAIR plus a high-resolution coronal T2 through the hippocampi
Repeat the same axial protocol with gadolinium, since epileptogenic lesions enhance once they are mature
Add diffusion and perfusion to the same axial protocol, which will expose the abnormal cortical region
Move directly to intracranial electrodes, since a study reported as normal ends the structural work-up
quiz.explain: A routine brain MRI is built to exclude a mass or a bleed, and it is the wrong instrument for this question. Thick axial slices partial-volume the cortical ribbon, so the blurred grey and white matter junction of a dysplasia is averaged away, and an axial plane cuts the hippocampus obliquely so that mild volume loss and signal change go unseen. The HARNESS-MRI protocol from the ILAE neuroimaging task force fixes exactly this: millimetric isotropic 3D T1, millimetric isotropic 3D FLAIR, and a two-dimensional coronal T2 with submillimetric in-plane resolution angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, preferably at 3T. Contrast adds almost nothing to a first-pass epilepsy protocol because the common lesions do not enhance. Diffusion and perfusion do not resolve the cortical ribbon. And a negative outside study is a reason to rescan properly, not to abandon imaging.

quiz.prompt: A routine two-dimensional FLAIR is acquired at 1.0 mm by 1.0 mm in-plane with 5 mm slices. The 3D FLAIR of an epilepsy protocol is 1.0 mm isotropic. By what factor is the voxel volume of the routine sequence larger? Answer as a number to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The routine voxel is 1.0 by 1.0 by 5.0, which is 5 cubic millimetres; the isotropic voxel is 1 cubic millimetre. The ratio is 5.0. That single figure explains most missed lesions in epilepsy. Signal in a voxel is the average of everything inside it, so a 5 mm slice through the cortex blends grey matter, white matter and cerebrospinal fluid and quietly erases the two findings that matter most: subtle blurring of the grey and white matter junction, and a thin band of high FLAIR signal running toward the ventricle. Isotropic voxels also let you reformat in any plane from one acquisition, so an abnormality suspected on the axial reconstruction can be confirmed on coronal and sagittal reformats of the same data rather than requiring the patient back.

quiz.prompt: A radiographer asks you to specify the three core sequences of the HARNESS-MRI epilepsy protocol. Describe them in one or two sentences, including the geometry that matters.
quiz.answer: A millimetric isotropic 3D T1, a millimetric isotropic 3D FLAIR, and a high in-plane resolution coronal T2 angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, acquired at 3 tesla wherever possible.
quiz.explain: HARNESS-MRI, the harmonised structural protocol proposed by the ILAE neuroimaging task force, was designed to be short enough that any department can run it. The isotropic 3D T1 gives the cortical ribbon and supports post-processing and surface analysis. The isotropic 3D FLAIR carries the signal abnormality of dysplasia and hippocampal sclerosis and reformats freely. The two-dimensional coronal T2, with in-plane resolution well below a millimetre and angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, is what lets you judge hippocampal size, signal and internal architecture side by side. A susceptibility-weighted or gradient echo sequence is a sensible addition for blood products when a cavernoma is in question. Contrast is not part of the core protocol, and adding it before a proper structural study is a common way to waste a scan slot.

quiz.prompt: A coronal T2 shows a small right hippocampus with increased FLAIR signal and loss of the normal internal digitations, and the right temporal horn is dilated. Which additional finding on the same study would most support the diagnosis you are considering?
quiz.answer: Atrophy of the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body with a small ipsilateral temporal lobe
choices: Atrophy of the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body with a small ipsilateral temporal lobe
Avid nodular enhancement of the hippocampal head after gadolinium with surrounding oedema
Restricted diffusion throughout the hippocampal body persisting on the apparent diffusion map
Enlargement of the contralateral hippocampus with high signal in its adjacent white matter
quiz.explain: Hippocampal sclerosis is read on three primary features: reduced volume, raised T2 and FLAIR signal, and loss of the internal architecture, meaning the digitations of the head and the internal striations blur into a featureless block. Because the circuit degenerates as a whole, the supporting findings sit downstream: the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body atrophy, the temporal horn dilates to fill the space, the collateral white matter loses its grey-to-white distinction, and the whole temporal lobe may be slightly small. Those extras are what convert a suspicion into a confident lateralisation, and lateralisation is the whole point in a surgical candidate. Avid enhancement with oedema should redirect you to a tumour or encephalitis. Persistent restricted diffusion suggests a recent insult, not chronic sclerosis. A big contralateral hippocampus is not a recognised sign and risks lateralising to the wrong side.

quiz.prompt: Describe the transmantle sign in one or two sentences, and say what its presence tells you about the underlying lesion.
quiz.answer: It is a funnel-shaped band of T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity tapering from thickened, blurred cortex down to the ventricular surface, and it indicates a focal cortical dysplasia, characteristically the ILAE type IIb form with balloon cells.
quiz.explain: The sign traces the path abnormal cells took during radial migration, so it runs the full thickness of the mantle from the cortical surface to the ventricular ependyma, widest at the cortex and narrowing as it descends. On isotropic 3D FLAIR it is often the only unequivocal abnormality, which is why that sequence is a protocol core. Look for its companions in the same place: cortical thickening, blurring of the grey and white matter junction, an abnormal sulcal or gyral configuration, and sometimes a deep unusually oriented sulcus at the epicentre. Its value is practical rather than descriptive. A transmantle sign identifies a discrete, resectable target with a good chance of seizure freedom, and it turns an MRI-negative patient into an MRI-positive one, which changes both the surgical decision and the odds quoted to the patient.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old has had focal seizures with impaired awareness since childhood. MRI shows a cortically based, multicystic bubbly lesion in the left temporal lobe with a bright FLAIR rim, no surrounding oedema, no enhancement, and gentle scalloping of the inner table of the skull. What is the lesion and how should the report frame it?
quiz.answer: A DNET, framed as a long-standing epileptogenic cortical lesion rather than an aggressive tumour
choices: A DNET, framed as a long-standing epileptogenic cortical lesion rather than an aggressive tumour
A ganglioglioma, framed around the enhancing mural nodule and calcification that characterise it
A cavernoma, framed around the complete haemosiderin rim and the blooming seen on susceptibility
An acute infarct, framed around the cortical swelling and restricted diffusion in a vascular territory
quiz.explain: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumours are cortically based, wedge-shaped or bubbly on T2, and characteristically have a bright FLAIR rim around a cluster of microcysts. They cause no oedema and little mass effect, and the slow remodelling of the overlying inner table testifies to how long they have been there. Enhancement is usually absent or faint. The reporting framing matters as much as the label: this is a lesion whose significance is seizures, so the report should support a planned epilepsy surgery pathway rather than trigger an urgent oncological work-up. A ganglioglioma, the other classic long-standing temporal lesion, more often shows a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule and calcification. A cavernoma would show a complete haemosiderin rim with marked blooming. An infarct would be territorial, swollen and diffusion-restricted, and would not scallop bone.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old with focal seizures has MRI showing smooth ovoid nodules lining both lateral ventricles. The nodules follow grey matter signal exactly on T1, T2 and FLAIR, do not enhance, and show no blooming on susceptibility imaging. What do you conclude and advise?
quiz.answer: Periventricular nodular heterotopia: grey matter in the wrong place, so no biopsy is needed
choices: Periventricular nodular heterotopia: grey matter in the wrong place, so no biopsy is needed
Subependymal nodules of tuberous sclerosis: look for calcification and cortical tubers as well
Subependymal tumour spread: the nodules would enhance and follow cerebrospinal fluid pathways
Old subependymal haemorrhage: blood products lining the ependymal surface after a preterm bleed
quiz.explain: The discriminator is signal, and the rule is simple: heterotopic grey matter is grey matter, so it matches cortex on every sequence, does not enhance, and does not bloom. Subependymal nodules in tuberous sclerosis often calcify and bloom, frequently enhance, and travel with cortical tubers and radial migration lines. Metastatic or lymphomatous subependymal deposits enhance and are usually irregular. Old germinal matrix haemorrhage leaves susceptibility-positive residue. Once heterotopia is established the useful work begins: describe how extensive and how symmetric the nodules are, look for the associated cortical malformation and for a thin corpus callosum or cerebellar hypoplasia, and mention that bilateral diffuse periventricular nodular heterotopia is associated with FLNA variants, since that carries implications for the patient's family as well as for surgical planning.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these investigations in the order a presurgical epilepsy programme would usually deploy them for a patient whose first MRI was reported as normal.
quiz.answer: HARNESS-MRI morphometric-post-processing FDG-PET ictal-SPECT intracranial-EEG
quiz.explain: The ladder climbs from cheap and non-invasive toward expensive and invasive, and each rung is only worth attempting once the one below it has been done properly. First repeat the structural study with a dedicated protocol, because a large share of so-called MRI-negative patients simply had the wrong sequences. Then run morphometric post-processing on the isotropic 3D T1, comparing junction and thickness maps against a normal database to flag candidate regions for a targeted re-read. Interictal FDG-PET follows, showing regional hypometabolism that usually extends beyond the lesion but reliably lateralises. Ictal SPECT, ideally coregistered with MRI, requires an injection during a seizure and is therefore resource-heavy and reserved for continuing uncertainty. Intracranial EEG sits at the top: it defines the seizure onset zone directly but carries surgical risk, and it needs a hypothesis to sample, which is precisely what every earlier rung supplies.

quiz.prompt: You are planning the dedicated coronal T2 stack. The hippocampus measures 4.0 cm along its long axis and you will use 2 mm slices with no interslice gap. How many slices are needed to cover it end to end? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Forty millimetres of coverage divided by 2 mm per contiguous slice gives 20 slices, and in practice you would prescribe a few more at each end so that the head and tail are not clipped. The planning point behind the arithmetic is that this stack must be angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, prescribed on a sagittal or oblique reformat, and must run from in front of the hippocampal head to behind the tail. Coverage failures are a real cause of missed sclerosis, because the head is where the digitations live and the tail is where subtle atrophy declares itself. Thin contiguous slices also preserve the side-to-side comparison that the coronal plane exists to provide: symmetry is judged by looking at both hippocampi in the same slice, which an oblique or gapped acquisition quietly destroys.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old with focal seizures has a 12 mm lesion at the right frontal grey and white matter junction with a mixed-signal popcorn core and a complete dark rim on T2, blooming on gradient echo, with no oedema. A cousin had seizures and a brain haemorrhage. What do you add to the study and why?
quiz.answer: Whole-brain susceptibility-weighted imaging, to search for the additional lesions of the familial form
choices: Whole-brain susceptibility-weighted imaging, to search for the additional lesions of the familial form
Perfusion imaging through the lesion, to separate a cavernoma from a haemorrhagic metastatic deposit
Spectroscopy through the lesion, to demonstrate the choline elevation of a vascular malformation
Early and delayed contrast imaging, to demonstrate the rapid arteriovenous shunting that it contains
quiz.explain: The described lesion is a cavernous malformation: locules of blood of differing ages give the popcorn core, and the complete haemosiderin rim blooms heavily on susceptibility-sensitive sequences. With a family history the question is no longer what the lesion is but how many there are, because multiplicity defines familial cerebral cavernous malformation and changes counselling, surveillance and the genetic conversation for relatives. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is far more sensitive than gradient echo for the tiny punctate lesions that make the diagnosis, so it should cover the whole brain. Perfusion and spectroscopy add nothing to a lesion this characteristic. Cavernomas are angiographically occult and contain no arteriovenous shunt, so dynamic contrast imaging is misdirected, though it is worth looking for an associated developmental venous anomaly, which must be preserved if the cavernoma is resected.

quiz.prompt: Describe how polymicrogyria appears on a millimetric 3D T1 and name the associated finding that often accompanies it.
quiz.answer: The cortical ribbon looks irregular, stippled and overly folded, thin in reality but mimicking thickening at low resolution, most often around the sylvian fissure, and it is frequently accompanied by anomalous draining veins.
quiz.explain: Polymicrogyria is a disorder of late migration and cortical organisation in which many small gyri fuse at the surface. On a thick-slice study the packed miniature gyri average together and the cortical ribbon simply looks thick and lumpy, which is how it gets confused with pachygyria; on millimetric isotropic T1 the true stippled, bumpy inner surface with a shallow irregular sulcal pattern becomes visible. The perisylvian region is the commonest site, and bilateral perisylvian involvement produces a recognisable clinical syndrome with oromotor difficulty. Look for the companions: anomalous or enlarged draining veins over the affected cortex, an overlying arachnoid or subarachnoid space that appears too generous, and underlying white matter volume loss. Distribution matters for aetiology, since a unilateral perisylvian distribution raises congenital cytomegalovirus or an in utero vascular insult.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old with drug-resistant frontal lobe epilepsy has a full HARNESS protocol reported as normal. Scalp EEG and semiology both point to the right frontal lobe. What is the most useful next imaging step?
quiz.answer: Run morphometric post-processing against a normal database, then re-read with that hypothesis
choices: Run morphometric post-processing against a normal database, then re-read with that hypothesis
Report the study as normal and close the structural work-up before the surgical meeting is held
Repeat the identical MRI in twelve months and wait for the abnormality to declare itself over time
Rely on interictal FDG-PET alone and take the hypometabolic lobe as the resection target directly
quiz.explain: Around a quarter to a third of drug-resistant focal epilepsies are called MRI-negative, and a good share of those are really reader-negative: the lesion is on the images but is too subtle for an unguided read. Morphometric post-processing helps twice over. It builds junction, extension and thickness maps from the isotropic 3D T1 and compares them voxel by voxel against a normal cohort, generating candidate regions; and it then licenses a targeted second read, where a radiologist looks at one gyrus with the electroclinical hypothesis in hand.
