That combination converts a meaningful number of negative studies into positive ones, and finding the lesion improves the odds of seizure freedom after surgery. Simply repeating the same scan later rarely helps in an adult. FDG-PET is valuable but its hypometabolism is regional and typically wider than the lesion, so it lateralises rather than defines a resection margin.

nodes.title: Intracranial Haemorrhage in Head Trauma
nodes.goal: Assign an intracranial bleed to its compartment from the shape of its margins, and recognise the herniation it threatens.

quiz.prompt: A cyclist struck the top of his head. CT shows a biconvex high-attenuation collection at the vertex that extends from one side of the midline to the other but stops abruptly at the coronal suture on both sides. What is the collection?
choices: An extradural haematoma from the sagittal sinus
An interhemispheric subdural haematoma
Subarachnoid blood filling the vertex sulci
A subgaleal haematoma over the vertex
quiz.answer: An extradural haematoma from the sagittal sinus
quiz.explain: Two boundaries, two different rules, and here both are met by one answer: held at the sutures, free across the midline. A vertex extradural is classically venous, from a torn superior sagittal sinus or a fracture through the sagittal groove, and it behaves differently from the arterial temporal variety - it may accumulate slowly over hours to days, and at operation it bleeds from a sinus rather than from the middle meningeal artery, which is why the neurosurgeon wants to know the diagnosis before the bone flap is raised. It is also the extradural most often missed, because it sits at the top of the stack where axial images contain little brain and the collection is easily dismissed as volume averaging with the vault: coronal reformats are what show it. Subgaleal blood lies outside the skull, crosses sutures with the galea, and expands the scalp rather than indenting the brain.

quiz.prompt: An extradural haematoma measures 6.0 cm in its greatest axial diameter, 4.0 cm perpendicular to that on the same image, and extends over 3.0 cm in the craniocaudal direction. Using the ABC/2 estimate for an ellipsoid, what is its volume in millilitres? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: ABC/2 multiplies the three orthogonal diameters and halves the product: 6 x 4 x 3 / 2 = 36 mL. It approximates the ellipsoid volume, which is four-thirds pi times abc over eight, or about 0.52abc, close enough to the 0.5 the formula uses - and it takes seconds at the workstation, which is why it has survived every attempt to replace it. The number matters because published surgical guidance takes an extradural volume above 30 cm3 as warranting evacuation whatever the GCS, so this measurement decides the content of the phone call rather than merely decorating the report. Two cautions: the estimate overstates volume for irregular or multilobular collections, and the C dimension should be counted from the images - the number of slices containing blood multiplied by the slice thickness - rather than eyeballed from a single plane.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old on warfarin has been drowsy for a week, three weeks after a fall. The CT is reported as showing no haemorrhage. Reviewing it, you find that sulci are absent across the right convexity, the grey-white junction on that side is displaced several millimetres away from the inner table, and there is 4 mm of midline shift to the left. What explains this?
choices: An isodense subdural collection over that convexity
Cortical swelling from a subacute infarction
Diffuse cerebral oedema after a hypoxic insult
Subarachnoid blood layering within the sulci
quiz.answer: An isodense subdural collection over that convexity
quiz.explain: A subdural haematoma passes through an isodense phase at roughly one to three weeks as the clot degrades, and it can match cortex closely enough to disappear. What gives it away is displacement rather than density: effaced sulci over a convexity, a grey-white interface standing off from the inner table, a compressed ventricle, and midline shift with no visible cause. Bilateral isodense collections are the real trap, because the shift cancels and the study looks normal but tight - so look for ventricles that are too small for the age and cortex held away from the vault on both sides. Anaemia lowers clot attenuation as well, so an acute subdural in a profoundly anaemic or coagulopathic patient can be isodense from the outset, and a fluid-fluid level or a swirl of unclotted blood within a collection raises the question of continuing haemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced CT, which opacifies the displaced cortical veins, or MRI, settles an equivocal study.

quiz.prompt: A 76-year-old with no history of trauma has had several episodes of numbness spreading up the left hand and arm, each lasting a few minutes. CT shows blood confined to three adjacent sulci over the right parietal convexity, with nothing in the basal cisterns or the Sylvian fissures. What should be suspected?
choices: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy of leptomeningeal vessels
Rupture of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction after a headache
A cortical vein thrombosis with local extravasation
quiz.answer: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy of leptomeningeal vessels
quiz.explain: Distribution carries the whole argument. Aneurysmal blood arrives under arterial pressure into the basal cisterns and fills them, and an anterior communicating aneurysm loads the interhemispheric fissure and often the ventricles. Blood confined to a few convexity sulci comes from vessels lying on the surface, and in a patient over about sixty the commonest cause is amyloid angiopathy. The transient spreading sensory episodes are the classic companion - amyloid spells, probably cortical spreading depolarisation over the blood - and they matter because they are routinely mistaken for transient ischaemic attacks and treated with antiplatelets or anticoagulants, which is the worst available move in a brain full of fragile amyloid-laden vessels. Confirm on susceptibility-weighted MRI, looking for lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis that spare the deep grey matter. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction also produces convexity subarachnoid blood and is the right answer in a younger patient with thunderclap headaches, often postpartum or after serotonergic drugs.

quiz.prompt: A patient thrown from a vehicle has blood in five separate spaces on one CT of the head. Put the spaces in order from the scalp inwards.
quiz.answer: subgaleal extradural subdural subarachnoid intraparenchymal
quiz.explain: The order is scalp, skull, dura, arachnoid, brain. Subgaleal blood lies between the galea aponeurotica and the pericranium, outside the skull, and crosses sutures because the galea does - unlike the neonatal subperiosteal cephalhaematoma, which is bounded by them. Extradural blood strips dura from the inner table and is held at the sutures. Subdural blood spreads in the potential space between dura and arachnoid, crossing sutures freely but stopped by the falx and tentorium. Subarachnoid blood follows cerebrospinal fluid into sulci and cisterns and so takes the shape of the space rather than pushing the brain aside. Intraparenchymal blood is within the brain itself. Every shape question a trauma CT asks - biconvex, crescentic, sulcal, rounded - reduces to which of these five spaces the blood is in, and getting the space right is what determines whether the answer is an operation, an observation, or an angiogram.

quiz.prompt: A registrar can recite that an extradural haematoma does not cross a suture while a subdural haematoma does not cross the midline, but cannot say why. Explain both boundaries from the anatomy of the dura, and give the exception you would still be careful about.
quiz.answer: The dura has two layers. The outer periosteal layer is the inner periosteum of the skull and is continuous with the pericranium through the sutures, where it is firmly adherent, so an extradural collection, which forms by stripping dura off the inner table, is halted at sutural lines. The falx and tentorium are reflections of the inner meningeal layer alone and lie deep to the extradural space, so extradural blood crosses the midline without difficulty. Subdural blood collects deep to both layers, between dura and arachnoid, so it spreads under sutures freely but is walled off by the falx and tentorium. The exception to be careful about is a suture that has been fractured through or diastased, which an extradural can cross, and the unfused sutures of an infant, where the rule barely applies.
quiz.explain: Reading the two rules together gives a usable heuristic: a collection that crosses the midline is extradural, and a collection that crosses a suture is subdural. The one refinement is the interhemispheric subdural, which lies along one side of the falx and follows it without crossing to the other side, so it can look like midline blood without breaking the rule. The mechanism also explains the company each keeps. Extradural blood needs enough force to separate an adherent dura, so the great majority in adults have an overlying fracture crossing a vascular groove, most often the middle meningeal artery in the temporoparietal region. Subdural blood needs only a bridging vein to tear, which is why it appears in atrophic, anticoagulated and alcoholic patients after trivial injury, and why its volume tells you less about the force of the impact than its extradural counterpart.

quiz.prompt: A biconvex temporal collection 15 mm thick contains an irregular area of lower attenuation within an otherwise dense clot. The patient's GCS has fallen two points in twenty minutes. What does the low-attenuation area within the clot indicate?
choices: Fresh unclotted blood still entering the collection
Cerebrospinal fluid tracking through a dural tear
Fat from a fracture through the diploic space
An older collection that has begun to liquefy
quiz.answer: Fresh unclotted blood still entering the collection
quiz.explain: This is the swirl sign. Clotted blood is dense because it is retracted and packed with haemoglobin; blood that has not yet clotted attenuates less, so an active bleeding point shows as a swirl or lucency inside a dense haematoma. It means the collection is still growing, it is associated with rapid expansion and worse outcome, and paired with a falling GCS it argues for shortening the interval to theatre rather than repeating the scan in six hours. The near-miss worth thinking through is the older, liquefying collection: that takes days to weeks, is uniform rather than swirled, and does not occur in a patient injured within the hour. Cerebrospinal fluid entering through a dural tear would sit at water attenuation with a sharp margin rather than swirling through the clot. The same sign in an intraparenchymal haematoma carries the same meaning, and its contrast-enhanced relative is the spot sign.

quiz.prompt: An 18-year-old is unconscious with a GCS of 6 after a high-speed collision. The CT shows two punctate dense foci at the grey-white junction of the right frontal lobe, no mass effect and nothing else. The team is reassured by the CT. Explain the discrepancy, and say what imaging you would request and what you would look for.
quiz.answer: The discrepancy is typical of diffuse axonal injury, in which rotational acceleration shears axons where tissues of differing stiffness meet. Most of those lesions are non-haemorrhagic and therefore invisible on CT, so the CT badly underestimates the injury, and a near-normal CT with a very low GCS is evidence of axonal injury rather than grounds for reassurance; the two dense dots are the haemorrhagic minority. MRI is the study. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is the sequence that matters most, since it shows microhaemorrhages that gradient echo and certainly CT miss, and diffusion-weighted imaging shows the non-haemorrhagic lesions as foci of restricted diffusion. Look at the lobar grey-white junction, at the corpus callosum and particularly its splenium, and at the dorsolateral midbrain and upper pons, because depth of involvement grades the injury and carries the prognosis.
quiz.explain: The three depths are the classic staging: grade 1 lobar grey-white junction, grade 2 adding the corpus callosum, grade 3 adding the dorsolateral brainstem, with outcome worsening as the lesions go deeper. The mechanism explains the sites - the callosum is tethered by the falx and the midbrain by the tentorium, so both are shearing planes - and it also explains the company: intraventricular blood near the fornix, and small haemorrhages in the deep grey matter. Timing matters when requesting the study, because susceptibility lesions persist for months while diffusion lesions are most conspicuous in the first week. The final point is medico-legal as much as clinical: documenting axonal injury in a patient whose CT looks bland is often the only objective evidence of why the patient did not wake up.

quiz.prompt: On the axial CT at the level of the foramen of Monro, the distance from inner table to inner table is 140 mm, and the septum pellucidum lies 82 mm from the left inner table. What is the midline shift in millimetres? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The true midline is half the width, 70 mm; the septum sits at 82 mm, so it is displaced 12 mm to the right. Measure at the foramen of Monro, from a line joining the anterior and posterior attachments of the falx, and state where you measured, because shift at the septum, at the third ventricle and at the pineal can differ in a rotated or asymmetric head. The threshold to have in mind is that an acute subdural haematoma more than 10 mm thick, or producing more than 5 mm of midline shift, is generally taken as warranting evacuation whatever the GCS. The most useful thing this measurement does, though, is flag a mismatch: shift far out of proportion to the visible collection means either that swelling is doing the work - in which case evacuating a thin collection will not fix it - or that there is a second collection you have not seen, most often an isodense one on the other side.

quiz.prompt: Three days after evacuation of an acute subdural haematoma that had caused 14 mm of midline shift, a patient develops weakness of the left leg. CT now shows new hypoattenuation along the medial surface of the right frontal lobe. What has happened?
choices: Anterior cerebral artery compression beneath the falx
Posterior cerebral artery compression at the tentorium
Watershed infarction from intraoperative hypotension
Venous infarction from a thrombosed bridging vein
quiz.answer: Anterior cerebral artery compression beneath the falx
quiz.explain: Subfalcine herniation pushes the cingulate gyrus under the free edge of the falx, and the anterior cerebral artery and its callosomarginal branch travel with it, to be compressed against a rigid edge; the medial frontal cortex infarcts and the contralateral leg goes weak. It is the herniation easiest to see on a scan and easiest to leave out of a report, and it is worth naming explicitly because the resulting infarct appears days later and is otherwise attributed to the operation. The mirror image happens one level down: uncal herniation compresses the posterior cerebral artery against the tentorial edge and infarcts the occipital lobe, which is why a homonymous hemianopia after a temporal haematoma is not a coincidence. Watershed infarction from hypotension would be bilateral and in the borderzones rather than confined to one medial frontal lobe, and bridging vein thrombosis would not respect an arterial territory.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a right temporal extradural haematoma develops a dilated right pupil and a left hemiparesis. Over the next hour the left side improves while the right side becomes weak, and the right pupil stays dilated. What accounts for the change of side?
choices: The left cerebral peduncle is pressed on the tentorial edge
A second haematoma has developed on the left side
The left internal carotid artery has dissected acutely
A left middle cerebral artery embolus has occurred
quiz.answer: The left cerebral peduncle is pressed on the tentorial edge
quiz.explain: This is Kernohan's notch phenomenon, the classic false localising sign. Descending transtentorial herniation on the right displaces the whole midbrain across, and the contralateral cerebral peduncle is crushed against the opposite rigid tentorial edge. The corticospinal fibres in that peduncle have not yet decussated, so they serve the right side of the body, and the hemiparesis appears on the same side as the haematoma. The pupil is the honest sign: the third nerve is compressed by the uncus on the side of the mass, so a fixed dilated pupil localises the lesion reliably where the limbs do not. The clinical weight of the sign is that it marks an advanced herniation, and that it must not be read as a new contralateral lesion, because the operation the patient needs is decompression of the right-sided collection. The same mechanism, carried further, tears the perforators from the basilar artery and produces a Duret haemorrhage in the pons and midbrain.

quiz.prompt: A CT one hour after a fall onto the occiput is normal. Eight hours later the patient is confused, and a repeat CT shows haemorrhagic contusions in both inferior frontal lobes and the anterior right temporal lobe. Explain the distribution and the interval, and say what follows for any patient with a normal early CT and a persistent deficit.
quiz.answer: The distribution is contrecoup. An occipital blow accelerates the brain against the irregular anterior skull base, so the inferior frontal surfaces, the gyrus rectus and the temporal poles strike the orbital roofs, the sphenoid ridges and the petrous ridges; contusions concentrate at those sites whatever the point of impact, because it is the roughness of the bone rather than the direction of the blow that determines where the brain is grazed. The interval reflects the blossoming of contusions: what begins as scattered petechial haemorrhage and oedema expands and coalesces over the first six to twenty-four hours, so a very early CT systematically underestimates the injury. It follows that a normal CT in the first hour does not exclude significant contusional injury, and that a patient with a persisting deficit, a falling GCS, coagulopathy or anticoagulation needs a repeat CT rather than reassurance, with MRI if the CT still fails to explain the clinical state.
quiz.explain: The anatomy is why contusions are so predictable: the anterior and middle cranial fossae are ridged and sharp, while the occipital bone and the posterior fossa are smooth, so occipital contusions are comparatively rare and inferior frontal and anterior temporal ones are the default. Two practical consequences follow. First, when a CT of a head injury looks normal, those two sites deserve a deliberate second look on a narrow window, because a small contusion against dense bone is easily lost. Second, expansion is the rule rather than the exception in the first day, so the question after a head injury CT is not only what is on it but when it was done - and in an anticoagulated patient, a normal early scan is the beginning of the observation, not the end of it.

nodes.title: Intracranial Haemorrhage: Traumatic and Spontaneous
nodes.goal: Argue from the shape, compartment, distribution and density of intracranial blood to the vessel and the cause, and state the imaging or intervention that should follow.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old struck on the side of the head has a lucid interval and is now drowsy. CT shows a biconvex right temporal extra-axial collection 18 mm thick with an overlying undisplaced squamous temporal bone fracture. Within the dense collection are irregular low-attenuation swirls. What do those swirls tell you?
quiz.answer: Active arterial extravasation into unclotted haematoma, predicting rapid expansion and urgent evacuation
choices: Layering of cerebrospinal fluid within a chronic collection, indicating a long-standing previous injury
Beam-hardening artefact from the adjacent temporal bone fracture, carrying no clinical consequence here
Active arterial extravasation into unclotted haematoma, predicting rapid expansion and urgent evacuation
Mixed-age subdural blood from repeated minor injury, favouring conservative management and repeat CT
quiz.explain: The swirl sign is fresh, unretracted blood — still liquid and therefore lower in attenuation than the clotted blood around it — and it means the bleeding has not stopped. In an extradural haematoma from a torn middle meningeal artery, that is a surgical emergency: the collection can double in an hour, and the lucid interval described here is the classical prelude to rapid decompensation. The shape and the fracture together make the compartment clear. Extradural blood is biconvex because it has to strip the dura off the inner table against its firm attachment at the sutures, so it does not cross a suture, though it can cross the midline and the tentorium because it is not bounded by dural reflections. Subdural blood is the reverse: crescentic, crossing sutures freely, but halted at the falx and tentorium. Chronic collections are uniformly low in attenuation without the irregular internal swirls, and artefact from bone runs as linear streaks across the whole slice rather than sitting inside the clot.

quiz.prompt: A crescentic hyperdense extra-axial collection extends along the right frontal convexity, continues across the coronal suture onto the parietal region, and stops abruptly at the midline. Say which compartment the blood is in and give the anatomical reason that lets you be certain.
quiz.answer: It is subdural. The periosteal layer of the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, so extradural blood cannot cross a suture, whereas subdural blood can; but the falx is a dural reflection in the subdural space's midline boundary, so subdural blood stops at the midline. Crossing a suture while respecting the midline is therefore subdural.
quiz.explain: Two anatomical rules do almost all the work in the extra-axial compartment, and they are complementary rather than competing. The dura is two layers: an outer periosteal layer fused to the inner table and adherent at the sutures, and an inner meningeal layer that folds inwards to form the falx and tentorium. Blood in the extradural space lifts the periosteal layer off the bone and is arrested where that layer is tethered, at the sutures; nothing stops it crossing the falx or tentorium, because those structures lie deep to it. Blood in the subdural space slides under the sutures without difficulty but meets the falx and tentorium head on. So crossing a suture argues subdural; crossing the midline argues extradural. Neither rule is absolute — a fracture that runs through a suture and diastases it lets extradural blood across — which is why shape, the presence of a fracture and the clinical story are read together. Look for interhemispheric or tentorial layering, which is subdural blood in profile and easily mistaken for subarachnoid.

quiz.prompt: On axial CT a spontaneous right basal ganglia haematoma measures 5.0 cm in its longest axial diameter and 3.0 cm perpendicular to that on the same slice, and it is visible on 8 contiguous slices of 5 mm each. Estimate its volume with the ABC/2 method. Answer in millilitres to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: ABC/2 approximates the ellipsoid: A is the largest diameter on the slice where the clot is biggest, B is the diameter perpendicular to A on that same slice, and C is the craniocaudal extent, obtained here as 8 slices times 0.5 cm, giving 4 cm. So 5.0 times 3.0 times 4.0, divided by 2, is 30.0 mL. It takes a few seconds and it is the number the medical and surgical teams actually use, because volume is one of the strongest predictors of 30-day mortality in spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, along with the Glasgow Coma Scale score and intraventricular extension. Two caveats keep you honest. ABC/2 systematically overestimates irregular or lobar haematomas, so a segmented volume is better when the shape is complex, and for the C measurement count only slices where the clot occupies a reasonable fraction of the largest area rather than every slice with a trace of blood. Record the baseline volume clearly, because the definition of significant expansion is relative to it.

quiz.prompt: A 66-year-old presents 2 hours after sudden left hemiparesis. CT shows a 22 mL right putaminal haematoma. On the arterial phase CT angiogram there is a 3 mm rounded focus of 150 Hounsfield units lying within the clot, not continuous with any adjacent vessel, which enlarges on the delayed acquisition. What does this predict?
quiz.answer: A high risk of haematoma expansion, warranting monitored care and early repeat imaging
choices: A high risk of haematoma expansion, warranting monitored care and early repeat imaging
An underlying ruptured aneurysm, warranting immediate catheter angiography and coiling
Calcification in a long-standing cavernous malformation, warranting outpatient MRI only
Contrast within a normal lenticulostriate branch, warranting no change to the current plan
quiz.explain: This is the spot sign: a focus of contrast extravasation within the haematoma, conventionally at least 1.5 mm, with attenuation clearly above the surrounding clot, discontinuous from any normal or abnormal vessel, and growing on delayed phases. It marks bleeding that is still happening and is one of the better predictors of haematoma expansion in the first few hours, with more and larger foci predicting more growth. Expansion itself is conventionally defined as growth of at least 33% relative or at least 6 mL absolute on repeat CT, and it is strongly associated with deterioration. The consequence is practical rather than glamorous: a monitored bed, prompt blood pressure control, urgent reversal of any anticoagulant, and a repeat scan rather than waiting for the patient to declare themselves. Trials of haemostatic therapy targeted at spot-positive patients have not shown a clear outcome benefit, so the sign informs vigilance, not a specific drug. Unenhanced markers point the same way: the blend sign, black hole sign, island sign and an irregular heterogeneous clot.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these MRI stages of an intraparenchymal haematoma in the order they occur from the moment of bleeding onwards.
quiz.answer: hyperacute acute early-subacute late-subacute chronic
quiz.explain: The sequence is driven by what happens to the haemoglobin iron and by whether it is inside or outside intact red cells. Hyperacute, within the first day, the clot is oxyhaemoglobin and diamagnetic: isointense to slightly hypointense on T1 and bright on T2, essentially looking like water with a rim. Acute, roughly days one to three, oxygen is stripped to deoxyhaemoglobin, which is paramagnetic but sequestered inside cells, so T2 goes dark while T1 stays middling. Early subacute, from about day three, deoxyhaemoglobin oxidises to intracellular methaemoglobin: T1 becomes bright, T2 stays dark. Late subacute, from about a week to a month, the cells lyse and methaemoglobin becomes extracellular, so both T1 and T2 are bright — the easiest stage to recognise. Chronic, beyond a month, iron is stored as haemosiderin and ferritin in macrophages at the rim, dark on T1 and T2 and blooming heavily on gradient echo and susceptibility imaging. The practical use is dating: a haematoma that does not follow this progression, or that has non-haemorrhagic enhancing tissue within it, should raise the question of an underlying tumour or malformation.

quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old has thunderclap headache. CT shows blood centred in the interpeduncular and prepontine cisterns with a little in the ambient cisterns, no extension into the anterior interhemispheric fissure or the lateral sylvian fissures, and no intraventricular blood. A good quality thin-section CT angiogram is negative. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
quiz.answer: Manage as non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic haemorrhage; the yield of further angiography is very low
choices: Treat as aneurysmal regardless and repeat catheter angiography at one week and again at three months
Assume a missed posterior inferior cerebellar aneurysm and proceed directly to surgical exploration
Attribute the blood to a spinal arteriovenous fistula and image the whole spinal cord urgently instead
Manage as non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic haemorrhage; the yield of further angiography is very low
quiz.explain: The perimesencephalic pattern is defined by distribution, and the definition is strict: blood centred immediately anterior to the midbrain or pons, with no more than a trace in the proximal sylvian or anterior interhemispheric fissures, and no frank intraventricular blood. Held to that standard, with a technically good CT angiogram that clearly demonstrates the basilar tip and both posterior inferior cerebellar arteries, the probability of an aneurysm is very low, the course is benign, and vasospasm and rebleeding are rare. Many units therefore stop there, although practice still varies and some perform one catheter angiogram; what almost nobody now does is a repeated cycle of angiography. The reason to be strict is the mirror image: a diffuse basal pattern with a negative angiogram deserves repeat imaging, because a small or thrombosed aneurysm is genuinely missed in a few percent. The presumed source in perimesencephalic bleeding is venous or from a small perforator, which is consistent with its confinement and its benign natural history.

quiz.prompt: A CT after thunderclap headache shows the densest blood filling the anterior interhemispheric fissure, a small haematoma in the left gyrus rectus, and blood layering in both lateral ventricles. State which aneurysm you would look for first on the angiogram and one complication you should specifically warn the team about.
quiz.answer: Look first at the anterior communicating artery complex, because interhemispheric and gyrus rectus blood points there. Warn about acute obstructive hydrocephalus from the intraventricular blood, which may need an external ventricular drain urgently.
quiz.explain: The clot points at the hole. Blood centred in the anterior interhemispheric fissure, especially with a haematoma in the gyrus rectus or blood tracking into the septum pellucidum and lateral ventricles, indicates the anterior communicating complex. Blood filling one sylvian fissure with a temporal haematoma indicates a middle cerebral bifurcation aneurysm. Blood in the suprasellar and ambient cisterns on one side, particularly with a third nerve palsy, indicates a posterior communicating origin aneurysm. Blood predominantly in the fourth ventricle and around the foramen magnum indicates a posterior inferior cerebellar artery aneurysm. Saying which one you favour makes the angiogram faster and the interventional plan sharper. The complication to flag with intraventricular extension is acute hydrocephalus, which can develop within hours and is reversible with a drain — so look every time at the temporal horns and the third ventricle. Beyond that, warn about rebleeding before securing, and delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm from about day four to day fourteen.

quiz.prompt: An 81-year-old on no anticoagulant has a spontaneous right occipital lobar haematoma. Susceptibility-weighted imaging shows numerous cortical and subcortical microbleeds with sparing of the basal ganglia, thalami and pons, plus curvilinear low signal over two convexity sulci. What should you conclude and convey?
quiz.answer: Probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy on the Boston criteria version 2.0, which argues against anticoagulation
choices: Hypertensive small vessel disease, whose microbleeds concentrate in the basal ganglia, thalami and pons
Probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy on the Boston criteria version 2.0, which argues against anticoagulation
Haemorrhagic metastases, which would show enhancing nodules and disproportionate surrounding vasogenic oedema
Multiple cavernous malformations, which would show complete haemosiderin rims around popcorn-like cores
quiz.explain: The location argument is the strongest tool you have in spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage. Hypertensive bleeds arise from lipohyalinotic deep perforators and sit in the putamen and external capsule, the thalamus, the pons and the cerebellar dentate; their chronic microbleeds sit in the same deep places. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy affects leptomeningeal and cortical vessels, so its bleeds are lobar and corticosubcortical, with an occipital predilection, and its microbleeds spare the deep grey. The curvilinear sulcal low signal is cortical superficial siderosis, and the Boston criteria version 2.0 of 2022 incorporate it explicitly: in a patient aged 50 or over with lobar haemorrhage and no other cause, probable amyloid angiopathy can be reached with two or more haemorrhagic lesions, or with one haemorrhagic lesion plus a white matter feature such as severe centrum semiovale perivascular spaces or a multispot white matter pattern. The consequence is a conversation about anticoagulation, since amyloid angiopathy carries a high annual recurrence risk. Metastases and cavernomas look different, and the stem's distribution excludes both.

quiz.prompt: An arteriovenous malformation has a nidus measuring 4.2 cm in maximum diameter, lies within the left precentral gyrus, and drains through a subependymal vein into the internal cerebral vein. Give its Spetzler–Martin grade. Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The Spetzler–Martin scale sums three components. Size scores 1 for a nidus under 3 cm, 2 for 3 to 6 cm and 3 for over 6 cm, so 4.2 cm scores 2. Eloquence of adjacent brain scores 1 if present and 0 if not; the precentral gyrus is eloquent, along with sensory cortex, language cortex, visual cortex, the internal capsule, thalamus, hypothalamus, brainstem, cerebellar peduncles and deep cerebellar nuclei, so that adds 1. Venous drainage scores 1 if any component is deep and 0 if it is entirely superficial; drainage into the internal cerebral vein is deep, so that adds 1 more. Total 4. The scale predicts surgical morbidity, and grades 4 and 5 are usually managed conservatively or with staged embolisation and radiosurgery rather than primary resection. Your report should therefore state each component explicitly rather than only the total, and add the features that carry independent bleeding risk: prior haemorrhage, an intranidal or flow-related aneurysm, venous stenosis and exclusively deep drainage.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old with a small cerebellar haemorrhage has MRI showing a 12 mm lesion with a mixed-signal core and a complete low-signal rim on susceptibility imaging, immediately adjacent to a tuft of small veins converging on a single enlarged transcortical draining vein. How should this be managed?
quiz.answer: Leave the venous anomaly alone and direct treatment at the cavernous malformation beside it
choices: Embolise the venous anomaly, since it is the arteriovenous shunt responsible for this bleed
Resect both lesions together, since the anomaly recruits arterial supply once it has bled
Leave the venous anomaly alone and direct treatment at the cavernous malformation beside it
Report an arteriovenous malformation and grade it for radiosurgery on the Spetzler–Martin scale
quiz.explain: Two lesions, only one of which bleeds. The caput medusae of small medullary veins draining into a single large collecting vein is a developmental venous anomaly, an anatomical variant of normal venous drainage rather than a malformation with a shunt. It carries essentially no bleeding risk of its own, and crucially it drains normal brain, so occluding or resecting it causes venous infarction — which is why the correct action is to leave it and to say so plainly in the report. The lesion with the mixed-signal popcorn core and the complete haemosiderin rim is a cavernous malformation, and cavernomas are the things that bleed. They are associated with venous anomalies often enough that finding one should prompt a careful search for the other. If surgery is contemplated, the surgeon must preserve the draining vein. An arteriovenous malformation would show enlarged feeding arteries, a compact nidus and early venous filling on angiography, none of which is described here.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old fell three weeks ago and the CT is reported as normal. Looking again, the sulci over the left convexity are effaced, the grey–white junction is displaced inwards, and the left hemisphere looks subtly compressed. State what is most likely happening and give one manoeuvre at the workstation that will confirm it.
quiz.answer: This is most likely an isodense subacute subdural haematoma, at the stage where its attenuation matches cortex. Confirm it by widening the display to subdural windows, around 150 to 200 units wide, which separates the collection from the underlying cortex, and compare the two sides at identical slices.
quiz.explain: Acute extravasated blood measures around 50 to 70 Hounsfield units and then loses roughly 1.5 units a day as the clot breaks down, so somewhere between about one and three weeks it passes through the attenuation of cortex and becomes invisible on standard brain windows. The trap is real: the scan looks unremarkable until you notice the secondary signs — effaced sulci on one side, inward displacement of the grey–white interface, a cortex that appears abnormally thick, midline shift out of keeping with any visible lesion. Widening the window compresses the greyscale of the brain and lets the collection separate from cortex; comparing the two hemispheres on the same slice is the other half of the trick. If doubt persists, MRI is definitive because subacute blood is bright on T1, and a contrast-enhanced CT shows the enhancing displaced cortical veins. Bilateral isodense collections are the hardest of all, since there is no shift and no asymmetry to alert you — look for the absent sulci at the vertex.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old with haemoglobin 68 g/L after a gastrointestinal bleed falls and strikes their head. CT shows a 9 mm crescentic collection over the right convexity measuring 38 Hounsfield units, without internal septation, and the injury is definitely recent. How should you interpret the density?
quiz.answer: Acute blood becomes isodense to cortex at very low haemoglobin, so an acute subdural remains possible
choices: The density proves a chronic collection at least three weeks old, so this trauma cannot be the cause
The density indicates a subdural hygroma, so the collection is cerebrospinal fluid rather than any blood
The density indicates an early empyema, so contrast and inflammatory markers should be the next step
Acute blood becomes isodense to cortex at very low haemoglobin, so an acute subdural remains possible
quiz.explain: The attenuation of blood on CT is driven mostly by the protein in haemoglobin, so it falls with the haemoglobin concentration. At a haemoglobin of around 80 to 100 g/L, fresh blood can measure close to grey matter, and below that it can look frankly hypodense, meaning an acute subdural haematoma in a profoundly anaemic patient can be reported as chronic or missed altogether. Density alone therefore never dates a collection; you read it alongside the history, the shape, and the presence of a fluid–fluid level or a mixed-density clot, which suggests active bleeding or rebleeding into an older collection. A hygroma is genuinely cerebrospinal fluid density, near zero, typically after trauma or shunting, and it lacks the internal complexity of chronic haematoma. An empyema is usually loculated with an enhancing membrane and restricted diffusion, with a septic patient attached. Coagulopathy is the other setting that changes appearance, producing unclotted low-density blood layered against denser clot.

quiz.prompt: A clinician asks whether adding a susceptibility-weighted sequence changes anything when the CT has already shown a lobar haematoma in a 78-year-old. Give the strongest reason to acquire it and one caveat about interpreting what it shows.
quiz.answer: The strongest reason is that susceptibility imaging detects lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis, which support cerebral amyloid angiopathy and directly influence whether anticoagulation is restarted. The caveat is that blooming exaggerates lesion size, and calcification, cavernomas and small vessels can mimic microbleeds, so phase images and a second sequence are needed before counting them.
quiz.explain: Susceptibility-weighted imaging exploits the phase difference between paramagnetic blood products and surrounding tissue and is substantially more sensitive to microbleeds than conventional gradient echo, which is itself far more sensitive than CT. In an elderly patient with a lobar haemorrhage, that sensitivity is what turns a single event into a pattern: strictly lobar microbleeds with deep sparing and cortical superficial siderosis fulfil elements of the Boston criteria version 2.0 for probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and cortical superficial siderosis in particular predicts recurrent lobar haemorrhage. That is exactly the evidence a cardiologist needs when weighing atrial fibrillation against bleeding risk. The interpretive caveats are worth stating in the report. Blooming makes every lesion look larger than it is and the apparent size varies with echo time and field strength, so counts are not comparable between scanners. Calcification also blooms, and phase imaging distinguishes it from haemorrhage. Finally, do not count microbleeds within or immediately around the acute haematoma — they are part of the index bleed.

nodes.title: Multiple Sclerosis and the White Matter Differential
nodes.goal: Apply the McDonald 2024 imaging criteria to a real study, use the central vein sign and the paramagnetic rim to argue for demyelination, and separate multiple sclerosis from the mimics that carry different treatment.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old presents with painful loss of vision in the right eye. MRI shows an enhancing lesion in the right intraorbital optic nerve and two ovoid periventricular T2 lesions lying perpendicular to the callosal margin. The cord is clear and the cortex looks normal. What can you say about dissemination in space?
quiz.answer: It is satisfied: the optic nerve is a topographical region in its own right under McDonald 2024
choices: It is satisfied: the optic nerve is a topographical region in its own right under McDonald 2024
It is not satisfied: the optic nerve is excluded from the regions that may be counted
It is satisfied by the periventricular lesions alone, with no need to invoke the optic nerve
It cannot be assessed at all until a dedicated spinal cord study is added to the protocol
quiz.explain: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria recognises five typical topographies rather than four: periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, and the optic nerve, which may be demonstrated by MRI, optical coherence tomography or visual evoked potentials. Dissemination in space requires involvement of at least two of them, and this patient has periventricular disease plus an optic nerve lesion, so it is met. The third option is the common trap: several lesions in one region remain one region, however convincing their morphology. Cord imaging is genuinely useful here for prognosis and for flushing out mimics, but the criteria do not require it once two regions are already shown. Note also that the symptomatic lesion counts toward dissemination in space, which was not always the case in earlier versions.

quiz.prompt: A patient has three ovoid periventricular lesions, one lesion abutting the cortex in subcortical white matter, one lesion in the left middle cerebellar peduncle, a normal whole-spine study and normal dedicated optic nerve imaging. How many of the five McDonald 2024 topographical regions are demonstrated? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Periventricular counts once no matter how many lesions sit there, the juxtacortical lesion counts as the cortical or juxtacortical region, and the middle cerebellar peduncle lesion counts as infratentorial. The cord and the optic nerve are clear, so three of five regions are demonstrated. Counting regions rather than lesions is the discipline the criteria demand, and it is where reports most often go astray by implying that a heavy periventricular burden alone is enough. Two regions satisfy dissemination in space, so this study clears that bar comfortably. What it does not do by itself is establish dissemination in time, and it does not exclude the mimics: the same region count could be produced by small vessel disease or migraine, which is exactly why the supportive biomarkers such as the central vein sign have been brought into the diagnostic conversation.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old with hypertension and long-standing migraine has multiple T2 hyperintense white matter lesions and is being assessed for possible multiple sclerosis. A high-resolution susceptibility-weighted acquisition shows a single small vein running through the centre of most of the lesions. How do you interpret this?
quiz.answer: These lesions carry the central vein sign, which favours demyelination over small vessel disease
choices: These lesions carry the central vein sign, which favours demyelination over small vessel disease
These lesions carry the central vein sign, which is the expected finding in small vessel disease
The veins are incidental, since a perivenular arrangement is as common in migraine lesions
The finding is a paramagnetic rim, which marks chronic active lesions rather than vein position
quiz.explain: Demyelinating plaques form around a central venule, so on susceptibility-based imaging, or on a combined FLAIR and T2-star acquisition, a thin vein is seen traversing the lesion and emerging from it in at least one plane. Ischaemic small vessel lesions, migraine-associated lesions and most other mimics arise from arteriolar territory and lack that central vessel, which is why the sign carries real discriminating power in exactly this middle-aged, vascular-risk-factor patient. Practical caveats belong in the report: assess only lesions above about 3 mm, exclude confluent lesions where the vein cannot be assigned to one plaque, and confirm the vein runs centrally on two planes. A paramagnetic rim is a different sign entirely, describing a dark iron-laden edge to a chronic active lesion, and the two may be present in the same patient.

quiz.prompt: A neurologist asks what a paramagnetic rim lesion is and why you have highlighted one in your report. Answer in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: It is a chronic active lesion whose edge of iron-laden microglia forms a dark paramagnetic rim on susceptibility-weighted imaging or quantitative susceptibility mapping; it does not enhance with gadolinium and is highly specific for multiple sclerosis.
quiz.explain: Chronic active, or smouldering, lesions have a quiescent demyelinated core surrounded by a ring of iron-laden microglia and macrophages that continue to expand the plaque slowly. That iron is paramagnetic, so it appears as a dark ring on susceptibility-weighted imaging and as a bright ring on quantitative susceptibility mapping. Two things make the sign useful. First, specificity: a paramagnetic rim is rarely produced by vascular, migrainous or other mimicking lesions, so even one strengthens a demyelinating interpretation, and the 2024 criteria bring it in as a supportive biomarker alongside the central vein sign. Second, prognosis: a higher rim lesion burden tracks with more severe disability and greater progression. Do not confuse it with an enhancing acute lesion; a rim lesion has an intact blood-brain barrier and takes no gadolinium.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old woman develops severe paraparesis over three days. Sagittal T2 shows a swollen, centrally placed cord lesion extending from C2 to C7, and the brain shows a lesion in the dorsal medulla at the area postrema with no ovoid periventricular lesions. What do you advise?
quiz.answer: Test for AQP4 antibodies and manage as NMOSD, because several MS drugs make this disease worse
choices: Test for AQP4 antibodies and manage as NMOSD, because several MS drugs make this disease worse
Start a multiple sclerosis disease-modifying drug, as this cord pattern lies within its spectrum
Call it idiopathic transverse myelitis, since a long cord lesion carries no antibody association
Call it cord infarction, since the central grey matter pattern and the length are typical of that
quiz.explain: Two findings define this study. A longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, conventionally three or more vertebral segments, sitting centrally within the cord and involving grey matter, is characteristic of aquaporin-4 antibody disease; multiple sclerosis produces short, peripherally placed, often dorsolateral cord lesions spanning fewer than two segments. The area postrema lesion is the second: it explains intractable hiccups and vomiting and is close to specific for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which also favours periependymal surfaces around the third and fourth ventricles and the optic chiasm. Getting this right is urgent because it is not merely a labelling exercise. Several multiple sclerosis therapies, including interferon beta and natalizumab, can worsen NMOSD, and treatment moves instead to complement, IL-6 or CD19 targeted agents. Cord infarction is hyperacute and usually anterior in distribution.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old develops simultaneous painful visual loss in both eyes. MRI shows long segments of both optic nerves enhancing, most marked anteriorly, with enhancement extending into the nerve sheath and adjacent orbital fat. The brain is otherwise normal. What do you recommend?
quiz.answer: Send MOG antibodies: bilateral anterior optic neuritis with perineural enhancement fits MOGAD
choices: Send MOG antibodies: bilateral anterior optic neuritis with perineural enhancement fits MOGAD
Send AQP4 antibodies only: this appearance represents posterior chiasmal disease in a child
Diagnose multiple sclerosis: bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis is its usual first presentation
Diagnose orbital inflammatory disease: sheath and fat enhancement place the process outside the nerve
quiz.explain: Antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein produce a recognisable optic neuritis: bilateral, longitudinally extensive along the nerve, anteriorly predominant with disc swelling, and characteristically spilling beyond the nerve into the sheath and surrounding orbital fat as perineural enhancement. Aquaporin-4 disease tends to hit the posterior nerve and chiasm and is rarer in children. Multiple sclerosis optic neuritis is usually unilateral and short-segment, with brain lesions to accompany it. Orbital inflammatory disease is a reasonable thought given the fat enhancement, but the intrinsic long-segment nerve enhancement makes it secondary here. Elsewhere MOGAD may look ADEM-like in a child, produce fluffy poorly marginated brainstem and deep grey lesions, or involve the conus. It matters clinically because MOGAD lesions often resolve completely and relapse risk and treatment differ from both multiple sclerosis and NMOSD.

quiz.prompt: A registrar asks how acute disseminated encephalomyelitis differs on imaging and clinically from a first attack of multiple sclerosis. Answer in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: ADEM is monophasic and usually follows an infection or vaccination in a child, with large, poorly demarcated, bilateral but asymmetric white matter lesions of similar age that commonly involve the deep grey matter of the thalami and basal ganglia.
quiz.explain: The strongest discriminator is that the lesions all look the same age, because they arose in one wave: they tend to enhance, or not enhance, together, whereas multiple sclerosis is defined by lesions of different vintages coexisting. Morphology helps too. ADEM lesions are large, fluffy and ill-defined rather than ovoid and sharply marginated, they are bilateral though asymmetric, and involvement of thalami and basal ganglia is common while it is unusual in multiple sclerosis. Clinically, encephalopathy is required for the diagnosis and the illness is monophasic. Many paediatric cases are MOG antibody positive, so testing is worthwhile, and it also identifies the minority who will relapse. Follow-up imaging is informative: ADEM lesions often resolve substantially, whereas new lesions appearing later should prompt reconsideration of a chronic demyelinating disease.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these deep white matter appearances in order from Fazekas grade 0 to Fazekas grade 3.
quiz.answer: absent punctate-foci early-confluence large-confluent-areas
quiz.explain: The Fazekas scale is scored in two compartments. In the deep white matter, grade 0 is no lesion, grade 1 punctate foci, grade 2 the beginning of confluence between those foci, and grade 3 large confluent areas. The periventricular compartment is scored separately: caps or a pencil-thin lining is grade 1, a smooth halo grade 2, and irregular hyperintensity extending into the deep white matter grade 3. Two cautions apply in a demyelination service. First, Fazekas describes presumed small vessel disease and is not a way to quantify multiple sclerosis burden, so do not use it to grade plaques. Second, in a middle-aged patient the two processes coexist, and disentangling them rests on morphology and on the central vein sign rather than on a severity score. Grading well still matters, because it anchors follow-up comparison.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has been on natalizumab for three years and is JC virus antibody positive with a high index. New subtle cognitive slowing prompts an MRI, which shows an asymmetric confluent subcortical lesion in the left frontal lobe involving the U-fibres, T1 hypointense, without mass effect or enhancement, with punctate T2 foci at its advancing margin. What do you do?
quiz.answer: Raise PML, recommend stopping the drug and arrange cerebrospinal fluid JC virus PCR today
choices: Raise PML, recommend stopping the drug and arrange cerebrospinal fluid JC virus PCR today
Call it a new demyelinating plaque, continue the drug and repeat the MRI in three months
Call it immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, which swells and enhances at this stage
Call it a tumefactive plaque, which shows an incomplete ring opening toward the adjacent cortex
quiz.explain: Every described feature belongs to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: asymmetric subcortical white matter involvement that reaches the U-fibres, marked T1 hypointensity, no mass effect out of proportion to size, absent enhancement while the patient remains immunosuppressed, and punctate T2 or diffusion-hyperintense foci at the leading edge, sometimes described as a milky-way appearance. Multiple sclerosis plaques are usually periventricular, ovoid and U-fibre sparing, and a new plaque does not creep. The risk profile fits too, since JC virus seropositivity with a high index, natalizumab beyond two years and prior immunosuppression together define the high-risk group who need short-interval surveillance MRI. Enhancement and swelling appear later, once the drug is withdrawn and immune reconstitution begins, and that phase can be clinically worse than the infection. Confirmation is cerebrospinal fluid JC virus PCR, and delay costs brain.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old develops subacute right hemiparesis. MRI shows a 35 mm left frontal white matter lesion with incomplete ring enhancement whose open edge faces the cortex, mass effect that is modest for the size of the lesion, and relative cerebral blood volume lower than in normal white matter. What do you favour and advise?
quiz.answer: Tumefactive demyelination: the open ring and the low perfusion argue against a high grade glioma
choices: Tumefactive demyelination: the open ring and the low perfusion argue against a high grade glioma
A high grade glioma: the incomplete ring and the low perfusion are characteristic of that tumour
A pyogenic abscess: the ring thins medially and the centre restricts diffusion markedly in that entity
A solitary metastasis: a ring lesion with modest oedema is the usual appearance of that diagnosis
quiz.explain: Three findings converge. The incomplete or open ring, with the deficient segment facing the cortical grey matter, reflects the inflammatory front advancing through white matter and is far more typical of demyelination than of tumour. Mass effect and oedema that look too mild for a lesion of this size point the same way, as neoplasms of 35 mm generally behave more aggressively. Perfusion is the clincher, since a high grade glioma raises relative cerebral blood volume while a demyelinating lesion does not, its enhancement reflecting a permeable barrier rather than neovascularity. An abscess would show a thin ring that is thinner on its ventricular side and a centre with striking diffusion restriction. The practical consequence is large: recognising this can avoid a biopsy, whose demyelinating hypercellularity is itself readily misread as tumour, and short-interval follow-up after steroids usually settles the question.

quiz.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences how the distribution of small vessel disease differs from that of multiple sclerosis on brain MRI.
quiz.answer: Small vessel disease spares the U-fibres, the corpus callosum and the cord, and comes with lacunes, basal ganglia perivascular spaces and deep microbleeds, whereas its lesions rarely carry a central vein.
quiz.explain: This is the everyday reporting problem, because after the fifth decade almost everyone has some white matter signal change. The distributions differ in a way that is reliable when applied carefully. Multiple sclerosis lesions sit against the callososeptal interface, are ovoid and oriented perpendicular to the ventricle, reach the juxtacortical U-fibres and the cortex itself, and are frequently accompanied by short dorsolateral cord lesions. Small vessel disease favours deep and subcortical white matter with periventricular caps and haloes, spares the callosum and the cord, and travels with lacunes, enlarged basal ganglia perivascular spaces and deep microbleeds. When the pattern is genuinely ambiguous, susceptibility-based imaging settles it more often than any distribution rule, since demyelinating plaques are perivenular and vascular lesions are not.

quiz.prompt: State in one or two sentences what imaging must show for dissemination in time, including how a single scan can achieve it.
quiz.answer: Dissemination in time needs either a new T2 or enhancing lesion on a follow-up scan, or, on a single scan, the simultaneous presence of an enhancing lesion and a non-enhancing lesion.
quiz.explain: The idea is simply that the disease has been active at more than one point in time, and imaging can demonstrate that in two ways. Comparing with a prior study, any new T2 lesion or any new enhancing lesion counts, regardless of when the baseline was performed. On a single study, an enhancing lesion sitting alongside a non-enhancing one implies lesions of different ages, because gadolinium enhancement in a plaque generally persists for only a few weeks. This is the practical reason a first study in suspected demyelination should be performed with contrast: without it a diagnosis that could be made today may take another six months. Cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands, or kappa free light chains, can substitute for dissemination in time in patients who satisfy dissemination in space, which is why the lumbar puncture is not merely confirmatory.

nodes.title: Spine MRI: Degeneration, Compression and Trauma
nodes.goal: Report displaced lumbar disc material in the agreed nomenclature, and separate the spinal emergencies from the incidental findings.

quiz.prompt: On the sagittal T2 image at L5/S1 the displaced disc material behind the vertebral body measures 13 mm craniocaudally at its widest, while its neck where it leaves the disc space measures 7 mm in the same plane. It occupies about 15 per cent of the disc circumference and remains continuous with the parent disc. How should this be reported in the standard lumbar disc nomenclature?
choices: A disc extrusion
A disc protrusion
A broad-based bulge
A sequestered fragment
quiz.answer: A disc extrusion
quiz.explain: The rule is geometric, and it is the only thing separating the first two words. Measure the greatest distance between the edges of the displaced material, then the distance between the edges of its base in the same plane: if the material beyond the disc space is wider than its base - 13 mm against a 7 mm neck - it is an extrusion, and if it is narrower or equal it is a protrusion. Continuity with the parent disc keeps it out of the sequestration category, which is reserved for a fragment that has lost that continuity. A bulge is a different animal altogether: disc tissue extending beyond the ring apophyses around more than a quarter of the circumference, a contour rather than a herniation, and 15 per cent is too little in any case. The words are not interchangeable in a report, because extrusions are more often symptomatic, more likely to migrate, and - counter-intuitively - more likely to resorb spontaneously, since exposed nucleus pulposus provokes a vascularised inflammatory response. Measure in the plane where the ratio is greatest: a herniation that looks contained on the sagittal may be an extrusion on the axial, and one plane is enough to make it one.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old with severe right L5 radiculopathy has an ovoid mass in the right lateral recess at the level of the L4 vertebral body, separate from the L4/5 disc, slightly brighter than that disc on T2, with a thin rim of enhancement after gadolinium and no central enhancement. What is it most likely to be?
choices: A migrated sequestered disc fragment
A synovial cyst from the facet joint
A nerve sheath tumour on the root
An early epidural abscess collection
quiz.answer: A migrated sequestered disc fragment
quiz.explain: Three features do the work. A fragment lying separate from its parent disc, having travelled cranially or caudally in the epidural space, is a sequestration; it is often brighter than the degenerate parent disc on T2 because it is hydrated and inflamed; and it typically shows a thin peripheral rim of enhancement from surrounding granulation tissue with a non-enhancing avascular centre. A nerve sheath tumour enhances solidly and throughout, is centred on the root rather than in the recess, and over time widens the foramen or scallops bone. A synovial cyst arises from a degenerate facet joint, sits posterolaterally against it, and usually has a low-signal rim and a demonstrable connection to the joint. An abscess would come with disc and endplate destruction, marrow oedema and systemic signs. The reporting consequence is practical: a fragment resorbs in a substantial proportion of patients, and if it is to be removed the surgeon needs to be told the parent level and the direction and distance of migration, because a fragment behind a vertebral body is not reached through a standard interlaminar approach to the disc.

quiz.prompt: A patient with recurrent left leg pain nine months after L5/S1 microdiscectomy has soft tissue in the left anterior epidural space at the operated level. Explain how you would use contrast to decide whether this is fibrosis or recurrent disc material, and why the timing of the post-contrast images matters.
quiz.answer: Give gadolinium and image early, within roughly ten to fifteen minutes. Epidural fibrosis is vascularised granulation tissue: it enhances immediately, homogeneously and throughout its substance, and it tends to be retractile rather than mass-like, drawing the thecal sac and root towards it. Recurrent disc material is avascular and does not enhance itself; what enhances is the vascularised tissue around it, so on early images it shows a peripheral rim of enhancement with a non-enhancing centre, and it is polypoid, has mass effect, and is continuous with the disc space. The timing matters because contrast diffuses passively into disc material over time, so on images acquired thirty minutes or more after injection the recurrent disc fills in and becomes indistinguishable from scar, turning a reliable sign into a misleading one.
quiz.explain: The distinction changes management directly, which is why it is worth protocolling properly: recurrent disc material can be re-operated, whereas re-operating on scar tends to make the patient worse and is the classic route into failed back surgery syndrome. Two refinements keep the sign honest. The two often coexist, so the question in practice is which component accounts for the mass effect on the symptomatic root, not which one is present. And mass effect is itself part of the argument - scar retracts and follows the contours of the thecal sac, disc material pushes. If the study cannot be done early after injection, say so in the report rather than calling the appearance for one or the other.

quiz.prompt: CT and MRI of the thoracolumbar junction show a burst fracture of L1 with retropulsion, the patient is neurologically intact, and STIR shows a widened interspinous space with high signal through the interspinous and supraspinous ligaments. What is the TLICS total? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: TLICS adds three components. Morphology: compression 1, burst 2, translation or rotation 3, distraction 4 - here 2. Neurological status: intact 0, nerve root 2, complete cord or conus injury 2, incomplete cord or conus injury 3, cauda equina 3 - here 0. Posterior ligamentous complex: intact 0, indeterminate 2, disrupted 3 - here 3, because interspinous widening with frank ligamentous high signal is disruption rather than suspicion. Total 5. A score of 3 or less is managed non-operatively, 4 is equivocal, and 5 or more points to surgery, so the MRI has just moved a neurologically intact patient into the operative group. That is the reason MRI is added to CT when the CT shows a burst fracture and the posterior elements are in doubt, and it is why the system weights the posterior ligamentous complex so heavily: it is the structure that governs mechanical stability and the one CT judges least well.

quiz.prompt: Put these four descriptions of displaced lumbar disc material in order of increasing displacement from the disc space, as the standard nomenclature grades them.
quiz.answer: bulge protrusion extrusion sequestration
quiz.explain: A bulge is not a herniation at all: it is disc tissue extending beyond the ring apophyses around more than a quarter of the circumference, a generalised change of contour that usually reflects age and degeneration. A protrusion is a localised herniation whose base is at least as wide as any part of the material beyond the disc space. An extrusion is a localised herniation that is wider beyond the disc space than at its base, so its neck is narrower than its dome. A sequestration is an extrusion that has lost continuity with the parent disc altogether. One term is often confused with this last: migration describes displacement away from the site of extrusion, cranially or caudally, and a migrated fragment may or may not be sequestered - the two words answer different questions, one about position and one about continuity.

quiz.prompt: A woman with metastatic breast cancer is referred for lumbar MRI because of two weeks of back pain. The lumbar study shows an epidural soft-tissue mass at T12 indenting the conus, and she has brisk reflexes in the legs and a sensory level. What is the most important next imaging step?
choices: MRI of the whole spine before treatment is planned
CT of the same level to assess the bony detail
Bone scintigraphy to stage the rest of the skeleton
Repeat MRI after dexamethasone has been started
quiz.answer: MRI of the whole spine before treatment is planned
quiz.explain: Roughly a third of patients with metastatic epidural spinal cord compression have compressive disease at more than one level, and the second site is often clinically silent because the first one is producing all the symptoms. Radiotherapy fields and surgical plans are drawn from the full extent of disease, so imaging only the symptomatic level risks treating one deposit and leaving another to compress the cord a fortnight later; national guidance accordingly asks for urgent whole-spine MRI in anyone with suspected metastatic cord compression. The distractors each answer a real but secondary question: CT characterises bone and vertebral body integrity for surgical planning, scintigraphy stages the skeleton, and steroids are started immediately - but none of them changes the immediate decision the way the extent of compressive disease does, and starting steroids is never a reason to delay or repeat the MRI.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have a large central disc extrusion: one at T9/T10 and one at L4/L5. Explain what determines whether the picture is cord compression or cauda equina compression, what each looks like clinically, and how far the MRI must extend.
quiz.answer: The determinant is the level of the conus medullaris, which in adults ends at about T12 to L1, with the lower limit of normal around the L2/L3 disc; a compressive lesion above it presses on the cord, one below it presses on the cauda equina. The T9/T10 extrusion therefore causes cord compression, with upper motor neurone signs below the level: spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, a sensory level, and T2 signal change within the cord if compression has been sustained. The L4/L5 extrusion compresses nerve roots and gives lower motor neurone signs: flaccid weakness, absent reflexes, bilateral radicular pain, saddle anaesthesia, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence. The MRI must cover the whole lumbosacral spine down to the sacrum, because a compressive lesion below the volume scanned is simply missed, and it must extend upwards whenever the signs are of cord rather than root disease, since the true upper level of the lesion may lie well above the symptomatic dermatome.
quiz.explain: Getting the compartment right is what makes the request sensible, because a referral for 'cord compression' at L4/5 asks for something anatomically impossible and often produces a scan that stops too high. Two refinements matter at the bedside. A conus lesion mixes the two pictures - early and severe bladder involvement with a combination of upper and lower motor neurone signs - and is the reason the transition zone is described separately. And retention is a late feature of cauda equina compression rather than an early one, so waiting for it before requesting the scan is how the diagnosis gets made too late; a raised post-void residual and loss of perianal sensation are the findings that should trigger imaging out of hours.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old with back pain after lifting has a collapsed L2 vertebral body. MRI shows a band of low T1 and high STIR signal running parallel to and beneath the superior endplate, with normal fatty marrow preserved through the rest of the body, retropulsion of the posterosuperior corner, normal pedicles and no paravertebral soft tissue. What does this favour?
choices: An acute osteoporotic insufficiency fracture
Metastatic collapse from an occult primary
Vertebral osteomyelitis with early collapse
Myelomatous involvement of the body
quiz.answer: An acute osteoporotic insufficiency fracture
quiz.explain: Five features in the stem point the same way. Band-like oedema parallel to the fractured endplate with normal marrow preserved elsewhere in the body means the marrow has been bruised, not replaced, whereas tumour replaces marrow diffusely and completely. Retropulsion of the posterosuperior corner is a mechanical failure pattern, while a convex bulge of the posterior cortex suggests an expanding tumour. Sparing of the pedicles matters because metastatic disease reaches the vertebra through the vascular supply of the posterior body and commonly takes the pedicle with it. And the absence of paravertebral or epidural soft tissue is decisive: tumour and infection both make soft tissue, mechanical failure does not. A fluid sign - a linear T2-bright cleft within the body - is another benign feature. Infection separates itself on the disc, which it destroys along with both adjacent endplates, whereas a fracture leaves the disc alone. Where the picture is genuinely equivocal, follow-up at six to twelve weeks showing resolving oedema, or a biopsy, settles it; diffusion helps but overlaps.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old with chronic mechanical back pain has low T1 and high T2 signal in the marrow on both sides of the L4/5 disc. The disc space is narrowed, the disc itself is dark on T2 with a preserved intranuclear cleft, the endplates are irregular but continuous, and there is no paraspinal or epidural soft tissue. Inflammatory markers are normal. What does this represent?
choices: Type 1 degenerative endplate marrow change
Pyogenic discitis with early osteomyelitis
Metastasis crossing the L4/5 disc space
An acute Schmorl node with marrow oedema
quiz.answer: Type 1 degenerative endplate marrow change
quiz.explain: The marrow signal is identical in the two leading diagnoses - that is the trap, and it is why the disc rather than the marrow decides the case. In degenerative type 1 change the disc is desiccated and dark on T2 and keeps its intranuclear cleft, the endplates are irregular from wear but their cortical line is continuous, and there is no soft tissue. In pyogenic infection the disc is bright on T2 and loses the cleft early, the endplates are eroded with loss of the cortical line, and there is paraspinal or epidural inflammatory tissue that enhances. Type 1 change is vascularised fibrous marrow with oedema, and its natural history is to convert to type 2, fatty (bright on T1, iso to bright on T2), and later to type 3, sclerotic (dark on both). It matters because type 1 is the type most associated with pain and the one most often mistaken for infection. The exception that keeps a reader honest is tuberculous spondylitis, which tends to spare the disc and spread beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament, so a preserved disc does not exclude infection when the clinical picture fits.

quiz.prompt: A restrained front-seat passenger in a frontal collision has a fracture line running horizontally through the spinous process, both pedicles and the posterior body of L2, with anterior wedging, and bruising across the lower abdomen. Beyond the spine, what does this pattern oblige you to look for on the same CT?
choices: Bowel and mesenteric injury in the abdomen
Renal pedicle avulsion at the vascular hilum
Diaphragmatic rupture on the left side
Aortic injury at the level of the isthmus
quiz.answer: Bowel and mesenteric injury in the abdomen
quiz.explain: This is a flexion-distraction, or Chance, injury: the lap belt acts as a fulcrum across the abdomen, the spine hinges over it, the posterior elements fail in tension and the anterior body fails in compression. The same mechanism crushes bowel and mesentery between belt and spine, and the association is strong enough that the fracture should be treated as a marker for visceral injury - small bowel perforation, mesenteric tear and delayed devascularisation being the injuries that get missed on the first pass. Look for free fluid without solid organ injury, mesenteric fat stranding, bowel wall thickening and extraluminal gas. The spinal half of the answer is that this is a distraction morphology with a disrupted posterior ligamentous complex, which places it in the operative range even in a neurologically intact patient. It is also easy to miss on axial images alone, because a horizontal fracture line can run between slices: the sagittal reformats are where it is seen.

quiz.prompt: On a lateral radiograph of the thoracic spine a wedged vertebral body measures 13 mm in anterior height and 24 mm in posterior height, and the vertebrae above and below are of normal shape. Taking the posterior height as the reference, what percentage of the anterior height has been lost? Give the answer to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: The loss is (24 - 13) / 24, which is 11/24, or 45.8 per cent, so 46 per cent. The semiquantitative Genant grading reads those bands as roughly 20 to 25 per cent height loss for grade 1 (mild), 25 to 40 per cent for grade 2 (moderate), and more than 40 per cent for grade 3 (severe), applied to anterior height (wedge), middle height (biconcave) or posterior height (crush). This vertebra is a grade 3 wedge deformity. Two practical points travel with the arithmetic. The reference should be the posterior height of the same vertebra when the neighbours are themselves deformed, since comparing with an abnormal neighbour understates the loss. And a vertebral fracture found on any imaging, including one seen incidentally on a CT requested for something else, is an osteoporotic fracture until proved otherwise and is among the strongest predictors of the next one, so it belongs in the conclusion of the report rather than buried in a list of degenerative findings.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows an L1 burst fracture in a neurologically intact patient, and the surgical team asks whether the posterior ligamentous complex is intact. State the sequence you would rely on, the findings that indicate disruption, and why the determination changes the plan.
quiz.answer: Sagittal STIR, or another fat-suppressed T2-weighted sequence; fat suppression is what makes ligamentous and interspinous oedema visible against fatty marrow and epidural fat. Disruption is indicated by high signal within or frank discontinuity of the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments and the ligamentum flavum, widening of the interspinous distance compared with the levels above and below, fluid or widening in the facet joints, a perched or dislocated facet, and avulsion at a ligamentous attachment. It changes the plan because the posterior ligamentous complex is the principal restraint against progressive kyphosis and translation: with it intact, a burst fracture in a neurologically intact patient is usually braced, and with it disrupted the same fracture scores into the operative range and is stabilised. CT can only infer the state of the ligaments from bony spacing, which is why MRI is added whenever the answer would change management.
quiz.explain: The reason the classification systems put so much weight here is that the posterior ligamentous complex heals poorly, so a disrupted complex means the deformity will progress even if the bone unites. Two cautions keep the report defensible. MRI over-calls: isolated high signal in the interspinous fat or in the ligamentum flavum alone is common after any injury and is not by itself disruption, which is why the classification offers an 'indeterminate' category worth two points rather than forcing a binary. And the findings should be read together - widened interspinous distance with fluid in the facet joints and discontinuous ligaments is a different report from one equivocal finding in isolation. Say which of the three states you believe the complex is in, because the score, and the operation, follow from that word.

nodes.title: Cervical Node Levels and the Malignant Node
