nodes.goal: Place a cervical node in its level from the anatomy on the image, decide whether it is malignant, and say what your call changes about the stage, the operation and the search for a primary.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old smoker with a supraglottic laryngeal carcinoma has a 15 mm necrotic node on the right. On the sagittal reformat its centre lies below the lower border of the cricoid arch and above the clavicle; on the axial images it sits anteromedial to a line drawn along the posterior edge of the sternocleidomastoid, just lateral to the common carotid artery. Which level does it belong in, and what follows from that?
quiz.answer: Level IV, so the dissection reaches the clavicle
choices: Level IV, so the dissection reaches the clavicle
Level III, so the dissection stops at cricoid
Level VB, so the accessory nerve is at risk
Level VI, so the central compartment is opened
quiz.explain: The jugular chain is cut into three by two horizontal landmarks: the lower body of the hyoid divides level II from III, and the lower border of the cricoid arch divides III from IV. A node below cricoid and above the clavicle is therefore level IV, provided it lies anteromedial to the oblique line joining the posterior edge of the sternocleidomastoid to the posterolateral edge of the anterior scalene; behind that line the same node would be level VB, which matters because the spinal accessory nerve runs there and its dissection carries a shoulder cost. Level VI is the central compartment between the carotid arteries, the territory of thyroid and subglottic disease, not of a lateral jugular node. Supraglottic larynx drains to levels II, III and IV, so this node is entirely in keeping with the primary; the practical consequence is that the neck dissection and the radiotherapy volume must extend down to the clavicle.

quiz.prompt: On axial CT a level II node measures 16 mm in its longest axis and 10 mm in its shortest. Divide the long axis by the short axis and give the ratio. Answer as a number, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Sixteen divided by ten is 1.6. A reactive node is ovoid and stretched along the chain, with a long-to-short ratio of about 2 or more; as tumour fills a node it becomes spherical and the ratio falls, so a value under 2 is the shape criterion for suspicion. Note what the size criterion alone would have done here. Using the widely applied minimal-axial-diameter thresholds, a node needs 11 mm short axis at level II and 10 mm elsewhere before size alone calls it involved, so at 10 mm this node would have passed. Shape, loss of the fatty hilum, central necrosis and irregular margins all carry more weight than a millimetre either side of a size cut-off, and necrosis carries the most of all. Measure the ratio in the axial plane, on the same image, and record the short axis in your report so that the next reader can compare.

quiz.prompt: Staging MRI for a nasopharyngeal carcinoma shows a lateral retropharyngeal node with a short axis of 7 mm and no necrosis. State whether you would report it as involved, and give the short-axis figure above which a retropharyngeal node in an adult is treated as malignant.
quiz.answer: Report it as involved: in an adult a lateral retropharyngeal node of 5 mm or more in short axis is treated as malignant, and this one at 7 mm is beyond that.
quiz.explain: The lateral retropharyngeal nodes sit between the prevertebral muscles and the pharyngeal wall, above the hyoid, and they are the first echelon for the nasopharynx, the posterior pharyngeal wall and the sinonasal cavities. In adults they are ordinarily involuted and invisible, which is why the threshold is so much lower than in the neck proper: 5 mm short axis is the figure in common use, and some readers reserve a confident call for 8 mm or a node with necrosis. Children are different — reactive retropharyngeal nodes are a normal finding. The reason to hunt for these nodes is that a standard neck dissection does not reach them, so they are covered by the radiotherapy volume rather than by the surgeon. In the AJCC 8th edition staging of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, retropharyngeal nodal involvement counts within N1, so calling it changes the stage as well as the plan.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old who has never smoked has a painless 3 cm cystic mass at level IIA. Ultrasound shows a thin wall with a 6 mm solid mural nodule, and there is no preceding infective illness. What is the appropriate next step?
quiz.answer: Ultrasound-guided aspiration with p16 testing
choices: Ultrasound-guided aspiration with p16 testing
A course of antibiotics and repeat ultrasound
Excision, assuming a branchial cleft cyst
Aspiration to dryness for symptom relief
quiz.explain: A cystic level II node in an adult is a metastasis from a human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma until proved otherwise, and the primary in the tonsil or tongue base is often tiny and impalpable. These nodes are famously mistaken for second branchial cleft cysts, which sit in the same place; the discriminators are a thicker or irregular wall, a mural nodule, and the patient's age, and the safe rule is that a first branchial cleft cyst presenting in adult life is a node until the cytology says otherwise. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration with p16 immunostaining or HPV testing on the aspirate answers the question with the least harm. Antibiotics simply delay. Simple aspiration decompresses the cyst, loses the specimen and lets it refill. Proceeding straight to excision performs an open biopsy on an undiagnosed squamous carcinoma, which spills tumour into a neck that has not yet been staged or planned.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the work-up of an adult with a cystic level II node and no visible mucosal primary, from the first step to the last.
quiz.answer: contrast-CT ultrasound-guided-FNA PET-CT panendoscopy-with-biopsies open-excision
quiz.explain: The sequence is driven by one principle: every step should be taken before the step that would spoil it. Cross-sectional imaging comes first, while the mucosa is undisturbed, because post-biopsy oedema and haemorrhage mimic a primary. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is the least invasive way to prove malignancy and to run p16 or HPV testing. PET-CT then goes before instrumentation, since biopsy sites and a recently traumatised tonsil take up tracer avidly and a false-positive there sends the surgeon to the wrong place; PET is also the step most likely to find the occult primary or a synchronous tumour. Panendoscopy with directed biopsies, guided by the PET, and usually with ipsilateral tonsillectomy, comes next. Open excision of the node is last and is a confession that everything else failed: it violates an unstaged neck, and in a patient with squamous carcinoma it is the step you most want to avoid having taken.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old smoker has a p16-negative tonsillar carcinoma and a single ipsilateral level II node of 2.5 cm. Its margin is spiculated, the perinodal fat is infiltrated and the sternocleidomastoid is invaded; the node is fixed on palpation. Using the AJCC 8th edition, what does the clinical nodal category become?
quiz.answer: N3b, which brings adjuvant chemoradiotherapy
choices: N3b, which brings adjuvant chemoradiotherapy
N1, unchanged by the perinodal appearances
N2a, taken from the 2.5 cm nodal diameter
N2b, because two compartments are involved
quiz.explain: The 8th edition, which is the edition head and neck staging still runs on, brought extranodal extension into the N category for the first time. For a p16-negative tumour, clinically overt extranodal extension makes the neck N3b whatever the size or number of nodes, so a 2.5 cm node that would otherwise be N1 leaps to the top of the N ladder. That is not bureaucracy: extranodal extension roughly halves survival, and its presence on the specimen is one of the two classic indications, with a positive margin, for concurrent chemotherapy alongside post-operative radiotherapy. Two cautions. Pathological staging is graded differently — a single ipsilateral node of 3 cm or less with extranodal extension is pN2a — and for p16-positive oropharyngeal cancer extranodal extension is deliberately excluded from the clinical N categories. On imaging, reserve the call for unequivocal signs: matted nodes and irradiated fat both mimic it.

quiz.prompt: A staging CT for an oral tongue carcinoma shows a level IB node of 8 mm short axis containing a rounded low-attenuation centre with an enhancing rim. Give the call you would make and the reason it outranks the measurement.
quiz.answer: Call it a metastatic node: central necrosis is the most specific sign of nodal metastasis and holds at any size, so a node under the 10 mm short-axis threshold is still reported as malignant.
quiz.explain: Size is the weakest of the nodal criteria; it is simply the one that is easiest to measure. A node enlarges for a fortnight of tonsillitis, and a node harbouring a 2 mm deposit may be entirely normal in calibre, so thresholds of 10 mm short axis in general and 11 mm at level II buy sensitivity at a heavy cost in specificity. Central necrosis is the opposite: an ovoid or round low-attenuation centre with an enhancing rim, in a node draining a known squamous primary, is close to diagnostic, and it is reported as involved at any size. The mimics worth holding in mind are a suppurative node in acute infection and a caseating node in tuberculosis, which is why the clinical setting is part of the reading. On ultrasound the same finding appears as an anechoic or heterogeneous centre; on MRI as a high-T2, non-enhancing core.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old has a firm 2 cm node in the left supraclavicular fossa. Flexible nasendoscopy, a dedicated contrast-enhanced neck CT and an ultrasound of the thyroid are all unremarkable. Where should the search for a primary now be directed?
quiz.answer: Below the clavicles, to chest, abdomen and pelvis
choices: Below the clavicles, to chest, abdomen and pelvis
To the nasopharynx, with blind directed biopsies
To the ipsilateral tonsil and the tongue base
To the thyroid bed, with a repeat ultrasound scan
quiz.explain: The level of the node is a map of where to look. The left supraclavicular fossa receives the thoracic duct, so a node there commonly reflects an infraclavicular primary — lung, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, colon, kidney, ovary, testis or breast — and the appropriate next test is a CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis, often followed by PET-CT. The other options each describe a real pattern that does not fit this case. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma announces itself with retropharyngeal nodes and level V disease, usually in a younger patient, and the neck CT would rarely be clean. An HPV-associated oropharyngeal primary drains to a cystic level II node, not to the supraclavicular fossa. Thyroid carcinoma spreads to levels VI, III and IV and would be sought on ultrasound of a gland that is here normal. Learning the drainage territories is what turns an unexpected level from a curiosity into a direction of travel.

quiz.prompt: A node is measured three ways on the same CT: 14 mm transverse and 9 mm anteroposterior on the axial image, and 22 mm craniocaudal on the coronal reformat. Give the figure you would enter in the report as the short axis. Answer in millimetres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The short axis is the smallest diameter in the axial plane, so it is 9 mm here. The craniocaudal measurement is not part of the criterion at all, and quoting it is the commonest way a normal node is reported as enlarged: nodes are cigar-shaped along the chain, so their long axis in the coronal plane is routinely twice the short axis. Measuring in the axial plane also keeps the number reproducible between readers and between studies, which is what makes follow-up comparisons mean anything. At 9 mm this node falls below the 10 mm threshold used outside level II and the 11 mm used at level II, so size alone does not call it. That is precisely the moment to look at everything else: is it round rather than ovoid, has it lost its fatty hilum, is there a necrotic centre, is the margin irregular?

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old has bilateral rubbery non-tender nodes up to 3 cm at levels II and V with preserved fatty hila, and CT shows mediastinal nodes as well. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration returns atypical lymphoid cells. State the sampling you would arrange next and why aspiration was the wrong tool here.
quiz.answer: Arrange a core biopsy, and an excision if the core is not diagnostic: lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture and immunophenotype, and an aspirate of dispersed cells cannot show architecture.
quiz.explain: Fine-needle aspiration is superb where the question is whether malignant epithelial cells are present — squamous carcinoma in a neck node, a thyroid nodule — because a cytological diagnosis needs only the cells. Lymphoma is diagnosed on how the cells are arranged as well as on what they are, and it is subclassified with immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry on tissue, so an aspirate yields the unhelpful answer this patient received. A core biopsy under ultrasound usually suffices and is the sensible next step; excisional biopsy of a whole node remains the reference standard when cores are equivocal. Note that the general warning against open biopsy of a neck node applies to suspected squamous carcinoma, not to suspected lymphoma, where excision is the right operation. When sampling, choose the node with the most abnormal cortex and vascularity rather than the largest, and avoid a node that is largely necrotic.

quiz.prompt: Ultrasound of the right neck in a patient with a 12 mm thyroid nodule shows two level III nodes. The first is oval, 6 mm in short axis, with an echogenic fatty hilum and hilar flow on Doppler. The second is round, 9 mm in short axis, with no hilum, punctate echogenic foci within it and peripheral subcapsular flow. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Sample the second node; its features outweigh size
choices: Sample the second node; its features outweigh size
Sample the first node, being the more accessible
Sample neither, as both are under 10 mm short axis
Rescan in six months to see which node grows
quiz.explain: Every feature of the second node argues for malignancy except its size, and size is the criterion to abandon first. Loss of the fatty hilum, a rounded contour, and vascularity that enters through the capsule instead of the hilum together carry far more weight than a millimetre of short axis, and punctate echogenic foci in a lateral neck node alongside a thyroid nodule point hard at metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma; cystic change in such a node points the same way. Waiting six months in a patient with a thyroid nodule and an abnormal node forfeits the chance to plan a single operation that clears the lateral compartment. Sampling the first node would return reactive tissue and falsely reassure. When a papillary carcinoma is suspected, the aspirate can be supplemented with a thyroglobulin washout from the needle, which is more sensitive than cytology alone in a cystic node.

quiz.prompt: Eighteen months after resection of an oral tongue carcinoma, surveillance CT shows a new 12 mm node at level IV with a necrotic centre. Levels I to III are clear and the primary site looks normal. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: Metastasis; tongue can drain straight to level IV
choices: Metastasis; tongue can drain straight to level IV
Reactive node, given the clear upper levels
Post-radiation change in a treated nodal bed
A thyroid primary presenting in its first echelon
quiz.explain: Two things settle this. Necrosis in a node draining a treated squamous primary is a metastasis whatever its size, and the oral tongue is the classic site for a skip deposit: lymphatic channels from the tongue can run directly to levels III and IV, bypassing the submandibular and upper jugular nodes altogether. That is why an elective dissection for an oral tongue primary is often extended beyond the levels I to III of the supraomohyoid operation, and why a clean upper neck is no reassurance about the lower neck. Reactive nodes do not develop necrotic centres in this setting. Radiotherapy change is diffuse, involves fat and skin, and does not produce a discrete new node. A thyroid primary would drain first to level VI and would be visible in the gland. The report should state the level, the size, the necrosis and whether the node abuts the carotid or the scalene muscles.

nodes.title: Deep Neck Spaces: Supra- and Infrahyoid
nodes.goal: Use the fascial spaces to localise a neck mass or a collection, read the displacement of the parapharyngeal fat as evidence of where it arose, and report the airway, the mediastinum and the routes of perineural spread.

quiz.prompt: A 47-year-old has trismus and numbness of the chin. Contrast CT shows a mass centred lateral to the pterygoid plates, with enlargement of the left masseter and pterygoid muscles and erosion of the mandibular ramus; the fat of the left parapharyngeal space is pushed posteriorly and medially. Where has the lesion arisen, and what must be traced next?
quiz.answer: Masticator space; trace V3 to the foramen ovale
choices: Masticator space; trace V3 to the foramen ovale
Parotid space; trace VII to the stylomastoid
Carotid space; trace the sheath to the base
Pharyngeal mucosal space; assess the tonsil
quiz.explain: The parapharyngeal fat is the compass of the suprahyoid neck, because every surrounding space pushes it in a different direction. A masticator space lesion lies anterolateral to it and drives it posteromedially, which is what has happened here; a parotid lesion lies lateral and drives it medially; a carotid space lesion lies posterior and drives it anteriorly; a pharyngeal mucosal lesion lies medial and drives it laterally; and a mass arising within the space itself simply widens the fat. Trismus, mandibular erosion and numbness of the chin all point the same way, since the masticator space carries the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve to the inferior alveolar canal. The obligation that follows is to follow V3 upwards through the foramen ovale to Meckel's cave, looking for nerve thickening, loss of the surrounding fat and asymmetrical enhancement, because perineural spread changes the surgical and radiotherapy plan entirely.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old has a pulsatile neck mass and a hoarse voice. CT angiography shows an avidly enhancing mass at the carotid bifurcation that splays the internal and external carotid arteries apart, with internal flow voids on MRI, and the parapharyngeal fat is displaced anteriorly. What should the report say to do?
quiz.answer: Carotid body tumour; avoid percutaneous biopsy
choices: Carotid body tumour; avoid percutaneous biopsy
Vagal schwannoma; it displaces, it does not splay
Nodal metastasis; arrange ultrasound-guided FNA
Second branchial cleft cyst; arrange excision
quiz.explain: Everything here places the lesion in the carotid space: the parapharyngeal fat pushed forwards, and a mass sitting between the two carotid arteries at the bifurcation. Splaying of the internal from the external carotid is the signature of a paraganglioma arising in the carotid body, and the avid enhancement with flow voids fits. That vascularity is exactly why percutaneous biopsy is the wrong move — the diagnosis is made on imaging, and the patient goes on to catecholamine screening, assessment for multicentric disease, and genetic testing for succinate dehydrogenase mutations. A vagal paraganglioma sits higher and pushes the internal carotid anteromedially rather than splaying it, while a vagal schwannoma displaces both vessels together and enhances less avidly; both remain reasonable considerations until the splaying is seen. A cystic lesion is excluded by the enhancement, and a nodal metastasis would not sit between the vessels.

quiz.prompt: On the sagittal reformat of a neck CT, a retropharyngeal collection has reduced the anteroposterior diameter of the airway at C3 from an expected 14 mm to 4 mm. Express the residual airway as a percentage of the expected anteroposterior diameter. Answer as a percentage, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Four divided by fourteen is 0.286, so 29 per cent of the airway remains — a figure worth calculating because it is the number that changes what happens in the next hour. The instinct on seeing a deep neck collection is to measure the abscess; the anaesthetist needs the airway. A report that leads with the calibre and the level of narrowing, the degree of laryngeal or tracheal deviation, and whether the epiglottis and supraglottis are involved, will be acted on faster than one that opens with the volume of pus. Two other measurements matter as much: how far the collection extends craniocaudally, and whether it reaches below the thoracic inlet, since descent into the posterior mediastinum turns a neck problem into a thoracic emergency. Say plainly if the airway looks unsafe for a supine, sedated examination.

quiz.prompt: Contrast CT in a child with fever and neck stiffness shows a 3 cm low-attenuation area in the retropharyngeal space with a thick, irregularly enhancing wall, a non-enhancing centre and a few locules of gas. State how you would report this rather than as phlegmon, and what your wording changes.
quiz.answer: Report a drainable abscess rather than phlegmon: a rim-enhancing collection with a non-enhancing centre and locules of gas is mature pus, so it goes to surgical drainage with the airway secured, not to antibiotics alone.
quiz.explain: Phlegmon and abscess are two points on one continuum, and the CT distinction is what decides between a ward and a theatre. Phlegmon is oedematous, infiltrated tissue that enhances more or less uniformly with stranding of the fat and no non-enhancing centre; it is treated with antibiotics and observed. An abscess has a definable rim that enhances around a centre that does not, and gas within it settles the matter. CT is not infallible in that judgement — small non-enhancing areas of necrosis inside a phlegmon are over-called as abscesses, which is one reason a collection under about 2 cm is often managed medically at first. Whatever the wording, the airway comes first in the report, the craniocaudal extent second, and the vessels third: look for thrombus in the internal jugular vein, which with septic pulmonary emboli would raise the possibility of Lemierre syndrome.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the stations of perineural spread from an adenoid cystic carcinoma of the hard palate along the maxillary nerve, from the primary towards the skull base.
quiz.answer: greater-palatine-canal pterygopalatine-fossa foramen-rotundum Meckel-cave
quiz.explain: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is the tumour that taught radiologists to look along nerves, and the hard palate is its classic address. The greater palatine nerve leaves the palate through the greater palatine canal and rises into the pterygopalatine fossa, which is the crossroads of the mid-face: it connects to the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure, to the nose through the sphenopalatine foramen, to the infratemporal fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure, and to the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum, which delivers the maxillary nerve to the trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave. The findings to hunt for are the loss of the normal fat in the pterygopalatine fossa, enlargement and enhancement of the nerve, widening of the foramen, and a convex bulge in Meckel's cave. Perineural spread is frequently painless and can skip, so a normal-looking segment does not end the search.

quiz.prompt: A 63-year-old with diabetes has neck pain and fever. MRI shows a rim-enhancing fluid collection lying anterior to the longus colli muscles and flattening them posteriorly, with a bow-tie configuration across the midline; the C4-C5 disc and its endplates are normal. Which space holds it, and what follows?
quiz.answer: Retropharyngeal; drain it and image the mediastinum
choices: Retropharyngeal; drain it and image the mediastinum
Prevertebral; look for discitis and treat medically
Danger space alone; the mediastinum will be spared
Carotid space; assess for jugular vein thrombosis
quiz.explain: Two features localise this. The collection lies in front of the prevertebral muscles, so it is retropharyngeal rather than prevertebral, and it takes a bow-tie shape because the median raphe tethers the space in the midline. A prevertebral collection would displace or involve the longus colli from behind and would almost always be accompanied by spondylodiscitis, classically tuberculous, which the normal disc here excludes. That distinction is not academic: a retropharyngeal collection is drained transorally or transcervically, while a prevertebral one is a spinal infection needing prolonged antimicrobial treatment and often instrumentation. The danger space lies immediately behind the retropharyngeal space, between the alar and prevertebral layers, and runs from the skull base to the diaphragm; retropharyngeal pus reaches the posterior mediastinum through it, which is why the chest is imaged rather than assumed to be clear.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old with a decayed lower molar has bilateral floor-of-mouth swelling and an elevated tongue. CT shows oedema and small locules of gas in the sublingual and submandibular spaces on both sides, with no drainable collection. State the single priority your report should lead with and the anatomical reason for it.
quiz.answer: The airway: bilateral sublingual and submandibular cellulitis lifts the floor of the mouth and pushes the tongue up and back, so the report leads with the threatened airway and the team secures it before anything else.
quiz.explain: This is Ludwig's angina, and the reason it kills is geometry rather than sepsis. The sublingual space sits above the mylohyoid and the submandibular space below it, the two communicate around the posterior free edge of the muscle, and both are bounded by a rigid mandible in front and below. Swelling therefore has nowhere to go but upwards and backwards, carrying the tongue against the palate and the pharynx. The imaging often shows no abscess at all, which tempts an unwary report into reassurance; the finding that matters is the extent of the cellulitis and the position of the tongue base and the airway. Say so in the first line, and be explicit about whether the patient looks safe to lie flat. Dental origin is the rule, so name the culprit tooth, and follow the process posteriorly into the parapharyngeal space and downwards towards the mediastinum.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old has a soft, non-tender lateral neck mass. MRI shows a thin-walled cystic lesion at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, displacing the muscle posteriorly, the submandibular gland anteriorly and the carotid space medially, with a small beak extending between the internal and external carotid arteries. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: Second branchial cleft cyst; excise cyst and tract
choices: Second branchial cleft cyst; excise cyst and tract
Cystic nodal metastasis; arrange FNA and PET-CT
Lymphatic malformation; expect fluid-fluid levels
Plunging ranula; trace its tail through mylohyoid
quiz.explain: The three displacements plus the beak between the carotid arteries are the signature of a second branchial cleft cyst in its usual position, at the angle of the mandible along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid. The beak follows the embryological tract, which runs from the tonsillar fossa between the carotids to the skin, and it is the reason the whole tract must come out or the lesion recurs. The other congenital lesions of the neck have their own addresses: first cleft anomalies sit around the parotid and the external auditory canal, third cleft lesions in the posterior triangle, fourth cleft sinuses on the left at the apex of the piriform fossa causing recurrent thyroiditis, thyroglossal duct cysts in or near the midline embedded in the strap muscles, lymphatic malformations crossing fascial planes with fluid-fluid levels, and a plunging ranula herniating through mylohyoid with a tail. Age is the caveat: past about forty the same appearance is a metastatic node until disproved.

quiz.prompt: A man treated two years ago for a cutaneous squamous carcinoma of the cheek now has numbness of the chin. MRI shows a widened left foramen ovale with loss of the fat that normally surrounds the nerve there, and the left masseter and pterygoid muscles are small and fatty. State what you will report, and the two findings that support it.
quiz.answer: Report perineural tumour spread along the mandibular division: the nerve is enlarged at a widened foramen ovale with loss of the perineural fat, and the wasted fatty muscles of mastication are chronic denervation from that same nerve.
quiz.explain: Cutaneous squamous carcinoma of the face and adenoid cystic carcinoma are the two tumours that most reliably travel along nerves, and they can do so years after the primary was treated and with clear margins at the time. The direct signs are nerve thickening, abnormal enhancement, loss of the fat that outlines a nerve at its foramen, and widening or erosion of the foramen itself; fat-saturated post-contrast sequences make them visible. The indirect sign is denervation of the muscles the nerve supplies, which passes through an acute oedematous phase, bright on T2 and enhancing, into chronic fatty atrophy — the appearance here. Because the auriculotemporal nerve links V3 to the facial nerve, always follow both, and look at the geniculate ganglion and the stylomastoid foramen before concluding. Report the most proximal level involved, since that dictates whether surgery can reach it.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with a hoarse voice has a mass in the left thyroid lobe extending posteromedially into the tracheo-oesophageal groove; on CT the left vocal cord is medialised and the left laryngeal ventricle is dilated. What should the report warn the surgeon about?
quiz.answer: Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement in the groove
choices: Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement in the groove
Carotid space invasion with encasement of the sheath
Retropharyngeal spread towards the skull base
Masticator space extension along the mandible
quiz.explain: Below the hyoid the organising space is the visceral space, bounded by the middle layer of the deep cervical fascia and containing the larynx, hypopharynx, trachea, oesophagus, thyroid and parathyroid glands, the level VI nodes and, in the tracheo-oesophageal grooves, the recurrent laryngeal nerves. A thyroid tumour that extends posteromedially is therefore heading straight for the nerve, and the imaging signs of a palsy are already present: a medialised cord, a dilated ipsilateral ventricle and piriform sinus, and often a thickened aryepiglottic fold. Saying so matters because it changes consent and operative planning, and because a pre-existing palsy alters what can be sacrificed on the other side. The other spaces named lie outside the reach of this tumour; the carotid space is the one to check next, along with the trachea and oesophageal wall for direct invasion, since that determines resectability.

quiz.prompt: An asymptomatic 50-year-old has a 3 cm well-defined, T2-hyperintense mass in the prestyloid part of the right parapharyngeal space. A thin band of fat separates it from the deep lobe of the parotid gland, and the carotid artery is displaced posteriorly. Where has it most likely arisen?
quiz.answer: Minor salivary gland tumour arising in the space
choices: Minor salivary gland tumour arising in the space
Deep lobe parotid tumour extending medially
Vagal schwannoma of the carotid space
Nodal metastasis in the retropharyngeal group
quiz.explain: The fat plane is the whole answer. The parapharyngeal space is divided by the styloid process and its muscles into a prestyloid compartment, which contains fat and rests of minor salivary tissue, and a retrostyloid compartment, which is effectively the carotid space. A mass in the prestyloid compartment separated from the parotid by preserved fat is a primary lesion of the space, usually a pleomorphic adenoma from a minor salivary rest. A deep lobe parotid tumour would efface that fat and stay continuous with the gland, often waisted as it passes through the stylomandibular tunnel. A carotid space lesion would sit behind the fat and displace it forwards rather than being pushed by it, and retropharyngeal nodes sit medial to the carotid arteries in front of the prevertebral muscles. The distinction decides the approach: transcervical for a true parapharyngeal lesion, parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection for a deep lobe one.

quiz.prompt: A neck CT in an adult shows a retropharyngeal abscess extending from C2 down to the thoracic inlet, where the study ends. State what you would add to the examination and the anatomical route that makes it necessary.
quiz.answer: Extend the scan through the chest: the danger space lies immediately behind the retropharyngeal space and runs from the skull base to the diaphragm, so pus can descend into the posterior mediastinum and cause necrotising mediastinitis.
quiz.explain: The retropharyngeal space itself ends somewhere between the first and the sixth or seventh thoracic vertebrae, where the alar fascia fuses with the visceral fascia, but the danger space behind it has no such barrier and continues to the diaphragm. That is why a neck study that stops at the thoracic inlet in a patient with deep neck sepsis is an incomplete study: descending necrotising mediastinitis carries a mortality that dwarfs the neck infection, and it is treated by drainage rather than antibiotics. Look on the chest images for mediastinal fat stranding, gas, fluid collections, pleural and pericardial effusions, and empyema. The same reasoning applies to any suprahyoid odontogenic infection that has reached the parapharyngeal space, since that space opens inferiorly towards the submandibular region and the mediastinum. Add the chest at the time, rather than recalling a septic patient.

nodes.title: Orbit: Trauma, Inflammation and Tumour
nodes.goal: Localise an orbital lesion to its compartment, separate trauma, infection, inflammation and tumour by the findings in front of you, and say what has to happen next.

quiz.prompt: Ethmoid sinusitis in a child spreads laterally across the lamina papyracea. Arrange these five orbital complications into the classical staging sequence of increasing severity.
quiz.answer: preseptal-cellulitis orbital-cellulitis subperiosteal-abscess orbital-abscess cavernous-sinus-thrombosis
quiz.explain: The classical five stages track the infection across one anatomical barrier at a time. It begins in the lid soft tissues in front of the orbital septum, where the eye itself is untouched. Once it crosses the septum the orbital fat is inflamed and the eye becomes proptosed, painful on movement and at risk. Pus then collects first between the periorbita and the medial wall, lifting the periosteum off the bone as a lentiform collection, before breaking through it into the orbital fat as a true intraorbital abscess. Finally it travels back along the valveless ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus. Two practical consequences: the septum is the line your report must comment on, because it separates an oral-antibiotic problem from an admission, and the direction of travel is medial and posterior, so it is the medial wall and the apex you scrutinise. In real children the stages blur and can be skipped, so the staging is a way of describing severity rather than a timetable.

quiz.prompt: A 6-year-old has a hot, swollen right upper lid. Eye movements are full and painless, acuity and colour vision are normal, and there is no proptosis. Contrast CT shows swelling of the lid soft tissues in front of an intact orbital septum, clean retroseptal fat, and an opacified ipsilateral ethmoid cell. Which additional finding on the same scan would most change what happens that day?
quiz.answer: A thin lentiform rim-enhancing collection along the lamina papyracea
choices: A thin lentiform rim-enhancing collection along the lamina papyracea
Mucosal thickening in the ipsilateral maxillary antrum as well
Reactive enlargement of the ipsilateral submandibular lymph nodes
A small quantity of fluid within the ipsilateral middle ear cavity
quiz.explain: A rim-enhancing lens-shaped collection hugging the medial wall is a subperiosteal abscess, and it moves the child from oral antibiotics and review to admission, intravenous antibiotics and a surgical conversation, with drainage if there is any visual compromise, a large collection, or failure to improve within about 48 hours. It is the one finding here that crosses the septum. Look for it deliberately on the coronal images, because a thin collection is easy to mistake for thickened periorbita on axial slices alone, and measure the medial rectus displacement. The other three findings are all common travelling companions of paediatric sinonasal infection and change nothing on the day: maxillary mucosal thickening simply confirms that the sinuses are inflamed, reactive nodes are expected, and middle ear fluid is incidental. None of them tells you where the eye stands.

quiz.prompt: Coronal and sagittal reformats after a blunt orbital injury show a floor defect measuring 18 mm anteroposteriorly by 14 mm transversely. The intact floor of the opposite orbit measures 30 mm by 24 mm. Treating both as rectangles, what proportion of the floor is defective? Answer as a percentage to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: The defect is 18 x 14 = 252 square millimetres against an intact floor of 30 x 24 = 720, so 252/720 = 35 per cent. The reason to do this arithmetic rather than eyeball it is that defect size is one of the few reproducible things imaging contributes to the repair decision. The widely used surgical rule of thumb is that a defect of roughly half the floor or more tends to produce late enophthalmos and is offered repair, while smaller defects are often watched for one to two weeks and repaired only if enophthalmos of about 2 mm or more, or persistent diplopia in the functional field of gaze, declares itself. Note that this is a rule of thumb and not a graded classification, so give the surgeon the measurements rather than a verdict. And it never overrides true muscle entrapment, which is repaired on its own merits and urgently, however small the crack.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old is struck in the eye by a football. He cannot elevate the left eye, is retching, and his pulse is 46. CT shows a hairline linear crack in the orbital floor with a small tag of soft tissue in the antral roof and almost no herniated fat. The on-call team plan to see him in fracture clinic in two weeks. Say what is going on and what should happen instead.
quiz.answer: This is a paediatric trapdoor fracture with genuine entrapment of the inferior rectus, and the bradycardia and vomiting are the oculocardiac reflex. The child's elastic bone has sprung back on the muscle, so the CT looks unimpressive while the muscle is being strangled. He needs urgent ophthalmology and maxillofacial referral for release within hours, not a clinic appointment in two weeks.
quiz.explain: This is the orbital fracture that punishes a proportionate CT report. In children the floor is greenstick rather than comminuted: it hinges open, the inferior rectus or its surrounding fat slips through, and the bone recoils and grips it. Because almost nothing herniates, the scan shows only a hairline defect and perhaps a small soft-tissue tag in the antrum, so the imaging looks trivial while the clinical picture is severe. The tell is the mismatch: marked restriction of upgaze, pain on movement, and the oculocardiac reflex of bradycardia, nausea and vomiting from traction on the extraocular muscles. Ischaemic muscle necroses, so this is repaired within hours to a day, not after the usual two-week wait for swelling to settle. Adults get the comminuted version and rarely the entrapment, which is why the same CT in a 40-year-old would not be urgent. When your scan looks mild and the referrer describes a fixed eye and a slow pulse, believe the referrer.

quiz.prompt: On an axial CT through the lenses, a line is drawn between the two zygomatic frontal processes. The right globe measures 24.0 mm in anteroposterior diameter, and 9.0 mm of it projects anterior to that line. What proportion of the globe lies behind the line? Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Fifteen of the 24 millimetres lie behind the line, which is 62.5 per cent. The convention worth carrying is that at least two-thirds, about 66.7 per cent, of a normal globe sits posterior to the interzygomatic line, so this eye is proptosed. The other common cut-off measures from the line to the anterior corneal surface, with more than about 21 to 23 millimetres taken as abnormal; both are rules of thumb rather than a graded system, and both are worth stating with the raw numbers so the clinician can follow them over time. Two cautions. First, the measurement is only valid on a straight axial slice through both lenses, because head tilt fakes asymmetry. Second, proptosis is a sign, not a diagnosis: what matters next is why. Bilateral and painless suggests thyroid eye disease, painful and unilateral suggests inflammation or infection, and pulsatile with an enlarged superior ophthalmic vein suggests a carotid-cavernous fistula.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old woman has bilateral proptosis and lid retraction. Coronal CT shows fusiform enlargement of both inferior and medial recti with tendinous insertions of normal calibre, and an increased volume of orbital fat. She has no orbital pain. Which finding on that same study would most urgently alter her management?
quiz.answer: Crowding of the orbital apex effacing the perineural fat
choices: Crowding of the orbital apex effacing the perineural fat
Enlargement of the superior ophthalmic vein bilaterally
Bowing of the medial orbital wall into the ethmoid cells
Increased retrobulbar fat displacing the globes forwards
quiz.explain: The muscle bellies enlarged with the tendons spared, bilaterally and painlessly, is thyroid eye disease, and the classical order of recruitment is inferior, then medial, then superior, then lateral rectus. The complication that threatens sight is dysthyroid optic neuropathy, produced not by the proptosis but by the swollen muscles crowding the optic nerve at the apex, and its imaging surrogate is loss of the fat plane around the nerve on posterior coronal slices. That finding triggers visual field testing, high-dose steroids and consideration of urgent decompression. Medial wall bowing is the opposite of a worry: it is spontaneous decompression, and orbits that bow tend to be the ones that spare the nerve. An enlarged superior ophthalmic vein is common in congested thyroid orbitopathy and is only alarming if it is thrombosed or if the picture suggests a fistula. Increased fat drives proptosis and exposure keratopathy, which is a corneal problem treated with lubricants and taping, not an emergency for the nerve.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old man has painless bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement and mildly enlarged lateral recti. The glands are hypointense on T2 and enhance homogeneously. A colleague has called it idiopathic orbital inflammation. What additional imaging finding would push you towards IgG4-related disease instead, and what would you ask the physicians to send?
quiz.answer: Enlargement of the infraorbital nerve in the orbital floor, together with disease elsewhere such as the pancreas, kidneys or salivary glands, favours IgG4-related disease over idiopathic orbital inflammation. Ask for a serum IgG4 level, and where the diagnosis will change treatment, tissue showing IgG4-positive plasma cells and storiform fibrosis.
quiz.explain: Both conditions are fibro-inflammatory, both are T2 dark because of that fibrosis, and both enhance, so signal alone will not separate them. Three things tilt the balance towards IgG4-related disease: bilateral and painless involvement, enlargement of the infraorbital nerve as it runs in the floor of the orbit, which is unusual enough in other orbital disease to be worth hunting for on coronal fat-saturated images, and extra-orbital sites, so widen your review to any prior chest or abdominal imaging for autoimmune pancreatitis, a sclerosing kidney lesion, retroperitoneal fibrosis or an enlarged submandibular gland. Idiopathic orbital inflammation is more often unilateral, painful, acute and steroid-responsive, and when it involves a muscle it involves the tendon insertion too, which is the point of difference from thyroid eye disease. The distinction matters because IgG4 disease relapses on steroid withdrawal and is increasingly managed with rituximab, and because a small number of orbital lymphomas hide in exactly this appearance, so a persistent or atypical case earns a biopsy.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old woman has slowly progressive visual loss in the right eye. Post-contrast fat-saturated T1 shows enhancing tubular thickening surrounding the right optic nerve with a non-enhancing linear structure running through its centre, and CT shows fine calcification along it. What follows from these appearances?
quiz.answer: A sheath lesion: the nerve is spared but endangered by resection
choices: A sheath lesion: the nerve is spared but endangered by resection
A nerve lesion: the nerve is expanded and buckles within the orbit
A perineuritis: the enhancement should resolve on corticosteroids
Perineural spread: search the face and sinuses for a primary tumour
quiz.explain: Enhancement surrounding a dark central nerve is the optic nerve sheath meningioma, seen as tram-track thickening on axial images and as a doughnut on coronals, in a middle-aged woman, and calcification on CT is close to confirmatory. The reason the distinction is worth making is surgical: the tumour is in the sheath, so the nerve itself is anatomically intact but takes its blood supply through the very tissue that would have to be removed. Resection therefore blinds the eye, and management is observation while vision holds and fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy when it does not. An optic nerve glioma expands the nerve itself, kinking and buckling it, occurs in children, does not calcify, and is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, bilateral involvement being effectively diagnostic of it. Optic perineuritis enhances the sheath too but is painful, acute and steroid-responsive without calcification. Perineural tumour spread reaches the orbit along the trigeminal branches, not along the optic nerve, which is a central nervous system tract.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old has two years of slowly progressive painless proptosis. MRI shows a well-defined encapsulated ovoid intraconal mass lateral to the optic nerve, bright on T2, enhancing patchily in the early phase and filling in progressively on delayed images. The referrer has suggested an orbital varix. Which observation would settle the question at the scanner?
quiz.answer: Whether the lesion swells when the patient performs a Valsalva manoeuvre
choices: Whether the lesion swells when the patient performs a Valsalva manoeuvre
Whether the lesion contains fluid-fluid levels on the T2 sequence
Whether the lesion contains internal flow voids on the T2 sequence
Whether the lesion abuts the periosteum of the lateral orbital wall
quiz.explain: A varix is a distensible venous channel in continuity with the orbital venous system, so it enlarges with Valsalva, with jugular compression or in the prone position, and collapses when the patient sits up. That single manoeuvre, added to the end of the study, answers the question. What is described here is a cavernous venous malformation, the commonest intraconal mass in adults: encapsulated, slow-growing, and characterised by patchy early enhancement that fills in centripetally on delayed imaging because contrast seeps slowly through its low-flow spaces. Its capsule is what makes it resectable when it becomes symptomatic. Fluid-fluid levels would point instead to a lymphatic malformation, which is transspatial, unencapsulated, presents in childhood and can enlarge abruptly after haemorrhage. Internal flow voids would suggest a high-flow lesion such as an arteriovenous malformation or a carotid-cavernous fistula, where you would also expect an enlarged superior ophthalmic vein and swollen extraocular muscles. Contact with the periosteum discriminates nothing.

quiz.prompt: A 7-year-old has developed proptosis and downward displacement of the left globe over three weeks. He is afebrile with a normal white cell count. MRI shows a superomedial extraconal soft-tissue mass, intermediate on T2, enhancing avidly, with erosion of the adjacent bone. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Urgent tissue biopsy and staging: this behaves like a malignant lesion
choices: Urgent tissue biopsy and staging: this behaves like a malignant lesion
Intravenous antibiotics and review: this behaves like an orbital abscess
A course of corticosteroids: this behaves like orbital inflammation
Interval imaging at six months: this behaves like a slow malformation
quiz.explain: Rapid painless proptosis in a well child with a bone-eroding extraconal mass is rhabdomyosarcoma until proved otherwise: it is the commonest orbital malignancy of childhood, arises from undifferentiated mesenchyme rather than from the extraocular muscles themselves despite the name, favours the superior and superomedial extraconal compartment, and grows over weeks. It is treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy after biopsy, with orbital preservation the norm, so the job of imaging is to get tissue and stage rather than to plan an exenteration. An abscess would come with fever, sinus disease and a rim-enhancing collection, and it displaces bone rather than destroying it. Idiopathic orbital inflammation is painful and steroid-responsive, and giving steroids blind here obscures the histology, which is the classic way to lose weeks. A lymphatic malformation is long-standing and shows fluid-fluid levels. The other paediatric bone-destroying orbital lesion to hold in mind is metastatic neuroblastoma, typically bilateral, centred on the sphenoid wing, with periorbital bruising.

quiz.prompt: An 18-month-old is referred with a white pupillary reflex on the right. Ultrasound shows an echogenic mass arising from the posterior retina containing foci that shadow, and the globe is of normal size. What imaging should follow, and for what reason?
quiz.answer: MRI of orbits and brain, to seek nerve, choroidal and pineal disease
choices: MRI of orbits and brain, to seek nerve, choroidal and pineal disease
CT of the orbits, to confirm the calcification within the retinal mass
Ultrasound of the opposite eye alone, repeated again in three months
Catheter angiography, to map the ophthalmic arterial supply first
quiz.explain: Shadowing foci in a retinal mass in a toddler with leukocoria are the calcification of retinoblastoma, and ultrasound has already shown them, so CT would add ionising radiation without adding information to a child who may carry a germline RB1 mutation and is therefore at raised lifetime risk of second malignancies. MRI answers the questions that change treatment: post-laminar optic nerve invasion, choroidal and extrascleral extension, the state of the fellow eye, and a pineal or suprasellar primitive neuroectodermal tumour, which makes the disease trilateral. The differential for leukocoria is worth carrying alongside. Coats disease gives exudative subretinal fluid that is bright on T1, in an older boy, without calcification. Persistent fetal vasculature gives a small globe with a stalk running from disc to lens and no calcification. Toxocariasis gives a granuloma with vitreous inflammation. Scanning only the good eye abandons the diseased one, and angiography belongs later, if intra-arterial chemotherapy is chosen.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old was grinding steel without eye protection and now has a painful watering right eye with reduced acuity. The eye clinic has requested an MRI of the orbits to look for a foreign body. What do you do with that request, and why?
quiz.answer: Do not send him to MRI yet. Get orbital CT first, or at least orbital radiographs, to exclude a metallic intraocular foreign body, because a ferromagnetic fragment can be torqued or displaced by the magnet and blind him. CT also shows an open globe and localises the fragment; MRI can follow if the fragment proves non-metallic or none is present.
quiz.explain: The history is the whole item: grinding, striking or hammering metal without protection is the classic mechanism for a small, fast, sometimes painless intraocular foreign body, and it is the standard screening question before any orbital MRI. A ferromagnetic fragment sitting against the retina can rotate or migrate in the static field and cause irreversible damage, so the sequence is imaging that cannot move it first. Thin-section CT is the workhorse: it detects metal and glass reliably, shows globe contour, lens position and intraocular gas, and localises the fragment relative to the sclera for the surgeon. Plain radiographs are an acceptable screen where CT is not available but miss small fragments. Wood and some plastics are poorly seen on CT and are the situation where MRI genuinely helps, but only once metal has been excluded. Do not let the urgency of the visual loss reverse the order; the eye that needs MRI today will still need it in an hour.

quiz.prompt: A patient struck in the eye by a bungee hook has a right globe of reduced volume with an irregular posterior contour, a few tiny locules of gas within the vitreous, and the lens lying dependently in the posterior segment. What does this combination require?
quiz.answer: Urgent surgical exploration, with a rigid shield and no pressure on the eye
choices: Urgent surgical exploration, with a rigid shield and no pressure on the eye
Topical antibiotics, a firm pad over the eye and clinic review tomorrow
Immediate lateral canthotomy to relieve raised intra-orbital pressure
Digital and applanation tonometry to establish the intraocular pressure
quiz.explain: A collapsed, irregular globe, intraocular gas and a dislocated lens are the CT signature of an open globe, and each of the three would raise the question on its own. The management consequence is immediate and mostly about what not to do: nothing may press on the eye, because pressure expresses vitreous, uvea and retina through the wound. So no pad, no tonometry, no forced lid retraction; a rigid shield instead, systemic antibiotics, tetanus cover, antiemetics, nil by mouth and theatre. Reviewing tomorrow risks endophthalmitis, which is the reason repair is measured in hours. Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis is the right answer to a different emergency, the orbital compartment syndrome of retrobulbar haemorrhage, where the globe is tense and tented posteriorly with a hard, proptosed eye. Performing it on an open globe would be actively harmful. Finish the read by looking for an intraocular foreign body and by checking the optic canal and orbital walls.

nodes.title: Paranasal Sinuses: Anatomy, Variants and Disease
nodes.goal: Read a sinus CT the way the endoscopic surgeon needs it read: work out which drainage pathway is blocked, flag the variants that put the skull base, optic nerve, carotid and orbit at risk, and separate inflammatory from neoplastic disease.

quiz.prompt: Coronal CT shows complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus, the right anterior ethmoid cells and the right frontal sinus, with a clear right sphenoid and clear right posterior ethmoid cells. The left side is clear throughout. Where is the obstruction, and what does that imply for treatment?
quiz.answer: The right ostiomeatal complex, which drains those three sinuses
choices: The right ostiomeatal complex, which drains those three sinuses
The right sphenoethmoidal recess, which drains those three sinuses
The right inferior meatus, which drains those three sinuses
The right superior meatus, which drains those three sinuses
quiz.explain: The ostiomeatal complex, meaning the maxillary ostium, the ethmoid infundibulum, the uncinate process, the hiatus semilunaris, the ethmoid bulla and the middle meatus, is the shared final pathway for the maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal sinuses. Block it and exactly this triad opacifies while the posterior ethmoid cells and the sphenoid, which drain to the superior meatus and the sphenoethmoidal recess, stay clear. That is why the pattern of opacification is diagnostic of the level of the obstruction and why the report should describe it as a pathway rather than a list of sinuses. The mirror image, an opaque sphenoid and posterior ethmoid with clear anterior sinuses, sends you to the sphenoethmoidal recess. The inferior meatus receives no sinus at all, only the nasolacrimal duct, so its obstruction causes a watering eye rather than sinusitis. The surgical consequence is that clearing the middle meatus treats three sinuses at once, which is the whole logic of functional endoscopic surgery.

quiz.prompt: A sinus CT shows complete opacification of the left posterior ethmoid cells and the left sphenoid sinus, while the maxillary, frontal and anterior ethmoid sinuses are clear on both sides. Which drainage pathway should you inspect, and where does it lie?
quiz.answer: The left sphenoethmoidal recess. It lies between the superior turbinate and the nasal septum, above and behind the superior meatus, and it receives the sphenoid ostium; the posterior ethmoid cells drain into the adjacent superior meatus, which is why the two opacify together while the ostiomeatal complex sinuses stay clear.
quiz.explain: This is the posterior counterpart of the ostiomeatal pattern, and it is the one most often missed because the sphenoid sits at the edge of the field on coronal images and gets skipped. The recess is a narrow cleft medial to the superior turbinate, and the sphenoid ostium opens into it high on the anterior sinus wall, which is why sphenoid secretions drain badly when the patient is upright and why isolated sphenoid opacification can persist for months. Two things follow. First, isolated sphenoid disease in an adult is never quite routine: it causes vertex or retro-orbital headache rather than facial pain, it sits against the cavernous sinus, the optic nerves and the carotids, and the differential includes fungal disease and neoplasm as well as bacterial sinusitis. Second, the surgical route to the recess passes close to the skull base and the sphenopalatine artery, so your report should describe the recess itself, not just record that the sphenoid is opaque.

quiz.prompt: A pre-operative coronal CT shows the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate measuring 10 mm on the right and 5 mm on the left. By how much does the right measurement exceed the upper limit of Keros type II? Answer in millimetres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The Keros classification grades the depth of the olfactory fossa by the height of the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate: type I is 1 to 3 mm, type II is 4 to 7 mm, and type III is 8 to 16 mm. Ten millimetres exceeds the type II ceiling of 7 mm by 3, and puts the right side in type III. This matters because the lateral lamella is the thinnest bone of the entire anterior skull base, and the deeper the fossa the longer and more exposed that lamella is to an instrument working in the ethmoid roof. Type III therefore carries the highest risk of iatrogenic penetration, cerebrospinal fluid leak and, rarely, intracranial injury. Two further points belong in the report: state the depth on each side separately, because marked asymmetry is itself a hazard and the surgeon may not expect it, and note any asymmetry of the ethmoid roof height, which is a related and equally dangerous variant.

quiz.prompt: On a pre-operative sinus CT the most posterior ethmoid air cell extends above and lateral to the sphenoid sinus, and coronal images show a horizontal septation dividing the two. Which structure is now at particular risk, and what must the report say?
quiz.answer: The optic nerve, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
choices: The optic nerve, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
The internal carotid, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
The infraorbital nerve, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
The vidian nerve, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
quiz.explain: A posterior ethmoid cell pneumatising superolaterally over the sphenoid is the Onodi or sphenoethmoidal cell, and its significance is entirely about the optic nerve. The nerve, normally safely tucked in the lateral wall of the sphenoid, ends up indenting or crossing the wall of this ethmoid cell, sometimes with dehiscent bone over it. A surgeon who believes he is in the last ethmoid cell and is working laterally is then working alongside the optic nerve, and the classic sign on coronal images is exactly the one described: a horizontal septation above the sphenoid, where the sphenoid septation would be vertical. Say it explicitly in the report and say which side. The internal carotid is the structure endangered by the lateral wall of a well-pneumatised sphenoid itself and by a septum inserting on its canal. The infraorbital nerve is put at risk by a Haller cell along the orbital floor, and the vidian nerve runs in the pterygoid canal below the sphenoid floor.

quiz.prompt: The sphenoid sinus is well pneumatised and its intersinus septum runs obliquely to insert on the bony canal of the left internal carotid artery, where the bone appears thinned. A transsphenoidal approach is planned. What should the report emphasise?
quiz.answer: Do not avulse the septum: it is anchored on the carotid canal
choices: Do not avulse the septum: it is anchored on the carotid canal
Do not resect the floor: it is anchored on the vidian canal
Do not open the recess: it is anchored on the optic canal
Do not drill the rostrum: it is anchored on the ethmoid roof
quiz.explain: The sphenoid intersinus septum is very often off-midline and oblique, and when its posterolateral end lands on the carotid canal, twisting or avulsing it during surgery can strip or fracture the thin bone and tear the artery. That is one of the few genuinely lethal complications of endoscopic sinus and pituitary surgery, so the finding earns an explicit sentence rather than a mention among variants. Describe which septum, which side it inserts on, and whether the bone over the carotid looks dehiscent, which on CT means no perceptible cortex over the vessel. Two related observations belong in the same paragraph: how far laterally the sphenoid pneumatises, since pneumatisation into the pterygoid process or greater wing brings the carotid and the maxillary nerve into the operative field, and whether the optic nerve canal is similarly dehiscent. None of the other three combinations described is an anatomical relationship that exists.

quiz.prompt: On a pre-operative CT the right uncinate process attaches superiorly to the lamina papyracea. What does that mean for the drainage of the right frontal sinus, and what does the surgeon need to be told?
quiz.answer: When the uncinate attaches laterally to the lamina papyracea, the ethmoid infundibulum ends blindly above as a terminal recess, so the frontal sinus cannot drain into it; the frontal recess instead drains medial to the uncinate, directly into the middle meatus. Tell the surgeon the frontal outflow is medial to the uncinate, so frontal disease can coexist with a clear infundibulum.
quiz.explain: The superior attachment of the uncinate process decides where the frontal sinus empties, and it varies from patient to patient and sometimes side to side. If the uncinate runs up to the lamina papyracea, the top of the infundibulum is closed off as a blind terminal recess and the frontal recess drains medial to the uncinate straight into the middle meatus. If it attaches instead to the skull base or to the middle turbinate, the frontal recess drains laterally into the infundibulum, and then infundibular disease and frontal disease travel together. The practical consequences are two. Reading: a patient can have an opaque frontal sinus with an entirely clear infundibulum, which is not a contradiction. Operating: the surgeon needs to know which side of the uncinate to look for the frontal outflow, and removing the uncinate blindly in the lateral-attachment pattern risks entering the orbit through the lamina papyracea.

quiz.prompt: Trace the path taken by mucus leaving the maxillary sinus, from its own ostium outwards into the nasal cavity.
quiz.answer: maxillary-ostium ethmoid-infundibulum hiatus-semilunaris middle-meatus
quiz.explain: Mucus leaves the antrum through its ostium high on the medial wall, which is why gravity is no help and mucociliary clearance does all the work. It then travels up the ethmoid infundibulum, the narrow three-dimensional channel bounded medially by the uncinate process and laterally by the lamina papyracea, escapes through the hiatus semilunaris, the crescentic gap between the free edge of the uncinate and the ethmoid bulla, and enters the middle meatus. Every step is a place where a few millimetres of mucosal swelling closes the pathway, which is why maxillary sinusitis is so often a middle meatal problem rather than an antral one. Two variants narrow the route further: a Haller cell hanging from the orbital floor into the roof of the antrum, and a large ethmoid bulla or concha bullosa crowding the hiatus. And an accessory ostium, when present, opens directly into the middle meatus and bypasses the infundibulum altogether, which is the route an antrochoanal polyp usually takes.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has had four months of nasal obstruction and facial pressure. CT shows circumferential mucosal thickening in both maxillary antra, thickened sclerotic bony walls, and no air-fluid levels anywhere. Which conclusion does the study support?
quiz.answer: Long-standing inflammation: sclerotic walls take months to develop
choices: Long-standing inflammation: sclerotic walls take months to develop
Acute bacterial infection: the mucosal thickening is a recent change
Aggressive infiltration: the bone reaction indicates tumour involvement
Post-surgical change: the antral walls remodel after previous surgery
quiz.explain: Reactive thickening and sclerosis of the sinus walls, sometimes called osteitis, is a marker of chronicity: it takes months of persistent inflammation to lay down, and it is the finding that lets you date the disease from a single scan. Acute rhinosinusitis looks different, with air-fluid levels, froth and oedematous mucosa over a normal-calibre bony wall, and in any case is a clinical diagnosis that rarely needs imaging at all; CT in chronic disease is done to map the anatomy for surgery, not to make the diagnosis. Tumour destroys or remodels bone rather than sclerosing it symmetrically and bilaterally, and would produce a unilateral soft-tissue mass, so unilateral is the word that should always slow you down on a sinus CT. Previous Caldwell-Luc surgery does thicken and sclerose an antral wall, but it is unilateral and comes with a defect in the anterior wall or a surgical antrostomy, neither of which is present here.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old has a persistently blocked left nostril. An MRI performed for headache is reported as showing clear sinuses. On review, the left maxillary sinus is markedly dark on T2 and intermediate on T1, with a thin rim of enhancing mucosa around it. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Obtain a CT: markedly T2-dark contents can mimic an aerated sinus
choices: Obtain a CT: markedly T2-dark contents can mimic an aerated sinus
Accept the report: a dark sinus on T2 indicates normal aeration
Obtain a CT: the darkness suggests an aggressive marrow-based tumour
Repeat the MRI with contrast: the enhancing rim needs characterising
quiz.explain: This is the trap that MRI sets in the sinuses. A fungus ball is a dense mat of hyphae with concentrated manganese, iron and magnesium and almost no free water, so it is profoundly hypointense on T2 and can be a true signal void; read alone, the sinus looks aerated, and the only clue is the enhancing mucosal rim that air would not have. CT rescues it immediately, showing hyperattenuating material with punctate or amorphous calcification in a sclerotic, occasionally expanded sinus, usually a single maxillary or sphenoid sinus in an immunocompetent adult. Treatment is endoscopic removal and ventilation, not antifungal drugs. The same physics explains the dark central material of allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, which differs by being multi-sinus, expansile and bone-remodelling in an atopic patient with polyposis and a raised IgE. Very inspissated bacterial secretions can also be T2 dark. The habit to build is simple: never call a sinus clear on MRI alone.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old with acute myeloid leukaemia is neutropenic and has facial pain with a numb right cheek. CT shows only mild mucosal thickening in the right nasal cavity and a little stranding in the fat behind the maxillary sinus; the bone appears intact. What are you worried about, what MRI finding would support it, and what has to happen today?
quiz.answer: Acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis. Infiltration of the periantral fat before any bone destruction is the earliest sign, and on MRI a turbinate that fails to enhance after contrast, the black turbinate of mucosal necrosis, supports it. He needs same-day ENT endoscopy with biopsy, urgent surgical debridement and systemic antifungal treatment, alongside correction of the neutropenia.
quiz.explain: In a neutropenic, transplanted or ketoacidotic patient, facial pain with a numb cheek is an emergency and the CT is characteristically underwhelming. The disease is angioinvasive, so it crosses tissue planes through vessels long before it destroys bone: the first sign is infiltration of the periantral fat, in front of the maxilla or behind it in the retroantral fat, with an intact sinus wall, together with unilateral nasal mucosal thickening. Waiting for bone destruction means waiting for orbital, cavernous sinus and intracranial spread. MRI adds the loss of contrast enhancement in necrotic turbinate mucosa, the so-called black turbinate, and shows perineural and intracranial extension. Mortality is high and falls with hours, not days, so the report should reach the clinician by telephone. Treatment is surgical debridement plus a systemic antifungal, commonly liposomal amphotericin B, together with reversal of the underlying immunosuppression or ketoacidosis; imaging alone never excludes it, and endoscopy with biopsy is the arbiter.

quiz.prompt: A pre-operative sinus CT shows: a right lateral lamella of 9 mm; a posterior ethmoid cell extending superolateral to the sphenoid on the right; the sphenoid intersinus septum inserting on the left carotid canal; a 4 mm dehiscence of the left lamina papyracea with fat bulging medially; a right concha bullosa; and a Haller cell along the right orbital floor. How many of these six findings place the skull base, optic nerve, carotid artery or orbit directly at risk? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Four of the six are hazards that belong in a highlighted paragraph. A 9 mm lateral lamella is Keros type III and exposes the thinnest bone of the anterior skull base. A posterior ethmoid cell reaching superolateral to the sphenoid is an Onodi cell and endangers the optic nerve. A septum landing on the carotid canal endangers the artery if it is twisted out. A dehiscent lamina papyracea with herniating fat endangers the orbit and the medial rectus, and is the variant behind the classic complication of a surgeon following what looks like polyp into orbital fat. The other two are worth reporting but are not in that category: a concha bullosa is a pneumatised middle turbinate that can narrow the middle meatus and may be resected, and a Haller cell narrows the infundibulum and sits near the infraorbital nerve, but neither threatens the four structures named. The discipline this builds is separating the checklist that changes the operation from the anatomy that merely describes it.

quiz.prompt: A 15-year-old boy has recurrent heavy epistaxis and progressive nasal blockage. Contrast CT shows an avidly enhancing mass centred on the right sphenopalatine foramen, widening the pterygopalatine fossa and bowing the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus forwards. What is the correct next step?
quiz.answer: Cross-sectional angiography and embolisation planning, without biopsy
choices: Cross-sectional angiography and embolisation planning, without biopsy
Endoscopic biopsy in clinic to establish the histology before surgery
A trial of intranasal corticosteroids with repeat imaging at 3 months
Simple polypectomy through the nose under local anaesthetic in clinic
quiz.explain: Adolescent male, epistaxis, and a vascular mass at the sphenopalatine foramen that widens the pterygopalatine fossa and bows the posterior maxillary wall forwards, is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. The imaging is characteristic enough that biopsy is avoided: the lesion is fed mainly by the internal maxillary artery, often with ascending pharyngeal and sometimes internal carotid contributions, and a clinic biopsy can produce torrential bleeding. The pathway is cross-sectional angiography to map supply and intracranial extension, pre-operative embolisation, then endoscopic or open resection. Two things to report: how far the tumour reaches into the pterygopalatine fossa and beyond it into the infratemporal fossa or the cavernous sinus region, and any internal carotid supply, which limits how completely it can be embolised. The two lesions this sits between are the antrochoanal polyp, which arises in the antrum, passes through a widened ostium to the choana and enhances only at its rim, and the inverted papilloma, which arises on the lateral nasal wall in middle age.

quiz.prompt: An adenoid cystic carcinoma fills the right nasal cavity. On fat-saturated post-contrast T1 the right pterygopalatine fossa is filled with enhancing tissue and its normal fat has gone. Which structure should you follow next, and what would its involvement mean for the plan?
quiz.answer: Foramen rotundum and the cavernous sinus, along the maxillary nerve
choices: Foramen rotundum and the cavernous sinus, along the maxillary nerve
Stylomastoid foramen and the mastoid, along the facial nerve trunk
Jugular foramen and the cerebellopontine angle, along the vagus nerve
Hypoglossal canal and the tongue base, along the hypoglossal nerve
quiz.explain: The pterygopalatine fossa is the crossroads of the face, and loss of its fat on fat-saturated T1 is the sign that tumour has reached it. Five routes leave it: the foramen rotundum, carrying the maxillary nerve back to Meckel's cave and the cavernous sinus; the pterygoid canal, carrying the vidian nerve towards the petrous carotid; the inferior orbital fissure into the orbit; the pterygomaxillary fissure into the infratemporal fossa; and the palatovaginal canal into the nasopharynx. Adenoid cystic carcinoma has the highest perineural propensity of the sinonasal tumours, and its spread is often discontinuous, so a skip lesion can sit well behind an apparently clean margin. Intracranial extension usually moves the patient out of curative resection and into radiotherapy planning, and it changes the fields. Look for nerve enlargement, enhancement, and foraminal widening on thin coronals. The other three nerves listed have no anatomical connection to this fossa.

nodes.title: Temporal Bone: Anatomy, Trauma and Pathology
nodes.goal: Report a temporal bone study from the anatomy that surgery depends on: separate cholesteatoma from chronic inflammation, grade otosclerosis and fractures by what they predict, work up a cerebellopontine angle mass, and answer the questions a cochlear implant team asks.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old with a foul-smelling discharging ear has a retraction of the pars flaccida on otoscopy. CT shows non-dependent soft tissue filling the lateral epitympanic recess, blunting of the scutum, and erosion of the long process of the incus, with the mastoid opacified. What should the report say, and what must it exclude?
quiz.answer: Cholesteatoma; check lateral canal, tegmen and VII
choices: Cholesteatoma; check lateral canal, tegmen and VII
Granulation tissue; the ossicles would be spared
Tympanosclerosis; expect dense calcified plaques
Congenital cholesteatoma behind an intact drum
quiz.explain: Soft tissue in the middle ear is soft tissue on CT whatever it is made of, so the diagnosis rests on where it sits and what it has destroyed. A mass in the lateral epitympanic recess, medial to the pars flaccida and lateral to the malleus neck, with a blunted scutum, is an acquired pars flaccida cholesteatoma; the long process of the incus, with its precarious blood supply, is usually the first ossicle to go. Granulation tissue and chronic inflammation opacify without eroding bone, and tympanosclerosis appears as dense calcification. The report earns its keep with the complications: erosion of the lateral semicircular canal, which is the commonest labyrinthine fistula and threatens hearing and balance; the tegmen tympani, opening the way to meningitis, temporal lobe abscess or an encephalocele; the tympanic segment of the facial canal; and the sigmoid plate. Say whether the antrum and aditus are involved, as that shapes the operation.

quiz.prompt: Three years after a canal-wall-up mastoidectomy for cholesteatoma, a patient has soft tissue in the mastoid antrum on CT and no way to tell scar from recurrence. Which examination answers the question best?
quiz.answer: Non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI
choices: Non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI
Echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI
Immediate post-contrast T1-weighted MRI
Repeat high-resolution CT in twelve months
quiz.explain: Keratin restricts diffusion; granulation tissue, fluid and fibrous scar do not. That single fact turned second-look surgery from routine into the exception. The technique has to be non-echo-planar, however: echo-planar diffusion suffers badly from susceptibility artefact at the skull base, where bone, air and soft tissue meet, and it misses the small residual pearls that matter. Non-echo-planar sequences give thin sections with far less distortion and reliably show lesions of only a few millimetres, with the caveat that a very small or very early recurrence can still be missed and that bone dust, cholesterol granuloma and wax can occasionally mimic restriction. Delayed post-contrast imaging at around forty-five minutes, where granulation enhances and cholesteatoma does not, is the older approach and is now reserved for problem cases. Repeating CT gains nothing: both tissues have the same attenuation, which is why the question arose.

quiz.prompt: A child with progressive sensorineural hearing loss has a vestibular aqueduct measuring 1.9 mm at its midpoint on axial CT. Using the Valvassori criterion of 1.5 mm at the midpoint, by how much does this exceed the threshold? Answer in millimetres, to one decimal place.
