quiz.explain: One point nine minus one point five is 0.4 mm, which sounds trivial and is not: an enlarged vestibular aqueduct is the commonest imaging finding in a child with sensorineural hearing loss. The Valvassori criterion measures the midpoint against 1.5 mm; the later Cincinnati criteria are more sensitive, taking more than 0.9 mm at the midpoint or more than 1.9 mm at the operculum as abnormal, so quote which you have used. The association to look for is incomplete partition type II, where a normal basal turn accompanies a cystic apex and a dilated vestibule, and the syndromic link is Pendred syndrome with its SLC26A4 mutations, so a thyroid history is relevant. Two practical consequences follow: the hearing loss is characteristically stepwise and provoked by minor head injury, so contact sport is discouraged, and there is a raised risk of a perilymphatic gusher if the ear is implanted.

quiz.prompt: A temporal bone CT after a road collision shows a fracture crossing the vestibule and the basal turn of the cochlea, with a few bubbles of air within the labyrinth. State the two complications you would place first in the report, and why this fracture pattern predicts them.
quiz.answer: Profound sensorineural hearing loss and facial nerve injury come first: a fracture violating the otic capsule tears the membranous labyrinth and commonly runs through the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion, and cerebrospinal fluid leak with meningitis follows close behind.
quiz.explain: The old longitudinal-versus-transverse division described the fracture line; the otic-capsule-sparing versus otic-capsule-violating division describes what the patient loses, which is why it has replaced it in reporting. Violating fractures are much the rarer of the two but carry several times the rate of profound sensorineural deafness, facial palsy, cerebrospinal fluid leak, perilymphatic fistula and meningitis. Pneumolabyrinth, as here, is a direct sign that the labyrinth has been opened. The facial nerve is most often injured at the geniculate ganglion and the labyrinthine segment, so inspect them specifically and say whether the canal is displaced or transected, since immediate complete palsy with a transected nerve may go to exploration while a delayed partial palsy is managed conservatively. Then look at the carotid canal, which if breached demands angiographic assessment, and at the tegmen for an encephalocele.

quiz.prompt: After a lateral blow to the head, a patient has a conductive hearing loss and haemotympanum. CT shows a fracture running along the long axis of the petrous bone, sparing the otic capsule, and on the axial image through the epitympanum the rounded malleus head has separated from the body of the incus. What should the report state?
quiz.answer: Incudomalleolar dislocation causing conductive loss
choices: Incudomalleolar dislocation causing conductive loss
Stapes footplate fixation causing conductive loss
Perilymphatic fistula causing sensorineural loss
Cochlear ossification causing sensorineural loss
quiz.explain: On an axial section through the epitympanum the malleus head and the body of the incus make a shape like a scoop of ice cream on a cone; when the joint separates, the ice cream falls off, and that is what has happened here. Otic-capsule-sparing fractures typically produce conductive loss from haemotympanum, tympanic membrane injury and ossicular disruption, and the incudostapedial joint is the commonest to separate because the incus is anchored least securely of the three ossicles. Say which joint, since it determines the reconstruction. Timing matters as much as the finding: much early conductive loss is blood in the middle ear and resolves, so ossicular surgery waits until the effusion has cleared and the loss has proved persistent. Footplate fixation belongs to otosclerosis, not trauma, and the two sensorineural options require the otic capsule to have been breached, which it has not.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the segments of the facial nerve in the order the nerve passes through them, from the brainstem to the stylomastoid foramen.
quiz.answer: cisternal meatal labyrinthine tympanic mastoid
quiz.explain: The nerve leaves the pontomedullary junction, crosses the cerebellopontine angle as the cisternal segment, runs in the anterosuperior quadrant of the internal auditory canal as the meatal segment, then turns anterolaterally as the labyrinthine segment to the geniculate ganglion, where it gives the greater superficial petrosal nerve and makes its anterior genu. It then runs backwards as the tympanic segment beneath the lateral semicircular canal and above the oval window, turns at the posterior genu into the vertical mastoid segment, gives the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani, and exits at the stylomastoid foramen. Two things follow. The labyrinthine segment is the narrowest and lacks an epineural sheath, which is where a swollen nerve is trapped in Bell's palsy. And mild enhancement of the geniculate, tympanic and mastoid segments is normal, from the perineural venous plexus, so it is enhancement of the cisternal, meatal or labyrinthine segments that should worry you.

quiz.prompt: A 35-year-old woman has progressive conductive hearing loss with a normal tympanic membrane and intact ossicles. High-resolution CT shows a small focus of lucency in the bone immediately anterior to the oval window, with a normal pericochlear capsule. What should be reported, and what does it open the way to?
quiz.answer: Fenestral otosclerosis; stapedotomy becomes an option
choices: Fenestral otosclerosis; stapedotomy becomes an option
Retrofenestral disease with a pericochlear halo
Congenital stapes fixation with a normal capsule
Paget disease of the skull base in its early phase
quiz.explain: The fissula ante fenestram is a narrow cleft of cartilage just anterior to the oval window and is where otosclerosis almost always begins, so a lucent focus there in a young adult with conductive loss and a normal drum is the finding to name. Lucency reflects the active, resorptive otospongiotic phase; later disease sclerose and can become hard to see, which is why a normal CT does not exclude the diagnosis. Retrofenestral disease is the same process spreading around the cochlea to give a lucent halo and a sensorineural component, and the report should state whether it is present because it affects the counselling. Describe the footplate thickness, the patency of the round window, any facial nerve overhanging the oval window and any persistent stapedial artery, since each of these can obstruct or complicate a stapedotomy. Paget disease and osteogenesis imperfecta produce more diffuse skull base change.

quiz.prompt: A 3-year-old deafened by pneumococcal meningitis is being assessed for cochlear implantation. State the single finding on the CT and MRI that would make you telephone the implant surgeon the same day, and why it cannot wait.
quiz.answer: New ossification, or loss of the normal fluid signal, in the basal turn of the cochlea: labyrinthitis ossificans after meningitis obliterates the scala tympani, so implantation becomes urgent before the cochlea closes.
quiz.explain: Post-meningitic labyrinthitis ossificans begins with fibrosis and proceeds to new bone, typically starting in the basal turn near the round window, which is exactly where the electrode array must go. MRI is the more sensitive test early, because loss of the bright fluid signal on high-resolution T2 precedes anything visible on CT; CT then shows the ossification once it is established. Because the window for a straightforward full insertion may close within months, this is one of the few findings in a paediatric hearing assessment that carries genuine urgency, and it can justify implanting sooner or implanting the less affected ear first. The rest of the assessment can proceed at its own pace: cochlear nerve calibre, malformations, facial nerve course, jugular bulb position, mastoid pneumatisation and the state of the middle ear.

quiz.prompt: A child with unilateral profound sensorineural hearing loss has a cochlear nerve canal measuring 0.8 mm on CT, and on the oblique sagittal T2 through the internal auditory canal only three nerves are visible, the anteroinferior quadrant being empty. What does this mean for implantation?
quiz.answer: Cochlear nerve deficiency; implantation may not help
choices: Cochlear nerve deficiency; implantation may not help
A normal variant; proceed to implant that side
Labyrinthitis ossificans; implant the other side
An enlarged vestibular aqueduct; expect a gusher
quiz.explain: The parasagittal T2 through the internal auditory canal is the image the implant team most wants, because it shows the four nerves in cross-section: facial anterosuperiorly, cochlear anteroinferiorly, and the two vestibular nerves behind, separated from the facial nerve by Bill's bar and from the superior compartment by the falciform crest. The cochlear nerve should be at least as thick as the facial nerve; an empty anteroinferior quadrant means it is absent or hypoplastic. The bony cochlear nerve canal corroborates it, with a width below about 1.4 mm widely taken as stenotic. An implant stimulates the cochlear nerve, so without one the result is poor and the discussion turns to an auditory brainstem implant instead. Report both the nerve and the canal, and check the internal auditory canal itself, since a narrow canal often accompanies the deficiency.

quiz.prompt: On CT of a child with sensorineural hearing loss the basal turn of the cochlea is normal but the middle and apical turns are replaced by a single cystic cavity. Taking a normal cochlea as 2.5 turns and the fused cavity as occupying the outer one, how many turns are identifiable? Answer as a number of turns, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: A normal cochlea makes two and a half turns around the modiolus; when the middle and apical turns fail to separate and merge into a single cystic cavity, one turn is lost and one and a half remain. That appearance, with a normal basal turn, is incomplete partition type II, the malformation long known by the eponym Mondini, and it usually travels with a dilated vestibule and an enlarged vestibular aqueduct. It is worth distinguishing from its neighbours. Incomplete partition type I gives a cystic cochlea with no modiolus at all alongside a dilated vestibule, and type III, the X-linked form, has a modiolus that is absent with an otherwise normal outer contour and a markedly widened fundus. Both type I and type III carry a high risk of a perilymphatic gusher at implantation, and type III often needs a specific electrode; type II is generally implanted with good results.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus has a 14 mm avidly enhancing extra-axial mass at the left cerebellopontine angle. It has a component filling and flaring the porus acusticus, makes acute angles with the petrous bone, and has no dural tail; the labyrinthine segment of the facial canal is normal. What is the most likely lesion, and on what grounds?
quiz.answer: Vestibular schwannoma, from the flared porus
choices: Vestibular schwannoma, from the flared porus
Meningioma, from a broad dural attachment
Epidermoid, which would restrict diffusion
Facial schwannoma, tracking to the geniculate
quiz.explain: The centre of gravity is the internal auditory canal and the porus is widened, which is what a vestibular schwannoma does as it grows out of the canal into the angle; the angles with the petrous bone are acute, and there is no dural tail. A meningioma sits eccentric to the canal on a broad dural base with obtuse angles, often with a tail, hyperostosis or calcification, and it may cap the porus without flaring it. An epidermoid does not enhance, insinuates around vessels and nerves, and restricts diffusion, while an arachnoid cyst follows cerebrospinal fluid on every sequence. The lesion always worth excluding before signing off is a facial nerve schwannoma, which is why the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion were inspected: extension there gives it away. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas mean NF2-related schwannomatosis. Record the maximal extrameatal diameter, since surveillance is judged on growth.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows complete opacification of the epitympanum, aditus, antrum and mastoid air cells, while the mesotympanum and protympanum are well aerated and the tympanic membrane is intact. State where the block must be, and the route air normally takes to reach the mastoid.
quiz.answer: The tympanic isthmus is blocked: air normally passes from the eustachian tube through the protympanum and mesotympanum, through the isthmus between the incus body and the tympanic facial nerve into the epitympanum, and then through the aditus into the antrum and mastoid cells.
quiz.explain: Middle ear ventilation is not one cavity filling uniformly; it is a series of narrow doors, and the pattern of opacification tells you which door has shut. Air enters the protympanum from the eustachian tube, crosses the mesotympanum, and reaches the epitympanum through the tympanic isthmus, the slot bounded by the incus body and malleus head laterally and the tympanic segment of the facial nerve medially. From the epitympanum the aditus ad antrum leads to the antrum and thence to the mastoid cells. Selective opacification of everything beyond the isthmus, with an aerated mesotympanum, therefore localises the obstruction precisely, and it is a recognised route to retraction of the pars flaccida and to cholesteatoma in Prussak's space. A blocked eustachian tube, by contrast, opacifies the whole middle ear from the protympanum outwards.

nodes.title: Thyroid Nodules: ACR TI-RADS and What Follows
nodes.goal: Score a thyroid nodule with ACR TI-RADS, decide between aspiration, surveillance and doing nothing, and respond proportionately to a nodule found incidentally on CT, MRI or PET.

quiz.prompt: Ultrasound shows a solid nodule that is hypoechoic, wider-than-tall, with a lobulated margin and a single macrocalcification. Score it using the ACR TI-RADS (2017) point system. Answer as a whole number of points.
quiz.explain: Solid composition scores 2, hypoechoic scores 2, wider-than-tall scores 0, a lobulated or irregular margin scores 2, and a macrocalcification scores 1, giving 7 points. Since TR5 begins at 7 points in the ACR TI-RADS (2017) chart, this is TR5 and needs aspiration at 1.0 cm or more, and follow-up from 0.5 cm. The item worth taking away is that a nodule can reach the highest category without either of the two features people think of as the frightening ones: it is neither taller-than-wide nor speckled with punctate foci. Points accumulate. The other habit to build is scoring composition, echogenicity, shape and margin once each, taking the single highest applicable value in each column, while echogenic foci are scored cumulatively because a nodule may carry more than one kind. Levels run TR1 at 0 points, TR2 at 2, TR3 at 3, TR4 at 4 to 6, and TR5 at 7 or more.

quiz.prompt: A nodule scores 5 points on ACR TI-RADS (2017) and measures 12 mm in its greatest dimension, with no suspicious cervical nodes. By how much would it have to grow before the ACR recommends fine-needle aspiration? Answer in millimetres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Five points is TR4, and the ACR TI-RADS (2017) recommendation for TR4 is aspiration at 1.5 cm or more, with imaging follow-up from 1.0 cm. At 12 mm this nodule is already in follow-up but 3 mm short of the biopsy threshold. Keep the full grid available, because the whole system turns on it: TR1 and TR2 need neither aspiration nor follow-up; TR3 is aspirated at 2.5 cm and followed from 1.5 cm; TR4 is aspirated at 1.5 cm and followed from 1.0 cm; TR5 is aspirated at 1.0 cm and followed from 0.5 cm. Follow-up intervals are years 1, 3 and 5 for TR3, years 1, 2, 3 and 5 for TR4, and annually to five years for TR5. Two caveats. Growth is judged generously, usually 20 per cent in two dimensions with at least 2 mm, because inter-observer measurement error is real. And a suspicious node overrides all of this.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these four echogenic-foci findings in ascending order of the points ACR TI-RADS assigns to them.
quiz.answer: large-comet-tail macrocalcifications peripheral-calcifications punctate-echogenic-foci
quiz.explain: The echogenic foci column runs 0, 1, 2, 3. Large comet-tail artefacts, longer than about a millimetre, score 0 because they are reverberation from inspissated colloid crystals and are a positively reassuring sign, seen in benign colloid nodules. Macrocalcifications score 1: coarse and shadowing, they are mostly degenerative, though they are not innocent and can sit within a papillary or a medullary carcinoma. Peripheral or rim calcification scores 2, and the finding that raises real concern is interruption of the rim with soft tissue extruding beyond it. Punctate echogenic foci score 3, the maximum, because non-shadowing specks correspond to psammoma bodies and are the most specific ultrasound feature of papillary carcinoma. The discrimination that matters at the machine is between a punctate focus and a small comet-tail: turn up the gain, zoom in, and look for the short tail. Getting that one call wrong moves a nodule three points, which is often a whole category.

quiz.prompt: A sonographer asks why ACR TI-RADS gives three points to a taller-than-wide nodule and three to punctate echogenic foci, when a lobulated margin gets only two. Answer her, and say in which plane the shape must be judged.
quiz.answer: Both carry three points because both are highly specific for malignancy even though neither is sensitive: a taller-than-wide nodule has grown across the normal tissue planes rather than along them, which is invasive behaviour, and punctate echogenic foci correspond to the psammoma bodies of papillary carcinoma. Shape is judged on the transverse image, comparing the anteroposterior dimension with the transverse one.
quiz.explain: The point weights in ACR TI-RADS are driven by specificity, not by how often a feature turns up. Benign nodules grow with the grain of the gland and end up wider than they are deep; a nodule taller than it is wide has ignored the tissue planes, which is what invasion looks like on a two-dimensional image. Punctate non-shadowing foci are the sonographic correlate of psammoma bodies, and although they appear in only a minority of papillary carcinomas, they are rarely seen in anything else. A lobulated or irregular margin scores less because it is common, is judged less reproducibly, and occurs in benign hyperplastic nodules too. Two practical notes. Shape is assessed on the transverse plane only, because a nodule can appear taller than wide on a longitudinal image without meaning anything. And an ill-defined margin scores 0 in this system, which surprises people: a fuzzy border proved not to predict malignancy, whereas frank invasion does.

quiz.prompt: A 1.4 cm solid hypoechoic nodule in the right lobe has a smooth border except posterolaterally, where it interrupts the thyroid capsule and a small tongue of tissue lies within the strap muscle. How should the margin be scored, and what does that do?
quiz.answer: Extra-thyroidal extension, 3 points, the highest margin score there is
choices: Extra-thyroidal extension, 3 points, the highest margin score there is
Lobulated or irregular, 2 points, the commonest malignant margin
Ill-defined, 0 points, because the border is simply hard to resolve
Smooth, 0 points, because most of the border is well demarcated
quiz.explain: Margin is scored once, taking the highest applicable value, and definite invasion of tissue beyond the capsule is the top of that column at 3 points in ACR TI-RADS (2017). Do not average around the circumference: one convincing area of extension outranks a smooth remainder. The finding is worth hunting for because it is one of the few sonographic features that changes more than a category. Gross extra-thyroidal extension into strap muscle or beyond alters the operation, the stage and the risk group, so it is worth stating exactly which structure is involved and over what length. Distinguish it from simple capsular abutment, where the nodule touches the capsule without interrupting it, which does not count. An ill-defined margin, meaning a border you cannot resolve, genuinely scores 0 in this system, because it did not predict malignancy in the data the committee reviewed; the concerning border is lobulated or irregular, at 2 points.

quiz.prompt: A registrar has scored a nodule at 3 points and wants to raise it because colour Doppler shows marked central vascularity and shear-wave elastography reads it as stiff. How should the report handle that?
quiz.answer: Report it at 3 points: neither finding is part of the point system
choices: Report it at 3 points: neither finding is part of the point system
Report it at 5 points: each of the two findings adds a point
Report it at 6 points: stiffness carries the same weight as shape
Report it at 4 points: vascularity adds one and stiffness adds none
quiz.explain: ACR TI-RADS deliberately restricted itself to five grey-scale categories. Doppler patterns were left out because intranodular vascularity is common in benign hyperplastic nodules and did not add independent, reproducible value, and elastography was left out because it is machine- and operator-dependent and was not available on every system the system had to work on. Nothing stops you describing either finding in prose; they simply do not move the score, and a score that has been quietly inflated is worse than no score, because the whole point of the system is that two readers reach the same number. Two other exclusions are worth knowing. TI-RADS is for adults; paediatric nodules carry a substantially higher malignancy risk and are managed differently. And it scores the nodule, not the neck: abnormal cervical lymph nodes sit outside the system and override it entirely.

quiz.prompt: A gland contains eleven nodules. Three score 4 points and measure 1.8, 1.6 and 1.1 cm. Two score 3 points and measure 2.9 and 2.6 cm. The remainder score 2 points. Which nodules should be aspirated?
quiz.answer: The 1.8 and 1.6 cm four-point nodules, and no more than those two
choices: The 1.8 and 1.6 cm four-point nodules, and no more than those two
The 2.9 and 2.6 cm three-point nodules, since they are the largest
The three four-point nodules and the two three-point ones as well
The 1.8 cm nodule alone, since one aspirate represents the gland
quiz.explain: Score every nodule separately, then rank by level rather than by size. The three 4-point nodules are TR4, whose aspiration threshold is 1.5 cm, so the 1.8 and 1.6 cm ones qualify while the 1.1 cm one enters surveillance instead. The 2.9 and 2.6 cm nodules are TR3, and they do cross their own 2.5 cm threshold, which is why this looks like five candidates. What settles it is the ACR recommendation that no more than two nodules be aspirated in one gland, choosing those at the highest level, because sampling many nodules multiplies indeterminate cytology and surgery without improving the detection of clinically important cancer. So the TR4 pair is aspirated and the TR3 pair goes to follow-up. Sampling the largest nodule is the reflex worth unlearning: size drives the threshold within a level, never the choice between levels. And one aspirate never speaks for the gland, because each nodule is a separate clone.

quiz.prompt: A 1.3 cm nodule scoring 8 points was aspirated and the cytology returns as Bethesda category I, nondiagnostic, with too few follicular cells. The clinic asks what to do. What do you advise, and what would change that advice?
quiz.answer: Repeat the aspiration under ultrasound guidance rather than accepting the result, aiming at the solid vascularised part of the nodule and away from any cystic component, since a nondiagnostic sample carries no reassurance at all. If a second attempt is again nondiagnostic in a nodule scoring this high, move to diagnostic lobectomy rather than a third pass.
quiz.explain: Bethesda I is not a result, it is a failed test, and the commonest error is to file it as though it were negative. The malignancy risk of the nodule is unchanged by a nondiagnostic sample, so a TR5 nodule remains a TR5 nodule. Repeat sampling under ultrasound guidance resolves most of them, provided the operator targets the solid, vascular portion rather than a cystic or necrotic area, and provided there is on-site adequacy assessment where available. If it fails again, the sonographic suspicion decides: for a high-scoring nodule the route is diagnostic lobectomy, whereas a repeatedly nondiagnostic TR3 nodule can reasonably be watched. The other Bethesda categories that come back to imaging are II, benign, which returns the patient to sonographic surveillance at an interval set by the TI-RADS level, and III, atypia of undetermined significance, which typically leads to repeat aspiration, molecular testing or diagnostic lobectomy rather than to more imaging.

quiz.prompt: A 3.2 cm nodule scoring 8 points was aspirated and the cytology is reported as Bethesda category II, benign. The patient is well and euthyroid. What imaging follow-up should be arranged?
quiz.answer: Ultrasound within a year, with repeat sampling at that same visit
choices: Ultrasound within a year, with repeat sampling at that same visit
No further ultrasound, because benign cytology settles the matter
Ultrasound in five years, matching the cytological risk alone
Immediate surgery, because sonographic risk overrides the cytology
quiz.explain: This is a discordant pair: a strongly suspicious nodule with reassuring cytology. Benign cytology has a low but real false-negative rate, and that rate matters more the higher the sonographic suspicion, partly because a large nodule is easier to miss within. The standard response, set out in the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline for a high-suspicion sonographic pattern with benign cytology, is repeat ultrasound with repeat ultrasound-guided aspiration within 12 months, rather than either discharging the patient or operating. Compare that with a benign result in a TR3 nodule, where a single ultrasound at a longer interval, or discharge, is entirely reasonable. Two habits follow. Always report the TI-RADS level alongside the cytology in your follow-up recommendation, because the pair is what determines the interval. And flag discordance explicitly in the report, since a benign cytology result filed without comment is the usual mechanism by which such nodules are lost to follow-up.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has a 1.4 cm nodule scoring 3 points, which at that size needs neither aspiration nor imaging follow-up. In the right level III chain there is a 12 mm rounded node with no fatty hilum, punctate echogenic foci within it and peripheral vascularity. What does that change?
quiz.answer: The node, not the nodule, becomes the target. A rounded shape, loss of the fatty hilum, punctate echogenic foci and peripheral rather than hilar vascularity describe a metastatic node, and nodal status sits entirely outside the TI-RADS score. Aspirate the node, send a thyroglobulin washout with the cytology, and treat the thyroid nodule as the likely primary regardless of its own points.
quiz.explain: TI-RADS scores a nodule in isolation, and this is the situation in which following it blindly does harm. The nodal features listed are the ones that matter: rounded rather than oval, absent fatty hilum, cystic change, punctate calcification, hyperechoic tissue resembling thyroid, and peripheral or chaotic rather than hilar vascularity. Punctate calcification and cystic change are the most specific of them for papillary carcinoma. When such a node is present, it is the node that is sampled, because it gives both the diagnosis and the stage in one pass, and washout of the needle for thyroglobulin markedly improves sensitivity over cytology alone, particularly in a cystic node. The 3-point nodule is then treated as the presumed primary and imaged carefully for extra-thyroidal extension, and the whole neck is mapped by level for the surgeon. Never let a low nodule score talk you out of a suspicious node.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old having a staging CT for colon cancer is found to have a 1.2 cm low-attenuation nodule in the right thyroid lobe. There is no local invasion and the cervical nodes are normal. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: No dedicated thyroid imaging: it is below the threshold at this age
choices: No dedicated thyroid imaging: it is below the threshold at this age
Dedicated thyroid ultrasound: a nodule of this size warrants scoring
Dedicated thyroid ultrasound and aspiration at the same attendance
Repeat CT of the neck in six months to look for interval growth
quiz.explain: The ACR white paper on incidental thyroid findings sets an age-dependent threshold for working up a nodule seen on CT or MRI: under 35 years, from 1 cm; at 35 and above, from 1.5 cm. At any age, a nodule accompanied by suspicious features on the same study, meaning local invasion or abnormal cervical nodes, is worked up regardless of size. At 62 with a 1.2 cm nodule and a clean neck, this falls below the threshold and the correct recommendation is none. The reasoning is proportionality: incidental thyroid nodules are extremely common, the great majority of the cancers found are indolent papillary carcinomas, and in a patient with colonic malignancy the cascade of ultrasound, aspiration, indeterminate cytology and hemithyroidectomy carries far more certain harm than the nodule does. Note also that repeating a CT characterises nothing: CT cannot assess composition, echogenicity, margin or echogenic foci, so only ultrasound can produce a TI-RADS score.

quiz.prompt: Two patients undergo PET-CT for lymphoma staging. In the first, the whole thyroid takes up FDG uniformly. In the second, a single intense 1.1 cm focus of uptake sits in the left lobe. What should each report recommend?
quiz.answer: Thyroid function tests for the first, and ultrasound for the second
choices: Thyroid function tests for the first, and ultrasound for the second
Ultrasound for the first, and thyroid function tests for the second
Ultrasound for both, since focal and diffuse uptake carry equal risk
Nothing for either, since uptake will settle after lymphoma therapy
quiz.explain: Diffuse thyroidal FDG uptake is almost always chronic autoimmune thyroiditis, and sometimes Graves disease, so it is a biochemical question and not an imaging one: thyroid function tests and antibodies, no ultrasound. Focal uptake is different. Reported malignancy rates for the focal thyroid incidentaloma cluster around a third, considerably higher than for a nodule found incidentally on ultrasound, so it earns a dedicated thyroid ultrasound and a TI-RADS score regardless of size, with aspiration if score and size call for it. Two riders. Avidity itself adds no points; it is a reason to look, not part of the score, and a benign-appearing nodule on ultrasound still carries some residual risk that many would biopsy in this setting. And proportionality applies at the other end too: in a patient with advanced disease and a short life expectancy, doing nothing may be the right answer, and the report should say so rather than leaving it unspoken.

quiz.prompt: A 3.1 cm nodule in the left lobe is anechoic with a thin smooth wall and no solid component, and several bright foci with long comet-tail artefacts drift within the fluid. The patient has no compressive symptoms and a normal TSH. What should be recommended?
quiz.answer: No aspiration and no imaging follow-up, since the nodule scores zero
choices: No aspiration and no imaging follow-up, since the nodule scores zero
No aspiration, but ultrasound at one, three and five years hence
Aspiration now, because the size has crossed 2.5 centimetres
Aspiration now, because the bright foci are worth three points
quiz.explain: Work the columns. Cystic composition scores 0, anechoic scores 0, wider-than-tall scores 0, a smooth margin scores 0, and large comet-tail artefacts score 0, giving a total of 0 points, which is TR1 in ACR TI-RADS (2017). TR1 needs neither aspiration nor follow-up at any size, so the 3.1 cm measurement is irrelevant here; the 2.5 cm threshold belongs to TR3. Aspiration may still be offered for compressive or cosmetic symptoms, but that is a therapeutic drainage and not a diagnostic test, and it is worth saying so in the report so the patient is not sent for cytology by mistake. The feature to get right is the comet tail. A bright focus with a long tapering tail, longer than about a millimetre, is reverberation from colloid crystals and scores 0; a bare non-shadowing speck is a punctate echogenic focus and scores 3. Zoom in and look for the tail before you commit.

nodes.title: Acute Pancreatitis: Revised Atlanta and its Complications
nodes.goal: Classify an episode of acute pancreatitis and its collections by the revised Atlanta criteria, time the CT to the question being asked, and recognise the vascular and infective complications that change management.

quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old man is scanned on day 6 of severe alcohol-related pancreatitis. Contrast-enhanced CT shows the pancreatic body failing to enhance over roughly 40% of the gland, and a heterogeneous collection containing both fluid and fat density tracking into the lesser sac, with no discernible wall. How should this be reported, and what follows from it?
quiz.answer: An acute necrotic collection; it is heterogeneous and unencapsulated, so intervention waits unless infection forces the issue
choices: An acute peripancreatic fluid collection; homogeneous fluid without necrosis, and most of these resolve with supportive care alone
A pancreatic pseudocyst; a mature wall has formed around simple fluid, so an endoscopic cyst-gastrostomy can be planned now
An acute necrotic collection; it is heterogeneous and unencapsulated, so intervention waits unless infection forces the issue
Walled-off necrosis; the necrosis has matured inside a defined capsule, so transmural necrosectomy can be undertaken safely
quiz.explain: The revised Atlanta classification (2012) sorts collections on two axes: does the collection contain necrotic debris, and is it older than four weeks. Heterogeneous content with fat density plus a non-enhancing gland means necrosis, and day 6 is inside the four-week window, so this is an acute necrotic collection. An acute peripancreatic fluid collection is the same age but arises in interstitial oedematous pancreatitis and is homogeneous fluid only. Pseudocyst and walled-off necrosis are the mature, encapsulated counterparts after four weeks. The distinction is not pedantry: a collection without a wall drains badly and tends to leave a persistent fistula, so unless there is infection or obstruction, the discipline is to wait for encapsulation before intervening.

quiz.prompt: A day-4 contrast-enhanced CT in acute pancreatitis shows an enlarged gland with peripancreatic fat inflammatory change but no collection, roughly 40% of the parenchyma failing to enhance, and a left pleural effusion. Score this using the modified CT severity index. Answer in points, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The modified CT severity index scores three things out of ten. Pancreatic inflammation: normal 0, intrinsic pancreatic abnormality with or without peripancreatic fat change 2, a pancreatic or peripancreatic collection or peripancreatic fat necrosis 4. Necrosis: none 0, 30% or less 2, more than 30% 4. Extrapancreatic complications (pleural effusion, ascites, vascular or gastrointestinal involvement) 2. Here that is 2 plus 4 plus 2, so 8 out of 10. The modified index differs from the original Balthazar-based CTSI by collapsing the grades and by adding the extrapancreatic component, which is why it correlates better with length of stay and organ failure. Do not let the score replace the clinical picture: the revised Atlanta severity categories are driven by organ failure, not by a CT number.

quiz.prompt: A patient presents 10 hours after the onset of epigastric pain with a lipase five times the upper limit of normal. The admitting team asks for a contrast-enhanced CT tonight to see how bad it is. What do you tell them, and why?
quiz.answer: Necrosis takes up to 72 hours to declare itself, so a scan this early will underestimate or miss it; unless the diagnosis itself is in doubt or a complication is suspected, delay the contrast CT to 72 to 96 hours after onset.
quiz.explain: Pancreatic necrosis is a perfusion phenomenon that evolves. In the first day the gland can enhance almost normally even when large territories are destined to infarct, so an early scan gives false reassurance and then has to be repeated. The revised Atlanta classification (2012) explicitly ties its collection terminology to time from onset for the same reason. Early CT still has proper indications: genuine diagnostic uncertainty where a perforated ulcer or ischaemic bowel is in the differential, or a patient deteriorating in a way that suggests haemorrhage or a hollow viscus problem. Otherwise the useful scan is at 72 to 96 hours, and severity in the first 48 hours is a clinical and biochemical judgement, not a radiological one.

quiz.prompt: A woman with gallstone pancreatitis becomes hypotensive on the evening of admission and needs 3 litres of fluid; her blood pressure and creatinine are normal again by the following afternoon, some 30 hours after the dysfunction began. She has a peripancreatic collection on day 5. How should the episode be graded, and what does that imply?
quiz.answer: Moderately severe: the organ failure was transient, resolving within 48 hours, and mortality is far lower than with persistent failure
choices: Severe: any documented organ dysfunction defines severe disease, whatever the duration, because it marks a systemic inflammatory response
Moderately severe: the organ failure was transient, resolving within 48 hours, and mortality is far lower than with persistent failure
Mild: dysfunction that corrects with fluid does not count as organ failure, and a collection on its own does not raise the grade
Severe: the peripancreatic collection is a local complication and it upgrades the episode independently of the organ failure course
quiz.explain: The revised Atlanta classification (2012) has three severity grades. Mild means no organ failure and no local or systemic complications. Moderately severe means transient organ failure that resolves within 48 hours, or a local complication such as a collection, or exacerbation of comorbid disease. Severe means persistent organ failure lasting beyond 48 hours. Organ failure itself is defined by a modified Marshall score of 2 or more in the respiratory, renal or cardiovascular system, so a blood pressure that responds to fluid is still counted while it lasts; the discriminator is duration, not whether it responded. This matters because persistent organ failure, especially when combined with infected necrosis, is where the mortality sits, and it is the trigger for critical care escalation and transfer to a pancreatic unit.

quiz.prompt: Symptoms began on day 0. A CT on day 26 shows a necrotic collection with a partially formed, incomplete wall. How many further days must elapse before the revised Atlanta terminology permits the report to say walled-off necrosis? Answer in days, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The revised Atlanta classification (2012) sets the boundary at four weeks from symptom onset, which is day 28, so from day 26 there are two days to go. Two cautions. First, the clock starts at symptom onset, not at admission or at the first scan, and patients often present late; take the history rather than the ward round date. Second, four weeks is necessary but not sufficient: walled-off necrosis also requires a mature, well-defined enhancing wall completely encircling the heterogeneous content. A day-40 collection with an incomplete rind is still best described as an evolving acute necrotic collection. Getting this right is what tells the endoscopist whether a lumen-apposing metal stent has something to seat against.

quiz.prompt: Three weeks into necrotising pancreatitis a patient drops his haemoglobin by 30 g/L and his known peripancreatic collection has enlarged and become denser. What scan do you ask for, what are you looking for, and what is the treatment?
quiz.answer: An arterial-phase CT angiogram, looking for a pseudoaneurysm, most often of the splenic artery, bleeding into the collection; the treatment is catheter angiography with embolisation.
quiz.explain: Enzyme-rich fluid digests the wall of an adjacent artery and a pseudoaneurysm forms; the splenic artery is the classic culprit, with the gastroduodenal and pancreaticoduodenal arteries next. Bleeding into a collection or into the gut through the duct produces exactly this picture: falling haemoglobin, a collection that grows and becomes hyperdense. A portal venous phase alone can miss it or make it look like a mural nodule, so the request must specify an arterial phase; a small pseudoaneurysm follows the aortic attenuation on arterial images and fades on delayed ones. Treatment is endovascular embolisation, which is both quicker and safer than operating in an inflamed field. Do not drain such a collection percutaneously until the vessel has been dealt with.

quiz.prompt: Six weeks after necrotising pancreatitis, CT shows a non-opacified splenic vein, a patent portal vein, and prominent gastric fundal and short gastric collaterals. The patient is well and has never bled. What should you advise?
quiz.answer: Report sinistral portal hypertension with gastric varices, note the bleeding risk, and reserve splenectomy for those who actually bleed
choices: Report the finding and recommend immediate splenectomy, since gastric varices from this cause bleed in the great majority of patients
Report the finding and recommend lifelong anticoagulation, which reliably recanalises the vein and makes the collaterals regress
Report sinistral portal hypertension with gastric varices, note the bleeding risk, and reserve splenectomy for those who actually bleed
Regard the collaterals as an incidental finding, since portal vein patency means that gastric varices in this setting carry no bleeding risk
quiz.explain: Peripancreatic inflammation thromboses the splenic vein, and splenic outflow reroutes through the short gastric and gastroepiploic veins into the gastric fundus. That produces isolated gastric varices with a normal portal pressure, which is why it is called left-sided or sinistral portal hypertension. Most patients never bleed, so prophylactic splenectomy is not justified; the operation is curative in the minority who do bleed, because removing the spleen removes the inflow. Anticoagulation is a debated option in acute, extensive splenic or portal vein thrombosis, particularly where the mesenteric axis is threatened, but it does not dependably recanalise a chronically occluded splenic vein. The one thing you must not do is stay silent: the endoscopist needs to know why the fundal varices are there.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a large walled-off necrosis at week 5 has new fever and rising inflammatory markers. CT shows several small gas locules within the collection. There has been no drain, no endoscopy and no gastrointestinal instrumentation. What do you conclude and recommend?
quiz.answer: Gas here indicates infected necrosis; recommend sampling and culture-directed antibiotics with a planned drainage pathway
choices: Gas is expected within maturing necrosis; recommend supportive care alone, with a repeat scan in a fortnight to reassess the collection
Gas indicates a fistula to the stomach or duodenum; recommend an urgent water-soluble contrast study before anything else
Gas mandates immediate open necrosectomy; recommend theatre today because delay in this setting is what drives mortality
Gas here indicates infected necrosis; recommend sampling and culture-directed antibiotics with a planned drainage pathway
quiz.explain: In an untouched collection, extraluminal gas is the one CT finding that is close to specific for infection. Everything else, including size, wall thickness and the patient's temperature, is suggestive at best, which is why fine-needle aspiration is still used where the picture is ambiguous. Two caveats keep you honest: a drain, a transmural stent or recent endoscopy puts gas in a collection innocently, and a spontaneous fistula to the gut can do the same, so the history matters more than the pixels. Sterile necrosis does not need antibiotics, and prophylactic antibiotics in necrotising pancreatitis have not been shown to help. Infection changes the plan to drainage, but it does not by itself mean an operation today.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the step-up management of infected walled-off necrosis from the first measure to the last resort.
quiz.answer: culture-directed-antibiotics catheter-drainage minimally-invasive-necrosectomy open-necrosectomy
quiz.explain: The step-up approach exists because primary open necrosectomy carried a punishing rate of organ failure, fistula and death. Antibiotics directed by culture come first and buy time for the collection to wall off. If the patient does not improve, the next step is drainage: percutaneous, ideally by a left retroperitoneal route that can later be upsized, or endoscopic transmural drainage through the stomach or duodenum. Roughly a third of patients need nothing further. If sepsis persists after several days, the existing tract is used for minimally invasive necrosectomy, either video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement or endoscopic necrosectomy through the stent. Open surgery is reserved for failure of that pathway or for abdominal catastrophe such as perforation or uncontrolled bleeding. The other principle is patience: delay intervention beyond four weeks where the patient allows it.

quiz.prompt: A woman admitted with pancreatitis has gallstones on ultrasound, a common bile duct of 9 mm, and a bilirubin that has risen over 24 hours. She is afebrile with no rigors and is otherwise improving. What is the right next imaging or intervention step?
quiz.answer: MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound to look for a retained duct stone, with ERCP reserved for cholangitis or persisting obstruction
choices: Urgent ERCP tonight with sphincterotomy, because a dilated duct after gallstone pancreatitis is an indication in its own right
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen tonight, which is the most sensitive test available for a stone in the distal bile duct
MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound to look for a retained duct stone, with ERCP reserved for cholangitis or persisting obstruction
No further duct imaging, and list her for cholecystectomy in three months once the pancreatic inflammation has fully settled
quiz.explain: Imaging in gallstone pancreatitis has to answer three questions: is the cause biliary, is a stone still obstructing, and is the gallbladder coming out. Ultrasound answers the first. For the second, MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are the accurate non-invasive tests; CT is poor at distal duct stones because many are not calcified. ERCP is a treatment, not a screening test, and its clear indications are cholangitis and persistent biliary obstruction, where early ERCP improves outcome. A rising bilirubin without fever or rigors is an equivocal picture that deserves MRCP or EUS first. The third question is the one juniors forget: in mild gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy on the index admission markedly reduces recurrence, and deferring it for months invites a second, worse attack.

quiz.prompt: You are supervising the first ultrasound in a patient admitted overnight with acute pancreatitis of unknown cause. What must that scan answer, and what decision hangs on each answer?
quiz.answer: Whether there are gallstones in the gallbladder, and whether the common bile duct is dilated or contains a stone; the first decides index-admission cholecystectomy, the second decides whether MRCP, EUS or ERCP is needed.
quiz.explain: Ultrasound in acute pancreatitis is not there to look at the pancreas, which is usually obscured by bowel gas and unhelpful in the first day anyway. It is there to settle aetiology and biliary obstruction, because those are the two findings that change what happens next. Stones in the gallbladder mean the patient needs cholecystectomy, ideally on the same admission for a mild attack. A dilated common bile duct, or a visible duct stone, moves the patient towards MRCP, endoscopic ultrasound, or straight to ERCP if there is cholangitis. Note the trap of the normal-calibre duct: a stone can pass and leave the duct entirely normal, so a normal ultrasound never excludes a biliary cause when the alanine transaminase is high.

quiz.prompt: Seven weeks after an episode of interstitial oedematous pancreatitis, a well patient has a 6 cm round collection anterior to the pancreatic body with homogeneous fluid content, a thin enhancing wall and no debris. She eats normally and is not jaundiced. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: Describe a pseudocyst and recommend observation, since an asymptomatic collection of this kind needs no drainage on size alone
choices: Describe walled-off necrosis and recommend endoscopic drainage, since encapsulated collections at this stage should be evacuated
Describe a pseudocyst and recommend observation, since an asymptomatic collection of this kind needs no drainage on size alone
Describe a mucinous cystic neoplasm and recommend resection, since a thin-walled unilocular cyst in a woman is neoplastic
Describe a pseudocyst and recommend drainage, since a collection above 5 cm at six weeks will rarely resolve on its own
quiz.explain: Homogeneous fluid, a defined wall and a preceding episode of interstitial rather than necrotising pancreatitis give a pseudocyst under the revised Atlanta classification (2012); by contrast walled-off necrosis contains heterogeneous solid debris, best appreciated on MRI or endoscopic ultrasound when CT looks deceptively simple. The old teaching that pseudocysts above 6 cm or older than 6 weeks must be drained has not survived; the indications now are symptoms, gastric or biliary obstruction, infection or growth. The differential worth pausing over is a mucinous cystic neoplasm or a branch-duct IPMN that caused the pancreatitis in the first place, so if the history of a genuine attack is thin, or there are septations, mural nodularity or peripheral calcification, do not label it a pseudocyst by assumption.

nodes.title: Appendicitis and its Mimics
nodes.goal: Choose the right first test for suspected appendicitis, judge the equivocal appendix on ultrasound and CT, recognise perforation and what it changes, and separate appendicitis from the conditions that share the right iliac fossa.

quiz.prompt: During graded compression ultrasound of the right iliac fossa a tubular structure is found at the caecal pole. Under gentle, progressive pressure it flattens completely, peristalsis is seen passing along it, and no blind end can be demonstrated. What follows from these three observations?
quiz.answer: This is small bowel rather than the appendix, and the search for a blind-ending tube should continue.
choices: This is small bowel rather than the appendix, and the search for a blind-ending tube should continue.
This is a normal appendix, and the study can be reported as having excluded acute appendicitis.
This is an inflamed appendix that has decompressed after perforating into the adjacent pelvis.
This is a mesenteric node imaged in its long axis, and the finding supports mesenteric adenitis.
quiz.explain: Three features identify the appendix and all three are needed: it ends blindly, it does not peristalse, and it arises from the caecal pole where the taeniae converge. A tube that peristalses is small bowel, and calling it a normal appendix is how a false negative is manufactured. Graded compression is the technique that makes the search possible — steady, increasing pressure with the linear probe displaces gas-filled bowel out of the field and brings the appendix closer, which both improves resolution and tests compressibility. The inflamed appendix is non-compressible, aperistaltic, over 6 mm outer-to-outer, often with an echogenic hyperaemic halo of inflamed fat around it. A perforated appendix may indeed decompress, but it does not acquire peristalsis. Nodes are ovoid with an echogenic hilum, not tubular in continuity along their length.

quiz.prompt: On graded compression ultrasound a blind-ending, aperistaltic, non-compressible tube arises from the caecal pole. Measured in true cross section, the near wall is 2.1 mm, the lumen 4.6 mm and the far wall 2.1 mm. Give the outer-to-outer diameter in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 2.1 plus 4.6 plus 2.1 gives 8.8 mm. The measurement that matters is outer wall to outer wall in a true transverse section, not the lumen and not an oblique cut through a curving appendix, both of which mislead. The conventional upper limit of normal is 6 mm, but the threshold behaves poorly on its own: a normal appendix can distend to 7 mm with gas or faecal material, and diameters between 6 and 8 mm are a genuine grey zone in which secondary signs decide — non-compressibility, mural hyperaemia on colour Doppler, an appendicolith, echogenic inflamed periappendiceal fat, and focal tenderness under the probe. At 8.8 mm with non-compressibility the diagnosis is secure. Beware the opposite error too: pressing too hard flattens the measurement and can talk you out of a real appendicitis.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old woman has had right iliac fossa pain for 30 hours. Ultrasound is careful and prolonged, but the appendix is not seen; there is no free fluid, no enlarged nodes and no echogenic fat. Write the conclusion you would put in the report, and say what happens next.
quiz.answer: Report that the appendix was not visualised, that this does not exclude appendicitis, and that the absence of secondary signs makes it less likely. If pain persists, proceed to CT - or MRI if she turns out to be pregnant - or re-examine clinically within a few hours.
quiz.explain: A non-visualised appendix is a common and honest result, and the report must say plainly that it is not a negative study. The causes are worth knowing because several are correctable: a retrocaecal or deep pelvic position, overlying gas, obesity, guarding that defeats compression, a perforated appendix that has decompressed, and inexperience with the technique. What softens the result is the complete absence of secondary signs — no free fluid, no echogenic fat, no nodes, no tenderness under the probe — which lowers the probability but never to zero. The next step depends on the patient in front of you: CT in a non-pregnant adult whose pain persists or whose inflammatory markers are rising, MRI in pregnancy, and structured clinical reassessment where the story is settling. What is not acceptable is a conclusion that reads as though appendicitis has been excluded.

quiz.prompt: CT in a 38-year-old man with two days of vague right-sided pain shows an appendix of 7 mm outer diameter, filled with gas along its whole length, with a thin wall, no periappendiceal stranding and no free fluid. What is the most defensible report?
quiz.answer: A borderline calibre appendix, gas-filled throughout with no periappendiceal change, argues against appendicitis.
choices: A borderline calibre appendix, gas-filled throughout with no periappendiceal change, argues against appendicitis.
A 7 mm appendix exceeds the accepted threshold, so acute appendicitis should be diagnosed and surgery advised.
Gas within the appendiceal lumen indicates perforation here, and urgent surgical exploration should be advised.
The study is uninterpretable at this calibre, and magnetic resonance imaging should be arranged the same day.
quiz.explain: Diameter alone is the weakest of the CT criteria. A normal appendix distended with gas or faecal material commonly measures 6 to 8 mm, so a 7 mm appendix is not a diagnosis. What resolves the equivocal case is the company it keeps. Against appendicitis: gas or oral contrast passing along the full length of the lumen, a thin non-enhancing-thickened wall, and clean surrounding fat. In favour: mural thickening beyond about 3 mm, mural hyperenhancement, periappendiceal fat stranding, an appendicolith, thickening of the caecal apex funnelling towards the base, and adjacent free fluid. Intraluminal gas is reassuring rather than alarming; extraluminal gas is the perforation sign. Reporting an equivocal appendix well means saying which secondary signs you looked for and did not find, so the clinician can weigh it against the patient.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old girl has right iliac fossa pain. Ultrasound shows a compressible 4 mm blind-ending tube at the caecal pole, mild terminal ileal wall thickening, and three ileocolic nodes with short-axis diameters of 4 mm, 6 mm and 8 mm. Using a short-axis threshold of 5 mm, how many of these nodes count as enlarged? Answer as a whole number, with no units.
quiz.explain: Two nodes — those of 6 mm and 8 mm — meet a 5 mm short-axis threshold. A commonly used working definition of mesenteric adenitis asks for three or more right iliac fossa nodes of at least 5 mm in short axis together with a normal appendix, sometimes with mild ileal or caecal wall thickening, so on this study the label is not fully earned even though the picture fits. That nuance matters less than the discipline behind it: nodes are non-specific, they are common in children and they are frequently present in appendicitis itself, so enlarged nodes never exclude an inflamed appendix. The finding that carries the weight here is the appendix — compressible, 4 mm, blind-ending — which is a genuinely normal appendix. Always measure nodes in short axis; long-axis measurements make reactive nodes look pathological.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old boy with a high body mass index has right-sided abdominal pain. CT shows a 7 cm heterogeneous, whorled fat-density mass lying between the ascending colon and the anterior abdominal wall, without a hyperattenuating rim, and a normal gas-filled appendix. What should be recommended?
quiz.answer: Conservative management with analgesia, since an omental infarct of this kind resolves without antibiotics or surgery.
choices: Conservative management with analgesia, since an omental infarct of this kind resolves without antibiotics or surgery.
Laparoscopy and excision, because a fatty mass of this size will not resolve and risks progressing to an abscess.
Antibiotics for a contained appendiceal phlegmon, with interval appendicectomy planned about six weeks later.
Staging CT of the chest and pelvis, since a fat-containing mesenteric mass of this size suggests a liposarcoma.
quiz.explain: Omental infarct and epiploic appendagitis are the two self-limiting fat lesions that imitate appendicitis and diverticulitis, and CT separates them confidently. Omental infarct is the larger of the two, typically over 5 cm, heterogeneous and whorled, sited between the colon and the anterior abdominal wall — most often on the right — and it is disproportionately a disease of children and of obese adults. Epiploic appendagitis is smaller, oval, under about 5 cm, with a thin hyperattenuating rim and sometimes a central dot representing a thrombosed vein, and it hugs the colonic serosa, usually the sigmoid. Neither needs antibiotics or an operation; both settle over weeks with analgesia. The normal appendix here rules out the phlegmon option. Liposarcoma is a mass with nodular soft tissue components in a patient without acute pain, not an inflamed omental fat lesion of sudden onset.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old man of East Asian background has right iliac fossa pain and tenderness. CT shows a normal, gas-filled 5 mm appendix, and a single inflamed outpouching arising from the caecum with focal adjacent wall thickening and pericolic stranding. What should the report advise?
quiz.answer: Solitary caecal diverticulitis: treat medically, since appendicectomy would not address the inflamed segment.
choices: Solitary caecal diverticulitis: treat medically, since appendicectomy would not address the inflamed segment.
Early appendicectomy, because the appendix is unreliably assessed on CT once the caecum is inflamed.
Right hemicolectomy, because focal caecal wall thickening at this age usually indicates a carcinoma.
Percutaneous drainage, because caecal diverticulitis nearly always harbours a drainable collection.
quiz.explain: Right-sided diverticulitis is clinically indistinguishable from appendicitis — same site, same age group, same tenderness — and it is relatively more common in patients of East and South-East Asian descent, in whom the diverticula tend to be solitary, true and right-sided. CT settles it by showing an inflamed outpouching with surrounding stranding and a demonstrably normal appendix. Most cases respond to antibiotics and supportive care, and the value of making the diagnosis before the operation is that it avoids a needless appendicectomy or, worse, an over-extensive resection of an inflamed caecum that the surgeon cannot distinguish from a tumour at the table. Carcinoma does deserve consideration when the wall thickening is asymmetric and shouldered rather than centred on a diverticulum, particularly in older patients — but at 32, with a visible inflamed diverticulum, medical treatment with later colonic assessment is the proportionate advice.

quiz.prompt: CT in a 29-year-old shows a dilated appendix with a focal defect in its enhancing wall, a 4.5 cm rim-enhancing pelvic collection containing gas, and a calcified body lying outside the appendiceal lumen. Say what has happened, and how it changes management.
quiz.answer: The appendix has perforated: there is a wall defect, an extraluminal appendicolith and a periappendiceal abscess. A collection of this size is generally managed with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage rather than immediate appendicectomy, with interval surgery considered afterwards.
quiz.explain: The signs of perforation on CT are a focal defect in the enhancing appendiceal wall, extraluminal gas, an extraluminal appendicolith and a rim-enhancing collection; a phlegmon is the same process without a drainable cavity. The distinction changes the operation rather than the diagnosis. A well-formed abscess of a few centimetres or more is usually treated first with antibiotics and image-guided percutaneous drainage, because immediate appendicectomy in a hostile, inflamed right iliac fossa carries a higher complication rate and sometimes forces a caecal resection. A phlegmon or small collection is treated with antibiotics alone. Interval appendicectomy afterwards is a matter of local policy and patient factors. Report the extraluminal appendicolith explicitly: one left behind after drainage is a recognised cause of recurrent abscess, and the surgeon needs to know it is there.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old with three months of loose stool has right iliac fossa pain. CT shows 20 cm of terminal ileum with mural thickening and layered enhancement, engorged vasa recta combed along the mesenteric border, fibrofatty proliferation, and a normal appendix. What should follow?
quiz.answer: Refer to gastroenterology for ileocolonoscopy with biopsy, and consider MR enterography to map disease extent.
choices: Refer to gastroenterology for ileocolonoscopy with biopsy, and consider MR enterography to map disease extent.
Refer for urgent appendicectomy, since terminal ileal change at this site is secondary to appendiceal inflammation.
Treat as infective ileitis with antibiotics alone, and repeat the CT at six weeks to confirm that it has resolved.
Arrange a barium follow-through as the definitive investigation before any endoscopic or cross-sectional imaging.
quiz.explain: A long segment of terminal ileum with mural stratification, engorged vasa recta along the mesenteric border and proliferation of the surrounding fat, in a young patient with months of diarrhoea, is ileocolic Crohn disease until proven otherwise. Diagnosis is made by endoscopy and histology, and the imaging job afterwards is mapping — MR enterography for disease length, activity, strictures, fistulae and abscesses, which spares a young patient repeated CT over decades of follow-up. Infective ileitis from Yersinia, Campylobacter or Salmonella can look identical on a single acute study, which is precisely why the history and the endoscopy matter rather than a repeat scan. Barium studies have been superseded for this indication. The normal appendix in a case like this is a finding to report positively, since it is what keeps the patient off the emergency list.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the imaging tests for suspected appendicitis in a 20-week pregnant woman in the order they should be attempted.
quiz.answer: ultrasound MRI CT
quiz.explain: Ultrasound comes first: no ionising radiation, immediately available, and in the first two trimesters graded compression still reaches the appendix in a useful proportion of women. As the uterus enlarges the appendix is displaced upwards and laterally and the success rate falls. MRI is second, performed without gadolinium, and it is very good at this question: an appendix above about 7 mm with wall thickening, periappendiceal fluid or high signal in the surrounding fat supports the diagnosis, while a normal appendix below 6 mm filled with gas is reassuring. CT is third rather than forbidden. The dose from a limited abdominopelvic study is well below the level associated with deterministic fetal injury, and a perforated appendix carries a far greater risk to the pregnancy than the scan. The pathway must keep moving to a decision.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old woman has sudden right iliac fossa pain and vomiting. Ultrasound shows a 6 cm oedematous right ovary with follicles displaced to the periphery and a twisted vascular pedicle, and a normal appendix. Arterial flow is still detectable within the ovary. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Refer for emergency gynaecological surgery, since detectable arterial flow does not exclude ovarian torsion.
choices: Refer for emergency gynaecological surgery, since detectable arterial flow does not exclude ovarian torsion.
Reassure and rescan in 24 hours, since detectable arterial flow makes ovarian torsion improbable here.
Treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease, and arrange outpatient follow-up imaging in two weeks.
Proceed to contrast-enhanced CT, which is considerably more sensitive than ultrasound for this diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Preserved arterial flow is the classic trap in ovarian torsion. The ovary has a dual supply from the ovarian and uterine arteries, torsion is often intermittent and partial, and venous outflow fails before arterial inflow does — so Doppler can look deceptively normal in a torted ovary. The diagnosis rests on the grey-scale findings: a unilaterally enlarged oedematous ovary, follicles pushed to the periphery by stromal oedema, an abnormal position of the ovary near the midline or above the uterus, a whirlpool of the twisted pedicle, and often a lead-point cyst or dermoid. Salvage depends on how fast detorsion happens, so this is a telephone call, not a routine referral. CT may be the study that happens to be done first in an undifferentiated abdomen, but ultrasound with Doppler is the test of choice, and a normal appendix does not close the case.

quiz.prompt: A 64-year-old man has CT-proven acute appendicitis. At the appendiceal base the caecal wall is asymmetrically thickened over about 3 cm with a shouldered margin, and there are two 8 mm pericolic nodes. State what you must add to the report, and why.
quiz.answer: Recommend colonoscopy after recovery, or interval imaging: appendicitis in an older patient may be caused by a caecal or appendiceal tumour obstructing the appendiceal orifice, and asymmetric shouldered caecal thickening with nodes is suspicious.
quiz.explain: Appendicitis is a disease of luminal obstruction, and in a patient over about 50 the thing doing the obstructing may be a neoplasm — a caecal carcinoma at the appendiceal orifice, or a mucinous neoplasm of the appendix itself. The clue is that the findings extend beyond what appendicitis alone explains: asymmetric caecal wall thickening with shouldered margins rather than symmetrical funnelling of the caecal apex, a soft tissue mass at the base, disproportionate lymph nodes, or a distended mucin-filled appendix with mural calcification. The report should name the concern and recommend colonoscopy or CT after the acute episode has settled, because that recommendation is often the only thing that carries the patient into a cancer pathway. Saying only 'acute appendicitis' in this situation is technically true and clinically incomplete.

quiz.prompt: A slim, cooperative 7-year-old boy has 18 hours of right iliac fossa pain and a raised C-reactive protein. Which pathway exposes him to the least harm while still answering the question?
quiz.answer: Ultrasound first, reserving CT or MRI for the child whose appendix is not seen and whose pain persists.
choices: Ultrasound first, reserving CT or MRI for the child whose appendix is not seen and whose pain persists.
Contrast-enhanced CT first, since ultrasound is too operator dependent to be relied upon in children.
Serial clinical review without imaging, since imaging seldom changes management in a child of this age.
MRI as the first test, since out-of-hours access to MRI matches ultrasound in most district hospitals.
quiz.explain: Children are the ideal ultrasound patients: thin abdominal walls, little intervening fat, and a short distance to the appendix, so a competent operator visualises it in a high proportion of cases. Radiation risk is also at its most consequential in a long life expectancy, which makes ultrasound first the right default. The pathway must not stall there, though. If the appendix is not seen and the child stays symptomatic, the options are a repeat ultrasound in experienced hands, MRI where it is genuinely available and the child will lie still, or CT. Withholding CT from a deteriorating child in order to avoid a dose is a false economy — perforation, abscess and sepsis are the greater harm. Out-of-hours MRI access is rarely comparable to ultrasound, which is why it cannot be the standing first test.

nodes.title: Biliary Obstruction, Stones and the Thickened Gallbladder
nodes.goal: Investigate a tender or jaundiced right upper quadrant, state the level and likely cause of biliary obstruction, and separate the inflamed gallbladder from the merely thick-walled one.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old with right upper quadrant pain has gallstones and a common bile duct of 9 mm on ultrasound, but the distal duct is obscured by duodenal gas. Bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are raised. State the next investigation you would recommend, and why.
quiz.answer: MRCP, because ultrasound is insensitive for stones in the distal common bile duct where duodenal gas obscures it; a dilated duct with obstructive liver tests needs direct imaging of the duct before cholecystectomy.
quiz.explain: Ultrasound is excellent for stones in the gallbladder — sensitivity comfortably above 90 per cent for a mobile shadowing echogenic focus — and poor for stones in the duct, where reported sensitivity is around half or less. The reason is anatomical: the retroduodenal and intrapancreatic segments lie behind gas-filled bowel, and small stones bathed in bile may not shadow at all. So a duct that is dilated with obstructive biochemistry is an indication for direct duct imaging, not for repeating the ultrasound. MRCP is the usual first choice; endoscopic ultrasound is more sensitive for stones under 5 mm where it is available, and ERCP is reserved for treatment rather than diagnosis. CT is a poor stone test, because many calculi are cholesterol-predominant and isodense with bile.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old with no previous biliary surgery has an incidentally noted common bile duct. Using the common convention that the upper limit of normal is 6 mm at 60 years and rises by 1 mm for each subsequent decade, calculate the upper limit for this patient. Answer in millimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Two decades beyond 60 adds 2 mm to the 6 mm baseline, giving 8 mm. Treat this as a convention rather than a law: the duct does tend to widen with age as its wall loses elastin, but the number is a reporting aid, and it should always be read alongside the liver enzymes and the symptoms. A duct at the upper limit in an asymptomatic patient with normal biochemistry rarely repays pursuit, while a 6 mm duct with a rising bilirubin certainly does. Two further adjustments matter in practice. After cholecystectomy the duct takes over some reservoir function and up to about 10 mm may be normal. And opiates cause sphincter of Oddi spasm, so a duct measured on a patient who has just had morphine can be transiently wide. Measure inner wall to inner wall, perpendicular to the duct, at the porta.

quiz.prompt: A patient is scanned after an appropriate period of fasting and the gallbladder is distended. Above what anterior gallbladder wall thickness, measured on ultrasound, is the wall conventionally regarded as thickened? Answer in millimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Three millimetres is the conventional upper limit, measured on the anterior wall, in a fasted and therefore distended gallbladder. Measure anteriorly because the posterior wall is degraded by through-transmission and reads falsely thick. The fasting condition carries most of the practical weight: a gallbladder that has contracted after a meal has a thick, layered wall as a matter of physiology, and this is the single commonest reason for a spurious call. Remember too that wall thickness on its own is a weak sign. It thickens in heart failure, hypoalbuminaemia, cirrhosis, hepatitis, renal failure and pancreatitis, none of which are surgical. What gives a high positive predictive value for acute cholecystitis is the combination — stones, a thickened wall, pericholecystic fluid, and above all a sonographic Murphy sign elicited by the probe over the visualised gallbladder.

quiz.prompt: A 72-year-old diabetic with four days of pain has a distended gallbladder containing stones, a thick wall with hypoechoic striations, sloughed intraluminal membranes, and a negative sonographic Murphy sign. What should you report and recommend?
quiz.answer: Gangrenous cholecystitis; the negative Murphy sign is not reassuring, and urgent surgical review is needed
choices: Gangrenous cholecystitis; the negative Murphy sign is not reassuring, and urgent surgical review is needed
Chronic cholecystitis; the negative Murphy sign makes acute inflammation unlikely at this presentation
Gallbladder carcinoma; recommend a staging CT and referral to the hepatobiliary multidisciplinary team
Adenomyomatosis; the intramural findings are Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses and no intervention is needed
quiz.explain: The trap sits in the negative Murphy sign. In gangrenous cholecystitis the wall is necrotic and its innervation destroyed, so focal tenderness is often lost — precisely in the patients who are sickest. Diabetes, age and analgesia compound this. The findings that make the diagnosis are the striated, heterogeneous wall, intraluminal membranes from sloughed mucosa, focal wall defects, and, on CT or contrast-enhanced ultrasound, segments of wall that do not perfuse. It matters because gangrene multiplies the risk of perforation and death and pushes management towards urgent cholecystectomy, or a percutaneous cholecystostomy if the patient is too unwell for theatre. Adenomyomatosis produces comet-tail reverberation from crystals in intramural sinuses in a gallbladder that is not tender, and carcinoma produces focal irregular solid thickening with invasion of the liver interface rather than membranes.

quiz.prompt: An unwell diabetic man has a CT showing curvilinear gas within the gallbladder wall, a few gas bubbles in the lumen, and pericholecystic fat stranding. Write what you would say when you telephone the surgical team.
quiz.answer: This is emphysematous cholecystitis, with gas in the gallbladder wall from gas-forming organisms; it carries a high risk of gangrene and perforation, so it needs immediate antibiotics and urgent cholecystectomy or percutaneous cholecystostomy.
quiz.explain: Gas in the wall means gas-forming organisms — commonly Clostridium perfringens or Escherichia coli — growing in an ischaemic gallbladder. The associations are diabetes and male sex, and roughly half the cases have no stones at all. Mortality is several times that of ordinary calculous cholecystitis and perforation is far more likely, so this is a telephone call, not a report line. Ultrasound is treacherous here: intramural gas produces bright echoes with dirty shadowing and ring-down that can be mistaken for a stone-packed gallbladder or overlying bowel, and if the lumen cannot be resolved at all the correct move is a CT rather than a confident report. Two look-alikes to keep separate. Porcelain gallbladder is mural calcification, dense and cleanly shadowing, with none of the dirty reverberation. Pneumobilia is central and branching, following the ducts towards the hilum.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient on day 12 of an intensive care admission after major burns develops a rising bilirubin. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a 6 mm wall and pericholecystic fluid, no stones, and sedation prevents any Murphy sign being elicited. What is the most appropriate course?
quiz.answer: Treat as acalculous cholecystitis; consider cholescintigraphy and percutaneous cholecystostomy
choices: Treat as acalculous cholecystitis; consider cholescintigraphy and percutaneous cholecystostomy
Attribute the findings to hypoalbuminaemia; no biliary imaging or intervention is warranted
Arrange MRCP to exclude a common bile duct stone before any biliary drainage is considered
Arrange urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy, since medical management is contraindicated here
quiz.explain: Acalculous cholecystitis is a disease of the critically ill — burns, sepsis, major trauma, prolonged parenteral nutrition, mechanical ventilation — driven by bile stasis and gallbladder wall ischaemia, and it gangrenes and perforates more readily than calculous disease. The difficulty is that intensive care itself produces every individual finding: hypoalbuminaemia and positive-pressure ventilation thicken the wall, fluid overload gives pericholecystic fluid, and fasting distends the gallbladder. So the diagnosis is a judgement built on the whole picture, supported where needed by cholescintigraphy showing non-filling of the gallbladder at 60 minutes with morphine augmentation, or by a wall perfusion defect on CT or contrast-enhanced ultrasound. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is frequently chosen over surgery because these patients tolerate anaesthesia and laparotomy badly, and drainage buys time for the underlying illness to be treated.

quiz.prompt: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis and gross ascites has a 7 mm gallbladder wall, no stones, no tenderness over the gallbladder, and normal liver enzymes. Explain what you would report and why.
