quiz.answer: Report the wall thickening as non-specific, most likely secondary to hypoalbuminaemia, ascites and portal hypertension rather than cholecystitis, since there are no stones, no focal tenderness and no obstructive biochemistry.
quiz.explain: A thick gallbladder wall is a finding, not a diagnosis, and the list of causes that are not cholecystitis is long: the physiologically contracted post-prandial gallbladder, hypoalbuminaemia of any cause, right heart failure and raised central venous pressure, cirrhosis and portal hypertension, acute hepatitis, renal failure, pancreatitis, adenomyomatosis and carcinoma. In cirrhosis the wall is thick for two reasons at once — low oncotic pressure and venous congestion — and Doppler may show varices within it. What should raise suspicion instead is focal rather than diffuse thickening, an irregular solid component, loss of the interface with adjacent liver, and internal vascularity, all of which point at gallbladder carcinoma. Writing this out matters: an unqualified line about a thickened wall in a cirrhotic patient generates surgical referrals and occasionally an operation that nobody needed.

quiz.prompt: A non-tender gallbladder has a focally thickened fundal wall containing tiny echogenic foci, each throwing a narrow V-shaped reverberation artefact that widens away from the transducer. There are no stones and no pericholecystic fluid. What should you conclude?
quiz.answer: Adenomyomatosis; the artefacts arise from crystals within Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses and it is benign
choices: Adenomyomatosis; the artefacts arise from crystals within Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses and it is benign
Chronic cholecystitis; the echogenic foci are tiny calculi embedded within a fibrotic scarred wall
Gallbladder carcinoma; focal fundal thickening of this kind warrants urgent staging and biopsy
Emphysematous cholecystitis; the artefacts arise from small volumes of gas within the gallbladder wall
quiz.explain: Comet-tail or ring-down artefact from cholesterol crystals lodged in intramural diverticula is close to diagnostic of adenomyomatosis, and MRI confirms it with the string of tiny T2-bright intramural cystic spaces sometimes described as a pearl necklace. It occurs in fundal, segmental and diffuse forms, it is benign, and it does not itself require cholecystectomy. Two cautions carry forward. Segmental adenomyomatosis creates an hourglass gallbladder whose narrowed segment can hide a coexisting carcinoma, so look carefully at both compartments. And focal thickening that is solid and vascular, without the cystic spaces or the comet tails, deserves suspicion rather than reassurance — MRI settles most of these. Stones shadow cleanly and darkly rather than ringing down; gas produces dirty shadowing and sits non-dependently, moving as the patient turns.

quiz.prompt: MRCP performed after a previous endoscopic sphincterotomy shows two rounded signal voids within the common bile duct. Both lie along the anterior, non-dependent wall, and both bloom on the gradient-echo sequence. What is the correct interpretation?
quiz.answer: Air bubbles introduced at sphincterotomy: non-dependent position and blooming distinguish them from stones
choices: Air bubbles introduced at sphincterotomy: non-dependent position and blooming distinguish them from stones
Two calculi: rounded filling defects within an instrumented duct should be treated as stones until disproved
Flow artefact from the right hepatic artery crossing the duct and producing a rounded signal void
Surgical clips from the earlier cholecystectomy, projected over the duct on the coronal acquisitions
quiz.explain: Pneumobilia is the classic MRCP mimic after sphincterotomy, a biliary-enteric anastomosis or stent placement. Two features separate it from a stone. Gas rises to the non-dependent surface — anterior in a supine patient — while a stone falls to the dependent wall; and gas blooms on gradient-echo sequences because of its susceptibility effect, whereas a stone does not. If real doubt persists, gas is unmistakable on CT. Other MRCP traps are worth carrying: pulsation of the right hepatic artery crossing the common hepatic duct makes a linear void, susceptibility from clips or a metal stent can obliterate a whole segment of duct, stones under about 5 mm are readily missed, and a calculus impacted at the ampulla can be mistaken for normal distal tapering. When the clinical suspicion is strong and MRCP is negative, endoscopic ultrasound is the more sensitive next step.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these levels of the biliary tree in order from within the liver towards the duodenum, as used when stating the level of an obstruction.
quiz.answer: intrahepatic-ducts hilar-confluence common-hepatic-duct common-bile-duct ampulla
quiz.explain: Stating the level narrows the differential more sharply than almost any other sentence in a biliary report, because the cause tracks the level. Intrahepatic and hilar obstruction, with dilated intrahepatic ducts and a collapsed, empty gallbladder, points to a hilar cholangiocarcinoma, to nodal disease at the porta, or to metastatic compression. Obstruction below the insertion of the cystic duct allows the gallbladder to distend, which is the anatomical basis of the old observation that a palpable, painless gallbladder in a jaundiced patient favours malignancy over stones. Distal and ampullary obstruction dilates both the bile duct and the pancreatic duct, which is where the double duct sign comes from. So work down the tree on the coronal images, find the last normal-calibre segment, and say where the transition is and whether it is abrupt or tapered.

quiz.prompt: A jaundiced 70-year-old has dilatation of both the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct, with an abrupt cut-off of both at the pancreatic head, and no visible calculus. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: A pancreatic head or ampullary tumour until proven otherwise; pancreatic protocol CT and MDT referral
choices: A pancreatic head or ampullary tumour until proven otherwise; pancreatic protocol CT and MDT referral
Chronic pancreatitis with a benign stricture; recommend a repeat MRCP in six months to reassess
A common bile duct stone that has already passed; recommend ERCP with sphincterotomy and clearance
Primary sclerosing cholangitis; recommend colonoscopy and serial liver function testing thereafter
quiz.explain: The double duct sign in a jaundiced older patient carries a high probability of pancreatic head adenocarcinoma, and next of ampullary or distal bile duct carcinoma. Chronic pancreatitis can produce it too, but usually with parenchymal calcification, a beaded and irregular pancreatic duct, and a long history. The essential point is that the sign obliges dedicated imaging even when no mass is visible, because a proportion of small head tumours are isoattenuating to pancreas on portal venous phase images alone. That means a pancreatic protocol CT with a late arterial pancreatic parenchymal phase and a portal venous phase, and endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle sampling where the CT remains negative. Read the morphology of the cut-off as well: abrupt and shouldered is the malignant pattern, whereas a smooth gradual taper over a centimetre or two favours a benign stricture.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have a stricture of the distal common bile duct. In the first the duct narrows over about 2 cm with a smooth gradual taper; in the second it stops abruptly with an irregular shouldered margin and there is subtle adjacent soft tissue. State what you conclude in each case and what you would do next.
quiz.answer: The smooth gradual taper favours a benign stricture — post-inflammatory, post-operative or from chronic pancreatitis — and can go to ERCP with brushings and follow-up; the abrupt shouldered narrowing with soft tissue favours malignancy and needs pancreatic protocol CT, endoscopic ultrasound with biopsy, and MDT referral.
quiz.explain: Stricture morphology is one of the few reliably discriminating observations in biliary imaging. Benign strictures are the product of diffuse fibrosis and taper gradually with preserved, concentric mucosal contour; the usual causes are chronic pancreatitis, previous surgery or instrumentation, ischaemia after transplantation, IgG4-related disease and passed stones. Malignant strictures are the product of a growing mass and end abruptly, with irregular shouldered margins, asymmetry, a long segment of involvement, associated periductal soft tissue and enhancement, and often upstream ductal wall thickening. Neither pattern is absolute, and brush cytology has poor sensitivity, so a persistent stricture with a negative brushing is not cleared — repeat sampling, cholangioscopy or resection may still be needed. State the length, the margin, and the presence or absence of enhancing soft tissue, because those three data points drive the next decision.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old with ulcerative colitis has MRCP showing multifocal short strictures with intervening mildly dilated segments throughout the intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts. Two years later one stricture has lengthened and there is now 2 cm of enhancing periductal soft tissue with new upstream dilatation. What should you report?
quiz.answer: Suspected cholangiocarcinoma arising in sclerosing cholangitis; urgent MDT review and tissue sampling
choices: Suspected cholangiocarcinoma arising in sclerosing cholangitis; urgent MDT review and tissue sampling
Progression of sclerosing cholangitis alone; continue annual MRCP and liver function monitoring
Recurrent bacterial cholangitis; recommend a course of antibiotics and repeat imaging in six weeks
Secondary sclerosing cholangitis from ischaemia; correlate with the state of the hepatic artery
quiz.explain: Primary sclerosing cholangitis produces the beaded pattern — multifocal short strictures alternating with normal or mildly dilated segments, plus pruning of the peripheral intrahepatic branches — and MRCP has displaced diagnostic ERCP for making the diagnosis. The reason these patients are imaged repeatedly is the substantial lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma, which typically arises at a dominant stricture. So a stricture that lengthens, acquires enhancing periductal soft tissue, or causes new upstream dilatation must be treated as malignant until sampled. Brush cytology has poor sensitivity here, so cholangioscopy, repeat sampling, FISH and serial CA19-9 are all used alongside imaging. Ascending cholangitis is common in these patients and produces duct wall thickening and enhancement, periportal oedema and sometimes small hepatic abscesses, but it does not create a focal enhancing periductal mass at a single site.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain has a CT showing thickened enhancing bile duct walls, periportal oedema, patchy ill-defined arterial hyperenhancement of the liver, and a calculus impacted in the distal common bile duct. The blood pressure is 85/50. What does the report need to drive?
quiz.answer: Urgent biliary decompression by ERCP, alongside resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics
choices: Urgent biliary decompression by ERCP, alongside resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics
Elective ERCP on the next available list, once the blood cultures have been reported
Percutaneous drainage of the hyperenhancing hepatic areas, which are developing abscesses
Urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy with operative cholangiography and peritoneal washout
quiz.explain: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain make Charcot's triad; add hypotension and confusion and it becomes Reynolds' pentad, meaning suppurative cholangitis in an obstructed duct. The imaging signs are circumferential duct wall thickening and enhancement, periportal oedema, patchy transient hepatic arterial hyperenhancement from inflammatory hyperaemia, and sometimes small abscesses. The patchy enhancement is perfusion change and there is nothing there to drain. What alters mortality is decompression within hours — ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction, or percutaneous transhepatic drainage if ERCP fails or the anatomy forbids it — so the report should name the obstruction, its level and its cause, and say that drainage is urgent. Cholecystectomy is deferred until sepsis is controlled. The Tokyo Guidelines 2018 grade severity, and organ dysfunction of this kind is grade III, the group in whom delay is least survivable.

nodes.title: Bowel Ischaemia and Wall Thickening Patterns
nodes.goal: Separate the four mechanisms of bowel ischaemia on CT, read wall thickening and enhancement against the phase you acquired, and decide when intramural gas means the patient needs an operation tonight.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old in atrial fibrillation has abdominal pain far out of proportion to a soft abdomen. CT angiography shows a sharply marginated filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery about 5 cm beyond its origin. The proximal jejunal branches and the middle colic opacify normally, the aorta is smooth with little calcification, and the mid ileal loops are thin-walled and barely enhance. What does that configuration point to?
quiz.answer: Embolus beyond the first branches, so the proximal jejunum is spared
choices: Embolus beyond the first branches, so the proximal jejunum is spared
Ostial thrombosis on plaque, so collaterals should have been visible
Low-flow ischaemia with a patent artery, so no clot will be retrieved
Venous outflow block, so the arterial defect is a timing artefact
quiz.explain: The level of the defect is the whole message. An embolus travels until the calibre steps down, which is typically a few centimetres beyond the origin and beyond the first jejunal branches and often the middle colic, so the proximal jejunum and the transverse colon are spared while the mid gut infarcts. Thrombosis behaves differently: it forms on an ostial plaque in a heavily calcified aorta, in a patient who has usually had months of post-prandial pain and weight loss, and by the time it occludes there are collaterals to see, through the arc of Riolan and the marginal artery. Low-flow ischaemia leaves the artery patent, so there is nothing to retrieve. Venous occlusion thickens the wall rather than thinning it. The distinction is operative: an embolus is taken out through the artery, whereas ostial thrombosis needs stenting or a bypass, and the surgeon plans differently for each.

quiz.prompt: Two patients arrive within the hour, both with infarcting bowel. In the first, the ileal loops are dilated, paper-thin and hypoenhancing, with almost no mesenteric fluid. In the second, the loops are thick-walled and layered, the mesenteric fat is oedematous and there is free fluid. What accounts for the difference in wall thickness?
quiz.answer: Arterial cut-off thins the wall; venous obstruction floods it with oedema
choices: Arterial cut-off thins the wall; venous obstruction floods it with oedema
The first is earlier in its course; both will look identical by day two
The second is inflammatory rather than ischaemic; look for an enteritis
Wall thickness follows the segment involved, not the vessel obstructed
quiz.explain: Thickening needs a delivery route. When the artery is cut off, nothing arrives: the wall loses tone, the loop dilates, and the wall becomes thin and unenhancing, which is why a paper-thin loop is one of the most ominous findings in the abdomen rather than a reassuring one. When the vein is obstructed, arterial inflow continues against a blocked outflow, so plasma and blood are driven into the wall and the mesentery: marked stratified thickening, mesenteric fat oedema, engorged vessels and ascites. Time modifies this but does not abolish it, because an arterial occlusion that reperfuses will then thicken and hyperenhance, which is a different appearance again and one worth naming in the report. The practical habit is to read wall thickness and the state of the mesentery together, and to ask which vessel would produce both.

quiz.prompt: On the unenhanced series a segment of ileal wall measures 64 HU. On the portal venous phase the same segment measures 71 HU, while an adjacent normal loop rises from 32 HU to 96 HU. By how many Hounsfield units does the abnormal segment enhance? Answer in Hounsfield units, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Seven Hounsfield units is not enhancement, it is noise. The adjacent loop, acquired in the same breath and at the same circulation time, gains 64 HU, which is the internal control that makes the comparison trustworthy: absolute mural attenuation depends on injection rate, cardiac output and phase, so a remembered number is a poor referee while the loop next door is an excellent one. Notice too that the 64 HU baseline is itself a finding. Wall that is already dense before contrast contains blood, and intramural haemorrhage is the signature of venous occlusion or reperfusion injury. Had the unenhanced series been omitted, the 71 HU wall could easily have been read as enhancing normally, and the diagnosis would have been missed twice over.

quiz.prompt: To save dose, your department proposes reducing the protocol for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia to a single portal venous acquisition. Name the findings that a dropped unenhanced series would cost you, and say what each would be mistaken for.
quiz.answer: Intramural or mesenteric haemorrhage, which on a single portal venous series is read as wall enhancement, and mural or vascular calcification and hyperdense thrombus in the vessel wall, which vanish once the lumen and vessels are opacified.
quiz.explain: A dense bowel wall after contrast has two explanations, and only the unenhanced series separates them: a wall that was already dense contains blood, and a wall that was not contains contrast. Getting this backwards inverts the diagnosis, since intramural haemorrhage belongs to venous occlusion, strangulation or reperfusion, whereas true hyperenhancement suggests inflammation or an early reperfused segment. The same series carries the vascular calcium that tells you whether an ostial defect sits on chronic plaque, and hyperdense thrombus in the mesenteric vein, both of which disappear once the lumen opacifies. The accepted protocol therefore acquires unenhanced, arterial and portal venous phases; the dose argument is real, but the phase to negotiate away is not the unenhanced one.

quiz.prompt: Thirty-six hours after a cardiac arrest, a 62-year-old on high-dose noradrenaline develops a rising lactate and a distended abdomen. CT shows a patent superior mesenteric artery and vein with no filling defect, branch vessels alternately narrowed and dilated, and thick-walled, poorly enhancing right colon and distal ileum. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Correct the shock and cut the vasopressors; consider an intra-arterial vasodilator
choices: Correct the shock and cut the vasopressors; consider an intra-arterial vasodilator
Take the patient for surgical embolectomy of the superior mesenteric artery
Start therapeutic anticoagulation for an occult mesenteric venous thrombosis
Treat this as an infective colitis, since the mesenteric vessels are patent
quiz.explain: This is non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia: splanchnic vasoconstriction in a low-output state, seen after cardiac arrest or cardiac surgery, in dialysis patients and with vasopressor or digoxin use. The vessels are patent, which is precisely why there is nothing to embolectomise, and the branch calibre alternates because the vasoconstriction is segmental. The treatment is haemodynamic: raise cardiac output, restore volume, withdraw the vasoconstrictor if the blood pressure allows, and in selected patients infuse a vasodilator such as papaverine into the superior mesenteric artery. Anticoagulation treats a clot that is not there. The trap is that the patient looks like every other unwell intensive care patient and the CT has no dramatic occlusion to point at, so the diagnosis rests on the pattern plus the physiology. Laparotomy is reserved for peritonitis or established infarction, and mortality remains high.

quiz.prompt: A 60-year-old with iron deficiency anaemia has two abnormal segments. One is 4 cm of jejunum with eccentric, homogeneous soft tissue thickening, abrupt shouldered margins and no layering. The other is a long ileal segment with symmetrical thickening and a low-attenuation middle layer. What should each be reported as?
quiz.answer: Short shouldered segment neoplastic; long stratified segment oedematous
choices: Short shouldered segment neoplastic; long stratified segment oedematous
Short shouldered segment ischaemic; long stratified segment neoplastic
Both segments neoplastic, one infiltrative and the other polypoid
Both segments oedematous, the shorter one simply less distended
quiz.explain: Two questions do most of the work: how long is it, and is the wall layered? Preserved stratification, with a water-attenuation middle layer between an enhancing mucosa and an enhancing serosa, means fluid has entered an intact wall, which is oedema from inflammation, ischaemia, venous congestion or hypoalbuminaemia, and it argues strongly against tumour. Tumour replaces the wall rather than swelling it: short, eccentric, homogeneous soft tissue, abrupt shoulders, loss of layering, sometimes with nodes or upstream obstruction. Length matters because infiltrating processes tend to be long and neoplasms short, with the notable exception of lymphoma, which can involve a long segment and dilate rather than obstruct it, replacing the muscularis and its nerve plexus. So a long aneurysmal segment with lost layering is not reassurance, it is a lymphoma until proven otherwise.

quiz.prompt: The middle layer of a thickened colonic wall measures about -40 HU. Say what that layer is made of and what it tells you about how long this disease has been present.
quiz.answer: It is fat laid down in the submucosa, a marker of long-standing disease such as chronic inflammatory bowel disease, so it is not an acute finding and does not support a diagnosis of acute ischaemia.
quiz.explain: Negative attenuation is the discriminator. In the target or halo pattern of acute disease the middle layer is water attenuation, roughly 0 to 20 HU, because it is oedema. At around -40 HU the submucosa contains fat, which takes time to accumulate: it is seen in long-standing ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, and also without any bowel disease at all in obesity, after steroids, after transplantation, and in the normal rectum and caecum of some patients. So it is a chronicity marker rather than a diagnosis, and its practical value is defensive. When an acutely unwell patient has a thickened colon with a fatty submucosa, some of that thickening predates today, and calling acute ischaemia on wall thickness alone would be an error.

quiz.prompt: Two patients have intramural gas. The first is a 70-year-old on chemotherapy, systemically well, with bubbly cystic gas in the descending colon wall, no portal or mesenteric gas and a normal lactate. The second is shocked, with linear gas in the wall of a dilated non-enhancing ileal segment, branching lucency at the liver periphery and gas in the mesenteric veins. How should they be handled?
quiz.answer: The first can be observed and treated medically; the second needs urgent surgery
choices: The first can be observed and treated medically; the second needs urgent surgery
Both need laparotomy, because intramural gas indicates a breached mucosa
Both can be observed, because intramural gas is a poor predictor of outcome
The first needs laparotomy for perforation risk; the second is drug-related
quiz.explain: Intramural gas is a sign, not a diagnosis, and the company it keeps decides its meaning. Bubbly, cystic, submucosal gas in a comfortable patient is the benign end: pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis, chemotherapy and immunosuppression, steroids, chronic lung disease, connective tissue disease, recent endoscopy, or bowel proximal to a stenosis. Linear or curvilinear gas following the contour of a loop that does not enhance, in a shocked and acidotic patient, is transmural infarction. Portal venous gas obeys flow, so it appears as fine branching lucency within a couple of centimetres of the liver capsule, which is what separates it from pneumobilia sitting centrally near the hilum. Portal gas alone is not a death sentence either, since it follows endoscopy and severe gastric distension, but portal gas with mural hypoenhancement and rising lactate is.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old with a previous appendicectomy has a U-shaped, fluid-filled dilated ileal segment, radially converging mesenteric vessels and a whirl of twisted mesentery. To call this a closed loop rather than a simple obstruction, how many transition points must you identify at the same site? Answer with a whole number.
quiz.explain: A closed loop is a segment obstructed at two adjacent points by a single lesion, most often an adhesive band, a hernia neck or a volvulus, so the two transitions lie side by side and can be within a centimetre of each other. Finding both is what converts a description of dilated bowel into a surgical emergency, because the same twist that closes the loop catches its mesentery, and venous return fails inside a compartment that cannot decompress in either direction. The supporting signs are the C-shaped or U-shaped loop, beaks at each transition, radially converging vasa recta, the whirl of twisted mesenteric vessels, and disproportionate fluid within the closed segment. A closed loop with impaired mural enhancement goes to theatre even when the patient looks comfortable, because the abdomen lags behind the bowel.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the events of a strangulating closed-loop obstruction in the order they occur.
quiz.answer: venous-outflow-occlusion mural-oedema-and-haemorrhage arterial-inflow-failure transmural-infarction
quiz.explain: The sequence explains everything you see. Thin-walled veins collapse first at the twisted neck, while the thicker-walled artery keeps delivering, so blood and plasma are pushed into a wall that cannot drain: mural thickening, high attenuation from haemorrhage on the unenhanced series, mesenteric fat oedema, engorged vasa recta and fluid in the mesentery. Rising interstitial pressure then defeats arterial inflow, and only at that point does the wall stop enhancing and the bowel begin to die. This is why the earliest CT signs of strangulation are mesenteric, not mural, and why a thick dense wall early and a thin unenhancing wall late can both be strangulation at different hours of the same illness. Reading enhancement without reading the mesentery loses the early window, which is the only window that saves bowel.

quiz.prompt: A hypotensive patient has segmental colonic wall thickening from the splenic flexure to the mid descending colon, with a normal rectum. Explain why that distribution is expected, and say what you would reconsider if the rectum were involved too.
quiz.answer: The splenic flexure is the watershed between the superior and inferior mesenteric territories and fails first in low flow, while the rectum has a dual supply that includes branches of the internal iliac and is usually spared, so rectal involvement argues against simple arterial ischaemia and towards infection, an inflammatory colitis, or occlusion low in the aorta or iliac vessels.
quiz.explain: Ischaemic colitis follows perfusion boundaries. The splenic flexure sits where the superior and inferior mesenteric territories meet, and the rectosigmoid junction sits where the inferior mesenteric supply meets the internal iliac branches, so both are vulnerable when flow falls. The rectum escapes because it draws on the middle and inferior rectal arteries from the internal iliac as well as the superior rectal artery, which is a genuinely dual supply. That escape is diagnostically useful: a thickened rectum in a hypotensive patient should send you looking for pseudomembranous or infective colitis, an inflammatory bowel disease, radiation change, or a low aortic or bilateral iliac occlusion, rather than accepting the ischaemic label. The corollary is that ischaemic colitis is usually segmental with an abrupt normal boundary, so pancolitis is also a reason to think again.

quiz.prompt: In an 80-year-old, ischaemic colitis involves the caecum and ascending colon rather than the left colon, and CT angiography shows ostial disease of the superior mesenteric artery. What does the right-sided distribution change?
quiz.answer: It carries a worse outcome and a higher chance of needing surgery
choices: It carries a worse outcome and a higher chance of needing surgery
It usually resolves faster because the right colon is thin walled
It makes an embolic source unlikely and suggests a venous cause
It runs the same course as left-sided disease and changes nothing
quiz.explain: Left-sided ischaemic colitis is usually a mucosal insult in a watershed, resolves with supportive care, and is often managed without a surgeon in the room. Isolated right colonic ischaemia is a different disease: it lies in the superior mesenteric territory, so it keeps company with small bowel ischaemia, with proximal arterial occlusion, and with the low-flow states of dialysis and cardiac failure. It carries a substantially higher rate of colectomy and death, so it justifies imaging the mesenteric vessels and involving surgery early rather than treating conservatively and reviewing in the morning. The other options invert the point: a thin wall does not aid recovery, and an arterial cause becomes more likely, not less, when the right colon alone is affected.

nodes.title: Bowel Obstruction, Closed Loop and Volvulus
nodes.goal: Establish whether bowel is mechanically obstructed, find and explain the transition point, recognise closed-loop obstruction and the signs of strangulation, and tell the surgeon what changes the timing of the operation.

quiz.prompt: A supine abdominal radiograph shows the widest small bowel loop at 3.6 cm, the transverse colon at 5.2 cm and the caecum at 11.0 cm. Using the conventional 3 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm upper limits of normal, how many of these three measurements are abnormal? Answer as a whole number, with no units.
quiz.explain: Two: the small bowel at 3.6 cm and the caecum at 11.0 cm. The transverse colon at 5.2 cm is within normal limits. The 3/6/9 rule — 3 cm for small bowel, 6 cm for colon, 9 cm for caecum — is a crude but durable bedside aid, and the caecal figure is the one that carries urgency. By Laplace's law, wall tension rises with radius, so the caecum, the widest and thinnest-walled segment, is where an obstructed colon perforates first, typically without any warning from the pain score. A caecum beyond about 12 cm is widely treated as demanding decompression. Radiographic measurement is approximate: magnification, projection and overlapping loops all distort it, so confirm on CT, where you can also assess wall enhancement and look for the cause.

quiz.prompt: CT in a 58-year-old woman with vomiting shows dilated fluid-filled jejunum and proximal ileum to 3.8 cm, collapsed distal ileum and colon, and an abrupt calibre change in the right iliac fossa with no mass, no hernia and no wall thickening at that point. She had an appendicectomy at 15. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: Adhesive small bowel obstruction with a right iliac fossa transition point and no current signs of strangulation.
choices: Adhesive small bowel obstruction with a right iliac fossa transition point and no current signs of strangulation.
Small bowel ileus, since an abrupt calibre change without a visible mass is not evidence of mechanical obstruction.
An obstructing small bowel tumour, which should be presumed whenever no external hernia can be demonstrated.
Gallstone ileus, which is the usual explanation for an abrupt ileal transition point in this particular age group.
quiz.explain: Adhesions cause most small bowel obstruction in adults with previous surgery, and they are diagnosed by what is absent: an abrupt transition with nothing at it — no mass, no wall thickening, no hernia, no intussusception, no inflammatory process. That makes the diagnosis a duty rather than a shrug. Before accepting it you must inspect every hernial orifice including femoral and obturator, look for a beak within the mesentery suggesting an internal hernia, and check for a lesion at the transition on thin reformats. Ileus is excluded here by the collapsed distal bowel and colon: an ileus dilates everything without a calibre change. Gallstone ileus has its own triad of pneumobilia, obstruction and an ectopic stone. The final clause — no signs of strangulation — is the part the surgeon reads first, because it is what permits a trial of conservative management.

quiz.prompt: A CT report on a small bowel obstruction lists five findings: mesenteric fluid, reduced small bowel wall enhancement, the small bowel faeces sign, pneumatosis of a dilated loop, and moderate ascites. How many of these five are recognised signs of strangulation? Answer as a whole number, with no units.
quiz.explain: Four. Mesenteric fluid and oedema, reduced or absent wall enhancement, pneumatosis and ascites all belong to the strangulation family, along with mural thickening, a hyperattenuating wall on the non-contrast series from haemorrhagic infarction, mesenteric venous engorgement and portal venous gas. Reduced wall enhancement is the most specific of them and the one to hunt for deliberately, comparing the suspect loop against a normal loop on the same image and on the same window. The small bowel faeces sign is the odd one out: it reflects stasis and delayed transit, not compromised perfusion. It is more common in higher-grade and longer-standing obstruction, which is why it feels ominous, but it does not by itself justify an emergency laparotomy. Grading the CT by how many of the real signs are present is how you communicate urgency.

quiz.prompt: In a patient with high-grade small bowel obstruction, a segment of dilated bowel immediately proximal to the calibre change contains particulate material mixed with gas bubbles. How should this influence what you do?
quiz.answer: Use it to point you towards the transition zone; by itself it says nothing about the blood supply of the loop.
choices: Use it to point you towards the transition zone; by itself it says nothing about the blood supply of the loop.
Treat it as an early sign of strangulation, and escalate the patient directly to an emergency laparotomy.
Take it as evidence against mechanical obstruction, since particulate content implies transit is preserved.
Take it as proof of a distal colonic cause, since particulate material can only originate within the colon.
quiz.explain: The small bowel faeces sign is gas bubbles suspended in particulate debris within dilated small bowel, produced by stasis, water resorption and bacterial overgrowth in a segment whose contents have not moved. Its practical value is topographical: it sits just proximal to the transition point, so when the transition is hard to find, follow the faecalised segment distally and it will usually take you there. It also tells you the obstruction is not brand new. What it is not is an ischaemia sign, and reading it as one leads to overcalling. It appears in Crohn disease, in some chronic strictures and occasionally without obstruction at all. Judge urgency on wall enhancement, mesenteric oedema, closed-loop configuration and the patient's physiology, and use the faeces sign for what it is good at — finding the level.

quiz.prompt: CT shows a C-shaped, fluid-filled dilated small bowel loop with two transition points at a single site, mesenteric vessels radiating towards that point, mesenteric oedema, and reduced enhancement of the loop wall. Say what you are describing and how quickly the surgical team needs to hear it.
quiz.answer: A closed-loop small bowel obstruction with signs of strangulation. Telephone the surgical team immediately rather than leaving a written report - the loop is at risk of infarction and this needs an emergency laparotomy, not a trial of conservative management.
quiz.explain: A closed loop is a segment obstructed at two points close together, usually by a single adhesive band or a hernial neck, and it is the configuration most likely to strangulate because the mesentery is caught in the same twist. Recognise it by the shape — a C or U-shaped, fluid-filled, disproportionately dilated loop — by two transition points converging at one site, and by mesenteric vessels stretched and radiating towards that point, sometimes with a whirl. Then look specifically for the viability signs: reduced or absent wall enhancement, mural thickening, mesenteric oedema and fluid, ascites, pneumatosis, portal venous gas. The report is not the communication. A closed loop with reduced enhancement is a phone call in minutes, because the interval between venous occlusion and transmural infarction is measured in hours and the operation is different if the bowel has to be resected.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the four questions to work through when reading a CT for suspected bowel obstruction, in the order they should be answered.
quiz.answer: confirm-dilatation locate-transition identify-cause assess-viability
quiz.explain: The sequence is forced by logic. First establish that bowel is genuinely obstructed rather than merely dilated: dilated proximal bowel with collapsed distal bowel and colon, against the 3/6/9 calibre limits. Second, find the transition point by following the dilated loops to where calibre changes, using coronal reformats, since the level determines whether this is a small or large bowel problem. Third, work out what is at the transition — adhesion, hernia, tumour, intussusception, volvulus, gallstone, inflammatory stricture — because the cause decides whether conservative management is even an option. Fourth, and never omitted, assess viability: wall enhancement, mural thickness, mesenteric fat and fluid, pneumatosis, portal venous gas. Viability comes last in the reading order but first in the conversation with the surgeon, because it is the finding that changes the timing of the operation rather than only its nature.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old has an obstructing sigmoid carcinoma. CT shows colonic dilatation from the caecum to the tumour, a caecum measuring 10.5 cm, no small bowel dilatation, and a thin caecal wall enhancing normally. What is the significance of the undistended small bowel?
quiz.answer: The ileocaecal valve is competent, making this a closed loop with the caecum at risk of perforating.
choices: The ileocaecal valve is competent, making this a closed loop with the caecum at risk of perforating.
The obstruction is incomplete, so the patient can safely wait for an elective operating list next week.
The tumour is more likely benign, since malignant strictures decompress into the small bowel early.
The caecal dilatation is passive, and the measurement therefore carries no prognostic weight here.
quiz.explain: A competent ileocaecal valve converts a distal colonic obstruction into a closed loop between the valve and the tumour. Nothing can escape proximally into the ileum or distally past the tumour, so the colon — and above all the caecum — takes the whole pressure. Because wall tension rises with radius, the caecum is the segment that ruptures, and it can do so with a deceptively comfortable abdomen. Paradoxically, the absence of small bowel dilatation is therefore the worrying feature, not the reassuring one: decompression into dilated small bowel means an incompetent valve and a lower immediate perforation risk. Report the caecal diameter as a number, comment on caecal wall enhancement and any pericaecal fluid or pneumatosis, and flag it for urgent decompression, whether by stent, defunctioning stoma or resection. This is not an elective list problem.

quiz.prompt: An 84-year-old nursing home resident with chronic constipation has gross distension. The radiograph shows an inverted U-shaped loop arising from the pelvis with its apex in the right upper quadrant and no rectal gas; CT confirms a whirl of twisted sigmoid mesentery with normal wall enhancement and no free gas. What is the appropriate first treatment?
quiz.answer: Endoscopic decompression with placement of a flatus tube, holding surgery for failure or for ischaemia.
choices: Endoscopic decompression with placement of a flatus tube, holding surgery for failure or for ischaemia.
Immediate laparotomy with sigmoid resection, since detorsion is seldom successful in this age group.
Water-soluble contrast enema for therapeutic reduction, which succeeds in the majority of volvulus cases.
Fluids and laxatives alone, since a sigmoid volvulus in a frail patient generally untwists without help.
quiz.explain: Sigmoid volvulus is a disease of the elderly, the immobile and the chronically constipated, and the classic radiograph is an enormously dilated inverted U arising from the pelvis, its apex often reaching above the transverse colon and pointing towards the right upper quadrant, with absent rectal gas. CT confirms it with a whirl of twisted mesentery and two beaks at the point of torsion, and — crucially — assesses viability. With enhancing wall and no free gas, first-line management is endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube left in place, which succeeds in most patients and converts an emergency into a planned procedure. Recurrence is high, so elective sigmoidectomy is usually considered afterwards. Perforation, peritonitis or CT evidence of ischaemia overrides all of this and sends the patient straight to theatre. Contrast enema is diagnostic at best and has been overtaken by CT.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old has acute distension and vomiting. CT shows a hugely dilated gas-filled loop in the left upper quadrant with a beak and a whirl of mesentery in the right iliac fossa, dilated small bowel, an empty right iliac fossa and a collapsed distal colon. State the diagnosis and why endoscopy is not the answer.
quiz.answer: This is a caecal volvulus. Unlike sigmoid volvulus it is rarely reduced endoscopically and recurs if it is, so it needs surgery - usually right hemicolectomy, or caecopexy in the unfit - and delay risks caecal infarction.
quiz.explain: Caecal volvulus needs a congenitally mobile caecum on an unfused mesentery, so it affects a much younger population than sigmoid volvulus. The giveaways are the empty right iliac fossa, the dilated caecum displaced towards the left upper quadrant, dilated small bowel proximal to it because the obstruction sits at the ileocaecal level, and a collapsed distal colon. On CT, look for the whirl of the twisted ileocolic pedicle and then for wall enhancement. The management diverges sharply from sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic reduction is technically difficult, frequently fails and recurs, so the answer is operative — right hemicolectomy where the patient can take it, caecopexy or caecostomy where they cannot. Say the diagnosis explicitly in the report rather than describing a distended loop, because the word caecal is what routes the patient to theatre instead of to endoscopy.

quiz.prompt: On day three after an open hysterectomy a woman is distended and not passing flatus. CT shows dilated small bowel and dilated colon with gas reaching the rectum, no calibre change anywhere, and no wall thickening or mesenteric fluid. State your conclusion and what it changes.
quiz.answer: Post-operative ileus rather than mechanical obstruction: bowel is dilated throughout with gas down to the rectum and no transition point. Management is conservative - nasogastric decompression, fluids, correcting electrolytes and reducing opiates - rather than a return to theatre.
quiz.explain: The distinction rests on one question: is there a transition point? An ileus dilates the whole gut uniformly, small bowel and colon together, with gas carried through to the rectum and no calibre change; mechanical obstruction dilates proximally and collapses distally around a discrete transition. Ileus follows surgery, electrolyte disturbance — especially hypokalaemia — opiates, sepsis, retroperitoneal inflammation and spinal injury, and it is treated by removing the cause. The trap is early post-operative mechanical obstruction, from an internal hernia or a tight closure, which can masquerade as a slow ileus and only declares itself when someone looks specifically for a transition point. So report the absence of a transition as a positive finding, and set a threshold: if the picture does not settle over the next couple of days, or the patient becomes tender or tachycardic, rescan and look again.

quiz.prompt: CT in a septic 70-year-old shows branching gas within the liver extending to within 1 cm of the capsule in the left lobe, together with gas in the wall of a dilated small bowel loop. What should be conveyed to the referring team?
quiz.answer: Gas of this peripheral distribution is portal venous, and with pneumatosis it points to infarcted bowel.
choices: Gas of this peripheral distribution is portal venous, and with pneumatosis it points to infarcted bowel.
Gas of this distribution within the liver is biliary, and is explained by a previous sphincterotomy.
The intramural gas is probably benign pneumatosis, so the hepatic gas can reasonably be disregarded.
The appearances suggest a gas-forming hepatic abscess, and image-guided aspiration should be arranged.
quiz.explain: Direction of flow separates the two. Portal blood runs from the hilum outwards, so portal venous gas is peripheral, fine and branching, typically reaching within 2 cm of the liver capsule and favouring the left lobe in a supine patient. Bile flows towards the hilum, so pneumobilia is central, coarser, and clusters around the porta — the expected finding after sphincterotomy, a biliary-enteric anastomosis or an incompetent sphincter. Portal venous gas together with pneumatosis in a septic patient is bowel infarction until proven otherwise and warrants immediate surgical discussion. The nuance to hold alongside it is that pneumatosis on its own is not always ischaemic: it occurs in chronic lung disease, with corticosteroids and some chemotherapy agents, after endoscopy, and in connective tissue disease. The company it keeps, and the patient, decide the meaning.

quiz.prompt: An 81-year-old inpatient recovering from a fractured neck of femur develops gross abdominal distension. CT shows dilatation of the entire colon including the rectum, a caecum of 12 cm, no transition point, no mass, and normal wall enhancement. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction: correct electrolytes and drugs, and consider neostigmine or endoscopic decompression.
choices: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction: correct electrolytes and drugs, and consider neostigmine or endoscopic decompression.
Mechanical obstruction of the distal colon, with a water-soluble contrast enema needed before any decompression.
Immediate laparotomy and subtotal colectomy, since a caecum of this diameter has by definition already infarcted.
Sigmoid volvulus, with urgent flexible sigmoidoscopy and placement of a flatus tube as the first intervention.
quiz.explain: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction is massive colonic dilatation with no mechanical cause, typically in an elderly inpatient after surgery, trauma or acute illness, and often with electrolyte disturbance, opiates or anticholinergics contributing. The distinguishing features on CT are gas carried right through into the rectum and the absence of any transition point — a sigmoid volvulus would show a whirl and beaks, and a tumour would show a shouldered stricture. First-line treatment is conservative: stop the offending drugs, correct potassium and magnesium, decompress nasogastrically, mobilise. Neostigmine under cardiac monitoring is effective in many patients, with colonoscopic decompression where it fails or is contraindicated. Report the caecal diameter and wall enhancement each time, because a caecum beyond about 12 cm, or one with pneumatosis, thinning or pericaecal fluid, is the trigger for escalation to surgery.

quiz.prompt: An 86-year-old thin woman with no previous abdominal surgery has a small bowel obstruction and pain radiating down the medial thigh. CT shows a loop of ileum passing between the pectineus and obturator externus muscles, with the transition point at that loop. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Refer urgently for surgical repair of an obturator hernia, stating the high risk of strangulation.
choices: Refer urgently for surgical repair of an obturator hernia, stating the high risk of strangulation.
Manage conservatively with a nasogastric tube, since hernias at this site usually reduce spontaneously.
Attribute the obstruction to adhesions, since the pelvic appearance is a recognised anatomical variant.
Book an outpatient hernia clinic appointment once the obstruction has settled with intravenous fluids.
quiz.explain: When there is no history of previous surgery, the transition point is far more likely to be a hernia than an adhesion, so the hernial orifices deserve a deliberate pass on the coronal images every time. The obturator hernia is the one most often missed: it occurs in thin, elderly, often multiparous women, the bowel passes through the obturator canal between pectineus and obturator externus, and compression of the obturator nerve produces pain referred to the medial thigh or knee — the Howship-Romberg sign. The neck is narrow and rigid, so strangulation is common and the reported mortality is high; this is an urgent operation, not a conservative trial. Check the femoral canals, the umbilicus, old incisions, and the mesenteric windows for internal hernias in the same sweep. Naming the hernia in the report changes both the urgency and the surgical approach.

nodes.title: CT in Abdominal Trauma and AAST Grading
nodes.goal: Choose and interpret the phases of a trauma abdominal CT, grade solid organ injury by the AAST scale, and separate the findings that go to the angiography suite from those that go straight to theatre.
articles: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma

quiz.prompt: A stable 30-year-old is scanned after a high-speed collision. The radiographer asks whether a single portal venous phase will do, or whether an arterial phase should be added. What is the best answer and its justification?
quiz.answer: Add an arterial phase where arterial bleeding is likely, because it separates arterial from venous bleeding and shows the embolisation target
choices: Use the portal venous phase alone in blunt trauma, because an added arterial phase raises dose without changing management decisions
Use an arterial phase alone in blunt trauma, because parenchymal lacerations and free fluid are shown at least as well on those images
Add a delayed phase rather than an arterial phase in routine practice, because it demonstrates the source of arterial bleeding far more reliably
Add an arterial phase where arterial bleeding is likely, because it separates arterial from venous bleeding and shows the embolisation target
quiz.explain: The portal venous phase at around 70 seconds is the workhorse: it shows parenchymal lacerations and haematomas, bowel wall enhancement, mesenteric injury and free fluid, and it is the phase on which AAST grading is largely done. An arterial phase adds real value where arterial haemorrhage is likely, which in practice means high-grade solid organ injury and pelvic fractures, because it distinguishes brisk arterial extravasation from a slow venous ooze and shows the vessel the interventional radiologist will target. A delayed phase, at three to five minutes, is a problem-solver rather than a routine, used to separate active extravasation from a contained vascular injury and to show urinary tract leak. Split-bolus techniques let some units combine phases and hold the dose down.

quiz.prompt: A splenic injury shows a rounded 8 mm focus of contrast within the parenchyma on the arterial phase, matching the aorta in attenuation. On the three-minute delayed images the focus is smaller, still round and sharply marginated, and it now matches the attenuation of the splenic vein. How do you interpret this and what do you advise?
quiz.answer: A contained pseudoaneurysm rather than active bleeding, since it stays discrete and follows the blood pool; advise angiographic embolisation
choices: Active extravasation, since a focus that matches aortic attenuation on the arterial phase represents haemorrhage escaping into the parenchyma
A contained pseudoaneurysm rather than active bleeding, since it stays discrete and follows the blood pool; advise angiographic embolisation
A calcified splenic artery branch, since the density persists across phases and vascular calcification is common at any adult age
An arteriovenous fistula requiring laparotomy, since early venous filling of this kind cannot be dealt with by endovascular means
quiz.explain: The delayed phase is what separates these. Active extravasation grows, changes shape, spreads irregularly and stays dense as more contrast pours out; it also usually enlarges beyond the organ or into the peritoneum. A contained vascular injury, that is a pseudoaneurysm or an arteriovenous fistula, stays round and well defined and washes out in step with the blood pool because it is still in continuity with the circulation. Calcification is distinguished by being present on the unenhanced series, if you have one, and by not changing at all. The management implication is that both active bleeding and a contained pseudoaneurysm in a stable patient are indications for angiography and embolisation, but a pseudoaneurysm may declare itself late, which is why it must be named in the report rather than dismissed as a blush.

quiz.prompt: A stable adult has a splenic laceration 4 cm deep, an intraparenchymal haematoma of 6 cm, and a 6 mm pseudoaneurysm within the parenchyma with no contrast beyond the splenic capsule. Give the AAST organ injury grade for the spleen under the 2018 revision. Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The 2018 revision of the AAST spleen scale made vascular injury an explicit upgrader. Any splenic injury containing a vascular injury, meaning a pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula, or active bleeding that remains confined within the splenic capsule, is grade IV, whatever the size of the laceration. Grade V is reserved for a shattered spleen, or a vascular injury with active bleeding extending beyond the spleen into the peritoneum. Without the pseudoaneurysm this injury would have been grade III on the laceration depth of more than 3 cm and the haematoma of 5 cm or more. This is exactly why the arterial phase earns its place: a grade III becomes a grade IV, and a stable patient who might have been observed goes to the angiography suite instead.

quiz.prompt: A stable patient kicked by a horse has a right renal laceration extending into the collecting system, with contrast in the perinephric space on the excretory phase, a normal renal artery and vein, and the haematoma confined within Gerota fascia. Give the AAST renal injury grade under the 2018 revision. Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Under the 2018 AAST kidney scale, a laceration involving the collecting system with urinary extravasation is grade IV, as are renal pelvic laceration or ureteropelvic disruption, a segmental vessel injury with a devascularised segment, and active bleeding extending beyond Gerota fascia. Grade III is a laceration deeper than 1 cm without collecting system involvement, or vascular injury and bleeding contained within Gerota fascia. Grade V means a shattered kidney or main renal artery or vein avulsion with a devascularised kidney. Note that the grade does not dictate the operation here: most grade IV renal injuries with urinary extravasation in a stable patient are managed without surgery, with a ureteric stent if the leak persists. This is also the injury you will miss without an excretory phase.

quiz.prompt: You have acquired arterial and portal venous phases in a stable patient with a renal and a splenic injury. Justify adding a delayed phase: what two distinct questions does it answer?
quiz.answer: It separates active extravasation, which enlarges and spreads, from a contained pseudoaneurysm, which stays discrete and washes out with the blood pool; and as an excretory phase it shows urinary leak from the collecting system or ureter.
quiz.explain: The delayed acquisition earns its dose twice. First, the behaviour of a hyperattenuating focus over time is the only reliable way to tell continuing haemorrhage from a contained vascular injury, and the two do not have identical urgency even though both point towards angiography. Second, at three to five minutes contrast has reached the collecting system, so a laceration communicating with the pelvicalyceal system or a ureteric injury shows as extraluminal excreted contrast; without this phase a grade IV renal injury can be graded as a III. Restrict the delayed acquisition to the region of interest rather than repeating the whole abdomen, and remember that it does not fill the bladder adequately, so it does not substitute for a retrograde CT cystogram.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these trauma CT acquisitions in the order they are performed within a single sitting.
quiz.answer: arterial-phase portal-venous-phase excretory-phase CT-cystography
quiz.explain: The arterial phase comes first, timed by bolus tracking, and answers the question of arterial haemorrhage and vascular injury. The portal venous phase at around 70 seconds is the diagnostic backbone for parenchymal injury, bowel and free fluid. The excretory phase at three to five minutes then serves two purposes: it resolves extravasation against pseudoaneurysm, and it opacifies the collecting systems and ureters. CT cystography comes last because it needs the bladder filled retrogradely through the catheter, and because the excreted contrast already in the system would otherwise confuse the picture. Not every patient needs all four; the sequence is a menu that the mechanism and the findings select from, and each added phase must be justified against dose in what is often a young patient.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a seat-belt mark across the abdomen has CT showing a segment of jejunum with discontinuous wall, adjacent extraluminal gas locules, a mesenteric haematoma and moderate free fluid. He is haemodynamically stable. What should you recommend?
quiz.answer: Immediate laparotomy: bowel wall discontinuity with adjacent extraluminal gas is a specific sign of perforation and is not managed expectantly
choices: Immediate laparotomy: bowel wall discontinuity with adjacent extraluminal gas is a specific sign of perforation and is not managed expectantly
Angiography and embolisation: the mesenteric haematoma is the dominant lesion here, and endovascular haemorrhage control should precede any operation
Admission for serial abdominal examination: stability makes bowel injury unlikely and repeat CT at 24 hours will settle the question
Oral contrast study and repeat CT: gas locules of this kind are usually artefactual and need confirmation before an operation
quiz.explain: Signs of blunt bowel injury divide into specific and suggestive. The specific ones, meaning discontinuity of the bowel wall, extraluminal gas adjacent to bowel, and extraluminal enteric or oral contrast, mandate laparotomy in a patient with the right mechanism. The suggestive ones, being focal bowel wall thickening, abnormal wall enhancement, mesenteric fat stranding, mesenteric haematoma, and interloop free fluid without solid organ injury, are individually unreliable but powerful in combination and warrant close observation and often surgery. Active mesenteric arterial extravasation is itself an indication for laparotomy or embolisation. Stability is no reassurance here: bowel and mesenteric injuries kill through delayed peritonitis rather than through haemorrhage, and every hour of delay after the first eight increases morbidity.

quiz.prompt: A stable adult with a seat-belt mark has moderate free fluid in the pelvis and both paracolic gutters on CT, with entirely normal liver, spleen, kidneys and pancreas. What is your interpretation and what do you recommend?
quiz.answer: Free fluid without solid organ injury after blunt trauma points to a bowel or mesenteric injury; scrutinise for bowel wall thickening, abnormal enhancement and mesenteric haematoma, and either take the patient to laparotomy or admit for serial examination with a low threshold for repeat imaging.
quiz.explain: Unexplained free fluid is one of the highest-yield observations on a trauma scan, because the fluid has to have come from somewhere. In a blunt-injured adult, the leading explanations are bowel or mesenteric injury, a bladder injury, and bleeding from an injury you have not yet seen. Small volumes of simple fluid in the pelvis of a woman of reproductive age can be physiological, and a modest amount may follow aggressive crystalloid resuscitation, but moderate or large fluid deserves a formal answer. Measure the attenuation: fluid at 30 to 45 Hounsfield units is blood, while low attenuation suggests bowel content, bile or urine. Do not sign off a normal report with unexplained free fluid on it.

quiz.prompt: A man with a pelvic fracture has CT cystography showing contrast tracking into the prevesical space and along the anterior abdominal wall, with none outlining bowel loops or reaching the paracolic gutters. He has no peritonism. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: An extraperitoneal rupture, which is usually treated by catheter drainage alone unless fracture fixation or a bladder neck injury forces repair
choices: An intraperitoneal rupture, which requires urgent operative repair, because urine within the peritoneal cavity causes a chemical peritonitis and sepsis
A urethral injury, which requires a retrograde urethrogram and precludes any attempt at urethral catheterisation before repair
An extraperitoneal rupture, which is usually treated by catheter drainage alone unless fracture fixation or a bladder neck injury forces repair
A normal study, since perivesical contrast after pelvic fracture reflects passive leakage around the catheter rather than a tear
quiz.explain: The two patterns are separated by where the contrast goes. Extraperitoneal rupture, which is far more common and nearly always accompanies a pelvic fracture, leaks into the prevesical space of Retzius and can track into the anterior abdominal wall, thigh or scrotum, producing the molar tooth appearance around the bladder base. Intraperitoneal rupture occurs at the dome, typically in a distended bladder struck by a direct blow, and contrast outlines bowel loops and fills the paracolic gutters; it needs surgical repair. Combined injuries occur and are managed surgically. The technique caveat is essential: the bladder must be filled retrogradely and distended with dilute contrast, since a passively filled bladder is the classic reason a rupture is missed.

quiz.prompt: A man arrives after a fall from height with a systolic blood pressure of 70 mmHg that does not improve after two units of blood. FAST shows fluid in Morison pouch and the pelvis. The registrar wants a trauma CT before deciding. What should be advised?
quiz.answer: Take him to theatre for laparotomy: with a positive FAST and no response to resuscitation, CT delays definitive haemorrhage control
choices: Scan him first with a portal venous phase alone, since an abbreviated protocol is quick enough to be safe even in a shocked patient
Take him to the angiography suite first: catheter angiography is faster than CT and can control any source of abdominal bleeding
Repeat the FAST in fifteen minutes: a single positive study is not sufficient grounds for laparotomy in blunt abdominal trauma
Take him to theatre for laparotomy: with a positive FAST and no response to resuscitation, CT delays definitive haemorrhage control
quiz.explain: CT is a test for the stable patient and for the transient responder in a department set up to scan them safely, ideally with the scanner in or beside the resuscitation room. A non-responder with free fluid needs the bleeding stopped, and the operating theatre does that; every minute in the scanner is a minute of ongoing haemorrhage, and the shocked patient is also the one who arrests on the table. Angiography has a defined role in pelvic arterial bleeding, often alongside packing, but it does not control splenic hilar or mesenteric haemorrhage in a crashing patient. Recognise the hypoperfusion complex when you do scan such patients: a flat inferior vena cava, intense bowel wall and adrenal enhancement, and a shocked pancreas.

quiz.prompt: A stable 25-year-old has a hepatic injury with parenchymal disruption of about 40 per cent of the right lobe and a focus of active contrast extravasation extending beyond the liver capsule into the peritoneum. The hepatic veins and inferior vena cava are intact. What is the appropriate recommendation?
quiz.answer: Grade IV liver injury; while he remains stable, hepatic angiography with embolisation is preferred to laparotomy for the active bleeding
choices: Grade III liver injury; parenchymal disruption below 50 per cent of a lobe means observation alone, with a repeat scan at 48 hours to reassess
Grade IV liver injury; while he remains stable, hepatic angiography with embolisation is preferred to laparotomy for the active bleeding
Grade V liver injury; extravasation beyond the capsule always denotes juxtahepatic venous injury and demands immediate laparotomy
Grade II liver injury; extravasation contained within the peritoneum without venous injury does not change the grade or the plan
quiz.explain: On the 2018 AAST liver scale, parenchymal disruption involving 25 to 75 per cent of a hepatic lobe is grade IV, as is active bleeding extending beyond the liver parenchyma into the peritoneum. Grade V is disruption of more than 75 per cent of a lobe or a juxtahepatic venous injury involving the retrohepatic inferior vena cava or the central major hepatic veins. Vascular injury contained within the parenchyma sits at grade III. Management has moved decisively towards non-operative care with angioembolisation for arterial bleeding in stable patients, because the liver is difficult to operate on and most venous bleeding tamponades. Anticipate the delayed complications you will be asked to image: biloma, abscess, haemobilia and delayed rupture of a subcapsular haematoma.

quiz.prompt: You are asked to perform CT cystography on a patient with a pelvic fracture and frank haematuria. Describe how you would fill the bladder and explain why clamping the catheter and relying on excreted contrast fails.
quiz.answer: Instil roughly 300 to 400 millilitres of dilute contrast retrogradely through the urethral catheter under gravity until the bladder is distended, then scan; passive antegrade filling with excreted contrast does not distend the bladder enough, so small tears stay apposed and the leak is missed.
quiz.explain: The whole sensitivity of the test lies in distension. A bladder that is not stretched keeps the edges of a tear in contact, and dilute urinary contrast simply sits in the dependent part without ever pressurising the wall, which is why the passively filled study has a well-earned reputation for false negatives. Fill retrogradely by gravity with dilute contrast, typically around 300 to 400 millilitres or until the patient reports discomfort, and scan through the pelvis; a post-drainage image helps where extraperitoneal leak is subtle. One absolute precaution: if there is blood at the meatus, a high-riding prostate or a suspected urethral injury, a retrograde urethrogram comes first, because passing a catheter through a partial urethral tear can complete it.

quiz.prompt: A hypotensive 7-year-old scanned after a road collision shows diffuse intense enhancement of thickened small bowel wall, a slit-like inferior vena cava, avid adrenal enhancement and a hypoenhancing pancreas, with no laceration or free gas. How should this be reported?
quiz.answer: As the hypoperfusion complex of hypovolaemic shock; it calls for urgent resuscitation and a search for bleeding, not laparotomy for bowel injury
choices: As diffuse blunt small bowel injury; the wall thickening and the abnormal enhancement together mandate laparotomy without any further resuscitation
As mesenteric venous thrombosis; the combination of bowel wall thickening with a collapsed vena cava indicates acute venous outflow occlusion
As the hypoperfusion complex of hypovolaemic shock; it calls for urgent resuscitation and a search for bleeding, not laparotomy for bowel injury
As a normal paediatric study; bowel wall enhancement and a narrow vena cava are expected findings at this age and carry no significance
quiz.explain: The hypoperfusion complex, sometimes called shock bowel, is a physiological pattern rather than an injury, and it is commonest in children. Low cardiac output produces a flattened inferior vena cava and small aorta, splanchnic vasoconstriction with intense mucosal enhancement and fluid-filled thickened bowel, avid adrenal enhancement, and reduced enhancement of the spleen, pancreas, liver and kidneys. Recognising it does two things. It stops the report from calling a diffuse enhancement pattern a bowel injury and sending a child who needs blood to theatre for the wrong operation. And it is an alarm: the child is decompensating on the table, so the scan should be curtailed, resuscitation intensified, and the bleeding source found. The pattern reverses within hours of adequate volume replacement.

nodes.title: Crohn Disease: MR Enterography and Ultrasound
nodes.goal: Run and read an MR enterography, separate active inflammation from fibrotic stricture so the team can choose drug or knife, and use bowel ultrasound to follow the response.

quiz.prompt: A patient managed only 400 mL of the oral agent before MR enterography. Several ileal loops are collapsed; their walls measure 5 mm and enhance briskly. There is no mural T2 signal, no comb sign, no restricted diffusion and no mesenteric fat change. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: Those loops are non-diagnostic, since collapsed bowel mimics mural thickening
choices: Those loops are non-diagnostic, since collapsed bowel mimics mural thickening
There is active ileal inflammation, since thickening with enhancement suffices
There is a fibrotic stricture, since the loops are narrowed and fail to distend
The bowel is normal, since the mesenteric and diffusion findings are absent
quiz.explain: Distension is the examination. A contracted loop has a genuinely thick, avidly enhancing wall, and the appearance is indistinguishable from disease if you look at the wall alone, which is why 1 to 1.5 litres of a biphasic agent over 45 to 60 minutes is a technical requirement rather than a courtesy. Two habits protect you. First, require corroboration before calling inflammation: mural T2 hyperintensity on fat-saturated images, restricted diffusion, ulcers, engorged vasa recta, creeping fat, upstream dilatation. Second, require persistence, since a peristaltic contraction changes between sequences while disease does not. Reporting the loops as normal is the mirror-image error and is just as unsafe, because you cannot exclude disease in bowel you have not seen. If the patient cannot drink, say so and offer bowel ultrasound instead.

quiz.prompt: Explain why the oral agent used for MR enterography is chosen to be bright on T2 and dark on T1, and say what the mannitol in it is doing.
quiz.answer: A bright lumen on T2 outlines the wall against fluid so thickening and ulcers stand out, while a dark lumen on T1 lets the wall show its intravenous contrast enhancement without competition; the mannitol is an osmotic agent that holds water in the bowel so the loops stay distended for the whole examination.
quiz.explain: The two signal requirements come from the two questions the study asks. On T2 you want the wall silhouetted, so bright luminal fluid is ideal and mural oedema shows as high signal within a dark wall. On post-contrast T1 you want mural enhancement to be the brightest thing in the field, so the lumen must stay dark; a positive luminal agent would swamp it. An agent that satisfies both is biphasic. Mannitol, sorbitol and polyethylene glycol are poorly absorbed solutes that keep water in the lumen by osmosis, which is what maintains distension over the 45 minutes of drinking and the 30 minutes of scanning, and also why they cause the cramping and diarrhoea patients complain about. Intravenous hyoscine butylbromide is added to stop peristalsis before the motion-sensitive sequences.

quiz.prompt: Post-contrast images are obtained at about 45 seconds and again at about 7 minutes. A terminal ileal segment enhances less than adjacent normal bowel at 45 seconds, but more than it at 7 minutes. What does that pattern favour?
quiz.answer: Fibrosis, where contrast accumulates late in a collagen-rich wall
choices: Fibrosis, where contrast accumulates late in a collagen-rich wall
Active inflammation, which peaks early and then washes out fast
A timing artefact, since two phases are not comparable this way
Ischaemia, since the wall enhances less than the neighbouring loops
quiz.explain: The enteric phase at roughly 45 seconds is when actively inflamed bowel is most conspicuous, because hyperaemic mucosa and submucosa take up contrast quickly and stratify. Fibrotic wall behaves in the opposite direction: contrast diffuses slowly into an expanded extracellular collagen matrix and leaves slowly, so a segment that looked unimpressive early is brighter than its neighbours on delayed imaging. Reading the two phases as a pair therefore separates the two processes better than either alone, and it is why a delayed acquisition earns its place in the protocol. Two cautions belong with it. Most strictures contain both processes, so this pattern shifts the balance rather than settling it; and the comparison must be made against normal bowel in the same acquisition, not against a remembered brightness.

quiz.prompt: A 25-year-old has a 6 cm terminal ileal stricture with 4.5 cm of upstream dilatation. The wall is 8 mm thick, dark on fat-saturated T2, shows no restricted diffusion, has no ulcers and no comb sign, and enhances progressively on the 7-minute images. The team asks whether to escalate the biologic.
quiz.answer: Predominantly fibrotic; escalating the biologic will not open this stricture
choices: Predominantly fibrotic; escalating the biologic will not open this stricture
Predominantly inflammatory; escalate the biologic before considering surgery
Indeterminate, since T2 signal and diffusion have no bearing on this question
Predominantly fibrotic, but a biologic is still the first line before surgery
quiz.explain: Every feature here points the same way. A wall dark on fat-saturated T2 holds no free water, absent restricted diffusion argues against a dense inflammatory infiltrate, there are no ulcers and no hyperaemic vasa recta, and enhancement is late and progressive rather than early and layered. That is scar, and no anti-inflammatory drug dissolves scar; the options are endoscopic balloon dilatation for a short stricture, strictureplasty, or resection. The upstream dilatation matters too, because the 2018 Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Gastroenterological Association consensus defines a stricture as luminal narrowing with unequivocal upstream dilatation, taken as greater than 3 cm, so 4.5 cm qualifies and the narrowing is doing real mechanical work. Where inflammation coexists, a drug trial is entirely reasonable; this scan is simply too clean to justify one.

quiz.prompt: At the next scan the same stricture is bright on fat-saturated T2, restricts diffusion and shows a deep ulcer, while still enhancing progressively on the delayed images. What should you tell the multidisciplinary meeting?
quiz.answer: This is now a mixed stricture, with active inflammation superimposed on the fibrosis, so a trial of medical therapy is justified first and dilatation or resection is held in reserve for the fibrotic component if the obstruction persists.
quiz.explain: Most Crohn strictures are mixed, and the honest report says so rather than forcing a binary. What the meeting needs is the proportion and its consequence: an inflammatory component can be treated medically and may relieve enough of the narrowing to defer an operation, whereas the fibrotic component sets a floor below which no drug will take the calibre. So the sequence is a defined trial of therapy with a stated endpoint and a planned reassessment, and an agreed intervention if symptoms of obstruction continue. Two practical points support this. Deep ulceration is a marker of severity and of poorer medical response, so it argues for close follow-up rather than complacency; and length matters to the surgeon, since a short stricture is a candidate for balloon dilatation while a long one is not.

quiz.prompt: On bowel ultrasound the terminal ileal wall measures 6.4 mm at its thickest, against the accepted upper limit of normal of 3 mm in adults. By how much does it exceed that limit? Answer in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Wall thickness is the workhorse of bowel ultrasound because it is the most reproducible thing the probe measures, and above 3 mm in an adult it is abnormal, with normal bowel usually under 2 mm. Technique decides whether the number means anything: use a high-frequency linear probe, measure perpendicular to the wall from the luminal interface to the serosa, exclude luminal content, and take the thickest point of the diseased segment rather than an average. The figure then feeds the composite activity scores such as the International Bowel Ultrasound Segmental Activity Score, alongside colour Doppler hyperaemia, loss of the layered pattern and mesenteric fat changes. MR enterography uses the same 3 mm threshold for adequately distended small bowel, which is why the two examinations can be used in series without recalibrating.

quiz.prompt: Coronal MR enterography shows the vasa recta on the mesenteric border of a thickened ileal segment splayed apart and engorged, with proliferation of the adjacent mesenteric fat and several small reactive nodes. What does this add to the assessment?
quiz.answer: It supports active transmural disease and helps localise the diseased segment
choices: It supports active transmural disease and helps localise the diseased segment
It indicates chronic burnt-out disease with no current inflammatory activity
It suggests mesenteric venous thrombosis rather than Crohn inflammation here
It is expected in well distended bowel and carries no diagnostic significance
quiz.explain: Engorged vasa recta standing perpendicular to the bowel are the vascular expression of active disease: flow to the segment has increased and the feeding vessels dilate to carry it. Fibrofatty proliferation around the same segment is the more chronic partner, a mesenteric response that tends to accumulate with disease duration but also tracks with activity. Both sit on the mesenteric border, which is where Crohn disease characteristically concentrates, sparing the antimesenteric side and producing the pseudosacculations seen there.
