Their practical value is twofold: they raise confidence that a thickened loop is truly diseased rather than contracted, and they mark the extent of involvement when the loops themselves are hard to follow. Be careful with the nodes, though; small reactive nodes belong here, whereas nodes over a centimetre deserve a separate thought.

quiz.prompt: MR enterography shows a blind-ending tract leaving the mesenteric border of a diseased ileal loop and ending in a 4 cm rim-enhancing collection that contains gas and restricts diffusion. The gastroenterologist would like to start infliximab this week.
quiz.answer: Drain the collection and treat the sepsis before any anti-TNF agent is started
choices: Drain the collection and treat the sepsis before any anti-TNF agent is started
Start the anti-TNF agent now, since it will close both the tract and the cavity
Resect the segment immediately, since any sinus tract mandates a resection
Repeat the enterography in three months before committing to an intervention
quiz.explain: Penetrating disease has a vocabulary worth keeping straight because it maps onto different actions. A sinus tract ends blind in the mesentery; a fistula reaches another epithelialised surface, whether bowel, bladder, vagina or skin; an abscess is a rim-enhancing collection, and restricted diffusion with gas is what distinguishes it from a fluid-filled loop. Starting potent immunosuppression into undrained sepsis is the one clearly wrong move, since it removes the containment the patient is relying on. So the order is drainage, percutaneous where the collection is accessible, with antibiotics, and then the biologic once the sepsis is controlled, which is also when the drug has the best chance of closing the tract. Immediate resection is not mandatory; many tracts settle once the cavity is drained and the inflammation treated.

quiz.prompt: Perineal MRI shows a primary tract crossing the external anal sphincter into the ischioanal fossa, with a secondary ramification and a 2 cm collection within that fossa. Using the St James's University Hospital MRI grading of perianal fistulas, which grade is this? Answer as a whole number from 1 to 5.
quiz.explain: The St James's grading runs from 1 to 5 and combines the anatomical course with whether there is a secondary tract or abscess. Grade 1 is a simple linear intersphincteric tract; grade 2 is intersphincteric with a secondary tract or abscess; grade 3 is a simple transsphincteric tract; grade 4 is transsphincteric with an abscess or secondary tract in the ischioanal or ischiorectal fossa; grade 5 is supralevator or translevator disease. Crossing the external sphincter makes it transsphincteric, and the ischioanal collection takes it to grade 4. This matters because grades 3 and above are complex disease: fistulotomy would divide sphincter and risk continence, so management moves to seton drainage plus medical therapy, and the report must state the relationship to the sphincter complex, the presence of collections and any secondary tracts.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the five sonographic layers of the bowel wall from the lumen outwards.
quiz.answer: lumen-interface mucosa submucosa muscularis-propria serosa
quiz.explain: High-frequency ultrasound resolves the wall into five alternating bands: a bright interface where the lumen meets the mucosa, dark mucosa, bright submucosa, dark muscularis propria and a bright serosal line. Reading them is the point rather than reciting them. In Crohn disease the thickening concentrates in the submucosa, so the bright band widens while the layering is preserved, and that preserved pattern is the reassuring finding. Loss of stratification, where the layers blur into a single hypoechoic mass, indicates severe transmural inflammation or deep ulceration and is associated with a poorer response to medical therapy and a higher chance of penetrating disease. Adding colour Doppler to a stratified thickened wall gives the hyperaemia score, and the two together are what a follow-up scan is really comparing.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old with terminal ileal Crohn disease needs assessment three times over the coming year to judge treatment response. Give the properties of bowel ultrasound that make it the right tool, and name the limitation that would send you back to MR enterography.
quiz.answer: It involves no ionising radiation, needs no oral preparation or sedation, is cheap and can be repeated at the bedside, giving wall thickness and Doppler hyperaemia at every visit; its limitation is poor access to the deep pelvis, the proximal jejunum and perianal disease, which need MR enterography or perineal MRI.
quiz.explain: Serial imaging has different requirements from diagnostic imaging. What matters over a year is that the test can be done often, quickly and identically, and bowel ultrasound wins on all three: no radiation, no drinking a litre of mannitol, no cannula, a few minutes in clinic, and quantitative outputs in wall thickness and Doppler signal that can be tracked visit to visit. That is why it has become a standard tool for monitoring response and for detecting relapse early. Its weaknesses are anatomical and operator-dependent rather than conceptual. Deep pelvic loops, the proximal jejunum, and anything perianal are beyond it, obesity degrades it, and reproducibility depends on training. So the usual arrangement is MR enterography to map the disease and ultrasound to follow it.

quiz.prompt: Another patient has continuous mucosal disease from the rectum to the splenic flexure, with symmetrical mildly thickened bowel, loss of haustration, no mesenteric fat proliferation, no deep ulcers and no fistulas. What does that combination favour, and what changes as a result?
quiz.answer: Ulcerative colitis; medical therapy and surveillance, with no hunt for fistulas
choices: Ulcerative colitis; medical therapy and surveillance, with no hunt for fistulas
Crohn colitis; the rectal involvement makes penetrating disease more likely
Infective colitis; a continuous distribution argues against a chronic process
Ischaemic colitis; the splenic flexure limit marks a watershed territory here
quiz.explain: Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum proximally, confined to mucosa and submucosa, and it does not penetrate: no creeping fat, no sinus tracts, no fistulas, and thickening that is usually modest compared with Crohn disease. Chronic change gives the smooth, foreshortened, haustra-free colon. Crohn colitis is the opposite in every respect that matters here, being discontinuous, asymmetric, mesenteric-border predominant, and prone to penetrating complications, which is why the distinction changes what you look for as well as what you call it. Two caveats keep you honest. Treated ulcerative colitis can become patchy and can spare the rectum after topical therapy, so distribution alone is unreliable in a patient already on treatment; and backwash ileitis gives a short, patulous, thin-walled terminal ileum, quite unlike the narrowed thickened ileum of Crohn disease.

nodes.title: Pancreatic Cancer Staging and Cystic Lesions
nodes.goal: Report a pancreatic protocol CT in the surgeon's language of vascular contact and resectability, and triage cystic and hypervascular pancreatic lesions to surveillance, sampling or resection.

quiz.prompt: A registrar wants to cancel the late arterial acquisition on a pancreatic protocol CT for a suspected head mass, arguing that the portal venous phase shows the liver and the veins perfectly well. What is the strongest argument against, in terms of what the study would lose?
quiz.answer: Tumour-to-parenchyma contrast peaks in the pancreatic parenchymal phase, and arterial mapping for coeliac and hepatic variants is lost
choices: Liver metastases from pancreatic cancer are hypervascular, and they are seen far better in the arterial phase than in the venous phase
Tumour-to-parenchyma contrast peaks in the pancreatic parenchymal phase, and arterial mapping for coeliac and hepatic variants is lost
The main pancreatic duct opacifies during the arterial phase, and its calibre cannot otherwise be assessed with reliability on a CT study
Portal and superior mesenteric vein contact is graded on arterial images alone, since venous walls are indistinct at 70 seconds
quiz.explain: Ductal adenocarcinoma is desmoplastic and hypovascular, so it shows up as a low-attenuation defect against enhancing parenchyma. That difference is greatest in the pancreatic parenchymal phase, roughly 40 to 50 seconds after injection or about 20 to 25 seconds after bolus tracking triggers, which is later than a pure angiographic arterial phase. The same acquisition maps the coeliac axis, the superior mesenteric artery and variants such as a replaced right hepatic artery, which the surgeon must know before opening. The portal venous phase at about 65 to 70 seconds is kept because it is better for the veins and for liver metastases, which in adenocarcinoma are typically hypovascular and most conspicuous then. The two phases answer different questions; dropping either degrades the report.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old has an incidental branch-duct IPMN. MRI shows a 3.4 cm cyst in the uncinate process, a main pancreatic duct of 6 mm, a thickened enhancing cyst wall, no mural nodule, no lymphadenopathy, a normal bilirubin and a normal CA 19-9. Count the worrisome features present under the international consensus (Fukuoka) criteria. Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The three are the cyst measuring 3 cm or more, a main pancreatic duct of 5 to 9 mm, and a thickened or enhancing cyst wall. The other worrisome features in the international consensus criteria (2017 revision, carried into the 2024 Kyoto update) are an enhancing mural nodule under 5 mm, an abrupt change in duct calibre with distal parenchymal atrophy, lymphadenopathy, a raised serum CA 19-9, a growth rate of 5 mm or more over two years, and acute pancreatitis attributable to the cyst. They are distinct from the high-risk stigmata, which are obstructive jaundice with a cystic head lesion, an enhancing mural nodule of 5 mm or more, and a main duct of 10 mm or more. Worrisome features send the patient to endoscopic ultrasound; high-risk stigmata send fit patients to the surgeon.

quiz.prompt: A pancreatic head adenocarcinoma abuts the superior mesenteric artery over about 90 degrees of its circumference, and encases the superior mesenteric vein over roughly 200 degrees with a narrowed but patent lumen and normal vein above and below the segment. There are no metastases. How do you report resectability?
quiz.answer: Borderline resectable: arterial contact is 180 degrees or less and the vein is reconstructible with normal vein above and below the segment
choices: Locally advanced: venous contact beyond 180 degrees with luminal narrowing places the tumour past the limit of surgical reconstruction
Resectable: the artery is not encased and venous involvement of any degree is dealt with routinely at operation without changing the plan
Borderline resectable: arterial contact is 180 degrees or less and the vein is reconstructible with normal vein above and below the segment
Locally advanced: contact with the superior mesenteric artery of any degree at all excludes an operation and commits to chemotherapy
quiz.explain: The categories that surgeons use turn on the degree of circumferential contact and on the shape of the vessel. Resectable means no arterial contact with the coeliac axis, superior mesenteric artery or common hepatic artery, and venous contact of 180 degrees or less without contour irregularity. Borderline resectable in a head or uncinate tumour includes superior mesenteric artery contact of 180 degrees or less, common hepatic artery contact that still permits reconstruction, venous contact above 180 degrees, or venous contact of 180 degrees or less with contour deformity or thrombus, provided there is suitable vein above and below for a graft. Locally advanced means superior mesenteric artery contact above 180 degrees, aortic involvement, or an unreconstructible venous occlusion. Report the numbers and the contour, and let the multidisciplinary team apply the label.

quiz.prompt: A jaundiced 70-year-old has a pancreatic protocol CT in which no mass is visible on any phase, yet the surgeon is convinced there is a tumour. What secondary signs would you go back and hunt for, and what would you do next?
quiz.answer: Look for an abrupt cut-off of the main pancreatic duct with upstream dilatation, distal parenchymal atrophy, a subtle contour bulge of the gland and loss of the fatty cleft around vessels, then proceed to endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle sampling.
quiz.explain: Around one in ten ductal adenocarcinomas is isoattenuating on every phase, more often when the tumour is small, and this is precisely the group where a confident negative report does harm. The secondary signs carry the diagnosis: an abrupt interruption of the main pancreatic duct, dilatation and parenchymal atrophy upstream, a focal convexity of the pancreatic contour, and effacement of the fat plane around the superior mesenteric vessels. The double duct sign, with both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct dilated and cut off at the same level, is the classic presentation in the head. When the CT is negative and suspicion persists, endoscopic ultrasound is the next test: it detects small isoattenuating lesions and it gives tissue in the same sitting.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with painless jaundice has CT showing a dilated common bile duct to 14 mm and a dilated main pancreatic duct to 6 mm, both terminating abruptly in the pancreatic head, with no discrete mass and no metastases. What is the most appropriate next step?
quiz.answer: Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle sampling of the head at the level of the duct cut-off, since a mass is present until proven otherwise
choices: Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle sampling of the head at the level of the duct cut-off, since a mass is present until proven otherwise
Repeat the pancreatic protocol CT in three months, since a lesion invisible on a dedicated study is very unlikely to be a carcinoma
Proceed directly to pancreaticoduodenectomy without tissue, since this pattern is diagnostic and sampling only delays the operation
Perform a FDG PET-CT as the next test, since it is the most sensitive available means of demonstrating a small primary pancreatic adenocarcinoma
quiz.explain: Simultaneous obstruction of both ducts at the same point in the head is a periampullary mass until disproved, whether or not you can see it. Endoscopic ultrasound is the right next test because it resolves small isoattenuating lesions and yields tissue, and because it may instead show an ampullary tumour, a duodenal lesion or focal autoimmune pancreatitis, each of which is managed differently. Waiting three months on a jaundiced patient risks losing a resectable window. Operating without any tissue does happen, in a fit patient with a convincing mass and a clear plan, but with no visible lesion it is indefensible. PET-CT has a role in occult metastatic disease at some centres, not in finding a small primary; and a benign stricture from chronic or autoimmune disease can reproduce this picture.

quiz.prompt: On axial CT the tumour abuts the superior mesenteric artery continuously from the 10 o'clock to the 2 o'clock position on the vessel circumference. Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number: what is the circumferential contact?
quiz.explain: Each hour on the clock face is 30 degrees, and 10 o'clock to 2 o'clock spans four hours, so the contact is 120 degrees. The number matters because 180 degrees is the dividing line in the consensus definitions used by NCCN and the Society of Abdominal Radiology: contact of 180 degrees or less with the superior mesenteric artery keeps a head tumour in the borderline resectable group, while contact above 180 degrees makes it locally advanced. Measure on the axial image where contact is greatest, and read the contact rather than the presence of fat stranding, which overcalls involvement after stenting or pancreatitis. Say the degree and the length of contact in your report; the word encasement without a number is not useful to the surgeon.

quiz.prompt: The hepatobiliary surgeon asks what your report needs to state about the superior mesenteric vein in a pancreatic head cancer. Give the three things.
quiz.answer: The degree of circumferential contact in degrees, whether the vein contour is deformed or thrombosed rather than merely touched, and the craniocaudal length of involvement with whether there is normal vein above and below for reconstruction.
quiz.explain: Venous resection and reconstruction is routine in high-volume practice, so the surgeon does not want a yes or no; they want to know whether they can get a clamp on normal vein above and below, and how long a segment they must replace. Contact of 180 degrees or less with a preserved round contour is resectable disease. Contact above 180 degrees, or any contact that deforms the contour into a teardrop shape or narrows the lumen, is borderline as long as reconstruction is feasible. An occlusion with no usable vein at either end, or one that extends to the confluence and the first jejunal branches, is what makes the case locally advanced. Mention the splenic and portal confluence and the gastrocolic trunk explicitly.

quiz.prompt: A 71-year-old woman has an incidental 4 cm pancreatic body lesion made of many small cysts each under 2 cm, with a central stellate scar containing calcification, no communication with the main pancreatic duct and no mural nodule. She is asymptomatic. What should you advise?
quiz.answer: The features are those of a serous cystadenoma, which is benign; advise no resection and no surveillance while she stays asymptomatic
choices: The features indicate a mucinous cystic neoplasm; advise distal pancreatectomy given the malignant potential of every mucinous lesion
The features indicate a branch-duct IPMN; advise endoscopic ultrasound and then annual MRI surveillance, given a size above the 3 cm threshold
The features suggest a walled-off collection after silent pancreatitis; advise a repeat scan at three months to confirm resolution
The features are those of a serous cystadenoma, which is benign; advise no resection and no surveillance while she stays asymptomatic
quiz.explain: The microcystic honeycomb with a central scar, sometimes with a sunburst calcification, is characteristic of serous cystadenoma, a lesion of older women with negligible malignant potential; the cyst fluid has low CEA and low amylase. Resection is for symptoms from mass effect, not for the diagnosis. The lesion to separate it from is the mucinous cystic neoplasm: also usually in the body or tail of a woman but typically in the fifth decade, unilocular or with few large locules, a thick wall with peripheral eggshell calcification, ovarian-type stroma histologically, and no ductal communication; it carries malignant potential and is resected in fit patients. Where the appearances are equivocal, especially the oligocystic variant of serous cystadenoma, endoscopic ultrasound with fluid analysis decides.

quiz.prompt: Give the features on cross-sectional imaging that let you separate a mucinous cystic neoplasm from a branch-duct IPMN, and say why the distinction changes what you recommend.
quiz.answer: A mucinous cystic neoplasm sits in the body or tail, has a thick wall sometimes with peripheral calcification, and does not communicate with the pancreatic duct; a branch-duct IPMN does communicate with the duct and favours the head and uncinate, so it can be surveilled while a mucinous cystic neoplasm is generally resected.
quiz.explain: Ductal communication is the single most useful sign and is best shown on heavily T2-weighted MRCP, where a branch-duct IPMN is a grape-like cluster joined to the main duct by a visible stalk. A mucinous cystic neoplasm is a closed cyst with its own thick, sometimes calcified wall, characteristically in the body or tail of a woman in middle age. The consequence is practical: a small branch-duct IPMN without worrisome features goes into surveillance, whereas a mucinous cystic neoplasm in a fit patient is usually resected because malignant transformation is a real risk and distal pancreatectomy is curative. The trap is calling a unilocular mucinous cystic neoplasm a pseudocyst on the strength of a vague history of abdominal pain.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the acquisitions of a pancreatic protocol CT in the order the scanner performs them.
quiz.answer: unenhanced-series bolus-tracking-monitoring pancreatic-parenchymal-phase portal-venous-phase
quiz.explain: The unenhanced series comes first and is useful for duct calculi, for a baseline against which faint enhancement is judged, and for calcification in a cystic lesion. Bolus tracking then monitors the abdominal aorta and triggers when a threshold, commonly around 100 Hounsfield units, is reached. The pancreatic parenchymal phase follows after a diagnostic delay of roughly 20 to 25 seconds, that is about 40 to 50 seconds after the start of injection, giving maximal difference between hypovascular tumour and enhancing gland along with the arterial map. The portal venous phase at about 65 to 70 seconds finishes the study for the veins and the liver. Thin collimation, a rate of 3 to 5 millilitres per second, and water as neutral oral contrast are the other ingredients; positive oral contrast obscures vessels on reformats.

quiz.prompt: A fit 66-year-old man has a main pancreatic duct dilated to 12 mm throughout the body and tail with no obstructing stone or stricture, diffuse parenchymal atrophy, and a 7 mm enhancing mural nodule within the duct. There is no jaundice and no mass. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: Refer for surgical assessment: duct dilatation of 10 mm or more and a nodule of 5 mm or more are both high-risk stigmata
choices: Arrange MRI surveillance at six months: without jaundice or a mass, duct dilatation alone does not warrant an operation
Refer for surgical assessment: duct dilatation of 10 mm or more and a nodule of 5 mm or more are both high-risk stigmata
Arrange ERCP with duct brushings first: cytology is required before any patient can be offered pancreatic resection
Attribute the appearances to chronic pancreatitis: duct dilatation with atrophy in this age group is usually a burnt-out gland
quiz.explain: This is main-duct IPMN, and it behaves quite differently from the branch-duct form. Under the international consensus criteria (2017 revision, carried into the 2024 Kyoto update), a main pancreatic duct of 10 mm or more and an enhancing mural nodule of 5 mm or more are each high-risk stigmata, which in a fit patient means resection rather than surveillance; the rate of high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma in main-duct disease is high. Chronic pancreatitis can dilate the duct, but it usually brings calcification and a history to match, and it does not produce an enhancing intraductal nodule. Brush cytology has poor sensitivity and a negative result would not change the plan. Report the duct calibre, the nodule size and its enhancement explicitly.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old with mild obstructive jaundice has a diffusely enlarged, sausage-shaped pancreas with a featureless border, a thin hypoenhancing rim around the gland, delayed homogeneous enhancement, a long narrowed main pancreatic duct without upstream dilatation, and bilateral renal cortical lesions. What should you suggest?
quiz.answer: Raise autoimmune pancreatitis, check the serum IgG4 level and look for other organ involvement before anyone commits to a resection
choices: Raise diffusely infiltrating adenocarcinoma and refer directly for staging laparoscopy, since the gland is expanded throughout
Raise acute interstitial pancreatitis and treat supportively, since gland enlargement with a peripheral rim is the usual pattern
Raise pancreatic lymphoma and arrange PET-CT, since diffuse enlargement with renal lesions is the characteristic combination
Raise autoimmune pancreatitis, check the serum IgG4 level and look for other organ involvement before anyone commits to a resection
quiz.explain: Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is the great mimic and its treatment is steroids, so the cost of missing it is an unnecessary Whipple. The features to hold on to are diffuse sausage-like enlargement with loss of the normal lobulated contour, a capsule-like rim that is hypoenhancing early and enhances late, delayed homogeneous parenchymal enhancement, and a duct that is narrowed over a long segment rather than cut off with upstream dilatation and atrophy. IgG4-related disease elsewhere clinches it: renal cortical lesions, retroperitoneal fibrosis, sclerosing cholangitis, salivary gland involvement. The harder problem is the focal form presenting as a mass, where the duct penetrating sign, the absence of marked upstream atrophy and a raised IgG4 tilt the balance; even then a mass that does not resolve on steroids must be treated as cancer.

quiz.prompt: An asymptomatic 60-year-old has a 1.2 cm solid lesion in the pancreatic tail that enhances avidly in the arterial phase and becomes nearly isoattenuating in the portal venous phase, with a normal duct and a normal liver. What is the most appropriate management recommendation?
quiz.answer: Probable neuroendocrine tumour: confirm with endoscopic ultrasound and somatostatin receptor imaging, then consider surveillance for a small grade 1 lesion
choices: Probable neuroendocrine tumour: confirm with endoscopic ultrasound and somatostatin receptor imaging, then consider surveillance for a small grade 1 lesion
Probable small ductal adenocarcinoma: refer for urgent distal pancreatectomy, since a solid tail lesion at this age is malignant until disproved
Probable hypervascular metastasis: search for a renal primary, since an isolated hypervascular pancreatic deposit nearly always arises from the kidney
Probable intrapancreatic accessory spleen: take no further action, since arterial hyperenhancement in the pancreatic tail has no other explanation
quiz.explain: Arterial hyperenhancement with venous washout towards the parenchyma is the signature of a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, which is why the arterial phase must be preserved when these are suspected, and why their liver metastases are missed on portal venous imaging alone. Grade follows Ki-67: grade 1 below 3 per cent, grade 2 from 3 to 20, grade 3 above 20. Small non-functioning grade 1 lesions, conventionally 2 cm or less, are increasingly watched rather than resected, whereas functioning tumours are removed regardless of size and gastrinomas in particular are often malignant. Two mimics deserve respect: an intrapancreatic accessory spleen, which follows splenic attenuation on every phase and can be confirmed with heat-damaged red cell scintigraphy, and a hypervascular metastasis, classically from renal cell carcinoma, sometimes many years after nephrectomy.

nodes.title: Peritoneum, Mesentery and the Abdominal Wall
nodes.goal: Track disease through the peritoneal recesses, distinguish carcinomatosis from its mimics in the peritoneum and mesentery, and read the abdominal wall for the hernia that needs an operation tonight.

quiz.prompt: CT in severe pancreatitis shows a large collection filling the space behind the stomach and in front of the pancreas, while the paracolic gutters and pelvis are almost dry. The team asks how this can be so localised, and how it might be drained.
quiz.answer: It lies in the lesser sac, a compartment draining through one narrow foramen
choices: It lies in the lesser sac, a compartment draining through one narrow foramen
It lies in the greater sac, so it will redistribute along the paracolic gutters
It lies in the retroperitoneum, so a transperitoneal route would be safest
It lies in the right subphrenic space, which is continuous with the gutter
quiz.explain: The peritoneal cavity is a set of communicating recesses rather than one bag, and the lesser sac is the most sequestered of them. It sits behind the stomach and lesser omentum and in front of the pancreas, and it communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen alone, a slit bounded in front by the free edge of the lesser omentum carrying the portal triad and behind by the inferior vena cava. That single narrow communication is why a pancreatic collection can fill it while the rest of the abdomen stays dry, and it is also why such collections are so often approached transgastrically at endoscopic ultrasound, since the stomach is the wall in front of them. Fluid in the greater sac behaves quite differently, obeying gravity into the gutters and the pelvis.

quiz.prompt: Two CTs each show about 500 mL of intraperitoneal fluid: one is simple ascites, the other a loculated collection. Give the features that separate them, and say why the distinction matters before a drain is placed.
quiz.answer: Ascites conforms to the shape of the recesses, has thin margins, shifts when the patient is repositioned and displaces nothing; a loculated collection is rounded or lentiform, exerts mass effect on adjacent bowel, may have an enhancing rim and stays put, so the drain must be sited into that specific cavity rather than into the free cavity.
quiz.explain: The question a drain asks is whether the fluid is one connected space or several. Free ascites fills the recesses passively, takes their outline, has no wall, and redistributes when the patient rolls, so a single catheter anywhere dependent will empty it. A loculated collection has been walled off by fibrin and adhesions, so it has convex margins, pushes bowel away rather than insinuating between loops, often has an enhancing rim if infected, and does not move. Drain the free fluid beside it and you will report a technically successful procedure while the abscess stays where it is. So the report should state the number of collections, the safest window to each, and whether any of them communicate, and the patient may need repositioned imaging or a repeat scan to answer that.

quiz.prompt: CT shows a thick nodular sheet of soft tissue replacing the greater omentum, with smooth concave indentations of the surface of the liver and spleen, while the hepatic parenchyma itself is normal. What do the indentations tell you?
quiz.answer: Extrinsic serosal deposits pressing on the capsule, not parenchymal disease
choices: Extrinsic serosal deposits pressing on the capsule, not parenchymal disease
Subcapsular hepatic metastases eroding the surface from within the liver
Chronic hepatic fibrosis remodelling the outline of the liver and spleen
Compression by tense ascites distributed around the whole upper abdomen
quiz.explain: Scalloping is a mechanical sign: material sitting on the outside of a solid organ, firm enough to indent a capsule, which means it belongs to the peritoneal surface rather than to the organ. It is the fingerprint of bulky serosal disease, most characteristically gelatinous mucin in pseudomyxoma peritonei but also mucinous carcinomatosis from the colon, appendix, stomach or ovary. Parenchymal metastases do the opposite, bulging the contour outwards from within and enhancing as discrete lesions, and simple ascites indents nothing because a liquid cannot deform a capsule. The finding changes the referral pathway rather than just the wording, since extensive surface disease with an omental cake is the territory of cytoreductive surgery with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy in a specialist centre.

quiz.prompt: Using the Sugarbaker peritoneal cancer index, a staging laparotomy records lesion size 2 in region 0, lesion size 3 in region 1, lesion size 1 in region 3, lesion size 3 in region 6, lesion size 2 in region 9, and no disease in any other region. What is the peritoneal cancer index? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The index is the sum of the regional lesion size scores, so 2 plus 3 plus 1 plus 3 plus 2 gives 11. The abdomen is divided into thirteen regions, nine abdominopelvic regions numbered 0 to 8 and four small bowel regions numbered 9 to 12 covering upper and lower jejunum and upper and lower ileum. Each region scores 0 for no disease, 1 for deposits up to 0.5 cm, 2 for deposits up to 5 cm and 3 for deposits over 5 cm or confluent disease, giving a maximum of 39. The number carries prognostic weight and helps select patients for cytoreduction, with thresholds that depend on the primary tumour, and it is worth saying in the report that CT systematically underestimates it, particularly for deposits under 5 mm and for small bowel serosal disease.

quiz.prompt: Before planned cytoreductive surgery, CT shows moderate ascites, an omental cake, and multiple small nodules along the small bowel serosa with tethering and angulation of the mesentery at its root. What is the most important thing to convey to the surgeon?
quiz.answer: Small bowel and mesenteric root disease, which threatens complete cytoreduction
choices: Small bowel and mesenteric root disease, which threatens complete cytoreduction
The volume of ascites, which is the strongest predictor of the operative result
The omental cake, which is removed at omentectomy and rarely alters the plan
That CT overstates disease burden, so the index will fall at the laparotomy
quiz.explain: Survival after cytoreduction depends more than anything on whether the resection can be complete, so the report should be organised around the findings that make completeness unlikely. Diffuse small bowel serosal disease is the classic one, because the surgeon cannot strip every loop and still leave a functioning gut; retraction at the mesenteric root, encasement of the superior mesenteric vessels, and disease at the hepatoduodenal ligament or porta hepatis carry the same weight. Ascites is common and by itself decides little. The omental cake is real disease but is resected as a block. The fourth option inverts the truth that matters most in this setting: CT underestimates peritoneal burden, especially miliary deposits, which is why diffusion-weighted MRI and staging laparoscopy are used when the decision is close.

quiz.prompt: A man has a slowly distending abdomen. CT shows loculated low-attenuation material with fine septa and curvilinear calcification, scalloping the liver and spleen, with small bowel loops held centrally and posteriorly rather than floating. The appendix is expanded and filled with mucin.
quiz.answer: Mucinous spread from an appendiceal neoplasm; refer for peritonectomy
choices: Mucinous spread from an appendiceal neoplasm; refer for peritonectomy
Simple ascites from portal hypertension; look for cirrhosis and varices
Tuberculous peritonitis; send fluid for culture and start antituberculous drugs
Ovarian carcinomatosis; the appendiceal finding is an incidental mucocele
quiz.explain: Mucin does not behave like fluid, and the CT says so in three ways. It loculates and septates instead of layering; it is viscous enough to indent the liver and spleen; and it displaces bowel rather than letting it float, so the loops sit centrally and posteriorly instead of drifting anteriorly as they do in true ascites. Add a distended mucin-filled appendix and the source is announced, since most pseudomyxoma arises from a ruptured low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm. Calcification within the material supports it further. Treatment is complete cytoreduction with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy in a specialist centre, and long survival is possible, so the referral matters. In a woman the ovaries are often involved secondarily, so an ovarian mass in this setting does not settle where the disease began.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old from a country with a high incidence of tuberculosis has ascites, peritoneal thickening and omental infiltration, and a raised CA-125. Give the CT features that would move you towards tuberculosis rather than peritoneal carcinomatosis.
quiz.answer: Smooth, regular, thin peritoneal enhancement rather than discrete nodular implants, ascites of higher attenuation than water because of its protein and cell content, and lymph nodes with low-attenuation necrotic centres and rim enhancement; ileocaecal thickening and splenic lesions support it further.
quiz.explain: These two diseases overlap almost completely in their clinical presentation, and CA-125 is raised in both, so the imaging has to carry the discrimination. Tuberculous peritonitis tends to thicken the peritoneum smoothly and uniformly with avid thin enhancement, produce ascites denser than water because it is proteinaceous and cellular, and give nodes with caseous low-attenuation centres and enhancing rims, particularly in the mesenteric and peripancreatic stations. Carcinomatosis favours discrete nodules and plaques, irregular thickening, scalloping of solid organ surfaces and nodes that enhance homogeneously. Neither pattern is diagnostic, and the omental caking of the fibrotic form of tuberculosis is a well-known trap. The safe report names the features on both sides and asks for tissue or fluid, because the treatments could hardly be further apart.

quiz.prompt: The same appearance of increased mesenteric fat attenuation is reported twice in one clinic: once in a patient with decompensated cirrhosis and hypoalbuminaemia, and once in a patient with weight loss and 2 cm mesenteric nodes. How should it be handled in each?
quiz.answer: Attribute it to oedema in the first; pursue lymphoma or deposits in the second
choices: Attribute it to oedema in the first; pursue lymphoma or deposits in the second
Attribute it to panniculitis in both; a follow-up scan at one year will suffice
Attribute it to oedema in both; the nodes are reacting to the fat inflammation
Biopsy the mesentery in the first; observe the second, since nodes are common
quiz.explain: Hazy mesenteric fat is a finding with a wide differential and almost no specificity on its own, so it must be read against the patient. The causes group into oedema from cirrhosis, cardiac failure, hypoalbuminaemia or venous and lymphatic obstruction; inflammation from pancreatitis, diverticulitis or mesenteric panniculitis; haemorrhage after trauma or in an anticoagulated patient; and tumour, particularly lymphoma, carcinoid with its desmoplastic reaction, and carcinomatosis. The nodes are the most useful modifier. Small nodes with surrounding preserved fat fit an inflammatory or oedematous cause, whereas nodes above about a centimetre in short axis, a discrete mass, or vascular encasement should not be dismissed as panniculitis. A calcified spiculated mesenteric mass with tethering of adjacent bowel is a different pattern again and points at carcinoid.

quiz.prompt: A well 60-year-old has an incidental fat-attenuation mass at the root of the small bowel mesentery containing several 4 mm nodes, with preserved fat immediately around the vessels and nodes and a thin hyperattenuating rim around the whole lesion. The mesenteric vessels are patent and undisplaced.
quiz.answer: Sclerosing mesenteritis; interval imaging rather than biopsy at this stage
choices: Sclerosing mesenteritis; interval imaging rather than biopsy at this stage
Mesenteric lymphoma; arrange a core biopsy of the mesenteric mass promptly
Carcinoid deposit; arrange somatostatin receptor imaging and small bowel MR
Peritoneal carcinomatosis; search for a gastrointestinal or ovarian primary
quiz.explain: Two features do the work here. The fat ring sign, where a halo of normal fat is preserved immediately around the vessels and nodes within the mass, and the pseudocapsule, a thin dense rim demarcating the lesion from surrounding fat, together favour sclerosing mesenteritis strongly. Lymphoma behaves differently: it encases and displaces vessels, obliterates perivascular fat, and gives nodes larger than a centimetre. Carcinoid produces a spiculated, frequently calcified soft tissue mass with retraction and tethering of adjacent loops, and it is a soft tissue mass rather than a fat-attenuation one. Most cases of sclerosing mesenteritis are incidental and stable, which is why interval imaging is a reasonable first move in a well patient, but a minority accompany lymphoma or IgG4-related disease, so a lesion that grows or changes character earns tissue.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the peritoneal spaces a leak from a perforated appendix passes through as it ascends on the right.
quiz.answer: right-iliac-fossa right-paracolic-gutter hepatorenal-recess right-subphrenic-space
quiz.explain: The right paracolic gutter is deeper than the left and runs uninterrupted from the iliac fossa to the subhepatic region, so fluid arising on the right ascends freely with respiratory and postural movement and reaches the hepatorenal recess, which is the most dependent part of the upper abdomen in a supine patient, and then the subphrenic space. On the left the phrenicocolic ligament interrupts the gutter and blunts that ascent, which is one reason left-sided collections behave less predictably. Knowing this path tells you where to hunt for an abscess after appendicitis, and the same anatomy explains the classic sites of peritoneal deposit in carcinomatosis: the pouch of Douglas, the right subphrenic space and paracolic gutter, the sigmoid mesocolon and the ileocaecal region at the end of the small bowel mesentery.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old woman with vomiting has a small bowel loop passing below the inguinal ligament and medial to a flattened femoral vein. The neck of the defect measures 8 mm, the herniated loop is thick-walled and there is fluid in the sac. What follows from the site and the neck?
quiz.answer: A femoral hernia with a tight neck; the strangulation risk demands urgent repair
choices: A femoral hernia with a tight neck; the strangulation risk demands urgent repair
A direct inguinal hernia; attempted reduction in the department is appropriate
An indirect inguinal hernia; elective repair on a routine operating list is fine
An obturator hernia; the loop lies between pectineus and obturator externus here
quiz.explain: Site is decided by relations, not by where the lump appears. A femoral hernia passes below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein, which it commonly flattens, through a ring bounded medially by the lacunar ligament, and that rigid narrow neck is why femoral hernias strangulate so often and why they should be repaired promptly rather than listed routinely. Inguinal hernias emerge above and medial to the pubic tubercle: direct ones through the posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, indirect ones through the deep ring lateral to those vessels. An obturator hernia takes a different route through the obturator canal and lies between pectineus and obturator externus; it too strangulates readily, and it should be looked for specifically in a thin elderly woman with unexplained obstruction.

quiz.prompt: A hernia contains a loop of small bowel that cannot be reduced, with dilated bowel proximal to it. Give the single CT observation that separates incarceration from strangulation, and two further findings that support the latter.
quiz.answer: Reduced or absent enhancement of the herniated bowel wall is the observation that marks strangulation, since incarceration is only mechanical irreducibility; supporting findings include fluid within the sac with fat stranding around the neck, mural thickening, mesenteric vascular engorgement and pneumatosis.
quiz.explain: Incarceration is a mechanical statement, meaning the contents will not go back, and an incarcerated hernia can sit unchanged for years. Strangulation is a vascular statement, and the wall is where you read it: enhancement that is reduced compared with non-herniated loops on the same acquisition, judged against a neighbouring loop rather than against a remembered attenuation, is the finding that changes the timing of the operation. Everything else is supportive. Fluid in the sac and haziness of the fat at the neck indicate venous congestion, mural thickening and mesenteric vascular engorgement follow it, and pneumatosis in the herniated loop is late and grave. A narrow neck raises the risk, which is why femoral and obturator hernias declare themselves this way more often than wide-necked incisional ones.

quiz.prompt: An anticoagulated 75-year-old with a week of violent coughing has a tender abdominal wall mass. Unenhanced CT shows a 9 cm haematoma in the right rectus muscle extending across the midline into the space in front of the bladder. Explain the anatomy that permits that spread, and say what you would do next.
quiz.answer: Below the arcuate line the posterior rectus sheath is absent, so blood is no longer confined by it or by the linea alba and tracks across the midline into the preperitoneal and prevesical space; the next step is an arterial phase acquisition to look for active extravasation from the inferior epigastric artery, which would be treated by embolisation.
quiz.explain: A rectus sheath haematoma usually comes from tearing of the inferior epigastric artery or its perforators, in an anticoagulated patient, after coughing, straining or an injection. Above the arcuate line the intact posterior sheath and the linea alba hold the blood on one side, so the collection is spindle-shaped and confined to the muscle. Below the arcuate line there is no posterior sheath, and blood spreads into the preperitoneal and prevesical space, crosses the midline, and can become very large, which is why the haemoglobin can fall dramatically and the appearance can be mistaken for intraperitoneal haemorrhage. A fluid-fluid level within the haematoma reflects an anticoagulated patient still bleeding. Most cases are managed with reversal and support; contrast extravasation on the arterial phase is what selects the patient for embolisation.

nodes.title: Rectal Cancer: MR Staging, Restaging and Perianal Fistula
nodes.goal: Stage and restage a rectal cancer on high-resolution MR, report the circumferential resection margin and extramural venous invasion in terms that change treatment, and map a perianal fistula for the surgeon.

quiz.prompt: A mid-rectal tumour arrives for staging. The axial T2 stack was planned straight through the pelvis, in the same plane as the rest of the abdominal series, but the tumour-bearing segment runs obliquely. The outer border of the muscularis propria looks blurred and indistinct all the way round the tumour. What should happen before you commit to a T stage?
quiz.answer: Re-plan the high-resolution T2 stack perpendicular to the long axis of the tumour-bearing segment and repeat it
choices: Re-plan the high-resolution T2 stack perpendicular to the long axis of the tumour-bearing segment and repeat it
Give intravenous gadolinium and stage the tumour from fat-suppressed post-contrast images through the same block
Add fat suppression to the existing axial T2 stack so the mesorectal fat is darkened around the outer muscle border
Accept the images as acquired and take the measurements from the sagittal T2 sequence, which crosses the wall twice
quiz.explain: Obliquity is the commonest avoidable cause of overstaging. When the slice cuts the wall at an angle, the muscularis propria is partial-volumed with the mesorectal fat and its outer border smudges, so a T2 tumour reads as T3 and a shallow T3 reads as deep. The fix is geometric, not chemical: plan a small field-of-view T2 turbo spin echo, about 3 mm thick, perpendicular to the long axis of the bowel at the tumour, using the sagittal image to set the angle. Fat suppression is deliberately avoided here, because the contrast between intermediate-signal tumour, dark muscle and bright mesorectal fat is exactly what you are reading. Gadolinium adds nothing to T staging in the MERCURY-style protocol. For a low tumour, add an oblique coronal plane parallel to the anal canal to see the sphincters.

quiz.prompt: A mid-rectal cancer extends 4 mm beyond the muscularis propria. The deepest tumour edge lies 0.9 mm from the mesorectal fascia. There is no venous invasion and no node meets malignant criteria. How should the margin be reported, and what does it drive?
quiz.answer: Predicted CRM involved at 0.9 mm, which moves the patient towards neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before surgery
choices: Predicted CRM involved at 0.9 mm, which moves the patient towards neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before surgery
Predicted CRM clear at 0.9 mm, since involvement is called when tumour actually reaches and touches the fascia
Predicted CRM clear, because it is the T category that selects neoadjuvant therapy and this tumour is still T3
Predicted CRM indeterminate, so the decision should be deferred until the resected specimen has been reported
quiz.explain: The mesorectal fascia is the plane the surgeon dissects in a total mesorectal excision, so the shortest distance from any tumour-bearing structure to that fascia predicts whether the specimen will have a positive margin. One millimetre or less is reported as involved; many multidisciplinary teams treat 1 to 2 mm as threatened and manage it the same way. The MERCURY study established that this MR measurement matches the pathological margin closely enough to select treatment before an operation is done, which is why margin, not T category alone, drives neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Waiting for histology defeats the purpose: once the specimen is out, the chance to downstage the margin has gone. Note that the measurement is taken to the nearest tumour-bearing structure of any kind, which is the point of the next item.

quiz.prompt: On T2 images, tumour signal of the same intermediate intensity as the primary tracks along a vessel running out of the tumour into the mesorectal fat. The vessel has lost its flow void, its contour is nodular and its calibre exceeds that of the matching vein on the other side. The primary is otherwise mrT3b with a margin of 6 mm. What does this add to the report?
quiz.answer: Extramural venous invasion, which independently predicts distant relapse and strengthens the case for systemic therapy
choices: Extramural venous invasion, which independently predicts distant relapse and strengthens the case for systemic therapy
Peritumoural desmoplastic reaction, a common finding at the invasive edge that does not change the risk category
Direct invasion of a mesorectal structure, which upgrades the tumour from mrT3b to mrT4b and alters the operation
A mesorectal tumour deposit, which should be counted and reported within the nodal category rather than separately
quiz.explain: The MR signature of extramural venous invasion is tumour-signal material inside a vein that the tumour has reached, with expansion of the calibre, loss of the flow void and an irregular or nodular contour. It is an independent adverse prognostic factor, associated with synchronous and metachronous distant metastases and with worse disease-free survival, and it is often what tips a borderline case towards neoadjuvant and adjuvant systemic treatment. It does not change the T category, which is a measure of depth. It is also not a tumour deposit, which is a discrete nodule of tumour in the mesorectum without a nodal or vascular structure. One practical trap: a tumour-filled vein counts as tumour for margin purposes, so if it approaches within a millimetre of the mesorectal fascia the predicted margin is involved even when the primary itself is nowhere near it.

quiz.prompt: A mid-rectal cancer has three mesorectal nodes: one measures 4 mm in short axis and is round with a smooth border and uniform signal; one measures 6 mm with an irregular border and mottled internal signal; one measures 10 mm and is smooth-bordered and homogeneous. Applying the 2016 ESGAR consensus criteria, how should these be reported?
quiz.answer: The 6 mm and the 10 mm nodes are malignant; the 4 mm node would need all three morphological features
choices: The 6 mm and the 10 mm nodes are malignant; the 4 mm node would need all three morphological features
Only the 10 mm node is malignant, because below 9 mm a mesorectal node is reported as reactive
Only the 6 mm node is malignant, because a smooth homogeneous node is benign whatever its size
All three are malignant, because a round mesorectal node is sufficient evidence of tumour spread
quiz.explain: The 2016 ESGAR consensus grades a mesorectal node on short axis plus three morphological features: round shape, irregular border and heterogeneous internal signal. At 9 mm or more the node is called malignant regardless of morphology. Between 5 and 8 mm it needs at least two of the three features. Below 5 mm it needs all three. So the 6 mm node with an irregular border and mottled signal qualifies on two features, the 10 mm node qualifies on size alone, and the small round but otherwise bland node does not. Be honest about the accuracy of nodal MR: it is the weakest part of rectal staging, which is one reason the field shifted towards the circumferential margin and extramural venous invasion as the decision drivers. Report node counts and location, but do not let a borderline node override a clear margin.

quiz.prompt: An upper rectal cancer on the anterior wall extends beyond the muscularis propria, and on sagittal and oblique axial T2 images tumour signal reaches and thickens the anterior peritoneal reflection at its insertion onto the bowel. The bladder and seminal vesicles remain separated by preserved fat. What stage do you report, and why does it matter?
quiz.answer: mrT4a: the visceral peritoneum is breached, which carries an added risk of peritoneal relapse
choices: mrT4a: the visceral peritoneum is breached, which carries an added risk of peritoneal relapse
mrT3d: the extramural spread is deep, but the peritoneum is not a structure counted in T staging
mrT4b: contact with the peritoneal reflection counts as invasion of an adjacent pelvic organ
mrT2: the peritoneal reflection lies outside the bowel wall, so the muscularis propria is intact
quiz.explain: Anterior upper rectal tumours are the ones where the peritoneal reflection matters, because above the reflection the rectum has a serosal surface and below it the mesorectum is the only barrier. Tumour that reaches, thickens or nodularly elevates the reflection is mrT4a, invasion of the visceral peritoneum, and it changes the conversation: peritoneal breach adds a route of spread that the mesorectal envelope does not contain, and these patients are watched for peritoneal disease. T4b is reserved for invasion of an adjacent organ or structure, such as prostate, vagina, bladder or pelvic sidewall, and here the fat planes are preserved. The measurement of extramural depth still belongs in the report, but depth cannot substitute for the peritoneal finding. Note also that above the reflection there is no mesorectal fascia anteriorly, so the margin concept is applied differently at that level.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks after long-course chemoradiotherapy, a patient is being considered for organ preservation. The tumour bed is mostly low-signal fibrosis, but a 9 mm focus of intermediate T2 signal sits within the scar, bright on high b-value diffusion images with a correspondingly dark ADC. Endoscopy shows a small persistent ulcer. What follows?
quiz.answer: This is residual tumour: the case fails clinical complete response and resection should be planned
choices: This is residual tumour: the case fails clinical complete response and resection should be planned
This is post-radiation inflammation: it is compatible with complete response and can be rescanned at 3 months
This is T2 shine-through on the diffusion images, so the surrounding fibrosis should settle the decision
This ambiguity cannot be resolved, so the pre-treatment stage should determine the operation offered
quiz.explain: A clinical complete response has three legs and needs all of them: a flat white scar with telangiectasia and no ulcer or nodule at endoscopy, no palpable abnormality on digital examination, and MRI showing only low-signal fibrosis without restricted diffusion. A discrete intermediate-signal focus that restricts diffusion, with a low ADC rather than shine-through, alongside a persistent ulcer, is residual disease until proved otherwise. Watch and wait is a legitimate pathway, but only for the complete responders and only inside a programme with intensive surveillance, typically three-monthly for the first two years, since most regrowth appears in that window and is usually still salvageable by surgery. Offering it to a partial responder converts a curable cancer into a missed one. When the scan and the endoscopy disagree, the more suspicious finding wins.

quiz.prompt: On the oblique axial T2 images of a mid-rectal cancer, the deepest edge of the primary tumour lies 4.2 mm from the mesorectal fascia. A tumour-filled vein tracks laterally and comes within 0.8 mm of the fascia, and a node meeting malignant criteria sits 6.0 mm from it. State the distance you should report as the predicted circumferential resection margin, in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The predicted circumferential resection margin is the shortest distance from the mesorectal fascia to any tumour-bearing structure, and that means the primary, a tumour-filled vein, a malignant node or a tumour deposit, whichever is closest. Here the vein is nearest at 0.8 mm, so the margin is reported as 0.8 mm and, being 1 mm or less, as involved. Radiologists most often go wrong by measuring only from the primary and reporting a comfortable margin while an extramural venous invasion track quietly abuts the fascia. Say in the report which structure the measurement came from and where on the clock face it lies, because that tells the surgeon whether the plane is threatened where it can be worked around or where it cannot. A margin of 1 to 2 mm is widely treated as threatened and managed as if involved.

quiz.prompt: Beyond the outer border of the muscularis propria, tumour signal extends 3 mm anteriorly, 8 mm laterally and 11 mm posteriorly on the oblique axial images. State the extramural depth of invasion you should report, in millimetres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Extramural depth is a single number: the greatest perpendicular distance from the outer border of the muscularis propria to the deepest edge of tumour, so you take the deepest point rather than an average. Eleven millimetres puts this tumour in the mrT3c band, using the widely applied subdivision of T3a under 1 mm, T3b 1 to 5 mm, T3c 5 to 15 mm and T3d over 15 mm. The subdivision earns its place because depth beyond about 5 mm carries prognostic weight comparable to nodal status and feeds the risk stratification that selects neoadjuvant treatment. The measurement trap is desmoplasia: fine low-signal spicules radiating into the fat are fibrous reaction and should not be measured, while a broad nodular intermediate-signal front is tumour and should. When you cannot separate the two, say so and let the margin do the work.

quiz.prompt: MRI of a perianal fistula shows a track leaving the anal canal at the 6 o'clock position, crossing both the internal and external sphincters into the right ischioanal fossa. In that fossa there is a 2 cm collection with an enhancing rim, and a secondary track runs anteriorly from it. Give the St James University Hospital MRI grade as a whole number from 1 to 5.
quiz.explain: The St James grading maps MR findings onto surgical difficulty in five steps. Grade 1 is a simple linear intersphincteric track; grade 2 is intersphincteric with an abscess or a secondary track; grade 3 is an uncomplicated transsphincteric track; grade 4 is transsphincteric with an abscess or secondary track in the ischioanal or ischiorectal fossa; grade 5 is supralevator or translevator disease. Crossing the external sphincter makes this transsphincteric, and the fossa collection with its secondary extension takes it to grade 4. The grade is useful because grades 1 and 3 can usually be laid open or treated with a simple sphincter-sparing repair, while an undrained collection or an unrecognised secondary track is the standard reason a fistula recurs after apparently successful surgery. Always state the level of the internal opening on the clock face too.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks after chemoradiotherapy the tumour bed is mostly low-signal fibrosis but contains a 12 mm area of very high T2 signal with the glassy quality of mucin. The patient is being considered for organ preservation. State what you should report about that area and what has to happen next.
quiz.answer: Report it as a mucinous area within the treated tumour bed and say that MRI cannot separate acellular mucin, which is a good response, from mucin containing viable tumour cells, so it must not be called a complete response on imaging alone; endoscopy with biopsy and digital examination has to decide.
quiz.explain: Pools of acellular mucin are a recognised and generally favourable consequence of chemoradiotherapy, and they are very bright on T2. The difficulty is that mucin containing scattered viable cells looks the same, and diffusion imaging does not rescue you because mucin itself can be bright on high b-value images. The tumour regression grade scale was built for fibrosis versus residual tumour signal and applies poorly to a mucinous bed, so grading it mrTRG1 because there is no intermediate signal would be a false reassurance. Report the mucin, state the uncertainty explicitly, and hand the decision to clinical assessment. Remember also that mucinous rectal cancers respond less well overall, so a mucinous appearance before treatment should already have lowered your expectation of a complete response.

quiz.prompt: A tumour whose lower edge is 2 cm from the anal verge extends through the internal sphincter, while the intersphincteric fat plane and the external sphincter remain intact on the oblique coronal images. State what you should report about the sphincter complex and how it shapes the operation offered.
quiz.answer: Report that the tumour breaches the internal sphincter but stops at the intersphincteric plane, with the external sphincter and levators uninvolved, so a sphincter-preserving intersphincteric resection is feasible rather than an extralevator abdominoperineal excision.
quiz.explain: In the low rectum the mesorectum tapers to nothing, so the mesorectal fascia stops being the relevant margin and the sphincter complex takes over. What the surgeon needs is a statement of how far outwards the tumour has gone: confined to the wall, through the internal sphincter but not across the intersphincteric plane, into the external sphincter or puborectalis, or beyond into the ischioanal fat or levator. The first two allow an intersphincteric resection with a coloanal anastomosis; the last two mean an extralevator abdominoperineal excision with a permanent stoma. This is only assessable on an oblique coronal plane aligned parallel to the anal canal, which is why that sequence is added for every low tumour. Give the distance from the anal verge and the internal opening of the plane you think is threatened.

quiz.prompt: A fistula track leaves the intersphincteric space, arches upward over the top of the puborectalis sling, then turns down through the levator plate into the ischioanal fossa to reach the skin. State which Parks category this fits and why laying the track open would be the wrong operation.
quiz.answer: It is a suprasphincteric fistula, and because the track passes above the puborectalis, laying it open would divide the entire external sphincter and the puborectalis and leave the patient incontinent, so it is managed with a seton or a sphincter-sparing repair instead.
quiz.explain: Parks divides perianal fistulas by their relation to the sphincter complex: intersphincteric tracks stay between internal and external sphincters; transsphincteric tracks cross the external sphincter into the ischioanal fossa; suprasphincteric tracks run up over the puborectalis before descending through the levator; extrasphincteric tracks begin above the levator, from pelvic sepsis, Crohn disease or an iatrogenic injury, and enter the anal canal from outside the sphincters altogether. The classification is not academic, because how much sphincter would have to be divided determines whether the track can be laid open at all. The radiologist's job is to state the internal opening, the course relative to both sphincters and the levator, and every secondary track or collection, since undrained sepsis is the usual reason a repair fails.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these post-chemoradiotherapy appearances of the treated tumour bed from the most complete response to the least, as the mrTRG scale runs from grade 1 to grade 5.
quiz.answer: fibrosis-only dense-fibrosis-with-minimal-residual-signal over-half-fibrosis-with-visible-tumour-signal little-fibrosis-mostly-tumour-signal tumour-signal-unchanged-or-larger
quiz.explain: The MR tumour regression grade, adapted from the pathological Mandard scale and validated in the MERCURY work, reads the treated bed as a proportion of dark fibrosis to intermediate tumour signal. Grade 1 is fibrosis only with no tumour signal; grade 2 is dense fibrosis with a barely perceptible residual focus; grade 3 is more than half fibrosis with clearly visible tumour signal; grade 4 is scant fibrosis with mostly tumour; grade 5 is no change or growth. Grades 1 and 2 constitute a good response and carry better disease-free survival, and they are the group in which organ preservation is even discussed. Two caveats to carry: interobserver agreement is only moderate, so read it with diffusion imaging and with the endoscopic findings, and scan at around eight weeks, since fibrosis is still maturing before that.

nodes.title: The Acute Abdomen
nodes.goal: Read an acute abdominal CT for free gas, obstruction and inflammation, find the transition point, and tell mechanical obstruction from ileus.

quiz.prompt: A supine abdominal radiograph is taken on the intensive care unit for distension. Gas outlines both the inner and the outer surface of a loop of bowel in the right upper quadrant, and a thin vertical line runs to the right of the midline from the liver towards the umbilicus. What do these two findings together indicate?
choices: Free intraperitoneal gas, visible on a supine film
Gas within the portal venous branches of the liver
Gas confined to the wall of the ascending colon
Colon interposed between liver and diaphragm
quiz.answer: Free intraperitoneal gas, visible on a supine film
quiz.explain: Both signs need gas outside the lumen. Rigler's sign is gas on both sides of the bowel wall, which can only happen when free gas lies against the serosa while luminal gas lies against the mucosa; the vertical line is the falciform ligament, visible because free gas has outlined it. That both appear on a supine film matters, because a supine film is often all a ventilated patient can manage and the classic erect view is unavailable. Portal venous gas is branching and lies within the liver, reaching its periphery, rather than tracing a bowel wall. Pneumatosis alone gives a curvilinear lucency in the wall but produces no falciform sign, and it is exactly what Rigler's sign is contrasted against. Colonic interposition, Chilaiditi's appearance, mimics free gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm on an erect film, but haustral folds run through the lucency and it does not outline anything from outside. Where doubt remains, CT settles it, and a left lateral decubitus film is the fallback where CT is not to hand.

quiz.prompt: A CT for abdominal distension measures the small bowel at 2.6 cm, the transverse colon at 7.2 cm and the caecum at 9.4 cm, each outer wall to outer wall. Taking the conventional 3, 6 and 9 cm calibre limits for those three segments, how many of the measurements exceed their own limit? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Small bowel at 2.6 cm is within its 3 cm limit; transverse colon at 7.2 cm exceeds 6; caecum at 9.4 cm exceeds 9. Two of the three. The caecum is the one to watch: it is the widest part of the colon, and by Laplace's law wall tension at a given pressure rises with radius, so it is where a distal large bowel obstruction perforates when the ileocaecal valve stays competent and turns the colon into a closed loop. Treat the numbers as a prompt to look rather than as a diagnosis. Calibre says only that bowel is distended; whether that distension is mechanical depends on finding a point where the calibre changes, and a colon dilated evenly through to the rectum is far more likely to be ileus or acute colonic pseudo-obstruction than a blockage.

quiz.prompt: A CT is reported for a suspected closed-loop small bowel obstruction. Put these steps of the search in the order that first identifies the closed loop and then judges whether it is still viable.
quiz.answer: dilated-loops first-transition second-transition mesenteric-whirl wall-enhancement
quiz.explain: Recognise dilated small bowel; track it distally to the point where calibre drops, which is the first transition; then look immediately around that point for a second transition, because a closed loop is bowel obstructed at two points close together, usually where a band or a hernial neck catches it. The C-shaped or U-shaped loop between them has its own mesentery, and following that mesentery back shows the vessels converging and twisting, the whirl. Only then ask about viability, on wall enhancement, mural thickening, mesenteric fluid and venous engorgement. The order is not arbitrary: viability is judged on the loop you have identified, and a reader who starts by hunting for signs of ischaemia across the whole abdomen finds thickened bowel everywhere and localises nothing. A closed loop is the configuration that strangulates, so finding the second transition is what converts an overnight obstruction into a theatre case.

quiz.prompt: Four days after an open colectomy a patient is distended and not passing flatus. CT shows small bowel loops to 3.4 cm, several air-fluid levels and mildly oedematous folds, and no point at which the bowel calibre changes. Which single further observation would most strongly support ileus rather than mechanical obstruction?
choices: Gas and faecal residue reaching the rectum
Fluid levels at different heights in one loop
Circumferential thickening of the dilated wall
A collapsed segment of distal small bowel
quiz.answer: Gas and faecal residue reaching the rectum
quiz.explain: The absence of a transition point is a negative finding, and negatives are weak: a transition can be subtle, and a low-grade or intermittent obstruction hides one. The positive finding is that content is still moving the whole way through. Gas and residue in a non-dilated rectum say the lumen is patent from duodenum to anus, which no complete mechanical obstruction permits. A collapsed segment of distal small bowel is the opposite observation, and is precisely what a transition point looks like. Differential air-fluid levels within a single loop have been taught for decades as a sign of obstruction; they are neither sensitive nor specific enough to decide a case, but they lean towards a mechanical cause rather than away from it. Wall thickening happens in both and comments on oedema or perfusion, not on mechanism. Postoperative ileus settles with time and correction of electrolytes and opiates; the reason to keep looking is that early postoperative mechanical obstruction, from adhesions or an internal hernia, is indistinguishable at the bedside.

quiz.prompt: CT in a patient with three days of vomiting shows dilated jejunal and proximal ileal loops. In the 20 cm of ileum immediately upstream of a calibre change there is mottled, particulate material mixed with gas that resembles colonic content. What does that material signify?
choices: Stasis in obstructed small bowel, marking the level
Ischaemia of the wall of the obstructed segment
Reflux of colonic content across the ileocaecal valve
Bacterial overgrowth producing a functional ileus
quiz.answer: Stasis in obstructed small bowel, marking the level
quiz.explain: This is the small bowel faeces sign: undigested residue mixed with gas from bacterial fermentation, in a segment where water has been resorbed during prolonged stasis. Its practical value is topographic. It tends to sit just proximal to the transition, so on a study where the calibre change is hard to see, following the mottled material distally leads to it. It says the obstruction has been present for a while rather than that it is severe, and it appears in chronic partial obstruction too. It is not a sign of ischaemia: that question is answered by wall enhancement, mesenteric fluid and vascular engorgement, and a reader who takes the faeces sign as reassurance or as alarm has read it for the wrong thing. Nor is it retrograde colonic content, which does not cross a competent ileocaecal valve in this fashion.

quiz.prompt: A closed-loop small bowel obstruction is confirmed on CT. The loop is thick-walled, there is fluid in the adjacent mesentery, the mesenteric vessels converging on the twist are engorged, and one part of the loop takes up less contrast than the rest of the bowel on the portal venous phase. Which of these observations is the most specific for strangulation?
choices: Enhancement of the wall reduced against other loops
Free fluid tracking through the adjacent mesentery
Circumferential thickening of the obstructed wall
Engorgement of the vessels running to the twist
quiz.answer: Enhancement of the wall reduced against other loops
quiz.explain: Reduced or absent mural enhancement is the sign that speaks directly to perfusion, and it is the most specific of the four for strangulation; where it is unequivocal, the bowel in question is at risk now. The other three are sensitive and unspecific. Mesenteric fluid, mural thickening and vascular engorgement all follow venous congestion, which begins long before arterial supply fails and is present in plenty of obstructions that recover without resection. The trap is the reverse of the usual one: their absence is reassuring, but their presence is not damning, and a report that lists them without commenting on enhancement has answered the easy question. Two cautions on the enhancement itself. Compare like with like, against non-obstructed loops on the same phase, since a hypotensive patient enhances poorly everywhere; and remember that a thin, poorly enhancing wall can look deceptively normal on a single phase, which is why the finding is sought on the portal venous phase where mural enhancement is at its most uniform.

quiz.prompt: A CT in a 26-year-old with right iliac fossa pain shows an appendix of 7 mm outer diameter with a normal thin wall, no periappendiceal fat stranding, no free fluid, and gas throughout its lumen. The registrar wants to report appendicitis on the diameter alone. Set out why the diameter by itself will not carry that report, and say what you would look for instead.
quiz.answer: A diameter above about 6 mm is sensitive but poorly specific: normal appendices are distensible and commonly measure between 6 and 10 mm, particularly when gas-filled, so 7 mm on its own separates nothing. The findings that make the diagnosis are the secondary ones, and they should be sought together: mural thickening with hyperenhancement, periappendiceal fat stranding, free fluid, an appendicolith, thickening of the adjacent caecal apex, and failure of the lumen to fill with gas or with oral contrast. An appendix that is gas-filled along its length, thin-walled and surrounded by clean fat is very unlikely to be inflamed whatever its calibre, and a report should say so rather than hedge.
quiz.explain: The 6 mm figure entered practice from graded-compression ultrasound, where the appendix is compressed and a distended one cannot be flattened. Transposed to CT, where nothing compresses the appendix, the same number keeps its sensitivity and loses much of its specificity, because a normal appendix filled with gas or with a little fluid readily exceeds it. That is why every published CT series reads diameter alongside secondary signs, and why the confident negative report rests on gas through the lumen, a thin wall and clean surrounding fat rather than on a measurement. The corollary matters for the report a surgeon can act on: hedging over a normal-looking appendix at 7 mm generates observation, repeat imaging and sometimes an operation, all of which cost more than a clear statement supported by the findings actually present.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with free gas remote from the colon and free fluid across the peritoneum; at laparoscopy there is generalised purulent contamination with no faeculent soiling. Which modified Hinchey stage does that describe? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The modified, imaging-based Hinchey scheme runs: stage I, inflammation confined to the pericolic tissues, with Ia a phlegmon and Ib a pericolic abscess; stage II, a pelvic, distant intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal abscess; stage III, generalised purulent peritonitis; stage IV, generalised faecal peritonitis. Purulent contamination without faecal soiling is III. The grades are not a taxonomy for its own sake. I and II are usually managed with antibiotics and, where the collection is large enough to warrant it, percutaneous drainage; III and IV go to theatre, and whether the peritoneum contains pus or faeces separates the two operative grades and tracks with mortality. Free gas by itself does not fix the stage: a small locule beside an inflamed segment sits comfortably within stage I, and it is the distribution of gas and fluid, read against the state of the patient, that says how far the perforation has spread.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old has left iliac fossa pain. CT shows sigmoid wall thickening with numerous diverticula and pericolic fat stranding. Which additional finding would shift the reading furthest towards carcinoma rather than diverticulitis?
choices: Enlarged pericolic nodes beside a short thick segment
Fluid tracking at the root of the sigmoid mesentery
Engorged vasa recta feeding the thickened segment
Inflammation out of proportion to the wall thickening
quiz.answer: Enlarged pericolic nodes beside a short thick segment
quiz.explain: The two diseases share the sigmoid, the wall thickening and, often enough, the diverticula, and a carcinoma can perforate and inflame exactly as diverticulitis does. The features that discriminate are the length of the abnormal segment and the company it keeps. A short segment with shouldered, abrupt margins and enlarged pericolic nodes is the carcinoma pattern; a long segment, more than about 10 cm, with fat stranding out of proportion to the degree of mural thickening, engorged vasa recta and fluid at the root of the sigmoid mesentery is the diverticulitis pattern. The three distractors are all diverticulitis findings, which is what makes them tempting to a reader who has already settled on the diagnosis. Carry away the limit of the exercise: none of these signs is decisive, CT cannot exclude a carcinoma hidden in an inflamed segment, and that is why an episode of complicated diverticulitis is followed by colonoscopy once the inflammation has resolved.

quiz.prompt: Five days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy a well, afebrile patient with a soft abdomen has an erect chest radiograph for a cough, and gas is seen beneath both hemidiaphragms. Explain how you would interpret that film, and what would make you treat the same finding as a leak.
