quiz.answer: Not on the CT alone, because non-functioning adenomas are common at this size and the true source may be the other gland or bilateral hyperplasia, so adrenal vein sampling is needed to lateralise aldosterone secretion before adrenalectomy.
quiz.explain: Adrenal incidentalomas are found in around 4 per cent of abdominal CT studies and become commoner with age, so the presence of a small nodule beside a positive biochemical screen does not establish that the nodule is the culprit. Bilateral hyperplasia is a frequent cause of primary aldosteronism and may look normal or near normal on CT, and a genuine aldosteronoma can be smaller than the scanner can resolve. Adrenal vein sampling remains the reference standard for lateralisation and regularly contradicts the CT. The recognised exception is a young patient, usually under 35, with florid biochemistry and an unequivocal unilateral adenoma. This is the general lesson of the adrenal: imaging characterises tissue, while function is a separate question answered by an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, plasma metanephrines and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the three acquisitions of a dedicated adrenal washout CT protocol in the order they are obtained during the study.
quiz.answer: unenhanced portal-venous-60-seconds delayed-15-minutes
quiz.explain: The unenhanced series comes first for two reasons: it supplies the baseline value that the absolute washout formula needs, and it can end the study on the spot, because a homogeneous nodule measuring 10 HU or less is already a lipid-rich adenoma and there is no reason to give contrast at all. Building that stopping rule into the protocol spares the patient two further acquisitions. The enhanced phase is acquired at around 60 to 75 seconds, and the delayed phase at 15 minutes. That fifteen minute delay is not arbitrary: the 60 per cent absolute and 40 per cent relative thresholds were derived at it, so acquiring the delay at ten minutes and applying the same numbers will systematically under-call adenomas. Keep the region of interest identical in size and position across all three phases.

nodes.title: Bladder Cancer and VI-RADS
nodes.goal: Assign a VI-RADS category from a multiparametric bladder MRI, defend it when the sequences disagree, and stage urothelial carcinoma beyond the bladder wall and into the upper tract.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old man with painless visible haematuria has a 2.5 cm broad-based tumour on the left lateral bladder wall at cystoscopy. The urologist asks for multiparametric MRI before taking him to theatre. Which management question is the MRI being asked to answer?
quiz.answer: Whether tumour extends into the muscularis propria, since that separates transurethral resection from cystectomy with neoadjuvant chemotherapy
choices: Whether tumour extends into the muscularis propria, since that separates transurethral resection from cystectomy with neoadjuvant chemotherapy
Whether the tumour is high grade, since that separates simple surveillance from a course of intravesical BCG after resection
Whether the histology is urothelial rather than squamous or glandular, since that changes which systemic agents are chosen
Whether residual papillary tumour will be left at the base, since that decides if a second-look resection is required
quiz.explain: Bladder cancer splits into two diseases at one anatomical line. Non-muscle-invasive disease (Ta, Tis, T1) is managed endoscopically with intravesical therapy and surveillance; muscle-invasive disease (T2 and above) earns neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy and radical cystectomy or bladder-preserving chemoradiation. That single question is what VI-RADS was built to answer, and it is the one thing cystoscopy cannot settle, because the scope sees only the luminal surface. Grade and histological subtype come from the pathologist, not from MRI. Residual tumour at the base is a resection-quality question answered by re-resection. And note the sequencing: TURBT itself causes oedema, granulation and enhancement at the base, so the most informative MRI is the one done before the resection, not after it.

quiz.prompt: Your bladder MRI protocol asks patients not to void for one to two hours before the scan. State the degree of bladder filling you are aiming for, and say what goes wrong on the images when the bladder is under-filled and when it is over-filled.
quiz.answer: Aim for moderate distension. An under-filled bladder produces apparent diffuse wall thickening and can hide a small tumour against the crumpled wall; an over-filled bladder stretches and thins the wall, flattens an exophytic tumour against it, and provokes movement from discomfort.
quiz.explain: VI-RADS rests on seeing a continuous low-signal muscularis propria, and that line only behaves predictably in a moderately distended bladder. Empty the bladder and the wall folds on itself: it looks thickened everywhere, a small sessile tumour disappears into the folds, and the dark muscle line becomes impossible to follow. Fill it too far and the wall is stretched thin, a papillary tumour is pressed flat and loses its stalk, and the patient cannot lie still for a diffusion series. The practical instruction is to void, then wait one to two hours, or to drink a measured volume beforehand. If the study is done at either extreme, say so in the report — a VI-RADS category assigned on an under-distended bladder is not the same evidence as one assigned on a good study.

quiz.prompt: A bladder multiparametric MRI is technically good on all three sequences. The T2 structural category is 3, the diffusion-weighted score is 4 and the dynamic contrast-enhanced score is 4. Give the overall VI-RADS category as a single whole number.
quiz.explain: VI-RADS scores each of the three sequences from 1 to 5 and then combines them into one category, but the combination is not an average and not a majority vote. Diffusion is the dominant sequence, with dynamic contrast enhancement second and T2 providing the structural framework. Here diffusion and the dynamic series both say 4, so the overall category is 4 — muscle invasion is likely — and the T2 score of 3 does not pull it down. VI-RADS 4 means the low-signal muscularis propria is breached on the sequences that matter, and it should push the team towards staging for muscle-invasive disease rather than towards a purely endoscopic plan. Most published series use a cut-off of VI-RADS 3 or above to call muscle invasion, gaining sensitivity; a cut-off of 4 or above trades some of that sensitivity for specificity.

quiz.prompt: A 1.8 cm papillary bladder tumour is bright on high b-value diffusion imaging, while the stalk at its base is dark on diffusion and bright on ADC. The low-signal muscularis propria beneath the tumour is unbroken on T2, on diffusion and on the early dynamic images. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: Muscle invasion is unlikely: this reads as VI-RADS 2, and complete transurethral resection with sampling of the base is the appropriate step
choices: Muscle invasion is unlikely: this reads as VI-RADS 2, and complete transurethral resection with sampling of the base is the appropriate step
Muscle invasion is likely: restricted diffusion within the tumour itself makes this VI-RADS 4 regardless of what the muscle line does
Muscle invasion is equivocal: a dark stalk on diffusion is a post-resection change, so the study should be reported as VI-RADS 3
The study is not interpretable: a stalk that is dark on diffusion means the b-value was too low, and the sequence needs repeating
quiz.explain: This is the inchworm sign, and it is one of the most useful patterns in bladder MRI. A papillary tumour has a fibrovascular submucosal stalk. The tumour is cellular and restricts diffusion, so it is bright on high b-value images with a low ADC; the stalk is loose oedematous connective tissue, so it is dark on high b-value images and bright on ADC. The bright cap sitting on a dark base gives the arched look of an inchworm, and its presence tells you the tumour is exophytic on a stalk with the wall beneath it intact — the picture of non-muscle-invasive disease. Restricted diffusion inside a urothelial tumour is expected and says nothing about stage on its own; what matters is whether the dark muscle line is interrupted. Under VI-RADS, an exophytic tumour with a stalk and an intact muscle line scores 1 if under 1 cm and 2 at 1 cm or more.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the tissue planes that a bladder tumour crosses as its T category rises, working from the luminal surface outward.
quiz.answer: urothelium lamina-propria muscularis-propria perivesical-fat prostatic-stroma
quiz.explain: The T categories of bladder cancer are simply a list of the layers a tumour has eaten through. Ta and Tis sit in the urothelium; T1 breaches the basement membrane into the lamina propria; T2 is in the muscularis propria, split into T2a for the inner half and T2b for the outer half; T3 reaches perivesical fat, microscopically as T3a and as a visible extravesical mass as T3b; T4a is direct contiguous invasion of an adjacent organ such as prostatic stroma, seminal vesicles, uterus or vagina, and T4b is pelvic or abdominal wall. Knowing the ladder tells you where imaging is strong and where it is weak. MRI is good at the muscularis propria step, which is the step that changes treatment. It cannot see microscopic perivesical spread, so it cannot reliably separate T2b from T3a — a limitation worth stating in the report rather than papering over.

quiz.prompt: A bladder MRI is excellent on T2 and on the dynamic contrast series, but the diffusion-weighted images are wrecked by susceptibility artefact from a right hip replacement. Say which sequence now carries the VI-RADS assessment, and what the report must state.
quiz.answer: The dynamic contrast-enhanced series carries it. Diffusion is normally the dominant sequence, and the dynamic series takes over when diffusion is non-diagnostic. The report must say that the diffusion images are unusable, that the category rests on the DCE and T2 findings, and that confidence is correspondingly reduced.
quiz.explain: The VI-RADS hierarchy is diffusion first, dynamic contrast second, T2 as the structural scaffold — but the hierarchy assumes each sequence is diagnostic. Echo-planar diffusion is the sequence most easily destroyed by metal, bowel gas and motion, and a hip prosthesis on the side of interest will do it. When diffusion fails, the dynamic series inherits the decision: on early dynamic images tumour and the inner layer enhance before the muscularis propria does, so an intact non-enhancing dark muscle band in that early window is reassuring, and early enhancement extending into the muscle is not. Say this explicitly in the report. A category assigned without its dominant sequence carries less weight, and the urologist deciding between resection and cystectomy is entitled to know which evidence the number rests on.

quiz.prompt: An MRI is requested six days after transurethral resection because the specimen contained no muscle. At the resection base there is wall thickening, restricted diffusion and early enhancement that would otherwise read as VI-RADS 4. What is the right response?
quiz.answer: Report the appearance but state that post-resection change cannot be separated from residual tumour here, and advise reassessment at least two weeks after the resection
choices: Report the appearance but state that post-resection change cannot be separated from residual tumour here, and advise reassessment at least two weeks after the resection
Report VI-RADS 4 at face value, since restricted diffusion at a resection base reflects residual tumour rather than granulation tissue in most patients
Report VI-RADS 2, since enhancement and restricted diffusion this soon after a resection are granulation tissue and carry no diagnostic weight at all
Report the bladder as normal for the interval, since wall thickening at a resection base always settles and no further imaging is warranted
quiz.explain: A fresh resection bed does everything a tumour does. Granulation tissue is cellular and hyperaemic, so it restricts diffusion and enhances early; oedema and haemorrhage thicken the wall and blur the dark muscle line; a perforation of the detrusor during resection may leave inflammatory change tracking into perivesical fat that mimics T3. This is the single commonest cause of overstaging on bladder MRI. The VI-RADS recommendation is to scan before resection wherever possible, and if the study must follow a resection, to leave an interval of at least two weeks so the acute inflammatory phase settles. Neither of the confident extremes is defensible: calling it tumour risks a cystectomy on granulation tissue, and calling it nothing risks missing residual disease. Report what you see, state the confounder, and give the interval at which the question can be answered.

quiz.prompt: A woman on maintenance intravesical BCG for high-grade T1 disease has surveillance MRI. There is smooth diffuse wall thickening around the whole bladder with early enhancement and mildly restricted diffusion, and no focal mass anywhere. How should this be handled?
quiz.answer: Read it as granulomatous inflammatory change from BCG, report the absence of any focal mass, and correlate with cystoscopy and urine cytology
choices: Read it as granulomatous inflammatory change from BCG, report the absence of any focal mass, and correlate with cystoscopy and urine cytology
Read it as diffuse carcinoma in situ, assign VI-RADS 4, and recommend cystectomy on the strength of the enhancement and diffusion findings
Assign VI-RADS 3 to the bladder as a whole, since diffuse enhancement is equivocal and that category conveys the uncertainty faithfully
Repeat the study in 48 hours with a fuller bladder, since diffuse thickening of this degree is an artefact of poor distension alone
quiz.explain: Intravesical BCG sets up a granulomatous cystitis. The wall thickens, enhances and shows mild diffusion restriction, often circumferentially and often for months after the last instillation. VI-RADS was designed for, and validated on, a bladder containing a visible tumour that has not been recently instilled or resected; applied to a diffusely inflamed bladder it will overcall. The discriminator is focality and asymmetry — a discrete mass with its own stalk or a segmental interruption of the dark muscle line means something, while smooth symmetrical change does not. Carcinoma in situ is flat and is essentially invisible on MRI, which is precisely why cystoscopy with biopsy and urine cytology remain the arbiters of BCG failure. Report the pattern, name the confounder, and hand the question back to the endoscopist rather than manufacturing a category the system was not built to give.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT for a muscle-invasive bladder cancer shows a 12 mm short-axis left obturator node and a 9 mm short-axis right common iliac node. There is no nodal disease above the aortic bifurcation. Give the N category as a single whole number.
quiz.explain: Bladder nodal staging is anatomical before it is numerical. N1 is a single node in the true pelvis — perivesical, obturator, internal iliac, external iliac or sacral. N2 is multiple nodes within that same true pelvic group. N3 is disease in a common iliac node, which sits above the true pelvis but is still regional. Anything higher, in the retroperitoneum, is no longer nodal staging at all: it counts as distant disease. Here the obturator node alone would be N1, but the common iliac node overrides it and makes the case N3. Size thresholds are conventions rather than rules — 8 mm short axis is commonly used for pelvic nodes and 10 mm above the bifurcation — and shape, necrosis and clustering matter as much as the caliper. The distinction is not academic: N3 disease remains within the field a radical lymphadenectomy or a radiotherapy volume can cover.

quiz.prompt: A bladder tumour at the trigone extends through the full thickness of the wall, and there is intermediate-signal tumour replacing the adjacent prostatic stroma in direct continuity with the bladder mass. The pelvic side walls and obturator internus are clear. How should T be reported?
quiz.answer: T4a, since tumour spreading contiguously from the bladder into prostatic stroma is what that category describes and it still points towards radical surgery
choices: T4a, since tumour spreading contiguously from the bladder into prostatic stroma is what that category describes and it still points towards radical surgery
T3b, since extension of any degree towards the prostate beyond the detrusor is graded simply as macroscopic extravesical disease
T4b, since involvement of a neighbouring pelvic organ by direct spread is the category used to denote surgically unresectable disease
T2b, since the prostatic stroma lies deep to the outer half of the detrusor and is therefore staged together with the muscle layer
quiz.explain: T4 divides into two very different prognoses. T4a is contiguous invasion of an adjacent organ — prostatic stroma, seminal vesicles, uterus or vagina — and remains resectable, so it belongs in the radical cystectomy conversation. T4b is fixation to the pelvic side wall or abdominal wall, and that is the category that generally takes surgery off the table. T3b is a macroscopic perivesical soft tissue mass without organ invasion, which is not what is described here. One nuance to keep: prostatic stromal invasion counts as T4a when tumour reaches it directly through the bladder wall, but urothelial carcinoma spreading along the prostatic urethra and into the stroma from within is staged under the urethral rules instead. On MRI, look for intermediate-signal tumour replacing the normally heterogeneous prostatic tissue rather than merely abutting it.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old with previously treated bladder cancer presents with fresh right-sided haematuria and a CT urogram is booked. Say which acquisition on that study answers the upper tract question, and what you are hunting for in the collecting system.
quiz.answer: The excretory or delayed acquisition, taken several minutes after injection once the collecting systems and ureters are opacified. Look for a fixed filling defect, focal urothelial thickening or an enhancing soft tissue mass, an irregular stricture, and hydronephrosis or calyceal dilatation above the level of the lesion.
quiz.explain: CT urography is a multiphase study and each phase does a different job. Unenhanced images find calculi and give a baseline density. The nephrographic phase, at around 100 seconds, is where renal parenchymal tumours are seen. Only the excretory phase, obtained several minutes later, distends and opacifies the urothelium so that a filling defect can be identified — and upper tract urothelial carcinoma lives in the urothelium. The three appearances to know are a filling defect, focal or circumferential wall thickening, and an infiltrative stricture with upstream obstruction. Enhancement is what separates tumour from clot: a clot does not enhance, and it moves between phases or between studies. Compare the two sides on the same image, because subtle asymmetric thickening reads far better as a comparison than as an absolute measurement.

quiz.prompt: The CT urogram shows a 1.5 cm enhancing filling defect in the right renal pelvis with mild upstream calyceal dilatation, alongside the separately confirmed bladder tumour. What does this add to the plan?
quiz.answer: It signals a synchronous upper tract primary that needs ureteroscopy and its own staging, since the urothelium behaves as a single field at risk
choices: It signals a synchronous upper tract primary that needs ureteroscopy and its own staging, since the urothelium behaves as a single field at risk
It most likely represents blood clot shed from the bladder tumour, so a repeat urogram in three months is the proportionate response here
It represents a metastasis from the bladder primary, so systemic chemotherapy replaces any local treatment of the renal pelvic lesion
It has little staging consequence, since the bladder tumour drives management and the renal pelvic lesion is treated only if it obstructs
quiz.explain: Urothelium runs continuously from renal calyx to urethra and is exposed to the same carcinogens along its whole length, so urothelial carcinoma is characteristically multifocal in space and metachronous in time. A patient with a bladder tumour and a separate enhancing renal pelvic lesion has two primaries until proved otherwise, and the upper tract one is staged and treated in its own right — ureteroscopy with biopsy, and radical nephroureterectomy including a bladder cuff for high-risk disease, or kidney-sparing treatment for low-risk lesions. Enhancement is the point that excludes clot, which is avascular and mobile. The field effect also runs the other way: after nephroureterectomy for an upper tract tumour, bladder recurrence is common enough that cystoscopic surveillance is routine. Report the lesion, its length and site, the degree of obstruction, and the contralateral kidney, because renal function shapes whether cisplatin is an option.

nodes.title: Ovarian Lesions: O-RADS on Ultrasound and MRI
nodes.goal: Categorise an adnexal lesion with O-RADS on ultrasound and MRI, decide when to escalate and when to say nothing, and recognise the classic benign lesions, torsion and peritoneal spread.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old woman has pelvic ultrasound for right iliac fossa pain. The appendix is normal. The right ovary contains a 2.4 cm anechoic thin-walled avascular cyst with posterior acoustic enhancement, and the left ovary is unremarkable. What should the report say about the cyst?
quiz.answer: Call it a normal follicle and give no follow-up, since a simple cyst of this size in a premenopausal ovary is a physiological structure
choices: Call it a normal follicle and give no follow-up, since a simple cyst of this size in a premenopausal ovary is a physiological structure
Call it a simple cyst and arrange repeat ultrasound in six to twelve weeks to document that it has resolved as would be expected
Call it an O-RADS 3 lesion and recommend pelvic MRI, since a discrete cyst warrants characterisation before it is dismissed as benign
Call it an O-RADS 2 lesion and recommend a serum CA-125, since simple cysts in this age group carry a low but genuine risk
quiz.explain: O-RADS US 1 is the normal premenopausal ovary, and it includes a follicle up to 3 cm and a corpus luteum up to 3 cm. These are physiology, not findings; describing them, following them and measuring them generates anxiety and repeat scans for nothing. Above 3 cm and up to 10 cm a simple cyst becomes O-RADS 2 — almost certainly benign, under 1% risk — and even then most need no imaging follow-up. The postmenopausal ovary is different: category 1 does not apply to it, because it should not be making follicles, so a simple cyst there is scored 2 rather than 1. Even so, the Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound consensus regards a simple cyst of 1 cm or less in a postmenopausal woman as clinically inconsequential and not worth describing. Knowing what to leave out is part of the skill.

quiz.prompt: A premenopausal woman has a unilocular, entirely anechoic ovarian cyst with a smooth thin wall, no septation and no solid tissue, measuring 12.3 cm in maximum diameter. Give the O-RADS US category as a single whole number.
quiz.explain: Morphology alone would keep this in O-RADS 2: a simple cyst has anechoic contents, a smooth thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement, and there is no solid tissue anywhere. But O-RADS US applies a size rule on top of morphology. A simple cyst above 3 cm and below 10 cm is category 2, almost certainly benign. At 10 cm or more it becomes category 3 — low risk, in the 1% to under 10% band — because very large cysts carry a small but real chance of a cystadenoma or a borderline tumour, and because their size itself raises the risk of torsion or rupture. The same 10 cm rule pushes the other classic benign lesions, such as a haemorrhagic cyst, an endometrioma or a dermoid, from category 2 into category 3. The practical consequence is that this woman needs gynaecological assessment, with MRI or specialist ultrasound as an option, not simple discharge.

quiz.prompt: A 6 cm multilocular ovarian cyst has smooth inner walls, thin septations, no solid tissue and no papillary projections. On Doppler interrogation there is very strong flow within the septations, corresponding to colour score 4. What category applies and what follows from it?
quiz.answer: O-RADS 4: very strong flow lifts a smooth multilocular cyst into the intermediate-risk band, so MRI or gynaecological oncology assessment follows
choices: O-RADS 4: very strong flow lifts a smooth multilocular cyst into the intermediate-risk band, so MRI or gynaecological oncology assessment follows
O-RADS 3: a multilocular cyst under 10 cm with smooth walls stays in the low-risk band, and Doppler findings within septations are disregarded
O-RADS 5: a colour score of 4 anywhere within an adnexal lesion places it in the high-risk band and mandates gynaecological oncology referral
O-RADS 2: septations without solid tissue are benign, so neither imaging follow-up nor any specialist referral is required for this woman
quiz.explain: The O-RADS US colour score comes from the IOTA lexicon: 1 is no flow, 2 minimal, 3 moderate and 4 very strong. For a multilocular cyst with no solid tissue, the category depends on three things — size, the smoothness of the inner wall, and the colour score. Smooth, under 10 cm, colour score 1 to 3 gives category 3. Reaching 10 cm, or having an irregular inner wall, or a colour score of 4, moves it to category 4, the 10% to under 50% band. Colour score 4 does not by itself produce a category 5; that requires solid tissue behaviour, four or more papillary projections, an irregular solid lesion, or ascites with peritoneal nodularity. Category 4 is the band where MRI earns its place, because most category 4 lesions are reclassified downwards once the tissue is characterised.

quiz.prompt: A 7 cm unilocular adnexal cyst in a 58-year-old contains four discrete papillary projections, each more than 3 mm high, with detectable internal flow. There is no ascites and no peritoneal nodularity. How should this be reported and referred?
quiz.answer: O-RADS 5, the high-risk band: four or more papillary projections put the lesion there, and referral to gynaecological oncology is the next step
choices: O-RADS 5, the high-risk band: four or more papillary projections put the lesion there, and referral to gynaecological oncology is the next step
O-RADS 4, the intermediate band: papillary projections in a unilocular cyst stay there whatever their number, so pelvic MRI is the next step
O-RADS 3, the low-risk band: without ascites or peritoneal nodules the lesion cannot climb higher, so interval ultrasound is the next step
O-RADS 4, the intermediate band: internal vascularity must be absent before the high-risk band applies, so pelvic MRI is the next step
quiz.explain: A papillary projection in the O-RADS lexicon is solid tissue at least 3 mm high protruding into the cyst lumen, and it is counted whether or not it shows flow — vascularity raises suspicion but is not required for it to count. The number is what moves the category: a cystic lesion with one to three projections is O-RADS 4, and four or more takes it to O-RADS 5, the band at 50% risk or above. Other routes into category 5 are a solid lesion with an irregular outer contour and any colour score, a smooth solid lesion with colour score 4, and the presence of ascites with peritoneal nodules regardless of the lesion itself. Category 5 means the referral is to gynaecological oncology, because outcomes in ovarian cancer depend heavily on who performs the primary surgery.

quiz.prompt: Your ultrasound report ends at O-RADS 4 for a 5 cm adnexal lesion with an enhancing solid component in a 42-year-old. Say what O-RADS MRI is expected to add here, and describe the situation in which MRI would not be the right next step.
quiz.answer: MRI restratifies the lesion by characterising the solid tissue — fat, dark T2 and dark diffusion fibrous tissue, or genuinely enhancing tumour with a time-intensity curve — and most intermediate-risk lesions are moved down to a lower risk band. MRI is not the next step when there is already ascites with peritoneal nodularity or unambiguous high-risk morphology, where the referral goes straight to gynaecological oncology.
quiz.explain: The purpose of O-RADS MRI is to rescue lesions from the indeterminate middle. Ultrasound can see that there is solid tissue but often cannot say what kind, and the intermediate-risk band spans 10% to just under 50% — too high to ignore and too low to justify oncological surgery. MRI answers the tissue question three ways: fat suppression identifies a dermoid, uniformly dark tissue on T2 and on high b-value diffusion identifies benign fibrous tissue, and dynamic contrast gives a time-intensity curve that separates low, intermediate and high risk. In practice a large share of O-RADS US 4 lesions come down to MRI 2 or 3. What MRI cannot do is add value when the diagnosis is already made: ascites with peritoneal nodularity is O-RADS 5 on ultrasound alone, and the delay of a further scan costs the patient time.

quiz.prompt: On O-RADS MRI a 6 cm adnexal lesion contains enhancing solid tissue. On the dynamic series that tissue begins to enhance earlier than the outer myometrium, rises steeply and then plateaus above it. What does the curve mean for the score and the referral?
quiz.answer: It is the high-risk curve: the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 5, and referral to a gynaecological oncology service should be made
choices: It is the high-risk curve: the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 5, and referral to a gynaecological oncology service should be made
It is the intermediate-risk curve: the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 4, and surgery under a general gynaecologist is appropriate
It is the low-risk curve: the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 3, and imaging follow-up rather than surgery is the proportionate step
The curve shape is not scored: the presence of enhancing solid tissue is what matters, so the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 4
quiz.explain: O-RADS MRI uses the outer myometrium as an internal reference standard, which neatly removes the effect of injection rate and cardiac output. Three curve types are recognised. The low-risk curve rises gradually without an early shoulder and stays below the myometrium; it gives a score of 3, roughly a 5% risk. The intermediate curve has a shoulder and then a plateau but enhances later and less than the myometrium; that is a score of 4, around 50%. The high-risk curve enhances earlier than the myometrium and plateaus above it, reflecting neovascular shunting; that is a score of 5, around 90%. If dynamic imaging is unavailable, the fallback is a single comparison with the outer myometrium at 30 to 40 seconds. Note that the curve is only needed for solid tissue that is not uniformly dark on T2 and diffusion — that tissue is already benign.

quiz.prompt: A 4 cm solid adnexal mass is uniformly very low signal on T2 and low signal on high b-value diffusion imaging, with only mild enhancement. There is a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas and no peritoneal nodularity. How should it be scored and managed?
quiz.answer: O-RADS MRI 2: uniformly dark solid tissue on T2 and on diffusion is benign fibrous tissue, so no oncological referral is required here
choices: O-RADS MRI 2: uniformly dark solid tissue on T2 and on diffusion is benign fibrous tissue, so no oncological referral is required here
O-RADS MRI 4: enhancing solid tissue within an adnexal mass reaches the intermediate band, so surgical assessment should be arranged
O-RADS MRI 5: free pelvic fluid alongside a solid adnexal mass counts as ascites and places the lesion in the high-risk band
O-RADS MRI 3: dark solid tissue sits in the low-risk band but still needs a time-intensity curve before a category can be given
quiz.explain: Solid tissue that is homogeneously dark on T2 and dark on high b-value diffusion is the signature of dense fibrous stroma, and O-RADS MRI treats it as almost certainly benign — category 2, under 0.5% risk — without requiring a time-intensity curve at all. The lesions in this group are ovarian fibroma and fibrothecoma, Brenner tumours, and pedunculated subserosal fibroids masquerading as adnexal masses. A small volume of physiological free fluid in the pouch of Douglas is not ascites; ascites in the O-RADS sense means fluid beyond the pelvis or fluid with peritoneal nodularity. This item is also the argument for MRI: on ultrasound a fibroma is a hypoechoic shadowing solid mass with colour score 1, which scores O-RADS US 3 and generates a referral. Remember Meigs syndrome, where a benign fibroma is accompanied by ascites and a pleural effusion that both resolve after removal.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old has a 5 cm ovarian cyst containing fine lacy internal strands and an avascular retracting clot with straight margins. State the conclusion you would report, the features that exclude a solid neoplastic nodule, and the follow-up you would advise.
quiz.answer: Report a haemorrhagic cyst. The strands are thin and fishnet-like and the clot is avascular with straight or concave margins, unlike a papillary projection, which has convex margins and detectable internal flow. Under 10 cm in a premenopausal woman this is O-RADS 2 and needs no follow-up; if there is any doubt, repeat the scan in six to twelve weeks, by which time it should have resolved.
quiz.explain: The haemorrhagic cyst is the commonest cause of an anxious adnexal report, and it has a reliable signature. Early on, fibrin strands make a fine reticular or fishnet pattern with no flow. As the clot organises it retracts from the wall, producing a solid-looking element that is nonetheless avascular and has straight or concave margins where it has pulled away — the opposite of the convex bulging outline of a true papillary projection. Nothing inside a haemorrhagic cyst should show Doppler flow, although flow in the surrounding ovarian tissue is normal. The lesion evolves and disappears, usually within about eight weeks, which is why the classic safety net is a repeat scan in the six to twelve week window, timed just after a period. On MRI it is bright on T1 and on fat-suppressed T1, variable on T2, and it does not enhance.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these peritoneal spaces in the order that ascitic fluid, and the ovarian tumour cells carried within it, normally reaches them.
quiz.answer: pouch-of-Douglas right-paracolic-gutter Morison-pouch right-subphrenic-space
quiz.explain: Ovarian cancer spreads chiefly by shedding cells into peritoneal fluid, and that fluid follows a predictable circulation. Gravity takes it first to the most dependent recess, the pouch of Douglas. From there the flow generated by respiration and bowel movement carries it up the right paracolic gutter, which is the wider and less obstructed of the two; the left gutter is partly barred by the phrenicocolic ligament and the spleen. It then reaches the subhepatic recess, Morison's pouch, and finally the right subphrenic space beneath the diaphragm, where absorptive lymphatics draw fluid in and implants take hold. Those four sites, together with the omentum and small bowel serosa, are where you should look first on a staging study. Right diaphragmatic disease matters disproportionately at the multidisciplinary meeting, because stripping the diaphragm is what often stands between the surgeon and complete cytoreduction.

quiz.prompt: A 3.5 cm adnexal cyst is homogeneously hyperintense on fat-suppressed T1 imaging and loses signal centrally on T2, leaving a dependent very dark focus. There is no enhancing solid tissue and no fat. What score applies and what should the report add?
quiz.answer: O-RADS MRI 2: the signal behaviour is that of an endometrioma, and the report should flag the likelihood of deep endometriosis elsewhere in the pelvis
choices: O-RADS MRI 2: the signal behaviour is that of an endometrioma, and the report should flag the likelihood of deep endometriosis elsewhere in the pelvis
O-RADS MRI 2: the signal behaviour is that of a mature teratoma, and the report should confirm macroscopic fat on the fat-suppressed sequence
O-RADS MRI 4: loss of T2 signal within a cyst indicates solid tissue, and the report should recommend prompt surgical assessment of the lesion
O-RADS MRI 3: haemorrhagic cysts and endometriomas cannot be separated on MRI, so the report should recommend short interval repeat imaging
quiz.explain: Two signal facts do the work here. Staying bright on fat-suppressed T1 means the content is blood, not fat — a dermoid loses its signal the moment fat saturation is applied. Losing signal on T2 is shading, caused by chronically degraded blood products with high protein and iron concentration, and it is characteristic of the endometrioma rather than the acute haemorrhagic cyst. The very dark dependent focus, the T2 dark spot, is more specific still. That combination is O-RADS MRI 2, almost certainly benign. Two things belong in the report nonetheless. First, endometriomas travel with deep infiltrating disease, so the uterosacral ligaments, torus, rectovaginal septum and bowel deserve a look. Second, malignant transformation, although uncommon, is announced by an enhancing mural nodule, loss of the usual shading, or interval growth, most often in women over 45.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old has sudden severe right iliac fossa pain with vomiting. The right ovary measures 6 cm and looks oedematous with follicles displaced to the periphery, there is a twisted vascular pedicle at the hilum, and colour Doppler shows preserved arterial flow within the ovary. What should you do?
quiz.answer: Report torsion as very likely and escalate for urgent surgical assessment, since preserved arterial flow does not exclude the diagnosis
choices: Report torsion as very likely and escalate for urgent surgical assessment, since preserved arterial flow does not exclude the diagnosis
Report torsion as excluded by the preserved arterial flow, and look instead for a haemorrhagic cyst or pelvic inflammatory disease
Report an oedematous ovarian mass and arrange contrast-enhanced MRI to confirm torsion before making any surgical referral
Report a physiological polycystic appearance, since peripherally arranged follicles are the expected pattern in this age group
quiz.explain: The commonest error in suspected torsion is trusting the Doppler. The ovary has a dual arterial supply, from the ovarian artery and from the ovarian branch of the uterine artery, and torsion is often intermittent or incomplete, so arterial flow may persist in an ovary that is nonetheless twisted and dying. Venous and lymphatic drainage fails first, which is exactly why the grey-scale findings — a unilaterally enlarged oedematous ovary, follicles pushed to the periphery by stromal oedema, a whirlpool of twisted vessels at the pedicle, the ovary sitting in an abnormal midline or superior position, and free fluid — carry more weight than the colour box. In adults a lead mass is usually present, most often a dermoid. Torsion is a surgical emergency in which detorsion salvages ovarian function, so the report should escalate rather than defer to further imaging.

quiz.prompt: In FIGO staging of ovarian, fallopian tube and primary peritoneal carcinoma, macroscopic peritoneal deposits beyond the pelvis are divided into two substages by the greatest dimension of the largest deposit. Give that threshold in centimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Stage III of the FIGO system is subdivided by how much extrapelvic peritoneal disease there is. IIIA1 is retroperitoneal nodal disease alone, further split by whether the largest node is at or below 10 mm. IIIA2 is microscopic extrapelvic peritoneal involvement. IIIB is macroscopic extrapelvic peritoneal deposits measuring 2 cm or less, and IIIC is deposits larger than 2 cm — a category that also captures tumour on the capsule of the liver or spleen without invasion of the parenchyma. That capsule-versus-parenchyma distinction is the one radiologists are asked to make most often, because parenchymal liver metastasis is stage IVB. Stage IVA is a malignant pleural effusion with positive cytology, and IVB covers parenchymal metastases, transmural bowel involvement and disease outside the abdomen, including inguinal nodes. Measure the largest deposit, and say plainly whether liver disease is on the surface or within it.

quiz.prompt: You are reporting a staging CT for newly diagnosed advanced ovarian carcinoma ahead of the multidisciplinary meeting. Set out the sites of disease you must comment on specifically, because they are the ones that predict that complete debulking will not be achieved.
quiz.answer: Comment specifically on the porta hepatis and gastrohepatic ligament, the lesser sac, the root of the small bowel mesentery, the diaphragmatic surfaces, suprarenal retroperitoneal nodes, any liver or splenic parenchymal disease as distinct from capsular deposits, and the volume of ascites.
quiz.explain: The surgeon's question is not what stage the disease is, but whether residual disease of zero is achievable, because that is what drives survival. A handful of sites make that unlikely, and they are hard to see unless you go looking. Disease at the porta hepatis or in the gastrohepatic ligament threatens vascular and biliary structures; lesser sac disease is easily overlooked behind the stomach; a retracted, thickened small bowel mesenteric root implies disease that cannot be excised without catastrophic bowel loss; extensive diaphragmatic plaques require stripping and sometimes resection; suprarenal nodal disease lies outside the standard field. Distinguish surface deposits on liver or spleen, which remain stage III and are resectable, from parenchymal metastases, which are stage IV. Large-volume ascites tends to accompany all of the above. Reporting these explicitly is what lets the meeting choose between primary surgery and neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

nodes.title: Prostate MRI
nodes.goal: Score a prostate MRI by PI-RADS v2.1 and tell real lesions from benign mimics.

quiz.prompt: A 1.2 cm anterior mid-gland lesion has its epicentre in the transition zone, with one edge abutting the anterior horn of the peripheral zone. It is lens-shaped, its margin fading into the surrounding gland rather than being sharply drawn, and it is uniformly and moderately dark on T2W. On diffusion it is focally hypointense on ADC and mildly hyperintense at b=1500. How should it be assessed?
quiz.answer: Assess it in the transition zone; T2 governs, giving PI-RADS 4
quiz.explain: PI-RADS v2.1 assigns a lesion straddling the zones to the zone it appears most likely to have arisen from, and the epicentre is the practical guide to that; the choice then fixes which sequence dominates, T2W in the transition zone and DWI in the peripheral zone. Lenticular or non-circumscribed, homogeneous, moderately hypointense and under 1.5 cm is a transition zone T2W score of 4, which is exactly what the described lens shape, fading margin and uniform moderate darkness amount to, and a transition zone T2W score of 4 is PI-RADS 4 whatever diffusion shows. Diffusion moves a transition zone lesion at two points and no others: a T2W score of 2 with DWI 4 or 5 becomes PI-RADS 3, and a T2W score of 3 with DWI 5 becomes PI-RADS 4. Neither applies here. 'Let DCE break the tie between T2 and DWI, giving PI-RADS 4' arrives at the right number down a road that does not exist, since DCE plays no part in the transition zone whatever it shows.
choices: Assess it in the peripheral zone; DWI governs, giving PI-RADS 3
Assess it in the transition zone; T2 governs, giving PI-RADS 4
Take the lower of the two sequence scores, giving PI-RADS 3
Let DCE break the tie between T2 and DWI, giving PI-RADS 4

quiz.prompt: A 9 mm posterolateral peripheral zone focus is discretely but not markedly hypointense on ADC and mildly hyperintense at b=1500, giving a DWI score of 3. On DCE there is focal enhancement at that site, appearing before the surrounding normal peripheral zone. What follows for the report?
quiz.answer: The category becomes 4, so biopsy usually follows
quiz.explain: DCE has exactly one job in PI-RADS v2.1: a peripheral zone lesion scored 3 on DWI becomes PI-RADS 4 if DCE is positive, meaning focal enhancement that is earlier than or contemporaneous with adjacent normal prostate and corresponds to the T2W or DWI finding. It is a binary read, so 'The category stays 3 unless washout appears later on' fails twice over: v2.1 abandoned curve typing, and the upgrade has already been earned. What DCE cannot buy is a higher ceiling, so 'The category becomes 5, as two sequences are positive' is wrong too; a DWI 4 lesion stays 4 however it enhances, since only a size of 1.5 cm or more, or definite extraprostatic extension, makes 5. The move from 3 to 4 is the one that matters clinically, because 3 is equivocal and may be watched, while v2.1 says biopsy should be considered for 4 or 5.
choices: The category stays 3, since DCE does not alter DWI
The category becomes 5, as two sequences are positive
The category becomes 4, so biopsy usually follows
The category stays 3 unless washout appears later on

quiz.prompt: A 65-year-old man has a transition zone nodule that is homogeneous and circumscribed but not encapsulated. On diffusion the nodule is discretely, though only mildly, hypointense on ADC and mildly hyperintense at b=1500. A colleague wants to call it PI-RADS 3 on the diffusion finding. Why should you resist?
quiz.answer: Mild restriction is expected in stromal hyperplasia nodules
quiz.explain: Score it first. A homogeneous circumscribed nodule without encapsulation is the atypical nodule, a T2W score of 2; a discrete focus that restricts only mildly on both ADC and high b-value is a DWI score of 3. PI-RADS v2.1 blocks precisely that upgrade: mildly or moderately restricted diffusion is common in mostly encapsulated and unencapsulated transition zone lesions, much of it stromal hyperplasia, so a T2W score of 1 or 2 is not raised on a DWI score of 3. The nodule stays PI-RADS 2. 'Diffusion has no bearing whatever on transition zone scores' overshoots: diffusion does count there, but only above that threshold, and v2.1 added exactly that step, a T2W score of 2 with DWI 4 or 5 becoming PI-RADS 3, and a T2W score of 3 with DWI 5 becoming PI-RADS 4.
choices: The nodule must exceed 1.5 cm before diffusion is counted
Mild restriction is expected in stromal hyperplasia nodules
Diffusion has no bearing whatever on transition zone scores
Restriction counts here if the nodule also enhances early on

quiz.prompt: Three weeks after systematic TRUS biopsy, T1W images show diffuse hyperintensity through much of both peripheral zones. Within it, a 14 mm right posterolateral area is conspicuously T1 hypointense, and that same area is T2 hypointense with markedly reduced ADC and marked b=1500 signal. What does the T1-dark area most likely represent?
quiz.answer: Tumour, spared by the blood and standing out as a T1 defect
quiz.explain: This is the haemorrhage exclusion sign. The explanation usually offered is that tumour has markedly reduced citrate, and that citrate is anticoagulant, so blood collects in the benign peripheral zone and spares the cancer; that mechanism is a published hypothesis rather than a measured fact, but the pattern it predicts is reliable. Read the T1W series as a map of where cancer is not, and a dark hole in a bright field is the suspicious finding; reading T1 brightness itself as tumour inverts the sign. 'Older blood whose signal has decayed back towards low T1' is the tempting answer, since v2.1 grants that chronic blood products may appear hypointense on all sequences, but the surrounding blood is the same three weeks old and still bright, so blood of that age has no reason to be dark in one 14 mm patch, and marked b=1500 signal with a low ADC indicates restricted diffusion rather than the signal loss susceptibility from old blood would produce. PI-RADS v2.1 does suggest considering a gap of six weeks or more when the study is for staging, but here the haemorrhage has made the lesion more conspicuous, not less.
choices: Older blood whose signal has decayed back towards low T1
Prostatitis, which tends to bleed less than the normal gland
Tumour, spared by the blood and standing out as a T1 defect
Artefact from a needle track running across the posterior zone

quiz.prompt: At the prostatic base, bands of low T2W and low ADC signal encircle both ejaculatory ducts and converge towards the verumontanum. Bulky transition zone hyperplasia has displaced the left band so that it is visibly larger than the right, but signal is equal on the two sides on T2W, ADC and b=1500, and neither side enhances early. How should this be handled in the report?
quiz.answer: Report it as the normal central zone, with no lesion score
quiz.explain: Separate the two asymmetries. What PI-RADS v2.1 treats as suspicious in the central zone is asymmetry of signal between the two sides on T2W, ADC or high b-value images, or focal early enhancement; here the signal is equal on all three and neither side enhances. What is present is asymmetry of size, and v2.1 names that a normal variant, particularly when transition zone hyperplasia deforms or displaces the central zone at the base, which is the described mechanism exactly. Everything else fits the normal central zone as v2.1 describes it: low T2W and ADC signal wrapping the ejaculatory ducts from base to verumontanum, mildly hyperintense at high b-value. 'Score it PI-RADS 4 on the strength of the low ADC signal' is the trap, because it scores a normal structure on one sequence read in isolation and turns it into a biopsy target.
choices: Score it PI-RADS 4 on the strength of the low ADC signal
Call it bilateral tumour arising at the base, PI-RADS 5
Score it PI-RADS 3, because the appearance is equivocal
Report it as the normal central zone, with no lesion score

quiz.prompt: A prostate DWI acquires b = 100 and b = 1000 s/mm^2. In a peripheral zone lesion the mean signal falls from 800 to 400 arbitrary units between those two b-values. Fitting a mono-exponential decay through the two points only, what ADC does this give, in units of 10^-3 mm^2/s? Give it to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: Mono-exponential decay is S(b) = S0 exp(-b x ADC), so ADC = ln(S1/S2) / (b2 - b1) = ln 2 / 900 = 7.70 x 10^-4 mm^2/s, that is 0.77 x 10^-3. Now resist the obvious next step. PI-RADS v2.1 offers 750-900 micrometre^2/s as the range within which a threshold may be set, and says that values below the chosen threshold correlate with clinically significant cancer. 770 sits inside that range, which makes it indeterminate rather than positive: suspicious if your unit has settled on 900, unremarkable if it has settled on 750. That is not a fault in the arithmetic but the reason the number is not a verdict, since ADC depends on which b-values were used and varies between vendors, and it is why v2.1 keeps visual assessment of the ADC map as the primary method rather than a numerical cut-off.

quiz.prompt: Your protocol acquires b = 50 and b = 800 s/mm^2, and the scanner then synthesises a b = 1500 image by extrapolation. A trainee asks why the b = 1500 data is not simply acquired directly and folded into the mono-exponential ADC fit as a third point. Give the two separate reasons, and state the b-values PI-RADS v2.1 requires for the high b-value image set and permits for the ADC calculation.
quiz.answer: Two reasons of different kinds. The first is practical: a directly acquired b = 1500 series needs strong diffusion gradients and so a longer echo time, and the signal-to-noise ratio falls as b rises, so it costs scan time and image quality and is more prone to artefact, which is why an image calculated from the acquired low and intermediate data is often the cleaner one. The second is about the model: prostate signal decay stops behaving in a mono-exponential way above roughly b = 1000 because of diffusion kurtosis, so folding a b = 1500 point into the fit would bias the calculated ADC and break comparability between studies. PI-RADS v2.1 requires a high b-value image set of at least 1400 s/mm^2, obtained either from a separate acquisition or calculated from the low and intermediate b-value images, and recommends that the maximum b-value used to calculate ADC be no greater than 1000 s/mm^2.
quiz.explain: The two reasons are of different kinds, and conflating them is the usual error. One is practical: strong diffusion gradients force a long echo time and the signal-to-noise ratio falls as b rises, so a directly acquired b = 1500 series costs time and quality. PI-RADS v2.1 accepts either route for the high b-value set, acquired separately or calculated, and notes only that calculating it avoids the longer echo times the strong gradient pulses would need. The other reason is about the model: the mono-exponential fit that defines ADC holds to roughly b = 1000 and then departs from the data, because kurtosis flattens the decay curve. A point at b = 1500 sits above the fitted line, drags the fitted slope shallower, and so lowers the reported ADC for reasons that have nothing to do with cellularity, which is why v2.1 recommends 1000 s/mm^2 as the maximum b-value used in the calculation while requiring at least 1400 s/mm^2 for the high b-value images. Those images earn their keep by suppressing signal from benign tissue with high diffusivity, lifting conspicuity at the apex, the base, subcapsular sites and beside the anterior fibromuscular stroma.

quiz.prompt: A 1.1 cm posterolateral peripheral zone lesion is markedly hypointense on ADC and markedly hyperintense at b=1500. It contacts the capsule over 16 mm, the rectoprostatic angle is obliterated, and a small tongue of tumour signal is measurable outside the gland beside the neurovascular bundle. Which category follows, and on what grounds?
quiz.answer: PI-RADS 5, since definite extraprostatic extension overrides size
quiz.explain: A DWI score of 4 and a DWI score of 5 are separated by two things, not one: a size of 1.5 cm or more, or definite extraprostatic extension or invasive behaviour. Tumour measurably outside the gland is the second of those, so an 11 mm lesion is PI-RADS 5 and its size never comes into it. The grounds matter as much as the number. PI-RADS v2.1 lists several features used to assess extraprostatic extension, among them a bulging contour, an irregular or spiculated margin, obliteration of the rectoprostatic angle, neurovascular bundle asymmetry or invasion, a tumour-capsule interface over 1 cm, and breach of the capsule with direct tumour extension; it ranks none of them, and only the last is demonstrable extraglandular tumour. 'PI-RADS 5, since the lost rectoprostatic angle settles the point' therefore reaches the right category on the wrong ground: a lost angle, like a long contact length, raises suspicion but occurs in organ-confined disease too, and on its own supports an indeterminate margin rather than a definite one.
choices: PI-RADS 4, since the lesion measures well under 1.5 cm across
PI-RADS 5, since definite extraprostatic extension overrides size
PI-RADS 4, with the extraprostatic disease called indeterminate
PI-RADS 5, since the lost rectoprostatic angle settles the point

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old man's seminal vesicles are diffusely low in T2W signal on both sides. There is no restricted diffusion and no abnormal enhancement in the walls, the angles with the prostatic base are preserved, and the sole prostatic finding is a small apical PI-RADS 3 focus. How do you report the vesicles, what benign process most likely accounts for the appearance, and what would have changed your mind?
quiz.answer: Report them as uninvolved. Bilateral symmetric T2W hypointensity with no restricted diffusion, no abnormal enhancement, preserved angles at the base and no contiguous tumour is the picture of senile seminal vesicle amyloidosis, or of age-related atrophy, rather than invasion. Invasion would show some combination of focal or diffuse low T2W signal with restricted diffusion or abnormal enhancement within or along the vesicle, obliteration of the angle between the prostatic base and the vesicle, and tumour continuous with the gland extending along the ejaculatory duct; no single one of those is strictly required, but low T2W signal is the weakest of them and is the only one present here. Geography argues the same way, since an apical lesion is at the wrong end of the gland to reach the vesicles.
quiz.explain: Low T2W signal is the least specific of the seminal vesicle invasion features, and in an elderly man amyloid deposition in the vesicle walls is the commoner cause. The features that carry weight are the ones invasion cannot easily avoid: a diffusion or enhancement abnormality in the vesicle itself, loss of the angle at the base, and physical continuity with tumour extending from the prostate. PI-RADS v2.1 gives these as features of invasion rather than as a checklist every case must complete, so the call is a weighing and not a tally, and real invasion can be diagnosed on two of them. Here bilateral symmetry argues against tumour, three of the four are absent, and a small apical focus is at the wrong end of the gland to reach the vesicles at all.

quiz.prompt: A staging study at 3T uses an endorectal coil whose balloon has been inflated with air. The T2W images are high in resolution and diagnostic, but DWI shows marked geometric distortion and signal dropout across the posterior gland. What is the most appropriate correction?
quiz.answer: Re-inflate the balloon with a liquid such as barium suspension
quiz.explain: Air in the balloon sits in a steep susceptibility gradient right against the posterior peripheral zone, and echo-planar DWI is the sequence least able to tolerate field inhomogeneity, which is why the T2W images survive and the diffusion images do not. The distortion grows with field strength, so 3T is where it bites hardest. PI-RADS v2.1 answers this directly: expel the air and distend the balloon with a liquid such as perfluorocarbon or barium suspension, or use a rigid coil that needs no balloon. 'Rescan at 1.5T, where the same balloon causes less trouble' would indeed shrink the distortion, and dropping field strength is the right move when the source of inhomogeneity cannot be removed, as with a metal prosthesis; here it can be removed, so 1.5T surrenders the signal-to-noise and resolution a staging study was booked for in order to solve a problem a syringe of barium solves. Raising the b-value lowers signal-to-noise without touching the inhomogeneity, and dropping the coil throws away the resolution the staging question depends on.
choices: Repeat the diffusion sequence after raising the b-value further
Re-inflate the balloon with a liquid such as barium suspension
Remove the coil and accept the lower-resolution T2W images
Rescan at 1.5T, where the same balloon causes less trouble

quiz.prompt: A 1.2 cm transition zone nodule is heterogeneous with obscured margins on T2W imaging, which scores 3. On diffusion it is markedly hypointense on the ADC map and markedly hyperintense at b=1500, which scores 5. Which PI-RADS v2.1 assessment category does the lesion take? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: In the transition zone T2W is the dominant sequence, and diffusion acts only as an upgrade in one specific place: a T2W score of 3 becomes an assessment of 4 when the DWI score is 5, and only then. A T2W score of 3 with any DWI score of 4 or below stays at 3. The neighbouring rule runs the other way for a T2W score of 2, which is upgraded to 3 when DWI is 4 or 5. Note what does not happen here. Dynamic contrast enhancement has no role at all in the transition zone; its single defined job in v2.1 is to lift a peripheral zone DWI score of 3 to an assessment of 4. Size does not enter either, since 1.5 cm separates a score of 4 from a score of 5 within a sequence, not across the zonal rules.

quiz.prompt: The prostate measures 4.8 cm by 3.6 cm by 4.2 cm on T2W imaging, and the volume is derived with the ellipsoid formula, multiplying the three dimensions by 0.52. The serum PSA is 8.4 ng/mL. What PSA density does that give? Answer in nanograms per millilitre per millilitre, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The gland volume is 4.8 x 3.6 x 4.2 x 0.52 = 37.7 mL, and 8.4 / 37.7 = 0.22 ng/mL/mL. The point of the calculation is that PSA alone cannot distinguish a large benign gland making a lot of protein from a small gland harbouring cancer, and dividing by volume does much of that work. A density of 0.15 or above is the threshold in common use to support proceeding to biopsy, and it earns its keep in exactly the situation this domain keeps returning to: a PI-RADS 3 lesion, where the imaging is equivocal and something else has to break the tie. Measure the three dimensions carefully and say which they were, since the ellipsoid figure is an approximation and a sloppy anteroposterior measurement moves the density more than anything else in the sum.

quiz.prompt: Put these local staging findings on prostate MRI into the order of increasing tumour stage.
quiz.answer: organ-confined extraprostatic-extension seminal-vesicle-invasion rectal-wall-invasion
quiz.explain: Disease confined within the capsule is T2 however large it is; extraprostatic extension is T3a; invasion of a seminal vesicle is T3b; and tumour fixed to or invading an adjacent structure such as the rectum, the external sphincter, the levator or the pelvic wall is T4. The ladder is worth holding because each rung changes a different decision. Extraprostatic extension at a particular site is what a surgeon needs in order to decide whether the neurovascular bundle on that side can be spared, so the report should say where along the gland the extension lies and how confident you are. Seminal vesicle involvement carries a distinctly worse prognosis and usually moves the conversation towards radiotherapy with androgen deprivation. T4 is uncommon at presentation and is often visible before anyone thinks about scoring.

quiz.prompt: You are reporting a study containing three lesions that score 3, 4 and 5, together with two further areas scoring 2. Say which sequence you measure each lesion on and how, how many lesions the report should carry, and which lesion is designated the index lesion.
quiz.answer: Measure each lesion on the sequence on which it was scored: the ADC map or high b-value images for a peripheral zone lesion, the T2W images for a transition zone lesion, taking the longest diameter on the axial image and using another plane only where the lesion is genuinely better seen there. PI-RADS v2.1 asks for up to four lesions of category 3 or above, so the three suspicious lesions are described individually and the two areas scoring 2 need no separate entry. The index lesion is the one with the highest category, here the lesion scoring 5; where two lesions share the highest category, the index is the one showing extraprostatic extension.
quiz.explain: These conventions exist so that two reports of the same gland can be compared, and so that a urologist reading yours can find the target again on the biopsy platform. Measuring on the sequence that generated the score keeps the size and the category describing the same thing, and the axial default keeps serial studies comparable. The cap of four lesions is a deliberate limit on clutter, since a report listing nine areas of low suspicion is harder to act on than one naming three. The index lesion is the one that will drive treatment, which is why the tie is broken by extraprostatic extension rather than by size: the lesion breaching the capsule is the one that changes the operation.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old man's peripheral zone shows several thin bands of low T2W signal radiating towards the capsule with indistinct margins. The ADC map is mildly and diffusely low across the same regions, there is no focal mass, and the high b-value images show nothing focal. How is this scored and reported, and what is the likely explanation?
quiz.answer: Linear or wedge-shaped hypointensity with indistinct margins in the peripheral zone is a T2W score of 2, and with nothing focal on the high b-value images and no focal defect on the ADC map the diffusion score is 1 or 2, so the assessment is PI-RADS 2 and no target is offered for biopsy. The likely explanation is chronic prostatitis with post-inflammatory fibrosis and atrophy, which is common at this age. Cancer is the exception here rather than the rule, because it usually forms a focal rounded or ill-defined mass with markedly restricted diffusion, not a thin band running along the course of the ducts.
quiz.explain: The peripheral zone is normally bright on T2W, so any darkening draws the eye, and the commonest cause of a dark peripheral zone in a man of this age is not cancer at all. Shape and margin do most of the discrimination: benign post-inflammatory change is linear, wedge-shaped or diffuse and fades into the surrounding gland, while tumour is focal and mass-like. Diffusion then decides, since a genuine lesion is focally and markedly restricted rather than mildly and diffusely so. The important discipline is not to be pushed by a rising PSA into scoring bands as a lesion; prostatitis raises PSA too. If the clinical suspicion stays high, PSA density and follow-up carry the argument, not an inflated category.

nodes.title: Uterus and Cervix: MR Staging, Endometriosis and Anomalies
nodes.goal: Use uterine zonal anatomy on MRI to stage cervical and endometrial cancer, map fibroids and deep endometriosis for the surgeon, and separate the Mullerian anomalies that change the operation.

quiz.prompt: In a 68-year-old being staged for endometrial carcinoma, the junctional zone cannot be identified anywhere on T2 and the myometrium is uniformly intermediate in signal. How should that affect your assessment of the depth of invasion?
quiz.answer: Measure invasion as a proportion of the whole myometrial thickness using the contrast and diffusion images, since the junctional zone is often absent after the menopause
choices: Measure invasion as a proportion of the whole myometrial thickness using the contrast and diffusion images, since the junctional zone is often absent after the menopause
Report the study as non-diagnostic for depth of invasion, since an absent junctional zone means the T2 sequence was mistimed and should be repeated
Assume deep invasion is present, since loss of the junctional zone in this setting reflects tumour having replaced the inner myometrium throughout
Report diffuse adenomyosis, since generalised loss of the junctional zone across the whole uterus is the diagnostic appearance of that disease
quiz.explain: The three-layer T2 appearance of the uterus — bright endometrium, dark junctional zone, intermediate outer myometrium — is a feature of the reproductive years. The junctional zone is the inner myometrium, where smooth muscle cells are packed more densely with less extracellular water, and it is hormonally responsive. After the menopause, and on the combined oral contraceptive or a gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonist, it commonly becomes thin or invisible, and the uterus looks uniformly intermediate. That is normal, not disease and not a technical failure. It does mean you lose your inner reference line, so depth is judged against total myometrial thickness on the sequences with the best tumour-to-muscle contrast. Diffuse adenomyosis is not a plausible reading in a 68-year-old with an atrophic uterus, and assuming deep invasion would overtreat. The lesson generalises: interpret zonal anatomy against the patient's hormonal state.

quiz.prompt: On sagittal T2 imaging in a 41-year-old with heavy painful periods, the junctional zone measures 7 mm at its thinnest and 14 mm at its thickest. Give the junctional zone differential in millimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: The junctional zone differential is simply the maximum thickness minus the minimum, here 14 minus 7, giving 7 mm. It matters because adenomyosis is judged on three related measurements rather than one. A maximum junctional zone thickness of 12 mm or more is taken as diagnostic; 8 to 12 mm is equivocal and needs supporting features; a differential of more than 5 mm and a ratio of junctional zone to total myometrial thickness above about 40% both support the diagnosis. This patient meets the maximum-thickness criterion and the differential criterion. The ancillary signs seal it: punctate high signal foci on T2 representing ectopic endometrial glands and cystic change, high signal foci on T1 from haemorrhage, linear striations radiating from the endometrium, and an ill-defined lesion that widens the myometrium without displacing the cavity. Measure perpendicular to the endometrium and avoid measuring through a contraction.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has a 3.2 cm squamous carcinoma of the cervix. On oblique axial T2 the low-signal cervical stroma forms a complete dark ring around the tumour and the parametrial fat is clean. All pelvic nodes measure under 8 mm in short axis. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: Parametrial invasion is effectively excluded, the tumour is stage IB2, and radical hysterectomy remains a realistic option
choices: Parametrial invasion is effectively excluded, the tumour is stage IB2, and radical hysterectomy remains a realistic option
Parametrial invasion is present because the tumour exceeds 3 cm, the tumour is stage IIB, and chemoradiation is indicated
Parametrial invasion cannot be judged on T2 alone, so dynamic contrast imaging is needed before any stage is assigned
Parametrial invasion is probable because the dark ring is only a partial barrier, so the tumour should be staged as IIB
quiz.explain: The intact low-signal cervical stromal ring is one of the most useful negative predictors in pelvic MRI: when a complete rim of dark fibrous stroma surrounds the tumour on a properly planned oblique axial T2, parametrial invasion is very unlikely, and the negative predictive value is high enough to plan surgery on. Parametrial invasion is called when that ring is disrupted full thickness with irregular tumour signal extending into the parametrial fat, sometimes encasing vessels or reaching the ureter. Under FIGO 2018, size subdivides stage IB: IB1 is under 2 cm, IB2 is 2 cm to under 4 cm, and IB3 is 4 cm or more, so a 3.2 cm tumour confined to the cervix is IB2. Tumour size alone does not create parametrial invasion, although the probability rises with size. Stage IIB, meaning parametrial disease, generally shifts management from radical hysterectomy to chemoradiation.

quiz.prompt: In FIGO 2018 staging of cervical carcinoma, give the depth of stromal invasion above which a microscopically diagnosed tumour is no longer stage IA and becomes stage IB. Answer in millimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: FIGO 2018 defines stage IA as invasive carcinoma diagnosed only by microscopy, with IA1 invading 3 mm or less in depth and IA2 invading more than 3 mm and up to 5 mm. Above 5 mm the tumour is stage IB regardless of how it was found. A notable change from earlier editions is that the horizontal extent criterion, previously 7 mm, was dropped altogether, so depth of stromal invasion is now the only measurement that separates IA1 from IA2 from IB. This matters for radiology in a mostly negative way: stage IA disease is a pathological diagnosis made on a cone or loop excision, and lesions of that depth are usually invisible on MRI. Reporting a normal-looking cervix does not exclude IA disease. MRI's contribution begins at IB, where tumour size, parametrial extension, vaginal involvement and nodal status are the questions it can genuinely answer.

quiz.prompt: A woman with a 3 cm cervical carcinoma that appears confined to the cervix on MRI has a 14 mm short-axis right external iliac node that is rounded and shows restricted diffusion. What stage should be reported and what does it change?
quiz.answer: Stage IIIC1r: nodal disease raises the stage in its own right under FIGO 2018, and the treatment shifts towards chemoradiation
choices: Stage IIIC1r: nodal disease raises the stage in its own right under FIGO 2018, and the treatment shifts towards chemoradiation
Stage IB2 with the node reported separately: nodal status does not enter the FIGO stage for carcinoma of the cervix
Stage IIIC2r: iliac nodal disease is grouped with para-aortic disease when it is detected on imaging rather than at surgery
Stage IVB: a malignant node outside the cervix constitutes distant disease, so treatment becomes palliative systemic therapy
quiz.explain: The most consequential change in FIGO 2018 was the creation of stage IIIC, which lets nodal disease raise the stage independently of the local extent of the tumour. IIIC1 is pelvic nodal disease and IIIC2 is para-aortic nodal disease. Because the finding may come from imaging or from pathology, the stage carries a suffix — r when assigned on imaging and p when assigned on histology — so this case is IIIC1r. A small primary confined to the cervix with one positive pelvic node is therefore stage III, which sounds startling until you remember that nodal status is among the strongest prognostic factors in this disease. Practically, it usually moves the patient from surgery to definitive chemoradiation, and it changes the radiotherapy volume. Judge nodes on shape, necrosis, irregular border and diffusion as well as size; PET-CT is often added to check the para-aortic chain before the field is drawn.

quiz.prompt: You are supervising the acquisition for a cervical cancer staging MRI. Say how you would plan the small field-of-view T2 stacks on the cervix, and explain why the plane matters for the numbers you will go on to report.
quiz.answer: Plan a sagittal T2 first, then prescribe an oblique axial stack perpendicular to the long axis of the endocervical canal, with an oblique coronal parallel to it. An off-axis plane cuts the cervix obliquely, which exaggerates the measured tumour diameter and blurs the low-signal stromal ring, so both the FIGO size threshold and the assessment of parametrial invasion become unreliable.
quiz.explain: Cervical staging turns on two things that are both geometry-dependent: a size measurement that decides between IB1, IB2 and IB3, and the integrity of a thin dark ring of stroma that decides between stage I and stage IIB. A straight axial stack through a cervix that is anteverted or retroverted slices it obliquely, so the cervix appears as an ellipse, the tumour is measured across its longest oblique dimension, and the stromal ring is partial-volumed into a blur that looks disrupted. Both errors push the patient up a stage. So plan from the sagittal every time: an oblique axial perpendicular to the endocervical canal, a matching oblique coronal, thin slices, small field of view, and no fat suppression on the T2 stacks, since parametrial invasion is read against bright parametrial fat. Antiperistaltic agents help, and vaginal gel can open the fornices when vaginal involvement is the question.

quiz.prompt: An endometrial carcinoma fills the uterine cavity. On sagittal T2 and on the contrast-enhanced images, tumour extends beyond half the thickness of the fundal myometrium, while the low-signal cervical stroma is intact throughout. What does the report need to convey?
quiz.answer: Deep myometrial invasion without cervical stromal involvement, a combination that raises nodal risk and shapes how extensive the surgery should be
choices: Deep myometrial invasion without cervical stromal involvement, a combination that raises nodal risk and shapes how extensive the surgery should be
Superficial myometrial invasion alone, since tumour must reach the serosal surface before invasion is graded as deep in this setting
Cervical stromal involvement is present, since tumour filling the cavity necessarily extends downward into the endocervical canal as well
Depth cannot be assessed without diffusion imaging, since T2 and contrast-enhanced images both systematically overestimate the depth
quiz.explain: The threshold that has survived every revision of endometrial staging is 50%: tumour invading less than half the myometrial thickness is superficial, and half or more is deep. Deep invasion correlates strongly with lymphovascular space invasion and nodal metastasis, which is why it influences whether nodal assessment or sentinel node mapping is performed. Cervical stromal involvement is a separate question and requires tumour to breach the dark cervical stroma; tumour merely extending along the endocervical mucosa does not count. Measure depth perpendicular to the serosa at the point of deepest invasion and express it as a fraction, not in millimetres. The traps are worth knowing: adenomyosis and fibroids distort the myometrium, the cornual myometrium is thin so invasion looks deeper than it is, and a distended cavity thins the wall. Modern FIGO staging also incorporates molecular classification, so imaging depth is one input among several.

quiz.prompt: Your endometrial MRI protocol is being rewritten. Say which sequences and which post-contrast timing you would insist on for judging the depth of myometrial invasion, and what each one contributes.
quiz.answer: Sagittal T2 plus an oblique axial T2 planned perpendicular to the long axis of the endometrial cavity for the anatomy; diffusion-weighted imaging with ADC, where tumour is bright at high b-value against darker myometrium; and dynamic contrast imaging read at the equilibrium phase around two to three minutes, when tumour-to-myometrium contrast is greatest and the subendometrial enhancing band can be followed.
quiz.explain: Three sequences, three jobs. Oblique axial T2 perpendicular to the cavity is the geometric foundation, because a tangential slice through a curved fundus manufactures apparent deep invasion. Diffusion adds lesion conspicuity: endometrial carcinoma is cellular and bright on high b-value images with a low ADC, while myometrium is not, and combining diffusion with T2 improves accuracy for depth in most series. Contrast timing is the detail people get wrong. Very early images show the thin subendometrial enhancing band, whose interruption suggests myometrial invasion, but the band is unreliable in an atrophic or fibroid uterus. The most consistently useful window is the equilibrium phase at roughly two to three minutes, when relatively hypoenhancing tumour is best set off against enhancing myometrium. Read the three together, and if they disagree, say which one you have believed and why.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old with heavy menstrual bleeding has a 2.6 cm fibroid whose bulk sits within the endometrial cavity, with roughly a third of its volume extending into the myometrium. She wishes to preserve fertility. What should the report drive?
quiz.answer: A FIGO type 1 submucosal fibroid, amenable to hysteroscopic resection, so report the intramural depth and the residual myometrial thickness
choices: A FIGO type 1 submucosal fibroid, amenable to hysteroscopic resection, so report the intramural depth and the residual myometrial thickness
A FIGO type 3 fibroid, which abuts the endometrium but requires abdominal myomectomy rather than any hysteroscopic approach
