A FIGO type 5 fibroid, largely intramural with a subserosal component, for which uterine artery embolisation is the first-line option
A FIGO type 0 fibroid, sitting on a stalk within the cavity, for which no measurement of intramural depth is needed at all
quiz.explain: The FIGO leiomyoma subclassification runs 0 to 8 and describes position rather than size. Type 0 is entirely intracavitary on a stalk; type 1 is submucosal with less than half its volume intramural; type 2 is submucosal with half or more intramural; type 3 lies wholly within the myometrium but contacts the endometrium; type 4 is purely intramural; type 5 is subserosal with half or more intramural; type 6 is subserosal with less than half; type 7 is pedunculated subserosal; type 8 covers cervical and parasitic fibroids. Types 0 to 2 are the hysteroscopically resectable group, which is why this classification changes the operation. For type 1 and type 2 the surgeon also needs the intramural depth and the thickness of myometrium left between fibroid and serosa, because a thin margin raises the risk of perforation and fluid overload.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these FIGO leiomyoma subtypes by position, from the one lying entirely within the endometrial cavity to the one lying entirely outside the serosa.
quiz.answer: type-0 type-2 type-4 type-6 type-7
quiz.explain: The numbering is a gradient that walks outward from the cavity to the peritoneal surface, which is why it is worth learning as a sequence rather than as a list. Type 0 is pedunculated within the cavity; type 2 is submucosal with half or more of its bulk in the myometrium; type 4 is wholly intramural, touching neither surface; type 6 is subserosal with less than half embedded; type 7 is pedunculated outside the serosa. Treatment tracks the gradient. Types 0 to 2 come out hysteroscopically through the cervix. Types 3 to 6 need myomectomy, open or laparoscopic, or medical management. Type 7 is a laparoscopic problem, and a narrow-stalked type 7 is a relative caution for uterine artery embolisation, as is a type 0, which can be expelled or slough into the cavity. Before embolisation also check for coexisting adenomyosis and confirm the fibroids enhance, since a degenerated fibroid will not shrink.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old has an ill-defined 4 cm area of low T2 signal in the posterior myometrium containing tiny bright foci, with no cleavage plane from surrounding muscle and an endometrial stripe that runs through it undisplaced. What is the discriminating reading, and what does it mean for treatment?
quiz.answer: Focal adenomyosis: ill-defined margins with little mass effect separate it from a fibroid, so hysteroscopic resection is not an option here
choices: Focal adenomyosis: ill-defined margins with little mass effect separate it from a fibroid, so hysteroscopic resection is not an option here
An intramural fibroid: low T2 signal within the myometrium indicates smooth muscle, so myomectomy would be expected to relieve symptoms
A degenerating fibroid: bright foci within a dark myometrial lesion indicate cystic degeneration and predict a poor response to embolisation
Endometrial carcinoma invading the myometrium: an undisplaced stripe crossing a low signal myometrial lesion is the sign of invasion
quiz.explain: Fibroid and adenomyoma both look dark on T2, so the discriminators are shape and behaviour rather than signal. A fibroid is a discrete round lesion with a pseudocapsule, a visible cleavage plane, often a rim of dilated vessels, and it displaces whatever lies next to it, including the endometrial stripe. Adenomyosis infiltrates: its margins are ill-defined, it is elliptical rather than round, it widens the myometrium with minimal mass effect, and the endometrium runs through it undisturbed. The tiny T2-bright foci are ectopic endometrial glands and small cysts; corresponding T1-bright foci from haemorrhage are more specific still. The distinction changes the plan, because there is no plane to shell an adenomyoma out of and no cavity lesion to resect hysteroscopically. Options are medical treatment, focused ultrasound or ablation, embolisation with a less durable response than for fibroids, or hysterectomy.

quiz.prompt: A 33-year-old with dysmenorrhoea and dyschezia has bilateral endometriomas that meet in the midline behind the uterus. Say what that appearance predicts, and set out the specific sites your report must address before the surgical planning meeting.
quiz.answer: Kissing ovaries predict dense posterior compartment adhesions and a high likelihood of deep infiltrating disease, particularly bowel disease. The report must address the torus uterinus and uterosacral ligaments, the rectovaginal septum and posterior vaginal fornix, the rectosigmoid with lesion length, depth of wall involvement and distance from the anal verge, whether the pouch of Douglas is obliterated, the bladder dome and vesicouterine pouch, and the ureters with any hydronephrosis.
quiz.explain: Ovaries that touch across the midline are not simply two endometriomas; they are tethered there by adhesions, and the sign is strongly associated with severe deep infiltrating endometriosis, especially of the bowel. MRI is asked to map disease by compartment. Anteriorly: bladder dome, vesicouterine pouch and the distal ureters. Middle: uterus, ovaries, torus uterinus, uterosacral ligaments, the retrocervical region, the rectovaginal septum and the posterior vaginal fornix. Posteriorly: the rectosigmoid, where the surgeon needs the number of lesions, the craniocaudal length, whether the lesion reaches muscularis or mucosa, and the distance from the anal verge, since those determine shaving versus disc excision versus segmental resection. Say explicitly whether the pouch of Douglas is obliterated. Ureteric involvement and hydronephrosis change the consent conversation and may require a stent, so they must never be left implicit.

quiz.prompt: A woman with two second-trimester pregnancy losses has pelvic MRI. The cavity is divided by a low-signal T2 midline band reaching the internal os, the internal indentation is 2.2 cm deep with an acute apex, and the external fundal contour is smooth with a 4 mm dip. What operation does this support?
quiz.answer: Hysteroscopic resection of the septum, since an external fundal contour indented by less than 10 mm places this in the septate group
choices: Hysteroscopic resection of the septum, since an external fundal contour indented by less than 10 mm places this in the septate group
Abdominal metroplasty to unify two horns, since a deep internal indentation defines a bicornuate uterus whatever the external contour
No surgery at all, since a low-signal midline band in the fundus is a normal muscular variant with no reproductive consequence
Laparoscopic excision of a rudimentary horn, since a divided cavity with an indented contour indicates a unicornuate configuration
quiz.explain: The whole distinction rests on the outside of the uterus, not the inside. Both a septate and a bicornuate uterus have a divided cavity; what separates them is the external fundal contour. Under the ASRM 2021 criteria a uterus is septate when the external contour is flat or indented by 1 cm or less while the internal indentation exceeds 1 cm with an acute angle, and bicornuate when the external indentation exceeds 1 cm. Here the outer contour dips only 4 mm, so this is septate. That matters because a septum can be divided transcervically at hysteroscopy, a low-morbidity day procedure, whereas separating two true horns needs an abdominal metroplasty that is rarely performed and leaves a scarred uterus. Note that the ESHRE and ESGE classification uses different thresholds, so state which system you are applying. Always look at the kidneys, since Mullerian anomalies travel with renal agenesis.

nodes.title: Breast Calcifications: Reading the Morphology
nodes.goal: Read a group of breast calcifications by morphology and distribution together, decide whether it needs sampling, and carry a stereotactic biopsy through to a concordant result.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old is recalled from screening. Magnification craniocaudal and true lateral views show a 9 mm group of calcifications: on the craniocaudal view they are smudgy and ill-defined, but on the true lateral they settle into thin crescents with flat upper borders. What do you do?
quiz.answer: Report milk of calcium in microcysts and return her to routine screening
choices: Report milk of calcium in microcysts and return her to routine screening
Report fine pleomorphic calcification and book a stereotactic biopsy this week
Report amorphous calcification and offer six-month short-interval magnification views
Report dystrophic calcification and retrieve the previous operation note first
quiz.explain: This is the one appearance that is defined by how it changes between projections. Calcium sediments to the bottom of tiny cysts, so with the vertical beam of a craniocaudal view you look down the column and see a smudge that can mimic amorphous calcification; with the horizontal beam of a 90-degree lateral you look across it and see a meniscus, the teacup. The mediolateral oblique is not good enough, because its angled beam blurs the layering; ask specifically for a true lateral. Milk of calcium is BI-RADS 5th edition category 2 and needs nothing further. The trap runs the other way too: if the group looks identical on both projections, the layering argument is not available to you and the morphology must stand on its own.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old has a new 2.5 cm run of calcifications extending back from the nipple in a wedge that points to the nipple. On magnification they are thin, of varying calibre, some branching in a dot-dash pattern. How do you assess and act?
quiz.answer: Category 4C: biopsy now, and warn the team that high-grade DCIS is likely
choices: Category 4C: biopsy now, and warn the team that high-grade DCIS is likely
Category 3: repeat magnification views in six months, since it has not changed
Category 2: benign secretory calcification, so return her to routine screening
Category 0: add ultrasound and MRI before any decision on this group is taken
quiz.explain: Fine linear and fine-linear-branching calcification carries the highest positive predictive value of any morphology in the BI-RADS 5th edition atlas, around 70 per cent, which places it above the 50 per cent floor of subcategory 4C. Category 5 is reserved for at least 95 per cent likelihood and would need supporting features such as an associated mass or skin change. The segmental distribution compounds the suspicion because it follows a duct system, exactly the territory high-grade comedo DCIS necrosis casts. Category 3 is not available for suspicious morphology; it is reserved for findings with a 2 per cent ceiling. Tell the surgeon the span, because the calcification often maps the disease better than any other test and drives the choice between wide excision and mastectomy.

quiz.prompt: Your unit biopsies 40 groups of fine-linear-branching calcification over a year. Using the positive predictive value of 70 per cent that the BI-RADS 5th edition atlas quotes for this morphology, how many benign results should you expect? Answer as a whole number of biopsies.
quiz.explain: Thirty per cent of 40 is 12. The arithmetic matters more than it looks. Even the most suspicious calcification morphology in the lexicon sends roughly three women in ten home with a benign result, and if you tell a woman before her biopsy that the appearance is worrying, you should also be able to tell her how often this worry proves unfounded. Run the same sum for the other suspicious morphologies and the counselling changes shape: amorphous sits near 21 per cent, coarse heterogeneous near 13 per cent, fine pleomorphic near 29 per cent, so for amorphous calcification roughly four out of five biopsies are benign. That is not an argument against biopsy; it is the reason a benign result must still be checked against the imaging for concordance rather than simply accepted.

quiz.prompt: In the BI-RADS 5th edition, what is the minimum likelihood of malignancy a finding must carry before it may be assessed as category 5? Answer as a whole-number percentage.
quiz.explain: Category 5 in the BI-RADS 5th edition means highly suggestive of malignancy, at least 95 per cent. The practical consequence is that a category 5 assessment licenses definitive one-stage management: if the core comes back benign, the result is discordant by definition and cannot be accepted. Category 4 spans everything above 2 per cent and below 95, subdivided as 4A above 2 to 10 per cent, 4B above 10 to 50 per cent, and 4C above 50 to below 95 per cent. Category 3, probably benign, has a 2 per cent ceiling and carries a surveillance rather than a biopsy pathway. Knowing where the boundaries fall is what lets you convert a positive predictive value quoted for a morphology into a subcategory the rest of the team can act on.

quiz.prompt: You perform a stereotactic vacuum-assisted biopsy for grouped amorphous calcification. The specimen radiograph clearly shows calcification in three cores, but histology reports fibrocystic change with no calcification identified. In one or two sentences, say what you do next and why.
quiz.answer: Treat this as discordant: ask the pathologist to cut deeper levels and to examine the block under polarised light for calcium oxalate, and if calcification still cannot be matched to the histology, repeat the sampling or proceed to excision.
quiz.explain: Radiological-pathological concordance is the safety net of the whole calcification pathway, and it fails silently if nobody checks it. Two things can go wrong here. The calcium may simply lie in a part of the block that has not yet been sectioned, which deeper levels solve. Or it may be calcium oxalate, which is transparent on routine haematoxylin and eosin staining and only becomes visible as a birefringent crystal under polarised light; oxalate tends to accompany benign processes, while the calcium phosphate of hydroxyapatite is what malignancy usually produces. If neither manoeuvre finds calcium, the pathologist has not examined the lesion you targeted, and a benign report tells you nothing about it. Say so explicitly in the report rather than filing the case.

quiz.prompt: A surgeon challenges you at the multidisciplinary meeting: why keep biopsying calcification when the clinical examination and the ultrasound are both normal? In one or two sentences, explain what calcification contributes to the detection of DCIS.
quiz.answer: Most DCIS is impalpable and invisible on ultrasound, so calcification is frequently the only sign it produces, and it is the morphology and distribution of that calcification that let mammography find the disease before it becomes invasive.
quiz.explain: DCIS is confined within the duct, so it usually creates no mass to feel and no hypoechoic lesion to see. What it does create is necrotic debris and secretory material that mineralises inside the duct lumen, which is why calcification is its dominant, and often its sole, imaging manifestation. The pattern reflects the grade: high-grade comedo necrosis casts the duct and gives fine linear and branching forms, while low-grade cribriform and micropapillary disease produces rounder, finer, more amorphous granules that are much easier to dismiss. This is also the honest answer to the overdiagnosis question the surgeon is really asking: calcification detection is why screening finds DCIS at all, and the debate about which DCIS needs treating is a separate one from whether we can see it.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these BI-RADS 5th edition distribution descriptors from the one that argues most strongly for a benign cause to the one that argues most strongly for malignancy.
quiz.answer: diffuse regional grouped linear segmental
quiz.explain: Distribution is the second axis, and it can override morphology in both directions. Diffuse calcification scattered randomly through both breasts is almost always benign, however unimpressive the individual particles look, because cancer does not arise everywhere at once. Regional means a large volume of tissue, over 2 cm across, that does not conform to a duct system, so it too is usually a benign process. Grouped, at least five particles in a centimetre of tissue, focuses suspicion because the volume is small enough for one duct system. Linear and segmental follow ducts and are the most worrying: segmental implies a whole lobe drained by one duct, the territory DCIS occupies. Always report the pair together, because grouped amorphous calcification and diffuse amorphous calcification lead to opposite decisions.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the steps of a stereotactic vacuum-assisted biopsy for calcification in the order you would carry them out.
quiz.answer: magnification-views stereotactic-pair vacuum-sampling specimen-radiograph clip-deployment post-biopsy-mammogram
quiz.explain: Each step protects the one after it. Magnification craniocaudal and true lateral views come first because they establish morphology, extent and the best approach, and they are much harder to obtain once a cavity and a haematoma exist. The stereotactic pair at plus and minus 15 degrees provides the depth coordinate. Sampling follows, then the specimen radiograph, which is the only proof that the calcification is in the pot rather than still in the breast; if it is absent, you resample now, not next week. The clip is deployed once you know the target has been hit, since it marks the site for the surgeon and for future comparison. The two-view post-biopsy mammogram closes the loop by recording where the clip actually ended up, and how much calcification remains.

quiz.prompt: Three years after wide local excision and radiotherapy, a woman's mammogram shows a new 2 cm cluster of coarse irregular calcifications at the scar, several with lucent centres, alongside an oval fat-density lesion with a thin calcified rim. What is your report?
quiz.answer: Benign dystrophic calcification and an oil cyst; complete the routine annual mammogram
choices: Benign dystrophic calcification and an oil cyst; complete the routine annual mammogram
Suspicious pleomorphic calcification at the scar; arrange stereotactic biopsy of the group
Probably benign findings; bring her back for magnification views of the scar at six months
Incomplete assessment; obtain contrast-enhanced MRI of both breasts before deciding
quiz.explain: Fat necrosis writes itself into the mammogram in a recognisable way. Dystrophic calcification is coarse, irregular and usually more than half a millimetre across, often with lucent centres, and it appears in irradiated or operated tissue over months to years. The oval fat-density lesion with a thin calcified rim is an oil cyst, and a lesion containing fat is benign; that is one of the few genuinely reliable rules in breast imaging. Recurrent disease at a scar tends to produce fine pleomorphic calcification, an enlarging mass, or increasing distortion rather than lucent-centred coarse particles. What earns a second look is any part of the group whose particles are thin, of varying calibre and without lucent centres, because dystrophic and malignant calcification can coexist at an operated site.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old has dense, smooth, rod-shaped calcifications more than a millimetre wide scattered through both breasts, several with lucent centres, all oriented along lines converging towards the nipples. Some branch, but each limb is continuous and smooth. What is the right report?
quiz.answer: Secretory calcification of duct ectasia: benign, with no further imaging required
choices: Secretory calcification of duct ectasia: benign, with no further imaging required
Comedo DCIS spanning both breasts: stereotactic biopsy of the densest group
Vascular calcification: report the cardiovascular risk and repeat imaging in a year
Skin calcification: confirm with tangential views before returning her to screening
quiz.explain: This is the benign appearance most often mistaken for high-grade DCIS, because both fill ducts and both can branch. The discriminators are calibre and continuity. Secretory, or plasma-cell mastitis, calcification is large and rod-like, typically over half a millimetre wide, smooth-edged, of even thickness along its length, often with a lucent centre because the calcium coats the duct wall around retained secretions, and it is usually bilateral and roughly symmetrical in an older woman. Malignant fine linear calcification is thin, irregular in calibre, discontinuous in a dot-dash rhythm, and confined to one segment. Vascular calcification runs as parallel tram-tracks that do not converge on the nipple, and skin calcification is polygonal with lucent centres and sits in the skin line on a tangential view.

quiz.prompt: On both screening projections a 42-year-old has a group of small lucent-centred polygonal calcifications that keep the same relationship to one another and lie close to the medial skin surface on each view. What is the most useful next step?
quiz.answer: A tangential view of the marked skin site, to project the group into the skin line
choices: A tangential view of the marked skin site, to project the group into the skin line
A stereotactic vacuum biopsy of the group with a marker clip left at the site
Targeted ultrasound of the medial breast, with biopsy of any correlate found
Six-month magnification follow-up of both breasts to establish that it is stable
quiz.explain: Dermal calcification is a classic false alarm, and it is cheap to exclude. The clue is the fixed internal arrangement: because the group lies in a flat sheet of skin rather than in three-dimensional breast tissue, the particles keep the same pattern relative to one another whatever the projection, whereas deep calcification changes its configuration as the breast is compressed differently. The particles themselves are small, polygonal and lucent-centred, lying in sweat glands. The confirmatory manoeuvre is an alphanumeric grid localisation of the skin surface followed by a tangential projection, which throws the group into the skin line where it becomes unmistakable. Ultrasound will not show them, and biopsying skin calcification is an avoidable harm that a single extra view prevents.

quiz.prompt: A 51-year-old's mammogram shows hundreds of amorphous calcifications scattered randomly and roughly symmetrically through both breasts, with no group standing out and no associated mass or distortion. How should you assess this?
quiz.answer: The bilateral random scatter makes them benign; return her to routine screening
choices: The bilateral random scatter makes them benign; return her to routine screening
Amorphous morphology stays suspicious wherever it lies; biopsy the largest group
Assess as probably benign and repeat magnification views of both breasts at six months
Assess as incomplete and add tomosynthesis and ultrasound of both breasts today
quiz.explain: Morphology and distribution are read together, never in isolation, and this is the case that proves it. Amorphous calcification carries a positive predictive value of roughly 21 per cent in the BI-RADS 5th edition atlas when it is grouped, which is squarely biopsy territory. Spread diffusely and bilaterally, the same particles reflect fibrocystic change, sclerosing adenosis or involuting lobules, and biopsy of one arbitrarily chosen area answers no question, because there is no reason to think the sampled millilitre differs from the rest. What would change this is asymmetry: a group that is denser, more numerous, or newer than the surrounding background, or one that has appeared since the last round. Compare with the previous films before you settle on diffuse.

quiz.prompt: After an uneventful stereotactic vacuum biopsy of an upper outer quadrant calcification group, the two-view post-biopsy mammogram shows the marker clip lying about 3 cm away from the residual calcification and biopsy cavity. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: Clip displacement is common; record the offset so that localisation still targets the calcification
choices: Clip displacement is common; record the offset so that localisation still targets the calcification
The clip is correctly sited, which means the device removed all of the calcification
Repeat the biopsy today, because the wrong quadrant has clearly been sampled instead
No action is needed, since the surgeon will locate the cavity by palpation at operation
quiz.explain: The clip is deployed while the breast is compressed. When compression is released the tissue re-expands like a concertina and the clip can travel several centimetres along the axis of compression, most often towards the skin; this is the accordion effect, and it is a property of the technique rather than an error. The post-biopsy two-view mammogram exists precisely to document it. What matters is that the report states where the residual calcification actually lies, so that a subsequent wire or seed is placed to the calcification rather than to the clip. Assuming the clip marks the target is how a wrong-site excision happens. Absence of visible residual calcification does not confirm complete removal either, and does not change the need for surgical clearance if the histology is malignant.

nodes.title: Breast MRI, Ultrasound and Staging
nodes.goal: Choose breast MRI and ultrasound for the situations in which they change surgical management, and interpret enhancement, kinetics, nodes, implants and the treated breast accordingly.

quiz.prompt: Four women are referred to your breast unit asking about supplemental MRI screening. Which of them should be offered annual contrast-enhanced breast MRI alongside mammography?
quiz.answer: A 31-year-old who had mantle radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma when she was seventeen
choices: A 31-year-old who had mantle radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma when she was seventeen
A 47-year-old whose mother developed a breast cancer at the age of seventy-four
A 52-year-old with heterogeneously dense breasts and no relevant family history
A 39-year-old whose fibroadenoma was surgically excised six years ago and confirmed
quiz.explain: Chest irradiation between roughly ages 10 and 30 confers a lifetime breast cancer risk approaching that of a BRCA carrier, which is why supplemental MRI is recommended, usually beginning about eight years after treatment and not before age 25. The threshold in general use is a lifetime risk of 20 to 25 per cent or more, which also captures BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers and their untested first-degree relatives, TP53, PTEN, CDH1 and PALB2. A single second-degree or late-onset first-degree relative does not reach that threshold. Dense tissue alone raises risk modestly and lowers mammographic sensitivity, but it is handled by supplemental ultrasound or contrast-enhanced mammography in most services rather than by MRI. Excised benign fibroadenoma confers no meaningful excess risk at all.

quiz.prompt: On a high-risk screening MRI a 6 mm mass is dark on T2, has an irregular margin and heterogeneous internal enhancement, and its kinetic curve rises steeply then falls away after two minutes. Nothing is visible on the mammogram. What do you do?
quiz.answer: Assess as suspicious, arrange second-look ultrasound, and biopsy under whichever guidance shows it
choices: Assess as suspicious, arrange second-look ultrasound, and biopsy under whichever guidance shows it
Assess as benign, since persistent type 1 kinetics permit return to annual screening
Assess as probably benign and repeat the whole examination at six months for stability
Assess as artefactual, re-shim the magnet, and repeat the dynamic series after re-injection
quiz.explain: A steep initial rise with a fall after the two-minute mark is a type 3 washout curve, the most worrying of the three delayed patterns, and here it agrees with a morphology that is already suspicious: irregular margin, heterogeneous internal enhancement, and low T2 signal. When morphology and kinetics disagree, morphology wins, because plenty of malignancies, particularly DCIS and invasive lobular carcinoma, show type 1 persistent enhancement, and plenty of fibroadenomas wash out. The practical route is second-look targeted ultrasound of the correct quadrant and depth, which finds a correlate for a substantial minority of MRI-detected lesions and makes biopsy quicker, cheaper and better tolerated. If nothing is found, biopsy under MRI guidance rather than downgrading the lesion because ultrasound was negative.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old having high-risk screening MRI has moderate background parenchymal enhancement that obscures the study, and you cannot exclude a small lesion. In one or two sentences, say how you would change the timing of the repeat examination and why.
quiz.answer: Rebook her for the second week of her menstrual cycle, around days seven to fourteen, because background parenchymal enhancement is lowest then, whereas late-cycle enhancement both conceals small cancers and generates false positives.
quiz.explain: Normal fibroglandular tissue enhances, and how much it enhances is under hormonal control. It is greatest in the late luteal phase and lowest in the follicular phase after menstruation, which is why premenopausal women are booked in the second week of the cycle wherever the service can manage it. The BI-RADS 5th edition MRI lexicon grades background enhancement as minimal, mild, moderate or marked, and this should be stated in every report because it qualifies the sensitivity of the study in the same way breast density qualifies a mammogram. Marked enhancement does not just hide lesions; it produces recalls and benign biopsies. Exogenous oestrogen and recent cessation of hormone therapy also raise it, so ask about both before assuming poor timing.

quiz.prompt: A woman with silicone implants has MRI for a change in breast shape. On silicone-selective sequences several curvilinear low-signal lines float within the silicone, well away from the periphery, and no silicone lies outside the fibrous capsule. In one or two sentences, report the finding and its consequence.
quiz.answer: This is the linguine sign of intracapsular rupture: the elastomer shell has collapsed inside an intact fibrous capsule, so the silicone remains contained and she needs elective implant exchange rather than urgent surgery.
quiz.explain: Implant imaging turns on two boundaries: the implant's own elastomer shell and the fibrous capsule the body builds around it. When the shell tears but the capsule holds, silicone escapes the shell yet stays inside the capsule, and the collapsed shell floats within it as the wavy dark lines of the linguine sign. Lesser degrees give the subcapsular line, or the keyhole and teardrop signs where a little silicone tracks into a radial fold. Radial folds alone, with no silicone between the layers, are a normal finding and the commonest source of overcalling. Extracapsular rupture is the different and more consequential diagnosis: silicone outside the capsule, in the parenchyma or in axillary nodes, giving the snowstorm appearance of dirty shadowing on ultrasound.

quiz.prompt: On a dynamic breast MRI a lesion has a signal intensity of 180 before contrast and 468 on the first post-contrast acquisition. Calculate the initial percentage enhancement. Answer as a whole-number percentage.
quiz.explain: Initial enhancement is the rise divided by the baseline: 468 minus 180 is 288, and 288 divided by 180 is 1.6, so 160 per cent. The number matters because the initial phase, before roughly two minutes, is graded slow, medium or rapid, and the fast rise of a malignancy reflects leaky neovascular capillaries with wide endothelial gaps. Curve typing then uses the delayed phase after that point: type 1 continues to rise, type 2 plateaus, type 3 falls away. Do the arithmetic on a region of interest placed in the most avidly enhancing part of the lesion, avoiding necrosis and avoiding the edge, because a region straddling normal tissue flattens the curve. Absolute signal intensities are not comparable between scanners, but the ratio is.

quiz.prompt: On axillary ultrasound before breast cancer surgery, above what uniform cortical thickness is a node conventionally regarded as suspicious and worth sampling? Answer in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Cortical thickness above about 3 mm is the threshold most units use, but the shape of the thickening matters as much as the number. Tumour arrives through the afferent lymphatics and first deposits in the subcapsular sinus, so the earliest sign is a focal eccentric bulge of cortex, not uniform thickening, and a node with an eccentric 5 mm lobe and a perfectly preserved fatty hilum can still be involved. Later changes are loss of the hilum, rounding with a shortened long-to-short axis ratio, non-hilar peripheral vascularity, and matting. Sensitivity is moderate at best, so a normal axillary ultrasound does not replace sentinel node biopsy; a positive needle sample, however, changes the operation and can spare the patient a two-stage procedure.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the acquisitions of a standard dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI in the order they are obtained and processed.
quiz.answer: localiser t2-weighted pre-contrast-t1 first-post-contrast delayed-post-contrast subtraction-images
quiz.explain: The order is not arbitrary. T2-weighted imaging is acquired before contrast because it must be uncontaminated: it is what tells you a mass is a cyst, a lymph node with a fatty hilum, or a T2-bright fibroadenoma with dark internal septations. The pre-contrast T1 series is the arithmetic baseline for everything that follows, so patient movement between it and the post-contrast series is what ruins subtractions. The first post-contrast acquisition, obtained within about 90 seconds of injection, carries most of the diagnostic weight because that is when malignant enhancement peaks against a still-quiet background; delayed acquisitions out to five or seven minutes define the curve type. Subtraction images are computed last, and should always be read alongside the source images rather than instead of them.

quiz.prompt: A 9 mm enhancing mass is seen only on MRI, and targeted ultrasound of the correct quadrant finds no correlate. Arrange the steps of the resulting work-up in the order they occur.
quiz.answer: mri-detection second-look-ultrasound mri-guided-biopsy clip-placement post-biopsy-mammogram
quiz.explain: Second-look ultrasound comes before MRI-guided biopsy for practical reasons: it is quicker, cheaper, better tolerated and available on any list, and it succeeds in a useful proportion of cases if you scan the right quadrant at the right depth with the MRI open beside you. When it fails, the lesion must still be sampled under MRI guidance rather than dismissed, because a negative second look does not downgrade a suspicious enhancing mass. A clip is deployed through the biopsy device before the patient leaves the magnet, since the lesion may be invisible by any other means and enhancement can vanish once the lesion has been sampled. The two-view post-biopsy mammogram records the clip position for future localisation and for comparison at follow-up.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old has a firm mobile lump. Ultrasound shows an 18 mm oval hypoechoic mass, wider than tall, circumscribed with three gentle lobulations, homogeneous internally, with mild posterior enhancement and no vascular distortion. What is the appropriate management?
quiz.answer: Probably benign: document it and offer six-month ultrasound follow-up, or biopsy if she prefers
choices: Probably benign: document it and offer six-month ultrasound follow-up, or biopsy if she prefers
Suspicious: perform a core biopsy today, because a palpable mass at any age needs tissue
Malignant features: arrange staging MRI and axillary ultrasound before taking a biopsy
Simple cyst: aspirate it under ultrasound guidance and discard the fluid if it is clear
quiz.explain: Every feature here is on the benign side of the BI-RADS ultrasound lexicon: oval shape, parallel orientation, circumscribed margin with no more than three gentle lobulations, homogeneous hypoechoic internal echoes, and posterior enhancement rather than shadowing. That combination in a woman of this age fits a fibroadenoma and carries a malignancy risk of around 2 per cent or less, which is category 3 territory. The features that would overturn it are a taller-than-wide orientation, an angular, microlobulated or spiculated margin, an echogenic halo, posterior acoustic shadowing, or internal calcification. A palpable mass is not itself a reason to biopsy, but it is a reason to take the woman's preference seriously, and many will choose tissue diagnosis over two years of surveillance.

quiz.prompt: Staging ultrasound in a woman with a 15 mm invasive carcinoma shows a level I axillary node with a preserved fatty hilum but an eccentric 5 mm bulge of cortex on one side. What is the right course?
quiz.answer: Sample the node with a needle and mark it with a clip before any systemic treatment
choices: Sample the node with a needle and mark it with a clip before any systemic treatment
Report it as reactive, since the fatty hilum is preserved throughout the whole node
Proceed directly to axillary node clearance without needle sampling of the node first
Repeat the axillary ultrasound once the primary tumour has been surgically removed
quiz.explain: An eccentric cortical bulge with a preserved hilum is the earliest morphological sign of metastasis, because deposits land in the subcapsular sinus and expand the cortex focally long before they efface the hilum. Preserved hilar fat is therefore reassuring only in a node whose cortex is uniformly thin. A fine needle or core sample of the most abnormal node converts imaging suspicion into a fact that changes the operation and the sequence of treatment. Marking the sampled node with a clip is what makes targeted axillary dissection possible if she has neoadjuvant chemotherapy, because a node that responds completely becomes impossible to find again. Clearance without sampling overtreats the substantial proportion of morphologically abnormal nodes that prove reactive.

quiz.prompt: A woman with a biopsy-proven 12 mm invasive ductal carcinoma has staging MRI. Beyond the mass, enhancement extends 5 cm posteriorly in a wedge converging on the nipple, with a clustered ring internal pattern. How should this change the plan?
quiz.answer: It suggests DCIS extending well beyond the mass: discuss wider excision or mastectomy
choices: It suggests DCIS extending well beyond the mass: discuss wider excision or mastectomy
It is benign fibrocystic enhancement: proceed with the planned wide local excision
It is background parenchymal enhancement: repeat the study in the second week of her cycle
It is post-biopsy change: attribute it to the recent core biopsy and disregard it entirely
quiz.explain: Non-mass enhancement is described by distribution and by internal pattern, and both are informative here. A segmental distribution occupies the territory of a single duct system, which is precisely how DCIS spreads. The clustered ring internal pattern, thin rings of enhancement around ducts filled with non-enhancing debris, is the most specific of the internal patterns for malignancy; homogeneous and heterogeneous patterns are far less discriminating. Background enhancement is bilateral and symmetrical rather than confined to one segment, and post-biopsy change is focal around the tract. Before converting a woman to mastectomy on MRI alone, obtain histology from the far end of the segment, because MRI overestimates extent often enough that a single wide excision plan should not be abandoned on imaging alone.

quiz.prompt: Fourteen months after wide local excision and radiotherapy, a woman has an area of nodular enhancement at the lumpectomy bed with a washout curve. The mammogram shows scarring only, and there is no fat signal within the enhancing tissue. What is your interpretation?
quiz.answer: Nodular washout enhancement at this interval is recurrence until histology proves otherwise
choices: Nodular washout enhancement at this interval is recurrence until histology proves otherwise
This is expected scar enhancement at fourteen months; repeat the study in twelve months
This is fat necrosis, whose enhancement follows fat on every sequence and needs no action
This is radiotherapy oedema; report the skin thickening and continue annual mammography
quiz.explain: Granulation tissue in a healing surgical bed does enhance, but its enhancement is typically thin and linear along the cavity wall, and it fades over the first year to eighteen months. Nodular enhancement, particularly with washout kinetics, at more than a year from surgery, is the pattern of recurrence and warrants biopsy. Fat necrosis is the important mimic and is excluded here by the absence of internal fat signal: fat necrosis contains a central component that follows fat on every sequence and loses signal with fat suppression, usually with a smooth enhancing rim. Radiotherapy change causes diffuse skin thickening and oedema that settles over two to three years. Comparison with the earliest post-treatment baseline study is what makes this judgement reliable.

quiz.prompt: A woman presents with an axillary nodal deposit of adenocarcinoma consistent with a breast primary, but mammography and whole-breast ultrasound are both normal. What is the most useful next imaging step?
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced breast MRI, which finds the primary in most such patients and can spare mastectomy
choices: Contrast-enhanced breast MRI, which finds the primary in most such patients and can spare mastectomy
Whole-body PET-CT alone, reserving breast MRI for those with dense fibroglandular tissue
Bilateral mastectomy without further breast imaging, to clear the presumed occult primary
Six-monthly mammographic follow-up, until the primary tumour grows to a detectable size
quiz.explain: Occult primary presenting as axillary nodal metastasis is one of the strongest indications for breast MRI, because it locates a mammographically and sonographically invisible tumour in the majority of cases. That matters practically rather than academically: if MRI shows a small unifocal primary, the woman can have breast-conserving surgery and radiotherapy instead of the mastectomy that historically followed a negative work-up, and if MRI is genuinely negative, whole-breast radiotherapy with axillary treatment becomes a defensible alternative. PET-CT contributes to distant staging and may show the primary, but its spatial resolution is poor for small breast lesions. Delay while awaiting growth is not an option once nodal disease is established.

nodes.title: Reading the Mammogram
nodes.goal: Work up a mammographic finding, assign the BI-RADS category that names the next action, and say when ultrasound or MRI adds something.

quiz.prompt: A screening mammogram in a 54-year-old shows a new group of calcifications in the upper outer left breast that were not present two years ago. The reader is tempted to call them probably benign and repeat the study in six months. Explain what must happen first, and how the category is then chosen.
quiz.answer: The screening study is incomplete, so the correct assessment is category 0 and a recall for further imaging rather than a probably-benign category assigned from a screening film. The further imaging is magnification views in the craniocaudal and true lateral projections, which resolve the morphology of individual particles and let milk of calcium layer into teacup shapes on the horizontal-beam lateral, with ultrasound if an underlying mass is suspected. Probably-benign is an assessment made after a complete diagnostic workup, precisely because magnification so often reclassifies a group in one direction or the other. Once the morphology and distribution are seen, typically benign forms such as vascular, coarse popcorn-like, large rod-like, round, rim, dystrophic, milk of calcium and suture calcifications take category 2 and routine screening. A group of round or punctate calcifications with no suspicious feature may take category 3 with the six-month follow-up protocol. Amorphous, coarse heterogeneous, fine pleomorphic and fine linear or fine-linear branching morphologies are suspicious and take category 4, rising through the subcategories with more suspicious morphology and with a linear or segmental rather than grouped distribution, and are sampled by stereotactic or tomosynthesis-guided vacuum-assisted biopsy, with a specimen radiograph to prove the calcifications were retrieved and a marker clip left at the site.
quiz.explain: Category 0 exists because the screening examination and the diagnostic examination are different tests with different purposes, and a suspicion level cannot honestly be assigned until the second one has been done. The workup is not a formality: magnification changes the apparent morphology of calcifications more than any other manoeuvre in mammography, turning apparently grouped amorphous particles into either unmistakable milk of calcium or unmistakable fine pleomorphic ones. The specimen radiograph and the marker clip are the two steps most often forgotten and the two that determine whether the pathology result can be trusted and whether the surgeon can find the site again.

quiz.prompt: The BI-RADS lexicon lists the distribution descriptors for calcifications in a deliberate sequence. Put these distributions in order of increasing suspicion of malignancy.
quiz.answer: diffuse regional grouped linear segmental
quiz.explain: The order follows how closely the arrangement of the particles imitates the anatomy of a duct system. Diffuse calcifications scattered randomly through both breasts are essentially always benign. Regional calcifications occupy a large volume of tissue that does not correspond to a duct distribution and are usually benign, though the volume alone means they warrant a look. Grouped calcifications occupy a small volume — the lexicon defines this by number within a defined distance — and can be either. Linear calcifications lie along a line, with or without branching, because they are sitting in a duct. Segmental calcifications occupy a duct and its branches, which is why they raise the possibility of extensive or multicentric disease in one lobe. Distribution and morphology are always read together: benign-morphology particles in a segmental distribution stay benign, while fine pleomorphic particles in a segmental distribution are as suspicious as calcifications get.

quiz.prompt: At diagnostic workup a woman has a solitary, circumscribed, oval, non-calcified mass that is not palpable, and the radiologist assigns BI-RADS 3 with a six-month follow-up rather than a biopsy. That category carries an agreed ceiling on the likelihood of malignancy. What is that ceiling, as a percentage? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Probably benign means a likelihood of malignancy greater than zero but no more than two per cent — low enough that surveillance is safer than biopsying every such lesion, but not low enough to ignore. The obligation the category carries is a protocol, not a vague plan: a unilateral study at six months, then bilateral at twelve and twenty-four months, and stability across two to three years permits a downgrade to benign. Three constraints go with it. The category should be assigned after a complete diagnostic workup rather than from a screening study, it is not appropriate for a palpable finding or where the patient cannot or will not comply with follow-up, and the findings for which the evidence supports it are few: a solitary circumscribed non-calcified mass, a focal asymmetry that effaces on spot compression, and a group of round or punctate calcifications. A finding that enlarges or changes during surveillance is biopsied.

quiz.prompt: On the mediolateral oblique view a small mass sits in the upper half of the breast; the craniocaudal view places it laterally. A true lateral mediolateral view is then taken to establish its position for biopsy. Compared with the oblique, where should the mass lie if the craniocaudal reading is correct?
choices: Lower on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
Higher on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
At the same height, since both are lateral projections
Further from the nipple on the true lateral projection
quiz.answer: Lower on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
quiz.explain: Rotating the tube from the oblique to a true lateral swings the lateral part of the breast downwards and the medial part upwards, so a lateral lesion drops and a medial lesion rises — the aide-memoire is that lead sinks and muffins rise. Watching the lesion move in the predicted direction is how you prove that the two views show the same object rather than two different ones, which is the whole point of triangulation and the reason a mass seen on one view alone gets a second projection before anything else. The true lateral also supplies the vertical coordinate a biopsy or wire localisation needs, and it is the projection on which milk of calcium layers into teacup shapes that the craniocaudal view shows only as smudges.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old presents with a palpable lump. Targeted ultrasound at the site of the lump shows a 15 mm anechoic structure with a circumscribed margin, an imperceptible wall, posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal vascularity or mural nodule. What follows?
choices: Assess as benign and reassure; no biopsy or imaging follow-up
Assess as probably benign and repeat the scan in six months
Aspirate the lesion and send the fluid for cytological study
Take a core biopsy, since a palpable lump requires tissue
quiz.answer: Assess as benign and reassure; no biopsy or imaging follow-up
quiz.explain: A structure meeting every criterion for a simple cyst is a category 2 finding, and imaging follow-up adds nothing; the criteria have to be met in full, though, because it is the combination of anechoic contents, an imperceptible wall, a circumscribed margin and posterior enhancement that gives the near-perfect negative predictive value. Aspiration is a treatment for a symptomatic cyst rather than a diagnostic step, and clear or greenish fluid from a simple cyst is discarded rather than sent for cytology, which has a poor yield and a real false-positive rate. The categories that do require action are the neighbours: a complicated cyst with homogeneous low-level internal echoes is followed or aspirated, and a complex cystic and solid mass with a thick septation or a vascularised mural nodule is biopsied. In a woman of this age ultrasound is the right first test for a palpable lump, with mammography added when the ultrasound is suspicious or the clinical concern persists.

quiz.prompt: A spiculated irregular mass with associated fine-linear branching calcifications and overlying skin retraction is worked up, and the radiologist must decide between category 4C and category 5 before the multidisciplinary meeting. For a finding to be placed in category 5, the likelihood of malignancy must be at least what percentage? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Category 4C runs from above fifty per cent to below ninety-five; category 5 begins at ninety-five per cent and means the imaging alone is close to diagnostic. The distinction is not cosmetic, because the category changes what happens after the biopsy. A benign core biopsy result against a category 5 finding is by definition discordant and obliges repeat sampling or surgical excision, whereas a benign result against a 4A finding may reasonably be accepted with imaging follow-up. Category 5 is also the level of confidence at which definitive surgical and oncological management can be planned around the biopsy result before it returns. Category 6 sits outside this scale altogether: it is reserved for a malignancy already proved by biopsy and awaiting definitive treatment, and it is not a way of expressing very high suspicion.

quiz.prompt: A spiculated mass with an irregular margin in the upper outer quadrant is assessed as category 5. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy returns fibrocystic change with no atypia, and the pathologist confirms that representative breast tissue was sampled. What should be done?
choices: Treat the result as discordant and proceed to excision biopsy
Accept the benign result and return her to routine screening
Accept the result but repeat the mammogram in six months
Repeat the core biopsy under stereotactic guidance instead
quiz.answer: Treat the result as discordant and proceed to excision biopsy
quiz.explain: Radiological-pathological concordance is the last step of every image-guided biopsy and the one that catches the sampling error. A finding carrying at least a ninety-five per cent likelihood of malignancy cannot be explained by fibrocystic change, so the benign result is discordant whether or not the pathologist is confident about what is on the slide, and the pathway is repeat sampling or, more usually at this level of suspicion, surgical excision. Accepting it and returning the patient to screening is the failure mode this check exists to prevent. Repeating the biopsy stereotactically is the wrong technique for a mass that ultrasound can see, and short-interval mammography leaves a probable cancer in place. The same discipline governs the lesions that are excised despite a benign core result because of their upgrade rate at excision — atypical ductal hyperplasia, a radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion, papillary lesions, and a discordant result of any kind.

quiz.prompt: A multidisciplinary meeting reviews six mammograms, each assigned a different BI-RADS assessment category. Put the categories in order of increasing likelihood of malignancy.
quiz.answer: category-2 category-3 category-4A category-4B category-4C category-5
quiz.explain: Each category is a probability band, and each band names an action. Category 1 and category 2 both carry an essentially zero likelihood and both mean routine screening; category 2 differs only in that a benign finding has been described. Category 3 is above zero but no more than two per cent and means short-interval surveillance. The three category 4 subdivisions run above two to ten, above ten to fifty, and above fifty to below ninety-five per cent, and all three mean tissue diagnosis — the subdivision guides how the result is then handled rather than whether to biopsy. Category 5 is ninety-five per cent or more. Two categories deliberately sit outside this ladder: category 0 is not a suspicion level at all but a statement that the workup is incomplete, and category 6 is a cancer already proved by biopsy.

quiz.prompt: Comparison with prior mammograms shows a focal asymmetry in the right breast that is larger and denser than on the study two years earlier, visible on both projections, containing no mass and no calcification. Spot compression shows it persists rather than effacing, and targeted ultrasound of the area is normal. What should be done?
choices: Biopsy it, because a developing asymmetry carries real risk
Return to routine screening, since ultrasound was normal here
Assess as probably benign and reimage the area in six months
Report it as summation of normal tissue on both projections
quiz.answer: Biopsy it, because a developing asymmetry carries real risk
quiz.explain: An asymmetry that is new or has increased, is visible on both projections and persists on spot compression has a positive predictive value high enough to demand tissue, and it is one of the presentations of invasive lobular carcinoma, the type that most often grows without forming a mass. A normal ultrasound does not overturn that, because a lesion with no discrete mass frequently has no sonographic correlate; it changes only the technique used to sample it, which becomes stereotactic or tomosynthesis-guided rather than ultrasound-guided, or MRI-guided if MRI is used to localise. Tomosynthesis is the tool that separates a true asymmetry from summation of overlapping normal tissue, and summation is precisely what a finding that persists on spot compression is not.

quiz.prompt: Five years after wide local excision and radiotherapy, a mammogram shows a spiculated density at the upper outer quadrant with overlying skin thickening. It lies exactly at the surgical site with surgical clips within it, and it has been unchanged over four annual studies, having been denser on the earliest of them. What should be done?
choices: Report the postsurgical scar and continue annual surveillance
Assess as suspicious and take a core biopsy from the density
Request MRI, since a scar and a recurrence look the same
Assess as probably benign and reimage the breast in six months
quiz.answer: Report the postsurgical scar and continue annual surveillance
quiz.explain: Four things identify a scar: it is at the operative site, marked by clips; it changes shape markedly between the two projections, because it is a plane of fibrosis rather than a mass; it has no central density; and above all it becomes less conspicuous or stays stable over successive studies, since scar tissue and post-radiotherapy oedema regress. Recurrence does the opposite — a scar that becomes denser, develops a central mass, or acquires new calcifications is the finding that triggers biopsy. MRI is genuinely useful where the mammogram is equivocal, because mature scar beyond about a year typically enhances little while recurrence enhances, but ordering it against a four-year stable appearance buys false positives rather than information. Comparison with the previous films is the whole of the argument here, which is why the prior studies are part of the examination and not an optional extra.

quiz.prompt: A 47-year-old has a biopsy-proven invasive lobular carcinoma of the left breast, and the mammogram shows only a subtle architectural distortion, so the extent of disease is uncertain. Separately, a 30-year-old whose mother and sister had premenopausal breast cancer asks whether she should be screened by MRI instead of mammography. Give the reasoning in each case.
quiz.answer: In the first case MRI earns its place. Lobular carcinoma grows in single-file strands without forming a discrete mass or a desmoplastic reaction, so it is the type that mammography most often misses or underestimates, particularly in dense tissue; MRI has the highest sensitivity of any breast technique for invasive disease and is used here to measure the extent of the tumour, to look for multifocal or multicentric disease and for a contralateral cancer that would change the operation. The condition attached is that MRI also finds lesions that prove benign, so any additional finding that would alter surgery is biopsied first, usually under ultrasound after a targeted second-look scan, rather than acted on directly. In the second case supplemental MRI is offered to women at high lifetime risk — carriers of a pathogenic BRCA1, BRCA2 or comparable variant and their untested first-degree relatives, women whose family history puts their lifetime risk above roughly a fifth on a model that accounts for it, and women irradiated to the chest in adolescence or early adulthood — but it is an addition to mammography rather than a replacement, because MRI is poor at showing calcifications, which is how a large share of ductal carcinoma in situ presents. In a premenopausal woman the study is booked for the second week of the menstrual cycle to limit background parenchymal enhancement, which otherwise obscures small lesions and generates recalls.
quiz.explain: The two halves are the same argument used in opposite directions. MRI's strength is sensitivity to enhancing invasive tumour, so it is worth doing where the question is how much invasive disease there is and mammography cannot answer it, and where a woman's prior risk is high enough that the extra cancers found outweigh the extra benign biopsies. Its weakness is calcification, which is why it supplements rather than replaces mammography in screening, and why an MRI-detected finding is a hypothesis to be tested rather than a diagnosis. The cycle timing and the second-look ultrasound are the two practical steps that make the difference between an MRI service that adds cancers and one that mainly adds recalls.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old whose screening mammogram was reported as normal, with the density assessed as extremely dense, presents nine months later with a 2 cm palpable invasive cancer. On review of the earlier film the unit finds nothing to see even in retrospect. What does the case say about mammographic density?
choices: Dense tissue masks cancer, and it also raises the risk itself
Dense tissue masks cancer but carries no risk of its own
Dense tissue is a reader effect and not a property of tissue
Dense tissue lowers sensitivity but raises specificity to match
quiz.answer: Dense tissue masks cancer, and it also raises the risk itself
quiz.explain: Fibroglandular tissue attenuates x-rays much as a tumour does, so a cancer surrounded by it has little contrast against its background and mammographic sensitivity falls with increasing density — the masking effect that produced this interval cancer. Separately and independently, high breast density is itself a risk factor for developing breast cancer, so the two effects compound rather than offset. That is the argument for supplemental imaging in dense breasts: tomosynthesis raises cancer detection and lowers recall by separating overlapping tissue, and supplemental ultrasound, contrast-enhanced mammography and MRI each find additional cancers, with MRI shown to reduce the interval cancer rate in extremely dense breasts. The honest caveat is that a mortality benefit from supplemental screening has not been demonstrated, and every additional test brings false positives with it. Density is a qualitative judgement made on the current study and can change over time, with hormonal status and with weight.

nodes.title: Ankle Fractures and the Painful Foot
nodes.goal: Decide who needs an ankle or foot radiograph, classify an ankle fracture in the terms that predict instability, and work up the tendon, midfoot and heel causes of a painful foot.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old inverted her ankle stepping off a kerb. She is tender over the base of the fifth metatarsal and describes midfoot pain. There is no tenderness over either malleolus, and she walked four steps in the department without help. What imaging follows from the Ottawa rules?
quiz.answer: Radiograph the foot but not the ankle, since only the midfoot criterion is met
choices: Radiograph the foot but not the ankle, since only the midfoot criterion is met
Radiograph the ankle but not the foot, since weight bearing has been preserved
Request no radiograph at all, because she managed to take four steps unaided
Radiograph the foot and ankle together with a whole-length view of the fibula
quiz.explain: The Ottawa rules are two separate rules sharing a structure. A foot radiograph is indicated when there is midfoot pain plus bone tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or at the navicular, or an inability to take four steps both at the time of injury and in the department. An ankle radiograph is indicated when there is malleolar pain plus bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus over its distal 6 cm, or the same weight-bearing failure. Here the fifth metatarsal base is tender with midfoot pain, so the foot rule fires and the ankle rule does not. The rules are highly sensitive for clinically significant fractures, which is why a negative result is safe to act on, but their specificity is low, so a positive result simply means imaging is justified rather than that a fracture is likely.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old has a spiral fracture of the distal fibula beginning at the level of the tibial plafond. The medial malleolus is intact but the medial clear space measures 6 mm on the mortise view. How should this be reported and what does it imply?
quiz.answer: Weber B with medial-sided injury, so the ankle is unstable and needs fixation
choices: Weber B with medial-sided injury, so the ankle is unstable and needs fixation
Weber B with an intact deltoid ligament, so a walking cast will be sufficient
Weber A, below the syndesmosis, and therefore a stable avulsion-type injury
Weber C, above the syndesmosis, with an obligate proximal fibular fracture
quiz.explain: Weber classifies by the level of the fibular fracture relative to the syndesmosis. Type A is below it, typically a transverse avulsion from supination and adduction, with the syndesmosis intact and the injury usually stable. Type B is at the level of the syndesmosis, typically a spiral fracture from external rotation, and stability is the open question. Type C is above it, and the syndesmosis is torn up to the level of the fracture. The Weber grade alone does not settle treatment for a type B: what settles it is the medial side. A widened medial clear space, above about 4 mm and wider than the superior joint space, means the deltoid ligament has failed, giving a bimalleolar-equivalent injury with a talus free to shift. That combination is unstable and goes for fixation, whereas an isolated Weber B with an intact medial side can be treated non-operatively.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these injuries in the order that the Lauge-Hansen sequence predicts for a supination and external rotation ankle injury.
quiz.answer: anterior-tibiofibular-ligament spiral-fibular-fracture posterior-malleolus medial-malleolus
quiz.explain: Lauge-Hansen names the position of the foot first and the direction of the deforming force second, and each mechanism fails in a fixed order, so the classification is genuinely predictive rather than merely descriptive. Supination with external rotation is the commonest pattern. Stage 1 tears the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, sometimes avulsing the Tillaux-Chaput or Wagstaffe fragment. Stage 2 produces the characteristic spiral fibular fracture running from anteroinferior to posterosuperior at the level of the plafond. Stage 3 involves the posterior structures, either the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament or a posterior malleolar fragment. Stage 4 completes the ring medially, with a transverse medial malleolar fracture or deltoid rupture. The practical value is that finding a late stage obliges you to look for the earlier ones, and finding an early stage tells you which structures to scrutinise before calling the ankle stable.

quiz.prompt: A colleague asks which radiographic measurements you use to judge the syndesmosis on ankle films. Give them and say where they are taken.
quiz.answer: Measured 1 cm above the plafond, the tibiofibular clear space should be under 6 mm on both anteroposterior and mortise views, tibiofibular overlap should be present, and the medial clear space should be under 4 mm and no wider than the superior joint space.
quiz.explain: All three syndesmotic measurements are taken at the same level, 1 cm proximal to the tibial plafond, and they are read together rather than singly. The tibiofibular clear space, the gap between the lateral border of the posterior tibial malleolus and the medial border of the fibula, is the most reliable because it varies least with rotation of the limb; under 6 mm is normal. Tibiofibular overlap is generous on the anteroposterior view and much narrower on the mortise view, and it disappears as the syndesmosis opens, but it is rotation-sensitive so a lone abnormal value warrants a repeat with correct positioning. The medial clear space reports the talus rather than the syndesmosis itself. Normal static films do not exclude a dynamic syndesmotic injury, so external rotation stress views or weight-bearing CT are the next step when the clinical suspicion is high.

quiz.prompt: A 35-year-old has a transverse medial malleolar fracture with a widened medial clear space. The ankle series shows no fibular fracture at all, and on re-examination the patient is tender high over the proximal calf. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Image the whole fibula; a proximal fracture with syndesmotic rupture is likely
choices: Image the whole fibula; a proximal fracture with syndesmotic rupture is likely
Repeat the ankle series in ten days to look for an occult distal fibular fracture
Treat as an isolated medial malleolar injury in a below-knee walking cast
Arrange an MRI of the ankle first to assess the deltoid before further radiographs
quiz.explain: The ankle behaves as a ring, and a ring rarely breaks in only one place. A medial injury with a widened mortise and no lateral fracture at the ankle means the force escaped proximally, and that is the Maisonneuve pattern: the extreme of the pronation and external rotation mechanism, in which the interosseous membrane and syndesmosis tear from the ankle upwards to a spiral fracture of the proximal fibula, often near the neck. It is missed whenever the radiograph is coned to the ankle, which is why palpating the whole leg and imaging the full length of the fibula is the standing rule in any medial-sided injury without a lateral fracture. It matters because the syndesmosis needs stabilisation and the fracture itself may need nothing, and because the common peroneal nerve runs around the fibular neck and can be injured.

quiz.prompt: After a forced inversion injury, a 28-year-old has persistent ankle pain. MRI shows a shallow, wafer-shaped osteochondral fragment at the anterolateral corner of the talar dome with a thin line of fluid signal along its deep surface. What is the correct characterisation?
quiz.answer: A lateral talar dome lesion, typically traumatic, shallow and prone to displace
choices: A lateral talar dome lesion, typically traumatic, shallow and prone to displace
A medial talar dome lesion, typically atraumatic, deeper and cup-shaped in profile
A subchondral insufficiency fracture of the talus in a low bone density patient
An accessory ossicle below the lateral malleolus of no clinical consequence here
quiz.explain: Talar dome osteochondral lesions divide by location and behave differently. Lateral lesions sit anterolaterally, are shallow and wafer-shaped, and are nearly always traumatic, following inversion with dorsiflexion; because they are thin and lie at the edge, they detach and displace more readily. Medial lesions sit posteromedially, are deeper and cup-shaped, and are more often atraumatic and degenerative in origin. The stability of the fragment is what the surgeon wants, so look for the features that suggest it has lifted: a continuous high signal line along the interface on fluid-sensitive sequences, subchondral cysts, a breach of the overlying cartilage, or a displaced fragment in the joint. A stable lesion is treated conservatively, whereas an unstable or displaced one goes to fixation, microfracture or grafting. An os subfibulare lies below the malleolus, outside the joint surface, with a corticated margin.

quiz.prompt: A 45-year-old felt a blow to the back of the calf during squash and cannot push off. Ultrasound shows complete discontinuity of the Achilles tendon 5 cm above its calcaneal insertion, with retraction of the torn ends and blood filling the gap. What is the most useful thing to add to the report?
quiz.answer: A mid-substance rupture in the hypovascular zone; state the gap in plantar flexion
choices: A mid-substance rupture in the hypovascular zone; state the gap in plantar flexion
Insertional tendinopathy with a Haglund deformity and retrocalcaneal bursal fluid
A partial tear of the plantaris tendon with the Achilles tendon itself intact
Oedema in the Kager fat pad after a sprain, with a normal underlying tendon
quiz.explain: Most Achilles ruptures occur 2 to 6 cm above the insertion, in the relatively hypovascular watershed segment, which is also where mid-substance tendinopathy sits. The diagnosis is usually clinical; the imaging question is what the treating team cannot get from examination, and that is the size of the gap and whether it closes. Ultrasound answers it dynamically: measure the separation between tendon ends in neutral and again in plantar flexion, because a gap that apposes in equinus supports functional non-operative management in a boot, whereas a gap that stays wide favours repair. Note the tendon ends themselves, since frayed, degenerate ends behave differently from clean ones. Insertional disease is a separate entity at the calcaneus, associated with a Haglund prominence and retrocalcaneal bursitis. An intact plantaris tendon running medially is a common finding beside a ruptured Achilles and should not be mistaken for intact fibres.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old has chronic lateral ankle pain after repeated sprains. Axial images at the level of the lateral malleolus show the peroneus brevis tendon splayed into a C shape wrapped around peroneus longus, with a small avulsed fragment from the posterolateral fibular rim. What do you report?
quiz.answer: A peroneus brevis split tear with injury of the superior peroneal retinaculum
choices: A peroneus brevis split tear with injury of the superior peroneal retinaculum
A peroneus longus tear at the os peroneum with retraction of the proximal stump
A normal low-lying peroneus brevis muscle belly sitting within the fibular groove
Tenosynovitis alone, with a trace of physiological fluid within the tendon sheath
quiz.explain: Peroneus brevis lies directly against the fibula in the retromalleolar groove and is the tendon that splits, taking on a C or boomerang shape that partly envelops peroneus longus on axial images. The mechanism is chronic subluxation over the sharp posterolateral fibular ridge, so the superior peroneal retinaculum is nearly always implicated, and a fleck of bone avulsed from the fibular rim is direct evidence of retinacular failure. Report both, because repairing the tendon without addressing the retinaculum invites recurrence. Look also for predisposing anatomy: a low-lying peroneus brevis muscle belly extending below the tip of the malleolus, or an accessory peroneus quartus, both of which crowd the groove. A small volume of fluid in the peroneal sheath is normal; fluid that exceeds the calibre of the tendons, or that is present without any tendon abnormality, needs care in interpretation.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old crushed the midfoot when a load fell on it. The non-weight-bearing anteroposterior radiograph shows the medial border of the second metatarsal base lying 2 mm lateral to the medial border of the middle cuneiform, and a tiny bone fragment sits in the interval between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal base. What follows?
quiz.answer: A Lisfranc injury; the fleck and malalignment need weight-bearing views or CT
choices: A Lisfranc injury; the fleck and malalignment need weight-bearing views or CT
A normal variation in tarsometatarsal alignment as seen on non-weight-bearing films
An avulsion at the peroneus brevis insertion on the base of the fifth metatarsal
A navicular stress fracture, which would account for the small cortical fragment
quiz.explain: Two alignment rules carry most of the diagnosis. On the anteroposterior view the medial border of the second metatarsal base should line up with the medial border of the middle cuneiform; on the oblique the medial border of the fourth metatarsal should line up with the medial border of the cuboid. The fleck sign, a small avulsed fragment lying in the Lisfranc interval between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal base, represents avulsion of the Lisfranc ligament and is close to pathognomonic. These injuries are missed on a substantial proportion of initial radiographs because a non-weight-bearing film lets a subluxed midfoot reduce itself. Weight-bearing or comparison views unmask it, and CT shows the fracture pattern for planning. Missing it leads to midfoot collapse and post-traumatic arthritis, so the threshold for further imaging should be low.

quiz.prompt: Comparison weight-bearing views are obtained. The gap between the medial cortex of the second metatarsal base and the lateral cortex of the medial cuneiform measures 4.6 mm on the injured side and 1.9 mm on the uninjured side. Report the side-to-side difference in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 4.6 minus 1.9 is 2.7 mm. Absolute widths at the first and second metatarsal interval vary considerably between individuals, which is exactly why the contralateral weight-bearing film is worth the extra exposure: it makes each patient their own control. A side-to-side difference greater than about 2 mm indicates diastasis and an unstable Lisfranc injury, and a difference of 2.7 mm on weight bearing takes this out of the equivocal zone and towards fixation, whether by open reduction and internal fixation or primary arthrodesis. If the patient cannot bear weight, the alternatives are stress views under anaesthesia or weight-bearing CT where available. Report the measurement itself rather than only the conclusion, since the surgical decision hangs on the number and the treating team will want to see it.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old fell three metres from scaffolding and landed on both heels. On the lateral radiograph of the right foot, Bohler angle measures 12 degrees and there is a broadened, sclerotic heel. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: A depressed intra-articular fracture; add CT and image the thoracolumbar spine
choices: A depressed intra-articular fracture; add CT and image the thoracolumbar spine
A normal Bohler angle, so no imaging beyond the standard ankle series is needed
An extra-articular anterior process avulsion, treatable in a below-knee cast
A calcaneal stress fracture of the type seen in runners, best assessed with MRI
quiz.explain: Bohler angle is formed by a line from the highest point of the anterior process to the highest point of the posterior facet and a line from that point to the superior aspect of the tuberosity. It normally measures 20 to 40 degrees, and it flattens when the posterior facet is driven downwards, so 12 degrees indicates a depressed intra-articular fracture. Two things follow. CT with coronal reformats defines the posterior facet, which is what the Sanders classification grades and what determines whether the fracture is reconstructable. And the mechanism obliges a wider search: axial loading fractures the calcaneus but also transmits force up the axial skeleton, so bilateral heels and the thoracolumbar spine should be imaged, with spinal fractures accompanying roughly one in ten calcaneal fractures. The critical angle of Gissane, normally about 120 to 145 degrees, is the second measurement to check.

quiz.prompt: On a lateral radiograph, relative to the highest point of the posterior facet, the highest point of the anterior process lies 40 mm anterior to it and 10 mm below it, and the superior point of the tuberosity lies 30 mm posterior to it and 10 mm below it. Bohler angle is the sum of the inclinations of these two lines to the horizontal. Calculate Bohler angle in degrees, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The anterior limb falls 10 mm over a horizontal run of 40 mm, so its inclination is the arctangent of 0.25, which is 14.0 degrees. The posterior limb falls 10 mm over 30 mm, giving the arctangent of 0.333, which is 18.4 degrees. Their sum is 32.5 degrees, comfortably within the normal range of 20 to 40 degrees, so the posterior facet has not been depressed.
