Working it out this way is worth doing once, because it shows why the measurement behaves as it does: depression of the posterior facet lifts the apex out of the angle and flattens both limbs together, which is why the value falls so sharply with even modest impaction. It also shows why positioning matters, since an obliquely projected lateral distorts both limbs. Compare with the uninjured side when the value sits near the boundary.

quiz.prompt: A 50-year-old runner has heel pain that is worst on the first steps of the morning. Say what you would look for on ultrasound and MRI, and what you would say about the heel spur seen on the radiograph.
quiz.answer: I would look for thickening of the plantar fascia beyond about 4 mm at its calcaneal origin with loss of the normal fibrillar pattern on ultrasound and perifascial oedema on MRI, and I would report the heel spur as an incidental degenerative finding rather than the cause of the pain.
quiz.explain: Plantar fasciitis is a degenerative enthesopathy rather than an inflammatory one, and the imaging findings mirror that. On ultrasound the proximal fascia at the medial calcaneal tuberosity thickens beyond roughly 4 mm, loses its tight fibrillar echotexture, becomes hypoechoic, and may show neovascularity on Doppler. On MRI the same segment thickens with intermediate signal, surrounded by perifascial oedema and often with marrow oedema in the adjacent calcaneus. Compare with the asymptomatic side, since fascial thickness varies. The spur is the finding to be careful with: plantar calcaneal spurs sit within the flexor digitorum brevis origin, occur in a large fraction of asymptomatic feet and are found in only some symptomatic ones, so calling it the cause misleads the patient about what treatment should target. In a young patient with bilateral enthesopathy and erosive change, consider seronegative spondyloarthropathy.

quiz.prompt: On a forefoot MRI there is a small mass in the third intermetatarsal space. Say how you would distinguish a Morton neuroma from intermetatarsal bursitis.
quiz.answer: A Morton neuroma lies plantar to the intermetatarsal ligament, is teardrop-shaped and stays low in signal on T2 because it is fibrous, whereas intermetatarsal bursitis sits dorsal to the ligament and follows fluid, appearing bright on T2.
quiz.explain: Two features separate them and both are visible on a single coronal fluid-sensitive image. Position relative to the deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament comes first: a Morton neuroma arises from the plantar digital nerve and therefore sits plantar to the ligament, whereas the intermetatarsal bursa lies dorsal to it. Signal comes second: the lesion is perineural fibrosis rather than a true neuroma, so it stays intermediate to low on T2 and enhances, while a bursa follows fluid and is uniformly bright. Neuromas favour the third intermetatarsal space, then the second. Ultrasound is a good alternative and adds the dynamic Mulder manoeuvre, in which squeezing the forefoot displaces the lesion plantarwards with a palpable and visible click. The two conditions coexist often enough that finding one should prompt a look for the other, since injection targets differ.

nodes.title: Bone Marrow, Stress Injury, Muscle and the Diabetic Foot
nodes.goal: Separate normal marrow and reactive oedema from disease, grade stress and muscle injury by what changes management, and decide osteomyelitis in a neuropathic foot.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old woman who smokes twenty a day and runs marathons has a knee MRI for pain. Both the distal femoral and proximal tibial metaphyses contain patchy, symmetric, ill-defined intermediate T1 signal that stays brighter than adjacent skeletal muscle. The epiphyses and subchondral bone are entirely fatty, the cortex is intact and there is no soft-tissue mass. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: Normal marrow reconversion; no further marrow imaging is required
choices: Normal marrow reconversion; no further marrow imaging is required
Diffuse marrow infiltration; recommend haematology referral and biopsy
Multifocal marrow oedema; recommend a repeat examination in three months
Marrow replacement by tumour; stage with whole-body imaging next
quiz.explain: Conversion from red to yellow marrow runs from the periphery inwards and from distal to proximal within a limb, with epiphyses and apophyses turning fatty within months of their ossification centre appearing; the adult pattern — red marrow confined to the axial skeleton and the proximal femoral and humeral metaphyses — is settled by the mid-twenties. Reconversion simply runs the film backwards: axial skeleton first, then proximal to distal, and it spares epiphyses. Its drivers are smoking, obesity, altitude, chronic anaemia, endurance training and marrow-stimulating drugs, and this patient has two of them. The rules that protect you are on the T1 image: normal red marrow is brighter than muscle and than a normal disc, is symmetric and ill-defined, and does not touch cortex. Signal at or below muscle, epiphyseal involvement, or a focal well-defined lesion moves you the other way.

quiz.prompt: A focal marrow lesion is interrogated with in-phase and opposed-phase gradient-echo imaging. A region of interest gives a signal intensity of 612 on the in-phase images and 401 on the opposed-phase images. Calculate the opposed-phase signal drop as a percentage of the in-phase signal, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The arithmetic is (612 minus 401) divided by 612, which is 0.345, or 34.5 per cent. The interpretation rests on one idea: fat and water protons in the same voxel cancel on the opposed-phase image, so any tissue containing both loses signal. Normal red marrow is a mixture of haematopoietic cells and fat and typically drops by more than about 20 per cent, whereas a lesion that has replaced the marrow has pushed the fat out and holds its signal or gains a little. A drop of this size therefore favours red marrow or a benign process. Know the failure modes: sclerotic and treated lesions, diffusely infiltrated marrow that still retains some fat early on, and haemorrhagic or iron-laden marrow. At 1.5 T the echo times sit near 2.3 ms opposed and 4.6 ms in phase; at 3 T both halve.

quiz.prompt: You are handed a lumbar spine MRI and asked whether the marrow is normal. Using the sagittal T1 images alone, state the internal comparisons you make and what would make you call the marrow abnormal.
quiz.answer: Compare the marrow with adjacent skeletal muscle and with a normal intervertebral disc on the same T1 image. Normal marrow, red or yellow, is brighter than both. Marrow that is equal to or darker than muscle or disc, whether diffuse or as a focal well-defined lesion, is abnormal and should be characterised further with fluid-sensitive, chemical-shift or diffusion imaging.
quiz.explain: Window and level settings vary, monitors vary, and absolute signal on MRI means nothing, so every marrow judgement is a comparison made inside the same image. Muscle and disc are convenient internal standards because both are reliably present and neither is usually altered by marrow disease. The comparison has real teeth: diffuse marrow signal below that of muscle on T1 in an adult is one of the more reliable signs of infiltration, whether from myeloma, leukaemia or widespread metastasis, and it can be the first clue in a patient scanned for back pain. Two traps: in young children red marrow is normally darker, so the rule is an adult rule; and in a marrow packed with fat by chemotherapy or radiotherapy, an ordinary red marrow island can look startlingly dark against its background.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old man has six weeks of worsening left hip pain and can barely weight-bear. MRI shows diffuse low T1 and high STIR signal through the left femoral head and neck, extending to the intertrochanteric line, with a small effusion, no subchondral low-signal line, no double-line sign and an intact subchondral plate. What is the appropriate report?
quiz.answer: Bone marrow oedema syndrome; protect weight-bearing and reimage later
choices: Bone marrow oedema syndrome; protect weight-bearing and reimage later
Avascular necrosis with collapse; refer for core decompression now
Septic arthritis of the hip; arrange aspiration of the joint today
Subchondral insufficiency fracture; the pattern here is diagnostic
quiz.explain: Marrow oedema is a sign, not a diagnosis, and it is the company it keeps that tells you which one. Here the oedema is diffuse and undemarcated, crossing from head into neck without a boundary, and the subchondral bone is clean — the picture of transient osteoporosis of the hip, or bone marrow oedema syndrome, which affects middle-aged men and women in late pregnancy and settles over six to twelve months with protected loading. Avascular necrosis is defined by its border: a geographic serpiginous low-signal line on T1 and the double line on T2, with oedema appearing late as pain and collapse approach. A subchondral insufficiency fracture shows a low-signal line running parallel to and abutting the subchondral plate. Sepsis is worth a thought with an effusion, but that decision is driven by fever and inflammatory markers, and if they are up you aspirate regardless of the marrow pattern.

quiz.prompt: A distance runner has anteromedial shin pain. MRI shows periosteal oedema and marrow oedema in the posteromedial tibial diaphysis, the marrow abnormality being visible both on the fluid-sensitive images and as low signal on T1, with no discernible fracture line. Using the Fredericson grading of tibial stress injury, what grade is this? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The Fredericson scale escalates with what the marrow does: grade 1 is periosteal oedema with normal marrow, grade 2 adds marrow oedema seen only on fluid-sensitive sequences, grade 3 is marrow oedema also visible as low signal on T1, and grade 4 is a visible fracture line — commonly subdivided into 4a, intracortical signal, and 4b, a discrete line. Higher grades take longer to return to running, which is the grading's real use. But the site outranks the grade. This injury is on the posteromedial cortex, the compression side, and it heals with load modification. The same grade on the anterior cortex, which is loaded in tension, is a high-risk lesion prone to non-union. Report the grade if the referrer uses it, but report the surface without fail.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old basketball player has four months of anterior shin pain, worse on landing. Radiographs show fusiform thickening of the anterior tibial cortex at the mid-diaphysis with a transverse lucency crossing the outer cortex. What should the report advise?
quiz.answer: A tension-side high-risk lesion; stop loading and refer for surgical review
choices: A tension-side high-risk lesion; stop loading and refer for surgical review
A benign compression-side injury; a graded return to running is safe
An osteoid osteoma is likely; arrange thin-section CT to find a nidus
A chronic osteomyelitis; arrange MRI to look for a sequestrum
quiz.explain: The anterior tibial cortex is loaded in tension, and a stress fracture there tends not to heal: the lucency persists for months, may go on to complete fracture across the bone, and often needs intramedullary nailing rather than rest. That is what earns it high-risk status. The wider list of tension-side or poorly vascularised sites is worth carrying: the superolateral femoral neck, the medial malleolus, the tarsal navicular, the base of the fifth metatarsal at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction, the great toe sesamoids, the patella and the talus. Low-risk sites — posteromedial tibia, fibula, calcaneus, metatarsal shafts, femoral shaft, the compression side of the femoral neck — heal with rest. Osteoid osteoma is a fair differential, since it too thickens cortex, but its nidus is round and centred rather than a transverse line, and CT settles it.

quiz.prompt: Two patients have sacral fractures with no history of a fall: a 24-year-old army recruit six weeks into basic training, and a 79-year-old woman on long-term corticosteroids. Explain what separates the two mechanisms, and what each obliges you to do beyond reporting the fracture.
quiz.answer: The recruit has a fatigue fracture: abnormal repetitive loading of normal bone, so the action is load modification and a look at training error. The older woman has an insufficiency fracture: normal loading of abnormal, osteoporotic bone, so the report should prompt bone density assessment and treatment of the osteoporosis, and should also raise metastasis or myeloma if the marrow signal or the bone elsewhere does not fit a simple fracture.
quiz.explain: The two words are not interchangeable, and the distinction changes who gets referred where. Sacral insufficiency fractures run vertically through one or both alae, often with a horizontal component across the body, giving the H or Honda configuration classically seen on bone scintigraphy and equally visible as oedema on MRI; they are easy to miss on radiographs and are a common cause of sudden immobility in an older patient. Steroids, radiotherapy, osteomalacia, renal disease and long-term bisphosphonates are the usual soil. The trap is the middle ground: a sacral or pelvic fracture in an older patient may be the presenting feature of myeloma or a metastasis, so look at whether the marrow signal outside the fracture line is normal, and whether there is a soft-tissue mass or cortical destruction that a fracture would not explain.

quiz.prompt: A 76-year-old woman who has taken alendronate for nine years has six weeks of dull right thigh pain. Radiographs show focal thickening of the lateral cortex of the right femoral diaphysis with a transverse lucency in the outer cortex and no comminution. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: Image the opposite femur too, since these lesions are often bilateral
choices: Image the opposite femur too, since these lesions are often bilateral
Reassure; lateral cortical thickening is a normal variant at this age
Treat as a metastasis and stage with CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis
Continue the bisphosphonate; the appearance is unrelated to treatment
quiz.explain: This is an atypical femoral fracture: subtrochanteric or diaphyseal, originating at the lateral cortex, transverse or short oblique, non-comminuted, with localised periosteal or endosteal beaking, and following minimal or no trauma. Prodromal thigh pain of weeks to months is characteristic, and the contralateral femur is involved often enough that imaging both is standard practice, whether by radiographs, a dedicated MRI or the femora already included on a dual-energy absorptiometry study. The referral is for orthopaedic assessment with a view to prophylactic fixation and for a review of the drug. Two balances to hold: a metastasis is the differential but is usually permeative rather than confined to the lateral cortex, and the absolute risk of this complication remains small against the hip and vertebral fractures that bisphosphonates prevent.

quiz.prompt: A sprinter pulls up mid-race. MRI shows a proximal biceps femoris injury with high signal disrupting the intramuscular tendon over 3 cm, oedema extending 10 cm craniocaudally, and no retraction. A team-mate with the same symptom has feathery oedema at the musculotendinous junction with an intact tendon. What separates their prognoses?
quiz.answer: Tendon involvement predicts a longer absence and a higher reinjury rate
choices: Tendon involvement predicts a longer absence and a higher reinjury rate
The length of the oedema is the single predictor of time to return
They are equivalent, since neither tendon has retracted from its origin
The second is worse, because junctional oedema implies an avulsion
quiz.explain: Muscle fails at the myotendinous junction under eccentric load, and the long head of biceps femoris is the classic casualty in sprinting. What the report has to establish is whether tendon is involved. The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grades 0 to 4 and adds a letter for the site: a for myofascial, b for musculotendinous, c for intratendinous. The c lesions, where the intramuscular or free tendon is disrupted, keep athletes out longest and re-tear most often, which is exactly the first case here. Oedema length and cross-sectional area correlate with time lost but far more loosely, so they are descriptors rather than the decider. Proximity to the ischial tuberosity also lengthens recovery, and frank retraction or a tuberosity avulsion moves the patient to a surgeon. Describe the structures; the grade is a summary, not the finding.

quiz.prompt: Order the imaging appearances of post-traumatic heterotopic ossification in a thigh haematoma, from earliest to latest.
quiz.answer: ill-defined-oedema faint-peripheral-calcification mature-cortical-rim shrinkage-and-remodelling
quiz.explain: In the first fortnight there is a cellular, oedematous, enhancing mass with extensive surrounding oedema, and it can look exactly like a sarcoma on MRI — which is the whole danger of this lesion, because the early histology mimics sarcoma too, and an ill-timed biopsy has cost patients limbs. At around three to six weeks faint peripheral floccular calcification appears, and this zonal pattern is the diagnostic key: mature at the rim, immature in the centre, the reverse of an extraskeletal osteosarcoma, which mineralises most densely centrally and is most aggressive at its edge. Over a few months the rim corticates and a lucent cleft usually separates it from adjacent bone, and thereafter it commonly shrinks. The practical rule: when the appearance is early and worrying, repeat radiographs or CT in a few weeks rather than reaching for a needle. CT shows the rim before MRI does.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old swimmer has a weak, aching shoulder. MRI shows uniformly increased STIR signal throughout infraspinatus with normal muscle bulk and normal T1 signal, while supraspinatus, teres minor and deltoid are normal. There is no rotator cuff tear. What should be looked for and reported?
quiz.answer: A cyst at the spinoglenoid notch and a posterior labral tear
choices: A cyst at the spinoglenoid notch and a posterior labral tear
A mass at the suprascapular notch compressing the whole nerve
An inflammatory myositis confined to a single rotator cuff muscle
A quadrilateral space lesion affecting the axillary nerve branches
quiz.explain: Denervation oedema respects a nerve territory rather than a compartment or a vascular territory, and that is what makes it recognisable. Isolated infraspinatus signal places the lesion distal to the branch supplying supraspinatus, at the spinoglenoid notch, where a paralabral cyst is the usual culprit — and the cyst is usually fed by a posterior labral tear through a one-way valve. That tear is the finding that changes the operation, so search for it deliberately. A lesion at the suprascapular notch, higher up, would denervate supraspinatus as well. Teres minor with or without deltoid is the axillary nerve and the quadrilateral space. Multiple territories that fit no single nerve suggest Parsonage-Turner syndrome. Timing matters as much as location: acute denervation keeps normal bulk and normal T1, whereas chronic disease brings fatty T1 signal and volume loss, which does not reverse.

quiz.prompt: A diabetic patient has an ulcer over the fifth metatarsal head, and the fluid-sensitive images show extensive oedema throughout the forefoot. State the sequence and the finding you rely on to call osteomyelitis, and say why the oedema by itself will not do.
quiz.answer: Rely on the T1 images: confluent, geographic low signal replacing the medullary fat of the bone subjacent to the ulcer, in a marrow rather than a periarticular distribution. Oedema on STIR is reactive and surrounds any inflamed, fractured or overloaded bone, so it is sensitive but not specific; confluent T1 marrow replacement makes the diagnosis, supported by cortical erosion, a sinus tract, an adjacent ulcer, abscess or loss of the soft-tissue fat planes.
quiz.explain: Almost every painful diabetic forefoot lights up on STIR, so a report built on fluid-sensitive images alone will over-call infection and cost patients bone. The T1 image is the discriminator because osteomyelitis physically replaces marrow fat, and replacement is confluent and geographic rather than hazy and subcortical. Anatomy helps too: infection reaches bone by contiguous spread from the skin, so it sits directly beneath an ulcer at a pressure point — metatarsal heads, malleoli, the calcaneus — and a tract or a rim-enhancing collection joining ulcer to bone effectively closes the case. Two refinements. Post-contrast fat-suppressed sequences are for tracts and abscesses, not for making the marrow diagnosis. And say which bones are involved and how far the marrow signal extends, because that determines the level of resection.

quiz.prompt: A diabetic with a rocker-bottom midfoot deformity has an ulcer over the plantar prominence. MRI shows tarsometatarsal subluxation with periarticular cysts and debris and, separately, the plantar aspect of the cuboid is indistinct on T1 but its outline reappears on the post-contrast fat-suppressed images, with a tract running from the ulcer to that surface. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: Neuropathic arthropathy with superimposed osteomyelitis of the cuboid
choices: Neuropathic arthropathy with superimposed osteomyelitis of the cuboid
Neuropathic arthropathy alone; the cuboid change is reactive oedema
Osteomyelitis alone; the midfoot changes are infective in origin too
Neither process; the appearances are those of an acute Charcot foot
quiz.explain: Distribution normally separates the two conditions. Neuropathic arthropathy is a midfoot, periarticular disease — tarsometatarsal and naviculocuneiform subluxation, subchondral cysts, fragmentation, debris and deformity — while osteomyelitis is medullary and lies beneath an ulcer at a pressure point. The difficulty is that a rocker-bottom deformity manufactures a new pressure point, an ulcer forms over it, and the two then coexist, which is the situation described. The ghost sign is the useful pointer in that setting: a bone whose margins disappear on T1 within the surrounding oedema and then reappear after contrast or on T2 indicates infection rather than the ill-defined T1 loss of neuropathic marrow change. The tract from ulcer to cortex seals it. Name the infected bones explicitly, because that, not the diagnosis alone, is what the surgeon operates on.

nodes.title: Bone Tumours: Lytic, Sclerotic and Cartilage
nodes.goal: Read a bone lesion in order of age, site, margin, periosteal reaction and matrix, and decide what to leave alone, what to follow and what must reach the sarcoma unit before anyone puts a needle in it.

quiz.prompt: Two incidental lesions arrive on the same list. A 14-year-old has an eccentric, lobulated lucency in the distal tibial metaphysis with a thick sclerotic rim and an intact cortex, seen after a sprain. A 61-year-old has a lucency in the femoral diaphysis with a wide zone of transition and a moth-eaten margin. How should each be handled?
quiz.answer: Leave the first alone without follow-up, and stage and refer the second one urgently
choices: Leave the first alone without follow-up, and stage and refer the second one urgently
Follow the first with radiographs at six months, and follow the second in the same way
Biopsy both, since a lucent lesion in bone is not characterised on radiographs alone
Refer both to the sarcoma unit, since the age of the patient is not a discriminator
quiz.explain: The margin is the best radiographic index of how fast a lesion is growing, because it shows whether the bone has had time to wall the lesion off. A thick sclerotic rim around an eccentric metaphyseal lucency in a teenager is a non-ossifying fibroma, a lesion that involutes and needs nothing, not even a follow-up film; putting a note in the report that it requires no action is more useful than a date. A moth-eaten margin with a wide zone of transition means destruction is outrunning repair, and in a patient past 40 the leading candidates are metastasis, myeloma and lymphoma, with primary sarcoma less common but still on the list. Age is the strongest single prior in bone tumours, which is why it belongs at the top of the read rather than in the clinical details you skipped. Biopsying the first lesion would be an avoidable operation on a normal variant.

quiz.prompt: A 17-year-old has months of night pain in the mid-femur, relieved within half an hour of taking ibuprofen. The radiograph shows a fusiform band of dense solid periosteal new bone along the cortex, with no soft tissue mass and no destruction. What imaging should follow, and why?
quiz.answer: Thin-slice CT of the segment, to find the small lucent nidus buried inside the reaction
choices: Thin-slice CT of the segment, to find the small lucent nidus buried inside the reaction
Contrast-enhanced MRI alone, since the reactive marrow oedema will localise the lesion
Radiographs of the opposite femur, to compare the thickness of the two cortices
A whole-body isotope scan, to establish that the lesion is solitary before any biopsy
quiz.explain: Dense, solid, uninterrupted periosteal new bone is the signature of a slow process, and combined with night pain that responds to a non-steroidal drug in a teenager, it points to an osteoid osteoma with its nidus hidden inside the thickened cortex. Thin-slice CT is the test that finds the nidus, typically under 15 mm and often with a central density. MRI is the classic trap here: the florid marrow and soft tissue oedema around the lesion can be read as infection or as an aggressive tumour, and the small nidus is lost inside it, which is why CT rather than MRI settles the diagnosis. The report should state where the nidus sits, whether it is intracortical, subperiosteal or intramedullary, and how far it lies from skin and neurovascular structures, because thermal ablation is the usual treatment and those are the numbers the operator needs. Isotope imaging is sensitive but non-specific.

quiz.prompt: A 12-year-old has three weeks of pain and fever, and radiographs of the femoral diaphysis show a permeative pattern with lamellated periosteal reaction. MRI shows an enhancing soft tissue mass encircling the shaft that is considerably larger than the area of bone destruction, with no rim-enhancing collection. What is the most useful conclusion for the referrer?
quiz.answer: A solid mass out of proportion to the bone destruction favours tumour over infection here
choices: A solid mass out of proportion to the bone destruction favours tumour over infection here
The permeative pattern with fever makes acute osteomyelitis much the likelier diagnosis
The lamellated periosteal reaction is specific for infection and excludes a bone sarcoma
No useful comment is possible until an aspirate has been taken and sent for culture
quiz.explain: Ewing sarcoma and osteomyelitis overlap almost completely on the plain film in this age group: both are diaphyseal, both are permeative, both raise inflammatory markers, and both can produce fever and a lamellated reaction. The discriminator is what MRI shows outside the bone. Ewing sarcoma builds a solid, enhancing, circumferential mass that is often far larger than the bone destruction that produced it, spreading through the cortex without destroying much of it. Osteomyelitis produces oedema, subperiosteal pus and a rim-enhancing abscess, sometimes with a sequestrum, and the soft tissue change is inflammatory rather than mass-like. The practical output is not a diagnosis but a route: this child should reach the sarcoma service before anyone aspirates, because a tract or a drain placed for a presumed abscess contaminates compartments and can convert a limb-sparing resection into something larger.

quiz.prompt: A staging CT in a woman with breast cancer shows a 9 mm sclerotic focus in the L2 vertebral body. It has spiculated margins that blend into the surrounding trabeculae, and it was present and unchanged on a CT from four years ago. What do you report, and what evidence do you use to justify it?
quiz.answer: Report it as a benign bone island needing no follow-up: it has been stable for four years, its brush-border margins interdigitate with the surrounding trabeculae, and its uniform very high attenuation is greater than an osteoblastic deposit would show; if there had been no prior study, absent or minimal uptake on a bone scan would carry the same argument.
quiz.explain: Three lines of evidence separate an enostosis from an osteoblastic deposit, and the strongest is an old study: a sclerotic focus that has not changed over years is not a metastasis. Morphology is the second, since an enostosis has the thorny brush border that merges with normal trabeculae, while a deposit tends to have a rounded, ill-defined edge that pushes trabeculae aside. Attenuation is the third: enostoses are very dense and homogeneous, and published CT thresholds of roughly 885 HU for the mean and 1060 HU for the maximum have been used to separate them from osteoblastic deposits, which are typically less dense. On MRI an enostosis is low signal on every sequence with no surrounding marrow oedema, and on isotope imaging it is usually cold, although a large one can take up a little tracer. The trap in an oncology patient is the healing deposit that has sclerosed under treatment, which is another reason the old films matter.

quiz.prompt: MRI of the proximal humerus shows a lobulated cartilage lesion. On the axial images the adjacent cortex measures 6 mm thick, and the deepest endosteal scalloping measures 4.5 mm. Express the depth of scalloping as a percentage of the cortical thickness. Answer as a percentage, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Four and a half divided by six is 0.75, so the scalloping is 75 per cent of the cortical thickness, and that clears the commonly used threshold of two thirds, or about 67 per cent, which is one of the features that shifts a cartilage lesion out of the enchondroma category. It rarely stands alone. The others worth measuring or describing are length beyond about 5 to 6 cm, cortical expansion or remodelling, periosteal reaction, any soft tissue extension, and pain arising from the lesion itself rather than from the rotator cuff or the joint. Nomenclature matters when reporting: in the long bones of the arms and legs, a low-grade cartilage tumour is now called an atypical cartilaginous tumour and is often managed by curettage or by surveillance, whereas identical histology in the pelvis, scapula, ribs or spine is treated as chondrosarcoma because it behaves worse. Enchondromas in the hands are the standing exception, since they scallop and expand while remaining benign.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old has a 7 cm lobulated lesion with rings-and-arcs mineralisation in the proximal femoral diaphysis, with deep endosteal scalloping, cortical thickening, and localised pain at that site with no history of injury. What is the right course?
quiz.answer: Refer to the sarcoma service for staging and biopsy, since these features suggest malignancy
choices: Refer to the sarcoma service for staging and biopsy, since these features suggest malignancy
Report an enchondroma and reassure, since rings-and-arcs mineralisation indicates benignity
Arrange a repeat radiograph in twelve months, since cartilage lesions change very slowly
Arrange a local curettage, since low-grade cartilage lesions are cured by curettage alone
quiz.explain: Rings and arcs tell you the matrix is cartilage and nothing whatever about its grade, since enchondroma and chondrosarcoma mineralise in the same way. The features that carry the weight here are size beyond 5 to 6 cm, deep endosteal scalloping, cortical thickening or remodelling, and unexplained pain localised to the lesion: in a long bone that combination is a chondrosarcoma until histology says otherwise. Local curettage would be the wrong operation performed by the wrong team, and it also spills tumour into the surrounding tissue. Twelve-month surveillance is a reasonable strategy for a small, asymptomatic, incidental cartilage lesion, which this is not. Once the lesion is referred, remember that cartilage tumours are heterogeneous, so a biopsy from a low-grade area of a high-grade tumour under-grades it, and the imaging appearances have to be weighed against the histology rather than being overruled by it.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with anaemia, renal impairment and a paraprotein has a normal skeletal survey. The haematologist needs to know whether there is bone disease before deciding whether to treat. What imaging do you recommend?
quiz.answer: Whole-body low-dose CT or whole-body MRI, both far more sensitive than the skeletal survey
choices: Whole-body low-dose CT or whole-body MRI, both far more sensitive than the skeletal survey
An isotope bone scan, which detects myeloma deposits earlier than the skeletal survey
A repeat skeletal survey in three months, which will demonstrate progression of the lysis
Targeted radiographs of each painful area, which match cross-sectional imaging for yield
quiz.explain: Myeloma destroys bone through osteoclast activation while suppressing the osteoblastic response, which has two consequences for imaging. First, the isotope bone scan depends on osteoblastic activity and is characteristically cold, so it is the wrong test. Second, a radiograph needs a large proportion of trabecular bone to be lost before a lesion becomes visible, so a normal skeletal survey excludes very little. Whole-body low-dose CT and whole-body MRI have replaced it, and current International Myeloma Working Group criteria count one or more osteolytic lesions of 5 mm or more on radiograph, CT or PET-CT as myeloma-defining bone disease, while more than one focal marrow lesion of 5 mm or more on MRI is itself a myeloma-defining event under the SLiM additions to the CRAB criteria. MRI is also the only way to see the diffuse infiltration pattern, which destroys no cortex at all and is invisible on CT.

quiz.prompt: A patient with metastatic disease is about to start systemic treatment. Baseline CT with 5 mm slices shows lung nodules of 14 mm, 12 mm and 8 mm, liver deposits of 20 mm and 15 mm, and one purely sclerotic deposit in the ilium with no soft tissue component. Applying RECIST 1.1, how many of these lesions may be selected as target lesions? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Four: two lung nodules and two liver deposits. Under RECIST 1.1 a non-nodal lesion is measurable when its longest diameter is at least 10 mm on CT with a slice thickness of 5 mm or less, so the 8 mm nodule is non-measurable and is recorded as non-target disease. At most two target lesions are chosen per organ and five in total, so both liver deposits and the two larger lung nodules qualify and the count sits comfortably under the ceiling. A purely blastic bone deposit is non-measurable in RECIST 1.1, whereas a lytic or mixed deposit with an identifiable soft tissue component of 10 mm or more can be selected. For completeness, lymph nodes are the exception that is measured on the short axis and are only measurable at 15 mm or more. Everything not selected still has to be followed, since unequivocal progression of non-target disease is progression regardless of what the targets do.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the steps in the work-up of a suspected primary bone sarcoma of the femur, from the first investigation to definitive treatment.
quiz.answer: radiograph sarcoma-referral staging-MRI planned-biopsy resection
quiz.explain: The radiograph comes first and still carries most of the diagnostic information, since age, site, margin, periosteal reaction and matrix are all read from it. Referral comes next, before any needle is passed, because the tract has to be chosen by the surgeon who will later resect it. Local staging MRI of the whole bone follows, and it must precede the biopsy: haemorrhage and tract oedema degrade the images afterwards and can lead to over-staging of marrow and soft tissue extent. The biopsy is then performed at the treating centre along the line of the planned incision, ideally by or with the operating surgeon, with cores taken from viable tumour rather than from necrotic centre or reactive rim. Resection removes the tumour and the tract in one piece. Staging of distant disease, principally CT of the chest, is added around the same time and does not change this order.

quiz.prompt: A general radiologist is asked by an orthopaedic colleague to biopsy a destructive proximal tibial lesion this afternoon, before the sarcoma meeting has seen it. Give the reason to decline, in terms the colleague will accept.
quiz.answer: The needle tract is seeded with tumour and has to be excised in one piece with the specimen, so it must run through tissue the surgeon plans to remove and along the line of the planned incision; a tract chosen elsewhere can cross an uninvolved compartment or a neurovascular plane and turn a limb-sparing resection into a much larger operation, which is why the biopsy belongs to the treating unit.
quiz.explain: Everything the needle passes through is contaminated, and haematoma spreads that contamination along fascial planes, so the tract is treated as part of the tumour and is resected with it. That is why the position of the skin entry, the angle and the muscles crossed are surgical decisions rather than technical conveniences: a transverse entry, a tract crossing from one compartment into another, or one that runs alongside the neurovascular bundle can each remove the option of saving the limb. Published series comparing biopsies performed at referral centres with those done elsewhere have repeatedly found more complications, more changes of plan and more unnecessary amputations in the latter group, which is the argument that carries weight in a corridor conversation. The practical steps are to agree the tract with the surgeon, mark and record the entry point, use image guidance, and take enough cores from viable tissue to allow grading and molecular work.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old has knee pain. Radiographs show an eccentric lucent lesion in the distal femur that extends to the subchondral bone, with a narrow but non-sclerotic margin, no mineralised matrix, and thinning of the adjacent cortex. What should the report conclude and advise?
quiz.answer: A giant cell tumour is most likely, so refer for local staging, biopsy and surgical treatment
choices: A giant cell tumour is most likely, so refer for local staging, biopsy and surgical treatment
A simple bone cyst is most likely, so nothing beyond a repeat radiograph is required here
A chondroblastoma is most likely, since this age and this site are typical for that lesion
An osteoblastic metastasis is most likely, so look for the primary tumour before doing more
quiz.explain: The combination that matters is a lesion reaching the subchondral plate in a skeletally mature adult between 20 and 40, eccentric, with a narrow but non-sclerotic margin and no matrix. That is a giant cell tumour, and its margin, geographic but unsclerosed, marks it as locally aggressive rather than indolent. Chondroblastoma occupies the epiphysis of a patient whose physis is still open, usually with a thin sclerotic rim and often with chondroid matrix, so the age here is wrong for it. A simple bone cyst is central and metaphyseal in a child, most often in the proximal humerus or femur. An osteoblastic metastasis would be sclerotic, not lucent, and metastasis in this age group is uncommon. Report also whether there are fluid-fluid levels, since secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change is common, and whether the cortex is breached, since these tumours recur locally and occasionally seed to the lungs.

quiz.prompt: You are staging a distal femoral osteosarcoma with MRI before neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Which set of observations most changes the operation the surgeon plans?
quiz.answer: Whole-bone extent, skip lesions, joint involvement and contact with the popliteal vessels
choices: Whole-bone extent, skip lesions, joint involvement and contact with the popliteal vessels
Matrix signal intensity, degree of enhancement and apparent diffusion coefficient values
Extent of surrounding oedema, amount of periosteal new bone and marrow fat percentage
Number of vessels within the mass, its enhancement curve and its calcified proportion
quiz.explain: Local staging is an anatomical exercise done for the surgeon. The resection level is planned from the proximal extent of marrow replacement measured against a fixed landmark such as the joint line, which is why the whole bone is imaged rather than the lesion alone, and imaging the whole bone is also how skip metastases in the same bone are found. Transphyseal spread, intra-articular extension and involvement of the popliteal vessels and nerve are the findings that decide between an endoprosthetic replacement and an amputation. Judge marrow extent on T1, where tumour replaces fat, since peritumoural oedema on fluid-sensitive sequences will over-estimate it. The tissue characterisation measurements are interesting but do not move the operation, and response to chemotherapy is judged mainly on the percentage of necrosis in the resected specimen rather than on any change in size. Staging is completed with CT of the chest.

quiz.prompt: Two lytic lesions in the same bone are compared. The first has a fine sclerotic rim you could trace with a pencil; around the second you could not draw a line at all. What does the difference in margin tell you, and what does it not tell you?
quiz.answer: The margin measures the speed of the lesion against the speed of bone repair: a sclerotic rim means the bone has had time to wall the lesion off, so growth is slow, whereas a wide zone of transition means destruction is outrunning repair and the lesion is aggressive. It does not tell you whether the lesion is malignant, since infection and eosinophilic granuloma can look aggressive while some metastases and myeloma deposits look slow.
quiz.explain: Lodwick built his grading on exactly this observation: grade IA is geographic with a sclerotic margin, IB geographic and well defined without sclerosis, IC geographic with an ill-defined margin or partial cortical destruction, grade II is moth-eaten and grade III permeative. The scale is a measure of growth rate, not of histology, and that is both its strength and its limit. It is why the differential is assembled from age plus site plus margin rather than margin alone: a permeative lesion in a child brings up Ewing sarcoma, leukaemia, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and osteomyelitis together, while the same pattern past 40 brings up metastasis, myeloma and lymphoma. Assess the margin on the radiograph rather than on CT or MRI, since the radiograph averages the whole thickness of bone and shows the transition zone better than a cross-section through part of it.

nodes.title: Describing a Fracture
nodes.goal: Turn a radiograph of a broken bone into a description a surgeon can act on, and know where the first film hides an injury.

quiz.prompt: A report on a mid-shaft femoral fracture states that the proximal fragment is displaced laterally by half a shaft width. The surgeon reads it, reaches for the films, and asks the radiologist to rewrite the sentence. What is wrong with it?
choices: Displacement is stated for the distal fragment, not the proximal
Displacement should be given in millimetres, not in shaft widths
Displacement needs a true lateral before it can be judged
Displacement and angulation are the same measurement here
quiz.answer: Displacement is stated for the distal fragment, not the proximal
quiz.explain: The convention exists because of what the surgeon does with it. The proximal fragment is held by the trunk and cannot be moved; the distal fragment is the one reduced onto it, so every element of the description is stated for the distal fragment relative to the proximal. Written the other way round the sentence inverts the direction of the correction, and a team acting on it plans to push the limb the wrong way. Translation expressed as a fraction or percentage of the shaft width is in fact the standard, so the millimetre option corrects something that is not broken; and while two orthogonal projections are needed before displacement can be described at all, this report already has them and would still be wrong.

quiz.prompt: On the lateral view of a distal radius fracture in an elderly woman who fell on the outstretched hand, the articular surface of the distal fragment tilts towards the dorsum, and the fragment is displaced dorsally. How should the angulation be recorded?
choices: Dorsal angulation of the distal fragment, apex volar
Volar angulation of the distal fragment, apex dorsal
Dorsal angulation of the distal fragment, apex dorsal
Dorsal tilt of the proximal fragment, apex volar
quiz.answer: Dorsal angulation of the distal fragment, apex volar
quiz.explain: Two fragments meeting at an angle make a wedge, and the apex points away from the side the distal fragment tilts towards: a distal fragment tilted dorsally opens the angle dorsally, so the apex lies volar. That is the Colles pattern, and both halves of the phrase are in circulation, which is exactly why a report should give the direction the distal fragment tilts and let the apex follow rather than leaving the reader to guess which convention was used. Recording the apex on the same side as the tilt describes a deformity that cannot exist, and stating the tilt of the proximal fragment repeats the error of describing the piece the surgeon cannot move.

quiz.prompt: Take the normal palmar tilt of the distal radial articular surface as 11 degrees. On the injured lateral the surface is tilted 15 degrees towards the dorsum. Through how many degrees must the distal fragment be rotated to restore the normal tilt? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Tilt is signed about a neutral surface that faces straight along the shaft. Fifteen degrees of dorsal tilt is minus fifteen on a scale where palmar tilt counts as positive, so reaching plus eleven means turning the fragment through twenty-six degrees, not through the four you get by subtracting one figure from the other. The sign error is the common one and it halves the correction the surgeon plans for. The same arithmetic applies to radial inclination on the posteroanterior view and to radial height, and it is the reason a report gives numbers rather than adjectives: how much residual dorsal tilt is acceptable depends on the patient's age and demands, and that judgement is not the radiologist's to make on the reader's behalf.

quiz.prompt: A tibial shaft fracture treated in a cast is followed with radiographs from the day of injury to a year later. Put these radiographic appearances in the order they appear on the films.
quiz.answer: crisp-lucency margin-resorption soft-callus bridging-callus remodelling
quiz.explain: On the day of injury the fracture is a sharply defined lucency between two crisp cortical edges. Over the following one to two weeks osteoclasts resorb the dead bone at the fracture margins, so the line becomes wider and less distinct, and a fracture invisible on the first film can declare itself here — which is the whole basis of the ten-to-fourteen-day repeat radiograph. Ill-defined periosteal new bone, the soft callus, follows at around two to three weeks; it mineralises and bridges the cortices over the next several weeks; and remodelling then reshapes the bone along its lines of loading over months to years, in a child to the point that the fracture becomes untraceable. The clinically useful trap is the middle step: a line that looks worse at two weeks than at presentation is usually healing normally, not displacing.

quiz.prompt: An adult falls on the outstretched hand. The lateral elbow radiograph, taken correctly at 90 degrees of flexion, shows a lucency lifted off the posterior aspect of the distal humerus and a raised triangular lucency anteriorly. No cortical break is visible on either projection. What should be done?
choices: Treat as an occult radial head fracture and immobilise
Report a normal elbow, since no cortical break is seen
Attribute the appearance to the flexed position of the arm
Proceed to CT of the elbow before any immobilisation
quiz.answer: Treat as an occult radial head fracture and immobilise
quiz.explain: The posterior fat pad sits deep in the olecranon fossa and is invisible on a normal elbow; anything that distends the joint lifts it into view. On a properly positioned lateral, a visible posterior fat pad therefore means a haemarthrosis, and in an adult who has fallen on the hand the commonest cause by far is an undisplaced radial head fracture. The anterior fat pad is visible normally and becomes a sail only when displaced, so it is the less specific of the two. Management is a sling or collar and cuff with early movement and a repeat film at seven to ten days; CT is reserved for a fracture already known to be displaced or comminuted, where it changes the operation. A lateral taken away from 90 degrees can lift the fat pads without an effusion, which is why the positioning is stated before the sign is trusted — and in a child the same finding points to a supracondylar fracture instead.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial loading of the thumb after falling on the outstretched hand. Four-view scaphoid radiographs are reported as normal. Set out how the wrist should be managed and justify each step.
quiz.answer: Treat the wrist as fractured until it is proved otherwise: immobilise it and arrange definitive imaging rather than discharging on the strength of a normal radiograph, because a substantial minority of scaphoid fractures are invisible on the first films. MRI is the most accurate second-line test and can be done within days; it shows the fracture line and the surrounding marrow oedema on the day of injury, and a normal MRI allows the splint to come off and the patient to be discharged. Where MRI is not available, CT displays cortical detail well but is less sensitive for the undisplaced fracture, and repeat radiographs at ten to fourteen days depend on resorption widening the line, which works but delays the diagnosis by a fortnight. The effort is justified by the blood supply: the scaphoid is perfused retrogradely through its distal pole, so a missed waist or proximal pole fracture risks non-union and avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment, with wrist collapse and secondary arthritis to follow.
quiz.explain: Everything here follows from a single anatomical fact and a single statistical one. The statistical fact is that normal initial radiographs do not exclude a scaphoid fracture, so the negative film changes nothing about the immediate management of a clinically suspicious wrist. The anatomical fact is the retrograde blood supply, which makes the cost of a missed fracture disproportionate: the proximal fragment is fed through the fracture, and immobilisation is what protects it. MRI has displaced the traditional repeat radiograph in most units on cost-effectiveness grounds as much as accuracy — an early definitive answer releases the many patients who have no fracture from weeks of unnecessary immobilisation and time off work.

quiz.prompt: A horizontal-beam lateral radiograph of the knee, taken after a fall from a ladder, shows a fluid-fluid level in the suprapatellar recess with the upper layer less dense than the lower. No fracture line is visible on the anteroposterior or lateral projection. What follows from the level?
choices: Marrow fat is in the joint, so a fracture enters it
Blood alone has layered, which follows a ligament tear
The level is an artefact of the horizontal beam technique
Synovial fluid has separated, which suggests an effusion
quiz.answer: Marrow fat is in the joint, so a fracture enters it
quiz.explain: Fat floats on blood, and the fat in question is marrow fat, which can reach the joint cavity by one route: a fracture that crosses the cortex within the capsular attachment. A fat-fluid level is therefore proof of an intra-articular fracture even when no line is visible, and the usual culprit at the knee is a depressed lateral tibial plateau fracture; CT is the next step, and MRI where the ligaments and menisci also need assessing. A pure haemarthrosis after a twisting injury does suggest an anterior cruciate tear, but blood does not separate into two layers of different density. The horizontal beam is what makes the level visible rather than what creates it — a level cannot form on a film shot with the beam vertical, which is why the technique is specified in the trauma series.

quiz.prompt: The elbow radiographs of a six-year-old are checked against the sequence in which the ossification centres appear, so that a displaced medial epicondyle is not mistaken for a trochlear centre. Put the centres in the order they ossify.
quiz.answer: capitellum radial-head medial-epicondyle trochlea olecranon lateral-epicondyle
quiz.explain: The centres appear at roughly one, three, five, seven, nine and eleven years, earlier in girls, and the ages matter far less than the order, which is reliable. The order is a diagnostic tool rather than a piece of trivia: a fragment of bone at the trochlea in a child whose medial epicondyle is not visible is an avulsed medial epicondyle that has migrated, sometimes into the joint after a transient dislocation, and calling it a trochlear centre leaves an intra-articular fragment in a growing elbow. The corollary is that the medial epicondyle should be identified before the trochlea is accepted, on every paediatric elbow. The centres fuse in a different order from the one in which they appear, so this sequence applies to appearance only.

quiz.prompt: After a generalised seizure a man cannot externally rotate his shoulder. The anteroposterior radiograph shows the humeral head overlapping the glenoid, and the head is rounded and symmetrical rather than showing its usual greater tuberosity profile. What is the next step?
choices: Obtain an axillary or scapular-Y view of the same shoulder
Report an anterior dislocation and reduce it in the department
Report a normal shoulder and treat the pain conservatively
Request MRI to look for a rotator cuff tear before reduction
quiz.answer: Obtain an axillary or scapular-Y view of the same shoulder
quiz.explain: A posterior dislocation locks the humerus in internal rotation, so the head presents its smooth articular surface to the beam and loses the tuberosity step, and the joint can look almost congruent on the frontal view alone. That is why the diagnosis is missed: the single view is unreliable, and the fix is a projection orthogonal to it — an axillary, a modified Velpeau axillary if the arm will not abduct, or a scapular-Y — with CT if the patient cannot be positioned at all. Seizures and electric shock are the classic mechanisms, and both can produce bilateral dislocations, so the other shoulder is examined too. Reducing what is assumed to be an anterior dislocation without a second view risks manoeuvring the wrong way against a locked head and an impaction fracture of its anteromedial surface.

quiz.prompt: A registrar telephones the orthopaedic team with 'a fracture of the distal radius'. Give four further elements the description must carry before the team can choose between a cast and theatre, and say what each one changes.
quiz.answer: Whether the fracture line enters the radiocarpal or distal radioulnar joint, and if so the size of the articular step or gap, because an articular step is what pushes the decision towards fixation rather than casting. The displacement and angulation of the distal fragment, given as translation as a fraction of the shaft width and as the direction in which the distal fragment tilts, in degrees, because that is the deformity the surgeon has to reverse and the figures determine whether it can be held. Whether the metaphysis is comminuted, particularly dorsally, because a comminuted metaphysis loses its buttress and collapses again after a closed reduction, which argues for fixation from the start. Whether the skin is broken over the fracture, and the state of the median nerve and the radial pulse, because an open fracture or an acute carpal tunnel syndrome goes to theatre whatever the alignment. Radial height, radial inclination and palmar tilt, the state of the ulnar styloid and any associated carpal injury complete the description.
quiz.explain: The four elements map onto the four questions the surgeon is actually asking: does this joint need to be rebuilt, how far out is it, will it stay where I put it, and does it need to go to theatre tonight. Naming the bone and saying 'fracture' answers none of them. The habit worth acquiring is to describe every fracture in the same fixed sequence — which bone and which part of it, whether it is open, the pattern of the line, the position of the distal fragment in translation, angulation, rotation and shortening, whether it reaches an articular surface, and what the adjacent joints and soft tissues show — because a fixed sequence is what stops the rotational deformity, or the second fracture at the joint above, from being the one thing left out.

quiz.prompt: A workman falls from a height and lands on his heels. On the lateral calcaneal radiograph the angle is measured between a line from the superior margin of the posterior tuberosity to the posterior facet and a line from that facet to the superior aspect of the anterior process. Below how many degrees is this angle regarded as reduced, indicating depression of the posterior facet? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The tuber joint angle described by Boehler measures 20 to 40 degrees in the intact calcaneus; flattening below 20 degrees means the posterior facet has been driven downwards into the body of the bone, and the angle can go negative in a severe injury. It is worth measuring precisely because the fracture line in an axial loading injury runs obliquely and can be genuinely invisible until the facet is seen to have dropped, and because the uninjured side gives a within-patient control. Two further habits belong with the finding: CT in the coronal plane through the posterior facet is what grades the fracture and plans the operation, and axial loading injuries travel up the body, so the other calcaneus, both tibial plateaus and the thoracolumbar junction are examined in the same patient.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old woman cannot bear weight after a fall onto her hip. An anteroposterior pelvis and a lateral of the hip are reported as showing no fracture, and she remains unable to stand the next morning. Which test resolves the question, and why?
choices: MRI, which shows the marrow oedema of an undisplaced line
CT, which is as sensitive as MRI for an undisplaced line
Repeat radiographs in ten days, once resorption widens it
Bone scintigraphy, which is positive within the first hours
quiz.answer: MRI, which shows the marrow oedema of an undisplaced line
quiz.explain: MRI is the reference standard for the radiographically occult hip fracture. It shows the low-signal line on T1 and the surrounding oedema on a fluid-sensitive sequence from the day of injury, and a limited two-sequence coronal protocol takes only a few minutes. CT misses a proportion of undisplaced femoral neck fractures, particularly in osteoporotic bone where the trabecular detail it depends on has already been lost, so a negative CT does not exclude the diagnosis — though CT is the reasonable substitute where MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. Scintigraphy needs a day or more in an elderly patient before it becomes reliable. Waiting ten days is the worst option of the four: it leaves an undisplaced intracapsular fracture to displace in a patient who is immobile in the meantime, and displacement is what converts a fixable fracture into an arthroplasty.

nodes.title: Hip: Impingement, Arthroplasty and the Painful Hip
nodes.goal: Measure the impingement and coverage angles that decide hip surgery, stage osteonecrosis, find the fracture the radiograph hides, and work up a failing arthroplasty.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old footballer has anterior groin pain on flexion and internal rotation. Oblique axial MR images show an aspherical anterolateral head-neck junction with an alpha angle of 72 degrees. The lateral centre-edge angle is 31 degrees and there is no crossover sign. Where do you expect the joint damage to be, and of what kind?
quiz.answer: Anterosuperior chondral delamination running from the rim inward, the labrum spared at first
choices: Anterosuperior chondral delamination running from the rim inward, the labrum spared at first
Anterosuperior labral crushing with a narrow rim of chondral loss and posteroinferior contrecoup injury
Posterior chondral loss with anterior capsular thickening and an otherwise normal acetabular labrum
Global cartilage thinning with medial joint space narrowing and central acetabular subchondral cysts
quiz.explain: The alpha angle of 72 degrees marks a cam bump, and the coverage numbers are normal: a lateral centre-edge angle of 31 degrees sits in the usual 25 to 39 degree range, and the absence of a crossover sign argues against focal retroversion. So this is cam impingement, where the aspherical junction is jammed into the joint on flexion and internal rotation and shears the cartilage off the subchondral plate from the acetabular rim inward. The delamination often runs well ahead of any labral tear, which is why the arthroscopist finds a carpet of loose cartilage under a labrum that still looks reasonable. The second option describes the pincer mechanism instead, where an over-covering rim pinches the labrum, chondral loss is confined to a thin rim strip, and the head levers into the posteroinferior socket to give the contrecoup lesion. Posterior chondral loss with capsular change is a pattern of trauma or instability, and global thinning with medial narrowing belongs to established or inflammatory arthritis, not to a young athlete with mechanical pain.

quiz.prompt: On a well-centred AP pelvis of a 24-year-old with lateral hip pain, the lateral centre-edge angle of Wiberg measures 18 degrees. Coverage of 25 degrees or more is taken as normal, 20 to 25 degrees as borderline and below 20 degrees as dysplastic. By how many degrees short of the normal range is this hip? Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Twenty-five minus eighteen is seven, and the arithmetic matters less than what it puts the hip into. The lateral centre-edge angle is built from a vertical line through the centre of the femoral head and a second line from that centre to the lateral edge of the acetabular sourcil, so it measures how much roof sits over the head. Below 20 degrees the hip is dysplastic, 20 to 25 is a borderline zone that is argued over, 25 to 39 is normal, and 40 or more is over-coverage of the kind that produces global pincer impingement. The direction of travel is the point: a dysplastic hip is short of coverage, so it overloads the rim, hypertrophies its labrum and tears it, and it is treated by adding coverage with a periacetabular osteotomy. Trimming the rim, the operation for pincer morphology, would make it worse. Measure only on a properly centred film, because pelvic rotation and tilt shift the apparent rim.

quiz.prompt: An AP pelvis shows the anterior acetabular wall line crossing lateral to the posterior wall line in the upper third of the socket. The coccyx lies 2 cm off the midline of the symphysis and the obturator foramina are markedly asymmetric. What do you do with that crossover?
quiz.answer: Repeat the radiograph properly centred, because rotation and tilt both create and erase this sign
choices: Repeat the radiograph properly centred, because rotation and tilt both create and erase this sign
Report cranial acetabular retroversion and refer for arthroscopic trimming of the anterior rim
Report the sign as valid, because the wall lines are unaffected by the position of the pelvis
Disregard the wall lines and measure the alpha angle, which answers the same question about version
quiz.explain: The crossover sign is only as good as the film. On a valid AP pelvis the coccyx sits in the midline above the symphysis, roughly 1 to 3 cm from it, and the obturator foramina and iliac wings look symmetric. Rotation towards one side swings the anterior wall of the opposite acetabulum laterally and manufactures a crossover in a normally orientated socket; rotation the other way hides a real one. Increasing pelvic tilt does much the same. Here the coccyx is off midline and the foramina are asymmetric, so the film cannot support the call, and the correct move is a properly centred repeat before anyone discusses a rim trim. When the film is valid, look for the supporting features of true retroversion: a prominent ischial spine projecting into the pelvis and a posterior wall line running medial to the head centre. The alpha angle describes the femoral side and says nothing at all about acetabular version.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old with mechanical groin pain has a non-contrast 3 T hip MRI reported as showing a possible anterosuperior labral abnormality. The surgeon asks whether direct MR arthrography would add anything before arthroscopy. What does the intra-articular injection actually do for you, and when is it worth it?
quiz.answer: Intra-articular dilute gadolinium contrast distends the capsule and drives fluid into the substance of the labrum, so a tear or a detachment is shown directly rather than inferred from a line of intermediate signal; it earns its place when the non-contrast study is equivocal and the answer will decide arthroscopy, and adds little when a dedicated small field-of-view study is already unambiguous.
quiz.explain: Distension is the whole mechanism. Without it, a partial detachment lies collapsed against the rim and reads as a vague grey line; with a few millilitres of dilute gadolinium the capsule is opened, the contrast is forced into the cleft, and the tear is outlined. Direct arthrography also lets the operator inject local anaesthetic, so a patient whose pain abates for an hour has told you the pain is intra-articular, which is diagnostic information no sequence provides. Against that, it is an invasive procedure, usually guided by fluoroscopy or ultrasound, and a good small field-of-view non-contrast study on a modern scanner is often enough. The commonest error either way is over-calling normal anatomy: a sublabral sulcus at the anterosuperior junction, the perilabral sulcus, and the labral base where the physis once ran can all mimic a cleft. A paralabral cyst next to the finding is the reassuring secondary sign that the tear is real.

quiz.prompt: A 42-year-old man has six weeks of hip pain and now limps. MRI shows diffuse marrow oedema through the whole femoral head, the neck and the intertrochanteric region with a small effusion, no demarcated subchondral segment and no low signal line. Radiographs show mild osteopenia of the head and neck. What follows?
quiz.answer: Protected weight-bearing and repeat imaging, since this pattern usually settles over several months
choices: Protected weight-bearing and repeat imaging, since this pattern usually settles over several months
Urgent core decompression, since the oedema marks the necrotic segment before it can collapse
Immediate arthroplasty referral, since collapse of the femoral head is already under way here
CT-guided biopsy of the femoral neck, since diffuse oedema of this extent implies a tumour
quiz.explain: Transient osteoporosis of the hip, or bone marrow oedema syndrome, produces exactly this: oedema that fills the head, crosses the neck and reaches the intertrochanteric region without a demarcated lesion inside it, in a middle-aged man or a woman in the third trimester, and it resolves over six to twelve months. Osteonecrosis looks different even when oedematous, because there is a geographic subchondral segment bounded by a serpiginous line, and on T2 the double line sign, an inner bright band of granulation tissue with an outer dark sclerotic band. Core decompression is aimed at that demarcated lesion, so it has nothing to work on here. Nothing has collapsed, so arthroplasty is premature, and a biopsy would sample oedematous marrow and tell you nothing while risking a fracture. The one thing that does matter is protection: the bone is transiently weak, and subcapital fracture during the oedema phase is the known complication.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these findings of femoral head osteonecrosis in the order they appear as the disease progresses, earliest first.
quiz.answer: marrow-signal-change sclerotic-demarcation crescent-sign head-flattening joint-space-loss
quiz.explain: This is the ARCO 2019 sequence in imaging terms. Stage 1 is MRI-only disease: the radiograph is normal and the marrow signal has changed, with the reactive interface giving the double line on T2. Stage 2 adds radiographically visible sclerosis, osteolysis or focal osteoporosis, still with no subchondral fracture and no flattening. Stage 3 is the subchondral fracture, the crescent of gas or fluid immediately beneath the plate, with or without collapse of the contour; ARCO 2019 splits it by the depth of femoral head depression, 3A at 2 mm or less and 3B beyond that. Stage 4 is secondary arthritis, when the acetabular cartilage finally gives way and the joint space narrows. The clinically useful part of the order is that the joint space stays normal all the way through stage 3, which is what separates osteonecrosis from arthritis on a plain film, and the frog lateral view shows the crescent best because the anterosuperior segment is thrown into profile.

quiz.prompt: Two hips have osteonecrosis of similar volume, both involving the anterosuperior weight-bearing segment. In one the subchondral bone plate is intact; in the other a thin fluid-signal line lies immediately beneath it on the T2 images. Why does that line change what you recommend?
quiz.answer: The line is a subchondral fracture, so the head has already lost its mechanical support and will go on to collapse; core decompression and the other joint-preserving procedures are aimed at the pre-fracture hip and rarely rescue a head once the crescent is present, so this patient moves towards osteotomy or arthroplasty rather than decompression.
quiz.explain: The crescent is a fracture through dead trabecular bone under the articular plate, and it is the point at which the natural history stops being reversible. That is why ARCO 2019 makes it the boundary between stage 2 and stage 3 rather than treating collapse as a matter of degree. MRI and CT both find it earlier than the radiograph, and CT is particularly good at showing a subtle break in the subchondral plate when the MRI is equivocal. Size and site are the other predictors that belong in the report: a lesion occupying more than about a third of the head, or one that involves the lateral pillar under the weight-bearing dome, will collapse whatever is done, whereas a small medial lesion may be watched. So the report should state the stage, the proportion of head involved, whether the lateral pillar is included, and whether a subchondral fracture is present.

quiz.prompt: An uncemented total hip replacement is reviewed for pain. On the immediate post-operative AP radiograph the acetabular component inclination measures 42 degrees; on a film taken three years later, measured against the same landmarks, it is 49 degrees. By how many degrees has the inclination changed? Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Seven degrees, and that is enough to matter. A change in cup inclination beyond about five degrees, or migration of the component by more than two or three millimetres, is taken as evidence of loosening whatever the lucent lines are doing, because a fixed implant does not move. The measurement is only meaningful if the two films are comparable, so use the same reference line each time, usually the inter-teardrop or inter-ischial line, and check that rotation and tilt are similar. The other half of the assessment is the interfaces: describe acetabular lucency by the three zones of DeLee and Charnley and femoral lucency by the seven Gruen zones, and treat a thin, non-progressive lucency of under 2 mm as acceptable while a wide or progressive one is not. Note also that the starting figure of 42 degrees sits inside the traditional Lewinnek target of 40 plus or minus 10 degrees of inclination, so this cup was well placed and has since moved.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old woman cannot weight-bear after a fall. An AP pelvis and a lateral of the hip show no fracture, but she has groin pain on any rotation of the leg and is unable to lift it from the trolley. What imaging do you arrange next?
quiz.answer: MRI of the hip with coronal T1 and STIR, which will show or exclude the fracture today
choices: MRI of the hip with coronal T1 and STIR, which will show or exclude the fracture today
Repeat radiographs in ten days, when resorption at the fracture line makes it visible
An isotope bone scan today, which is the most sensitive test in the first 24 hours
No further imaging, with full mobilisation, analgesia and physiotherapy review
quiz.explain: A normal radiograph does not exclude a hip fracture in an osteopenic patient, and a missed one that displaces converts a screw fixation into a hemiarthroplasty. MRI is the reference standard: a limited protocol of coronal T1 and STIR through the pelvis takes a few minutes, shows the fracture line as low signal on T1 within hours of the injury, and needs no contrast. It also answers the question when the hip is normal, because pubic rami fractures, greater trochanteric and abductor injuries, and occasionally a metastatic deposit are the alternative explanations, and they are all in the same field of view. CT is the fallback when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, but it does miss undisplaced trabecular fractures in porotic bone. A bone scan can stay negative for one to three days in the elderly, and repeating radiographs at ten days leaves an unprotected fracture to displace in the interval.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old on long-term corticosteroids has low back and buttock pain that came on without injury. Radiographs and MRI of the lumbar spine show only degenerative change. Pain is reproduced by pressure over the sacroiliac region. What is the most useful next step?
quiz.answer: Image the sacrum and pelvic ring, looking for vertical alar and pubic ramus fractures
choices: Image the sacrum and pelvic ring, looking for vertical alar and pubic ramus fractures
Inject the L4/5 and L5/S1 facet joints under fluoroscopic guidance to treat the pain
Arrange flexion and extension views of the lumbar spine for degenerative instability
Arrange a whole-body isotope scan to search for the primary tumour causing the pain
quiz.explain: The sacrum sits below the field of view of most lumbar spine studies, so a sacral insufficiency fracture is missed by a protocol aimed at the discs. Steroids, osteoporosis and previous pelvic radiotherapy are the classic settings. On STIR the fractures run vertically through the sacral ala parallel to the sacroiliac joints, often with a transverse component across the body, which is the H or Honda pattern that isotope imaging shows so memorably. CT confirms the line and the surrounding sclerosis. Because the pelvis is a ring, always look for the second break: pubic rami fractures accompany alar fractures in a large proportion of cases. The trap is calling the marrow change a metastasis, so look for a fracture line and an absent soft tissue mass; conversely, a lesion that destroys the cortex and has a mass is not an insufficiency fracture. Treatment is analgesia and mobilisation, sometimes sacroplasty, not a facet injection.

quiz.prompt: Four months after a cemented total hip replacement, radiographs show a 4 mm lucency around the whole cement-bone interface of the stem, new periosteal reaction along the proximal femur, and ultrasound shows a joint effusion. The patient has rest pain and a raised C-reactive protein. What is the leading explanation?
quiz.answer: Periprosthetic infection, given the speed of change, the periosteal reaction and the raised CRP
choices: Periprosthetic infection, given the speed of change, the periosteal reaction and the raised CRP
Aseptic loosening from polyethylene wear particles, which produces the same appearances
Stress shielding by a stiff stem that transfers load to the distal femur instead
Heterotopic ossification in the abductor mass, which often follows this surgical approach
quiz.explain: Timing carries most of the weight. Particle disease and aseptic loosening take years to produce a wide lucency, and they do not raise inflammatory markers; a wide, circumferential lucency at four months with rest pain and a raised CRP is infection until an aspirate says otherwise. Periosteal reaction is the other strong pointer, being uncommon in aseptic loosening and characteristic of infection, and the effusion supports it. The next step is aspiration before any antibiotic is given, so the culture is not sterilised, and the report should say so explicitly. Stress shielding produces the opposite appearance, proximal bone resorption and calcar rounding with a well-fixed distal stem, and no pain. Heterotopic ossification is new bone in the soft tissues around the joint, not a lucency at the interface. For reference, a thin, non-progressive lucency of under 2 mm at the cement-bone interface can be entirely normal.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a metal-on-metal hip resurfacing has groin pain and a rising blood cobalt level, and the clinician wants MRI for adverse reaction to metal debris. Say what you ask the radiographer to change from a standard protocol, and what each change buys.
quiz.answer: Scan at 1.5 T rather than 3 T; use turbo spin echo rather than gradient echo sequences, with a high receiver bandwidth, a short echo time and a short echo spacing; use thin slices with a fine matrix; and use STIR rather than spectral fat saturation. Each change either reduces the off-resonance frequency shift near the metal or spreads it across fewer millimetres, so the pseudotumour and the abductor muscles remain visible next to the implant.
quiz.explain: Metal distorts the local field, and the size of the resulting displacement is the frequency shift divided by the bandwidth per pixel, so raising the receiver bandwidth is the single most effective lever, at a cost in signal to noise. Gradient echo sequences have no refocusing pulse to recover dephasing and are the worst offenders, so they are dropped. Spectral fat saturation depends on a uniform field and fails precisely where you need it, whereas STIR nulls fat by inversion time and tolerates inhomogeneity. Lower field means a smaller shift, and orienting the long axis of the prosthesis along the main field reduces distortion further. Where they exist, the multispectral techniques MAVRIC and SEMAC do the job properly. What you are looking for is a periprosthetic fluid collection or solid mass with a thickened capsule, plus atrophy or frank necrosis of the abductors and osteolysis, since abductor destruction is what makes revision urgent.

quiz.prompt: An elderly man falls and breaks his femur around a cemented stem.
