CT shows a spiral fracture around the distal stem, a fractured cement mantle, and the stem sitting in a slightly different position from the film taken a year ago; the bone stock elsewhere looks good. What should the report emphasise, and what does it mean for the operation?
quiz.answer: The stem is loose, so this needs revision of the stem rather than fixation of the fracture alone
choices: The stem is loose, so this needs revision of the stem rather than fixation of the fracture alone
The stem is stable, so plate fixation around the retained implant is all that is required
The bone stock is inadequate, so this needs proximal femoral replacement rather than a stem
The fracture lies below the stem, so it can be managed as an isolated femoral shaft break
quiz.explain: The Vancouver classification divides periprosthetic femoral fractures into type A at the trochanters, type B around or just below the stem, and type C well distal to it, and type B is subdivided by exactly the two things the radiologist can report: B1 has a stable stem and is fixed, B2 has a loose stem with adequate bone and needs a revision stem, and B3 has a loose stem with deficient bone and needs proximal femoral reconstruction or replacement. Here a change in stem position against a previous film and a fractured cement mantle both say the implant is loose, while the bone stock is preserved, so this is B2. That is why the sentence the surgeon needs is not the shape of the fracture but whether the stem has moved and whether the bone will hold a new one. Always compare with the earliest post-operative film rather than the most recent one, since loosening is a slow drift.

nodes.title: Knee: Meniscus, Ligament and Cartilage
nodes.goal: Report a knee MRI so that you name the meniscal tear pattern and its mechanical consequence, recognise ligament injury from direct and secondary signs, and grade cartilage and patellofemoral injury in terms that change management.

quiz.prompt: A 25-year-old footballer has a locked knee. On the sagittal images through the intercondylar notch there is a low-signal band lying anterior and roughly parallel to the posterior cruciate ligament. On the same 4 mm sagittal series the body of the medial meniscus produces a bow tie on only one slice. What do you report?
quiz.answer: A displaced bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus, fragment lying in the notch
choices: A displaced bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus, fragment lying in the notch
A prominent meniscofemoral ligament of Wrisberg passing behind the posterior cruciate
A torn anterior cruciate bundle displaced forwards to form a cyclops lesion
A normal transverse geniculate ligament crossing the anterior intercondylar area
quiz.explain: Three findings converge. The double PCL sign is a displaced meniscal fragment sitting in the notch beneath the true PCL, and because the medial meniscus is longer and more tethered it accounts for the great majority of these. The absent bow-tie sign is its companion: with 4 to 5 mm sagittal slices a normal meniscal body should produce a bow tie on at least two consecutive images, so a single bow tie means tissue has left the periphery. A locked knee ties it together clinically. Wrisberg runs posterior to the PCL, not anterior, and is a thin band that can be traced to the lateral meniscal posterior horn. A cyclops lesion is a nodule of arthrofibrosis anterior to a reconstructed graft. The transverse geniculate ligament lies anteriorly, between the anterior horns, well away from the notch.

quiz.prompt: Describe the signs you would systematically look for before committing to a diagnosis of a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear.
quiz.answer: I look for the double PCL sign in the notch, the flipped fragment or double anterior horn sign, an absent bow-tie on fewer than two consecutive sagittal slices, and a truncated or diminutive parent meniscus at the donor site.
quiz.explain: A bucket-handle tear is a longitudinal vertical tear whose inner fragment has hinged into the joint, and every reliable sign is really the same observation made twice: tissue is missing from where it should be and present where it should not. The double PCL sign shows the fragment in the notch. The flipped fragment, or double anterior horn sign, shows it folded forwards on top of the anterior horn, which is the pattern to expect when the handle displaces anteriorly rather than centrally. The absent bow tie quantifies the loss at the donor site. Always confirm that the parent meniscus is truncated, because the displaced fragment has to have come from somewhere; if the meniscus looks intact, reconsider the diagnosis. Reporting it is urgent in a locked knee, since early repair of a peripheral vascular tear preserves the meniscus.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old felt a pop while squatting. The coronal images show a vertical cleft at the posterior attachment of the medial meniscus with no meniscal tissue visible on the slice through the root, the meniscal body lies 5 mm beyond the tibial margin, and there is marrow oedema in the medial femoral condyle. What is the mechanical significance?
quiz.answer: A posterior medial root tear; the extruded meniscus no longer carries hoop stress
choices: A posterior medial root tear; the extruded meniscus no longer carries hoop stress
A degenerative horizontal cleavage tear with a parameniscal cyst at the root
Chondrocalcinosis producing linear meniscal signal that stops short of the surface
A ramp lesion at the meniscocapsular junction of the posterior horn medially
quiz.explain: The meniscal roots anchor the circumferential collagen bundles to bone. Cut the root, or make a full radial tear near it, and the meniscus can no longer convert axial load into hoop tension: it simply squeezes outwards. That is why root tears and extrusion travel together, and why a root tear is biomechanically close to a total meniscectomy. The signs are a ghost meniscus on the slice through the root, a vertical cleft on coronal images and extrusion of the body of 3 mm or more measured at the level of the medial collateral ligament. Marrow oedema signals the load now going straight into bone, and subchondral insufficiency fracture is the feared sequel. Report it explicitly, because root repair in the right patient is a different operation from a meniscectomy. A horizontal cleavage tear splits the meniscus into upper and lower leaves and does not abolish hoop stress. Chondrocalcinosis gives linear intrameniscal signal without a surface-reaching cleft.

quiz.prompt: On the coronal image at the level of the medial collateral ligament, the outer margin of the medial meniscal body lies 8.2 mm beyond the mid-coronal tibial plateau margin, but a marginal osteophyte projects 3.4 mm beyond that true plateau margin and must be excluded from the measurement. Report the true meniscal extrusion in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 8.2 minus 3.4 leaves 4.8 mm. Extrusion is measured on the mid-coronal image at the level of the medial collateral ligament, from the outermost meniscal edge to the peripheral tibial cortex, and osteophytes are deliberately excluded because they push the reference line outwards and inflate the figure. Anything at or beyond about 3 mm counts as significant extrusion, and 4.8 mm is well past that. The finding matters because extrusion is a marker of lost hoop-stress function rather than a diagnosis in itself: look immediately for a posterior root tear or a large radial tear, and check the cartilage and subchondral bone of the same compartment, which is where the consequence shows up. Extrusion also increases with weight bearing, so a borderline value on a supine scan may understate the problem.

quiz.prompt: A single sagittal image shows a thin line of high signal reaching the inferior articular surface of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. The images either side of it are normal, the coronal series is normal, and there is no marrow oedema or joint effusion. How should you handle this?
quiz.answer: Treat it as a single-slice finding and do not yet call a tear; specificity is poor
choices: Treat it as a single-slice finding and do not yet call a tear; specificity is poor
Call a definite tear, since one surface-contacting slice is sufficient evidence
Call a bucket-handle tear whose fragment has displaced out of the imaging plane
Attribute it to magic angle effect, expected on short echo time sequences at 55 degrees
quiz.explain: The two-slice-touch rule says a meniscal tear should be called when abnormal signal contacts an articular surface on two or more consecutive images, in either plane. A single contacting slice has a positive predictive value barely better than chance, because volume averaging, vascular remnants, the concave meniscal undersurface and normal insertional signal all generate one-slice findings. Applying the rule lifts specificity substantially at very little cost in sensitivity, and it stops a stream of unnecessary arthroscopies. Say what you saw and say you are not calling it: a one-line comment protects the next reader. Magic angle is a real phenomenon at 55 degrees to the main field on short echo time sequences, but it affects the popliteus and the patellar tendon rather than producing a surface-reaching line in the meniscus. A displaced bucket-handle fragment would leave a truncated parent meniscus, which is absent here.

quiz.prompt: List the normal anatomical structures that most often produce a false-positive meniscal tear, and say where each of them sits.
quiz.answer: The transverse geniculate ligament at the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus, the popliteus tendon and popliteomeniscal fascicles at the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus, and the meniscofemoral ligaments of Humphrey and Wrisberg near the lateral posterior root.
quiz.explain: Almost every classic meniscal pseudo-tear is on the lateral side, and each is a normal structure creating a fat or fluid cleft where it meets the meniscus. The transverse geniculate ligament crosses the anterior intercondylar fat and inserts on the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus, producing an oblique line at that junction. The popliteus tendon passes through its hiatus beside the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus, and the superior and inferior popliteomeniscal fascicles create two further clefts. The meniscofemoral ligaments, Humphrey in front of the posterior cruciate and Wrisberg behind it, insert near the posterior root and can mimic a tear or a fragment. The defence is anatomical rather than statistical: follow the suspect line onto adjacent slices and into the orthogonal plane, and if it can be traced to a named structure, it is not a tear.

quiz.prompt: A knee with an acute anterior cruciate rupture is being reported. Say what a ramp lesion is and why it is easy to miss.
quiz.answer: A ramp lesion is a tear at the meniscocapsular junction of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus; it is missed because it lies at the posteromedial corner, shows only as a thin fluid line between meniscus and capsule, and attention is usually on the ACL itself.
quiz.explain: The posteromedial meniscocapsular attachment is a secondary restraint to anterior tibial translation, so it fails alongside the anterior cruciate ligament in a meaningful minority of acute ruptures. The MRI sign is subtle: fluid or high signal interposed between the peripheral edge of the posterior horn and the capsule on fluid-sensitive sagittal and coronal images, sometimes with posteromedial tibial marrow oedema as the only clue. It is also hard to see arthroscopically from the standard anterior portals, which is why the finding is valued. It matters because an unrepaired ramp lesion leaves residual rotational laxity and is associated with graft failure after reconstruction. Make a habit of looking specifically at the posteromedial corner on every acute ACL study rather than trusting incidental detection.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old had a non-contact twisting injury. The knee is too swollen for the cruciate to be traced with confidence, but there is marrow oedema in the sulcus terminalis of the lateral femoral condyle and in the posterolateral tibial plateau, together with a thin vertical cortical avulsion at the lateral tibial rim. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: A pivot-shift contusion pattern with a Segond fracture: the anterior cruciate is torn
choices: A pivot-shift contusion pattern with a Segond fracture: the anterior cruciate is torn
A dashboard contusion pattern with a reverse Segond, so the posterior cruciate is torn
A hyperextension kissing contusion pattern of the anterior tibia and anterior femur
A lateral patellar dislocation pattern with medial patellar and lateral condylar oedema
quiz.explain: Secondary signs rescue the study when the ligament itself cannot be judged. The pivot shift drives the posterolateral tibial plateau against the lateral femoral condyle at the sulcus terminalis, so that pair of contusions is close to diagnostic of an anterior cruciate rupture even when the ligament is obscured. The Segond fracture is a vertical avulsion from the lateral tibial rim at the attachment of the anterolateral capsular structures, and its association with ACL rupture is around ninety per cent, with a high rate of meniscal injury alongside. Other useful secondaries are anterior tibial translation beyond about 5 to 7 mm, an uncovered lateral meniscus and a deep lateral femoral notch. A reverse Segond is a medial tibial rim avulsion and points to the posterior cruciate. The dashboard pattern bruises the anterior tibia. Patellar dislocation bruises the inferomedial patella and the anterolateral condyle, not the posterolateral plateau.

quiz.prompt: Eight months after a hamstring anterior cruciate reconstruction, a patient with a clinically stable knee has an MRI for anterior ache. The graft is continuous, correctly angled along Blumensaat line, with well-placed tunnels, but shows diffuse intermediate signal through its substance and no fluid-filled cleft. What should you say?
quiz.answer: Expected graft remodelling signal at this interval; report the graft as intact
choices: Expected graft remodelling signal at this interval; report the graft as intact
Graft rupture; the raised intrasubstance signal indicates fibre discontinuity
Roof impingement from an anterior tibial tunnel producing the abnormal signal
A cyclops lesion of arthrofibrosis lying in front of the graft and limiting extension
quiz.explain: A new graft is low signal throughout, but between roughly four and twelve months it undergoes revascularisation and remodelling, and diffuse intermediate signal during that window is normal and should not be read as failure. What signals a genuine problem is fluid-signal discontinuity, an abnormally horizontal graft that no longer parallels Blumensaat line, anterior tibial translation, or the graft draping over the intercondylar roof. Tunnel position is worth checking on every post-operative study: an anteriorly placed tibial tunnel causes roof impingement with signal concentrated at the distal graft and a fluid-filled ganglion, while an anteriorly placed femoral tunnel makes the graft tighten in flexion. A cyclops lesion is a discrete nodule of scar anterior to the graft in a patient who cannot fully straighten the knee, which is a different clinical picture from a dull ache.

quiz.prompt: A patient sustained a varus blow. The radiograph shows a small avulsed fragment off the tip of the fibular styloid. On MRI there is fluid around the popliteus tendon at its femoral origin and the lateral collateral ligament is lax and thickened. What must the report emphasise?
quiz.answer: A posterolateral corner injury; missing it is a recognised cause of graft failure
choices: A posterolateral corner injury; missing it is a recognised cause of graft failure
An isolated Segond fracture of the lateral tibial plateau with an intact corner
An avulsion of biceps femoris from the fibular head without ligamentous injury
A normal fabella lying posterolateral to the lateral femoral condyle in the capsule
quiz.explain: The arcuate sign is an avulsion at the fibular styloid, where the arcuate ligament complex and the popliteofibular ligament insert, and it is a flag for injury to the whole posterolateral corner: lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament and the posterolateral capsule. It is rarely isolated, so search deliberately for cruciate injury alongside it. The reason to be emphatic is surgical: an unrecognised posterolateral corner injury leaves persistent varus and external rotation laxity that stretches out a cruciate reconstruction, and it is one of the commonest causes of graft failure. Check the common peroneal nerve too, since it is injured in a significant minority. A Segond avulsion comes off the tibia, not the fibula, and points anterolaterally. A fabella is a corticated sesamoid within the lateral head of gastrocnemius, well away from the styloid.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these articular cartilage appearances in order of increasing Outerbridge grade.
quiz.answer: softening shallow-fissuring deep-fissuring exposed-subchondral-bone
quiz.explain: Outerbridge was written for what the surgeon sees through the arthroscope and has been adapted for MRI, so the language crosses over usefully. Grade 1 is softening and swelling with an intact surface, which on MRI appears as focal signal change without contour loss. Grade 2 is fissuring or fragmentation through less than half the cartilage thickness. Grade 3 is fissuring deeper than half thickness with the subchondral plate still covered. Grade 4 is full-thickness loss with subchondral bone exposed, usually accompanied by marrow oedema and often by a subchondral cyst. The step that changes management is the one from 3 to 4: full-thickness loss over a defined area in a young patient opens the conversation about resurfacing, whereas partial-thickness change is managed conservatively. Always state the size and location of the defect as well as the grade, because a 5 mm and a 25 mm grade 4 lesion are different problems.

quiz.prompt: A 16-year-old netball player felt the knee give way with the leg planted, and it swelled immediately. MRI shows oedema in the inferomedial patella and the anterolateral aspect of the lateral femoral condyle, disruption of the medial patellofemoral ligament at its femoral attachment, and a 10 mm osteochondral fragment lying in the lateral gutter. What most changes management?
quiz.answer: A transient lateral patellar dislocation with a loose osteochondral fragment to retrieve
choices: A transient lateral patellar dislocation with a loose osteochondral fragment to retrieve
An osteochondritis dissecans of the medial femoral condyle with a stable in-situ fragment
A direct blow to the front of the knee with avulsion of the quadriceps tendon insertion
A bucket-handle meniscal fragment that has displaced laterally into the lateral gutter
quiz.explain: The bone bruise pair is diagnostic even after the patella has relocated: the medial facet of the patella strikes the anterolateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle as it reduces, so oedema appears in both. The medial patellofemoral ligament is the primary restraint and usually fails at the femoral attachment near the adductor tubercle. What alters the immediate plan is the loose fragment: an osteochondral body of that size in a young patient is taken to theatre for removal or fixation, whereas the ligament injury and the predisposing features are managed afterwards. Look for and report those predisposing features too, since they drive the decision about stabilisation: trochlear dysplasia, patella alta and a raised tibial tuberosity to trochlear groove distance. Osteochondritis dissecans classically involves the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle, without this bruise pattern or a torn ligament.

quiz.prompt: On the sagittal image of the same knee, the patellar tendon measures 57 mm from the inferior pole of the patella to its tibial insertion, and the greatest diagonal length of the patella is 38 mm. Calculate the Insall-Salvati ratio, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 57 divided by 38 is 1.5. The Insall-Salvati ratio compares patellar tendon length with the greatest diagonal length of the patella; the normal range is about 0.8 to 1.2, so 1.5 is patella alta. That is a meaningful finding in a dislocator, because a high-riding patella engages the trochlear groove later in flexion and is therefore less constrained in the range where the knee is most vulnerable. Report it alongside the other structural risk factors, since together they decide whether the patient is offered a soft-tissue reconstruction alone or a bony procedure. A ratio below 0.8 is patella baja, seen after tibial tuberosity transfer, in chronic arthrofibrosis, or acutely with a quadriceps tendon rupture. Note that the ratio is measured on a lateral radiograph or a sagittal image with the knee in modest flexion, since it is insensitive to knee position compared with some alternatives.

nodes.title: Musculoskeletal MRI
nodes.goal: Choose the MRI sequence a joint question needs, and tell artefact from disease.

quiz.prompt: On a shoulder study the distal supraspinatus shows intermediate signal on the short-TE proton-density images, in the segment where the tendon curves over the humeral head. That same segment is normal in thickness and contour, and uniformly dark on the long-TE T2 images. What follows?
quiz.answer: The signal is an orientation effect and the tendon is intact
quiz.explain: Tendon collagen is dark because tightly bound water dephases fast, and the dipolar term that does the dephasing scales as 3cos-squared(theta) minus 1, which vanishes near 55 degrees to B0. Where the fibres pass through that angle T2 lengthens, so signal appears on sequences whose TE is short compared with the lengthened T2 and fades once TE is long. A tear holds fluid and stays bright as TE lengthens; tendinosis keeps at least intermediate signal at long TE and usually thickens the tendon. A segment that returns to uniform low signal at normal calibre does neither, so 'The finding is tendinosis that needs an arthrogram to grade' fails on both counts, and calling a tear here treats a geometry effect as disease.
choices: An interstitial tear is present and hidden on T2 imaging
The finding is tendinosis that needs an arthrogram to grade
The signal is an orientation effect and the tendon is intact
A partial-thickness bursal-side tear should be reported

quiz.prompt: Take the proton resonant frequency at 1.5 T as exactly 64 MHz, with fat precessing 3.5 ppm below water. A knee sequence is read out at a bandwidth of 100 Hz per pixel. By how many pixels is fat displaced along the frequency-encoding direction? Give the number of pixels to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Convert the chemical shift to hertz, then hertz to pixels. 64 MHz times 3.5 ppm is 224 Hz, and frequency encoding turns that offset into a position offset of 224 divided by 100, which is 2.24 pixels, or 2.2 to one decimal place. Using the true 1.5 T frequency of 63.87 MHz gives 2.235 and rounds to the same figure. The same arithmetic governs metal, whose induced off-resonance is far larger, which is why raising the receiver bandwidth is the first move next to a prosthesis; the price is signal-to-noise falling as one over the square root of bandwidth. At 3 T the offset doubles to about 447 Hz, so the same bandwidth buys half as much protection.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a cobalt-chrome hip arthroplasty needs MRI for suspected periprosthetic infection, and both a 1.5 T and a 3 T scanner are free. Give three protocol decisions that shrink the metal artefact, with the physical reason each one works.
quiz.answer: Scan at 1.5 T rather than 3 T, because the off-resonance spread the metal induces scales with field strength. Raise the receiver bandwidth, because the displacement produced by a given off-resonance equals that offset divided by the bandwidth per pixel. Suppress fat with STIR rather than a spectral pulse, because inversion recovery nulls by T1 and does not need the fat resonance to sit where the scanner expects it. Beyond the three asked for, thin slices, view-angle tilting and SEMAC or MAVRIC correct the residual in-plane and through-plane distortion.
quiz.explain: Each decision follows from one fact: metal warps B0, so protons near it precess at the wrong frequency and the scanner mislocates them. Lower field means a smaller absolute frequency spread; higher bandwidth means each hertz of error buys less displacement; STIR nulls by T1 recovery rather than by resonant frequency, so it tolerates a fat peak shifted out of the saturation band. Spin echo with its refocusing pulses is essential and gradient echo is the wrong family here, since gradient echo lets exactly this off-resonance dephasing accumulate.

quiz.prompt: Sagittal proton-density images show a linear high-signal line separating a small triangular structure from the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus on two adjacent slices. Coronal images show a band running transversely across the front of the joint into that point. What is the appropriate action?
quiz.answer: Report the meniscus intact; the band explains the cleft
quiz.explain: The transverse intermeniscal ligament crosses the front of the joint to the anterior horns, and the fat between ligament and meniscus makes a pseudotear line that can be traced onto contiguous coronal or axial images as a discrete band. The two-slice rule bites only on signal that reaches an articular surface; this line lies along the interface between ligament and meniscus and stops there, which is why persisting on adjacent slices does not make it a tear. So 'Report a tear of the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus' misapplies a criterion whose premise is missing, and ordering an arthrogram to confirm a structure the plain study already resolves adds a needle for nothing.
choices: Report the meniscus intact; the band explains the cleft
Report a tear of the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Recommend MR arthrography to confirm an anterior horn tear
Report a displaced flap in the anterior joint recess

quiz.prompt: Sagittal images through the lateral compartment show fluid signal separating the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus from the capsule, at the level where the popliteus tendon runs obliquely behind it. The meniscal substance is uniformly dark, both popliteomeniscal fascicles are continuous, and the meniscus sits in normal position. How should this be handled?
quiz.answer: Call it the normal popliteal hiatus and report no tear
quiz.explain: Over roughly a centimetre the lateral meniscus has no capsular attachment, because the popliteus tendon passes through the hiatus, and fluid or fat there imitates a peripheral detachment. What settles it is that the meniscal substance carries no signal reaching an articular surface, and that the gap follows the tendon's course rather than continuing along the meniscal margin beyond the hiatus. 'Attribute the appearance to a torn popliteomeniscal fascicle' is the real differential and the tempting one, but that diagnosis rests on disrupted fascicles and a hypermobile or displaced meniscus, and this study reports both fascicles continuous and the meniscus sited normally.
choices: Report a peripheral tear detaching the posterior horn
Describe a bucket-handle tear with the fragment displaced
Attribute the appearance to a torn popliteomeniscal fascicle
Call it the normal popliteal hiatus and report no tear

quiz.prompt: After a non-contact twisting injury a knee MRI shows marrow oedema in the lateral femoral condyle at the sulcus terminalis and in the posterior lateral tibial plateau. The cruciate images are degraded by motion. What does the oedema pattern support?
quiz.answer: Pivot-shift impaction, which places the ACL at high risk
quiz.explain: In the pivot shift a valgus load with rotation carries the tibia forward, and the lateral femoral condyle strikes the posterior lateral tibial plateau; the paired contusions record that collision and carry a strong association with a torn ACL. The motion-degraded cruciate images should therefore be repeated, or the ACL reported as suspect, rather than passed over. 'Dashboard impaction, which points to a posterior cruciate tear' is the closest rival, but dashboard loading drives the tibia backwards and bruises the anterior tibia instead, which is a different pattern in a different place.
choices: Dashboard impaction, which points to a posterior cruciate tear
Pivot-shift impaction, which places the ACL at high risk
Clip injury, which points to a medial collateral tear
Hyperextension impaction, which spares both cruciate ligaments

quiz.prompt: Eighteen months after partial medial meniscectomy a patient has recurrent locking, and conventional MRI shows intermediate signal touching the tibial surface of the small remnant. Why is direct MR arthrography preferred here to an intravenous gadolinium study?
quiz.answer: Contrast placed in the joint fills a re-tear cleft directly
quiz.explain: In an operated meniscus the usual criterion fails, because the cut surface and its granulation tissue produce surface-reaching intermediate signal for years; the question becomes whether a cleft is open to the joint. Dilute gadolinium injected into the joint tracks into an open cleft, which answers exactly that. 'Intravenous gadolinium fails to reach the joint space itself' is the tempting distractor and its premise is false: indirect arthrography does opacify the joint by diffusion from synovium, given a delay and some exercise. What it shows, though, is enhancement rather than filling, and enhancing granulation tissue is read as a sign of re-tear by some authors and as a confounder by others, so it settles the question less directly than contrast running into a cleft.
choices: Intravenous gadolinium fails to reach the joint space itself
Distension of the capsule is what displays the remnant
Contrast placed in the joint fills a re-tear cleft directly
Intra-articular injection carries a lower contrast dose

quiz.prompt: In-phase and opposed-phase gradient-echo images of the lumbar spine show a focus that loses more than a fifth of its signal on the opposed-phase image, and on T1 the focus is a little brighter than the adjacent disc. What does the signal drop indicate about the focus?
quiz.answer: Fat and water share the voxels, favouring a benign focus
quiz.explain: At the opposed-phase echo time fat and water magnetisation point in opposite directions, so a voxel loses signal in proportion to how much of each it holds, and a drop therefore requires both to be present. Haematopoietic marrow keeps interspersed adipocytes and drops; a marrow-replacing lesion has pushed the fat out and holds its signal, so 'The focus is cellular, so marrow replacement is likely' reads the drop backwards. The T1 comparison with disc and muscle is the independent check. Sclerosis and blood products act through T2-star, which attenuates the longer in-phase echo more than the shorter opposed-phase one, so they shrink or even reverse an apparent drop rather than creating one.
choices: The focus is cellular, so marrow replacement is likely
Blood products are present and dephase the gradient echo
The focus is sclerotic, which shortens T2* and darkens it
Fat and water share the voxels, favouring a benign focus

quiz.prompt: One distance runner with shin pain has periosteal and marrow oedema in the posteromedial tibia on fluid-sensitive images, with normal T1. A second runner has the same oedema plus a dark line crossing the cortex on T1. What separates the two?
quiz.answer: The second shows a fracture line, so a longer time unloaded
quiz.explain: Stress injury runs a continuum, and the established MRI grading climbs from periosteal oedema, through marrow oedema visible on fluid-sensitive images alone, to marrow signal change seen on T1, and finally a discrete fracture line, with return to sport lengthening at each step. T1 does the discriminating work because marrow fat, and its displacement, is what T1 shows. 'The two grade alike, because marrow oedema settles the grade' is the trap: fluid-sensitive sequences are sensitive but unspecific, and oedema by itself can follow a change in training load. MRI outperforms radiographs and CT at the early end, so sending the first runner for CT loses information rather than adding it.
choices: The second shows a fracture line, so a longer time unloaded
The first has the higher grade, since oedema outweighs a line
The two grade alike, because marrow oedema settles the grade
The first needs a CT, since MRI misses periosteal reaction

quiz.prompt: A suspected soft-tissue sarcoma of the thigh is imaged, and the radiographer, worried that spectral fat saturation will fail at the edge of the field, acquires the post-gadolinium sequence as a STIR. Why is that the wrong choice?
quiz.answer: STIR nulls by T1, and enhancement drives tumour T1 toward fat
quiz.explain: Inversion recovery suppresses whatever has recovered to the null point at the chosen inversion time, and that is a statement about T1 rather than about frequency. Gadolinium shortens the T1 of enhancing tissue, so enhancing tumour or granulation can be driven into the nulled band and erased, which defeats the purpose of giving contrast at all. Use spectral fat suppression on the post-contrast T1, or a Dixon water-only reconstruction, which separates fat from water by phase evolution and tolerates far more field inhomogeneity than a single saturation pulse. 'Gadolinium shifts the fat resonance, so the inversion mistimes' is the plausible-sounding rival, but gadolinium at clinical doses does not move the fat resonance, and inversion recovery would not care where that resonance sat even if it did.
choices: Gadolinium shifts the fat resonance, so the inversion mistimes
STIR nulls by T1, and enhancement drives tumour T1 toward fat
Inversion recovery images the tumour rim but not its centre
The inversion pulse breaks down the chelate in the contrast

quiz.prompt: Taking the T1 of fat at 1.5 T as 260 ms, at what inversion time does an inversion-recovery sequence cross zero for fat and so null its signal? Answer in milliseconds, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Longitudinal magnetisation recovers as 1 - 2exp(-TI/T1) after a 180 degree pulse, and it passes through zero when TI = T1 x ln2 = 0.693 x 260 = 180 ms. Two consequences follow. The first is why STIR survives conditions that defeat spectral fat saturation: nulling by T1 needs no assumption about where the fat resonance sits, so a poor shim, a large field of view or a lump of metal does not break it. The second is the price. Anything else whose T1 approaches that of fat is nulled too, which is why STIR after gadolinium is a mistake and why some subacute blood disappears. In practice scanners use a shorter time than the ideal figure, often around 150 to 170 ms at 1.5 T, because the repetition time is finite and the magnetisation never fully recovers between pulses.

quiz.prompt: A two-dimensional fast spin-echo protocol acquires 0.4 mm by 0.5 mm in plane at a slice thickness of 3.0 mm. An isotropic three-dimensional sequence on the same scanner acquires 0.6 mm in all three directions. By what factor is the two-dimensional voxel larger in volume than the three-dimensional one? Answer to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The 2D voxel is 0.4 x 0.5 x 3.0 = 0.6 cubic millimetres and the isotropic voxel is 0.6 cubed = 0.216, so the ratio is 2.8. That single number explains most of the trade. Signal-to-noise scales with voxel volume, so the isotropic acquisition starts with well under half the signal per voxel and has to buy it back with long echo trains and acceleration, which costs edge sharpness. What it buys is the loss of partial volume in the slice direction and the freedom to reformat along any plane the anatomy asks for, which is why isotropic 3D suits obliquely oriented structures and post-operative anatomy. The 2D protocol keeps better tissue contrast per unit time, which is why most joint protocols still hang on 2D sequences and add a 3D acquisition to answer a particular question.

quiz.prompt: Put these parts of a long bone into the order in which their red marrow converts to yellow marrow during normal childhood.
quiz.answer: epiphysis diaphysis distal-metaphysis proximal-metaphysis
quiz.explain: Conversion begins in the epiphysis within months of its ossification centre appearing, then takes the diaphysis, then the distal metaphysis, and reaches the proximal metaphysis last, so that in an adolescent or young adult the residual red marrow is exactly where it looks most alarming: the proximal humeral and proximal femoral metaphyses. Reconversion under demand, from anaemia, smoking, obesity or endurance training, runs the sequence backwards and repopulates the same regions in reverse. Knowing the order is what keeps a normal variant out of the report. Red marrow follows the rules: it stays higher in signal than skeletal muscle and than the intervertebral disc on T1, it is symmetrical and it has no mass effect, and it drops signal on opposed-phase imaging because fat still shares the voxels. Marrow that is darker than muscle on T1 is not red marrow.

quiz.prompt: On a large field-of-view coronal study of both thighs the fat is well suppressed centrally, but bright at both lateral edges of the image, and a fluid-sensitive series is being read there for muscle oedema. Explain what has gone wrong and give two ways to obtain a dependable fat-suppressed image.
quiz.answer: Spectral fat saturation assumes the fat and water resonances sit where the scanner expects them, which requires a uniform main field. At the edges of a large field of view the field is least uniform and the shim is poorest, so the saturation pulse misses fat there, and it may partly saturate water instead, which can also produce artefactual signal loss. The remedies are to shim over a smaller volume and bring the region of interest to isocentre, imaging one thigh at a time if necessary, or to change technique: STIR nulls by T1 and is indifferent to where the resonance sits, and a Dixon acquisition separates fat from water using the phase difference between echoes and tolerates inhomogeneity far better.
quiz.explain: The failure is regional, and that is the clue: an artefact of field uniformity gets worse with distance from isocentre, while a true absence of fat suppression would be uniform across the image. It matters clinically because both errors it produces are dangerous in opposite directions. Unsuppressed fat at the edge of the field hides oedema, so a myositis or an infected collection is missed at the very periphery. Partially suppressed water in the same region mimics oedema where there is none. Dixon has largely become the pragmatic answer for big fields and awkward geometry, since it yields fat-only, water-only, in-phase and opposed-phase images from one acquisition, and its water image is robust where a spectral pulse is not.

quiz.prompt: On an axial fluid-sensitive series of the knee, a row of evenly spaced bright and dark smudges runs across the image from the popliteal artery, and one of them lies over the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. Explain the appearance and say what you would change so that it stops obscuring the meniscus.
quiz.answer: Pulsatile flow in the popliteal artery changes signal from one repetition to the next, and since the phase-encoding direction is sampled one line per repetition, that inconsistency is mismapped along the phase-encode axis as a train of evenly spaced ghosts of the vessel. It is an artefact and not a lesion: the smudges repeat at a regular interval, they trace back to the artery, and they cross tissue planes. The first fix is to swap the phase-encoding direction so the ghosts run away from the structure being assessed; a saturation band placed over the vessel outside the slice, gradient moment nulling, and more signal averages all reduce them further.
quiz.explain: Ghosting is the classic artefact that reads as disease because it lands somewhere plausible. The discriminators are all geometric rather than anatomical: the repeats are regular, they run along one axis of the image, and that axis is the phase-encode direction rather than any plane in the knee. Swapping the phase-encode direction is worth understanding as more than a trick, since it moves the artefact without removing it, so the choice is really about where you are willing for the ghosts to fall. It also costs something in most protocols, because the field of view usually has to grow in the new phase direction to avoid wrap. When the same smudge persists in the same anatomical place after the direction is swapped, it was never a ghost.

nodes.title: Shoulder: Cuff, Labrum and Instability
nodes.goal: Read a shoulder MRI or ultrasound so that you separate normal labral variants from real lesions, grade a cuff tear in the terms the surgeon plans by, and say whether an unstable shoulder needs bony treatment.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old swimmer has an MR arthrogram for anterior pain. There is no labral tissue at all between roughly the one and three o'clock positions, and the middle glenohumeral ligament is thickened into a cord that runs across the front of the glenoid neck. The rest of the labrum is smooth, there is no paralabral cyst, and she has never dislocated. What should your report conclude?
quiz.answer: A Buford complex, a normal anterosuperior variant that should not be repaired
choices: A Buford complex, a normal anterosuperior variant that should not be repaired
An anterosuperior labral tear that needs arthroscopic repair to restore stability
An anterior labroligamentous periosteal sleeve avulsion of the anterior labrum
A sublabral recess extending posteriorly behind the long head of biceps anchor
quiz.explain: An absent anterosuperior labrum combined with a cord-like middle glenohumeral ligament is the Buford complex, found in roughly one to two per cent of shoulders. On axial images the cord is easily read as a detached labral fragment floating in contrast. Saying so matters in both directions: suturing a Buford cord down to the glenoid tethers the joint and leaves a stiff, painful shoulder, while omitting it invites the arthroscopist to make the same error. A genuine anterosuperior tear has irregular margins, often a paralabral cyst, and a history to match. An ALPSA lies anteroinferiorly, where the shoulder actually dislocates. A sublabral recess belongs at the biceps anchor superiorly, not at two o'clock.

quiz.prompt: A registrar asks you how you decide, on a superior labral image, whether the fluid line at the biceps anchor is a normal recess or a tear. Give the features you use.
quiz.answer: A sublabral recess is a smooth, thin cleft under 2 mm wide that follows the glenoid contour medially and stops at the biceps anchor, whereas a SLAP tear is irregular, wider, and extends laterally into the labral substance or posterior to the anchor, often with a paralabral cyst.
quiz.explain: The superior labrum is the single most over-called structure in the shoulder. A sublabral recess is a developmental cleft between the labrum and the glenoid rim: it hugs the glenoid contour, points medially, is thin and smooth-walled, and dies out at the biceps anchor. A type II SLAP tear runs the other way, extending laterally into the substance of the labrum or tracking posteriorly behind the anchor, with irregular walls and often a paralabral cyst tracking into the spinoglenoid notch. Width helps but is not decisive on its own. Age helps too: a smooth superior cleft in a 60-year-old is usually degenerative fraying, and reporting it as a repairable SLAP in that group has driven a good deal of unnecessary surgery.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old decorator has a painful arc. On the MR arthrogram, contrast tracks from the joint into the deep surface of the supraspinatus at the footprint and extends 4 mm into a tendon that measures 11 mm thick. The bursal surface fibres are continuous and no contrast reaches the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa. What do you report?
quiz.answer: An articular-sided partial tear involving less than half of the tendon thickness
choices: An articular-sided partial tear involving less than half of the tendon thickness
A full-thickness tear with contrast tracking into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa
A bursal-sided partial tear of the kind that responds poorly to conservative care
Tendinosis alone, with intrasubstance signal that stops short of either surface
quiz.explain: Contrast entering the deep surface but stopping before the bursa is a partial articular-sided tear, the PASTA pattern, and articular-sided tears outnumber bursal-sided ones roughly three to one because the deep fibres are thinner and more highly stressed. Depth is what the surgeon acts on: Ellman grade 1 is under 3 mm, grade 2 is 3 to 6 mm and grade 3 is over 6 mm, which for a 10 to 12 mm tendon corresponds to more than half thickness and is where takedown and repair start to be considered. Here 4 mm of an 11 mm tendon is a grade 2 lesion, under half depth. Fluid in the bursa would have made it full thickness. Bursal-sided tears sit on the superficial surface and often accompany impingement. Tendinosis raises signal without a fluid-filled cleft reaching a surface.

quiz.prompt: The same tendon is re-measured on the arthrogram: the supraspinatus is 10.0 mm thick at the footprint and the articular-sided defect extends 6.5 mm from the deep surface. Report the depth of the tear as a percentage of tendon thickness. Answer as a percentage, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: 6.5 of 10.0 mm is 65 per cent. The arithmetic is trivial; the point is that surgeons think in proportions, not millimetres, because the decision threshold sits near half thickness. Below about 50 per cent, most partial tears are managed with debridement and rehabilitation; above it, takedown and repair or a transtendon repair come into play, since the remaining fibres carry a load they were not built for and the tear tends to propagate. State both the absolute depth and the tendon thickness in your report, because a 5 mm defect means something quite different in a 12 mm tendon than in an 8 mm one. Measure on the coronal oblique image perpendicular to the tendon, at the point of maximum depth, and note whether the defect reaches the bursa.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old has a full-thickness supraspinatus tear whose free edge lies at the level of the glenoid. On the sagittal oblique image at the scapular Y, the supraspinatus belly contains more fat than muscle and lies below a line drawn from the coracoid to the scapular spine. What does this add to the report?
quiz.answer: Patte 3 retraction with Goutallier 4 atrophy, which predicts poor healing after repair
choices: Patte 3 retraction with Goutallier 4 atrophy, which predicts poor healing after repair
Patte 1 retraction with Goutallier 1 change, a combination that repairs very reliably
Denervation change from suprascapular nerve entrapment rather than tear-related atrophy
Reversible disuse change that recovers once the subacromial space has been decompressed
quiz.explain: Two separate scales are being applied. Patte grades retraction in the coronal plane: stage 1 near the footprint, stage 2 at the level of the humeral head, stage 3 back at the glenoid. Goutallier grades fatty infiltration of the muscle belly on the sagittal oblique Y view: 0 none, 1 fatty streaks, 2 more muscle than fat, 3 equal fat and muscle, 4 more fat than muscle. The muscle failing to cross the coracoid-to-spine line is the tangent sign, an independent marker of atrophy. Goutallier 3 or 4 does not reverse after repair and carries a high retear rate, so this combination usually steers the surgeon away from repair towards debridement, tendon transfer or reverse arthroplasty. Nerve entrapment produces oedema or atrophy in a nerve territory, typically infraspinatus with or without supraspinatus, without a retracted tendon.

quiz.prompt: The referring surgeon asks why you always state the Goutallier grade rather than just describing the tear itself. Explain what the grade changes.
quiz.answer: Goutallier grade 3 or 4 fatty infiltration is irreversible: the muscle does not recover after repair, the retear rate is high, and so a high grade pushes the surgeon away from cuff repair towards debridement, tendon transfer or reverse arthroplasty.
quiz.explain: Tear size tells the surgeon what has to be reached; muscle quality tells them whether it is worth reaching. Fatty infiltration is the muscle's response to chronic retraction and denervation, and once fat has replaced muscle it does not convert back, whatever is done to the tendon. That is why Goutallier grade, measured on the sagittal oblique image at the level of the scapular spine, sits alongside Patte retraction in every good cuff report. Grades 0 to 2 are compatible with a durable repair; 3 and 4 predict failure of the construct and, in a low-demand patient, may push the plan to a reverse arthroplasty that does not depend on the cuff at all. The tangent sign is a quick sanity check on the same image.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these stages of degenerative rotator cuff disease in the order in which they typically develop.
quiz.answer: tendinosis articular-sided-partial-tear full-thickness-tear tendon-retraction fatty-atrophy
quiz.explain: Degenerative cuff disease follows a fairly orderly course, and knowing it tells you what to look for next once you have found one step. Intrasubstance signal without a surface-reaching cleft is tendinosis. The deep fibres fail first, giving an articular-sided partial tear, because they are thinner and bear more strain than the bursal fibres. Propagation through the remaining thickness produces a full-thickness defect and fluid then reaches the subacromial bursa. Once the tendon is discontinuous the muscle unloads and the free edge retracts medially, which Patte grades. Chronic retraction and the associated denervation then convert muscle to fat, which Goutallier grades and which does not reverse. Traumatic tears in young patients can skip the early steps, but in the degenerative shoulder this is the sequence, and the last two steps are the ones that decide reparability.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old rugby player has axial MR images after a first anterior dislocation. There is a shallow concavity on the posterolateral humeral head, but on the slices passing through the coracoid process the head is perfectly round; the concavity appears only well below the coracoid. There is no marrow oedema. What is the correct interpretation?
quiz.answer: The normal bare area of the humeral head, rather than a Hill-Sachs impaction
choices: The normal bare area of the humeral head, rather than a Hill-Sachs impaction
An acute Hill-Sachs impaction that will engage the glenoid rim in abduction
A reverse Hill-Sachs impaction, indicating a posterior rather than anterior dislocation
An osteochondral defect of the humeral head following previous septic arthritis
quiz.explain: The posterolateral humeral head has a normal flattening and a bare area below the level of the coracoid, where the articular cartilage thins and small vascular channels sit. A Hill-Sachs impaction happens when the head strikes the anteroinferior glenoid rim, which is why a real one is found on axial slices at or above the level of the coracoid tip. Depth below that level, with no marrow oedema and no cortical irregularity, is anatomy. The distinction matters because calling a Hill-Sachs in a first-time dislocator invites a discussion about bony augmentation. A reverse Hill-Sachs sits anteromedially and accompanies posterior dislocation, often after a seizure or electric shock. Post-infective defects are irregular, cross the articular surface and come with cartilage loss and effusion.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old has recurrent anterior dislocations. On the en face sagittal CT reconstruction the glenoid diameter measures 26.0 mm and the anterior glenoid bone defect measures 4.0 mm. The glenoid track is 0.83 times the glenoid diameter, minus the width of the anterior defect. Calculate the glenoid track width in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 0.83 times 26.0 is 21.58 mm, and subtracting the 4.0 mm anterior defect leaves 17.6 mm. The track is the zone of the humeral head that stays in contact with the glenoid through abduction and external rotation. You then measure the Hill-Sachs interval, which is the width of the Hill-Sachs defect plus the width of the intact bone bridge between it and the rotator cuff footprint. If that interval is wider than the track, the lesion is off-track and will engage the glenoid rim, so a soft-tissue Bankart repair alone is likely to fail and a bone procedure such as a Latarjet or a remplissage is considered. If it is narrower, the lesion is on-track. This concept has largely replaced the older habit of quoting a single percentage of glenoid bone loss, and it is worth reporting both numbers so the surgeon can do the comparison.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old has recurrent instability after non-operative treatment of a first dislocation. The MR arthrogram shows the anteroinferior labrum displaced medially along the scapular neck and rolled up beneath an intact, stripped periosteum, with no free fragment and no glenoid rim fracture. What is the significance of this appearance?
quiz.answer: An ALPSA lesion, which heals in a medialised position and leaves the capsule lax
choices: An ALPSA lesion, which heals in a medialised position and leaves the capsule lax
A classic Bankart lesion, with the periosteum torn and the labral fragment free
A Perthes lesion, with the labrum in anatomical position and the periosteum intact
A GLAD lesion, with a labral tear and adjacent glenoid cartilage loss but stability
quiz.explain: The anteroinferior labroligamentous complex fails in several patterns and the periosteum decides which. In a classic Bankart the periosteum tears and the labrum sits free at the rim. In a Perthes lesion the periosteum stays intact and the labrum remains anatomically placed, so it can be almost invisible without abduction and external rotation positioning. An ALPSA is the intermediate: the periosteum is stripped rather than torn, and the labroligamentous sleeve slides medially down the scapular neck and scars there. It matters because a medialised, healed labrum still fails mechanically, the capsule remains lax, recurrence rates are higher, and the surgeon has to mobilise the scarred tissue off the neck before reattaching it. A GLAD lesion adds a cartilage defect but is usually a stable, painful shoulder rather than a dislocating one.

quiz.prompt: A 54-year-old with type 2 diabetes has a shoulder stiff in every direction. MRI shows capsule and inferior glenohumeral ligament thickened to 5 mm at the axillary recess, soft tissue thickening in the rotator interval with obliteration of the subcoracoid fat, and an intact cuff with no effusion. What should you report and recommend?
quiz.answer: Adhesive capsulitis; report it so hydrodilatation or injection can be arranged
choices: Adhesive capsulitis; report it so hydrodilatation or injection can be arranged
An occult full-thickness cuff tear; arrange arthrography before any surgery
Calcific tendinitis; arrange ultrasound-guided barbotage of the supraspinatus deposit
Glenohumeral osteoarthritis; report the joint space loss and inferior osteophyte
quiz.explain: Adhesive capsulitis is diagnosed clinically, but MRI has reasonably specific signs and they are worth knowing because the request usually asks about the cuff. Thickening of the capsule and inferior glenohumeral ligament at the axillary recess beyond about 4 mm, oedematous soft tissue in the rotator interval replacing the normal subcoracoid fat triangle, and avid enhancement of those tissues after contrast are the constellation. It is commoner in diabetes and in thyroid disease. Naming it changes the pathway: the patient goes to physiotherapy with an intra-articular steroid injection or hydrodilatation rather than to arthroscopy for a cuff that is intact. A cuff tear gives a fluid-filled defect, not global capsular thickening. A calcific deposit is low signal on all sequences and visible on the radiograph. Osteoarthritis narrows the joint and builds an inferior humeral osteophyte.

quiz.prompt: A clinician reports that a patient has a hooked acromion on their radiograph and asks you to confirm subacromial impingement on that basis. Explain how you would answer.
quiz.answer: Impingement is a clinical diagnosis, and acromion shape alone does not make it: I would look for supporting findings such as a subacromial spur, bursal-sided cuff tendinosis or tearing, and fluid in the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa, and report the shape only as one part of that picture.
quiz.explain: The Bigliani description of acromial shape, flat, curved or hooked, is easy to quote and poorly reproducible: the apparent shape shifts with the obliquity of the sagittal slice or the radiographic projection, and interobserver agreement is modest. Hooked acromia are common in asymptomatic shoulders. What earns a place in the report is mechanical evidence: a spur projecting from the anterior acromial undersurface or the acromioclavicular joint, narrowing of the subacromial space, reactive change or tearing on the bursal surface of supraspinatus, and fluid in the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa. Even then the diagnosis is made by the examining clinician, since a painful arc relieved by local anaesthetic is the actual test. Describing shape without the mechanical findings can send a patient to acromioplasty for pain that came from somewhere else.

quiz.prompt: The MRI waiting list is three months. A 60-year-old presents with weakness after lifting and the team wants an answer this week. What is the honest account of what shoulder ultrasound will give them?
quiz.answer: It detects full-thickness tears accurately and allows dynamic side-to-side comparison
choices: It detects full-thickness tears accurately and allows dynamic side-to-side comparison
It shows labral tears and marrow oedema about as reliably as MR arthrography does
It grades fatty atrophy of the cuff bellies more accurately than sagittal oblique MRI
It reliably excludes the occult proximal humeral fracture that radiographs have missed
quiz.explain: In experienced hands ultrasound matches MRI for full-thickness cuff tears, with sensitivity and specificity in the ninety per cent range, and it does several things MRI cannot: it moves the shoulder while looking, so subluxation of the long head of biceps or dynamic bursal bunching is visible; it compares directly with the asymptomatic side; it is cheap and repeatable; and the same probe guides the injection afterwards. Its limits are equally clear. The labrum is largely hidden by bone, marrow oedema is invisible, and an undisplaced fracture will be missed. Fatty atrophy can be judged crudely by echogenicity but is graded far better on the sagittal oblique MRI. The classic pitfall is anisotropy: a normal tendon looks hypoechoic and torn when the beam is not perpendicular to it, so rock the probe before calling a defect.

nodes.title: The Radiographic Pattern of Arthritis
nodes.goal: Read a hand, a knee or a pelvis and separate the arthritides by distribution, erosion, joint space, bone density and new bone.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old woman has six weeks of hand stiffness worst in the morning. Radiographs show fusiform soft-tissue swelling around the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints on both sides, reduced bone density around those joints, and small erosions at the radial margins of the metacarpal heads. The distal interphalangeal joints are normal and there is no new bone. What does the film support, and what should follow?
choices: Early rheumatoid arthritis; request MRI or ultrasound of the hands
Psoriatic arthritis; look for nail pitting and hidden skin plaques
Erosive osteoarthritis; treat symptomatically and repeat the film
Gouty arthropathy; aspirate the joint for crystal analysis
quiz.answer: Early rheumatoid arthritis; request MRI or ultrasound of the hands
quiz.explain: Four features move together here. The distribution is bilateral, symmetric and proximal — metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists — with the distal interphalangeal joints spared, which is close to the opposite of psoriatic disease. The density is reduced periarticularly, because hyperaemic synovitis resorbs the adjacent trabecular bone. The erosions sit at the margin, at the bare area between the edge of the articular cartilage and the capsular insertion, where synovium lies against unprotected bone. And there is no new bone at all, which is what separates rheumatoid arthritis from every spondyloarthritis. The action matters as much as the label: a visible radiographic erosion is already a late finding, so ultrasound or MRI, which show synovitis and bone marrow oedema before the cortex is breached, is what changes treatment inside the window in which treatment works best.

quiz.prompt: A 39-year-old man has one swollen, sausage-shaped fourth finger. The radiograph shows erosion at the fourth distal interphalangeal joint with irregular, ill-defined new bone along the adjacent phalangeal shaft and resorption of the terminal tuft. Bone density is normal, the other fingers are unaffected and the wrist is normal. What does the combination indicate?
choices: Psoriatic arthritis, with erosion and proliferation in one ray
Rheumatoid arthritis presenting atypically in a single finger
Erosive osteoarthritis, which favours the distal finger joints
Chronic tophaceous gout eroding the terminal phalanx
quiz.answer: Psoriatic arthritis, with erosion and proliferation in one ray
quiz.explain: Psoriatic arthritis destroys and builds at the same time, and the coexistence of erosion with fluffy periosteal new bone beside it is close to diagnostic; rheumatoid arthritis erodes without ever laying down new bone. The distribution is the second half of the argument: disease running along one digit through all its joints, asymmetrically, is a ray pattern, whereas rheumatoid disease picks out the same row of joints on both hands. Preserved bone density, distal rather than proximal predominance, tuft resorption and the swollen whole digit all belong to the same picture, and the advanced form gives the pencil-in-cup deformity and arthritis mutilans. Erosive osteoarthritis does favour the distal joints but erodes centrally and appears in an older patient alongside osteophytes; gout would preserve the joint space and produce a corticated erosion with an overhanging edge next to a soft-tissue tophus, not periostitis.

quiz.prompt: An untreated seropositive rheumatoid wrist and hand are radiographed at intervals over fifteen years. Put these radiographic changes in the order in which they first appear.
quiz.answer: soft-tissue-swelling periarticular-osteopenia marginal-erosion joint-space-narrowing carpal-ankylosis
quiz.explain: Synovitis comes first and shows as fusiform periarticular soft-tissue swelling; the hyperaemia that accompanies it resorbs trabecular bone next to the joint, giving periarticular osteopenia. Pannus then reaches the bare area at the joint margin, where no cartilage protects the bone, and erodes it. Only after that does the pannus thin the cartilage across the whole joint, which is why the narrowing of rheumatoid arthritis is uniform rather than confined to a loaded compartment as in osteoarthritis. Deformity, subluxation and finally bony ankylosis — commonest in the carpus — end the sequence. The order is the argument for imaging early with a modality that sees synovium: by the time the radiograph shows the third step, the damage that treatment was meant to prevent has happened.

quiz.prompt: A woman with twenty years of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is listed for a general anaesthetic, and the anaesthetist asks for flexion and extension lateral cervical radiographs before intubation. On the flexion view the distance is measured between the posterior cortex of the anterior arch of the atlas and the anterior cortex of the odontoid peg. Above how many millimetres is this distance abnormal in an adult? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Three millimetres is the upper limit of the anterior atlanto-dental interval in an adult; up to five is accepted in a child, whose ligaments are laxer and whose odontoid is incompletely ossified. Beyond the adult limit the transverse ligament has been destroyed by pannus and the atlas slides forward on the axis in flexion, which is precisely what happens when an anaesthetist positions a head for laryngoscopy. The interval that predicts neurological injury, though, is the one behind the peg — the space left for the cord between the odontoid and the posterior arch — because as the anterior gap opens, that posterior space closes. Radiographs answer the question of movement; MRI is what shows pannus, cord compression and cord signal change, and vertical migration of the peg through the foramen magnum is the more dangerous and easily missed second pattern.

quiz.prompt: A hand radiograph in a 58-year-old woman shows erosions at several distal interphalangeal joints. Set out the features that separate erosive osteoarthritis from psoriatic arthritis on the radiograph alone.
quiz.answer: Erosive osteoarthritis erodes centrally. The subchondral plate collapses in the middle of the joint while osteophytes hold up the margins, producing the gull-wing outline on the frontal view, and sometimes a saw-tooth appearance where the opposing surface is remodelled. It sits in a hand that shows osteoarthritis elsewhere — first carpometacarpal and proximal interphalangeal involvement, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts — with normal bone density and no periosteal reaction. Psoriatic arthritis erodes at the margins, where the bare area lies, and then lays down new bone: ill-defined fluffy periosteal reaction along the shaft next to the erosion, ossification at entheses, and in advanced disease pencil-in-cup deformity and acro-osteolysis of the tuft. Its distribution is asymmetric and follows a whole ray rather than a row of equivalent joints, the soft tissues may show a uniformly swollen digit rather than a joint-centred swelling, and bone density is preserved. Neither shows the periarticular osteopenia of rheumatoid arthritis, and neither spares new bone the way rheumatoid arthritis does.
quiz.explain: The two questions that settle almost every eroding hand are where in the joint the erosion sits and whether the bone is reacting. Central erosion with marginal osteophytes is a degenerative process eating through a thinned subchondral plate; marginal erosion with adjacent proliferation is an enthesis-driven inflammatory one. Distribution is the cross-check: osteoarthritis, erosive or not, picks out the same joints on both hands in a recognisable pattern, whereas psoriatic disease is asymmetric and runs down a ray. Where the film is genuinely equivocal, the clinical examination — nail pitting and onycholysis, a scalp or natal cleft plaque, dactylitis, enthesitis at the heel — usually decides it faster than more imaging will.

quiz.prompt: A 72-year-old has wrist pain and swelling. The radiograph shows a thin band of calcification in the triangular fibrocartilage and in the intercarpal cartilage, narrowing of the radiocarpal joint with subchondral cysts, and widening of the scapholunate interval with proximal migration of the capitate. The metacarpophalangeal joints are normal and bone density is preserved. What does the pattern indicate?
choices: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition with scapholunate collapse
Rheumatoid arthritis with carpal collapse and ligament failure
Primary osteoarthritis of the wrist following an old injury
Haemochromatosis arthropathy of the second and third heads
quiz.answer: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition with scapholunate collapse
quiz.explain: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposit in fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, and the triangular fibrocartilage is one of the four places worth looking for them, with the knee menisci, the symphysis pubis and the acetabular labrum. Their arthropathy is degenerative in character — narrowing, sclerosis and prominent subchondral cysts — but it appears in joints that primary osteoarthritis has little reason to visit, and the radiocarpal joint is the classic one: crystal-driven failure of the scapholunate ligament lets the interval widen and the capitate migrate proximally between scaphoid and lunate. Rheumatoid disease also destroys the carpus, but with periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions and erosion of the ulnar styloid rather than chondrocalcinosis. Haemochromatosis is the important companion diagnosis and produces chondrocalcinosis too, but its signature is hook-like osteophytes on the radial aspect of the second and third metacarpal heads, and those joints are stated to be normal here.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old man has had inflammatory back pain for two years. The anteroposterior pelvis shows erosion and sclerosis on the iliac side of the right sacroiliac joint with irregular widening of the joint space, and a normal left joint. Under the modified New York criteria, a unilateral abnormality must reach at least which sacroiliitis grade to satisfy the radiographic criterion? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The grading runs from 0 for a normal joint, through 1 for suspicious change, 2 for minimal sclerosis or small erosions without any alteration of joint width, 3 for unequivocal abnormality with erosion, sclerosis, widening, narrowing or partial ankylosis, to 4 for total ankylosis. The radiographic criterion is met by grade 2 or more on both sides, or grade 3 or 4 on one side alone, which is why a convincing unilateral change has to reach grade 3 while a milder bilateral change need only reach grade 2. The reason the whole exercise has been overtaken clinically is worth knowing: radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear, and MRI showing bone marrow oedema in the subchondral bone of the sacroiliac joints identifies active inflammation long before, which is what allows a diagnosis of non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis to be made at all. Grading a plain film also has poor interobserver agreement, and oblique or dedicated views add little over a good frontal view.

quiz.prompt: The lumbar spine of a man with ankylosing spondylitis is followed on lateral radiographs from his twenties into his fifties. Put these vertebral appearances in the order in which they develop.
quiz.answer: shiny-corner vertebral-squaring syndesmophyte bridging-ankylosis
quiz.explain: Inflammation begins at the enthesis where the outer annulus inserts into the vertebral corner. Erosion there provokes reactive sclerosis, and the dense corner against a normal body is the shiny corner of the Romanus lesion. Continued erosion of the anterior corners flattens the normal anterior concavity of the body, which is squaring. Ossification then advances vertically through the outer fibres of the annulus as a thin, marginal syndesmophyte, and successive syndesmophytes meet to bridge the disc, ending in the fused bamboo spine. The whole sequence is the argument for the distinction that matters on a spine film: the syndesmophyte of ankylosing spondylitis is thin, vertical and marginal because it follows the annulus, while the bulky, asymmetric, non-marginal paravertebral ossification of psoriatic and reactive arthritis does not, and the flowing anterior ossification of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis spares the sacroiliac joints and the disc heights altogether. A fused spine also fractures like a long bone, which is why new pain in this patient means CT rather than reassurance.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old has medial knee pain. Weight-bearing radiographs show loss of the medial tibiofemoral joint space with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes on the medial tibial plateau, a normal lateral compartment, and no erosion or periarticular osteopenia. A supine film taken a year earlier had been reported as normal. What accounts for the difference between the two studies?
choices: Load is needed to bring the worn compartment surfaces together
The earlier film was taken before any of the cartilage was lost
The osteophytes had not yet formed when the first film was taken
Sclerosis obscured the joint space on the earlier projection
quiz.answer: Load is needed to bring the worn compartment surfaces together
quiz.explain: Cartilage is radiolucent, so joint space is inferred from the gap between two cortical surfaces, and that gap closes to its true minimum in a worn compartment only when the joint is loaded. A supine knee film can therefore show a preserved space in a knee with advanced cartilage loss, which is why the standing anteroposterior view is the standard, and why a flexed posteroanterior weight-bearing view is added when the posterior femoral condyles are the suspected site, since that is where cartilage wears first. The rest of the description is a compact statement of osteoarthritis and its difference from an inflammatory arthritis: one compartment rather than the whole joint, new bone in the form of osteophytes and sclerosis, normal bone density, and no erosions.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old man has pain at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The radiograph shows a well-corticated erosion on the medial aspect of the metatarsal head with a thin spur of bone overhanging an adjacent soft-tissue mass, a preserved joint space and normal bone density. Argue from the film why this is gout rather than rheumatoid arthritis, and say what would confirm it.
quiz.answer: Three features argue against rheumatoid arthritis. The erosion is punched out with a sclerotic rim and an overhanging edge of bone, because a tophus enlarges slowly enough for the adjacent bone to react and to be lifted rather than simply destroyed, whereas the rheumatoid marginal erosion has neither a sclerotic margin nor an overhanging edge. The joint space is preserved, because urate deposits in and beside the joint and erodes bone long before it destroys cartilage, while rheumatoid pannus thins cartilage across the whole joint and narrows it early and uniformly. Bone density is normal, whereas periarticular osteopenia is an early rheumatoid sign. The soft-tissue mass is the tophus itself, occasionally containing dense internal calcification, particularly in renal impairment. Confirmation: ultrasound shows the double contour sign of urate deposited on the surface of the hyaline cartilage and hyperechoic aggregates within a tophus, dual-energy CT colour-codes urate deposits volumetrically, and aspiration showing negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarised light remains the definitive test.
quiz.explain: Gout is the arthritis that breaks the usual coupling between erosion and joint destruction, and that dissociation — substantial erosion with a joint space that still looks reasonable and bone that is still dense — is what should bring it to mind on any hand or foot film. The distribution helps: the first metatarsophalangeal joint, the midfoot, the olecranon bursa, the knee and the hands in longstanding disease, characteristically asymmetric. Two cautions on confirmation: the double contour sign and dual-energy CT are much less sensitive in the first attack than in established disease, so a negative study does not exclude gout in an acute joint, and an eroded joint with a soft-tissue mass that turns out to have no urate needs a different explanation, including infection.

quiz.prompt: Two men in their thirties have inflammatory back pain. The first has thin vertical ossifications running from the corner of one vertebral body to the corner of the next, with symmetric erosion and sclerosis of both sacroiliac joints. The second has bulky coarse ossification bridging vertebrae away from the disc margin, skipping levels, with sacroiliitis on one side. What separates them?
choices: The first is ankylosing spondylitis; the second, psoriatic disease
The first is psoriatic disease; the second, ankylosing spondylitis
Both are ankylosing spondylitis at different stages of the disease
Both are diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, not inflammation
quiz.answer: The first is ankylosing spondylitis; the second, psoriatic disease
quiz.explain: Where the ossification runs tells you which structure is ossifying. In ankylosing spondylitis it is the outer fibres of the annulus fibrosus, which run vertically from one vertebral corner to the next, so the syndesmophyte is thin, vertical and marginal, and the disease is symmetric — including its sacroiliitis, which is bilateral and equal. In psoriatic and reactive arthritis the ossification forms in the paravertebral tissues away from the disc margin, so it is bulky, coarse, asymmetric and often skips levels, matching an asymmetric or unilateral sacroiliitis. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is the third pattern and the one most often confused with the second: flowing ossification along the anterior longitudinal ligament across four or more contiguous vertebrae, with the disc heights preserved and the sacroiliac joints and facet joints uninvolved, which is why the sacroiliitis described here excludes it.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had a hot, swollen, painful knee for ten days. The radiograph shows loss of the entire joint space compared with a film taken three weeks earlier, ill-defined erosion of both articular surfaces, a large effusion, and no osteophytes. What must be excluded before anything else?
choices: Septic arthritis; aspirate the joint before treatment is started
Rheumatoid arthritis; start disease-modifying therapy promptly
Rapidly progressive osteoarthritis of the femorotibial joint
Neuropathic arthropathy from long-standing diabetic neuropathy
quiz.answer: Septic arthritis; aspirate the joint before treatment is started
quiz.explain: The tempo is the diagnosis. Bacterial enzymes and the host response destroy cartilage over days, so the whole joint space disappears at once and both articular surfaces erode, with no time for the new bone that any chronic arthropathy would have produced. Nothing else on the list moves that fast: rheumatoid arthritis does not destroy a knee in three weeks and is rarely monoarticular at onset, rapidly progressive osteoarthritis is a real but slower entity and a diagnosis of exclusion, and a neuropathic joint shows the triad of increased density, debris and dislocation with abundant fragmentation, in a patient whose pain is characteristically less than the film suggests. Aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystals comes before antibiotics wherever possible, since an aspirate taken afterwards may not grow the organism — and crystals and infection can coexist, so finding crystals does not close the question.

nodes.title: Wrist and Hand: Carpal Instability and Fractures
nodes.goal: Judge carpal alignment from the arcs and the carpal angles, chase the fracture the radiograph hides, and give the measurements and findings that decide each operation.
articles: Ulnar collateral ligament injury of the thumb

quiz.prompt: After a fall on the outstretched hand, a PA wrist radiograph shows a 4 mm gap between the scaphoid and lunate, a foreshortened scaphoid and a dense ring at its distal pole.
