The lateral shows the lunate tilted dorsally, with a scapholunate angle of 75 degrees. What does this combination tell you?
quiz.answer: The scapholunate ligament has failed and the carpus has collapsed into a dorsal intercalated pattern
choices: The scapholunate ligament has failed and the carpus has collapsed into a dorsal intercalated pattern
The lunotriquetral ligament has failed and the carpus has collapsed into a volar intercalated pattern
The lunate has dislocated volarly from its fossa while the capitate remains aligned with the radius
The distal radioulnar joint has dislocated, with the ulnar head displaced dorsal to the sigmoid notch
quiz.explain: Two findings on two views agree. On the PA, a scapholunate interval of 4 mm is well beyond the normal 2 mm or less, and the ring sign with a foreshortened scaphoid is the flexed bone seen end-on: freed from the lunate, the scaphoid rotates into flexion. On the lateral, the lunate is left tethered to the triquetrum and extends, giving a scapholunate angle above the normal 30 to 60 degrees, and that is the dorsal intercalated segment instability pattern. Lunotriquetral failure gives the mirror image: the lunate flexes with the scaphoid and the angle falls below 30 degrees, which is the volar pattern. A lunate dislocation would show a triangular lunate and broken arcs on the PA and a volarly tipped lunate on the lateral, not a widened interval with normal arcs. Distal radioulnar dislocation is judged on a true lateral by the position of the ulnar head, and does not alter carpal angles. Untreated, this hip of the wrist collapses into a predictable arthritis.

quiz.prompt: A distal radius fracture is reviewed on a lateral radiograph after a failed manipulation: the distal radial articular surface now tilts 12 degrees dorsally. Taking the normal palmar tilt as 11 degrees, through how many degrees would the articular fragment have to be rotated to restore that normal tilt? Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Palmar tilt is signed, so a surface tilted 12 degrees dorsally is at minus 12, and reaching plus 11 means rotating through 23 degrees. Learn the three normal values together and report all three: palmar tilt about 11 degrees, radial inclination about 22 degrees, and radial height about 11 mm. They matter because losing palmar tilt past neutral tips load onto the dorsal rim and the distal radioulnar joint, weakens grip, and provokes an adaptive midcarpal collapse that mimics dorsal intercalated instability. The commonly quoted limits that push a fracture towards fixation are dorsal tilt beyond 10 degrees, radial shortening beyond 3 mm and an intra-articular step-off beyond 2 mm, applied more strictly in a young, high-demand patient than in a frail one. Give the surgeon the numbers rather than an adjective, and say whether the distal radioulnar joint looks congruent on the lateral.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old carpenter has wrist pain a year after a fall. Standard PA radiographs show a 2.5 mm scapholunate interval with intact carpal arcs, and the clinical scaphoid shift test is positive. Which single additional radiograph is most likely to settle the question?
quiz.answer: A PA with the fist clenched, which drives the capitate up between scaphoid and lunate
choices: A PA with the fist clenched, which drives the capitate up between scaphoid and lunate
A lateral in full radial deviation, which flexes the scaphoid and opens the interval
A carpal tunnel view, which throws the hook of the hamate and the pisiform clear
A PA in ulnar deviation, which elongates the scaphoid and profiles its waist
quiz.explain: An interval of 2.5 mm sits in the equivocal band between the normal 2 mm and the clearly abnormal 3 mm, and a wrist with a competent secondary restraint can look normal at rest and come apart under load. The clenched-fist PA supplies that load: the capitate is driven proximally into the scapholunate space and an incompetent ligament lets the gap open, which is what dynamic instability means. Compare it with the same view of the other wrist, since intervals vary between people. Ulnar deviation elongates the scaphoid and is the view for a suspected waist fracture, not for the interval. Radial deviation flexes the scaphoid but does not stress the interval, and a lateral does not display it at all. A carpal tunnel view is for the hook of the hamate. If the stress views stay normal and suspicion persists, MR arthrography or arthroscopy is the next rung, arthroscopy still being the reference standard for a partial tear.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the stages of progressive perilunate instability in the order the ligaments fail as force travels around the lunate.
quiz.answer: scapholunate capitolunate lunotriquetral lunate-dislocation
quiz.explain: Mayfield showed that the injury propagates around the lunate from radial to ulnar in four stages, and the radiographic appearances follow the same order. Stage 1 is scapholunate failure, giving the widened interval and the flexed, ring-sign scaphoid, or its bony equivalent, a scaphoid waist fracture. Stage 2 carries the force through the space of Poirier into the capitolunate joint. Stage 3 tears the lunotriquetral ligament, and the whole carpus can now displace dorsally around a lunate that stays in its fossa, which is a perilunate dislocation. Stage 4 fails the dorsal radiotriquetral restraint and the lunate is squeezed volarly out of the fossa into the carpal tunnel, the spilled teacup on the lateral and the triangular piece of pie on the PA with all three of Gilula's arcs broken. Roughly a quarter of these are missed on the initial films, and the lateral is the view that saves you.

quiz.prompt: A motorcyclist has a swollen, painful wrist. The PA shows a triangular lunate with the three carpal arcs broken; the lateral shows the capitate in line with the radius and the lunate tipped volarly out of its fossa. Numbness is developing in the thumb and index finger. What is the priority?
quiz.answer: Urgent reduction, because the displaced lunate is compressing the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
choices: Urgent reduction, because the displaced lunate is compressing the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Urgent CT angiography, because the radial artery is at risk where it crosses the volar wrist crease
Outpatient MRI in two weeks, to grade the interosseous ligament injuries before any intervention
Splint and fracture clinic review, because these injuries settle as the soft tissue swelling resolves
quiz.explain: This is a lunate dislocation, the end stage of perilunate instability, and the lunate has rotated into the carpal tunnel where it presses directly on the median nerve. Developing numbness in the median distribution makes it a surgical emergency: reduction first, then ligament repair, with carpal tunnel decompression if symptoms persist. The lateral view is what separates it from a perilunate dislocation, where the lunate stays in the radial fossa and the capitate and the rest of the carpus displace dorsally; on the PA both look similar, with broken arcs and an abnormally shaped lunate, which is why these injuries are missed when only the PA is reviewed. Look also for the transscaphoid variant, in which the force passes through the scaphoid rather than around it, since a fracture will need fixing at the same operation. Delay costs nerve recovery and cartilage, so nothing here waits two weeks.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old has a fracture through the proximal third of the scaphoid. Explain, from the blood supply, why this site behaves so differently from a fracture of the distal tubercle, and say what your report should therefore state.
quiz.answer: Most of the scaphoid is supplied by branches of the radial artery entering the dorsal ridge distally, and flow to the proximal pole is retrograde through the bone, so a proximal fracture cuts that supply off and the proximal fragment risks avascular necrosis and non-union; the report should state the level of the fracture and the risk explicitly, because a proximal pole fracture goes to early fixation rather than a cast.
quiz.explain: The scaphoid is almost entirely covered in cartilage, so its vessels enter at two small non-articular areas, and the dominant supply comes from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery entering the dorsal ridge near the waist. Blood then runs backwards, distal to proximal, through the bone. That is why the further proximal the fracture, the worse the vascular consequence: distal tubercle fractures heal reliably, waist fractures develop necrosis in roughly a third when displaced or treated late, and proximal pole fractures are the ones that go on to necrosis and non-union most often. The practical output is the level, the displacement and any gap or angulation, since all three drive the decision between a cast and a percutaneous screw. On MRI, preserved fatty marrow signal on T1 in the proximal fragment is the reassuring finding; uniformly low T1 that fails to enhance is not.

quiz.prompt: A student falls on his hand and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox with pain on axial loading of the thumb. Four-view scaphoid radiographs show no fracture. He is a competitive rower and wants an answer this week. What do you advise?
quiz.answer: Immobilise and arrange MRI within days, which will show or exclude the fracture straight away
choices: Immobilise and arrange MRI within days, which will show or exclude the fracture straight away
Immobilise and repeat the radiographs at two weeks, which is as accurate as early MRI
Discharge with analgesia, since four dedicated normal views exclude a scaphoid fracture
Arrange an isotope bone scan today, which is highly specific for a scaphoid fracture
quiz.explain: Initial radiographs miss a substantial minority of scaphoid fractures, and the cost of missing one is a non-union in a young hand. MRI is the most accurate early test, showing the low signal fracture line on T1 within hours, and it has the added merit of explaining the wrist when the scaphoid is intact, since distal radius, triquetral and hamate hook fractures and ligament injuries all appear in the same study. CT resolves cortical detail and displacement better and is a reasonable alternative, but it is less reliable for an undisplaced trabecular fracture. Repeating the radiographs at two weeks was the traditional pathway and is both slower and less accurate, and it leaves an athlete in a cast on a maybe. Isotope imaging is sensitive after 24 to 72 hours but is not specific, since any bone or soft tissue injury nearby takes up tracer.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old builder has a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture. CT shows an intra-articular step-off of 1.5 mm, radial shortening of 4 mm compared with the other side, and the articular surface tilted 5 degrees dorsally. Using the commonly quoted limits of step-off under 2 mm, shortening under 3 mm and dorsal tilt under 10 degrees, how many of the three limits does this fracture breach? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Only the shortening breaches: 4 mm against a limit of 3 mm, while the 1.5 mm step-off and the 5 degrees of dorsal tilt are both inside their limits. Reporting it that way is the point of the exercise, because one clear breach in a manual worker in his thirties is an argument for fixation, whereas a vague phrase such as mild displacement is not. Radial shortening is the measurement that tracks most reliably with ulnar-sided pain, loss of forearm rotation and grip weakness, and it is read either as radial height or as a change in ulnar variance against the uninjured side. Two further things belong in the same report: the state of the distal radioulnar joint, including a fracture at the base of the ulnar styloid or an incongruent sigmoid notch, and the number and position of the articular fragments, since a die-punch fragment of the lunate fossa changes the fixation.

quiz.prompt: A 25-year-old has ulnar wrist pain and a clunking distal radioulnar joint after a fall. MR arthrography shows contrast tracking to the ulnar side of the triangular fibrocartilage at its attachment to the fovea, with the central disc intact and neutral ulnar variance. What does this mean for treatment?
quiz.answer: A peripheral tear at a vascular attachment, which is repairable and accounts for the instability
choices: A peripheral tear at a vascular attachment, which is repairable and accounts for the instability
A central perforation in an avascular zone, which is debrided back rather than being repaired
A degenerative lesion of ulnar impaction, which is treated by shortening the ulna instead
A radial avulsion from the sigmoid notch, which needs no more than a period of splinting
quiz.explain: The Palmer classification splits traumatic class 1 lesions from degenerative class 2 lesions, and within class 1 the site is what decides the operation: 1A is a central perforation, 1B an ulnar or foveal avulsion often with a fracture at the base of the ulnar styloid, 1C a tear of the volar ulnocarpal ligaments and 1D a radial-sided avulsion. The periphery of the complex carries a blood supply and heals if it is repaired, whereas the central disc is avascular and is debrided to a stable rim. Foveal detachment is the lesion that destabilises the distal radioulnar joint, which is exactly what the clunk describes, so it goes to repair. Neutral ulnar variance and an intact central disc argue against a degenerative class 2 lesion, and ulnar shortening would be an operation for a problem this patient does not have.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old has chronic ulnar-sided wrist pain. Radiographs taken with the shoulder abducted and the elbow flexed to 90 degrees show the ulna projecting 3 mm distal to the radial articular surface. Say what you would look for on MRI to confirm the mechanism, and what your findings imply for treatment.
quiz.answer: Look for subchondral oedema, sclerosis and cysts in the proximal ulnar corner of the lunate and the adjacent triquetrum, with thinning or a central perforation of the triangular fibrocartilage and chondral loss on the ulnar head; that combination with positive ulnar variance confirms ulnar impaction and points towards an ulnar shortening osteotomy rather than a ligament repair.
quiz.explain: Ulnar impaction is a load problem, not a torn structure: a long ulna hammers the ulnar corner of the lunate through the triangular fibrocartilage, and the imaging signature is marrow oedema, then sclerosis and cysts, in precisely that corner. The disc thins and eventually perforates centrally, which is a Palmer class 2 degenerative lesion, and the lunotriquetral ligament may fail as a late consequence. Ulnar variance is dynamic and rises with grip and pronation, so it must be measured on a standardised PA with the shoulder abducted 90 degrees, the elbow flexed 90 degrees and the forearm in neutral rotation, otherwise you will over- or under-call it. The differentials for ulnar-sided pain that this study also addresses are extensor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy or subluxation, a lunotriquetral tear and a foveal triangular fibrocartilage avulsion, each with a different operation.

quiz.prompt: A skier has a swollen thumb that is unstable to radial stress at the metacarpophalangeal joint. Ultrasound shows a rounded mass of ligament tissue lying proximal and superficial to the adductor aponeurosis, with the distal insertion empty. What follows from that appearance?
quiz.answer: Surgical repair, because the retracted ligament can no longer reach its insertion to heal
choices: Surgical repair, because the retracted ligament can no longer reach its insertion to heal
A thumb spica cast for six weeks, because most of these tears heal well in a cast
Stress radiographs of the joint, to quantify the laxity before any decision is made
Aspiration of the mass with injection of corticosteroid into the joint afterwards
quiz.explain: The ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb tears at its distal insertion on the proximal phalanx, and if the torn end flips proximal to the adductor aponeurosis, the aponeurosis interposes between ligament and bone. That is the Stener lesion, and it is the reason imaging is worth doing: a non-displaced tear heals in a cast, and a displaced one will not heal at all, so the two injuries look identical clinically but are managed differently. Ultrasound shows the rounded retracted stump above the aponeurosis, sometimes described as a ball on a string, and MRI shows it equally well. The other argument for imaging first is that vigorous stress testing can itself pull a non-displaced tear proximal and convert it into a Stener lesion. Look also for an avulsed fragment from the ulnar base of the proximal phalanx, which is displaced along with the ligament.

quiz.prompt: A boxer has an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal, with a small volar-ulnar fragment left in position and the shaft displaced proximally, dorsally and radially. What should the report say about why it displaced, and what does that mean for treatment?
quiz.answer: The volar fragment is held by ligament while abductor pollicis longus drags the shaft away
choices: The volar fragment is held by ligament while abductor pollicis longus drags the shaft away
The fragment is avulsed by flexor pollicis longus and the shaft remains stable in a cast
The articular surface is comminuted into several pieces, so this needs a primary fusion
The displacement is purely rotational, so a closed reduction will hold it without fixation
quiz.explain: This is a Bennett fracture-dislocation. The small volar-ulnar fragment stays put because the anterior oblique, or volar beak, ligament anchors it to the trapezium, while abductor pollicis longus pulls the metacarpal shaft proximally, dorsally and radially, with adductor pollicis adding an adduction force. It is therefore an unstable injury by definition, and a cast will not hold it: reduction with percutaneous wires or screw fixation is the usual treatment, because residual incongruity of the trapeziometacarpal joint leads to early and symptomatic arthritis in a joint that has to take load through the thumb. Its comminuted cousin, in which the base is broken into a T or Y with several articular fragments, carries a worse outlook and needs a different fixation. An extra-articular fracture of the metacarpal base looks similar on a poor film but tolerates far more angulation, so a true lateral or a dedicated thumb view is worth the extra exposure.

quiz.prompt: Nine months after an untreated scaphoid waist fracture, CT shows a persistent lucent line with cystic change, sclerosis of the proximal fragment and a flexed humpback deformity. The surgeon asks for MRI before planning the operation. What question is MRI being asked, and what will you look at to answer it?
quiz.answer: The question is whether the proximal pole is still viable, because that decides between a conventional bone graft and a vascularised graft; look at the T1 marrow signal of the proximal fragment, since preserved fatty marrow argues for viability, and confirm the absence of enhancement after contrast before calling the fragment dead.
quiz.explain: T1 is the sequence that carries the answer, because fatty marrow is what dies. Diffusely low T1 signal throughout the proximal fragment that fails to enhance after gadolinium is the strongest non-invasive evidence of necrosis; patchy low T1 with preserved enhancement usually means oedema and reactive change rather than a dead bone. Fluid-sensitive sequences are less useful, since oedema is everywhere in a non-union. The CT contributes the structural measurements the surgeon needs: the humpback angulation, the height-to-length ratio, the extent of resorption to be filled with graft, and any dorsal intercalated collapse of the lunate. Be honest about the limits, because both MRI and CT misclassify a proportion of cases and punctate bleeding at operation remains the reference standard. Left alone, the non-union progresses to a predictable arthritis that starts at the radial styloid, spreads across the radioscaphoid joint and finally reaches the capitolunate joint.

nodes.title: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip and the Child's Elbow
nodes.goal: Work up the unstable, painful or injured child's hip and elbow from ultrasound and plain film, and act correctly on what you find.

quiz.prompt: A six-week-old girl, born breech, has hip ultrasound. On a technically adequate Graf coronal image the iliac line is straight, the bony rim is angular, the alpha angle measures 64 degrees and the beta angle 48 degrees, and the femoral head is more than half covered by bony roof. Both hips look the same. What do you do with this study?
quiz.answer: Report a normal, mature hip and take her off the imaging pathway
choices: Report a normal, mature hip and take her off the imaging pathway
Report immaturity and bring her back for a repeat scan at three months
Report dysplasia and ask the surgeons to consider a Pavlik harness now
Report the scan as equivocal and arrange an AP pelvis radiograph today
quiz.explain: In the Graf method the baseline runs along the iliac wing, the bony roof line along the acetabular roof, and the angle between them is alpha. Alpha of 60 degrees or more is a mature hip — Graf type I — and a beta angle under 55 degrees puts it in subtype Ia. More than half the femoral head sitting under bony roof agrees. Breech presentation is a proper screening indication, and six weeks is the right moment: scanning in the first few weeks catches physiological laxity and generates false positives that lead to unnecessary harnesses. Repeat scanning belongs to the immature type IIa hip (alpha 50–59 degrees under three months), not to this one. Nothing here needs a harness, and a radiograph at six weeks is largely uninterpretable because the femoral head has not yet ossified.

quiz.prompt: On the standard Graf coronal image of an infant hip the alpha angle is subtended by the iliac baseline and the bony acetabular roof line. State the lowest alpha angle that still counts as a mature Graf type I hip. Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Sixty degrees is the line Graf drew between a mature hip and everything else, and it is worth holding on to because every other threshold in the system hangs off it. Alpha of 50–59 degrees is a deficient bony roof: type IIa if the infant is under three months (physiological immaturity, rescan), type IIb if over three months (true dysplasia, treat). Alpha of 43–49 degrees is a critical hip, subdivided by beta — type IIc if beta is under 77 degrees, type D if beta exceeds it, meaning the head is beginning to decentre. Below 43 degrees the hip is dislocated: type III with the labrum everted, type IV with it pressed down between head and roof. The alpha angle is only trustworthy on a correctly obtained coronal image with a straight iliac line, so judge the image before you trust the number.

quiz.prompt: A five-month-old is referred with asymmetric thigh creases and limited abduction on the left. She has never been imaged. Which examination do you put her down for?
quiz.answer: An AP pelvis radiograph, read with Hilgenreiner, Perkin and Shenton lines
choices: An AP pelvis radiograph, read with Hilgenreiner, Perkin and Shenton lines
A Graf coronal hip ultrasound with dynamic stress manoeuvres in flexion
An MRI of both hips without contrast, done under a feed-and-sleep protocol
A CT of the pelvis with three-dimensional surface reconstruction of the roof
quiz.explain: Ultrasound depends on the femoral head being cartilaginous and therefore sonolucent. From around four to six months the ossific nucleus appears and casts an acoustic shadow across the medial structures, so coverage and the alpha angle become unreliable exactly as the radiograph becomes readable. Past that age the plain film takes over. Hilgenreiner's line runs horizontally through the triradiate cartilages, Perkin's line vertically through the lateral acetabular margin, and the ossific nucleus should sit in the lower inner quadrant they make. Shenton's line, the arc from the inferior femoral neck to the superior border of the obturator foramen, breaks when the head rides up. The acetabular index, between Hilgenreiner's line and the acetabular roof, falls with age; above about 30 degrees in the first year is regarded as dysplastic. MRI and CT have roles after reduction, not at first presentation.

quiz.prompt: A fourteen-month-old walks with a waddle. On the AP pelvis the right capital femoral ossification centre sits lateral to Perkin's line and above Hilgenreiner's line, the arc from femoral neck to obturator foramen is discontinuous, and the acetabular index measures 38 degrees. Say what has happened to the hip and what the index adds.
quiz.answer: The right hip is dislocated superolaterally: the epiphysis has left the lower inner quadrant and Shenton's arc is broken, while an acetabular index of 38 degrees shows the roof is abnormally steep, so the acetabulum is truly dysplastic and not merely lax.
quiz.explain: Two separate statements are being made here and they carry different weight. Position — epiphysis lateral and superior, Shenton's arc broken — tells you where the head is now, and it is out. The acetabular index tells you what the socket has become in response, and a steep roof at 38 degrees at fourteen months is well outside the normal range, which is falling towards 25 degrees by the first birthday. That matters for management: a hip that is simply lax may reduce and remodel, whereas a steep, shallow, false-acetabulum-forming socket in a walking child usually needs open reduction with a pelvic osteotomy rather than a harness, which in any case is ineffective beyond about six months. Say both things in the report, because the surgeon plans from the acetabulum, not only from the head.

quiz.prompt: A six-year-old boy has limped for four months with mild groin and knee ache and no fever. The AP pelvis shows a slightly small and slightly dense left capital femoral epiphysis with a little medial joint space widening. The right hip looks normal. What is the most useful next step at the workstation?
quiz.answer: Add a frog-lateral view to look for a subchondral crescent line
choices: Add a frog-lateral view to look for a subchondral crescent line
Add inlet and outlet pelvic views to profile the acetabular roof
Go straight to CT of both hips to measure epiphyseal height loss
Report the study as normal and repeat the radiograph in six months
quiz.explain: This is the early face of Perthes disease — idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis, typically a boy of four to eight, insidious limp, pain often referred to the knee. The earliest reliable radiographic signs are a small dense nucleus, apparent medial joint space widening, and the subchondral fracture line, the crescent sign, which lies anterosuperiorly and is therefore hidden on the AP and shown on the frog-lateral. Finding it establishes the diagnosis and predicts the extent of the segment that will fragment. If both views stay normal and suspicion persists, contrast-enhanced or perfusion MRI shows the avascular segment weeks before the radiograph does. Inlet and outlet views belong to pelvic trauma. Waiting six months wastes the containment window, which is when treatment changes the outcome.

quiz.prompt: A twelve-year-old boy with a high BMI has had three weeks of aching in the left thigh and knee. On the AP pelvis a line drawn along the superior margin of the left femoral neck passes entirely above the epiphysis, and the left physis is wide and woolly. He walked into the department. What matters most now?
quiz.answer: Keep him from weight-bearing, refer the same day, and image the other hip
choices: Keep him from weight-bearing, refer the same day, and image the other hip
Send him home in a sling with a routine orthopaedic letter for next month
Arrange MRI first to confirm the slip before contacting the surgical team
Repeat the radiograph in six weeks to see whether the slip has progressed
quiz.explain: The line of Klein along the superior femoral neck should clip a sliver of the lateral epiphysis on the AP; when it misses entirely, the epiphysis has slipped posteromedially, and that failure carries Trethowan's name. A widened, irregular physis with loss of epiphyseal height supports it. Two things then drive management. First, a stable slip becomes unstable if he keeps walking, and an unstable slip carries a high rate of avascular necrosis, so he stops weight-bearing at once and goes to the orthopaedic team today. Second, the contralateral hip slips in a substantial minority — figures of roughly 20 to 40 per cent are quoted — so it is imaged and watched. A frog-lateral or cross-table lateral is more sensitive for a subtle slip, but positioning a frankly unstable hip in frog is avoided. MRI is unnecessary when the radiograph is this clear.

quiz.prompt: A three-year-old refuses to weight-bear on the right leg, is mildly febrile, and has an irritable hip. Hip ultrasound shows a 6 mm anterior capsular distension on the right and 1 mm on the left. Explain what the ultrasound has and has not settled, and what settles it.
quiz.answer: Ultrasound has confirmed a joint effusion but cannot separate transient synovitis from sepsis, because both distend the capsule; ultrasound-guided aspiration with Gram stain, cell count and culture of the fluid settles it, read alongside fever, refusal to weight-bear and inflammatory markers.
quiz.explain: The commonest error here is treating a positive scan as a diagnosis. Capsular distension of more than about 2 mm, or 2 mm more than the other side, is a real effusion, and it is present in transient synovitis, in septic arthritis, in early Perthes and in juvenile idiopathic arthritis alike. Echogenicity of the fluid does not reliably separate pus from serous fluid. What the scan genuinely does is exclude an effusion when there is none, and guide the needle when there is one. The clinical predictors — non-weight-bearing, temperature above 38.5 degrees, ESR above 40 mm/h, white cell count above 12 x 10^9/L — stratify probability but do not replace aspiration. If sepsis is plausible, the child goes to aspiration and washout, and MRI is added when osteomyelitis of the adjacent metaphysis or a subperiosteal collection is suspected.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the six elbow ossification centres in their usual order of radiographic appearance during childhood.
quiz.answer: capitellum radial-head internal-epicondyle trochlea olecranon external-epicondyle
quiz.explain: The sequence is worth knowing cold because it is a safety check, not a piece of trivia. Capitellum, radial head, internal (medial) epicondyle, trochlea, olecranon, external (lateral) epicondyle, appearing at roughly one, three, five, seven, nine and eleven years, with wide individual variation and earlier appearance in girls. Ages are approximate; the order is not. Two practical consequences follow. First, an unfused centre in the expected sequence is never a fracture, so knowing the order stops you overcalling normality. Second, and more importantly, the medial epicondyle always ossifies before the trochlea, so a fragment at the trochlea with no medial epicondyle in place means the medial epicondyle has been avulsed — usually into the joint after a dislocation. Compare with the other elbow when you are unsure; the two sides ossify near-symmetrically.

quiz.prompt: A nine-year-old is radiographed after a dislocated elbow has been reduced. You can see the capitellum, the radial head, and an ossification centre lying at the level of the trochlea, but nothing at the medial epicondyle. The joint is otherwise congruent. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: The apparent trochlear centre is the avulsed medial epicondyle, now inside the joint
choices: The apparent trochlear centre is the avulsed medial epicondyle, now inside the joint
The medial epicondylar centre is merely late in this child and may be disregarded
The trochlea has ossified ahead of sequence, a normal variant at this age and sex
The radiograph is technically inadequate and an oblique projection should be added
quiz.explain: Because the medial epicondyle ossifies before the trochlea, a trochlear-looking fragment without a medial epicondyle in its place is the medial epicondyle that has moved. In a child of nine after a dislocation, the fragment has been pulled off by the flexor-pronator mass and dragged into the joint, where it may be trapped after reduction. This is the single most useful application of the ossification sequence, and it changes management immediately: an entrapped fragment blocks motion, needs operative extraction, and sits next to the ulnar nerve, so the nerve is examined and documented. Isolated late ossification of the medial epicondyle with an ossified trochlea does not occur, and early trochlear ossification out of sequence is not a recognised variant. When in doubt, radiograph the uninjured elbow and compare.

quiz.prompt: Using the conventional one, three, five, seven, nine and eleven year scheme for the elbow ossification centres, state how many centres you should expect to see at the elbow of a healthy seven-year-old. Answer as a whole number of centres.
quiz.explain: Four: capitellum at about one year, radial head at about three, internal (medial) epicondyle at about five, trochlea at about seven. The olecranon at nine and the external (lateral) epicondyle at eleven have not yet arrived. The point of counting rather than reciting is that it gives you an expectation before you look, so a fifth fragment in a seven-year-old immediately raises the question of an avulsion or a fracture rather than a variant. Treat the ages as soft — girls ossify earlier, and there is a year or so of scatter either way — but treat the order as hard. The most reliable resolution of any doubt is a comparison view of the uninjured elbow, where the same child's own timetable is on display.

quiz.prompt: A five-year-old fell onto an outstretched hand. On the lateral elbow radiograph there is a clearly visible posterior fat pad and an elevated anterior fat pad. The anterior humeral line passes through the middle third of the capitellum and the radiocapitellar line is intact. No cortical break can be seen. What do you advise?
quiz.answer: Treat this as an occult fracture: immobilise and review with repeat radiographs
choices: Treat this as an occult fracture: immobilise and review with repeat radiographs
Report a normal elbow, since the alignment lines and the cortices are intact
Request urgent elbow MRI to characterise the collateral ligamentous injury
Request elbow CT to exclude an undisplaced condylar split before discharge
quiz.explain: A visible posterior fat pad on a true lateral in a child means a joint effusion, and after trauma that effusion is haemarthrosis until proved otherwise. Most such elbows harbour a fracture that the first films do not show, usually a supracondylar undisplaced injury and sometimes a radial neck or lateral condylar one, so the child is splinted and brought back rather than discharged. Normal alignment lines are reassuring about displacement, not about the presence of a fracture: the anterior humeral line through the middle third of the capitellum excludes a significant extension-type supracondylar displacement, and an intact radiocapitellar line on every projection excludes radial head dislocation. Cross-sectional imaging is rarely needed at this stage; repeat radiographs at ten to fourteen days, showing periosteal reaction, answer the question with no dose and no anaesthetic.

quiz.prompt: A five-year-old has lateral elbow tenderness after a fall. The AP view shows a lucency crossing the lateral condylar metaphysis and running into the physis with about 2 mm of gapping. The lateral view looks almost normal. What do you do?
quiz.answer: Add an internal oblique view, because the AP under-reads displacement here
choices: Add an internal oblique view, because the AP under-reads displacement here
Accept the reassuring lateral view and manage in a simple collar and cuff
Book outpatient MRI in two weeks to assess continuity of the cartilage hinge
Report a supracondylar fracture and splint the elbow in full extension today
quiz.explain: Lateral condylar fractures are usually Salter–Harris type IV, crossing metaphysis, physis and unossified epiphyseal cartilage into the joint, and the extensor origin pulls the fragment laterally and rotates it. The internal oblique projection profiles the fracture best and routinely shows more displacement than the AP, which is why it changes decisions: gapping beyond roughly 2 mm, or any widening on serial films, usually goes to fixation, while a genuinely undisplaced fracture may be casted with close review. Missing or under-treating one is expensive — non-union, cubitus valgus and a tardy ulnar nerve palsy years later. Where the cartilaginous hinge cannot be judged, ultrasound or MRI can be used acutely in some centres, but a delayed outpatient scan is no help. Splinting in full extension is wrong for any injured paediatric elbow.

quiz.prompt: A two-year-old was lifted by one hand and now holds the arm slightly flexed and pronated, refusing to use it. There is no swelling, no bruising and no bony tenderness. The registrar asks whether to radiograph before attempting anything. What is your advice and why?
quiz.answer: Radiographs are normal in a pulled elbow and are not needed with this history, because the annular ligament has slipped over the radial head rather than any bone breaking; reduction by supination and flexion or by hyperpronation is a clinical manoeuvre, and imaging is reserved for a poor history, swelling or failed reduction.
quiz.explain: In the classic presentation — a longitudinal pull on an extended pronated arm in a child of one to four, no swelling, no point tenderness, arm held quietly at the side — the diagnosis is clinical and the films add dose and delay. The annular ligament has subluxed proximally over the radial head; the bones are intact and the radiocapitellar line stays normal, so a radiograph cannot confirm the diagnosis, only exclude alternatives. Imaging earns its place when the history does not fit, when there is swelling, bruising or focal tenderness, when the child is outside the usual age range, or when two attempts at reduction have failed — then you are looking for a radial neck fracture, a supracondylar injury, or in a young infant with an unexplained mechanism, for signs of inflicted injury.

nodes.title: Imaging the Child
nodes.goal: Read the neonatal chest and abdomen, image the infant hip at the right age with the right test, and recognise the injuries that oblige a safeguarding referral.

quiz.prompt: Two infants are tachypnoeic in the first hours of life. The first, born at term by caesarean section without labour, has a film showing fluid in the horizontal fissure, prominent perihilar streaking and normal to slightly increased lung volumes. The second, born at 29 weeks, has uniformly low volumes, a fine granular pattern throughout both lungs and air bronchograms extending to the periphery. Interpret each film and say how the next 48 hours should differ.
quiz.answer: The first is transient tachypnoea of the newborn: fetal lung fluid that would normally be cleared during labour and the first breaths is still in the interstitium and the lymphatics, so it collects in the fissures and around the hila while the alveoli remain aerated, which is why the lung volumes are preserved or even increased. It is managed supportively, with oxygen if needed, and it clears as the fluid is absorbed, typically within 24 to 48 hours, so the follow-up film should look better rather than worse. The second is surfactant deficiency: without surfactant the alveoli collapse at end-expiration, so the volumes are low, the fine granularity is the summation of countless airless acini, and the air bronchograms are conspicuous because aerated bronchi stand out against airless lung. Untreated it worsens over the first day or two rather than clearing, and it is treated with exogenous surfactant and respiratory support, after which the film can clear strikingly and sometimes asymmetrically. Two cautions belong with the pair: group B streptococcal pneumonia can be radiographically indistinguishable from surfactant deficiency, so antibiotics are started while cultures are awaited, and a sudden deterioration on a ventilator should prompt a search for pulmonary interstitial emphysema or a pneumothorax rather than a change in the underlying diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Lung volume is the discriminator that does most of the work on a neonatal chest film, because it follows directly from where the abnormality sits. Fluid in the interstitium leaves the air spaces open and the lungs large; absent surfactant collapses the air spaces and makes the lungs small. Everything else — gestation, mode of delivery, the tempo over the following two days, and the response to surfactant — is confirmatory. The pair also illustrates why the neonatal film is read alongside the gestational age and the clinical course rather than in isolation: the same granular pattern in a term infant should raise pneumonia, and coarse patchy shadowing with hyperinflation in a term or post-term infant with a history of stained liquor points instead to meconium aspiration.

quiz.prompt: A radiograph of a preterm infant shows one umbilical catheter that dips into the pelvis, turns and ascends to the left of the vertebral bodies, with its tip at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra. A second catheter runs directly cephalad from the umbilicus with its tip at the level of the ninth thoracic vertebra. How should the lines be reported?
choices: Both are well sited; the descending course marks the artery
Both need withdrawal; the tips lie within the heart itself
The lines are swapped; the ascending one is the arterial line
The venous line is in the portal vein and must be pulled back
quiz.answer: Both are well sited; the descending course marks the artery
quiz.explain: The course identifies the vessel before the tip is judged. The umbilical artery runs caudally to the internal iliac artery before turning up the aorta, so an initial dip into the pelvis is the signature of an arterial catheter; the umbilical vein runs straight up through the falciform ligament and the left portal vein into the ductus venosus, so a catheter that only ascends is venous. Acceptable arterial tip positions are high, between the sixth and ninth thoracic vertebrae — above the coeliac axis and below the ductus arteriosus — or low, between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae, below the renal arteries; the intervening stretch is avoided because it lies across the origins of the visceral vessels. The venous tip should sit at the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium, around the eighth or ninth thoracic level. The two failures worth knowing are a venous tip that stops short in the liver, which risks portal vein thrombosis and extravasation of hypertonic infusate into the parenchyma, and a tip advanced into the right atrium, which risks arrhythmia, thrombus and pericardial tamponade.

quiz.prompt: A preterm infant on the neonatal unit has serial abdominal radiographs during an episode of necrotising enterocolitis. Put these radiographic findings in order of increasing severity.
quiz.answer: dilated-loops pneumatosis portal-venous-gas pneumoperitoneum
quiz.explain: Dilated, separated loops with a loss of the normal polygonal gas pattern are the earliest and least specific finding, and by themselves they support only a suspicion. Intramural gas — a bubbly or curvilinear lucency within the bowel wall, produced by gas-forming organisms in a damaged mucosa — is the finding that establishes the diagnosis. Branching lucencies over the liver are that gas carried back in the portal venous system, and they mark more extensive disease and a worse prognosis. Free intraperitoneal gas means the bowel has perforated and is the one finding that is an absolute indication for surgery; it appears as gas outlining the falciform ligament on the supine film, as both sides of the bowel wall becoming visible, or as a lucency over the liver on a left lateral decubitus view, which is the projection to request in an infant too unwell to be sat up. A loop that stays in the same position and the same shape across serial films is a further sign of a segment that is no longer viable, and ultrasound adds bowel wall thickness, perfusion and free fluid that the radiograph cannot show.

quiz.prompt: A term neonate aged three days vomits bile. Put the steps of the emergency pathway in the order in which they are carried out.
quiz.answer: nasogastric-decompression abdominal-radiograph upper-GI-contrast laparotomy
quiz.explain: Bile-stained vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proved otherwise, and the whole pathway is built around how quickly the midgut dies once its vascular pedicle twists. Resuscitation and a nasogastric tube come first, both to decompress the stomach and to confirm the character of the aspirate. The plain film is quick and can show a double bubble, a gasless abdomen or dilated loops — but it is very often normal, so it can raise the suspicion and cannot lower it. The upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the reference standard: it shows where the duodenojejunal flexure lies, which should be to the left of the left-sided pedicle at the level of the duodenal bulb, and in volvulus it shows a corkscrew or beaked duodenum. A twisted midgut then goes straight to a Ladd procedure. Ultrasound showing the superior mesenteric vein lying anterior or to the left of the artery, or a whirlpool of vessels wrapping the pedicle, is increasingly used and can make the diagnosis quickly, but in most units a normal ultrasound does not by itself exclude malrotation.

quiz.prompt: A 5-week-old boy has non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds and a palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium. Ultrasound of the pylorus is performed in the right lateral decubitus position with a high-frequency linear probe. At or above what single-wall muscle thickness, in millimetres, is the pylorus regarded as hypertrophied? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Three millimetres of single muscle wall thickness, measured on the short-axis image away from the near-field, together with a pyloric channel length of about fifteen to seventeen millimetres or more, defines the hypertrophied pylorus. The measurements matter less than the dynamic observation that accompanies them: the study is watched for several minutes, and in true hypertrophic pyloric stenosis vigorous gastric peristalsis fails to drive fluid through the channel, whereas pylorospasm relaxes and lets fluid pass. A borderline pylorus in a young infant is rescanned rather than operated on. The surgical point is that this is not a surgical emergency but a medical one: the persistent vomiting of gastric contents produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and that must be corrected before an anaesthetic, because alkalosis predisposes to postoperative apnoea. Ultrasound has replaced the contrast meal, and no ionising radiation is involved at all.

quiz.prompt: A neonate with trisomy 21 vomits in the first hours of life. The supine abdominal radiograph shows two gas-filled structures in the upper abdomen, one under the left hemidiaphragm and one to its right, with no gas anywhere beyond them. What does the absence of distal gas indicate?
choices: Complete duodenal obstruction, most likely an atresia
Midgut volvulus twisting a patent duodenum shut
A duodenal web with a central perforation in it
Annular pancreas causing a partial obstruction
quiz.answer: Complete duodenal obstruction, most likely an atresia
quiz.explain: The two bubbles are the distended stomach and the dilated duodenal cap proximal to the obstruction, and what discriminates among the causes is whether any gas has passed beyond them. Complete absence of distal gas means a complete obstruction, and in a neonate with trisomy 21 that is duodenal atresia, which needs no contrast study before surgery. Gas beyond the second bubble means the obstruction is incomplete — a fenestrated web, an annular pancreas, or malrotation with Ladd bands — and those do need a contrast study, both to define the anatomy and because malrotation carries the risk of volvulus. The trap to hold on to is the converse: a neonate vomiting bile whose film is normal or near-normal still needs an urgent upper gastrointestinal study, because a midgut volvulus can produce very little to see on a plain film and is the one diagnosis here that cannot wait.

quiz.prompt: A previously well 9-month-old has episodes of screaming with drawing up of the legs, and a sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound shows a 3 cm structure with concentric rings in the transverse plane. The abdomen is soft, there is no peritonism and the child is well perfused. What should follow?
choices: Fluoroscopically guided air enema reduction, with surgery on standby
Immediate laparotomy, since ultrasound has already made the diagnosis
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to search for a lead point
Observation with intravenous fluids, since most reduce spontaneously
quiz.answer: Fluoroscopically guided air enema reduction, with surgery on standby
quiz.explain: Ileocolic intussusception at this age is usually idiopathic, following lymphoid hypertrophy after a viral illness, and ultrasound is both sensitive and specific enough to be the diagnostic test — the target on the transverse image and the pseudo-kidney on the longitudinal one. Reduction by air, or by fluid under ultrasound guidance, is the treatment, and it succeeds in the large majority. It is done with a surgeon informed and theatre available, because of the small risk of perforation during the procedure and because a failed reduction goes on to operation. The contraindications are perforation, peritonitis and shock, none of which is present here. CT adds radiation to a child and delays a treatment that is already available; a lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, a duplication cyst, lymphoma or the bowel wall haematoma of Henoch-Schoenlein purpura is looked for in children outside the typical age range or after repeated recurrence. A short small-bowel-only intussusception found incidentally is usually transient and needs no intervention.

quiz.prompt: A girl born in the breech position at term has a normal hip examination at birth, and is referred for imaging because of the breech presentation alone. Coronal hip ultrasound is performed by the Graf method. At or above what alpha angle, in degrees, is the bony acetabular roof regarded as normal? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The alpha angle lies between the vertical line of the iliac wing and the slope of the bony acetabular roof, and sixty degrees or more is a mature hip. Between fifty and fifty-nine the roof is deficient, which may be physiological immaturity in the first weeks or genuine dysplasia depending on the infant's age; below fifty the hip is dysplastic and the femoral head is subluxed or dislocated. Two points about timing follow. Ultrasound is the technique before the femoral head ossifies at around four to six months, because the cartilaginous head and roof are invisible on a radiograph; after that an anteroposterior pelvis takes over, read with Hilgenreiner's and Perkin's lines, with the ossific nucleus expected in the lower inner quadrant, together with Shenton's line and the acetabular index. And a risk-factor scan of this kind is deferred to about six weeks of age, because physiological laxity in the first weeks produces findings that resolve on their own and would lead to over-treatment. An infant with an abnormal clinical examination is a different matter and is imaged and referred sooner.

quiz.prompt: A girl born at term in the breech position has a normal hip examination at birth. At two weeks of age the department receives a request for an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph to screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip. What should the department do?
choices: Perform hip ultrasound instead, and book it at about six weeks
Perform the radiograph, which shows the cartilage well enough
Perform hip ultrasound at once, before the laxity settles down
Perform MRI of the hips under sedation to assess the labrum
quiz.answer: Perform hip ultrasound instead, and book it at about six weeks
quiz.explain: Both halves of the answer matter. The modality is wrong because the femoral head is entirely cartilaginous until around four to six months, so a neonatal radiograph shows an empty acetabulum and unreliable landmarks, while ultrasound images the cartilaginous head and the acetabular roof directly and adds a dynamic assessment of stability under stress. The timing is wrong because physiological ligamentous laxity in the first weeks of life produces immature-looking hips that resolve spontaneously, so scanning too early converts normal newborns into patients; a scan at around six weeks is the compromise that finds the hips that need treating without treating the ones that do not. This applies to screening on the basis of a risk factor — breech presentation, a first-degree family history, oligohydramnios — in an infant whose examination is normal. An infant with a positive Ortolani or Barlow test is imaged and referred to orthopaedics sooner, and a frankly dislocated irreducible hip is discussed immediately.

quiz.prompt: A term neonate has not passed meconium by 48 hours and the abdomen is distended. The radiograph shows many dilated bowel loops throughout the abdomen. A water-soluble contrast enema shows a small-calibre colon with a change in calibre at the rectosigmoid junction, and the rectum narrower than the sigmoid above it. What does the enema indicate?
choices: Hirschsprung disease; the aganglionic rectum stays narrow
Meconium ileus; inspissated pellets fill an unused colon
Ileal atresia; the colon is unused and small along its length
Functional immaturity of the colon in an infant of a diabetic
quiz.answer: Hirschsprung disease; the aganglionic rectum stays narrow
quiz.explain: In a normal neonate the rectum is the widest part of the large bowel, so a rectum narrower than the sigmoid — a rectosigmoid index below one — is abnormal in itself, and a transition in calibre above it marks the boundary between the aganglionic distal segment, which cannot relax, and the dilated ganglionic bowel proximal to it. Suction rectal biopsy is what confirms the diagnosis; the enema shows where to expect the transition and how much bowel is involved. Two technical points determine whether the study works: it is done without a preceding rectal examination or washout, either of which can decompress the transition zone and hide it, and delayed films are taken, since retention of contrast beyond 24 hours supports the diagnosis. The alternatives differ in the calibre of the colon along its whole length: meconium ileus gives a microcolon with filling defects in the terminal ileum and points to cystic fibrosis, ileal atresia gives an unused microcolon with no pellets, and small left colon syndrome shows an abrupt calibre change at the splenic flexure in an infant of a diabetic mother and resolves without surgery.

quiz.prompt: A five-month-old who is not yet crawling is brought in with a swollen thigh, and the radiograph shows a transverse mid-shaft femoral fracture. The parents describe a roll from a sofa onto a carpeted floor. Set out the imaging that should follow and the findings that would raise the concern further.
quiz.answer: The starting point is that the injury is not explained by the history: a femoral shaft fracture requires substantial force, and in an infant who cannot yet crawl, cruise or weight-bear, a short fall of this kind is an inadequate mechanism. The mismatch between the injury, the mechanism offered and the child's motor development is itself the concerning feature. A full skeletal survey to a national standard is indicated in any child under two years with suspected physical abuse: a defined set of collimated, coned, high-detail views of the whole skeleton rather than a single film of the entire baby, reported by a radiologist experienced in the work, and a limited follow-up survey at about eleven to fourteen days shows healing periosteal reaction at sites that were invisible acutely. Neuroimaging is added in an infant, because occult abusive head trauma is common at this age and clinical signs are unreliable. The findings carrying the highest specificity are classic metaphyseal lesions at the ends of the long bones, posterior and posteromedial rib fractures, and scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures; fractures of clearly different ages, multiple fractures, and any fracture whose mechanism does not match the history or the developmental stage add further weight. The imaging is one contribution to a multi-agency safeguarding assessment made with the clinical team, and is not a verdict on its own.
quiz.explain: The single most useful question in this area is whether the injury fits what the child is physically capable of doing. Fractures in non-ambulant infants are uncommon and are the group in which inflicted injury is most frequent, which is why the developmental history is recorded before the film is reported. The survey is a protocol rather than an ad hoc set of films because its purpose is to find fractures that are clinically silent, and the follow-up survey exists because callus makes visible what the acute study could not — particularly rib and metaphyseal injuries. The last sentence is the one that is easiest to get wrong in either direction: imaging can describe the injuries and their probable ages and mechanisms, and it can say whether the account offered fits, but the determination is made by the safeguarding process rather than by the radiologist alone.

quiz.prompt: A skeletal survey in an 8-month-old, carried out after a reported fall from a bed, shows a healing fracture of the posterior sixth left rib near the costovertebral junction, a linear parietal skull fracture and a mid-clavicular fracture. The parents point out that the child was resuscitated by a paramedic at the scene. How should the rib fracture be weighed?
choices: Highly specific for abuse; chest compressions seldom fracture there
Adequately explained by the chest compressions given at the scene
A common birth injury at this age, and of no further concern
Of no more weight than the skull fracture in the same survey
quiz.answer: Highly specific for abuse; chest compressions seldom fracture there
quiz.explain: Posterior and posteromedial rib fractures arise when an infant is gripped around the chest and squeezed front to back, levering the rib over the transverse process, and they are among the findings with the highest specificity for inflicted injury. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation does fracture ribs in a small minority of infants, and the fractures it produces are predominantly anterior or anterolateral, although posterior fractures after resuscitation have been reported with the two-thumb technique; a documented resuscitation is therefore weighed as a possible contributor rather than accepted as a complete explanation, and it does not on its own dispose of the finding. The other two fractures illustrate the difference between specificity and presence. A linear parietal skull fracture is common and non-specific, follows an ordinary household impact as readily as an inflicted one, and cannot be dated, because the skull heals without callus. A clavicular fracture is the commonest birth injury but would have remodelled long before eight months, and in any case is non-specific. Classic metaphyseal lesions carry specificity comparable to posterior rib fractures and are the other finding to hunt for on the survey.

nodes.title: Non-accidental Injury: The Imaging Duty
nodes.goal: Conduct, interpret and report imaging for suspected physical abuse to a standard that will hold up in a courtroom.

quiz.prompt: A five-month-old is admitted with an unexplained spiral femoral fracture and no history of injury. The night radiographer offers a single anteroposterior film covering the whole infant to save handling. What do you insist on instead?
quiz.answer: A full survey of coned, dedicated views of every region, with oblique rib views
choices: A full survey of coned, dedicated views of every region, with oblique rib views
A limited survey of the long bones and chest, adding skull views if bruised
A whole-body low-dose CT, which resolves ribs and skull in one acquisition
A whole-body MRI, which shows marrow oedema at every fracture that is present
quiz.explain: The single whole-body film — the babygram — fails because it images most of the skeleton off-axis, at the wrong exposure, with the divergent beam obliquing the metaphyses and ribs it most needs to show. The standard survey is a set of individually collimated projections: two views of the skull, lateral cervical and thoracolumbar spine, frontal chest with left and right oblique rib views, abdomen and pelvis, and separate frontal views of humeri, forearms, hands, femora, tibiae and feet. Coning and correct positioning are what make a classic metaphyseal lesion visible at all. CT delivers a dose that cannot be justified as a screening survey, though targeted CT of head and, with reformats, of skull and ribs has a role. Whole-body MRI complements the survey by finding marrow and soft-tissue injury, but it misses metaphyseal and rib fractures and does not replace it.

quiz.prompt: Below a certain age a full skeletal survey is performed in every child in whom physical abuse is suspected, without needing a specific bony complaint. State that age in months, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Twenty-four months. Under two years the survey is mandatory in suspected physical abuse because occult fractures are common, the child cannot report pain or localise it, and the yield is high enough that a negative survey is itself informative. Between two and five years the survey is used selectively, guided by findings and by the clinical account, and above five it is rarely productive because a child of that age reports the injured part and occult fractures are unusual. Age also shapes the interpretation, not just the decision to image: any fracture in a child who is not yet independently mobile demands an explanation, and a femoral or humeral shaft fracture in a non-ambulant infant is a serious concern in a way that the same fracture in a running four-year-old is not.

quiz.prompt: The first skeletal survey on a seven-month-old with an unexplained subdural collection shows no fractures at all. The safeguarding team asks whether imaging of the skeleton is now finished. What do you tell them?
quiz.answer: Repeat a limited survey about two weeks later; healing changes disclose new injuries
choices: Repeat a limited survey about two weeks later; healing changes disclose new injuries
The survey is complete, and a repeat adds radiation dose without new information
Substitute a bone scintigram, which will detect every fracture the survey missed
Repeat the entire survey with skull views on the morning of hospital discharge
quiz.explain: A normal first survey does not exclude skeletal injury, because the two most specific fractures are the two hardest to see acutely. Undisplaced posterior rib fractures and classic metaphyseal lesions frequently become visible only as subperiosteal new bone and callus appear, and the accepted interval for that is eleven to fourteen days. The repeat is limited: chest with obliques, long bones, and any region of concern. Skull films are generally omitted, since fractures of the skull heal without callus and a repeat film adds nothing. Scintigraphy is sensitive for rib and shaft injury but is poor at the skull and at symmetrical metaphyseal disease, and it cannot characterise what it detects. Repeating on the day of discharge, if that is day four, wastes the examination — timing is the whole point.

quiz.prompt: A four-month-old's survey shows, at the distal femur, a thin lucency parallel to and just beneath the growth plate, with a small triangular density at each margin; on the follow-up film the same lesion has a curved rim of bone around it. Describe what has fractured and what evidential weight it carries.
quiz.answer: This is a classic metaphyseal lesion, a planar fracture through the primary spongiosa of the metaphysis, projecting as a corner fragment or a bucket-handle depending on beam angulation, and in an infant it sits at the top of the specificity ranking for inflicted injury.
quiz.explain: The lesion is a disc-shaped fracture running across the metaphysis just below the zone of provisional calcification, undercutting a thin rim of bone that stays attached to the periphery. Tangential to the beam it looks like a corner fragment; en face, with a little obliquity, the same rim projects as a bucket handle. It is produced by shearing and torsion of the limb, the forces of gripping and wrenching a small limb, not by axial loading, which is why it is rare in accidental falls. It heals with little periosteal reaction, so it can be invisible acutely and obvious a fortnight later. Its differential is real and must be addressed: rickets frays, cups and splays the metaphysis and widens the physis; the classic metaphyseal lesion does neither, and the surrounding bone is normally mineralised.

quiz.prompt: A four-month-old resuscitated after an apnoeic episode has healing fractures of the left fifth to eighth ribs posteriorly, close to the costovertebral junctions. The parents ask, through the paediatric team, whether the chest compressions caused them. How do you frame the answer in your report?
quiz.answer: Posterior rib fractures arise from anteroposterior compression of the chest by encircling hands
choices: Posterior rib fractures arise from anteroposterior compression of the chest by encircling hands
Infant resuscitation frequently fractures posterior ribs and readily explains this pattern
Fractures at this site in an infant point to an underlying metabolic disorder of bone
Fractures here follow direct blows to the back and suggest a fall onto a hard edge
quiz.explain: The mechanism is levering. When an infant's chest is gripped front and back and squeezed, the posterior rib is forced over the fulcrum of the transverse process and snaps close to the costovertebral junction. That geometry is not reproduced by accidental trauma, and posterior rib fractures accordingly sit in the highest-specificity group alongside classic metaphyseal lesions and scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation in infants rarely fractures ribs at all, and when it does the fractures tend to be anterior or anterolateral, from two-thumb compression, rather than posterior. Say the mechanism plainly and in general terms; describe the fracture, state its specificity and state that resuscitation does not account for it, and leave the question of who did what to the investigation.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these features of a healing long bone fracture in the order in which they become visible on radiographs.
quiz.answer: soft-tissue-swelling subperiosteal-new-bone soft-callus hard-callus remodelling
quiz.explain: Soft-tissue swelling is there from the day of injury and fades within a week or so. Subperiosteal new bone, a fine line of mineralisation lifted off the shaft by the periosteal haematoma, appears from roughly four to fourteen days and is the first true sign of healing. Soft callus follows, becoming visible around the second week, then hard, well-mineralised bridging callus in the third to sixth weeks, and finally remodelling, which reshapes the cortex over months to years. Use these as overlapping bands rather than as dates. The bands are wide, they run faster in infants than in older children, and they differ between a rib, a metaphysis and a diaphysis. That imprecision is exactly why a report should describe the stage of healing and not name a day.

quiz.prompt: A solicitor asks you, from your report, to state the date on which each of an infant's four fractures was inflicted. Two show fine periosteal new bone, one shows dense bridging callus, and one is a parietal skull fracture with sharp margins. Set out what your imaging can and cannot support.
quiz.answer: Imaging can place each fracture in a broad range — acute, healing or old — and can state that fractures of differing ages are present, but it cannot date any of them to a particular day, and a skull fracture cannot be dated at all because it heals without callus.
quiz.explain: Fracture dating is one of the places where a radiologist can do real harm by overreaching. The evidence supports wide, overlapping windows: subperiosteal new bone from about four to fourteen days, soft callus around ten to fourteen days, hard callus from roughly two to six weeks, remodelling over months. Rates vary with the child's age, the bone involved and whether the fracture was immobilised. Classic metaphyseal lesions and rib fractures may heal with minimal periosteal reaction, blunting the usual markers. Skull fractures neither form callus nor reliably narrow, so a sharply marginated linear fracture may be hours or months old. What the imaging supports powerfully is multiplicity and difference: several fractures at demonstrably different stages of healing means several occasions, and that statement is defensible in court while a specific date is not.

quiz.prompt: A three-month-old has CT showing bilateral subdural collections, partly hyperdense and partly of near-water attenuation, with an interhemispheric component. The referring clinician asks you to confirm in writing that there were two separate assaults. What do you report?
quiz.answer: Mixed attenuation has several explanations and does not by itself establish two events
choices: Mixed attenuation has several explanations and does not by itself establish two events
Mixed attenuation dates these injuries as one recent and one several weeks older
Interhemispheric blood on its own establishes the diagnosis of inflicted head injury
Water-density collections are the benign subarachnoid spaces of infancy, so no injury
quiz.explain: Attenuation is a poor clock. Hyperacute, unclotted blood is not markedly dense; a torn arachnoid lets cerebrospinal fluid dilute a collection within hours; rebleeding into an established collection produces layered density; and severe anaemia lowers the attenuation of fresh blood towards that of brain. So a mixed-density subdural is compatible with repeated injury but does not prove it. MRI characterises blood products more finely and adds parenchymal information, yet it too gives ranges rather than dates. Interhemispheric and posterior falcine collections are strongly associated with inflicted injury but are not by themselves diagnostic. Benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces is a genuine mimic of chronic collections, but it does not explain a hyperdense component. Report the appearances, list what could produce them, and say what the imaging does and does not support.

quiz.prompt: A six-week-old with a parietal skull fracture and a thin subdural collection has already had a head CT. Before the strategy meeting the paediatricians ask what an MRI would add to what you already know.
quiz.answer: Parenchymal and hypoxic-ischaemic injury, small collections, and cervical spine damage
choices: Parenchymal and hypoxic-ischaemic injury, small collections, and cervical spine damage
A precise date for the subdural collection, reliable to within two or three days
Better depiction of the fracture line itself, which CT tends to under-represent
Confirmation that the fracture is linear rather than complex, altering specificity
quiz.explain: CT is the emergency test: fast, excellent for fracture and for acute blood, and with three-dimensional reformats it depicts the skull better than MRI does. MRI is added because it answers different questions. Diffusion-weighted imaging shows hypoxic-ischaemic injury, which is the strongest determinant of outcome in inflicted head trauma and is largely invisible acutely on CT. It resolves thin convexity and posterior fossa collections that CT loses against bone, characterises blood products, and can show bridging vein injury. Crucially it includes the whole spine, where ligamentous injury at the craniocervical junction and spinal subdural blood are found and are otherwise missed. Timing is usually two to five days from presentation, with a repeat at two to three months to assess established damage. What MRI cannot do is give the courtroom a precise date.

quiz.prompt: A two-year-old presents with vomiting and a bruised abdominal wall. ALT is 260 U/L and AST 190 U/L. Ultrasound shows a small volume of free fluid and no solid organ abnormality. What is the appropriate next step?
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, because ultrasound under-reads bowel and pancreas
choices: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, because ultrasound under-reads bowel and pancreas
Repeat the ultrasound at 24 hours, which will disclose a duodenal haematoma
A fluoroscopic upper gastrointestinal series as the first test for visceral injury
No further imaging, since transaminases at this level reflect muscle bruising
quiz.explain: Raised transaminases in a young child with an unexplained abdominal injury are a recognised trigger for cross-sectional imaging, with a threshold around 80 U/L widely used in practice. Inflicted abdominal trauma is uncommon but carries high mortality, largely because it presents late and because the injuries are hollow-viscus and pancreatic rather than the splenic injuries of road trauma. The duodenum and proximal jejunum are crushed against the vertebral column at their fixed points, producing intramural haematoma or perforation; the pancreatic body is transected across the spine and may present later as a pseudocyst; liver injury favours the left lobe from a midline blow. Ultrasound is insensitive for all of these, and free fluid without solid organ injury should itself raise suspicion of bowel or mesenteric damage. Contrast-enhanced CT is the test, with solid organ injuries described using the AAST grades.

quiz.prompt: Before a strategy meeting on an infant with three fractures at different stages of healing, you are asked which medical conditions you have considered and excluded on the imaging. Name the main ones and say what you looked for.
quiz.answer: Osteogenesis imperfecta, rickets and the metabolic bone disease of prematurity must be excluded, along with birth injury, by assessing bone density and modelling, the metaphyses and physes, the skull for wormian bones, and the age and site of any healing fracture.
quiz.explain: The differential deserves to be addressed explicitly in the report, because it will be raised later whether or not you raise it. Osteogenesis imperfecta shows generalised osteopenia, gracile or bowed bones, wormian bones in the lambdoid region and often a family history and blue sclerae, though mild type I can look near-normal, which is why clinical and genetic assessment sits alongside the imaging. Rickets frays, cups and splays the metaphyses, widens the physes and softens the bone; it is the mimic that matters most for metaphyseal lesions. Metabolic bone disease of prematurity does the same in an ex-preterm infant. Birth injury accounts for clavicular and humeral fractures, but these callus by two to three weeks and remodel, so a fresh fracture in a six-week-old is not birth-related. Copper deficiency, Menkes disease and congenital syphilis are rarer but real.

quiz.prompt: Your department repeats the skeletal survey once healing changes have had time to declare themselves; the accepted interval is quoted as a window of eleven to fourteen days. State the upper limit of that window, in days, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Fourteen days is the upper limit of the conventional eleven to fourteen day window, and the reason for both ends is physiological rather than administrative. Repeat too early and subperiosteal new bone has not yet mineralised enough to be seen on a plain film; leave it too long and a child is exposed to continuing risk while the investigation waits, and some rib callus begins to remodel. The repeat typically finds fractures the first survey missed in a meaningful minority of cases, chiefly posterior ribs and classic metaphyseal lesions, and it also reclassifies apparent findings as normal variants, which protects families as much as it protects children. It is limited rather than full — chest with obliques, long bones, and any site of concern — and the skull is normally left out because skull fractures do not heal with callus.

quiz.prompt: You have described a healing posterior rib fracture and two classic metaphyseal lesions in a five-month-old with no offered explanation. The consultant paediatrician asks you to write in your report that the mother's partner inflicted them. How do you frame the report?
quiz.answer: Describe the findings, state their specificity, and leave causation to the investigation
choices: Describe the findings, state their specificity, and leave causation to the investigation
Name the mechanism and the likely perpetrator, since the imaging is unambiguous here
Omit any interpretation and simply list the fractures without further qualification
Record the findings as indeterminate until the follow-up survey has been completed
quiz.explain: The report is a legal document that you may be cross-examined on years later, so write it as one. Describe each finding precisely, with site, appearance and stage of healing. Then interpret within your expertise: these injuries are of high specificity for inflicted trauma in an infant, no medical condition on the imaging accounts for them, and the pattern is not explained by the history given. That is a defensible clinical opinion. Identifying who caused an injury is not a radiological finding and belongs to the investigation. Saying nothing at all is also a failure, because the clinicians and the court need the specificity ranking that only you can supply. Add the practical duties: escalate to the safeguarding team the same day rather than waiting for the report to be typed, date what you write, and have a second radiologist review the images.

nodes.title: Paediatric Masses and Neonatal Neurosonography
nodes.goal: Characterise the common masses of childhood by age and origin, and read the neonatal head and spine on ultrasound with confidence.

quiz.prompt: A three-year-old has a smooth, painless flank mass. CT shows a large heterogeneous mass with a rim of renal cortex splayed around its edge, no calcification, the aorta displaced rather than surrounded, and a filling defect extending into the right renal vein. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: Manage it as a Wilms tumour and stage the chest, since spread follows the veins
choices: Manage it as a Wilms tumour and stage the chest, since spread follows the veins
Manage it as a neuroblastoma and arrange MIBG imaging with marrow sampling
Manage it as a renal abscess and drain it before any further cross-sectional work
Manage it as nephroblastomatosis and simply observe with serial renal ultrasound
