quiz.answer: Lymphoscintigraphy maps the true drainage basin before surgery and SPECT/CT localises the sentinel node anatomically, which matters on the trunk where drainage is unpredictable and may cross the midline or stop at an interval node.
quiz.explain: Blue dye tells the surgeon where a node is once the incision is open; it does not tell them which incision to make. Truncal melanoma drains unpredictably — bilaterally, across the midline, to axilla and groin simultaneously, or to an interval node sitting in the subcutaneous fat between the primary and the basin, which will simply be missed if nobody knows to look. Dynamic imaging immediately after intradermal injection of technetium-99m nanocolloid catches the first-order node before second-tier nodes label, and SPECT/CT then gives depth and the relation to vessels and muscle, allowing the skin to be marked accurately. Intraoperatively the gamma probe leads and the dye confirms. Previous wide local excision or prior nodal surgery can divert or obstruct lymphatics, and is worth knowing before you start.

quiz.prompt: A hydronephrotic kidney with a dilated pelvicalyceal system is being assessed for obstruction. Say what a MAG3 diuretic renogram gives you that ultrasound cannot.
quiz.answer: The diuretic renogram shows whether the dilated system actually drains under a furosemide challenge and measures relative function, so a prolonged clearance half-time indicates true obstruction rather than a capacious unobstructed system.
quiz.explain: Dilatation is anatomy; obstruction is physiology, and ultrasound can only see the first. MAG3 is secreted by the proximal tubule with high extraction, giving good images even in impaired kidneys. Furosemide, given either 20 minutes after the tracer or 15 minutes before it, generates a high urine flow to stress the system: clearance half-time under 10 minutes is normal drainage, over 20 minutes suggests obstruction and 10 to 20 minutes is equivocal. The curve shape matters as much as the number, and a rising curve that falls when the patient stands or empties the bladder was never obstructed. The study is invalid if the patient is dehydrated, the bladder is full, or renal function is too poor to respond to diuretic, all of which produce a falsely obstructed appearance.

quiz.prompt: Put the acquisitions of a three-phase bone scan, together with its optional late acquisition, into the order in which they are performed.
quiz.answer: dynamic-flow-images blood-pool-images delayed-three-hour-images twenty-four-hour-images
quiz.explain: The sequence is dictated by where the tracer is at each moment. Flow images are rapid frames acquired from the moment of injection over the first minute, showing regional arterial perfusion. Blood pool images follow within about five to ten minutes, while tracer is still largely in the extracellular space, and show hyperaemia and soft tissue inflammation. Delayed images at two to four hours, conventionally three, are acquired once soft tissue has cleared and the diphosphonate is bound to bone, and these are the only phase that reports osteoblastic activity. An optional 24-hour set improves bone-to-background contrast where perfusion is poor, classically in the dysvascular diabetic foot. Interpretation depends on which phases are positive, so a single delayed acquisition answers a narrower question than the full study.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these three investigations for gastrointestinal bleeding by the rate of blood loss each can detect, starting with the one that detects the slowest bleeding.
quiz.answer: labelled-red-cell-scintigraphy CT-angiography catheter-angiography
quiz.explain: Technetium-99m labelled red cells detect bleeding of roughly 0.1 to 0.2 mL per minute, CT angiography around 0.3 to 0.5, and catheter angiography needs approximately 0.5 to 1.0 mL per minute before contrast extravasation is visible. Scintigraphy has a second advantage that matters more than the threshold: the labelled cells circulate for hours, so delayed imaging can catch intermittent bleeding that was quiescent when the patient was first imaged. Its weakness is localisation — the finding you are looking for is a focus that appears where there was none, increases in intensity, and moves both antegrade and retrograde along a bowel loop, and it is that movement rather than the initial position that names the segment. A static focus is usually a vascular structure or renal activity. Its practical role is to tell the interventional radiologist whether catheter angiography is worth attempting.

nodes.title: FDG PET/CT in Oncology
nodes.goal: Read an oncological FDG PET/CT with its preparation, its physiological traps and its treatment timing in mind, and act proportionately on incidental uptake.

quiz.prompt: A lung primary measured SUVmax 8.4 on a staging PET/CT performed at another hospital and SUVmax 5.9 on your restaging scan six weeks later. No treatment was given in between and both studies were technically satisfactory. How should you handle the comparison in your report?
quiz.answer: Describe the appearances qualitatively and avoid a numerical comparison across the two scanners
choices: Describe the appearances qualitatively and avoid a numerical comparison across the two scanners
Report a 30% metabolic response, treating SUVmax as an absolute calibrated measurement
Report metabolic progression, since a lower SUV reflects a shorter uptake time
Report a partial response under RECIST 1.1, which grades response using SUVmax
quiz.explain: SUV is not a measurement of the tumour so much as a ratio: activity concentration in the region divided by injected activity per unit body weight. Everything in that chain travels badly between departments — uptake time, plasma glucose, any dose extravasation, scanner calibration, and reconstruction (point spread function and time-of-flight modelling both push small-lesion SUVmax up). Harmonisation programmes such as EARL exist precisely because raw numbers are not portable. Quantitative response assessment (PERCIST) therefore demands the same scanner, protocol and uptake time. RECIST 1.1 is an anatomical system; it uses FDG PET only in a limited way, to confirm that a new lesion is genuinely new, and it never grades response by SUV. A falling SUV would need a longer, not shorter, uptake time to be an artefact, since tumour uptake rises for the first hour or more.

quiz.prompt: A thin 22-year-old woman scanned in January for lymphoma staging has symmetrical intense uptake in both supraclavicular fossae, along the paravertebral gutters and around the aortic arch. The CT component shows only fat at these sites.
quiz.answer: Report brown adipose tissue and warm the patient thoroughly before any repeat study
choices: Report brown adipose tissue and warm the patient thoroughly before any repeat study
Report bilateral nodal disease and stage her as having supradiaphragmatic involvement
Report a paraneoplastic myositis and recommend creatine kinase and a muscle biopsy
Report probable sarcoidosis and recommend mediastinoscopy before treatment begins
quiz.explain: Brown fat is metabolically active, sympathetically driven and richest in young, thin, female patients scanned in cold weather. Its signature is symmetry and distribution: supraclavicular and lower neck, paravertebral, perirenal, around the aortic arch and in the mediastinal fat, always with fat attenuation on the co-registered CT rather than a soft tissue node. That co-registration is the whole reason PET is fused with CT. The clinical problem is not misdiagnosis so much as concealment — brown fat sits exactly where supraclavicular and mediastinal nodes sit and can mask them. Prevention is practical: a warm waiting room and blankets, avoiding cold exposure before injection, and in some departments a benzodiazepine or a beta blocker. If the neck genuinely has to be assessed, rescan the patient warm rather than argue with the images you have.

quiz.prompt: A patient with type 2 diabetes arrives for a staging PET/CT. His capillary glucose is 15 mmol/L (270 mg/dL) two hours after breakfast and his usual short-acting insulin.
quiz.answer: Rebook the study after better glycaemic control rather than inject the tracer today
choices: Rebook the study after better glycaemic control rather than inject the tracer today
Inject now and give short-acting insulin at the same time to bring the glucose down
Inject now and correct the reported SUV values afterwards for the measured glucose
Inject a doubled activity of tracer to overcome the competing plasma glucose load
quiz.explain: FDG and glucose compete for the same GLUT transporters and for hexokinase, so hyperglycaemia lowers tumour uptake while raising muscle and background activity: sensitivity falls and lesion contrast falls with it. Simple arithmetic correction of SUV for glucose is not reliable enough to rescue the study. Giving insulin at the time of injection is worse than doing nothing, because insulin drives FDG into skeletal muscle and produces a diagnostically useless scan; if short-acting insulin has been given, most departments wait at least four hours. Doubling the activity increases dose without improving the competitive block. Standard preparation is a four to six hour fast with water allowed, glucose checked at the door, and a working threshold around 11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL), above which the patient is better rescheduled with the diabetes team's help.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old smoker has a 3 cm right upper lobe adenocarcinoma. Staging PET/CT shows an avid 9 mm right lower paratracheal node (SUVmax 4.8) and no distant uptake. He is otherwise fit for lobectomy.
quiz.answer: Recommend endobronchial ultrasound sampling of the node before the stage is settled
choices: Recommend endobronchial ultrasound sampling of the node before the stage is settled
Report confirmed N2 disease and refer him directly for chemoradiotherapy instead
Report the node as reactive on size criteria and proceed straight to lobectomy
Recommend a repeat PET/CT in three months to see whether the node grows further
quiz.explain: PET is far better than CT at finding mediastinal disease, but a positive node is a probability, not a diagnosis. Granulomatous disease, anthracosis, reactive nodes draining a post-obstructive pneumonia and sarcoidosis all take up FDG happily, and in a population with any burden of tuberculosis or histoplasmosis the false positive rate is high enough to matter. The decision hanging on this node is enormous — single-station N2 disease moves a resectable patient into multimodality treatment — so guidelines require pathological confirmation of PET-positive mediastinal nodes, usually by endobronchial ultrasound with mediastinoscopy in reserve. Note also that lung cancer is staged by TNM 9th edition, which subdivides N2 by single versus multiple station involvement, making accurate nodal mapping more consequential than it used to be. Waiting three months simply lets a curable cancer grow.

quiz.prompt: A man with HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma and a bulky ipsilateral level II node completes chemoradiotherapy. The head and neck multidisciplinary team asks when to image the neck and what the imaging will decide.
quiz.answer: PET/CT at around 12 weeks, reserving neck dissection for residual nodal uptake
choices: PET/CT at around 12 weeks, reserving neck dissection for residual nodal uptake
PET/CT at around 3 weeks, reserving neck dissection for residual nodal uptake
Planned neck dissection at 6 weeks, with PET/CT used afterwards for surveillance
Contrast-enhanced CT at 6 weeks, with neck dissection decided on node size alone
quiz.explain: The PET-NECK randomised trial established the modern pathway: PET/CT-guided surveillance after chemoradiotherapy gave survival equivalent to planned neck dissection while sparing most patients an operation, and cost less. The timing is the substance of the item. Scan too early and radiation mucositis, dermatitis and reactive nodal uptake generate false positives, while incompletely regressed but sterilised nodes look like residual disease; around 12 weeks the inflammation has settled and residual uptake means something. Size criteria on CT are unreliable after chemoradiotherapy because necrotic sterilised nodes stay large for months. The same principle governs the rest of the body: allow roughly six weeks after surgery and around three months after radiotherapy before treating uptake as tumour.

quiz.prompt: Staging PET/CT for a biopsy-proven mucinous adenocarcinoma of the rectum shows only faint uptake in the primary (SUVmax 2.6) and nothing elsewhere. CT shows a 5 cm annular tumour and two 9 mm low-attenuation liver lesions, neither of which is FDG-avid.
quiz.answer: Treat the PET as insensitive in this histology and characterise the liver with MRI
choices: Treat the PET as insensitive in this histology and characterise the liver with MRI
Report the liver lesions as benign, since neither of them shows any FDG uptake
Report a complete metabolic response and defer any further staging investigation
Report the primary as a low-grade tumour that needs no further local staging
quiz.explain: Mucinous and signet ring adenocarcinomas have low cellular density and abundant extracellular mucin, so there are simply fewer glycolytic cells per voxel and uptake is modest even in large tumours. The same trap recurs across the false negative list: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours, lepidic-predominant lung adenocarcinoma, indolent lymphomas such as marginal zone and MALT, renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma, and prostate adenocarcinoma. Lesion size compounds it — below roughly 8 to 10 mm partial volume averaging dilutes true uptake towards background, so two 9 mm liver lesions could not be called benign on PET even in an avid tumour. Liver MRI with a hepatobiliary or diffusion-weighted protocol is the sensitive test here, and rectal MRI still does the local staging that PET cannot.

quiz.prompt: A patient with resected stage IIIC melanoma has a staging FDG PET/CT reported as negative from vertex to thigh. Three weeks later he presents with a first generalised seizure.
quiz.answer: Arrange contrast-enhanced brain MRI, which PET cannot replace because of cortical background
choices: Arrange contrast-enhanced brain MRI, which PET cannot replace because of cortical background
Repeat the PET/CT with a delayed brain acquisition, which resolves the cortical background
Arrange non-contrast CT of the head, which matches MRI for small parenchymal metastases
Reassure him, since a negative whole-body PET makes intracranial metastasis unlikely
quiz.explain: Normal grey matter is intensely glycolytic, so a small cortical metastasis sits inside a bright background and is easily invisible; delayed imaging does not fix this because the background is physiological, not a clearance problem. PET is likewise weak for sub-centimetre pulmonary nodules, where respiratory motion and partial volume averaging both work against it, which is why the CT component is read in its own right rather than as a map for the PET. Melanoma staging therefore pairs whole-body PET/CT with dedicated contrast-enhanced brain MRI in higher-stage disease, and non-contrast CT is a poor substitute for either. Where PET does earn its place in melanoma is in stage III and IV disease, finding unsuspected nodal, subcutaneous and visceral deposits that alter systemic treatment.

quiz.prompt: A restaging PET/CT in a woman taking metformin shows intense uptake continuously throughout the colon and, separately, one discrete intense focus in the sigmoid that is brighter than the surrounding bowel.
quiz.answer: Attribute the diffuse activity to metformin and refer the focal sigmoid uptake for colonoscopy
choices: Attribute the diffuse activity to metformin and refer the focal sigmoid uptake for colonoscopy
Attribute both the diffuse activity and the focal sigmoid uptake to metformin and stop there
Refer her for colonoscopy on the basis of the diffuse pattern and disregard the sigmoid focus
Attribute both patterns to an infective colitis and recommend stool culture with review
quiz.explain: Metformin produces striking, continuous FDG uptake through small bowel and colon, thought to reflect increased enterocyte glucose handling; where the bowel is the question, stopping it for around 48 hours before the scan clears the picture. That diffuse pattern is not itself an indication for colonoscopy. Focal colonic uptake is a different finding entirely and is the incidental most worth chasing: it appears in something like one or two per cent of oncological PET studies, and in pooled colonoscopy series a large minority — of the order of a third — prove to be an adenoma or a carcinoma. A polyp found this way is a cure. Report it explicitly and name the segment, because the endoscopist will otherwise not know where to look.

quiz.prompt: Fluorine-18 has a half-life of 110 minutes. A syringe is calibrated to contain 370 MBq of FDG at 08:00, but the patient is delayed and is not injected until 11:40 the same morning. What activity remains in the syringe at 11:40? Answer in MBq to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: From 08:00 to 11:40 is 220 minutes, exactly two half-lives, so the activity halves twice: 370 to 185 to 92.5 MBq. The arithmetic is trivial but the working day depends on it. Fluorine-18 is cyclotron-produced and shipped, so a department's schedule is written around decay: a delivery calibrated for a mid-morning slot is worth a quarter of that by early afternoon, which is why late-running lists get abandoned rather than rescued. It is also why administered activity must be recorded as the dose actually given, corrected for residual activity left in the syringe and line, since SUV divides by that number and an over-recorded dose falsely lowers every SUV on the study. Compare gallium-68, with a 68 minute half-life, which is eluted on site from a generator rather than delivered.

quiz.prompt: Two PET studies of the same patient on the same scanner give different SUVmax for the same node. Give three technical variables that could account for this, and say briefly why SUV is so sensitive to them.
quiz.answer: Uptake time before acquisition, the patient's blood glucose and the reconstruction algorithm can all change SUVmax, because SUV is only a ratio of measured activity concentration to injected dose per unit body weight.
quiz.explain: SUV = tissue activity concentration divided by (injected activity / body weight). Nothing in that expression is a property of the tumour alone. Tumour uptake continues to rise for 60 to 90 minutes, so a delayed acquisition raises the number; hyperglycaemia competitively lowers it; extravasated dose inflates it because the denominator overstates what actually circulated; body weight normalisation over-reads in obese patients, which is why PERCIST uses lean body mass (SUL) instead; and iterative reconstruction with point spread function or time-of-flight modelling raises small-lesion SUVmax substantially. Region-of-interest method matters too, SUVpeak being more reproducible than the single hottest voxel. The practical rule is unglamorous: compare like with like, and when you cannot, say so and read the images.

quiz.prompt: A staging PET/CT for lymphoma shows a single focus of intense uptake in the right thyroid lobe, with the rest of the gland quiet. State the proportionate next step and the reason for it.
quiz.answer: Recommend thyroid ultrasound, with fine needle aspiration if the nodule looks suspicious, because focal thyroid uptake carries a malignancy risk of roughly a quarter to a third.
quiz.explain: Focal thyroid incidentalomas appear on around one to two per cent of FDG studies, and pooled series put the malignancy rate at roughly 25 to 35 per cent — high enough that ignoring it is indefensible, low enough that most are benign. The proportionate response is ultrasound first, then risk-stratify by sonographic features using ACR TI-RADS or the local equivalent, and aspirate on that basis rather than on the PET alone. Diffuse thyroid uptake is a different finding, usually chronic autoimmune thyroiditis, and needs only thyroid function tests if there is a clinical reason. The same graded logic applies to incidental focal prostate uptake: check the PSA and refer for urological assessment rather than either ignoring it or launching straight into biopsy. Always weigh it against the prognosis of the cancer being staged.

quiz.prompt: A patient with oesophageal carcinoma finishes neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and the surgeon requests a PET/CT before oesophagectomy. Say when you would perform it and what the study is chiefly looking for.
quiz.answer: Scan at least six weeks after chemoradiotherapy, chiefly to find interval distant metastases that would make oesophagectomy futile, since earlier imaging is confounded by treatment inflammation.
quiz.explain: The honest purpose of restaging PET before oesophagectomy is not to grade the primary but to spare a patient a major operation they cannot benefit from, by detecting metastases that declared themselves during the months of neoadjuvant treatment. Grading the primary is unreliable, because radiotherapy leaves a band of intense oesophagitis exactly where the tumour was. Timing is the same family of judgements throughout oncological PET: allow around six weeks after surgery for the wound bed to quieten, roughly three months after radiotherapy, and for lymphoma end-of-treatment studies at least three weeks after the last chemotherapy cycle, since marrow rebound and growth factor support make the marrow and spleen light up diffusely, and thymic rebound produces an arrowhead of anterior mediastinal uptake in younger patients.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these reference levels of uptake in the order the Deauville five-point scale ranks them, from score 1 through to score 5.
quiz.answer: no-uptake-above-background at-or-below-mediastinal-blood-pool above-blood-pool-up-to-liver moderately-above-liver markedly-above-liver
quiz.explain: The Deauville scale, embedded in the Lugano criteria for Hodgkin and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, scores residual uptake visually against two internal reference organs: the mediastinal blood pool and the liver. Scores 1 to 3 are generally taken as a complete metabolic response in patients on standard therapy, and 4 to 5 mean residual metabolic disease, driving escalation, biopsy or a change of plan; score 5 also covers new lesions attributable to lymphoma. An additional score X is used for new uptake unlikely to be lymphoma at all. Two cautions: it is a visual comparison, not an SUV threshold, so the reference organs must be assessed on the same study; and it was validated in lymphoma, so importing it into solid tumour reporting is a category error.

quiz.prompt: Put the steps of a standard oncological FDG PET/CT into the order in which they happen on the day of the scan.
quiz.answer: fast-four-hours check-capillary-glucose inject-FDG rest-quietly-60-minutes void-bladder acquire-PET-CT
quiz.explain: Each step exists to remove a specific artefact. A four to six hour fast with water allowed lowers circulating insulin, which keeps FDG out of skeletal muscle and shifts the myocardium towards fatty acid metabolism. Glucose is checked before injection, not after, because a high reading changes the plan rather than the report. The uptake phase is roughly 60 minutes in a warm, quiet room: talking loads the vocal cords and larynx, chewing loads the muscles of mastication, exercise loads the limbs, and cold recruits brown fat. Voiding immediately before acquisition reduces bladder activity and the streak-like artefact around it, and matters most in pelvic malignancy. The low-dose CT then provides attenuation correction and anatomical localisation, which is what turns a blob of activity into a diagnosis.

nodes.title: PSMA, DOTATATE and Theranostics
nodes.goal: Select and follow patients for radioligand therapy using PSMA and DOTATATE imaging, and give sound radiation protection advice to the treated patient and their household.

quiz.prompt: A gallium-68 PSMA PET/CT performed for staging shows a focus of moderate uptake just lateral to the coeliac axis, along the anterior aspect of the left crus, arising from a slightly elongated 6 mm structure. The CT shows no discrete lymph node there.
quiz.answer: Report coeliac ganglion uptake rather than a retroperitoneal nodal metastasis
choices: Report coeliac ganglion uptake rather than a retroperitoneal nodal metastasis
Report a retroperitoneal nodal metastasis and upstage him to M1a disease
Report an adrenal metastasis, which characteristically lies anterior to the crus
Report a neuroendocrine tumour, since ganglia do not bind PSMA ligands at all
quiz.explain: Autonomic ganglia express PSMA, and the coeliac ganglion is the single most important false positive on these studies. The clues are morphological: a band-like or teardrop shape rather than a round node, a paired and symmetrical position hugging the crus adjacent to the coeliac trunk, uptake typically lower than a true nodal deposit, and no lymph node on the CT component. The stakes are high, because calling it a node moves a man from potentially curative local treatment to systemic therapy. Physiological uptake also occurs in lacrimal and salivary glands, liver, spleen, kidneys, small bowel and the urinary tract. Non-prostatic pathology that takes up PSMA ligands includes renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma, thyroid disease, glioma, Paget disease, fibrous dysplasia, healing rib fractures and reactive nodes in sarcoidosis.

quiz.prompt: A man with Gleason 4+5 prostate cancer and a PSA of 32 ng/mL is being assessed for radical treatment. The multidisciplinary team asks whether to stage him with CT and bone scintigraphy or with PSMA PET/CT.
quiz.answer: PSMA PET/CT, which was substantially more accurate than CT with bone scan in a randomised trial
choices: PSMA PET/CT, which was substantially more accurate than CT with bone scan in a randomised trial
CT with bone scan, which was substantially more accurate than PSMA PET/CT in a randomised trial
CT with bone scan first, reserving PSMA PET/CT for cases where the bone scan is equivocal
Whole body MRI, which a randomised trial showed to be superior to PSMA PET/CT for staging
quiz.explain: The proPSMA trial randomised men with high-risk prostate cancer before curative-intent treatment to gallium-68 PSMA-11 PET/CT or to conventional imaging with CT and bone scintigraphy. PSMA PET/CT achieved around 92 per cent accuracy for nodal and distant disease against roughly 65 per cent for conventional imaging, with fewer equivocal findings, less radiation exposure and more changes in management. On that basis it is now accepted as a first-line staging investigation in high-risk disease rather than a problem-solving add-on. One consequence worth carrying into the multidisciplinary meeting: a more sensitive test causes stage migration, so a cohort staged by PSMA PET is not directly comparable with historical series staged by CT and bone scan, and apparent improvements in outcome may be partly an artefact of better staging.

quiz.prompt: Six years after radical prostatectomy a man's PSA is 0.12 ng/mL on two separate occasions. His general practitioner has referred him for PSMA PET/CT to find the site of recurrence.
quiz.answer: Explain that detection at this PSA level is poor and follow the PSA before imaging him
choices: Explain that detection at this PSA level is poor and follow the PSA before imaging him
Proceed to PSMA PET/CT now, since detection rates are high below 0.2 ng/mL
Proceed to bone scintigraphy now, which outperforms PSMA PET at very low PSA
Explain that this PSA already satisfies the Phoenix definition of biochemical failure
quiz.explain: After radical prostatectomy, biochemical recurrence requires a confirmed PSA of 0.2 ng/mL or above, so 0.12 does not yet meet the threshold. The Phoenix definition, nadir plus 2 ng/mL, belongs to patients treated with radiotherapy and does not apply after surgery. Detection rate on PSMA PET rises steeply with PSA: pooled data give roughly 40 per cent at a PSA of 0.2 to 0.5, around 60 per cent at 0.5 to 1.0, about three-quarters between 1 and 2, and over 90 per cent above 2 ng/mL. A short PSA doubling time and high Gleason grade raise the yield at any given level. Scanning too early produces a negative study that answers nothing, delays nothing useful and consumes a slot, so the sensible advice is to repeat the PSA and image when the number will support the question.

quiz.prompt: A man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has progressed after abiraterone and docetaxel. Screening PSMA PET/CT shows avid bone and nodal disease with uptake well above liver background, but a 3 cm liver metastasis seen on CT shows no PSMA uptake at all.
quiz.answer: He is unsuitable, because a measurable metastasis without uptake would receive no treatment
choices: He is unsuitable, because a measurable metastasis without uptake would receive no treatment
He is suitable, because most of his disease shows uptake greater than the normal liver
He is suitable, because liver metastases are treated by the beta particles regardless
He is unsuitable, because previous docetaxel exposure excludes radioligand therapy
quiz.explain: The screening scan before lutetium-177 PSMA-617 asks two questions, and both must be answered favourably. First, is there at least one lesion with uptake greater than normal liver, confirming the target is expressed and bright. Second, is there any measurable lesion that lacks uptake, since a sizeable PSMA-negative deposit is disease the radioligand cannot reach and is likely to be what kills the patient. A 3 cm PSMA-negative liver metastasis fails the second test. In the VISION trial the regimen was 7.4 GBq every six weeks for up to six cycles added to standard care, improving median overall survival to about 15.3 months against 11.3. Prior taxane exposure was an entry requirement in that trial rather than an exclusion; the pre-taxane setting has been studied separately. Xerostomia from salivary uptake, fatigue and marrow suppression are the main toxicities.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a grade 3 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour has a DOTATATE PET showing only faint uptake, below that of normal liver, while an FDG PET performed a week later shows intense uptake in the same lesions.
quiz.answer: Report a discordant pattern that argues against peptide receptor therapy and suggests aggressive biology
choices: Report a discordant pattern that argues against peptide receptor therapy and suggests aggressive biology
Report a concordant pattern that supports proceeding with peptide receptor therapy at full dose
Report the DOTATATE study as technically inadequate and simply repeat it in a week's time
Report the FDG uptake as inflammatory in origin and proceed with peptide receptor therapy
quiz.explain: This is the dual-tracer flip-flop. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours express somatostatin receptor subtype 2 densely and are relatively FDG-quiet; as they dedifferentiate they lose receptor expression and switch to glycolysis. FDG-positive, DOTATATE-negative disease therefore carries a markedly worse prognosis and will not respond to peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, because there is nothing for the peptide to bind. Uptake at or below liver corresponds to a Krenning score of 2 or less and generally fails eligibility, which requires score 3 or 4. Two practical points: report the least avid lesion as well as the most avid, since heterogeneity determines what the therapy will miss; and long-acting somatostatin analogues can in principle compete for the receptor, so scans are usually scheduled shortly before the next depot injection.

quiz.prompt: A woman with papillary thyroid carcinoma underwent a staging CT with iodinated contrast three weeks ago. Her radioiodine ablation is currently booked for next week and the endocrine team asks whether to go ahead.
quiz.answer: Defer the ablation, because the stable iodine load will compete with the therapeutic dose
choices: Defer the ablation, because the stable iodine load will compete with the therapeutic dose
Proceed as booked, because iodinated contrast is fully cleared within a few days
Proceed as booked, but double the administered activity to overcome the iodine load
Defer the ablation, because iodinated contrast permanently blocks thyroidal uptake
quiz.explain: Iodinated contrast expands the stable iodide pool for weeks, and stable iodide competes with iodine-131 at the sodium-iodide symporter, so the therapeutic activity is diluted and taken up poorly. Most departments wait around four to eight weeks after contrast, some checking a urinary iodine before proceeding. Increasing the administered activity does not overcome competitive inhibition; it just increases dose to everything else. The rest of the preparation follows the same physiology: a low-iodine diet for one to two weeks, and TSH raised above about 30 mIU/L either by thyroid hormone withdrawal or by recombinant human TSH, since TSH drives symporter expression. Two further points of current practice: low-risk patients often need no radioiodine at all, and where remnant ablation is given, 1.1 GBq has been shown as effective as 3.7 GBq.

quiz.prompt: A man with castration-resistant prostate cancer has painful widespread bone metastases, no visceral disease, and a 4 cm retroperitoneal nodal mass. The oncologist asks whether radium-223 would be a reasonable choice for him.
quiz.answer: Radium-223 acts only within bone, so his bulky nodal disease would go untreated
choices: Radium-223 acts only within bone, so his bulky nodal disease would go untreated
Radium-223 treats nodal and skeletal disease alike, so it suits his pattern well
Radium-223 is unsuitable here because his skeletal disease is causing him pain
Radium-223 requires visceral metastases to be present before it can be offered
quiz.explain: Radium-223 is a calcium mimetic: it deposits at sites of high bone turnover, which in this disease means the osteoblastic reaction around metastases. Its alpha particles have a range of only a few cell diameters, under about 100 micrometres, which is exactly why it delivers high linear energy transfer damage to the tumour microenvironment while relatively sparing marrow — and equally why it does nothing whatever for soft tissue or nodal disease. The ALSYMPCA trial enrolled men with symptomatic bone-predominant disease and no visceral metastases, excluding bulky lymphadenopathy, and showed improved overall survival of roughly 14.9 against 11.3 months with fewer symptomatic skeletal events. Symptomatic bone disease is the indication, not a contraindication. Since ERA-223 found increased fractures when it was combined with abiraterone and prednisolone, that combination is avoided and bone-protective therapy is given.

quiz.prompt: A man treated with 3.7 GBq of iodine-131 for differentiated thyroid carcinoma is ready for discharge. He lives with his wife and a three-year-old daughter, and asks what he needs to do once he gets home.
quiz.answer: Sleep separately, keep his distance from the child, and use a separate toilet for some days
choices: Sleep separately, keep his distance from the child, and use a separate toilet for some days
Sleep separately for a single night, then resume close household contact from the next day
Stay away from the family home for six months, until the iodine has decayed completely
Take no precautions, since iodine-131 emits only beta particles of very short range
quiz.explain: Iodine-131 emits both a therapeutic beta particle and a 364 keV gamma photon that leaves the patient, so external dose to household contacts is real, and it is excreted in urine, saliva and sweat, so contamination matters as much as external exposure. Typical advice after ablation is to sleep alone, limit close contact time with young children and pregnant women, use a toilet carefully and flush it, wash hands thoroughly, avoid sharing utensils and towels, and avoid long journeys seated close to others. Durations are set by the dose rate measured at discharge and by local dose constraints, and run from a few days to a couple of weeks depending on activity and on who is at home. The physical half-life is around 8 days and the effective half-life shorter. Conception is deferred for about six months, and breastfeeding must cease permanently for that infant.

quiz.prompt: At discharge, the dose rate measured at 1 metre from a patient treated with iodine-131 is 45 microsieverts per hour. Assuming inverse square behaviour and no shielding, what is the dose rate at 3 metres? Answer in microsieverts per hour to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Tripling the distance divides the dose rate by nine: 45 divided by 9 gives 5.0 microsieverts per hour. This is the cheapest and most powerful protective measure available at the bedside, and it is the arithmetic behind almost every piece of household advice you will give. Since dose equals rate multiplied by time, a relative sitting on the far side of the room for an hour receives less than one sitting beside the patient for seven minutes. Discharge criteria in most jurisdictions are written in terms of measured dose rate at one metre and estimated dose to contacts and the public, rather than administered activity alone. Two caveats when you use the calculation clinically: a patient is not a point source, and self-attenuation within the body means measured rates in practice are usually lower than a pure inverse square estimate predicts.

quiz.prompt: A colleague asks what makes the PSMA and DOTATATE agents theranostic. Explain the principle in one or two sentences, and say what the diagnostic scan is actually deciding.
quiz.answer: The same targeting molecule carries either an imaging radionuclide or a therapeutic one, so the diagnostic scan shows whether the target is expressed and where, and it decides eligibility by proving the therapy will bind the patient's disease.
quiz.explain: Gallium-68 or fluorine-18 is used for imaging and lutetium-177, a beta emitter, or actinium-225, an alpha emitter, for treatment, mounted on the same vector molecule. The diagnostic study is effectively a whole-body biopsy of receptor expression, sampling every lesion at once — something no tissue sample can do, and the reason a single negative biopsy does not settle the question. It answers three things: is the target present, is it present in all the measurable disease, and is it bright enough against a reference organ. After treatment, imaging the small gamma yield of lutetium-177 confirms that the activity went where the diagnostic scan predicted, occasionally shows disease not previously seen, and provides the counts for dosimetry.

quiz.prompt: State why an amino acid infusion is given alongside lutetium-177 DOTATATE therapy, and which organ it is protecting.
quiz.answer: An infusion of lysine and arginine competitively blocks proximal tubular reabsorption of the radiopeptide, protecting the kidneys from radiation nephropathy, which is the dose-limiting organ toxicity of this treatment.
quiz.explain: Small radiolabelled peptides are freely filtered at the glomerulus and then reabsorbed by the megalin-cubilin receptor system in the proximal tubule, which concentrates activity in the renal cortex and makes the kidney the organ that limits how much can be given. Positively charged amino acids saturate that reabsorption pathway competitively, and are started before the radiopeptide and continued for several hours afterwards; the infusion is emetogenic, so antiemetic cover is routine. The NETTER-1 regimen was 7.4 GBq every eight weeks for four cycles in progressive, receptor-positive midgut neuroendocrine tumours, with a large gain in progression-free survival. Bone marrow is the other dose-limited tissue, and a small percentage of patients later develop myelodysplasia, which is worth mentioning at consent.

quiz.prompt: After each cycle of lutetium-177 PSMA therapy the patient returns for imaging at around 24 hours. Say what that post-therapy study is for.
quiz.answer: The post-therapy study images the gamma emission of lutetium-177 to confirm that the activity localised to the known lesions, to look for disease not seen before, and to provide the counts for dosimetry of the kidneys and marrow.
quiz.explain: Lutetium-177 conveniently emits low-abundance gamma photons at 113 and 208 keV alongside its therapeutic beta particles, so an ordinary gamma camera can image the treatment itself — a real advantage over pure beta and alpha emitters, where you administer the dose and hope. The study documents biodistribution and confirms delivery to the targets identified at screening; it occasionally reveals additional lesions; and with serial time points it supports patient-specific dosimetry of kidneys, marrow and salivary glands, which is moving steadily from research towards routine practice. The finding that should give you pause is a photopenic area where a known lesion sits, indicating heterogeneous target expression and a region that will not have been treated.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these reference levels of tumour uptake in the order the Krenning score ranks them, from score 1 up to score 4.
quiz.answer: very-low-uptake uptake-at-or-below-liver uptake-above-liver uptake-above-spleen
quiz.explain: The Krenning score grades somatostatin receptor expression visually against internal reference organs, with score 0 for no uptake at all, then very low uptake, uptake at or below normal liver, uptake above liver, and finally uptake exceeding normal spleen or kidney. It began with indium-111 octreotide scintigraphy and carried over to gallium-68 DOTATATE PET, where the reference organs are conveniently on the same images. Scores 3 and 4 indicate receptor density sufficient for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, and score 4 predicts the best response; score 2 or less generally fails eligibility. The discipline that separates a useful report from a decorative one is grading the least avid measurable lesion as well as the brightest, because heterogeneity is what the therapy will fail to control.

quiz.prompt: Put the steps of a first radioiodine treatment for differentiated thyroid carcinoma into the order in which they occur.
quiz.answer: total-thyroidectomy low-iodine-diet TSH-stimulation I-131-administration post-therapy-whole-body-scan
quiz.explain: Each step prepares the one after it. Surgery comes first because a bulky normal remnant takes up iodine avidly and would soak up the activity intended for residual tumour while irradiating the neck. A low-iodine diet for one to two weeks shrinks the competing stable iodide pool, for the same reason iodinated contrast must be avoided beforehand. TSH is then raised above roughly 30 mIU/L, either by withdrawing thyroid hormone or by giving recombinant human TSH, because TSH upregulates the sodium-iodide symporter that carries iodide into the cell. The capsule is administered, and a whole-body scan three to seven days later maps what actually took up the activity. That post-therapy scan is considerably more sensitive than any pre-therapy diagnostic scan, simply because far more activity is on board, and it not infrequently reveals unsuspected metastatic disease.
